units.la: AD LECTOREM PRÆFATIO.
units.tr: TO THE READER, A PREFACE.

units.la: Postquam Pandectarum juris professio, ab Ampliss. Senatu Trajectino mihi fuit demandata; id negotii datum mihi credidi, ut non tantum ore, sed & calamo singulis, & universis prodessem. Utque constaret magis, quam non mihi foret otium negotiosum, de tali juris materia cogitare coepi, quę & sapientioribus non ingrata, & in foro non minus utilis esset futura. Ubi, si quę ab aliis prætermissa supplerem, confuse dicta in ordinem digererem, iisque à me reperta noviter adjicerem, non dubitabam, quin aliquid mea Professione dignum, perfecissem. Commodum autem se mihi obtulit, Statutorum materia confusa, & diffusa satis; quę ut multorum ingenia virorum antehac torsit, ita hodierno tempore non minus, ea contorsit. In quà ipsa, fas sit dicere, qui in supremis positi subselliis, nonnunquam offendunt: etiam eas reperiunt difficultates, quas non sine novi legislatoris auctoritate facile superarint. Neque e-nim nim hic quicquam è trivio desumptum est, aut à vulgari ratione disputandi ; verum id ipsum, quod ex abditis juris regulis quę in rebus agendis obtinent , [?]etitum est penetralibus. Et licet bene multi, sparsim nonnulla huc facientia, sun[?]t scriptis inseruerint, quę equidem, vidi, & legi, nec contempsi; nulli tamen, quod sciam, universam illam de Jure statutario materiam, (minime illam ipsam partem, de quâ maximè laborandum erat), aut pertractarunt. aut ordine sunt complexi. Multo minus regulas exhibuerunt, quibus veluti thesibus premissis, multis hypothesibus, jure consuetudinario, atquė statutario firmatis, sua constaret ratio. Quod an meo libello confecero, non equidem velim affirmare; ut qui non ignorem alia multa hactenus à me traditis, superaddi posse. Sperarę tamen ausim, mē viris solidâ juris civilis scientiâ imbutis, inque praxi hodierna satis exercitatis, viam monstrasse, quam forte planam suâ industriâ planissimam, ac tutissimam sunt redditur[?]. Huic meo instituto si faveris lector judiciosè, me forte ad plura & majora proferenda in publicum instigabis.
units.tr: Since the professorship of the Pandects was entrusted to me by the most distinguished Senate of Utrecht, I have believed that the task given me was to be of service to each and all, not only by word of mouth but also with my pen. And so that it might be clear that my leisure was not idle but busy, I began to think about a subject of law of this kind, which would be neither unwelcome to the more learned nor less useful in the courts. If I might supply what others had passed over, set in order what had been said in a confused way, and add newly discovered matters of my own, I had no doubt that I would have produced something worthy of my professorship. Now the matter of Statutes presented itself to me as opportune, being rather confused and rather diffuse; and just as it has tormented the minds of many men in the past, so in the present age it has tormented them no less. In it, it is permitted to say, even those who sit on the highest benches sometimes stumble, and they meet with difficulties which could not easily be overcome without the authority of a new lawgiver. For nothing here has been drawn from the crossroads, nor from the common method of disputation; rather, the very matter that is treated has been sought out from the hidden recesses of the rules of law that hold in the conduct of affairs. And although very many have inserted scattered remarks bearing on this in their writings, which indeed I have seen and read, and did not despise, yet none, so far as I know, has either treated or arranged in order that whole body of doctrine concerning statutory law (least of all that very part in which the greatest labour was needed). Still less have they set forth rules by which, as with theses laid down beforehand and many hypotheses confirmed by customary and statutory law, their system might stand. Whether I have accomplished this in my little book I would not care to affirm, since I am not unaware that many other things handed down by me hitherto could be added. Yet I would venture to hope that, for men imbued with a solid knowledge of civil law and sufficiently practised in the present-day practice, I have shown a way which, made plain by their own diligence, may be rendered most plain and most safe. If you, reader, favour my undertaking with judgement, you will perhaps spur me on to bring forth more and greater works before the public.

units.la: Clarissimo, Consultissimo VIRO, PAULO VOET, Juris in illustri Academiâ Ultrajectinâ Professori ordinario, & Camerae Vianensis Senatori, Cùm erudite STATUTORUM Jura illustras- set.
units.tr: To the most distinguished and most learned man, PAULUS VOET, ordinary professor of law in the famous Academy of Utrecht and senator of the Chamber of Vianen, since he has learnedly illustrated the laws of STATUTES.

units.la: SCribite vos, alii, veterum dictamina legum, Et toties scriptum pandite juris opus; Quae Paulus responsa dabat, quae Scævola, Celsus, Ac Labeo, Latii dogmata mille fori.
units.tr: Let others write down the precepts of the ancient laws and open up the much-written work of jurisprudence: what Paulus gave as responses, what Scaevola, Celsus and Labeo gave, the thousand doctrines of the Latin forum.

units.la: Si placeat Romana Themis, placet altera Belgis, Nec proprium Romae condere jura fuit.
units.tr: If Roman Themis pleases, another Themis pleases the Belgians, nor was it ever proper for them to frame their laws at Rome.

units.la: Sunt non pauca, novis quae sanxit serior aetas Legibus, aut ratio congrua motve probat.
units.tr: There are not a few things which a later age has sanctioned by new laws, or which reason and fitting motive approve.

units.la: Sceptra tenet, justique modos praescribit ubivis
units.tr: Sovereignty holds the sceptre and prescribes the measures of justice everywhere,

units.la: Libera Majestas civibus ipsa suis.
units.tr: free in itself, for its own citizens.

units.la: Quod licet hîc, alibi licitum lex lata negabit;
units.tr: What a law once enacted allows here, it will deny elsewhere;

units.la: Quodque meum est, alibi non sinet esse meum.
units.tr: and what is mine here, it will not let be mine elsewhere.

units.la: Migramus; sedesque recens mutata prioris
units.tr: We migrate, and a place newly changed from the former

units.la: Jus negat, & lites parturit ipse locus.
units.tr: denies its law, and the place itself gives birth to lawsuits.

units.la: Quae mala dum passim vixarum pullulat hydra,
units.tr: While this evil hydra of troubles sprouts everywhere,

units.la: Magne Vir, has calamo tu, velut ense secas.
units.tr: great man, you cut these off with your pen as with a sword.

units.la: Jurâque qui penetras, jam sic nostra firmas,
units.tr: And you, who penetrate the laws, now so confirm ours

units.la: Errorum ut reseces hîc simul omne caput.
units.tr: that you cut off every head of error here at once.

units.la: Grande tibi statuet plaudens Themis ipsa trophaeum,
units.tr: Applauding Themis herself will raise a great trophy for you,

units.la: Dum tua stant stabili, PAULE, Statuta Pede.
units.tr: PAUL, while your Statutes stand on a steady foot.

units.la: D E JURE & CONCURSU STATUTORUM.
units.tr: ON THE LAW AND THE CONCURRENCE OF STATUTES.

units.la: SECT. I. CAP. I.
units.tr: SECTION I, CHAPTER I.

units.la: 1. Præcognitione, etiam in jure, opus esse.
units.tr: 1. That foreknowledge is needed, even in law.

units.la: 2. Quid sit jus in genere, definitur.
units.tr: 2. What law is in general is defined.

units.la: 3. Juris prima divisio proponitur.
units.tr: 3. The first division of law is set out.

units.la: 4. Jus Dei quid sit?
units.tr: 4. What is the law of God?

units.la: 5. Quid jus creaturarum?
units.tr: 5. What is the law of creatures?

units.la: 6. Quid jus humanum?
units.tr: 6. What is human law?

units.la: 7. Quotuplex jus humanum?
units.tr: 7. How many kinds of human law are there?

units.la: 8. Quo referendum jus sacrum?
units.tr: 8. To what is sacred law to be referred?

units.la: 9. Publicum unde collectum?
units.tr: 9. From what is public law collected?

units.la: 10. Jus naturale Dei & hominum sunt distincta.
units.tr: 10. The natural law of God and that of men are distinct.

units.la: 11. Explicatur jus naturale hominum.
units.tr: 11. The natural law of men is explained.

units.la: 12. Jus naturale hominum immutabile.
units.tr: 12. The natural law of men is unchangeable.

units.la: 13. Juri naturali matrimonium adscribitur.
units.tr: 13. Marriage is assigned to natural law.

units.la: 14. Liberorum itidem procreatio, amor & educatio.
units.tr: 14. Likewise the procreation, love and education of children.

units.la: 15. Sui defensio, & injuriae propulsatio. 16. Non nuda defensio bonorum.
units.tr: 15. Self-defence and the repelling of injury. 16. Not bare defence of goods.

units.la: 17. Religio juri natura adscribitur.
units.tr: 17. Religion is assigned to natural law.

units.la: 18. Amor itidem patria atque parentum.
units.tr: 18. Likewise love of country and of parents.

units.la: 19. Ut tamen amor patria fit præferendus amori patris.
units.tr: 19. That love of country is nevertheless to be preferred to love of father.

units.la: 20. An libertas?
units.tr: 20. Whether liberty?

units.la: 1. URis portionem implicatam magis, magisque receptam moribus, quam legibus Romanis, explicaturus; quod in ejus naturâ, & affectionibus elucidandis laborarint, atque etiamnum laborent excellentissima nostri seculi ingenia; quo nomine ipsa à multis neglecta jacet, à plerisque non intellecta satis, à paucis probe cognita : visum mihi, vice prologi, de Jure in universum, ejusq; generali divisione atque partibus agere; in quantum nihil eorum non scitu necessarium est in illâ ipsâ materiâ, quam pertractandam assumpsi. Si enim in foro causas dicentibus, nefas esse videtur, nullâ factâ præfatione, rem judici exponere, teste Cajo, in l. 1. D. de Orig. jur. quanto magis, rei cujusdam promittenti interpretationem, inconveniens erit, illotis quasi manibus protinus eam adhibere. Ut in omni specici tractatione ad Ulpiani imitationem congruum atque decens sit, in antecessum e juldem jusdem generis exhibere cognitionem l. 1. D. de Rebus credit. Quæ lectorem ad materiam propositam, quasi manuducat; cumque ibi pervenerit, evidentiorem præbeat intellectum. d. l. 1. D. de Orig. Jur.
units.tr: 1. Intending to explain a part of law more intricate, and more received by custom than by the Roman laws, a part whose nature and affections the most excellent minds of our own age have laboured, and still labour, to make clear; a part which for that reason lies neglected by many, is not sufficiently understood by most, and is well known to few: I have thought fit, by way of preface, to treat of law in general, of its general division and its parts, insofar as nothing of these is unnecessary to know in that very matter which I have undertaken to handle. For if, as Gaius teaches in l. 1, D. de Orig. jur., it seems wrong for those pleading causes in court to lay the matter before the judge without any preface, how much more will it be unfitting to take up the interpretation of a thing one has promised without, as it were, first washing one's hands? So that in every treatment of a subject, following the example of Ulpian, it may be fitting and proper to set forth beforehand a knowledge of the same kind, l. 1. D. de Rebus credit. which may lead the reader, as it were by the hand, to the matter proposed, and when he has arrived there, may give him a clearer understanding. d. l. 1. D. de Orig. Jur.

units.la: 2. Jus in propriâ & propiore significatione, pluribus omissis, de quibus JCti. in l. pen. & ult. D. de Just. & Jur. Hilliger. ad Donell. 1. comm. 3. Althus. prolixe in Dicaiologi. l. 1. c. 13. & seqq. mihi dicetur regula licitu & honesti, adeoque si manifestata, directio & norma agendorum. Id quod, meo judicio, juris singulis partibus, citra ullam difficultatem poterit applicari. Quod tamen de receptis dd. finitionibus vix ausim affirmare; non omnibus saltem juris speciebus, quæ generali juris nomine continentur. Clarum id erit ex sequentibus, in quibus neglectâ communi opinione sequar meam; quâ positâ & elucidatâ, illa suâ sponte ruet.
units.tr: 2. Law in its proper and closer meaning, leaving aside many things on which the jurisconsults speak, in l. pen. & ult. D. de Just. & Jur. Hilliger, ad Donell. 1. comm. 3. Althusius at length in Dicaiologica l. 1, c. 13 and following, I shall define as the rule of what is lawful and honourable, and therefore, when made known, the direction and norm of what is to be done. This, in my judgment, can be applied to every part of law without any difficulty. Yet I would hardly venture to affirm this of the definitions received among the learned, at least not of all the species of law which are comprehended under the general name of law. This will be clear from what follows, in which, setting aside the common opinion, I shall follow my own; once it has been laid down and explained, the other will fall of its own accord.

units.la: 3. Non enim cum Amesio Theologo de Consicnt. casibus libr. 5. congruenter scholasticorum pariter atque Jurisconsultorum placitis Donell. 1. comm 7. Hillig. ibid. &
units.tr: 3. For not in agreement with the theologian Amesius, De conscientia casibus lib. 5, nor agreeing with the opinions of the scholastics and jurists alike, Donellus, 1. comm. 7, Hilliger, ibid. &

units.la: 2. Comm. 2. jus partiar in divinum & humanum. Quasi illud Deum auctorem; hoc auctorem hominem laudet; nec jus naturale cum divino confundam, id quod fecit Fortatul. dial. 37. Verum distinctius hic meum pro mam sensum, ubi forte cæteri meram tradidere confusionem.
units.tr: 2. Comm. 2. law is divided into divine and human, as if the one praised God as its author and the other man. Nor will I confound natural law with divine law, which Fortunatus did, dial. 37. But here I shall express my own meaning more distinctly, where others perhaps have handed down a mere confusion.

units.la: 4. Generalissima hæc potius erit divisio, quod aliud sit jus Dei, aliud jus creaturarum. Illud est, secundum quod Deus semetipsum obligat, vel quasi, in ordine ad creaturarum, vel etiam sui ipsius directionem. Estque vel jus Dei naturale, vel positivum. Illud, quod citra divinæ naturæ destructionem, id est, abnegationem, aliter atque aliter se habere non potest. Sic ut illud ipsum Deus ne quidem antecedenter ad suâ ipsius voluntatem immutare valeat, aut aliter velle, quâ hactenus voluit. Cujus juris expressio elucescit in Primo decalogi præcepto: Non habebis Deos alienos in conspectu meo. Ejus quippe contrarium, in præjudicium suæ naturæ undiquaque perfectissimæ summæ & excellentissimæ, quæ parem non patitur, ne summa esse desinat, nec potest velle Deus, nec vult posse. Ne si illud obtineat, voluntas dicatur inefficax, & imperfecta. Ne si hoc locum reperiat, divina potentia, in sui detrimentum, & interitum suæ ὑπεροχῆς laboraret in vanum.
units.tr: 4. This will be rather the most general division: that one law is the law of God, another the law of creatures. The former is that by which God binds himself, either in relation to creatures, or to his own direction. And it is either the natural or the positive law of God. The natural law is that which cannot be otherwise, without the destruction of the divine nature, that is, its denial. So that God himself cannot, even prior to his own will, change it, or will otherwise than he has hitherto willed. The expression of this law shines forth in the first precept of the Decalogue: You shall have no other gods before me. For its contrary, to the prejudice of his nature, which is everywhere most perfect, supreme and most excellent, and admits of no equal, God neither can nor wills to will, lest he cease to be supreme. Otherwise his will would be called ineffective and imperfect. And if this law found a place, the divine power would labour in vain, to its own detriment and the destruction of its own pre-eminence.

units.la: Hoc, puta jus Dei positivum, consequenter ad divinam voluntatem tale est, ut ejus contrarium citra perfectionis suæ naturæ destructionem, vel ullum ejusdem præjudicium, possit velle & velit posse; scilic. in signo rationis, uti loquuntur scholastici, antecedenter ad decretum. Cujus exemplum suggerit secundum in primâ tabulâ decalogi præceptum; quod ut modum continet rite Deum colendi; ita etiam alium illi dissimilem, si sic Deo visum fuisset, praescribere potuisset. Alterum suppeditat, quartum ejusdem tabulae praeceptum, (ut alia secundae tabulae relinquam) quo Deus septimum diem sui sanctificationi nobis quidem immutabili lege, non tamen sibi, praescripsit. Ut vel nonum vel decimum quemque diem, siquidem id ei placuisset, suo cultui designare, potuisset.
units.tr: This, namely the positive law of God, follows from the divine will in such a way that its contrary, without destroying the nature of his perfection or any prejudice to it, could be willed by him and he could will it able to be done; namely, in the sign of reason, as the scholastics say, prior to the decree. An example of this is suggested by the second precept of the first table of the Decalogue, which, while it contains the due manner of worshipping God, could also have prescribed to him another dissimilar to it, had it so pleased God. Another is supplied by the fourth precept of the same table (I leave aside the others of the second table), by which God prescribed to us the seventh day for his sanctification, by an unchangeable law for us, but not for himself. So he could have designated for his worship the ninth or the tenth day, had this pleased him.

units.la: 5. Jus sequitur creaturarum, scil. quando creatura, proprie, sensu rationis praedita, ut excludantur animantia bruta, ad aliam sic ordinatur creaturam, seu refertur, ut eam vel obliget, vel ab ea vicissim obligetur, ad hoc vel illud agendum, vel, non agendum. Estque vel Angelicum, vel Humanum. Illius juris explicatio nihil pertinet ad jurisconsultum, multo minus quicquam facit ad farinam, uti loquuntur. Neque enim una societas est Angelorum & hominum; ut hominibus cum iis nullum sit commercium. Praeterquam, quod ea quae jure nostro traduntur, vel res, vel personas, id est homines, vel actiones spectent. At cum res ipsae hominum gratia sint productae; & actiones propter res & homines. Angelis nihil reliquum erit. §. sin. Instit. Jure natur. Gent. civil, §. 37. in sin. Instit. Rer. Divis. l. 1, 2. D. de Stat. Person.
units.tr: 5. The law of creatures follows, namely when a creature, properly endowed with reason (so that brute animals are excluded), is so ordered or referred to another creature that it either binds it, or is in turn bound by it, to do or not to do this or that. And it is either angelic or human. The explanation of the former law does not concern the jurisconsult, much less has anything to do with the bread-and-butter matters, as they say. For there is not one society of angels and men, so that men have no dealings with them. Besides, what is handed down by our law concerns either things, or persons, that is men, or actions. But since the things themselves were made for the sake of men, and the actions on account of things and men, nothing will be left for angels. §. sin. Instit. Jure natur. Gent. civil, §. 37. in sin. Instit. Rer. Divis. l. 1, 2. D. de Stat. Person.

units.la: 6. Agendum itaque de jure humano, quod inter hominem & hominem, sibi locum cum vindicat; sive hominem auctorem agnoscat, sive non, parum interest. Neque enim à causâ juris constitutivâ hæc mihi desumpta est divisio.
units.tr: 6. Therefore we must treat of human law, which claims its place between man and man; whether it acknowledges man as its author or not makes little difference. For this division has not been drawn by me from the constitutive cause of law.

units.la: Unde, si verum dicere liceat, inspectâ juris origine, omne jus, divinum appellabitur, quod Deum spectet auctorem. Nihil quippe à legitimâ humanâ potestate rectè conditum, aut constitutum censeri poterit, quod non congruenter rectæ rationi, naturæ legi, quæ divinæ legis indicium, moralis legis imago, sit constitutum.
units.tr: Hence, if it is permissible to speak the truth, looking at the origin of law, every law will be called divine which has God as its author. For nothing can be rightly held to have been established or constituted by lawful human authority, unless it has been constituted in agreement with right reason and the law of nature, which is the indication of the divine law and the image of the moral law.

units.la: Quinimo cum omnis origo justi & æqui sit à fonte primævo omnis justitiæ, Deo opt. Max. ut qui est ipsissima justitia; dicendum erit, nullum jus humanum, in rei veritate jus appellari, nisi pro principio, thesi, & fundamento naturalem servet honestatem, quæ Deum auctorem habet. Ut si illum verum ortum deserat, & in quantum deserit, à suo principio deviare, adeoque degenerare sit dicendum.
units.tr: Moreover, since every origin of the just and the equitable is from the primal fountain of all justice, God the best and greatest, who is justice itself, it must be said that no human law, in the truth of the matter, deserves the name of law unless it keeps, as its principle, thesis and foundation, natural honesty, which has God as its author. So if it forsakes that true origin, and insofar as it forsakes it, it must be said to deviate from its principle, and so to degenerate.

units.la: 7. Jus humanum, prout hoc ipsum à jurisconsultis explicari solet, aliud dicitur publicum, aliud Privatum. §. sin. Instit. de Just. & Jur. l. 1. D. eod. Illud definitur, quod ad statum rei Romanæ spectat. Id est, uti legit Rævardus, quod ad Rempublicam per se & primario, spectat utilitatem. Ravard. 5. varior. 12. Nam per consequentiam nonnunquam, si non plerumque, etiam civium singulorum respicit commoditatem. Cum si Reipublicæ bene sit, & singulis soleat esse bene : adeoque corpore recte constituto, singulis partibus in ordine ad corpus, probe sit prospectum.
units.tr: 7. Human law, as jurisconsults are accustomed to explain it, is said to be one thing public and another private. §. sin. Instit. de Just. & Jur. l. 1. D. eod. The former is defined as that which regards the state of the Roman commonwealth. That is, as Revardus reads, it regards primarily and in itself the utility of the Respublica. Revard. 5. varior. 12. For by consequence it sometimes, if not most often, also regards the convenience of individual citizens. For if it goes well with the commonwealth, it usually goes well with the individuals; and so, when the body is rightly constituted, provision is also made well for the single parts in relation to the body.

units.la: 8. Huic juri publico annumerandum est jus Sacrum, (de quo alibi tract. pecul.) quod in 12. Tabulis juris peculiarem speciem constituit. Legibus tamen Pandectarum, juris publici portionem facit. Id quod in sacris, in Sacerdotibus, in Magistratibus consistere dicitur. l. 1. §. 2. D. de Justit. & Jur. Contra tamen, quam voluit Imperator, qui divina atque publica, separata jura voluit ; uti sacerdotium, & imperium, jure merito, discriminavit. l. 2 3. in init. Cod. Sacrof. Eccles. Nov. 6. in init.
units.tr: 8. To this public law must be added sacred law (on which see elsewhere, in the treatise on peculium), which in the Twelve Tables formed a special kind of law. Yet in the laws of the Pandects it forms a part of public law. This is said to consist in sacred things, in priests and in magistrates. l. 1. §. 2. D. de Justit. & Jur. Contrary, however, to what the Emperor wished, he who wanted divine and public law kept separate, and who rightly distinguished priesthood from empire. l. 2 3. in init. Cod. Sacrof. Eccles. Nov. 6. in init.

units.la: Jus privatum est, quod directe & primario, singulorum spectat commoda ; universorum tamen per consequentiam, in quantum si singulis membris suus constet vigor, universo corpori etiam suum adest robur, atque firmamentum.
units.tr: Private law is that which directly and primarily concerns the advantages of individuals; yet it concerns the advantages of all by consequence, inasmuch as, when each member is strong, the whole body also has its vigour and firmness.

units.la: 9 Utrumque hoc jus, tam publicum, quam privatum : collectum est ex praeceptis naturalibus, gentium & civilibus. Arg. l. 2. D. de de Just. & Jur. l. ult. D. de legat. §. 2. Instit. de jure nat. gent. civil. l. 8. D. de Just. & jure. Neque enim, quod in universum à jure naturali&gentium recedit, juris nomen meretur l. 6. D. Just. & Jur.
units.tr: 9. Both kinds of law, public and private, are drawn from natural precepts, from the law of nations and from civil law. Arg. l. 2. D. de Just. & Jur. l. ult. D. de legat. §. 2. Instit. de jure nat. gent. civil. l. 8. D. de Just. & jure. For what departs in general from natural law and the law of nations does not deserve the name of law. l. 6. D. Just. & Jur.

units.la: Ut nec publicum jus (de quo potissimum difficultas) ab eo declinare sit dicendum: nisi in licentiâ, & Tyrannidem degeneret. Maximè cum ejusdem juris vestigia, vel simulacra, etiàm in ipsis animantibus brutis appareant: Certum indicium similiter atque privatum, Publicum, juri naturae, etiam naturali instinctui, abusive jus appellato, suum ortum debere. Quid quod apes regem ducem sequantur; grues aciem volando instruant, & si pericula metuant, custodem exponant, pro dormientium excubantem, securitate; formicae ordinem, & oeconomiam servent, & quae plura alia, naturalium rerum scriptores exempla, suppeditant. Duaren. D. Just. & Jure c. 5. Giffan. disp. 1. Instit. n. 20. 21. ad Thef. 8. Befold. ad l. 1. tit. 1. libr. 1. D. num. 19. & in delib. juris ad Pand. n. 9. p. 21. Wurmser. Nucl. jur. contr. libr. 1. tit. 1. controv. 9. diss. Cujac. in not. Wesemb. Parat, D. de Just. & Jur. Lyclam. pro parte. 7. Membr. eclog. 41. §. 1. Bacchov. ad §. 4 Instit. de Just. & Jur. Boer. Classs. 1. disp. 2. n. 5.
units.tr: Nor is public law (which is the chief difficulty) to be said to depart from this, unless it degenerates into licence and tyranny. The more so since traces or likenesses of this same law appear even in the brute animals themselves. Public law, like private law, owes its origin to natural law, or rather to natural instinct, though it is improperly called law. Why do bees follow a king as leader; why do cranes arrange their battle line by flying; and if they fear danger, why does one post a sentinel who keeps watch for the security of the sleeping flock; why do ants keep order and economy; and writers on natural history supply many other examples. Duaren. D. Just. & Jure c. 5. Giffan. disp. 1. Instit. n. 20. 21. ad Thef. 8. Befold. ad l. 1. tit. 1. libr. 1. D. num. 19. & in delib. juris ad Pand. n. 9. p. 21. Wurmser. Nucl. jur. contr. libr. 1. tit. 1. controv. 9. diss. Cujac. in not. Wesemb. Parat, D. de Just. & Jur. Lyclam. pro parte. 7. Membr. eclog. 41. §. 1. Bacchov. ad §. 4 Instit. de Just. & Jur. Boer. Classs. 1. disp. 2. n. 5.

units.la: 10. Hinc secunda juris elucescit divisio, quae maxime celebrata; quod aliud sit naturale, aliud gentium, aliud civile. Ubi in antecessum observandum, jus naturale Dei, de quo fuit actum, à jure naturali hominum esse distinctum. Non enim omne jus divinum est jus naturale Dei, eo quod etiam aliquod jus divinum sit positivum. Non itidem omne jus naturale, statim naturale divinum appellabitur, cum quoddam jus naturale etiam dicatur naturale hominum. Jus quippe Dei naturale, est prorsus immutabile; neque ullam patitur relaxationem aut dispensationem. Eoque spectant illa divina effata: Deus suam gloriam alteri dare non potest. Non potest creaturam rationalem à dependentiâ physicâ, vel morali, absolvere &c.
units.tr: 10. Hence there emerges the second and most celebrated division of law: that one kind is natural, another of nations, another civil. Here it must first be noted that the natural law of God, of which we have been speaking, is distinct from the natural law of men. For not all divine law is the natural law of God, since some divine law is also positive. Nor again is every natural law at once called divine natural law, since some natural law is also called natural law of men. Indeed the natural law of God is wholly unchangeable, and admits no relaxation or dispensation. To this belong those divine sayings: God cannot give his glory to another; he cannot release a rational creature from physical or moral dependence, and so on.

units.la: Jus naturale hominum dicetur, quod in jure nostro sic appellatur simpliciter, adeoque juris naturalis sine additamento venit nomine.
units.tr: That is called the natural law of men which in our law is so named simply, and so it goes by the name of natural law without any addition.

units.la: Estque etiam, ratione nonnullorum praeceptorum, juris divini positivi, & quidem liberrimi; sic ut à Deo, qui supra talem naturae legem, ejus oppositum mandari possit. Eo refero, legem ceremonialem atque forensem Mosaicam, qua talem, magnamque legis moralis portionem. Licet autem postremae legis, nullum praeceptum sit juris humani positivi, in quantum nemo mortalium, quamvis suprema in terris gaudeat potestate ejus contrarium mandare valet; est tamen aliqua ejus portio juris divini positivi. Quâ ratione in praeceptis secundae tabulae bene multa occurrunt, secundum nos immutabilia, non tamen inspectâ divinâ potestate. Sic, quae de Nuptiis, de monogamiâ, de gradibus nuptiarum prohibitis, de dominiorum distinctionibus, de homicidio, sunt juris naturalis hominum immutabilis, non ita à Deo sunt constituta pro juris ipsius necessitate, quin pro voluntatis beneplacito liberrimo mutationi subjacere possent. Accedit & aliud discrimen, quod jus naturale hominum, eosdem semper & ubique, & in omni statu obliget, in quantum lex est & quidem manifestata, & omnium cordibus inscripta, quo reddantur inexcusabiles, ex illo Paulino: ad Rom. c. 1. v. 19. 20. & c. 2. v. 12. & seqq. Non autem omne Jus divinum semper & ubique homines obligat, quia non semper & ubique manifestatum. Ut tum demum ad sui obedientiam constringat homines, cum in leges & præcepta sese diffundit, quæ non dirigunt, nisi humanis actibus sint applicata; adeoque sufficienter propositæ, sic ut ignorantia prætendi nequeat, ab iis, quibus ea præscribuntur. d. c. 2. v. 12. Arg. l. 1. §. 4. D. de Orig. Jur l. 9. Cod. de legibus. vid. de hâc materiâ Rever. Parentem meum differt. de Jur. & Just. Dei. Me. am Theologiam Natural. cap. de Justit. Divinâ.
units.tr: There is also, by reason of certain precepts, a positive divine law, and indeed a very free one, so that God, who is above such a law of nature, could command its opposite. To this I refer the Mosaic ceremonial and forensic law, as such, and a large part of the moral law. Although, however, no precept of the latter is positive human law, inasmuch as no mortal, however supreme his power on earth, can command its contrary, yet it is some part of positive divine law. For this reason, many precepts of the second table, which we hold to be unchangeable, nevertheless are not so in view of divine power. Thus what concerns marriage, monogamy, the degrees of prohibited marriage, the distinctions of property, and homicide, is of the unchangeable natural law of men; yet God did not establish these by the necessity of law itself, so that they could not, by his most free good pleasure, be subject to change. There is also another difference: the natural law of men binds always, everywhere and in every state, inasmuch as it is law, and indeed manifest, and written on the hearts of all, so that men are rendered inexcusable, from that saying of Paul: Rom. 1. 19, 20, and 2. 12 ff. But not all divine law binds men always and everywhere, because it is not always and everywhere manifest. It binds men to obedience only when it spreads itself into laws and precepts, which do not direct unless they are applied to human acts, and so is sufficiently set forth to those to whom it is prescribed, so that ignorance cannot be pleaded by them. d. c. 2. v. 12. Arg. l. 1. §. 4. D. de Orig. Jur l. 9. Cod. de legibus. See on this matter Rever. Parentem meum differt. de Jur. & Just. Dei. Me. am Theologiam Natural. cap. de Justit. Divinâ.

units.la: II. Jus autem naturale hominum est, quod recta ratio, inter omnes homines æqualiter dictat; solisque hominibus competit, si accurate, & proprie loquamur. Unde quæsitum, cur Ulpianus JC. omnia indistinctè animalia juris naturalis perita censeri velit? Respondendum est, in jure nostro, non uno modo jus accipi naturale. Quandoque enim pro lege naturæ sumitur, pro communibus honestatis principiis, quae omnibus innata sunt hominibus, & quidem solis. §. 1. in sin. instit. Si quadrup. Paup. feciss. dic. Quo etiam respicit Apost. Paul. Rom 2. v. 15. Gentes opus legis scriptum in cordibus gerere. Et alibi Ambros. Lex gemina est naturalis & scripta, naturalis in corde, scripta in tabulis. Quandoque minus proprie, magis abusive, pro instinctu & inclinatione aliquâ naturali, cujus beneficio, secundum legem naturae, certo quodam respectu agere videntur bruta. Sensualem enim aliquem habent discursum, quam aestimativam Philosophi appellant: ut secundum analogiam brutis jus aliquod naturale tribui posset. Quod tamen non legis naturae, sed potius Praecepti veniet nomine; hoc quippe vocabulum paulo largius accipitur, quam ipsa lex. Praeceptum enim apud latinos etiam monitum designat, vi obligandi carens. Lex autem vim obligandi continet, à ligando sic dicta. Per jus autem naturae, tantum praeceptum naturae, citra vim obligandi, JC. designare, partim ex antecedentibus, partim ex consequentibus colligitur manifeste. Quod enim in l. 1. D. Just. & Jur. appellatur jus naturae, antea naturae vocabatur praeceptum. Et quae exempla juris naturae in sequentibus d. l. verbis subjecta, non ad leges referenda, sed ad instinctum, impetum & incitamentum naturae. Neque enim
units.tr: II. The natural law of men, however, is that which right reason dictates equally to all men, and it belongs to men alone, if we speak accurately and properly. Hence the question arises why the jurist Ulpian wishes all animals without distinction to be counted as skilled in natural law. The answer must be that in our law natural law is not taken in one way only. For sometimes it is taken for the law of nature, for the common principles of honesty which are innate in all men, and indeed in men alone. §. 1. in sin. instit. Si quadrup. Paup. feciss. dic. To this the Apostle Paul also refers, Rom. 2. 15: The Gentiles having the work of the law written in their hearts. And elsewhere Ambrose: The law is twofold, natural and written; natural in the heart, written on tablets. Sometimes, less properly and more abusively, it is taken for an instinct and some natural inclination, by the benefit of which brute animals seem to act, in a certain respect, according to the law of nature. For they have a certain sensory reasoning, which the philosophers call estimative; so that by analogy some natural law could be attributed to brutes. This, however, will not bear the name of law of nature, but rather of precept; for this word is taken somewhat more widely than law itself. For among the Latins a precept means also an admonition, lacking the force of obligation. Law, however, contains the force of obligation, and is so called from binding. That jurists by natural law mean only a precept of nature, without force of obligation, is clear from what goes before and what follows. For what in l. 1. D. Just. & Jur. is called the law of nature was formerly called a precept of nature; and the examples of natural law that are added in the words following that law are to be referred not to laws but to the instinct, impulse and incitement of nature. For

units.la: jus naturale ad maris & fœminæ conjunctionem,ad liberorum procreationem,aliquem juris obligat necessitate, verum monendo incitat & instigat. Init. Inst. Jur. Nat.Gent. civ. l. i. D. Just. & Jur. Nec alio sensu apud probatos Scriptores H″ɔn (seu mores, virtutes & vitia, tribus brutis, exemplis patefecit. Sic Aristot. passim in histor. Anim. & Plinius de Apibus l. 11. cap. 5. quod maxime, inquit, mirum est, & mores habent. Et Virgil.
units.tr: natural law does not bind by any necessity of law to the union of male and female, or to the procreation of children, but advises and urges. Init. Inst. Jur. Nat. Gent. civ. l. i. D. Just. & Jur. Nor do approved writers use the term in any other sense; they have shown, by examples drawn from brute animals, the Hebrew term (that is, manners, virtues and vices). Thus Aristotle passim in the History of Animals, and Pliny on bees, book 11, chapter 5: what is most wonderful, he says, is that they have manners. And Virgil.

units.la: Totiusque ex ordine gentis, Mores & studia & populos & prælia dicam: Et Horat.
units.tr: I shall tell of the whole nation in its order: its manners and pursuits, its peoples and its battles. And Horace:

units.la: Est in juvenis, est in equis patrum virtus.
units.tr: In young men there is, and in horses, the virtue of their fathers.

units.la: Et Epiphanius de brutis loquens: ἔα ὃ ἐν αὐτοῖς ἡῆ Ἀλόφοςς τῶν πεόνοιων ὃ θεὸς αἰνιγ-μάτα. Ut immerito Valla grammaticus, elegant. 4. cap. 48. censuram strinxerit in Ulpianum, quasi, brutis eandem illam juris rationem, quæ in homines & pro ut in homines cadit, tributam velit. Revard. 1. var. cap. 1. Athenæus Casaubon. cap. 10. lib 1. p. mihi 34. Coras. ad l. 1. D. Just. & Jur. Bocer. Clas. 1. disp. 2. n. 6. Connan. comm. jur. civil. lib. 1. cap. 6. n. 1. Merend. Contr. jur. lib. 2. cap. 1. n. 13. Henric. Ern. Cathol. jur. cap. 9. in init. diff. ex part. Wurmser. Nucl. jur. contr. lib. 1. tit. 2. Besold. in delib. jur. & ad tit. D. Just. & Jur. n. 20.
units.tr: And Epiphanius, speaking of brute beasts: "Let these things pass, which among them are the enigmas of God's providence" [ἔα ὃ ἐν αὐτοῖς ἡῆ Ἀλόφοςς τῶν πεόνοιων ὃ θεὸς αἰνιγ-μάτα]. So Valla the grammarian unjustly censured Ulpian, as if he wished the same legal reasoning that applies to men, and applies in the way it applies to men, to be attributed to brute beasts. Revard. 1. var. cap. 1. Athenæus Casaubon. cap. 10. lib 1. p. mihi 34. Coras. ad l. 1. D. Just. & Jur. Bocer. Clas. 1. disp. 2. n. 6. Connan. comm. jur. civil. lib. 1. cap. 6. n. 1. Merend. Contr. jur. lib. 2. cap. 1. n. 13. Henric. Ern. Cathol. jur. cap. 9. in init. diff. ex part. Wurmser. Nucl. jur. contr. lib. 1. tit. 2. Besold. in delib. jur. & ad tit. D. Just. & Jur. n. 20.

units.la: 12. Quia vero, uti propositum, recta ratio inter homines, jus naturale hominum dictavit ; ideo etiam ejus est conditionis, ut per homines mutari nequeat. Recta enim ratio in homine nonnisi simplex est, & uniformis, nec dispositioni alicujus hominis subjacet. §. pen. Instit. jur. nat. gent. §. ult. Inst. leg. Agnat. tutel. Arg. §. 2. v. Ergo Senatus. Instit. Usufr Merend. jur. contr. lib. 2. c. 2, n. 6. Besold. jur delib. ad lib. 1. Pand. n. 7. Conn. Comment. jur. civil. loc. cit. n. 5. 6. Negandum tamen non est, quin in hypothesi quandoque variet, quin ejus effectus impediatur, quin naturæ author, jus naturale hominum, immutare & in thesi possit. vid Lyclam. ultim Memb. Eccl. 31. Pac. Enant. c. 1. q. 2. Bronch cent. 1. assert. 4. Grot. Introd. Jurisp. Holl. lib. 1. part. 2. Bacchov. ad tit. Inst. jur. nat. Gent. Boer. ibid. Rever. Parentem disp. de jure & justitia Dei. Azor. Inst. Mor. tom. 1. lib. 6. q 2. Molin. de Just. tom. 1. disput. 4. tract. 1.
units.tr: 12. But since, as proposed, right reason among men dictates the natural law of men, it follows that this law is of such a nature that it cannot be changed by men. For right reason in a man is only simple and uniform, and is not subject to the disposition of any man. §. pen. Instit. jur. nat. gent. §. ult. Inst. leg. Agnat. tutel. Arg. §. 2. v. Ergo Senatus. Instit. Usufr Merend. jur. contr. lib. 2. c. 2, n. 6. Besold. jur delib. ad lib. 1. Pand. n. 7. Conn. Comment. jur. civil. loc. cit. n. 5. 6. Yet it must not be denied that in a hypothesis it sometimes varies, that its effect is sometimes hindered, and that the author of nature can change the natural law of men, both in the hypothesis and in the thesis. See Lyclam. ultim Memb. Eccl. 31. Pac. Enant. c. 1. q. 2. Bronch cent. 1. assert. 4. Grot. Introd. Jurisp. Holl. lib. 1. part. 2. Bacchov. ad tit. Inst. jur. nat. Gent. Boer. ibid. Rever. Parentem disp. de jure & justitia Dei. Azor. Inst. Mor. tom. 1. lib. 6. q 2. Molin. de Just. tom. 1. disput. 4. tract. 1.

units.la: 13. Verum, inquiretur ulterius, quo constet, quid sit immutabile, quænam juri naturæ sint adscribenda? An matrimonium? Id affirmandum, per textum expressum in init. Inst. jur. nat. l. 1. D. Just. & Jur. Non quidem ut vagum designat concubitum, sed ut conjunctionem cum affectu gratiâ procreandi desideratam. Neque enim promiscuam commixtionem suadet instinctus naturæ, neque dictat recta ratio. Genef. 1. v. 22. & 28. Lactant. 6. Divin. Instit. Schneidw. init. Inst. de Nupt. Caraf. ad l. 1. D. Just. & Jur. n. 7. 8. Dill. Conan. comm. jur. Civil. lib. 1. c. 6. n. 10 Olemann. Prefat. ad antin. Giffan. Besoid. n. 21. ad l. 1. D. Just. & Jur. Henric. Ernst. in Cathol. jur. cap. 9. n. 1.
units.tr: 13. But it will be asked further, by what means it is established what is immutable, and what should be ascribed to the law of nature. Is marriage such? This must be affirmed, by an express text in init. Inst. jur. nat. l. 1. D. Just. & Jur. Not indeed as denoting vague intercourse, but as a conjunction with affection desired for the sake of procreation. For the instinct of nature does not urge promiscuous mixing, nor does right reason dictate it. Genef. 1. v. 22. & 28. Lactant. 6. Divin. Instit. Schneidw. init. Inst. de Nupt. Caraf. ad l. 1. D. Just. & Jur. n. 7. 8. Dill. Conan. comm. jur. Civil. lib. 1. c. 6. n. 10 Olemann. Prefat. ad antin. Giffan. Besoid. n. 21. ad l. 1. D. Just. & Jur. Henric. Ernst. in Cathol. jur. cap. 9. n. 1.

units.la: 14. An itidem liberorum procreatio, eorundem amor & educatio ? Idem dicendum Init. Institit. Jur. Nat. Gent. civil. l. 1. D. Just. & Jur. Naturalis quippe stimulus parentes hortatur ad eorum procreationem, & educationem; in tantum, ut si liberis alimenta denegent, eos necare videantur; ne dicam in propria sævire viscera, præsertim si non habeant, unde sese alant. l. liberorum §. ult. D. V. signif. l. unic. §. taceat. Cod. Rei Uxor. Act. l. 4. 5. D. Agnosc. & alend. lib. l. ult. Cod. Alend. lib. §. 7. Institit. Noxal. Act. l. iste. Quod Met. causf. Aristot. 1. Polit. c. 1. & 1. Phys. c. ult. Xenoph. Inst. Cyr. lib. 2. Coraf. loc. cit. 9. Bocer. Classf. 1. disp. 2. n. 8.
units.tr: 14. Is the same true of the procreation of children, of love for them, and of their upbringing? The same must be said. Init. Institit. Jur. Nat. Gent. civil. l. 1. D. Just. & Jur. For the natural impulse urges parents to bring children into being and to rear them, to such an extent that if they deny food to their children they seem to kill them, not to mention raging against their own vitals, especially if they have no means by which to sustain themselves. l. liberorum §. ult. D. V. signif. l. unic. §. taceat. Cod. Rei Uxor. Act. l. 4. 5. D. Agnosc. & alend. lib. l. ult. Cod. Alend. lib. §. 7. Institit. Noxal. Act. l. iste. Quod Met. causf. Aristot. 1. Polit. c. 1. & 1. Phys. c. ult. Xenoph. Inst. Cyr. lib. 2. Coraf. loc. cit. 9. Bocer. Classf. 1. disp. 2. n. 8.

units.la: Quo nomine improbandum est jus civile, utpote juri naturae adversum, dum incestuosis alimenta non deberi, decernit. Authent. ex complexu. Cod. incest. Nupt. Neque enim id potuit statuere jus civile, aut debuit. init. Institit. juncto §. 1 1. jur. Nat. Gent. civil. arg. §. 2. v. Ergo nec Senatus. Inst. Usufr. & l. 8. D. reg. jur. l. 4. D. Agnosc. lib. Ut potius hic laudanda sit æquitas juris canonici, quod etiam mores hic sequuntur, secundum quam ex incestu prognatos liberos, parentes alere tenentur. c. cum haberet. 5. X. de eo, qui dux. in matr. quam poss. Gail. 2. obs. 88. Bull. de trib. Gener. jur. Prac. in addit. n. 9.
units.tr: For this reason civil law is to be condemned, since, being contrary to the law of nature, it decrees that food is not owed to incestuous persons. Authent. ex complexu. Cod. incest. Nupt. For civil law could not, nor ought to, establish this. init. Institit. juncto §. 1 1. jur. Nat. Gent. civil. arg. §. 2. v. Ergo nec Senatus. Inst. Usufr. & l. 8. D. reg. jur. l. 4. D. Agnosc. lib. Rather, the equity of canon law is to be praised here, which also the customs follow, under which parents are bound to feed the children born of incest. c. cum haberet. 5. X. de eo, qui dux. in matr. quam poss. Gail. 2. obs. 88. Bull. de trib. Gener. jur. Prac. in addit. n. 9.

units.la: Etiam improbandi quarundam foeminarum mores, quae post positâ naturae lege, affectu repudiato, proprios lactare liberos decori esse censent. Parum memores, quod majus sit partum sanguine in utero aluisse, quam jam natum lacte nutrire. Parum memores, Deum & naturam non frustra eas uberibus ornasse. Parum memores & lactis alimoniam nonnihil ad ingenii similitudinem conferre. Parum memores, isthac ratione affectum deminui, & quid non. Id quod suadent exempla piarum foeminarum, suadent rationes allatae, suadet jus civile. DD. ad l. pen. Cod. Patr. potest. gloss. & Gothefr. ibid. Gell. noct. Attic. lib 12. c. 1. Tiraquell. de Nobilit. c. 20. n. 79. & seq. ubi etiam dissidentes allegat. Berneg. q. 115. in Tac. Germ. & Agricol. Bocer. loc. cit. Bull. addit. ad tria jur. Prac. n. 9.
units.tr: The conduct of certain women is also to be condemned, who, setting aside the law of nature and rejecting affection, think it becoming to let their own children be nursed by others. Being too little mindful that it is a greater thing to have nourished the child with blood in the womb than to feed it with milk once born. Too little mindful that God and nature did not adorn them with breasts in vain. Too little mindful that the nourishment of milk contributes something to likeness of disposition, and so on. Examples of pious women urge this, the reasons adduced urge it, and civil law urges it. DD. ad l. pen. Cod. Patr. potest. gloss. & Gothefr. ibid. Gell. noct. Attic. lib 12. c. 1. Tiraquell. de Nobilit. c. 20. n. 79. & seq. ubi etiam dissidentes allegat. Berneg. q. 115. in Tac. Germ. & Agricol. Bocer. loc. cit. Bull. addit. ad tria jur. Prac. n. 9.

units.la: 15. An sui defensio, & injuriae propulsatio?
units.tr: 15. Is self-defence and the repelling of injury (to be assigned to the law of nations)?

units.la: Resp. licet non negaverim, eam posse juri Gentium adscribi, in quantum apud omnes Gentes ea peraeque observatur: §. 2. Inst. jur. nat. Gent. & civil. ratione tamen originis rectius eam adscripseris juri naturali, quod nobis est quodammodo cum brutis commune. Et quia passim in Jure Ratio naturalis & ipsa Natura permittere dicitur, ut quivis adversus omne periculum se tueatur. Et quia omni animantium generi per Naturae instinctum attributum videtur, ut se, vitam, & corpus tueatur.l. 4. in princ. D. ad l. Aquil. l. 1. §. 27. D. de vi & vi armat. Init. Institut. de Jur. Nat. Gent. & Civil. l 1. §. 11. D. Si quadrup. paup. fec. dic. l. 5. §. 1. l. 45. §. 4. D. Ad leg. Aquil. Propert. 2. Eleg. 5. Cicer. pro Milone & 1. offic. Cujac. 5. observ. cap. 18. Donell. 1. comm. 7. Bullaeus de tribus Gener. jur. Precept n. 10. Wissenbach. disp. 3. Pand. n. 6. Dist. Bartol. ad l. 3. D. de just. & jur. Connan. 1. comm. 6. n. 8. Jo-hann. Coras. in comm. add. l. 3. n. 3. 4. 5. Lyclam. Membr. 7. Eclog. 42. Pacius Antinom. cent. 1. quaest. 1. Matth. Berlich. part. 4. concl. Pract. 13. n. 2. Haenon. disput. 1. Instit. §. 11. Ego ex professo in tractatu meo de Duellis.
units.tr: Reply: although I would not deny that this can be ascribed to the law of nations, insofar as it is observed equally among all nations (Inst. jur. nat. Gent. & civil. §. 2), yet by its origin you would more rightly ascribe it to natural law, which we share in some measure with the brutes. For it is said everywhere in the law that natural reason and Nature herself allow anyone to defend himself against every danger, and because it seems to be granted to every kind of living creature by the instinct of Nature, that it should protect itself, its life and its body (l. 4 in princ. D. ad l. Aquil.; l. 1 §. 27 D. de vi & vi armat.; Init. Institut. de Jur. Nat. Gent. & Civil.; l. 1 §. 11 D. Si quadrup. paup. fec. dic.; l. 5 §. 1; l. 45 §. 4 D. Ad leg. Aquil.; Propert. 2 Eleg. 5; Cicero, pro Milone and De officiis 1; Cujacius, 5 observ. cap. 18; Donellus, 1 comm. 7; Bullaeus, de tribus Gener. jur. Precept. n. 10; Wissenbach, disp. 3 Pand. n. 6; Bartolus, distinction on l. 3 D. de just. & jur.; Connanus, 1 comm. 6 n. 8; Johannes Coras, in comm. add. l. 3 n. 3, 4, 5; Lyclamus, Membr. 7 Eclog. 42; Pacius, Antinom. cent. 1 quaest. 1; Matthaeus Berlichius, part. 4 concl. Pract. 13 n. 2; Haenon, disput. 1 Instit. §. 11). I have treated this ex professo in my tractate on Duels.

units.la: 16. Idemne de bonorum defensione statuendum? Resp. Si solam rerum defensionem spectemus, non idem dicendum esse putarem. Si eam, quae cum defensione corporis est conjuncta, id equidem non negarem. Ratio prioris est, quod Jurisconsultus in l. 3. D. de Just. & Jur. defensionem cum propulsatione conjunctam ad tutelam corporis permissam statuat, ut recte inferatur, propter solam rerum defensionem ad caedem perveniri non debere l. 52. §. 1. D. Ad l. Aquil. Accedit, quod inter hominis vitam & bona caduca nulla sit proportio; cùm illa semel amissa resarciri nequeat: hæc verò possint; ut vita etiam rebus pretiosissimis sit præferenda. l. 21. in sin. Cod. de Sacros. Eccles. l. 44. in princ. D. de Ædil. Edict. Ratio posterioris est, quòd furem nocturnum occidere liceat; quia incertum est, an veniat animo furandi, an occidendi? Et diurnum non aliter, quàm si telo se defendat; ut cum bonorum defensione semper aliqua vitæ tuitio debeat esse conjuncta. l. 4. D. Ad leg. Aquil. l. 45. §. 4. D. eod. l. 2. 3. 4. Cod. l. Cornel. de Sicar. Fachin. 1. contr. 31. Bocer. de duell c. 9 Bachov. in not. ad Parat. Wesenb. ad l. Aquil. Branchorst. 4. Antin. 82. Diff. Jul. Clar. §. Homicidium. n. 25. Lessius Jesuita, lib. 2. de just. & jur. c. 9. dubit. 2.
units.tr: 16. Is the same to be decided concerning the defence of goods? Resp. If we consider only the defence of things, I would not think the same should be said. If we consider that defence which is joined with the defence of the body, I would certainly not deny it. The reason for the former is that the jurist, in l. 3. D. de Just. & Jur., holds that defence joined with repelling is permitted for the protection of the body, so that it is rightly inferred that one must not come to killing merely for the defence of goods (l. 52. §. 1. D. Ad l. Aquil.). Add that there is no proportion between a man's life and perishable goods, since the former, once lost, cannot be restored, whereas the latter can; so life is to be preferred even to the most precious things (l. 21. in sin. Cod. de Sacros. Eccles. l. 44. in princ. D. de Ædil. Edict.). The reason for the latter is that it is lawful to kill a thief by night, because it is uncertain whether he comes with intent to steal or to kill; and a thief by day may be killed only if he defends himself with a weapon. So with the defence of goods there must always be some protection of life joined. (l. 4. D. Ad leg. Aquil. l. 45. §. 4. D. eod. l. 2. 3. 4. Cod. l. Cornel. de Sicar. Fachin. 1. contr. 31. Bocer. de duell c. 9 Bachov. in not. ad Parat. Wesenb. ad l. Aquil. Branchorst. 4. Antin. 82. Diff. Jul. Clar. §. Homicidium. n. 25. Lessius Jesuita, lib. 2. de just. & jur. c. 9. dubit. 2.)

units.la: 17. Verum cui juri adscribenda Religio? Resp. illi juri Naturæ eam esse adscribendam, quod ratio dictat inter omnes homines: licet modum colendi Deum præscribat sacra Scriptura. Omnes enim homines, modò sint sanæ mentis, fateri coguntur, Deum esse colendum; cùm, si conscientiam examinent, dubitare non audeant de Numinis existentiâ. Et recta ratio suadet id, quod summum est, ratione suæ excellentiæ, omnem honorem mereri. Arg. l 2. D. de justitiâ & jur. Paulus ad Rom. 1. v. 19. Ut propterea Aristoteles
units.tr: 17. But to which law is religion to be assigned? Resp. It is to be assigned to that law of Nature which reason dictates among all men, although Holy Scripture prescribes the manner of worshipping God. For all men, provided they are of sound mind, are compelled to acknowledge that God is to be worshipped; since, if they examine their conscience, they dare not doubt the existence of the Deity. And right reason teaches that what is supreme deserves all honour by reason of its excellence (Arg. l. 2. D. de justitiâ & jur.; Paul to the Romans 1:19). Therefore Aristotle

units.la: teles eeles (1. Topic. cap. 9.) castigatione & pœnâ dignos judicaverit eos, qui, utrum Deus honorandus sit, dubitare audent? Cicer. 3. Tuscul. quæst. Boët. Consol. Philos. lib. 5. pros. 6. Lyclam. 7. Membr. Eclog. 41. Besold. ad l. 2. de justitiâ & jur. Bocer. Class. 1. disput. 2. n. 12. tract. de Jur. Univers. Wurmser. Nucl. jur. contr. lib. 1. tit. 2. contr. 2. n. 8. 9. Reverendus meus Parens in tractat. de Atheismo. Ego in Theologiâ Natur. Reformat. Diss. ex parte Cartefius, Sociniani, aliiqueAthei à me dicto tract. refutati.

Membr. Eclog. 41. Besold. ad l. 2. de justitiâ & jur. Bocer. Class. 1. disput. 2. n. 12. tract. de Jur. Univers. Wurmser. Nucl. jur. contr. lib. 1. tit. 2. contr. 2. n. 8. 9. My reverend father in his treatise on Atheism; I in the Natural Theology Reformed. The dissertation in part against the Cartesians, Socinians and other atheists refuted by me in the treatise mentioned.

units.la: 18. Cui juri adscribendus Amor, qui Patriæ debetur & Parentibus? Respondeo, juri naturali. Arg. l. 3. D. Just. & jur. Ratio enim naturalis suadet & Patriæ, in quâ vitam primitus accepimus, & Patri, à quo spiritum hausimus, post Deum in omnibus esse parendum. Suadet id ipsum 5. Decalogi præceptum, quæ juris est naturalis expressio. Suadent id effectus, quòd originarii plerumque extraneis in obeundis Patriæ muneribus sint fideliores. DD. Ad l. 1. D. Ad municip. Vid. l. habebat. De leg. 3. l. qui habebat. v. dulcissima patriæ meæ. D. eod. l. moveor. Cod. serv. export. & l. sin. ubi Bald. Cod. si serv. export. veniat. Gloss in l. veluti. D. just. & jur. & in l. fallaciter. Cod. de Aboliti. Georgius Vivien comm. ad lat. introit. Philippi 2. Hisp. Reg. tartic. 9. in sin. Besold. class. 1. disp. 2. n. 12.
units.tr: 18. To what law should we assign the love that is owed to one's country and to one's parents? I answer: to the natural law. Argument: Digest 1.1.3 (De justitia et iure). For natural reason suggests that, after God, one must obey both one's country, in which we first received life, and one's father, from whom we drew breath. The fifth precept of the Decalogue suggests the same, and it is a true expression of the natural law. The effects suggest it too, since natives are generally more faithful than foreigners in discharging the duties of their country. The jurists on Digest 1.1.1 (De municipibus): see Code 4.? (l. habebat), Digest 3.? (l. qui habebat, v. "dulcissima patriae meae"), Digest of the same title, l. moveor, Code (De servis exportandis) and l. sin., where Bartolus on Code (si serv. export.) veniat; the gloss on l. veluti in Digest 1.1 and on l. fallaciter, Code (De abolitionibus); Georgius Vivien, commentary on the Latin introduction of Philip II of Spain, tit. 9, at the end; Besold, class 1, disp. 2, n. 12.

units.la: 19. Verum, quid dicendum in concursu, an potiús parenti, an patriæ succurrendum erit? Resp. Affirm. Post. licet ordo in d. l. 2. D. Justitia & jur. à Juriscoufulto sit inversus. Quò enim finis est ulterior, eo melior: ut universali, quale est Patriæ bonum, cedat particularis finis, qualis est Parentis conservatio l. 1. §. 15. ibidemque varia à Gotefredo in Comm. cit. D. de ventr. in Poss mittend. d l. qui habebat. D. de leg. 3. l. 35. D. Religios & sumpt. fun. Docuerunt id exempla omnis ætatis, omniumque populorum; quæ ne huc conferam, vel unum, licet severum nimium, Damatriæ Spartanæ dabo, quæ, cùm accepisset filium ignavo erga Patriam esse animo, eundem domum reversum occdit, atque ejus sepulchro hosce versus inscribi curavit:
units.tr: 19. But what is to be said in a conflict: must one come to the aid of the parent or of the fatherland? Answer: Yes, the latter, although the order in the said law 2, D. Justice and Right, has been reversed by the jurist. For the further an end reaches, the better it is, so that the particular end, such as the preservation of a parent, yields to the universal good, such as that of the fatherland. See l. 1 §15, and the various remarks of Gothofredus in his cited commentary; D. de ventre in possessionem mittendo; l. qui habebat, D. de legatis 3; l. 35, D. de religiosis et sumptibus funerum. The examples of every age and of all peoples teach this. Rather than bring them all in here, I will give just one, though it is rather harsh: the Spartan mother Damatria, when she heard that her son had a cowardly spirit toward the fatherland, killed him on his return home, and had these verses inscribed on his tomb:

units.la: Hunc timidum mater Damatrion ipsa peremit.
units.tr: His own mother Damatrion herself slew this coward.

units.la: Nec dignum matre, nec Lacedæmonio.
units.tr: Worthy neither of a mother nor of a Lacedaemonian.

units.la: Valer. Maximus, lib. 2. cap. 7. Everhard. in Topicis, loco: ab ordine. Georgius Vivien, comment. ad let. introit. Philippi 2. artic. 13. litt. a. & d. Keckerm. disp. pract. 22. Problem. 24. Besold. ad l. 2. D. de just. & jur. n. 5, & 6. Wurmser. Nucl. jur. contr. lib. 1. tit. 2. q. 2.
units.tr: Valerius Maximus, book 2, chapter 7. Everhard, in Topics, under the heading "from order". Georgius Vivien, commentary on the introduction to Philip 2, article 13, letters a and d. Keckermann, practical disputation 22, problem 24. Besold, on D. 2, de iustitia et iure, nn. 5 and 6. Wurmser, Nucleus of Controverted Law, book 1, title 2, question 2.

units.la: 20. Cui denique juri adscribenda Libertas? Respondeo, licet plerique libertatem illi juri naturali adscriptam velint, quod nobis est cum brutis animantibus commune: argum. l. 4. v. quæ res à jure Gentium. D. de Justit. & Jur. & §. 1. Inst. de Jur. Person. Dicendum tamen, Libertatem non esse aut ab instinctu naturali, aut à ratione dispositivè. Est enim quædam facultas naturalis, quam in tantum non introduxit Ratio, ut potius eam minuat. Vel potius legibus congruenter dicatur, nec Libertatem, nec servitutem esse juris naturalis, indifferenter semet ad utrumque oppositum habentis; ut uno communi nomine omnes appellati sint homines, nullo posito discrimine, liberine essent an servi? Ut differentiæ duæ Libertatis, ejusque oppositæ servitutis, juris Gentium sint dispositive. Id quod satis colligitur (meo judicio) ex Instit. de libert. v. & cum uno communi nomine l. 4. v. sed postea quam. D. de just. & jur. Zoes. D. de just. & jur. n. §1. Diss. Donell. 1. comment. cap. 7. Besold. ad l. 4. n. 1. D. de Just. & jur. Bocer. class. 1. disp. 2. n. 8.
units.tr: 20. Finally, to what law is liberty to be assigned? I answer: although most people want liberty to be ascribed to natural law, since we share it with the brute animals (argument from l. 4, v. quæ res à jure Gentium, D. de Justitia et Jure, and §1 Inst. de Jure Personarum), it must be said that liberty is neither from natural instinct nor from reason as a disposing cause. For there is a certain natural faculty which Reason has not introduced in such a way as to diminish it; or rather, to speak in agreement with the laws, neither liberty nor servitude belongs to natural law, since man stands indifferently toward either opposite, so that by one common name all are called men, with no distinction made as to whether they are free or slaves. Thus the two differences of liberty, and its opposite servitude, belong to the law of nations as dispositive. This is sufficiently gathered (in my judgment) from Instit. de libert. v. and from l. 4, v. sed postea quam, D. de just. & jur., with one common name. Zoes. D. de just. & jur. n. §1. Diss. Donell. 1. comment. cap. 7. Besold. ad l. 4. n. 1. D. de Just. & jur. Bocer. class. 1. disp. 2. n. 8.

units.la: 1. Differentia inter jus gentium & naturae traditur.

units.la: 1. EXplicui quantum sufficit, jus Naturale, & quæ illi adscribenda. ordine recensui. Ad jus Gentium propero, quod à jure naturali distinctum esse, (licet quandoque à Jurisc. confundantur ut in §. 11. instit. de jure natur. Gent. & civil.) plus quàm manifestum est. l.pen. D. just. & jur. Jus enim naturale est, quod vel Natura, si improprie (id est, instinctus) vel ipsa Ratio, si proprie, quod est hominum tantùm, illos ipsos docuit: estque jus quoddam innatum. Quod si ad usum transferatur, mutat nomen suum, & à Gentibus, à quibus recipitur, jus gentium appellabitur. §. 1. Instit. de jur. nat. Gent. & Civil. Ut jus naturale non sit jus constitutum. Jus gentium, jus constitutum. d. §. 1. licet non tantùm. Cùm quoddam jus ab aliquo populo, seu natione, sit constitutum, quod civile appellatur. Ut, quod est à Gentibus plerisque & quidem moratioribus, & quidem morate constitutum,etiàm in quantum comprobatum, jus Gentium dicatur. Argum. §. pen. instit. Præam, §. 1. 2. junct. §. II. Inst. jur. Nat. Gent. Civil. c. jus gentium. 1. distinct. Non quod in unum aliquando convenerint Gentes : verùm quòd successivè plerisque tacitè id visum est placere ; ut totius orbis suisse decretum existimetur. Dissentiunt plerique,qui jus naturale hominum cum jure Gentium primævo confundunt. Merend. juris controv. lib. 2. c. 3. in sin. Besold. del. jur. ex lib. 1. Pand. n. 6. Bocer. class. 1. disp. 2. n. 10. Tract. jur. Univers. Wurmser. Nul. jur. coutr. lib. 1. tit. 2. concr. 1. in sin. & 2. in init. vide Grot. de jur. bell. & Pac. lib. 1. Cap. 1. n. 10.
units.tr: 1. I have explained the natural law as far as is sufficient, and have reviewed in order what is to be ascribed to it. I now turn to the law of nations, which is plainly distinct from the natural law, although jurists sometimes confuse the two, as in § 11, Inst. de jure natur. Gent. & civil. For the natural law is that which nature (improperly speaking, that is, instinct) or reason itself (properly speaking) taught to men alone; it is a certain innate law. But if it is put into use, it changes its name and is called the law of nations, from the nations by which it is received, § 1, Inst. de jur. nat. Gent. & Civil. So the natural law is not a constituted law, whereas the jus gentium is a constituted law, d. § 1. though not only that. For when a certain law is established by some people or nation, it is called civil law. Thus what is established by most nations, and indeed by the more civilised and in a civilised way, and indeed insofar as it is approved, is called the law of nations. Not because the nations ever came together into one place, but because it has tacitly seemed good to most of them one after another, so that it is regarded as having been decreed for the whole world. Most of those who confuse the natural law of men with the primary law of nations disagree. See Merend. juris controv. lib. 2 c. 3; Besold, del. jur. ex lib. 1 Pand. n. 6; Bocer. class. 1 disp. 2 n. 10; Wurmser, Nucl. jur. contr. lib. 1 tit. 2 concr. 1 and 2; and see Grotius, de jur. bell. & pac. lib. 1 cap. 1 n. 10.

units.la: 2. Jus Gentium, à jure naturali sic distinctum communiter dividi solet in Primævum & Secundævum. Illud appellant, quod Ratio (quæ etiam in statu Integritatis locum habuisset) inter homines constituit, atque firmum & immutabile permanet. Hoc quod Ratio quidem naturalis, sed propter depravatam hominum naturam inter gentes, constituit. Quæritur, Num rectè? Resp. quod ita. Neque enim hæc distinctio suo caret fundamento. Cùm enim aliquod jus Gentium dicatur immutabile, aliquod mutabile: aliquod cum ipso humano genere ortum sumpsisse: aliquod postea demùm, usu exigente & humanis necessitatibus: aliquod esse ex jure naturali: aliquod ei suo modo adversari: haecque omnia inferant aliquam oppositionem, quae distinctionis est fundamentum: negari non poterit. quin duplex jus gentium sit admittendum. Sive, illud appelletur Primaevum & secundaevum, sive Prius & posterius, sive superius & inferius parum refert. Verba enim non curanda modo in re sit consensus: neque leges verbis, sed rebus sunt datae, l. 2. in fin. Cod. comm. de legat. & fideicomm. §. 1. 2. 11. Inst. Jur. Natur. Gent. & Civil. & l. 3. 4. 5. D. eod. Pinell. ad l. 2. Cod. de Rescind. vendit. part. 1. n. 11. Donell. 1. comm. cap. 7. Besold. delib. jur. ex lib. 1. Pand. n. 6. Idem ad l. 1. D. de Just. & Jur. Wurmser. Nucl. jur. Contr. lib. 1. tit. 2. contr. 2. Bocer. classi. 1. disp. 2. n. 11. Bacchov. ad Institit. Com. de jur. nat. Gent. Civil. Henric. Ernst. Helmst. Catholi. jur. cap. 10. n. 1. Dist. Connan. comm. jur. Civil. lib. 1. cap. 5. Dist. Coraf. 6. Misc. cap fin. Bronchorst, cent. 1. Enant. assert. 3. Lyclam. 7. Membran. Eclog. 31. Zoes. D. de justit. & jur. n. 33. Qui ibidem Covarruviam & Valascum pro se allegat.
units.tr: 2. The law of nations, distinguished in this way from the natural law, is commonly divided into primary and secondary. The first is what reason (which would also have held sway in the state of integrity) established among men, and it remains firm and unchanging. The second is what reason, natural indeed, but because of the depraved nature of men, established among nations. Is this right? I answer that it is. For this distinction is not without its foundation. Since some law of nations is called unchangeable and some changeable; some arose together with the human race itself, some only later, as use and human needs required; some derive from the natural law, and some oppose it in their own way; and since all these things imply some opposition, which is the basis of the distinction, it cannot be denied that a twofold law of nations must be admitted. Whether it is called primary and secondary, or prior and posterior, or higher and lower, matters little: words are not to be regarded, provided there is agreement in the thing, for laws are given for things, not for words. See l. 2 in fin. Cod. comm. de legat. & fideicomm.; § 1, 2, 11 Inst. Jur. Natur. Gent. & Civil.; l. 3, 4, 5 D. eod.; Pinell. ad l. 2 Cod. de Rescind. vendit. part. 1 n. 11; Donell. 1 comm. cap. 7; Besold. delib. jur. ex lib. 1 Pand. n. 6; the same ad l. 1 D. de Just. & Jur.; Wurmser, Nucl. jur. contr. lib. 1 tit. 2 contr. 2; Bocer. classi. 1 disp. 2 n. 11; Bacchov. ad Institut. com. de jur. nat. Gent. Civil.; Henric. Ernst. Helmst. Catholi. jur. cap. 10 n. 1; Connan. comm. jur. civil. lib. 1 cap. 5; Coraf. 6 Misc. cap. fin.; Bronchorst, cent. 1; Enant. assert. 3; Lyclam. 7; Membran. Eclog. 31; Zoes. D. de justit. & jur. n. 33. He cites Covarruvias and Valasco there in support of himself.

units.la: 3. Verum quaenam ad jus Gentium primaevum erunt referenda? Resp. Eadem illa quae hactenus juri naturali fuerunt annumerata. Qualia sunt Matrimonium, Liberorum educatio, defensio sui ipsius, Religio, Amor patriae atque parentum. Ut ea omnia utrique juri (naturali scilicet, & gentium) sint communia, quæ semper fiirma atque immutabilia permanent. Argum. §. 11. Instit. de jur. natur. Gent. & Civil. Infrequens enim in jure non est, ut una eademque res diverso jure censeatur; adeoque pro variâ consideratione & juri naturali & gentium primævo accepta feratur. Argum. l. 45 §. 4. D. Ad l. Aquil. Cujac. 5. observ. cap. 18. Besold. ad l. 1. § 21. D. Just. & Jur. ad l. 2. §. 1. 2. D. eod. & l. 3. §. 1. in med. comm. D. eod. Wurmser. Nucl. jur. contr. lib. 1. tit. 2. confr. 2. n. 11. 12. Borer. class. 1. disp. 2. n. 13. vid. quæ notavi in disp. 1. Ad l. 2. Cod. l. Cornel. de Sicar. thes. 5.
units.tr: 3. But which things are to be referred to the primary law of nations? I answer: those same things that have hitherto been counted under the natural law, such as marriage, the education of children, self-defence, religion, love of country and of parents. So all those things are common to both laws (the natural and the law of nations) which remain always firm and unchangeable. See § 11, Inst. de jur. natur. Gent. & Civil. For it is not unusual in law for one and the same thing to be judged under different laws, and so to be taken as belonging to the natural law or the primary law of nations according to the different point of view. See l. 45 § 4 D. ad l. Aquil.; Cujac. 5 observ. cap. 18; Besold. ad l. 1 § 21 D. Just. & Jur.; ad l. 2 § 1, 2 D. eod. and l. 3 § 1 in med. comm. D. eod.; Wurmser, Nucl. jur. contr. lib. 1 tit. 2 contr. 2 n. 11, 12; Bocer. class. 1 disp. 2 n. 13. See what I have noted in disp. 1, ad l. 2 Cod. l. Cornel. de Sicar. thes. 5.

units.la: 4. Major difficultas est circa exempla juris Gentium secundævi; quænam scilicet illi juri sint annumeranda? An distinctio dominiorum? Respondeo, licet ea non tantum jure humano, sed & naturali & divino nitatur; quia tamen non directe & immediate ab initio natura rerum præcepit divisionem, verum tantum ex occasione humani generis multiplicati, & iniquitatis invalescentis, cupiditate hominum insatiabili viam monstrante; dicendum erit rerum divisionem seu dominiorum distinctionem ex jure gentium secundævo originem trahere. §. 3. Inst. jur. nat. gent. & civil. §. 11. Inst. Rer. divis. l. 5. D. eod. idque ad commodum generis humani. Nisi enim ea obtineret, pacifica & suavis rerum admiadministratio inter homines non esset. Communio quippe mater est litium atque discordiarum. Genes. 13. & 30. l. 79. §. dulcissimis fratribus. D. leg. 2. l. 5. D. Acquir. Rer. dom. Communio mater socordiæ est: cum quod ab omnibus possidetur, nemo quasi possideat: quotque omnes curant, nemo curet. l. 1. D. de rebus eorum qui sub tutel, vel cur. l. 3. §. 6. D. Adm. tutel. Præterquam quod suam quis partem corrumpi patiatur, dum invidet alienæ. l. 2. Cod. quando & quibus pars quart. debeatur. lib. 10. Ne jam dicam, in corruptâ hominum societate, Deum hominibus viam præmonstrasse divisionis, ut ita omnis occasio dissensionis evitaretur. Genes. 10. Deuteron. 32. Josuæ 9. 18. & Donell. 1. comment. 7. Besold. ad l.
units.tr: 4. The greater difficulty concerns examples of the secondary law of nations: which things, namely, are to be counted under that law? Is the distinction of dominions one of them? I answer: although it rests not only on human law but also on natural and divine law, yet because nature did not directly and immediately prescribe from the beginning the division of things, but only on the occasion of the multiplication of the human race and the growing of wickedness, human greed pointing the way, it must be said that the division of things, or the distinction of dominions, derives its origin from the secondary law of nations. §3 Inst. jur. nat. gent. & civil.; §11 Inst. Rer. divis.; l. 5 D. eod. And this was for the good of the human race. For unless this obtained, a peaceful and pleasant administration of things among men would not exist. Indeed communal ownership is the mother of lawsuits and quarrels. Genes. 13 and 30; l. 79 § dulcissimis fratribus D. leg. 2; l. 5 D. Acquir. Rer. dom. Communal ownership is the mother of carelessness: what is possessed by all is, as it were, possessed by no one, and as many as look after it, no one looks after it. l. 1 D. de rebus eorum qui sub tutel. vel cur.; l. 3 § 6 D. Adm. tutel. Besides this, a man allows his own share to be spoiled while he envies another's. l. 2 Cod. quando & quibus pars quart. debeatur, lib. 10. Not to mention that, in a corrupted human society, God showed men the way of division, so that every occasion of dissension might be avoided. Genes. 10; Deuteron. 32; Josuae 9, 18; and Donell. 1 comment. 7; Besold. ad l.

units.la: 5. An regna ex eodem jure nata? Affirm. Licet enim immediate à naturâ procedat, ut civiles sint hominum societates, adeoque in statu integritatis suavis fuisset harmonia superiorum & inferiorum; inque jubendo & parendo certus ordo, semotâ omni ambitione, finesque dilatandi cupidine; quia tamen hodie quæ regna constituta, pleraque dominandi libidine sunt constituta, ad prædas & depopulationes instituendas, potius quam ad societatem colendam erecta; concurrente rerum atque hominum defensione, quod se solos infirmos sentirent; per accidens malitiæ humanæ ab hominibus, regna esse condita, ac per hoc discretas gentes, statuendum erit. Genes. c. 10. §. 2. Instit. Jur. nat. gent. civil. l. 4. D. Just. & jur. Bocer. Besold. Zoes. loc. entea citat.
units.tr: 5. Do kingdoms arise from the same law? Affirmative. For although civil societies proceed immediately from nature, so that in the state of integrity the harmony between superiors and inferiors would have been pleasant, and in commanding and obeying there would have been a fixed order, with all ambition set aside and no desire for extending boundaries; yet because today most of the kingdoms that have been established were founded from a lust for domination, set up for plundering and laying waste rather than for cultivating society, and because men felt that they were weak only when alone, they joined together in defence of things and persons; thus kingdoms were founded by accident of human malice, and it must be held that the nations are distinct on that account. Gen. ch. 10. §. 2. Inst. Jur. nat. gent. civil. l. 4. D. Just. & jur. Bocer. Besold. Zoes. cited in the same place.

units.la: 6. An itidem bella? Idem dicendum. Licet enim simplex defensio, juri naturali adscribatur; non tamen bellum, quæ defensio est limitata & circumscripta, partim juri naturali accedens, partim ab ea recedens. Ut nonnisi usu exigente, & ut hominum malitiis obviam eatur, ea sint introducta. §. 2. Inst. Jur. natur. Gent. civil. l. 5. D. Just. & Jur. Argum. l. 6. D. eod. Zes. D. eod. n. 37. & seq. Besold ad l. 5. D. eod. n. 1. diff. Hottom. ad §. sed jus. Inst. de jur. nat. Gent. civil.
units.tr: 6. Likewise wars? The same must be said. For although simple defence is ascribed to the natural law, war is not; that defence is limited and circumscribed, partly agreeing with natural law and partly departing from it. Thus wars were introduced only by use, as the need required, and so that the malice of men might be met. §. 2. Inst. Jur. natur. Gent. civil. l. 5. D. Just. & Jur. Argument from l. 6. D. eod. Zoes. D. eod. n. 37. & seq. Besold on l. 5. D. eod. n. 1. diss. Hottom. on §. sed jus. Inst. de jur. nat. Gent. civil.

units.la: 7 An captivitates, hincque ortæ servitutes, & manumissiones? Quod Affirmandum. Etsi enim secundum Philosophum alii qui nascantur servi, aliqui domini; non alio sensu, quam quod nonnulli adeo bardi & stupidi, ut digni qui serviant, alii adeo ingeniosi, & sublimati pectoris, ut digni qui jubeant; hæc tamen non obstant, quo minus servitutes, non juris naturæ, sed gentium & quidem secundæ, esse dicantur. Si enim nim bella, unde captivitates, sint juris gentium; & nisi in bello fiant servi; (neque enim hic ago de modis juris civilis, quibus servi efficiuntur) sequitur & jur sgentium esse ipsas servitutes. §. 2. Instit. jur. nat. Gent. civil. Init. Inst. de libertin. §. 2 Inst. de jure Personar. l. 5. D. Just. & Jur. l. 32. D. de Reg. jur. l. 4. 5. D. stat. Homin Zoef d. l. n. 36. Besold, ad l. 4. D. Just & jur. n. 1. Accuratissime Jurisconsultum cum Aristotele in materia propositâ conciliatum vide in Epist. Nob. Daniel. Heinsii ad Georgium Richterum, Apud Janum Rutgersium Jur. lection. l. 4. c. 3.
units.tr: 7. Likewise captivities, and the servitudes arising from them, and manumissions? This must be affirmed. For although, according to the Philosopher, some are born slaves and others masters, this is only in the sense that some are so dull and stupid that they are fit to serve, and others so gifted and lofty of spirit that they are fit to command; yet these things do not prevent servitudes from being said to belong not to the natural law but to the law of nations, and indeed to the secondary law of nations. For if wars, from which captivities arise, belong to the law of nations, and men become slaves only in war (for I am not here treating of the modes of civil law by which slaves are made), it follows that servitudes themselves belong to the law of nations. §. 2. Inst. jur. nat. Gent. civil. Init. Inst. de libertin. §. 2 Inst. de jure Personar. l. 5. D. Just. & Jur. l. 32. D. de Reg. jur. l. 4. 5. D. stat. Homin. Zoes d. l. n. 36. Besold, on l. 4. D. Just & jur. n. 1. See most accurately the jurist reconciled with Aristotle on the matter proposed, in the Letter of our friend Daniel Heinsius to Georgius Richterus, in Janus Rutgersius, Jur. lection. l. 4. c. 3.

units.la: 8. An obligationes, & contractus?Resp. Sic videtur; non omnes tamen; ut dicendum, fere omnes ex jure gentium originem habere. Id quod non tantum de contractubus sed etiam quasi contractubus, reliquisque juris actubus statuendum erit. §. 2. Inst. Jur. natur. Gent. civil. l. 5. D. Just. & jur. l. 20. D. de Judic. Ut tamen constet quinam sint juri gentium, quinam alteri juri adscribendi, videndum an ne sic jus civile juris gentium contractus receperit, comprobaverit, reformaverit, ut tamen specificam iis formam, quam habent ex jure gentium reliquerit; & manebunt juris gentium, ut emptio venditio &c. An vero novam juris formam specificam superaddiderit; & desinent esse juris gentium; quod forma det esse rei. d. l.
units.tr: 8. Likewise obligations and contracts? Answer: It seems so; yet not all of them. It must be said that almost all have their origin in the law of nations. This must be held not only of contracts but also of quasi-contracts and the other acts of law. §. 2. Inst. Jur. natur. Gent. civil. l. 5. D. Just. & jur. l. 20. D. de Judic. Yet so that it may be established which are ascribed to the law of nations and which to another law, one must consider whether civil law has received, approved and reformed the contracts of the law of nations in such a way that it has left them their specific form as they have it from the law of nations, and they will remain of the law of nations, as sale and purchase etc.; or whether it has added a new specific form of law, and they cease to be of the law of nations, because form gives being to a thing. d. l.

units.la: 5. l. 6. D. eod. Cornan. comment. jur. l. 2. c. 3. Zoes. D. de Just. & jur. n. 43. Ernst. in Cathol. juris cap. 10. n. 2. Befold. ad l. 5. §. 4. D. eod Barbos. Axiom. & Princ. jur, in verbo :forma.
units.tr: Law 5, law 6, D. eod. (same title); Cornan, Commentary on Law, bk. 2, ch. 3; Zoes, D. de Just. & jur., n. 43; Ernst, in Cathol. juris, ch. 10, n. 2; Befold, on law 5, §4, D. eod.; Barbosa, Axioms and Principles of Law, under the word "forma".

units.la: 9. An per hoc actiones, quæ ex obligationibus, & contractubus oriuntur? Resp. licet actionum formulæ juris sint civilis, materia tamen juri gentium est adscribenda. l. 2. § 6. D. Orig. jur. Ratio in promtu est: Quod aliter ante 12. Tabulas, inanes suissent ex jure gentium obligationes & contractus, nisi & remedia exigendi, quales sunt actiones, locum habuissent. Arg. l. 7. in init. D. de Pact. Accedit, quod qualis est causa, etiam talis debeat esse effectus: ut si mater actionum sit ex jure gentium, & ipsæ illi juri suam debeant originem. Barbos. axiom. & Princ. jur. in verbo : causa. Coraf. ad §. 6. D. orig. jur. Treutl. disp. 1. Pand. thes. 4. Bacchov. ibid. Idem ad Init. Institut. de Action.
units.tr: 9. Likewise, do the actions that arise from obligations and contracts belong to the same?
