Answer: although the formulas of actions belong to civil law, their matter is nevertheless to be ascribed to the law of nations. l. 2. § 6. D. Orig. jur. The reason is ready to hand: otherwise, before the Twelve Tables, the obligations and contracts of the law of nations would have been empty, unless the remedies for exacting them, such as actions, had had a place. Cf. l. 7 in init. D. de Pact. Add that, as the cause is, so the effect ought to be; so if the mother of actions is of the law of nations, the actions themselves owe their origin to that law. Barbos. axiom. & Princ. jur. under the word: causa. Coraf. on §. 6. D. orig. jur. Treutl. disp. 1. Pand. thes. 4. Bacchov. ibid. The same on the beginning of the Institutes, de Action.

units.la: 10 An hypotheca, Constitutum, Emphyteusis, Donatio propter nuptias? Idem dicendum. Etsi enim ex jure civili obligent, eoque sensu, licet admodum improprie, dicantur juris civilis. l. 6. D. de pact. Et ita omnes juris gentium contractus, suo modo dicantur esse juris civilis: attamen quia nec Præthor, nec Zenon Imperator, nec Justinianus obligationibus, prænominatis novam formam addiderunt ; in terminis juris gentium remanserunt. Hypotheca enim & Constitutum tantum jure prætorio ad obligandum facta sunt efficacia. Et circa Emphyteusin, atque Donationes, neque Zenon, neque Justinianus, jura nova introduxerunt; quod isti contractus gentibus non essent incogniti, licet nonnulli forte iisdem proprium nomen imposuerint. Coraf. 1. Mistel. 21. Conuan. 7. comm. c. 12. Hænon. disp. Inst. 1. thef. 14. Henric. Ernst. Cathol. jur. c. 10. n. 7. & 8. diss. Zoef. ex parte. D. just. & jur. n. 44.
units.tr: 10. Likewise hypotheca, constitutum, emphyteusis, donatio propter nuptias? The same must be said. For although they bind by civil law, and in that sense, though very improperly, are called of civil law (l. 6. D. de pact.), and thus all the contracts of the law of nations are in their own way said to be of civil law; yet because neither the Praetor, nor the Emperor Zeno, nor Justinian added a new form to these obligations, they remained within the bounds of the law of nations. For hypotheca and constitutum were made effective for binding only by praetorian law. And concerning emphyteusis and donations, neither Zeno nor Justinian introduced new laws; because these contracts were not unknown to the nations, although some perhaps gave them their own proper name. Coraf. 1. Mistel. 21. Conuan. 7. comm. c. 12. Hænon. disp. Inst. 1. thef. 14. Henric. Ernst. Cathol. jur. c. 10. n. 7. & 8. diss. Zoef. ex parte. D. just. & jur. n. 44.

units.la: CAPUT III.
units.tr: CHAPTER III.

units.la: 1. Quid sit jus Civile in genere, describitur.
units.tr: 1. What civil law is in general is described.

units.la: 2. An mutabile?
units.tr: 2. Is it changeable?

units.la: 3. Quot modis aliquid dicatur juris civilis? Et an stipulatio? Acceptilatio?
units.tr: 3. In how many ways is something called civil law? And is stipulation so called? Acceptilation?

units.la: 4. An Testamenti factio, Tutela, &c.
units.tr: 4. Whether the power to make a will, guardianship, etc., belong to civil law.

units.la: 5. Unde dignoscatur aliquid esse juris civilis?
units.tr: 5. How can it be recognised that something belongs to civil law?

units.la: 1. HActenus egi de jure naturali & gentium, deque iis quæ utrique aut alterutri adscribuntur; superest jus civile, sic acceptum, ut & jus prætorium sub se contineat; ad distinctionem juris naturalis atque gentium. §. 1. Inst. de jur. nat. Gent. & civil. l. 9. D. de Just.
units.tr: 1. HITHERTO I have discussed the law of nature and the law of nations, and those things which are ascribed to one or the other or to both. There remains civil law, taken in such a way that it also comprises praetorian law, in distinction from the law of nature and of nations. §. 1. Inst. de jur. nat. Gent. & civil. l. 9. D. de Just.

units.la: Iust. & jur. Duaren. h. Revard. Varior. l. 1. cap. 1. Et est jus hominum, alicujus populi, vel unius aut alterius civitatis proprium. Idque vel in quantum eo jure tanquam suo civitas quæque utitur; quod in eam sit receptum. §. 2. Inst. Iur. nat. Gent. civil. Vel in quantum aliquid juris quæque civitas sibi constituit. §. 1. Inst. eod. Illud in totum ex naturali & gentium jure desumtum est; hoc cum quopiam additamento. Ut hic expiodenda nonnullorum distinctio. qui volunt jus civile aliud esse merum, aliud mixtum: cum quod esset juris civilis meri, mera esset injuria, utpote quæ nec ratione nec ratiocinatione humanâ niteretur. DD. ad. l. 6. D. Iust. & jur. Boer. class. 1. disp. 2. num. 15. 16. 17.
units.tr: Iust. & jur. Duaren. h. Revard. Varior. l. 1. cap. 1. It is the law of men, peculiar to some people, or to one or another state. This is so either inasmuch as each state uses that law as its own, because it has been received into it (§. 2. Inst. Iur. nat. Gent. civil.), or inasmuch as each state has established for itself some part of law (§. 1. Inst. eod.). The former has been taken entirely from the law of nature and of nations; the latter with some addition. Here the distinction of some writers must be set aside, who want civil law to be one thing pure and another mixed. For what was purely civil law would be pure injustice, since it would rest on neither reason nor human reasoning. DD. ad. l. 6. D. Iust. & jur. Boer. class. 1. disp. 2. num. 15. 16. 17.

units.la: 2. Ubi quæsitum, an omne jus civile mutabile? Resp. licet id velint nonnulli, idque ad oppositionem juris naturalis, & gentium secundævi, quod dicitur esse immutabile; ideoque jus civile positivum appellent; contrarium tamen statuendum, videtur. Et quia non omne jus positivum est mutabile: cum uti ex ante dictis patet, etiam jus gentiu primævum, suo modo positivum esse dicatur. Et quia non omne jus civile origine est positivum, licet assumptione & comprobatione posset dici tale. Unde non sine distinctione hæc quæstio expediri poterit. Aut igitur jus civile est, quod simpliciter ex jure natu-ræ ræ desumptum in civitatem est receptum; & est immutabile. Aut est tale, quod civitas ipsa sibi constituit, juri naturali aliquid addendo, vel detrahendo; & mutari quandoque poterit. Non tamen sine gravi causâ: quod omnis mutatio sit periculosa, atque reipublicæ præjudiciosa: Arg. §. 1. 2. & 11. Inst. jur. nat. Gent. civil. l. 6. D. Just. & Jur. l. 2. D de Const. Princip. Befold. ad l. 6. D. Just. & jur. n. 1. vid. Zoes. h. tit. n. 48. ex parte dissentientem. ut & Boerum classf. 1. disp. 2. n 18.
units.tr: 2. The question arises whether all civil law is changeable. I answer: although some wish this, and so set it against the law of nature and of nations, which they say is unchangeable, and therefore call civil law positive law, the contrary seems to be the case. For not all positive law is changeable, since, as is clear from what was said above, the primitive law of nations is also said to be positive in its own way. And not all civil law is positive in origin, although by adoption and confirmation it could be called so. Hence this question can be settled only with a distinction. Either civil law is that which has been taken simply from the law of nature and received into the state, and it is unchangeable; or it is that which the state itself has established, adding to or subtracting from the law of nature, and this can at some time be changed. Yet not without a serious cause, since every change is dangerous and prejudicial to the commonwealth. Arg. §. 1. 2. & 11. Inst. jur. nat. Gent. civil. l. 6. D. Just. & Jur. l. 2. D de Const. Princip. Befold. ad l. 6. D. Just. & jur. n. 1. vid. Zoes. h. tit. n. 48. ex parte dissentientem. ut & Boerum classf. 1. disp. 2. n 18.

units.la: 3. Verum ut eundem servem ordinem, quem in explicatione juris naturæ & gentiū adhibui, examinabo, quænam juri civili sint adscribenda? Ubi præ notandum, quandoque aliquid dici juris civilis privative, in quantum jus civile aliquod commodum aufert, quomodo servitus dici potest juris civilis. § 4. Inst. jur. Person. Quandoque approbative, in quantum, quod est juris naturalis probat; ut si pacto tribuat vim pariendi actionem; quod eo nomine legitimum appellatur. l. 6. D. de Pactis. Quandoque dispositive, dum jus civile alicui negotio peculiarem formam, aut differentiam specificam, aut integram naturam tribuit.
units.tr: 3. But, to keep the same order that I observed in explaining the law of nature and of nations, I shall examine which things are to be ascribed to civil law. Here it must be noted that something is sometimes called civil law privatively, inasmuch as civil law takes away some advantage; in this way servitude can be called civil law. § 4. Inst. jur. Person. Sometimes it is called approbative, inasmuch as it confirms what belongs to the law of nature, as when it gives a pact the force of producing an action; such a pact is called lawful on this account. l. 6. D. de Pactis. Sometimes it is called dispositive, when civil law gives a transaction a particular form, or a specific difference, or its whole nature.

units.la: Quo sensu postremo inquiritur, Num stipulatio, seu verborū obligatio juri civili sit annumeranda? Quod affirmandum. Licet enim negari vix posset, quin in genere sit juris gentium,quia conventionibus annumeratur.l. 1. §. 3 junct. l. 5. & 6. D. de Pactis. Ejus tamen differentia est juris civilis; ut cujus propria ratio in eo consistit, quod solennis & congrua oporteat esse rogatio, & responsio subsequens; id quod ita, uti apud Romanos obtinebat, gentibus erat incognitum §. 1. Inst. v. obligat. §. 9. Inst. de Action. Ejusdem juris est Acceptilatio propter peculiarem suam formam, quod sit contra veritatem dissolvendae obligationis modus. l. 19, §. 1. D. Accept. l. 13. l. 107. D. solut. Zoes. D. de Just. & jur. n. 44.
units.tr: In this last sense the question is asked whether stipulation, or the obligation by words, is to be reckoned among civil law. This must be affirmed. For although it could hardly be denied that in general it belongs to the law of nations, since it is counted among agreements (l. 1. §. 3 junct. l. 5. & 6. D. de Pactis.), its distinctive character nevertheless belongs to civil law; for its proper nature consists in this, that the question must be solemn and fitting, and the answer must follow. This, as it obtained among the Romans, was unknown to the nations (§. 1. Inst. v. obligat. §. 9. Inst. de Action.). Acceptilation belongs to the same law, on account of its peculiar form, since it is a mode of dissolving an obligation which is contrary to the truth (l. 19, §. 1. D. Accept. l. 13. l. 107. D. solut. Zoes. D. de Just. & jur. n. 44.).

units.la: 4. An itidem Testamenti factio, Tutela, Nuptiae, Patria potestas, Actus legitimi, Haereditas, Usucapio, juri civili accensebuntur. Id utique dicendum videtur. Argum. Init. Inst. de Testam. Ordin. l. 4. D. qui Testament. fac. poss. Argum. l. 7. D. de legat. 1. §. 2. Inst. de Tutel. l. 1. D. eod. Init. & §. pen. Inst. de Nupt. l. 19. l. 24. D. de Statu hom. §. 2. Inst. de Patria potest. l. 3. D. qui sui vel alien. jur. l. 11. D. liber. & posthum. hared. l. 77. D. de Regul. jur. ibidem Faber in Comm. Cicer. Orat. Pro Cecinn. Init. Inst. de Usuc. l. 1. D. eod. junct. l. 14. D. Condiction. Indeb.
units.tr: 4. Likewise, the power to make a will, guardianship, marriage, paternal power, legal acts, inheritance, and usucapion would seem to be reckoned under civil law. This is certainly to be said. Argument: Init. Inst. de Testam. Ordin. l. 4. D. qui Testament. fac. poss. Argum. l. 7. D. de legat. 1. §. 2. Inst. de Tutel. l. 1. D. eod. Init. & §. pen. Inst. de Nupt. l. 19. l. 24. D. de Statu hom. §. 2. Inst. de Patria potest. l. 3. D. qui sui vel alien. jur. l. 11. D. liber. & posthum. hared. l. 77. D. de Regul. jur. ibidem Faber in Comm. Cicer. Orat. Pro Cecinn. Init. Inst. de Usuc. l. 1. D. eod. junct. l. 14. D. Condiction. Indeb.

units.la: 5. Verum unde cognosci poterit indubitanter, aliquem actum juris esse civilis? An quia non nisi inter cives Romanos fieri poterat? Id quod videtur admittendum secundum Boet. comment. l. 3. In Topic. Cicer. Ut tamen hinc male ex adverso colligatur nihil posse fieri inter extraneos, quod juris sit civilis. l. 17. D. de Pœn. An itidem, quia nonnisi lingua Latina celebrari potest? Quod affirmandum. Olim enim in stipulationibus ut etiam in decretis judicialibus interponendis, nonnisi Latinâ linguâ usi fuerunt. l. 48. D. de Re judic. Et legatum Græce scriptum non valebat, licet valeret fideicommissum. Ulp. tit. 25. de fideic. Paul. 3. Sent. tit. 4. §. ex his. Cujac. ibid. Postmodum tamen, quæ sunt juris civilis, etiam aliâ linguâ celebrari poterant. Arg. §. 1. Inst. verb. Obl. l. 8. in sin. D. Accept. Cujac. in l. 1. §. 5. D. verb. obligat. Henric. Ernst. Cathol. jur. c. 10. vid. Montan. de tutel. c. 6. n. 20. & seqq.
units.tr: 5. But how can it be known with certainty that some act belongs to civil law? Is it because it could be done only between Roman citizens? This seems to be admitted, according to Boet. comment. l. 3. In Topic. Cicer. Yet it does not follow, from the opposite, that nothing done between foreigners can belong to civil law (l. 17. D. de Pœn.). Or is it because it can be performed only in the Latin language? This must be affirmed. For formerly they used only the Latin language in stipulations, as also in interposing judicial decrees (l. 48. D. de Re judic.). A legacy written in Greek was not valid, although a trust (fideicommissum) was valid (Ulp. tit. 25. de fideic. Paul. 3. Sent. tit. 4. §. ex his. Cujac. ibid.). Afterwards, however, those things which belong to civil law could also be performed in another language (Arg. §. 1. Inst. verb. Obl. l. 8. in sin. D. Accept. Cujac. in l. 1. §. 5. D. verb. obligat. Henric. Ernst. Cathol. jur. c. 10. vid. Montan. de tutel. c. 6. n. 20. & seqq.).

units.la: CAPUT IV.
units.tr: CHAPTER IV.

units.la: 1. Jus civile, secundum excellentiam, quid signet?
units.tr: 1. What does civil law signify in the pre-eminent sense?

units.la: 2. Eius divisio traditur.
units.tr: 2. Its division is set out.

units.la: 3. Quod portiones juris scripti?
units.tr: 3. What are the parts of written law?

units.la: 4. Utrum Responsa Jurisconsultorum jus faciant?
units.tr: 4. Do the responses of the jurists make law?

units.la: 5. Utrum Prætorum edictâ?
units.tr: 5. Do the edicts of the praetors make law?

units.la: 6. Utrum res judicata?
units.tr: 6. Does a thing adjudged make law?

units.la: 7. Utrum sententi a à Principe lata?
units.tr: 7. Does a sentence pronounced by the Prince make law?

units.la: 8. Utrum communis opinio Doctorum?
units.tr: 8. Does the common opinion of the doctors make law?

units.la: 1. HActenus per compendium præmisi, quæ spectabant jus in genere, ejusque divisiones. Ut ad propositum perveniam, juris civilis danda erit divisio. Quod secundum excellentiam jus Romanum, jus Cæsareum, Justinianæum, designat. Negandum tamen non est, quin etiam illud jus, quod post imperatorem Justinianum alii imperatores condiderunt, jus Cæsareum, denominari possit. Quale jus est, lex Conradi, Constitutiones Lotharii & Friederici imperatorum. Quarum nonnullæ in codice Justinianæo, aliæ in libris feudorum conspiciuntur. Quales etiam sunt constitutiones in imperio Romano-Germanico, à Goldasto editæ; quales imperii recessus. Mihi vero jus civile in genere accipitur, prout antea definiebatur.
units.tr: 1. Hitherto I have set out briefly what concerned law in general and its divisions. To come to my purpose, a division of civil law must be given. In the pre-eminent sense, civil law designates the Roman law, the Caesarean law, the Justinianic law. Yet it must not be denied that the law which the emperors after Justinian enacted may also be called Caesarean law. Such law is the law of Conrad and the constitutions of the emperors Lothar and Frederick. Some of these are found in the Justinianic code, others in the books of feuds. Such also are the constitutions of the Roman-German empire edited by Goldast, and the recesses of the empire. For my part, civil law is taken in the general sense, as it was defined above.

units.la: 2. Etiam sumptum duplex est; vel commune, vel particulare, municipale, seu statutarium appellatum. Quod est jus alicujus populi, sive à populo sit inventum, sive secundum jus omnium hominum receptum in civitatem. l. 9. D. Just. & Jur. Hoc est alicujus Provinciæ vel municipii proprium. Utrumque vel est sanctio, vel jus sine sanctione. Sanctio, nihil aliud est, quam jus simul ac semel ab eo latum, qui suprema gaudet potestate, vel qui juris condendi potestatem à suprema nactus est potestate. Jus sine sanctione est, vel æquitas, vel consuetudo. Ut bic hic explodenda veniat plerorumque divisio juris in scriptum, & non scriptum. Quasi illud sit, quod publicâ auctoritate in scripturam est redactum; hoc non item. Neque enim scriptura spectat essentiam ullius juris. Cum nihil interfit scriptæ sint leges, an non scriptæ, teste Arist. 10. Ethic. cap. 9. Ut per jus scriptum nihil aliud intelligi debeat, quam sanctio, seu jus latum. Scribere enim antiquitus designabat ferre; unde jus scriptum nihil aliud, quam lex; quæ simulac lata est, jus facit. §. 4. 5. 6. Inst. de Jur. nat. Gent. & civ. l. 1. D. Const. Princ. l. 32. §. 1. D. de legibus. Bodin. in jur. Univ. distr. Wurmser. Nucl. jur contr. l. 1. tit. 2. contr. 3: ibidem que multi citati. Besold. ad l. 6. n. 2. D. de Just. & jure; ibidemque DD. allegati. Ernst. Cathol. Jur. c. 12.
units.tr: 2. Civil law, taken in the general sense, is also twofold: either common, or particular, called municipal or statutory. The latter is the law of some people, whether it was devised by the people or received into the state according to the law of all men (l. 9 D. Just. & Jur.). It is the proper law of some province or municipality. Each of these is either a sanction or law without sanction. A sanction is nothing other than law enacted once and for all by one who enjoys supreme power, or who has received the power of making law from supreme power. Law without sanction is either equity or custom. Hence the division of law by most people into written and unwritten is to be dismissed here, as if the former were what has been committed to writing by public authority and the latter not. For writing does not touch the essence of any law, since it makes no difference whether laws are written or unwritten, as Aristotle testifies (Ethic. 10, c. 9). So by written law nothing else should be understood than sanction, or law enacted. For to write designated in antiquity to bring forward, so written law is nothing other than statute, which makes law as soon as it is enacted (§. 4. 5. 6. Inst. de Jur. nat. Gent. & civ.; l. 1 D. Const. Princ.; l. 32 §. 1 D. de legibus; Bodin. in jur. Univ. distr.; Wurmser. Nucl. jur contr. l. 1 tit. 2 contr. 3, and the many cited there; Besold. ad l. 6 n. 2 D. de Just. & jure, and the doctors alleged there; Ernst. Cathol. Jur. c. 12).

units.la: 5. Juris scripti seu potius sanctionis ut erat jus commune & quidem Principale; & quidem in Republica liberâ, tres sunt species; lex in specie, quod est populi jussum; plebis scitum, jussum plebis; Senatusconsultum constitutio Senatus. Quod jus triplex, præter consuetudinem, quæ erat jus non scriptum, in Romanâ obtinuit republicâ, antequam ea ad Monarchicum statum translata fuit. Quo sensu dixit Modestinus, one ne jus aut consensus fecit, intellige populi aut plebis, aut necessitas constituit, supple, senatusconsulta, aut firmavit consuetudo, quod accipe de jure non scripto. l. 40. D. de leg. Cujac. l. 18. Observ. c. 16. Bocer. class. 1. disp. 3. n. 11. ex parte dissentiens, Besold. ad l. 6. D. Just. & jur. n. 2. vid Bodin. 1. de Republ. 10. Hottom. ad § Senatus. inst. jur. nat. Joh. Sarius Samoszius de Senat. Popul. Romān. libr. 2. p. 6. & pass. Althus. dicajol. libr. 1. c. 14. n. 15. & c. 15.
units.tr: 5. Of written law, or rather of sanction, there were three kinds that were common law and indeed principal law in a free republic: the lex in the proper sense, which is the command of the people; the plebiscite, the command of the plebs; and the senatus consultum, the constitution of the Senate. These three kinds of law, besides custom, which was unwritten law, held sway in the Roman republic before it was transferred to a monarchical state. In this sense Modestinus said: "Neither law nor the consent of the people made it" (understand of the people or the plebs), "or necessity established it" (supply: senatus consulta), "or custom confirmed it", which is to be taken of unwritten law (l. 40 D. de leg.; Cujac. l. 18 Observ. c. 16; Bocer. class. 1 disp. 3 n. 11, partly dissenting; Besold. ad l. 6 D. Just. & jur. n. 2; see Bodin. 1 de Republ. 10; Hottom. ad §. Senatus, Inst. jur. nat.; Joh. Sarius Samoszius de Senat. Popul. Romān. libr. 2 p. 6 and passim; Althus. dicaiol. libr. 1 c. 14 n. 15 and c. 15).

units.la: 4. Quid itaque de Responsis Jurisconsultorum erit judicandum? Respondeo, non sunt praecise juris partes aut species. Sanctiones enim non sunt; quia non latae ab eo, qui suprema gaudet potestate. Neque etiam ante Justinianum erant jus non scriptum: uti nonnulli hic somniant, quia non erant consuetudo, ut juris nomen non mereantur. Idque vel inde colligitur, quod judicibus quibus responsa sua mittebant jurisconsulti, quandoque etiam ab iis recedere fuerit permissum, licet non facile, non temere. Non dubium enim, quin quandoque uterque litigantium pro se habuerit cujusdam jurisconsulti responsum, ut alterutrum a judice oportuerit fuisse neglectum. Argum. l. 2. §. 47. D. de Origin. jur. Hottom. ad. §. 8. Inst. de jur. nat. Gent. & civ. vid. hic Besold. ad l. 7. & 8. D. de Just. & jur. Bocer. class. 1. disp. 3. n. 32. Zoes. D. de Just. & jur. n. 62. vid. Merend. jur. contr. l. 2 c. 4.
units.tr: 4. What then is to be judged of the responses of the jurists? I answer: they are not precisely parts or species of law. For they are not sanctions, since they were not enacted by one who enjoys supreme power. Nor, as some here dream, were they unwritten law before Justinian, since they were not custom and so do not deserve the name of law. This is gathered even from the fact that judges, to whom jurists sent their responses, were sometimes permitted to depart from them, though not easily and not rashly. For there is no doubt that sometimes each of the litigants held the response of some jurist in his favour, so that one of the two must have been neglected by the judge (Argum. l. 2 §. 47 D. de Origin. jur.; Hottom. ad §. 8 Inst. de jur. nat. Gent. & civ.; see here Besold. ad l. 7 & 8 D. de Just. & jur.; Bocer. class. 1 disp. 3 n. 32; Zoes. D. de Just. & jur. n. 62; see Merend. jur. contr. l. 2 c. 4).

units.la: 5. Quid de Edictis Magistratuum, de jure honorario statuendum erit? Resp. Quod Praetorem spectat, certum est, eum olim non condendi, verum dicendi tantum habuisse auctoritatem, l. 2. §. 27 D de Orig. jur. Postmodum ut edicta conderet, quae prius annua, deinde perpetua, ei fuit permissum. §. 1. Inst. Perp. & Tempor. Act. Quae licet non modicam juris habuerint auctoritatem. §. 10. Inst. de jur. nat Gent. & civil. eoque nomine quandoque leges appellarentur: non tamen praecise leges constitutas abrogare, ei fuit permissum. Qui non juris conditor, sed disceptator, sed custos, fuit appellatus; etiam viva vox civitatis. §. 7. Instit. de jur. nat. Gent. civil. l. 7, 8. D. de Just. & jur. l. 12. §. 2. D. bonor. Poss. Bachov. ad §. 7. Inst. jur. nat. Gent. Ernst. Catholic. jur. c. 16. vid. accurate Anton. Merend. tom. 2. juris controv. libr. 12. c. 23.
units.tr: 5. What must be determined about the edicts of magistrates, the honorary law? Answer: as regards the praetor, it is certain that he once had not the authority of making law but only of declaring it (l. 2 §. 27 D. de Orig. jur.). Afterwards he was permitted to make edicts, at first annual, then perpetual (§. 1 Inst. Perp. & Tempor. Act.). Although these had no small authority of law, and on that account were sometimes called laws, yet it was not permitted to him to abrogate laws precisely enacted (§. 10 Inst. de jur. nat. Gent. & civil.). He was called not the maker of law but its arbiter, its guardian; he was also the living voice of the state (§. 7 Instit. de jur. nat. Gent. civil.; l. 7, 8 D. de Just. & jur.; l. 12 §. 2 D. bonor. Poss.; Bachov. ad §. 7 Inst. jur. nat. Gent.; Ernst. Catholic. jur. c. 16; see carefully Anton. Merend. tom. 2 juris controv. libr. 12 c. 23).

units.la: 6. Quid statuendum de rebus judicatis, an & illae jus faciant? Resp. Licet Tullius in Topic. juris scripti speciebus addiderit res judicatas; unde & praejudicia sumebantur, quae Asconio Pediano erant decreta; quae judicaturis exemplum adferrent, quod sequerentur. Quia tamen nullibi inter juris species enumerantur, ubi tamen de juris portionibus agitur. l. 7. D. just. & jur. Et non exemplis, sed legibus est judicandum. l. 12, D. off. Praef, inferendum erit, eas juris auctoritatem non habere. l. 13. Cod. de sent. & interloc. omnium judic. Ratio etiam id ipsum suadet: eo quod facti minima mutatio & diversam versam sententiam deposcat. Conn, 1. comm. jur. c. 15. n. 6. Pac. 1. Cent. Enant. quaest. 16. Sand. Praefat. ad decis.Frif. Pacius 1. Antin. 19. dis. Mynsing. ad §. Responsa. instit. jure natur. gent. & civil. Ex parte Speckh. centur. 2. classi. 4. q. 39. Dist nonnulli inter nos Pragmatici, qui juris debita cognitione destituti, tantam rotarum decisionibus auctoritatem tribuunt ut eas, pro Pythag. αὐτὸς ἔφα, habeant. Cum cogitandum fuisset rotam quandoque rotare, & praejudicia Cameralia invicem saepe adversari. Besold. ad l. 7. 8. D. justit. & jur. n. 7. Aliud forte de stylo curiae dicendum, quod habeat vim legis. Arg. §. ult. Inst. de Satisdat. quo refero l. 38. D. de legibus. Coras. ad l. 25. D. stat. homin. Hackel. illustr. 1. thes. 13. Speckhan. centur. 2. classi. 4 quaest. 39 Groenw. de ll. Abrog. ad l. ult. Cod. de legibus.
units.tr: 6. What must be determined about things adjudged: do they also make law? Answer: although Tully in the Topics added things adjudged to the species of written law, whence precedents were also taken, which Asconius Pedianus decreed, offering an example to those about to judge, which they would follow, yet since they are nowhere enumerated among the species of law, although the parts of law are treated there (l. 7 D. Just. & jur.), and judgment must be made not by examples but by laws (l. 12 D. off. Praef.), it must be inferred that they do not have the authority of law (l. 13 Cod. de sent. & interloc. omnium judic.). Reason too suggests this same thing, since the slightest change of fact calls for a different and contrary sentence (Conn. 1 comm. jur. c. 15 n. 6; Pac. 1 Cent. Enant. quaest. 16; Sand. Praefat. ad decis. Frif.; Pacius 1 Antin. 19 dis.; Mynsing. ad §. Responsa, Inst. jure natur. gent. & civil.). On the other side, Speckh. centur. 2 classi. 4 q. 39. Some of our Pragmatici, lacking due knowledge of law, dissent, and grant such authority to the decisions of the Rota that they hold them, in the words of the Pythagorean, "he himself said it" [αὐτὸς ἔφα], whereas they should have considered that the wheel sometimes turns, and that Camber precedents often conflict with one another (Besold. ad l. 7, 8 D. justit. & jur. n. 7). Perhaps something different must be said of the practice of the court, which has the force of law (Arg. §. ult. Inst. de Satisdat.), to which I refer l. 38 D. de legibus; Coras. ad l. 25 D. stat. homin.; Hackel. illustr. 1 thes. 13; Speckhan. centur. 2 classi. 4 quaest. 39; Groenw. de ll. Abrog. ad l. ult. Cod. de legibus.

units.la: 7. Aliud tamen dicendum, de sententia à Principe latâ. l. ult. in init. Cod de legibus. Quo de Moribus non immerito retuleris sententiam in revisione latam.
units.tr: 7. Something else, however, must be said about a sentence pronounced by the Prince. l. ult. in init. Cod. de legibus. On this point one may not unreasonably cite also the sentence given on revision.

units.la: 8. Quid igitur sentiendum de communi doctorum opinione? An & illa ius faciet? Ita quidem censent nonnulli, qui eandem juris auctoritatem nostri tempo is DD. tribuunt, quam habebant responsa veterum Jurisconsultorum. Wurmser. l. 1 tit. 2. contr. 6. ibidemque innumeri DD. Bocer. classi. 1. disp. 3.
units.tr: 8. What, then, is to be thought of the common opinion of the doctors? Does that too make law? Some indeed hold that it does, those who grant to the doctors of our own time the same authority in law that the responses of the ancient jurists once had. Wurmser. l. 1 tit. 2. contr. 6. ibidemque innumeri DD. Bocer. classi. 1. disp. 3.

units.la: n. 34. n. 34. Besold, ad l. 7. n. 6. D. de legibus. In tantum etiam, ut Judicem litem suam facere velint, si in judicando à communi & recepta deflectat opinione. Sichard ad Auth. Sacramenta puberum. Cod. si aav. vend. Verum quia sine jure loquuntur quotquot id statuunt, contraria sententia erit amplectenda. Tenetur enim judex in judicando sequi, quod legibus & moribus est proditum; quo nemo retulerit communem opinionem, qui saepe communis quispiam error est, adeoque juris nomen non meretur. Init. Inst. de Offic. judic. Novell. 82. §. pen. Arg. l. 1. §. sed neque. 5. Cod. Vet. jur. Enucl. Consentiunt Zas. 2. Sing. Resp. 1. Altiat. 1. Praes. §1. n. 3. Joh. Vuud. 1. qu. 10. Coras. ad l. unic. D. de offic. quaest. Pinhard. in comm. ad instit. tit. quod cum eo qui in alien potestat. §. 8. n. 6. Cubach. in sin. libri Brocardicorum. Hunn. ad Treutl. vol. poster. disp. 23. thes. 5. p. 390. Anton. Matth. disp. de judic. 11. n. 4. Nebelkra decis. 1. per totum.
units.tr: n. 34. n. 34. Besold, on l. 7, n. 6, D. de legibus. They even go so far as to want a judge to make the suit his own if, in deciding, he departs from the common and accepted opinion. Sichard on Auth. Sacramenta puberum, Cod. si adv. vend. But since all who maintain this speak without law, the contrary view is to be adopted. For a judge is bound in deciding to follow what has been handed down by laws and customs; and no one would call a common opinion that, since it is often some common error and so does not deserve the name of law. Init. Inst. de Offic. judic.; Novell. 82, §. pen.; Arg. l. 1, §. sed neque, 5. Cod. Vet. jur. Enucl. They agree: Zasius, 2 Sing. Resp. 1; Altiat. 1 Praes. §1 n. 3; Joh. Vuud. 1 qu. 10; Coras. on l. unic. D. de offic. quaest.; Pinhard, in comm. on Instit. tit. quod cum eo qui in alien potestat. §. 8 n. 6; Cubach. in the end of the book of Brocardica; Hunn. on Treutl. vol. poster. disp. 23 thes. 5 p. 390; Anton. Matth. disp. de judic. 11 n. 4; Nebelkra, decis. 1, throughout.

units.la: SECTIO SECUNDA
units.tr: SECTIO SECUNDA

units.la: CAPUT PRIMUM.
units.tr: CAPUT PRIMUM.

units.la: 1. In statu monarchico tantum Princeps jus facit.
units.tr: 1. In a monarchical state the Prince alone makes law.

units.la: 2. Lex regia multiplex.
units.tr: 2. The Royal Law is manifold.

units.la: 3. Ubi legis Regiae monumentum?
units.tr: 3. Where is the monument of the Royal Law?

units.la: 4. U4. Utrum ea unquam fuerit lata?
units.tr: 4. Was it ever enacted?

units.la: 5. Lex Regia, non est jus Regium Hebraeorum.
units.tr: 5. The Royal Law is not the royal right of the Hebrews.

units.la: 6. Quo tempore lata sit lex Regia?
units.tr: 6. At what time was the Royal Law enacted?

units.la: 7. A quo ea fuerit lata?
units.tr: 7. By whom was it enacted?

units.la: 8. Quis finis legis Regiae?
units.tr: 8. What was the purpose of the Royal Law?

units.la: 9. Quae occasio? 10. 11. An si metus fuerit occasio, lex valeat? 12. Quale jus in Principem sit collatum? 13. An communicative, an abdicative? 14. An aliqua potestas penes Senatum? 15. An Princeps legibus solutus? 16. 17. Sensus legis Regiae explicatur.
units.tr: 9. What was its occasion? 10. 11. If fear was the occasion, is the law valid? 12. What kind of right was conferred upon the Prince? 13. Was it a communicative or an abdicative right? 14. Is any power retained by the Senate? 15. Is the Prince released from the laws? 16. 17. The meaning of the Royal Law is explained.

units.la: 1. JUs, quod in Republicâ libera obtinebat, triplex erat, Lex, plebiscitum, & consultum senatus. Neque enim aut edicta praetorum, aut prudentium, responsa jus erant absolute. Suo tamen modo jus appellabantur uti id paulo ante fuit ostensum. Illa in quantum non modicam obtinebant juris auctoritatem. Haec in quantum non facile ab eorum responsis judici recedere permissum erat. §. Responsa §. praetorum. Instit. jur. nat. Gent. Civil. l. pen. D. just. & jur. l. 40. D. leg. Postquam autem status reipublicae liberae, in Monarchicum fuit translatus, non-
units.tr: 1. The law (jus) that held sway in a free republic was of three kinds: statute (lex), plebiscite, and decree of the Senate. For neither the edicts of the praetors nor the responses of the jurists were law in the strict sense. Yet in their own way they were called law, as was shown a little earlier: the former because they carried no small authority of law, the latter because it was not permitted to depart easily from the responses of such men. (See the Institutes, the law of nature, nations and civil law; the last law in the Digest, de iustitia et iure; and Digest 1.40, de legibus.) But after the state of the free republic was transferred into a monarchy, nothing was law except the constitution of the Prince, since to him alone belongs the power of making a law and of interpreting it once made. But because all that power is said to have been transferred to the Prince by the Royal Law, therefore, before we treat of the Prince's constitutions, the nature of the Royal Law must be explained. And since this part of law is rather intricate, on account of the manifold opinions of disagreeing authors, I thought I would be doing a worthwhile thing if I first set out the various senses of the Royal Law. This is so that I do not seem obscure through an ambiguous use of the term, and so that the nature of the controversy may be made sufficiently plain.

units.la: [illegible, ~3 letters] nisi Principis constitutio jus erat; utpote cujus solius est legem ferre, latamque interpretari. Verum quia omnis illa potestas lege Regiâ in Principem dicitur translata ideo antequam agatur de Principis constitutionibus, Regiæ legis natura erit explicanda. Et quia hæc juris materia satis est intricata, propter dissentientium autorum opiniones multiplices, operæ precium me facturum existimavi, si primitus varias legis Regiæ acceptiones protulero. Ne aliter sub ambigua Legis Regiæ acceptione, obscurus esse videar, neque quis sit controversiæ status, innotescat satis.
units.tr: [illegible] except the Prince's constitution was law, since the power to make law and to interpret it belongs to him alone. But because all that power is said to have been transferred to the Prince by the Royal Law, the nature of that law must be explained before we treat the Prince's constitutions. And since this part of the law is quite intricate, on account of the many differing opinions of the authors, I have thought it worth the effort to set out first the various meanings of the Royal Law. Otherwise I might seem obscure under the ambiguous use of the term, and the point of the dispute would not be made sufficiently clear.

units.la: 2. Eam itaque intueor vel ut dicta regia ab autore, ut ita appellata à contentâ materiâ, id est à Rege, quod de Rege ejusque potestate agat. Neque hæ leges nobis erunt confundendæ, ut quæ multis modis discriminentur. Illa quippe non semper populi consensu lata est; hæc vero à ipso lata populo. Illa est, quam Rex tulit ad populum, & quidem super populo; hæc vero quam populus tulit super jure Regis. Sicut illâ designetur Regis in ipsum populum imperium; hâc populi in omnes potestas, etiam ante translationem ejus potestatis in ipsum Regem. De illâ lege Regiâ, seu potius Regiis legibus, numero plurali, in jure non semel fit mentio. Olim, manu Regiâ, id est, uti interpretor, lege, à Rege latâ, omnes gubernabantur. l. 2. §. 1. 2. §. 1. & §. 36. D. orig. jur. Et post regia leges dictæ, quas Reges tulerunt ad populum. l. 2. §. 2. D. eod. l. 2. D. Mortu. infer. Cujac. §. 1. ad tit. D. eod. Unde recte cecinit poeta libr. 1. Æneid.
units.tr: 2. I regard it, then, either as a royal law named after its author, or as named after its subject matter, that is, after the King, because it deals with the King and his power. These laws should not be confused with one another, since they differ in many respects. The former was not always passed with the consent of the people; the latter was passed by the people itself. The former is the law which the King brought to the people, and indeed over the people; the latter is the law which the people passed concerning the King's right. The former designates the King's command over the people itself; the latter, the power of the people over everyone, even before that power was transferred to the King himself. The Royal Law, or rather the royal laws in the plural, is mentioned more than once in the law. Formerly everyone was governed by royal hand, that is, as I interpret it, by a law brought in by the King: l. 2 §1, 2 §1 and §36 D. orig. jur. Afterwards, the laws which the Kings brought to the people were called royal laws: l. 2 §2 D. eod.; l. 2 D. Mortu. infer.; Cujac. §1 ad tit. D. eod. Whence the poet rightly sang in book 1 of the Aeneid:

units.la: Remo cum fratre QuirinusJura dabat :
units.tr: "With his brother Remus, Quirinus gave laws."

units.la: Etiam de Priamo in hanc sententiam libr. 7. Hoc Priami gestamen erat cum jura vocatis More daret populis. Neque obstant antecedentia verba Pomponii. in l. 2. Quod populus non lege certa nec certo jure uteretur, Id enim significat non legibus à populo latis, nec certo jure scripto, id est perpetuo & immutabili usum esse populum, quod vel indies Reges pro arbitrio suo jura utare potuerint, etiam id facere consueverint.
units.tr: Also, to the same effect, of Priam in book 7: "This was Priam's sceptre, when with it he gave laws to the summoned peoples, as was the custom." Nor do the preceding words of Pomponius in l. 2 stand in the way, where it is said that the people did not use a fixed law nor a certain right. For this means that the people did not live under laws passed by the people, nor under a certain written right, that is, one that is lasting and unchangeable; since the Kings could, day by day, rule by their own will and often did so.

units.la: Quæ vero Regia dicta est ab autore, potissimum jam explicandum. Quod ut fiat commodissime, eam secundum varia tempora considerabo : ut est Antiquissima, ut Media, ut Nova. Antiquissima lex Regia ab autore sic appellata, quæ lata est regnante Romulo, primo Romanorum rege; adeoque simul cum urbe nata. Hottom de leg pop Rom.
units.tr: The new is so named, which holds a place in the declining empire; it is therefore that law by which the absolute power is not so much transferred to the emperor, as his power is limited, and as it were held in check by bridles and reins, so that he may not do everything that pleases him. Such is that Imperial capitulation which holds a place in the German empire (Carpzov, de lege regia Germanorum, c. 1, n. 11).

units.la: Nova appellata, quæ in imperio declinante locum habet, adeoque ea erit, qua non tam potestas absoluta in imperatorem transfertur, quam quidem ejusdem potestas limitatur, adeoque tanquam frænis ac retinaculis sistitur, coercetur; ne illi id omne liceat, quod libuerit, Qualis est illa capitulatio Cæsarea, quæ in imperio Germanorum locum habet. Carpzov. de l. Reg. Germanor. c. 1. n. 11.
units.tr: The so-called new law is that which holds sway in a declining empire. It is the law by which the emperor's power is not so much transferred to him absolutely as limited, and, as it were, reined in and restrained, so that he may not do everything that pleases him. Such is that Imperial capitulation which holds a place in the German Empire. Carpzov. de l. Reg. Germanor. c. 1, n. 11.

units.la: Media dicta Regia ; non tantum, quod de Regno sive imperio Principis agat, sed etiam de potestate à Populo in Principem translatâ. §. 6. Instit. jur. nat. Gent. civ. l. 1. in init. D. Const. Princ. §. 7 D. concept. digest. Adeo ut sine fundamento pro lege Regiâ Remniam substituant Alciat. in l. bona civit. n. 1. D. verb. Sign. & dubitanter Coraf. 6. Misc. c. 8. n. 2.
units.tr: The so-called middle royal law; not only because it deals with the kingdom or empire of the Prince, but also with the power transferred from the People to the Prince. §6 Instit. jur. nat. gent. civ. l. 1 in init. D. Const. Princ.; §7 D. concept. digest. So much so that without foundation they substitute the Remniam for the royal law: Alciat. in l. bona civit. n. 1 D. verb. Sign.; and doubtfully Coraf. 6 Misc. c. 8, n. 2.

units.la: Hæc eadem dicta, lex Augusti, l. 14 D. Manumiss. Augustum Privilegium. l. unic. §. antepen. Cod. Cad. Toll. Lex imperii, l.
units.tr: The same law is also called the law of Augustus, l. 14 D. Manumiss.; the Augustan privilege, l. unic. §. antepen. Cod. Cad. Toll.; the law of empire, l.

units.la: 2. Cod. Testam. Eamque sic ab initio dictam fuisse, non regiam, idque ad invidiam nominis evitandam, probabiliter colligitur ex illo Dion. l. 53. Ubi ita latinè: Cæsar quamvis Romuli nomen vehementer appetebat, tamen quum sentiret hinc se suspectum, affectati Regni fieri, eo omisso, Augustus, quasi hominis natura amplior ipse cognominatus est. Et post. Ad huius itaque modum ratione eorum nominum quæ in populari civitatis statu usurpantur, omnem totius rei publicæ potestatem accipiunt: ac regiam etiam, nisi quod invidiam nominis vitant. Quo cum facit illud Tacit. Annal. 1. non regno, nec dictatura, sed Principis nomine constitutam fuisse Rempublicam. & Annal. 3. Ti-berius berius tribunitiam Drusso petebat. Id summi fastigii vocabulum Augustus repperit, ne regis aut dictatoris nomen assumeret, ac tamen appellatione aliquâ cætera Imperia præmineret.
units.tr: 2 Cod. Testam. That it was originally so called, and not the royal law, in order to avoid the odium of the name, is probably gathered from that passage of Dio, l. 53. There, in Latin: Caesar, although he greatly desired the name of Romulus, yet, perceiving that he would thereby be suspected of aiming at kingship, dropped it, and Augustus, as a more exalted name, was given to him as a cognomen. And afterwards: In the same way, by the names used in a popular state, they take every power of the whole commonwealth, and the royal power too, except that they avoid the odium of the name. With this agrees what Tacitus says, Annals 1: the commonwealth was established not by the name of king or dictator, but of Prince. And Annals 3: Ti-berius sought the tribunician power for Drusus. Augustus devised this title of highest rank, so that he would not assume the name of king or dictator, and yet would still surpass the other magistracies by some designation.

units.la: 3. Hujus Regiæ legis verba, æneæ tabulæ (non marmoreæ, uti nonnulli censuerunt) incisa, non nisi secundum partem ultimam, Georg. Fabric. Antiq. 1. quam imperitum vulgus quondam Pontii Pilati sententiam continere credidit, Anton. August. dial. Antiq. 4. In Basilicâ Lateranensi extare communiter receptum Anton. August. d. l. Hottom. de Leg. pop. Rom. Licet verosimilior Eccardi opinio, qui disp. sing. de leg. Reg. hoc legis Regiæ monumentum è Laterano in Capitolium translatum, ibidemque etiamnum hodie extare, & asservari scribit.
units.tr: 3. The words of this Royal Law, engraved on bronze tablets (not marble, as some have thought), were, according to Georg. Fabric. Antiq. 1, known only in their last part, which the ignorant common people once believed contained the sentence of Pontius Pilate. Anton. August. dial. Antiq. 4. It is commonly held that it stands in the Lateran Basilica, Anton. August. d. l.; Hottom. de Leg. pop. Rom. Yet the opinion of Eccard is more probable, who in disp. sing. de leg. Reg. writes that this monument of the Royal Law was transferred from the Lateran to the Capitol, and that it is still there today and preserved.

units.la: 4. Circa hanc Regiam legem quæsitum, in principio, num ea unquam fuerit lata? Respondeo, licet Connan. 1. comm. 16. aliique statuant, eam latam à populo nunquam suisse, verum à postremis imperatoribus, ut sic aliquam suæ Tyrannidi legem obtenderent: at tamen quia non facilè, historiarum fides ut & auctoritates jurisconsultorum, in corpore juris occurrentes, sunt convellendæ, nisi manifestioribus probationibus contra veritatem multa scripsisse convincantur, non video cur non eam legem quondam latam fuisse sit admittendum. §. 6. Institit. jur. nat. Gent. civil. l. 2. §. 11. D. Orig. jur. l. 1. in init. init. D. Constit. Princip. §. 6. de D. Concept. l. unic. D. de off. Præf. Prætor. Strabo l. 17. Dion. lib. 53. Ammian. Marcell. lib. 14. p. 12. cujus aliquot loca postmodum proferenda; neque enim in jure sine Historicorum autoritate decidenda quæstio, quæ potissimum historicâ nititur fide. Argum. §. 2. Instit. empt. vendit. Nec quicquam obstat, quod Historici illius temporis legis Regiæ mentionem nullam faciant, uti qui contrarium tenent, asserunt. Et quia, inter illos nonnulli haud latenter, illius legis contentum expiimunt. Et quia, id affirmant tot fide digni jurisconsulti, qui ævo Augusti proximi fuere. Et quia argumentum ab autoritate desumptum, non concludit negativè. Neque enim sequitur, Suetonius Tranquillus, aliique non scribunt Legem Regiam fuisse latam: ergo lata non est. Præterquam quod nemo illorum auctorum, qui tacent, neget aut contradicat. Vid. in simili Discursum Rev. Parentis, de Transl. imper. à Græcis ad Francos. n. 6.
units.tr: 4. Regarding this Royal Law, the question arises at the outset whether it was ever enacted. I answer: although Connanus, 1 comm. 16, and others hold that it was never enacted by the people, but was later invented by the last emperors so as to put forward some law for their tyranny, nevertheless, since the testimony of the histories, as well as the authorities of the jurists found in the body of the law, are not to be overturned lightly, unless they are shown by clearer proofs to have written many things contrary to the truth, I do not see why it should not be admitted that this law was once enacted. §6 Instit. jur. nat. gent. civ.; l. 2 §11 D. orig. jur.; l. 1 in init. D. Const. Princip.; §6 de D. concept.; l. unic. D. de off. Praef. Praet.; Strabo l. 17; Dio lib. 53; Ammianus Marcellinus lib. 14 p. 12, some passages of which shall be cited later; for the question, which rests chiefly on historical evidence, is not to be decided in law without the authority of the historians. Argument from §2 Instit. empt. vend. Nor is there anything to stop us in the fact that the historians of that time make no mention of the Royal Law, as those who hold the contrary assert. For some of them, not obscurely, set out the content of that law. And because so many jurists of high credit, who lived close to the age of Augustus, affirm it. And because an argument drawn from authority does not prove a negative. For it does not follow: Suetonius Tranquillus and others do not write that the Royal Law was enacted; therefore it was not enacted. Besides, none of those authors who are silent would deny or contradict it. On a similar point, see the discourse of the Reverend Father, On the translation of empire from the Greeks to the Franks, n. 6.

units.la: 5. Quæsitum amplius, Num quæ de lege Regiâ in jure dicuntur, potius ad jus Regium à Samuele propositum sint referenda? Ita quidem velit Vultejus, quem refutat Bulæus in disp. de Trib. Gener. jur. Præcept. n. 10. quod ea opinio nullo fundamento nitatur. Qua enim ratione lex Regia, cum jure Regio à Samuele descripto, confunderetur ? Cum sit probabile Romanos de illo jure Regio Samuelis, diu ante erectum principatum lato, ne quidem per somnium cogitasse. Praeterquam quod lex illa Regia Romanorum vere fuerit lex, cum jus Regium Samuelis, non lex, sed consuetudo, sed modus Regis sit nuncupandus. Sic enim vocabulum Mispath, quod in textu Hebraeo occurrit, 1 Sam. 8. v. 11. in aliis scripturae locis usurpatur. Nam 1. Sam. 2. verf. 13. improbata filiorum Eli consuetudo. Et 1. Sam. 27. verf. 11. fraudulentum Davidis factum, Mispath appellatur. Dissent. Tholos. de Republ. l. 24. c. 7. n. 1. Accedit, quod eveniente principatu, populum Romanum jus illud, de quo diu ante in Palaestina verba fecerat propheta Israeliticus, obligare nullo modo potuerit. Quid enim juris erat Judaeis, in illas Gentes quas nunquam subegerant? Cumque caeterae leges Israelitarum Romanum populum nunquam obligaverint, quo jure, haec regia lex cum obligaverit, non video: cum omnium legum in ordine ad obligationem, una sit ratio. Quid quod ne quidem nos obligent leges a Judaeis latae, qui tamen in Republica degimus Christiana; tantum abest, ut Romanis, & quidem Gentilibus, ea latae dicantur. Besold. ad tit. D. const. Princip. Amef. lib. 5. caf. confc. c. 1. 7. Zepp. leg. Mosaic. l. 1. c. 12.
units.tr: 5. A further question arises: whether what the law says about the Lex Regia should rather be referred to the royal right proposed by Samuel. Vultejus indeed thinks so, and Bulæus in disp. de Trib. Gener. jur. Præcept. n. 10. refutes him, on the ground that this opinion rests on no foundation. For on what reasoning would the Lex Regia be confused with the royal right described by Samuel? It is probable that the Romans never even dreamed of that royal right of Samuel, which was enacted long before the principate was established. Besides, the Roman royal law was truly a law, whereas the royal right of Samuel should be called not a law but a custom, or the manner of a king. For the word Mispath, which occurs in the Hebrew text at 1 Sam. 8. v. 11, is used in other places of Scripture. At 1 Sam. 2. v. 13 the custom of Eli's sons, which was disapproved, is so called, and at 1 Sam. 27. v. 11 David's deceitful deed is called Mispath. See Tholosanus, De republica, l. 24, c. 7, n. 1. Add that when the principate came, the Roman people could in no way be bound by that right, about which the Israelite prophet had spoken long before in Palestine. For what right did the Jews have over those nations which they had never subdued? And since the other laws of the Israelites never bound the Roman people, I do not see by what right this royal law could have bound them, since there is one reason for all laws in regard to obligation. Indeed, not even laws enacted by the Jews bind us, though we live in a Christian commonwealth; so far is it from being the case that they were enacted for the Romans, and for Gentiles at that. Besold. ad tit. D. const. Princip.; Amef. lib. 5. caf. confc. c. 1.; Zepp. leg. Mosaic. l. 1. c. 12.

units.la: 6. Verum non minor inter autores dissensus sensus est quando ea fuerit lata? Alii eam ad imperium Romuli referri posse censent, ut quo tempore alicui legi Regiæ locum fuisse ex Liv. l. 34. testatur Hottom. loc. cit. Verum ea sententia mihi videtur esse improbabilis. Cessavisset quippe ipsa lex Regia, imo in totum fuisset sublata, post sublatum vetustius regnum, sic ut quæ postmodum diceretur renovata, non tam esset revocata, cum non eadem, quam alia quæpiam lex, de novo condita.
units.tr: 6. But there is no less disagreement among authors about when it was enacted. Some think it can be referred to the reign of Romulus, since, as Hottom. loc. cit. testifies from Liv. l. 34., some law of the royal kind had force at that time. But this view seems to me improbable. The Lex Regia itself would have lapsed, indeed would have been wholly abolished, once the older kingdom was abolished; so that what was said afterwards to be renewed would not so much have been revoked as newly established, being no more the same law than any other law enacted afresh.

units.la: Alii, legibus antiquioribus de quibus Cicer. 3. de legibus, eam ferunt acceptam, quibus Consulibus idem jus quod Regibus videtur esse tributum. Verum & hoc perperam statuitur. Licet enim illis legibus dictum sit; Consules nemini parento: Attamen non id de populo, ad quem à Consulibus erat provocatio, quam de aliis magistratibus quibus Consules non superant, est accipiendum.
units.tr: Others, citing the older laws of which Cicer. 3. de legibus speaks, hold that it was taken from them, laws by which the same right seems to have been granted to the consuls as to the kings. But this too is wrongly asserted. For although it was said in those laws, Consules nemini parento ("let the consuls obey no one"), this must be understood of the people, to whom there was appeal from the consuls, and not of the other magistrates, over whom the consuls have no superiority.

units.la: Alii ante Augusti tempora, Julio Cæsare imperante, legem regiam latam fuisse tenent. Alii eam primitus, (inter quos est etiam Zas. ad. l. 1. D. const. Princ.) Vespasiani temporibus obtinuisse, statuunt. Verum cum illi omnes abunde historicorum autoritatibus refutentur, dicam, quid hic sentiam, idque multis testimoniis firmatum ibo. Id quidem verum est nec inficias ire possum, quod ante Augusti tempora legis Regiæ placita obtinuerint, eaque incæpta ferri, cum solus propemodum omnia pro lubitu administraret Julius Cæsar; nondum tamen ea lata, forte quia regis specie solus imperio potiri voluit Cæsar, quod tamen minus feliciter succeßit. Hoc ipsum satis innuunt Suetonii verba in Jul. Cæs. Unus ex eo tempore omnia in republicâ, ad arbitrium administravit: ut nonnulli urbanorum, cum quid per jocum testandi gratiâ signarent, non Cæsare & Bibulo, sed Julio & Cæsare actum scriberent, bis eundem proponentes, nomine atque cognomine. utque vulgo mox feruentur hi versus,
units.tr: Others hold that the Royal Law (lex regia) was passed before the time of Augustus, while Julius Caesar was in power. Others maintain that it first came into force in the time of Vespasian (among them is Zas. ad l. 1 D. const. Princ.). But since all of these views are abundantly refuted by the authority of the historians, I will state what I think and confirm it with many testimonies. It is true, and I cannot deny, that the provisions of the Royal Law came into effect before the time of Augustus, and that they were already being proposed, since Julius Caesar almost alone administered everything as he pleased. Yet the law had not yet been passed, perhaps because Caesar wanted to hold sole power under the appearance of a king, though this did not succeed well for him. The words of Suetonius in the Julius Caesar sufficiently hint at this: From that time on he alone managed everything in the republic at his pleasure, so that some of the city wits, when they wanted to jest by way of signing a will, wrote that the act was done not by Caesar and Bibulus but by Julius and Caesar, putting the same man down twice, with both name and surname. And as these verses were soon commonly circulated,

units.la: Non Bibulo quicquam nuper, sed Cæsare factum est:
units.tr: Non Bibulo quicquam nuper, sed Cæsare factum est: ("Nothing was lately done under Bibulus, but under Caesar.")

units.la: Nam Bibulo fieri consule nil memini.
units.tr: Nam Bibulo fieri consule nil memini. ("For I remember nothing being done while Bibulus was consul.")

units.la: Et illud, Novissime dubium an ipso volente, oblata pro rostris ab Antonio consule, regni insignia. Flor. lib. 4. c. 2. & Paterc. l. 1. Dion. libr. 44. Quæ forte, ratio, quod sub initium legis Regiæ, uti ea proflat, Julii Cæsaris facta sit mentio. Vid. eam editam apud Hottom. loc. cit.
units.tr: And that line: Novissime dubium an ipso volente, oblata pro rostris ab Antonio consule, regni insignia. ("Lastly, it is doubtful whether with his consent the insignia of kingship were offered on the rostra by the consul Antony.") Florus, book 4, c. 2; Paterculus, l. 1; Dio, book 44. Perhaps this is the reason why mention of Julius Caesar is made at the beginning of the Lex Regia, as it has been published. See it published in Hottom. loc. cit.

units.la: Etiam id lubens admittam eandem renovatam fuisse temporibus Vespasiani Clapm. lib. 2. c. 15. Arian. domin. Revera tamen & quidem solemniter demum fuit lata, Augusto imperante, idque eodem annuente, quo populo Romano esset gratior, velut per manus ab eo suscepto imperio. Florus. 4. c. 3. Guil. Onciac. quæst. jur. Phil. 26.
units.tr: I will also gladly admit that the same law was renewed in the times of Vespasian (Clapm. lib. 2. c. 15. Arian. domin.). Yet in truth it was enacted solemnly only under Augustus, with his consent, at the time when it would be more pleasing to the Roman people, as if the empire had been received from his hands. Florus. 4. c. 3. Guil. Onciac. quæst. jur. Phil. 26.

units.la: Id quod confirmatur partim auctoritate l. 14. in sin. D. Manumiss. ubi appellatur lex Augusti. Partim ratione, quia sub Augusto demum Reipublicæ forma mutata, & ad Monarchicum statum translata est, sic ut ipsi hæc concessa potestas, ut rempublicam solus administraret.
units.tr: This is confirmed partly by the authority of l. 14 in sin. D. Manumiss., where it is called the lex Augusti, and partly by reason: under Augustus the form of the commonwealth was changed and transferred to a monarchical state, so that this power was granted to him, to administer the commonwealth alone.

units.la: Sub Augusto quippe, sunt verba Herodiani latinè translata, Romanorum potentia ad unius arbitrium est devoluta. lib. 1. in init. Et postquam bellatum ad Actium, omnium potestatem in unum conferri, pacis interfuit. Tacit. Histor. 1. Neque enim aliud discordantis patriæ remedium fuit, quam ut ab uno regeretur. Idem Annal. 1. Et qui nostram sententiam dilucide confirmat est Dion Cassius, cujus verba eo lubentius huc transferre decrevi. Is lib. 53. p. mihi 495. translatus, ita differentem introducit Augustum: Nihil aliud est, quod potius prædicem, aut quo magis glorier, quam quod regiam potestatem, & is à vobis datam (loquitur de Jul. Cæs.) repudiavit, & ego eam habens depono. & idem Historicus in iisdem p. 503. Ubi peroravit (scil. Augustus) multis eum verbis precati sunt, ut solus Imperii summam gereret, multisque, quibus id ei persuaderent adductis argumentis, eo tandem compulerunt, ut principatum solus gereret. Cui addatur locus ejusdem autoris, p. 507. quem Leunclavius supplevit. Hoc facto omne populi senatusque imperium ad Augustum transiit. ab eoque perfecta Monarchia Romanorum initiam accepit. Ex quibus testimoniis abunde patet, quo tempore lex regia fuerit lata. Quæ sequuntur magis ex jure civili, quam ex Historiis temporum sunt decidenda, sic tamen ut omnibus controversiis Regiam legem spectantibus, & historicis & rationibus aliquis sit relictus locus. Wurmser. nucl. jur. contr. libr. 1. tit. 2. contr. 4.
units.tr: Under Augustus, indeed (these are the words of Herodian, translated into Latin), the power of the Romans was transferred to the will of one man. Book 1, at the beginning. And after the war was fought at Actium, it was in the interest of peace that the power of all should be conferred upon one. Tacitus, Histories 1. For there was no other remedy for a divided country than that it be governed by one. The same author, Annals 1. And Dio Cassius, whose words I have decided to quote here all the more gladly, clearly confirms our opinion. In Book 53, p. 495 in my copy, translated, he introduces Augustus speaking thus: There is nothing else that I would rather proclaim, or in which I would take more pride, than that he (speaking of Julius Caesar) rejected the royal power which you had given him, and I, holding it, lay it down. And the same historian in the same work, p. 503: When he (namely Augustus) had finished speaking, they begged him with many words that he alone should hold the sum of the empire, and by bringing many arguments to persuade him, they finally brought him to the point where he alone held the principate. To this may be added a passage of the same author, p. 507, which Leunclavius supplied: By this act all the power of the people and senate passed to Augustus, and from him the complete monarchy of the Romans took its beginning. From these testimonies it is abundantly clear at what time the Royal Law was passed. What follows is to be decided more from civil law than from the histories of the times, yet in such a way that some room is left, both for the historians and for the reasoned arguments, in all the controversies concerning the Royal Law. Wurmser, Nucleus juris controversi, book 1, title 2, controversy 4.

units.la: 7. Imprimis itaque in causas erit inquirendum, & quidem, à quo lex illa Regia fuerit lata? Populum eam tulisse, colligitur iis allegationibus, quibus probatum fuit, legem Regiam unquam latam fuisse. Neque enim Rex sibi legem tulit, neque in se omne jus ipse transtulit, quod ejus transferendi nullam habuerit potestatem. Aut si ullam habuit, eam ut à populo sibi concessam vindicaverit. §. quod Principi. Instit. de jur. nat. Gent. & civil. l.
units.tr: 7. First, then, we must inquire into the cause, and indeed: by whom was that royal law enacted? That the people enacted it is gathered from the arguments by which it was proved that a royal law was ever enacted at all. For the king did not make a law for himself, nor did he transfer to himself all right, since he had no power to transfer it. Or if he had any such power, he claimed it as granted to him by the people. §. quod Principi. Instit. de jur. nat. Gent. & civil. l.

units.la: 1. D. de princ. Constit. Autores superius allegati.
units.tr: 1. D. de princ. Constit. The authors cited above.

units.la: 8. Non alius autem finis & scopus fuit dictæ legis quam salus populi seu universitatis: hæc saltem prophasis, hic prætextus. Licet, si verum loqui liceat, lubido dominandi fuerit Principum intentio. Eadem refertur fuisse occasio constituendi Senatum, eumque vice populi consulendi. §. Senatus conf. Instit. jur. nat. Gent. & civil. l. 2. §. 8. D. de Orig. jur. Scilicet intererat Reipublicæ ut uni populus subesset, & discordantis patriæ non aliud remedium erat, quam ut ab uno regeretur. Tacit. Annal. 1.
units.tr: 8. The purpose and aim of that law was none other than the safety of the people or community; this is at least the pretext, this the excuse. Yet, to speak truly, the lust for domination was the intention of the princes. The same occasion is said to have led to the establishment of the Senate, to consult in place of the people. §. Senatus conf. Instit. jur. nat. Gent. & civil. l. 2. §. 8. D. de Orig. jur. Of course it was in the interest of the commonwealth that the people be subject to one, and for a divided country there was no other remedy than that it be ruled by one. Tacit. Annal. 1.

units.la: 9. Occasio forte latæ Legis fuit metus, fuere minæ. Certum enim populum, vel potius senatum vice populi fungentem, eo ad actum fuisse nonnullorum potentia; adeoque armorum formidine coactum, ut in unum omnia conferret. Testatur hoc Sueton. in August. cap. 26. Idem quod Clapmarius post alios statuit, in tractatu de Arcan. Imperii libr. 2. cap. 15.
units.tr: 9. The occasion of the law passed was perhaps fear; there were threats. For it is certain that the people, or rather the Senate acting in place of the people, was driven to this act by the power of certain men, and so compelled by fear of arms that it handed everything over to one man. Suetonius testifies to this in Augustus, chapter 26. Clapmarius, following others, lays down the same in his treatise de Arcanis Imperii, book 2, chapter 15.

units.la: 10. Unde quæsitum, utrum hoc factum teneat, aut jus in posterum faciat quo populus in Principem metu aut minis sua transfuisse dicitur? Respondeo, licet forte rescindi possit, quod ita gestum est; quia tamen aliquis ibidem consensus adfuit, uti testatur Dion. loco superius allegato, contractum inter Principem & populum tenere dicendum est. Arg. §. 1. Instit. de Excep. l. 21. §. 5. & in sin. D. Quod Met. causa gest.
units.tr: 10. Hence the question arises whether this act holds, or whether it creates a right for the future, by which the people is said to have transferred its rights to the Prince through fear or threats. I answer that, although what was done in this way might perhaps be rescinded, nevertheless, since some consent was present, as Dio testifies in the passage cited above, the agreement between the Prince and the people must be held to be binding. Compare Institutes 1, de Exceptionibus; Digest 21, title 5, §5 and at the end; Digest, Quod metus causa gestum.

units.la: 11. Quid si tamen Princeps populum eo adegerit armorum terrore, & quidem contra protestantem, vel occultè, vel propalam; anne tali conventioni, aut contra eius stare tenebitur, adeoque Principi, subjectus erit? Resp. licet de facto subjectus sit, dum forte armis subigitur, non tamen de jure subesse tenetur, quod nullus populi in subjectionem fuerit consensus. In tantum etiam ut quacunque occasione impune jugum illud, modo virium satis habeat, abjicere valeat.
units.tr: 11. But what if the Prince compelled the people to this by the terror of arms, and indeed against their protest, either secretly or openly? Would they be bound to keep such an agreement, or to remain subject to the Prince against their will? I answer that, although they are in fact subject, since they are perhaps forced under arms, they are not bound by right to remain subject, because there was no consent of the people to subjection. So much so that on any occasion whatever they may cast off that yoke with impunity, provided they have strength enough.

units.la: C Argum. l. 6. §. ult. D. Acquir. vel omitt. hered. Argum. §. 10. Instit. de Rer. divis. Nec obst §. 17. Instit. eod.
units.tr: C Compare Digest 6, last paragraph, de acquirenda vel omittenda hereditate. Compare Institutes 2, title 1, §10, de rerum divisione. Nor does Institutes 2, title 1, §17 stand in the way.

units.la: 12. Sed quaesitum amplius quale jus in Principem sit collatum? Respondeo, Id omne quod antea populus aut Senatus habuit. Sic ut non tantum populus suum patrimonium regendum Principi permiserit, uti vult Ammian. Marcell. Histor. libr. 14. Verum etiam hoc ipsum, ut omnibus praeesset, in quantum Populo persuasum fuit, Reipublicae per unum consuli debere. l. 2. §. 11. de Orig. jur. Dion. p. mihi 498.
units.tr: 12. But it is further asked what right was conferred upon the Prince. I answer: all that the people or the Senate previously had. So that the people did not merely permit the Prince to manage its patrimony, as Ammianus Marcellinus, Histories, book 14 maintains; but also that he should preside over all, insofar as the people was persuaded that the commonwealth ought to be governed by one man. Digest 1, title 2, law 2, §11, de origine iuris; Dio, p. 498 in my edition.

units.la: 13. Unde quaesitum, utrum Populus Imperatori tantum omnem potestatem communicaverit, an etiam à se prorsus abdicaverit? Respondeo, licet Duarenus ad tit. D. de constit. Princ. cap. 1. posterius neget; argumento l. de quibus. D. de leg. videtur tamen contrarium de jure civili esse probabilius. Praesertim si quaestio de majestate personali. §. Principum placita. Instit. jur. nat. Gent. civ. Leges enim passim utuntur verbo concessionis, & translationis. l. ult. Cod. de leg. l. 3. Cod. crimin. Sacril. l. ult. Cod. de sent. & interloc. judic. l. 1. §. 7. Cod. de veteri jur. enucleand. Placent. Instit. ad tit. de jur. nat. Gent. civ. Carpzov. Ad l. Reg. German. cap. 3. sect. 8. num. 20.
units.tr: 13. Hence the question arises whether the people communicated all power to the Emperor only, or whether it also utterly renounced it for itself. I answer: although Duaren, on title de constitutionibus principum, chapter 1, denies the latter, and it seems more probable under civil law, by the argument of Digest, de legibus, law "de quibus", the contrary is the case, especially if the question concerns personal majesty. Institutes, de iure naturali, gentium et civili, §Principum placita. For the laws everywhere use the words concession and transfer. Code, de legibus, last law; Code, de crimine sacrilegii, law 3; Code, de sententiis et interlocutionibus, last law; Code, de veteri iure enucleando, law 1, §7; Placentinus, Institutes, on title de iure naturali, gentium et civili; Carpzov, on the Regulations of the German Empire, chapter 3, section 8, number 20.

units.la: 14. An igitur penes Senatum postmodum nihil juris, nihil virium remansit? Respondeo ; revera nihil remansit. Saltem nonnisi umbratilis quaepiam potestas vel simulacrum aliquod potestatis, idque Principe connivente. l. 2. D. const. Princ. Nov. 105. in init. – l. 9. D. de leg. l. 8. Cod. eod. l. quisquis. 5. Cod. Ad l. Juliam Majestat. Dion. p. mihi. 498. 507. in sin.
units.tr: 14. Then did no right and no power remain afterwards with the Senate? I answer: in truth nothing remained, or only some shadowy power or a certain semblance of power, and that only with the Prince's connivance. Digest, de constitutionibus principum, law 2; Novel 105 at the beginning; Digest, de legibus, law 9; Code, the same title, law 8; Code, ad legem Iuliam maiestatis, law 5 "quisquis"; Dio, p. 498 and 507 in my edition, at the end.

units.la: 15. An propterea postquam omnis illa populi potestas in Principem est translata, legum vinculis Principem exemptum dicemus? Respondeo, ita quidem velint ipsi Principes, quibus forte plebiscitum Atheniense placeret, ut quidquid Rex Demetrius jussisset, illud & apud Deos fas, & apud homines jus esset. Idem ex parte innuere videntur, omnes illae sententiae & phrases, quae adulationibus plenae, legibus nonnullis civilibus continentur; quasque procul dubio viri Principes ad suum arbitrium effinxerunt. §. ult. Instit. quibus Mod. Testam. Infirm. l. 31. D. de leg. l. ult. Cod. de leg. l. 3. Cod. Crim. Sacril.
units.tr: 15. Shall we therefore say that, after all that power of the people was transferred to the Prince, he is freed from the bonds of the laws? I answer: the Princes themselves would indeed wish it so, to whom perhaps the Athenian decree would have pleased, that whatever King Demetrius ordered should be both divine law among the gods and human law among men. The sentences and phrases which, full of flattery, are contained in certain civil laws, and which the Princes undoubtedly framed to suit their own judgment, seem in part to hint at the same thing. Institutes, last paragraph, quibus modis testamenta infirmantur; Digest, de legibus, law 31; Code, de legibus, last law; Code, de crimine sacrilegii, law 3.

units.la: Id tamen per omnia verum non esse, etiam ex leg. civilibus colligi potest. l. digna vox. Cod. de leg. vid. Donell. 1. comm. 17. Dan. Ethic. Christ. libr. 2. cap. 12. Bachov. ad §. ult. Instit. Quibus mod. Test. infirm. Speckhan. 1. q. 72. Barbos. coll. in Cod. ad l. 4. Cod. de leg. Ibidemque innumeri. Ut tamen audiendus non sit Cujacius obs. 15. c. 30. & obs. 26. cap. 35. Qui tantum legibus caducearius & pœnariis Principem velit esse solutum, aut aliquibus juris solemnibus. Id enim Principi non competeret, vi potestatis supremæ, sed ex singulari quodam beneficio. Augusta quippe talibus gaudet privilegiis, licet non habeat legibus solutam potestatem. l. 31. D. de leg. Befold. oiton. jur. tit. 4. libr.
units.tr: That this is not true in every respect can also be gathered from the civil laws. Digest, law "digna vox", Code de legibus; see Donellus, Commentaries 1, chapter 17; Dan, Ethica Christiana, book 2, chapter 12; Bachov on the last paragraph of the Institutes, quibus modis testamenta infirmantur; Speckhan, 1 q. 72; Barbosa, collectanea on Code, law 4, de legibus. And there are countless others there. Yet Cujas, Observations 15, chapter 30, and Observations 26, chapter 35, is not to be heard, who would have the Prince freed only from the laws concerning the caducary and penal matters, or from some solemn rules of law. For this would not belong to the Prince by virtue of supreme power, but by a certain special favour. Indeed Augustus enjoyed such privileges, although he did not possess power to be released from the laws. Digest, de legibus, law 31; Beyerlinck (Befold), Oiton iuris, title 4, book ...

units.la: 1. P. q. 7. ibidemque varii.
units.tr: 1 P. q. 7; and various others there.

units.la: 16. Verum quis sensus verborum; in d. l. Regiâ occurrentium: quod Principi placuit, legis habere vigorem? Quæ verba existant d. §. 6. Institit. & l. 1. D. de Constit. Princip. An autoritatis legislatoriæ diminutionem designabunt? Non equidem. Et quia Principi eadem concessa fuit potestas, quæ erat populi l. 3. in sin. D. de offic. Prætor. Igitur vere potuit leges condere. l. ult. Cod. de leg. Et quia ea verba referuntur ad Principis placita, postquam ei legum ferendarum potestas est tributa. d. §. 6. & d. l. 1. Et quia in locis allegatis, ea Principum placita, quæ legis vigorem habere dicuntur, leges esse, citra dubitationem asseritur. Ut hallucinetur Perezius, qui placita Principum tanta fuisse censet, ut appellari leges meruerint, quasi ideo duntaxat censeantur legis habere vigorem. Perez. tit. Cod. de legibus num. 2.
units.tr: 16. But what is the meaning of the words, occurring in the said law Regia: what pleased the Prince has the force of law? These words are found in the said paragraph 6 of the Institutes and in Digest, de constitutionibus principum, law 1. Do they designate a diminution of legislative authority? Certainly not. And because the same power was granted to the Prince which the people had, Digest, de officio praetoris, law 3, at the end, he could truly make laws. Code, de legibus, last law. And because those words refer to the Prince's decisions, after the power of enacting laws had been granted to him, said paragraph 6 and said law 1. And because in the places cited it is asserted without doubt that those decisions of the Princes which are said to have the force of law are laws. So Perezius is mistaken, who thinks the Princes' decisions were so great that they deserved to be called laws, as if they were therefore merely considered to have the force of law. Perezius, on the title Code de legibus, number 2.

units.la: 17. Verum quis sensus illorum verborum d. §. 6. & d. l. 1. quibus dicitur, ei & in eum populum suam potestatem transtulisse? Utrum emphatice erunt accipienda? sic ut populus Principi & in Principem suam transtulerit potestatem? Non videtur. Neque enim tam foret emphasis quam pleonasmus. Præterquam quod non videatur probabile, populum sic ostendere voluisse suam obnixam in Principem voluntatem, uti id perpetram vult Bacchov. ad d. §. 6. Instit. Utrum potius per vocem ei designabimus imperatorem, & per vocem, in eum, ipsum populum? Ita effectu inspecto dicendum videtur. Potestas enim Principi collata non tantum est in Provinciales, & subjectos populo Romano, sed & in ipsum populum Romanum. Neque hinc absurdus oritur sensus, si dicamus in ipsum populum Principi datam esse potestatem. Præsertim cum aliter frustra positum fuisset vocabulum ei. Cui non obstat, quod elegantiæ repugnare videatur, pronomen non reciprocum, pro reciproco usurpari: præsertim cum id in jure infrequens non esse ex variis juris locis colligatur. l. si quis. 22. in Princ. D. de leg. 3. l. 17. §. ult. D. Recept. Arbitr. Dion. p. mihi. 499. Theophil. ad d. §. 6. Instit. Duaren. cap. 1. de Potest. Princ. Coras. ad d. l. 1. Baro ad d. l. 1. D. de Princip. Constit.
units.tr: 17. But what is the meaning of those words in the said paragraph 6 and said law 1, by which it is said that the people transferred its power to him and into him? Are they to be taken emphatically, so that the people transferred its power to the Prince and into the Prince? That seems not so. For that would be not so much an emphasis as a pleonasm. Besides, it does not seem probable that the people wished in this way to show its firm will towards the Prince, as Bachovius wants to maintain on the said paragraph 6 of the Institutes. Shall we rather designate the Emperor by the word ei, and the people itself by the words in eum? That seems the right way to judge, looking at the effect. For the power conferred on the Prince extended not only over the provincials and subjects of the Roman people, but also over the Roman people itself. Nor does an absurd meaning arise from this, if we say that power was given to the Prince over the people itself. Especially since otherwise the word ei would have been placed in vain. Nor is it an objection that a non-reflexive pronoun seems to clash with good style when used for a reflexive one; especially since it is gathered from various places in the law that this is not uncommon in law. Digest, de legibus, law 22, beginning; Digest, Recepta arbitrium, law 17, §last; Dio, p. 499 in my edition; Theophilus on the said paragraph 6 of the Institutes; Duaren, chapter 1, de potestate principis; Coras on the said law 1; Baro on the said law 1, Digest de constitutionibus principum.

units.la: Quod si per eum intendamus ipsum Principem? Sensus juri civili atque rationi minus conformis admitteretur. Absurdum quippe esset alicui dare potestatem, quâ ipse adversum se utatur. Præterquam quod illam potestatem, sic concessam, non acceptassent Principes, ut qui potius ad absolutum ad spirassent imperium. Præter quam quod notissimum sit, Ineminem sibi jus dicere aut Imperare posse. l. 51. D. de Recept. Arbitr. l. 40. in sin. D. fidei commiss. libert. l. 7. §. 8. in sin. D. don. inter vir. & uxor, Besold, Oiconom. jur. ad tit. D. Constit. Princip.
units.tr: But if by "him" we understand the Prince himself? That sense would be admitted as less consistent with civil law and with reason. For it would be absurd to give someone a power by which he himself might act against himself. Besides, Princes would not have accepted a power granted in that way, since they aspired rather to absolute rule. Moreover, it is very well known that no one can pronounce law for himself or command himself. l. 51. D. de Recept. Arbitr. l. 40. in sin. D. fidei commiss. libert. l. 7. §. 8. in sin. D. don. inter vir. & uxor, Besold, Oiconom. jur. ad tit. D. Constit. Princip.

units.la: CAPUT. II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: 1. Quæ sint Majestatica?
units.tr: 1. What are the majestatica?

units.la: 2. Quid sint Constitutiones Principum in genere?
units.tr: 2. What are the constitutions of Princes in general?

units.la: 3. An omne Principis placitum lex sit?
units.tr: 3. Is every pleasure of the Prince a law?

units.la: 4. Quot generum sint Principum Constitutiones?
units.tr: 4. How many kinds of constitutions of Princes are there?

units.la: 5. Quid Decretum?
units.tr: 5. What is a decree?

units.la: 6. Quid Edictum?
units.tr: 6. What is an edict?

units.la: 7. Quid Oratio?
units.tr: 7. What is an oration?

units.la: 8. Quid Mandatum?
units.tr: 8. What is a mandate?

units.la: 9. Quando valeat?
units.tr: 9. When is it valid?

units.la: 10. Utrum omni Principis Mandato sit parendum? dist.
units.tr: 10. Whether every command of the Prince is to be obeyed? Distinguish.

units.la: 11. Objectionibus succurritur.
units.tr: 11. Objections are met.

units.la: 12. Quid sit Rescriptum?
units.tr: 12. What is a rescript?

units.la: 13. Quis possit supplicare Principi?
units.tr: 13. Who may petition the Prince?

units.la: 14. Utrum Rescriptum Principis habeat vim legis?
units.tr: 14. Whether a rescript of the Prince has the force of law?

units.la: 15. Utrum Principis interlocutio?
units.tr: 15. Whether an interlocution of the Prince?

units.la: 16. Utrum omne rescriptum valeat?
units.tr: 16. Whether every rescript is valid?

units.la: 17. Utrum per subr aut obreptionem vitiata valeant?
units.tr: 17. Whether rescripts vitiated by subreption or obreption are valid?

units.la: 18. 19. Quibus modis rescripta vitientur?
units.tr: 18. 19. By what modes are rescripts vitiated?

units.la: 20. An rescripti exemplum, an authenticum probet?
