units.la: 1. SUperest ut de Principum Pacitis, seu constitutionibus personalibus agatur; quæ privilegia sunt appellata. l. 1. D. Princ. constit.
units.tr: 1. It remains to treat of the decrees of princes, or personal constitutions, which are called privileges. l. 1. D. Princ. constit.

units.la: Quorum natura ut innotescat magis, juris Singularis habenda ratio, idque ad oppositionem juris universalis, quod est commune præceptum, communis vitæ regula, de eo, quod ut plurimum, quod sæpe, quod frequenter evenit. l. 2. 3. 4. D. de legibus. Ut jus Singulare dicatur, quod sub communi præcepto collocatum non est, ab eodem exemptum, quodque non ad omnes, aut in imperio, aut civitate spectat, verum ad certas tantum personas refertur, aut certis in casibus & causis obtinet.
units.tr: To make their nature better known, we must take account of singular law, as opposed to universal law, which is a common precept and the common rule of life, concerning what happens for the most part, often, or frequently. l. 2. 3. 4. D. de legibus. Singular law is said to be that which is not placed under the common precept, is exempted from it, and does not apply to all persons, either in the empire or in the state, but refers only to certain persons or holds in certain cases and matters.

units.la: Quale jus singulare contra rationem juris introductum esse dicitur. l. 14. D. de legibus. in quantum in speciem rationi juris communis contradicit; in quantum alicui regulæ juris receptæ & ratione quadam in commune collectæ.
units.tr: Such singular law is said to be introduced against the reason of law. l. 14. D. de legibus. It does so insofar as it contradicts, in a particular case, the reason of the common law, that is, insofar as it departs from a received rule of law and from a reason gathered in common.

units.la: Cæterum generaliter consideratum universo juri non contradicit, multo minus rationi naturali; verum illud supplet in eâ parte, salvâ tamen justitiâ ad quam porrigi aut extendi communis regula non potest. Ut etiamnum universo juri sit convenientissimum, vel ratione æquitatis, vel singularis auxilii, vel liberalitatis, vel indulti, vel dispensationis, vel gratiæ, vel humanitatis, vel clementiæ, vel utilitatis &c. l. 16. D. de leg. l. 15. D. de Rebus credit. l. 3. D. offic. Prætor. l. 11. in init. D. de Pœn. l. ad bestias 31. D. eod. §. 7. Institut. Testam. ordin.
units.tr: Considered in general, however, it does not contradict the whole of law, and still less natural reason. Rather it supplies law in that part, though saving justice, to which the common rule cannot be stretched or extended. Thus it is still wholly in agreement with the law as a whole, whether by reason of equity, of special help, of liberality, of indulgence, of dispensation, of grace, of humanity, of clemency, or of utility, and so on. l. 16. D. de leg. l. 15. D. de Rebus credit. l. 3. D. offic. Prætor. l. 11. in init. D. de Pœn. l. ad bestias 31. D. eod. §. 7. Institut. Testam. ordin.

units.la: Unde facile colligitur, quod jus singulare nihil aliud sit, quam quod contra communes juris civilis regulas, propter aliquam vel naturalis æquitatis, vel humanitatis, vel utilitatis &c. rationem, certâ supremorum auctoritate est introductum. d. l. 16. d. l. 31. l. ult. Cod. si Contra jus vel public. util. Parum ab hâc definitione dissentit Oldendorp. in tractatulo de jure singulari recte desin.
units.tr: Hence it is easily gathered that singular law is nothing other than what is introduced by the certain authority of the supreme power against the common rules of civil law, on account of some reason of natural equity, humanity, or utility, and so on. d. l. 16. d. l. 31. l. ult. Cod. si Contra jus vel public. util. Oldendorp, in his little treatise on singular law, rightly concludes, and differs little from this definition. (tractatulo de jure singulari recte desin.)

units.la: 2. Hoc jus singulare, sic definitum, sub se complectitur Privilegia, quæ nihil aliud signant, in strictiori sensu, quam jus aliquod Singulare seu proprium seu speciale, quo aliquai aliqua prærogativa contra jus commune tribuitur. l. 21 D. de Constit. Princ. l. 2. l. 3. l. 11. D. de Testam. Milit. l. 46. D. de contrah. Empt. l. 37. D. de jur. fisc. l. 1. D. Ad Munic. l. 2. l. 3. Cod. de leg. l. pen. Cod. de Prec. imper. offer. l. 9. Cod. de Testam. Azo in summa Cod. de jur. fisc. libr. 10. Accacius Enenck Bur. de Priv. jur. Civ. l. 1. cap. 3. num. 1. & seqq.
units.tr: 2. This singular law, so defined, includes under it privileges, which in the stricter sense signify nothing other than some singular law, whether proper or special, by which some prerogative is granted to some person against the common law. l. 21 D. de Constit. Princ. l. 2. l. 3. l. 11. D. de Testam. Milit. l. 46. D. de contrah. Empt. l. 37. D. de jur. fisc. l. 1. D. Ad Munic. l. 2. l. 3. Cod. de leg. l. pen. Cod. de Prec. imper. offer. l. 9. Cod. de Testam. Azo in summa Cod. de jur. fisc. libr. 10. Accacius Enenck Bur. de Priv. jur. Civ. l. 1. cap. 3. num. 1. & seqq.

units.la: 3. Et si vero Privilegia dicantur jus singulare, intellige singulorum legem; cum quae nos singulare veteres privata appellaverint. Gell 10. Mod. Attic. 20. Et Isidor. in origin.
units.tr: 3. And if privileges are called singular law, understand it as the law of individuals, since the ancients called what we call singulare by the name privata. Gell. 10. Mod. Attic. 20. Et Isidor. in origin.

units.la: Sintq; leges privatorum, quasi privatae leges. Etiam privilegia inde dicta, quod in privatos feratur lex. Non tamen cum jure singulari, de quo in l.14. D. de legibus, erunt confundenda. Etsi enim omne privilegium sit jus singulare: non omne tamen jus singulare statim dicendum erit Privilegium; à quo differt, ut genus à specie. Illud enim, supple jus singulare, paululum aberrat à regulis juris; sic introductam, propter aliquam vel utilitatem, vel humanitatem, uti dictum; non autem tantum lex in res singulas, aut personas constituta. Hoc, puta Privilegium, est contra jus commune, etiam in singulas res vel personas latū. Illud non semper complectitur favorem, aut beneficium, quo res vel persona afficitur. Hoc complectitur, si in bonam partem vocem accipiamus. Ita jus singulare est, quod tabularius pupillo stipuletur. Ut in casu absentiae gladii potestas demandari possit nec tamen Privilegium est. l. 2. D. Rem pupill. Sulc. l. 18. D. Adopt. l. 1. §. 15. D. Mag. conv. -- l.1. D. off. ejus cui mand. jurisd. Quibus adjiciatur casus. l. 1. Cod. Si per vim vel alio modo Absent. poss. l. 8. d. l. 14. l. 15. D. de legibus. Gotefred. in notis ibid. vid. Cujac. 15 obs. 8. Ut hic erret Oldendorp. in tract. de jur. sing. & plerique cum eo, qui jussingulare cum Privilegio confundunt.
units.tr: Private laws are laws of private persons, as it were private laws. Privileges too are so named because the law is brought to bear upon private persons. They are not, however, to be confused with singular law, of which we spoke in l. 14. D. de legibus. For although every privilege is singular law, not every singular law is at once to be called a privilege; the privilege differs from it as species from genus. For the one, namely singular law, departs a little from the rules of law, being introduced, as said, on account of some utility or humanity; but it is not merely a law laid down for particular things or persons. The privilege is against the common law, and is extended even to particular things or persons. The one does not always involve favour or benefit by which a thing or person is affected; the other does, if we take the word in a good sense. Thus it is singular law that a tabularius stipulates for a pupil, or that in a case of absence the power of the sword may be committed, yet this is not a privilege. l. 2. D. Rem pupill. Sulc. l. 18. D. Adopt. l. 1. §. 15. D. Mag. conv. l. 1. D. off. ejus cui mand. jurisd. To these may be added the case of l. 1. Cod. Si per vim vel alio modo Absent. poss. l. 8. d. l. 14. l. 15. D. de legibus. Gotefred. in notis ibid. vid. Cujac. 15 obs. 8. So Oldendorp errs here, and most others with him, who confuse singular law with privilege.

units.la: 5. Privilegia dividit Choppin.in.tract.de Priv. Rust. ab objecto, quod alia sint rerum, alia personarum, alia actionum. Communissima divisio est in realia & personalia. Meo judicio alia erunt realia, alia personalia, alia mixta. Quam etiam divisionem admittit Oldendorp. tractatulo de jur. singul. Illa, quæ rem sequuntur, nec extincta persona extinguntur. Ista, quæ cum persona amittuntur, ideoque nec ad alium dominum, aut hæredem, vel qualemcunq; successorem transeunt: extendi tamen nonnunquam de persona in personam per interpretationem possunt. Hæc sunt, quæ quidem transitoria, non tamen ad quamcunque personam; qualia sunt, quæ hæredibus prosunt, non autem fidejussoribus vel quæ certis prosunt hæredibus, non indistinctè omnibus, l. etiam filios. 18. in Princ. D. Salut. Matrim. l. 3. §. 1. & in sin. & l. seq. D. de Cens. l. 3. l. 4. D. jur. immun. l. 9. §. ista fere. D. de Pœn, l. 1. §. antepen. D. Aquaquot. & estiv l. 63. §. 1. D. pro soc. l. 42. D. Admin. Tutor. l. 196. D. de Reg. jur. l. 28. §. 1. D. de re judic. l. 3. D. de Veter. l. Divo. Cod. de Quæst. l. 3. l. 5. Cod. de Pœn. vid. Menoch. 3. Præsumpt. 103. Petr. Fabrum. Comm. ad Reg. jur. 196.
units.tr: 5. Choppin, in his treatise on rustic privileges, divides privileges by their object: some concern things, some persons, some actions. The most common division is into real and personal. In my judgment there will be real privileges, personal privileges, and mixed ones; Oldendorp also admits this division. Those which follow the thing are not extinguished when the person dies. Those which are lost along with the person, and therefore do not pass to another owner, heir, or any successor whatever, can nevertheless sometimes be extended from person to person by interpretation. Some are transmissible, yet not to any person whatever, such as those which benefit heirs but not sureties, or which benefit certain heirs and not all of them indiscriminately. l. etiam filios. 18. in Princ. D. Salut. Matrim. l. 3. §. 1. & in sin. & l. seq. D. de Cens. l. 3. l. 4. D. jur. immun. l. 9. §. ista fere. D. de Pœn. l. 1. §. antepen. D. Aquaquot. & estiv. l. 63. §. 1. D. pro soc. l. 42. D. Admin. Tutor. l. 196. D. de Reg. jur. l. 28. §. 1. D. de re judic. l. 3. D. de Veter. l. Divo. Cod. de Quæst. l. 3. l. 5. Cod. de Pœn. vid. Menoch. 3. Præsumpt. 103. Petr. Fabrum. Comm. ad Reg. jur. 196.

units.la: 6. Alii secundum DD. aliter partiuntur privilegia, quod quædam perpetuam, & constantem habeant rationem in naturâ positam, ut perpetuo competant iis, quibus data, ta, qualia in corpore juris inclusa esse dicuntur : ut sunt privilegia Minoris ætatis, Vellejani, &c. Quædam vero sint momentanea, nec causam habeant perpetuam, nec eo animo concessa, ut perpetui manerent : qualia, si forte alicui veniam delicti concedat Princeps, aut ædificandi in publico jus largiatur. l. 1. D. Const. Princip. l. 2. §. 10. 16. D. Ne quid in loc. public. Est & alia divisio, quod quædam privilegia sint mera, quædam mixta. Illa, quæ si impetrata, in totum jus aliquod singulare continent. Hæc quæ etiam præter jus singulare, aliquid juris communis continent, quales sunt nundinæ, seu magni mercatus. Alciat. 5. Respons. 23. n. 6.
units.tr: 6. Others, following the jurists, divide privileges differently. Some have a perpetual and constant basis fixed in nature, so that they belong permanently to those to whom they were granted, such as those included in the body of law, for example the privileges of minors, the Velleian privilege, and so on. Others are momentary: they have no perpetual cause and were not granted with the intention that they should last for ever. Examples are when a prince grants someone pardon for an offence, or gives the right to build on public land. l. 1. D. Const. Princip. l. 2. §. 10. 16. D. Ne quid in loc. public. There is also another division: some privileges are pure, others mixed. Pure privileges, once obtained, contain a single special right in its entirety. Mixed privileges, besides some special right, also contain something of common law, such as fairs or great markets. Alciat. 5. Respons. 23. n. 6.

units.la: 7. Insignis autem hic ventilanda quæstio: Si in diplomate (quod est instrumentum beneficium in aliquem collatum, continens) verba sint obscura, quale præsumendum sit esse privilegium, reale, personale, an mixtum? Resp. Si privilegium sit odiosum, præsumetur esse personale; ne extendatur nimiü. Ut si reipublicæ sit damnosum, quandoque si pœnam contineat, si juris tertii deminutionem. Si vero favorabile censebitur esse reale. Arg. l. 3. D. de Constit. Princ. l. 2. §. 10. 16. D. Ne quid in loc. Public. Tusc. concluf. Pract. Privilegium an reale an personale præsumatur. 741. & seqq. G. Everh. conf. 21. n. 8.
units.tr: 7. Here a notable question must be discussed: if the words of a diploma (that is, the instrument containing a benefit conferred on someone) are unclear, which kind of privilege should be presumed, real, personal or mixed? Answer: if the privilege is odious, it is presumed to be personal, so that it is not extended too far. For example, if it is harmful to the commonwealth, or if it contains a penalty, or a diminution of the right of a third party. But if it is judged to be favourable, it is taken to be real. Arg. l. 3. D. de Constit. Princ. l. 2. §. 10. 16. D. Ne quid in loc. Public. Tusc. concluf. Pract. Privilegium an reale an personale præsumatur. 741. & seqq. G. Everh. conf. 21. n. 8.

units.la: 9. Verum cujus erit privilegia interpretari? Resp. Uti pari passu ambulant legem ferre, eamque interpretari; ita ejus solius erit privilegia interpretari, qui ea concessit. Itaque Princeps à se data privilegia, solus interpretabitur. l. ex facto, & ibi Jason, ac Zasius. n. 6. D. de vulg. & pupill. Subst. l. ult. Cod. de legibus. l. 191. D. de Reg. jur. Coler. Conf. 56. num. 77. Gail. 1. obs. 1. num. 13. Zanger de Except. part. 2. c. 1. num. 138. Mindan. 1. Proceff. c. 20. in
units.tr: 9. But whose right is it to interpret privileges? Answer: just as the power to make a law and to interpret it go hand in hand, so the power to interpret privileges belongs solely to the one who granted them. Accordingly, a prince alone will interpret the privileges that he himself has granted. l. ex facto, & ibi Jason, ac Zasius. n. 6. D. de vulg. & pupill. Subst. l. ult. Cod. de legibus. l. 191. D. de Reg. jur. Coler. Conf. 56. num. 77. Gail. 1. obs. 1. num. 13. Zanger de Except. part. 2. c. 1. num. 138. Mindan. 1. Proceff. c. 20. in

units.la: Princ. Befold. delib. jur. ad l. 1. P. p. mihi 34.
units.tr: Princ. Befold. delib. jur. ad l. 1. P. p. mihi 34.

units.la: 10. Finiuntur autem Privilegia variis modis. Vel quia se indignum beneficio præbuit, delinquendo privilegiatus. Vel quia persona cui concessum Privilegium personale in fata conceßit, aut si reale, res interiit. Vel quia Privilegio renunciavit. Vel quia conditio aut tempus extitit ad quod concessu est. Vel quia fortius privilegium illud elidit. Vel quia incipit esse iniquum, & lædit enormius. Vel quia aliquis non usus est privilegio si modo utendi facultas sese obtulerit. Vel quia actum privilegio contrarium fecit, aut admisit, sine protestatione. Vel quia abusus quis est privilegio, adeoque meretur illud amittere, qui permissa sibi abutitur potestate. Vel quia per sub & obreptionem fuerat impetratum, dum fallitur Principis conscientia. Vel quia causa finalis, ob quam concessum est privilegium cessat. Cessante quippe causa, cessat effectus. Vel quia revocatio Privilegii publicam respicit utilitatem, quæ privatorum commodis est præferenda. Arg. §. pen. inst. Usufr. l. 4. §. 2. D. quod cum eo qui in alien. l. 37. D. interd. releg. l. 37. in sin. D. de Minor. l. ult. Cod. de Revoc. donat. l. 1. verf. omnem enim. Cod Ubi Senator. l.
units.tr: 10. Privileges are ended in various ways. Either because the privileged person, by offending, has shown himself unworthy of the benefit; or because a personal privilege has lapsed with the death of the person to whom it was granted, or, if it is real, because the thing has perished; or because he has renounced the privilege; or because the condition or time on which it was granted has arrived; or because a stronger privilege overrides it; or because it has become unfair and harms someone too greatly; or because someone has not used the privilege when the opportunity to use it has presented itself; or because he has done or allowed an act contrary to the privilege without protest; or because the privileged person abuses it, and so deserves to lose it, having misused the power given to him; or because it was obtained by subreption and obreption, while the prince's knowledge was deceived; or because the final cause for which the privilege was granted has ceased. For when the cause ceases, the effect ceases too. Or because the revocation of the privilege concerns public utility, which must be preferred to the private advantage of individuals. Arg. §. pen. inst. Usufr. l. 4. §. 2. D. quod cum eo qui in alien. l. 37. D. interd. releg. l. 37. in sin. D. de Minor. l. ult. Cod. de Revoc. donat. l. 1. verf. omnem enim. Cod Ubi Senator. l.

units.la: 11. Finiuntur denique privilegia, revocatione, tione ejus, à quo concessa, vel illius successoris. Unde quaesitum satis anxie, an beneficium à Principe alicui concessum ad vitam, ad placitum revocari possit, saltem à Principis successore? Variis adhibitis distinctionibus quaestionem terminant doctores. 1. Aut enim concessum est subdito, aut non subdito. Si huic; ad lubitum non revocabitur. Quod jus quaesitum per Principem illi nequeat auferri, qui Principis territorio non subest. Arg. l. sin. D. de jurisd. Peregrin. de jur. fisc. libr. n. 28. 29. Nisi tamen in Principis versetur territorio. Besold. ad libr. 1. Pand. de Privil. p. mihi 31.
units.tr: 11. Privileges are finally ended by revocation, or by the death of the one who granted them, or of his successor. Hence the question is asked rather anxiously: can a benefit granted by a Prince to someone for life be revoked at will, at least by the Prince's successor? The jurists settle the question with various distinctions. 1. For the benefit has either been granted to a subject or to a non-subject. If to a non-subject, it cannot be revoked at will; a right acquired in this way cannot be taken away by the Prince from one who is not subject to his territory. Arg. l. sin. D. de jurisd. Peregrin. de jur. fisc. libr. n. 28. 29. Unless, however, he is within the Prince's territory. Besold. ad libr. 1. Pand. de Privil. p. mihi 31.

units.la: 12. Si concessum subdito, & quidem in praejudicium publici boni, nullius censebitur esse momenti, adeoque nec eget revocatione. l. 2. 4. Cod. si contr. jus vel util. l. qui immunitatem. Cod. Muner. Patrim. l. quicquid Cod. de Vectig. l. actores. Cod. Exact. Tribut. Quod si concessum subdito non tamen in reipublicae detrimentum tendat; aut erit concessum omnino gratis, atque simpliciter, non addita temporis determinatione & revocari poterit. Arg. l. nihil tam naturale. D. de Reg. jur. l. 25. §. vis major. D. locat. Bald. in l. 2. v. item nota. Cod. de Servit. & aqua.
units.tr: 12. If it has been granted to a subject, and indeed to the prejudice of the public good, it will be judged to be of no force at all, and so it does not even need revocation. l. 2. 4. Cod. si contr. jus vel util. l. qui immunitatem. Cod. Muner. Patrim. l. quicquid Cod. de Vectig. l. actores. Cod. Exact. Tribut. But if it has been granted to a subject without tending to the detriment of the commonwealth, then either it was granted entirely freely and simply, without any time limit added, and it can be revoked. Arg. l. nihil tam naturale. D. de Reg. jur. l. 25. §. vis major. D. locat. Bald. in l. 2. v. item nota. Cod. de Servit. & aqua.

units.la: 3. Hac tamen adhibita cautela, ne id fiat frequenter aut facile. Tum quod nemo Principali auctoritate sit circumscribendus. l.
units.tr: 3. This caution, however, must be observed: that it not be done often or lightly. Then, because no one should be circumvented by the authority of the Prince. l. 1. Cod. qui ven. etat. impetr.

Ut in Principe dictorum & factorum constantia desideretur, l. inter claras. Cod. de Summo Trinit. Cujus os divinum, l. 1. §. 6. Cod. veter. jur. Enucl. Cujus dicta, consulta coelestia, l. 8. Cod. off. Rect. Prov. Cujus vox, oraculum, l. 4. Cod. de leg. & constitutiones sacratissimæ, statuta coelestia, l. 10. Cod. Muril. §.
units.tr: Then, because in private persons levity is blamed in those who wish to revoke a gift. l. 7. D. Cond. ob caus. dat. So constancy in the words and deeds of a Prince is to be expected. l. inter claras. Cod. de Summo Trinit. Whose mouth is divine. l. 1. §. 6. Cod. veter. jur. Enucl. Whose sayings are heavenly counsels. l. 8. Cod. off. Rect. Prov. Whose voice is an oracle. l. 4. Cod. de leg. And whose most sacred constitutions are heavenly statutes. l. 10. Cod. Muril. §.

units.la: 14. Aut concessum est beneficium propter bene merita, adeoque ad modum donationis, neque illud unquam revocari oportet. Et quod ex causa antecedente id contulerit ad quod naturæ lege tenebatur, cui etiam subjectus est Princeps. Et quod donatio jure gentium introducta, irrevocabilem obtineat vigorem. l. 1. §. 1. D. Precar. l. 27. D. Donat. Clarus 4. sent 3. Gail. 1. obs. 60. n. 17. Menoch. 3 Presumt. 103. & consil. libr. 4. conf. 307. 378.
units.tr: 14. Or the benefice has been granted on account of good services, and so by way of a gift, and it ought never to be revoked. Also because he conferred it from an antecedent cause, to which he was bound by the law of nature, and to which the Prince too is subject. And because a donation introduced by the law of nations obtains irrevocable force. l. 1. §. 1. D. Precar. l. 27. D. Donat. Clarus 4. sent 3. Gail. 1. obs. 60. n. 17. Menoch. 3 Presumt. 103. & consil. libr. 4. conf. 307. 378.

units.la: Unde non poterit revocari beneficium, quod alicui concessum est propter aliquod officium, quod in se suscepit. Neque enim cuiquam suum officium debebit esse damnosum. l. 7 D. Testam. Quemadm. Aperiunt. Et qui quid revocat, quod quis in se suscepit, is tenetur ei qui illud suscepit, ad id quod ejus interest. Arg. l. 8. §. Mandati. D. Mandat. Si scilicet per eum non stet, quo minus illud impleat. Arg. l. 38. D. locat. Perez. Cod Prof. & Medic. n. 9. Gail. 1. obs. 44. n. 12. post Minsf. cent. 3. obs. 7. & 8. vid. Sand. 5. decis. tit. 10. def. 2.
units.tr: Hence a benefit that has been granted to someone on account of an office he has undertaken cannot be revoked. For no one's office ought to be made damaging to him. l. 7 D. Testam. Quemadm. Aperiunt. And whoever revokes what someone has undertaken is bound to make good to the one who undertook it whatever his interest is. Arg. l. 8. §. Mandati. D. Mandat. That is, if it is not through him that he fails to fulfil it. Arg. l. 38. D. locat. Perez. Cod Prof. & Medic. n. 9. Gail. 1. obs. 44. n. 12. post Minsf. cent. 3. obs. 7. & 8. vid. Sand. 5. decis. tit. 10. def. 2.

units.la: 16. Si tamen publica utilitas suadeat revocandum esse privilegium, id revocari poterit, ut tamen in ejus locum succedat id quod interest. Arg. §. 2. Instit. qui sui vel alien. jur. Zoes. D. de constit. Princ. n. 30. & Felin. ibid.
units.tr: 16. If, however, public utility suggests that the privilege ought to be revoked, it may be revoked, provided that in its place there succeeds what concerns the party. Arg. §. 2. Instit. qui sui vel alien. jur. Zoes. D. de constit. Princ. n. 30. & Felin. ibid.

units.la: 17. Uti impune revocabitur, si quispiam indignum se gesserit illo beneficio, adeoque pro ingrato habeatur. Nam cessante causa finali beneficii, & ipsum cessabit: Arg. l. ult. Cod. de Revocand donat. l. Athleta. §. 1. l.
units.tr: 17. It will be revoked with impunity if someone has behaved himself unworthily of that benefit, and so is held to be ungrateful. For when the final cause of the benefit ceases, the benefit itself will cease too. Arg. l. ult. Cod. de Revocand donat. l. Athleta. §. 1. l.

units.la: 18. Quod si de successore Principis loquamur, immodica largitio privilegiorum à Prædecessore facta, præsertim eorum, quæ publicum jus spectant, omnino revocari poterit. Quod talis immoderata & irrationabilis concessio, reipublicæ sit perniciosa. c. ipsa pietas 23. q. 4. Bald. in l. jubemus. Cod. Sacros. Eccles.
units.tr: 18. But if we speak of a successor of the Prince, an immoderate largess of privileges granted by a predecessor, especially of those which concern public right, can certainly be revoked. For such an immoderate and irrational grant is pernicious to the commonwealth. c. ipsa pietas 23. q. 4. Bald. in l. jubemus. Cod. Sacros. Eccles.

units.la: 19. Cæterum, in casibus præcedentibus, quod privilegia publicâ nitantur fide, successores, eodem modo, quo antecessores obstringuntur. Enench. 3. de Priv. c. 7. c. 11. n. 44. n. 60. Besold. delib. jur. ex libr. 1. D. p. 34. 43. de Privil. vid. Vaz. Barbos. Axiom. litt. G. n. 15. Raubar. quest. jur. 11. part. II. ibique varios.
units.tr: 19. Moreover, in the preceding cases, since privileges rest on public faith, successors are bound in the same way as their predecessors. Enench. 3. de Priv. c. 7. c. 11. n. 44. n. 60. Besold. delib. jur. ex libr. 1. D. p. 34. 43. de Privil. vid. Vaz. Barbos. Axiom. litt. G. n. 15. Raubar. quest. jur. 11. part. II. ibique varios.

units.la: 1. POst explicationem speciersum seu partium juris scripti & quidem universalis, sequeretur jus scriptum particulare, verum quoniam ad ejus intellectum plenioriem multum confert juris non scripti cognitio, non immerito id erit præmittendum. Estque jus non scriptum duplex; consuetudo, vel æquitas. Utrumque jus sine sanctione. Illud est, quod usus seu mores approbarunt: ut à moribus distinguatur, tanquam effectus à causâ. Mores quippe sunt actus, jus consuetudinarium introducentes. Quod jus consuetudinarium, vel universale, quale populus introducit; vel singulare, quod est alicujus Municipii, vel collegii. Azo in summ. Cod. hic.
units.tr: 1. After explaining the kinds or parts of written law, and especially the universal written law, one would proceed to particular written law. But since a fuller understanding of that depends greatly on knowledge of unwritten law, it will not unreasonably be set out first. Unwritten law is twofold: custom, or equity. Each of these is law without sanction. Custom is that which usage or manners have approved, so that it is distinguished from manners as an effect from its cause; for manners are the acts that introduce customary law. Customary law is either universal, such as a people introduces, or particular, which belongs to some municipality or college. Azo in Summa on this title of the Code.

units.la: 2. Cujus occasione DD. inquirunt num ab unâ familiâ induci possit consuetudo? Respondeo, non videtur id affirmandum, nisi forte in quantum populus unius familiæ consuetudinem, pro justâ recipit, & admittit. Arg. l. 32. D. de legibus. Quo nomine affirmativam sententiam variis in casubus amplectuntur varii allegati apud Gabriel. Comm. opinion. libr. 6. de consuet. conclus. 5. cum limit.
units.tr: 2. On this occasion the doctors inquire whether a custom can be introduced by one family alone. I answer that this does not seem to be affirmed, except perhaps in so far as the people accepts and admits the custom of one family as just. Arg. l. 32. D. de legibus. On this point various authorities, cited by Gabriel. Comm. opinion. libr. 6. de consuet. conclus. 5. cum limit., embrace the affirmative opinion in various cases.

units.la: 3. Poterit consuetudo in genere definiti, per jus non scriptum, quod diuturni mores, tacito consensum utentium accedente, comprobarunt. Ut ad consuetudinem requirantur quatuor. 1. Ut adsit tacitus utentium consensus. 2. Ut sit justa & rationabilis. 3. Ut sit usus, seu mores. 4. Ut mores diuturni, seu longus usus. Giurba in proœm. consuet. Senatus Messanien. part. 1. num. 12. 13. 14. 15. & seqq.
units.tr: 3. A custom may be defined generally as unwritten law, which long-standing usage has confirmed with the tacit consent of those who use it. For a custom four things are required: (1) that there be tacit consent of the users; (2) that it be just and reasonable; (3) that there be use or practice; (4) that the practice be long-standing, or of long use. Giurba in proœm. consuet. Senatus Messanien. part. 1. num. 12. 13. 14. 15. & seqq.

units.la: 4. Primum requisitum erat tacitus utentium consensus; qualis est regulariter consensus universi populi, vel plerorumque, qui moraliter pro omnium consensu habetur. l. 32. D. legibus l. 3. D. quod cujusque univ. nomine. l. 2. D. decret. ab ordine fac. Ratio est, quia omne jus consensu latum est; etiam quod ipsa necessitas introduxit; quale Senatusconsultum, & responsa jurisconsultorum. Nec interest tacitus adsit consensus, an expressus. Ut quemadmodum in jure scripto desideratur expressus, simul & semel manifestatus, in consuetudine sufficiat tacitus; id est, qui reipsa, seu ipso facto paulatim tamen & pedetentim declaretur. l. 32. l. 39. D. de legibus. bus. Nec obst. l. pen. D. eod. Ubi jus quod consensus introduxit juri consuetudinario opponitur. Ibi quippe per consensum intelligit JC. expressum illum consensum, quo lex aut Plebiscitum, introducitur; ad oppositionem consensus taciti, in consuetudine desiderati. d. l. 32. Faber. in §. ex non scripto. num. 7. Instit. de jure natur. Gent. & civil. Mynsf. 6. obs. 41. n. 11. 12. Speckh. cent. 1. quaest. 73. n. 30. 31.
units.tr: 4. The first requirement is tacit consent of the users, which is ordinarily the consent of the whole people, or of most of them, who are morally held to stand for the consent of all. l. 32. D. legibus l. 3. D. quod cujusque univ. nomine. l. 2. D. decret. ab ordine fac. The reason is that all law is established by consent, even that which necessity itself introduced, such as a senatus-consultum and the answers of jurisconsults. Nor does it matter whether the consent is tacit or express. For while in written law express consent is required, made known at once and at a single time, in custom tacit consent suffices, that is, consent declared in fact, by the deed itself, yet gradually and step by step. l. 32. l. 39. D. de legibus. Nor does l. pen. D. eod. stand in the way, where law that consent has introduced is set against customary law. There the jurisconsult means by consent that express consent by which a law or plebiscite is introduced, in contrast to the tacit consent required in custom. d. l. 32. Faber. in §. ex non scripto. num. 7. Instit. de jure natur. Gent. & civil. Mynsf. 6. obs. 41. n. 11. 12. Speckh. cent. 1. quaest. 73. n. 30. 31.

units.la: 5. Nec tamen per consensum tacitum excluditur scriptura, quae recte ex post-facto superadvenit, ut eo certior sit consuetudo, & omnibus atque singulis innotescat magis; neque ignorantia possit allegari. Argum. l. 2. §. 4. verb. quas in tabulas. D. de Origin. jur. l. jubemus. 29. §. sed ne aliqua. Cod. de Testament. l. cum res 12. Cod. Probat. vid. Merul. libr. 1. Prax. civil. tit. 5. cap. 1.
units.tr: 5. Nor, however, is written record excluded by tacit consent. It may rightly be added afterwards, so that the custom may be more certain and become better known to all and to each, and so that ignorance cannot be pleaded. Argum. l. 2. §. 4. verb. quas in tabulas. D. de Origin. jur. l. jubemus. 29. §. sed ne aliqua. Cod. de Testament. l. cum res 12. Cod. Probat. vid. Merul. libr. 1. Prax. civil. tit. 5. cap. 1.

units.la: Ut eo ipso nomen consuetudinis non amittat; quod scriptura primordialem actus naturam non immutet, aut immutare queat; tantum mad hoc inventa, ut quod factum est, probetur melius. l. 4. in sin. D. Pignor. & hypothec. Arg. consuet. feudor. Vivius, decis. 240. n. 7. Bartol. Bald. Alexand. in l. 1. 2. D. vulg. substit. Cevall. quaest. comm. 357. n. 11. apud Giurbam in consuet. Senatus Messaviensis. Proem. part. 1. num. 25. Anton. Pichard. ad. §. 10. Instit. Testam. ordin. n. 23.
units.tr: 6. Yet error which is opposed to consent is not thereby excluded from custom. l. 15. D. de jurisdict. l. 39. D. de legibus. Nor does d. l. 39 stand in the way, since it is there sufficiently clear that an erroneous custom does not make law, when it is denied that such a custom holds in other similar cases. This, however, holds in those things which have the force of law. l. 12. D. de legibus. Besides, an erroneous custom is there called a custom only abusively, since it belongs not to law but to fact; such a custom one may rightly attribute even to brute animals. Arg. §. Pavorum. 15. Instit. de Rerum divis. Zoes. D. de offic. Prætor. It nevertheless has various limitations, Gabriel. comm. opinion. libr. 1. de Probat. conclus. 8. and the various authorities cited there.

units.la: 6. Ut tamen per consensum excludatur error, qui consensui adversatur. l. 15. D. de jurisdict. l. 39. D. de legibus. Neque obst. d. l. 39. Quia ibidem satis manifestum est, erroneam illam consuetudinem, jus non facere, quod negetur ea in aliis similibus obtinere. Id quod tamen obtinet in iis, quae habent vim legis. l. 12. D. de legibus. Praeterquam, quod consuetudo erronea, ibidem abusive appelletur consuetudo; ut quae non est juris, sed facti; qualem consuetudinem etiam merito brutis animantibus tribueris. Arg. §. Pavorum. 15. Instit. de Rerum divis. Zoes. D. de offic. Prætor. Habet tamen varias limitationes Gabriel. comm. opinion. libr. 1. de Probat. conclus. 8. ibique varii.
units.tr: 7. The second requisite of custom is that it be just and reasonable. For what has been introduced not by reason but by error does not hold in other similar cases. l. 39. D. de leg. c. ult. de consuet. Zasius after Bartolus on l. 32. D. de leg.; Mynsing. 6. observ. 41; Gail. 2. obs. 31. n. 11; Speckhan. cent. 1. quest. 73. num. 2; Bernegg. in Tacit. German. & Agricol. quest. ult.

units.la: 7. 2. Requisitum consuetudinis erat, ut sit justa & rationabilis. Quod enim non ratione sed errore introductum est, in aliis similibus non obtinet. l. 39. D. de leg. c. ult. de consuet. Zasius post Bartol. in l. 32. D. de leg. Mynsing. 6. observ. 41. Gail. 2. obs. 31. n. 11; Speckhan. cent. 1. quest. 73. num. 2. Bernegg. in Tacit. German. & Agricol. quest. ult.
units.tr: And just as no law has the force of law unless it is just, honourable and congruent with reason (since reason is the soul of law), so too a custom which imitates law will be a custom only if it is honourable and agrees with natural and divine law, or at least contains nothing opposed to it. Arg. l. 15. D. Condit. insit.

units.la: Et quemadmodum nulla lex vigorem legis habet, nisi quae justa, & honesta, & rationi congrua, quod ratio sit legis anima: Ita nec consuetudo, quae legem imitatur, erit consuetudo, nisi honesta, & juri naturali atque divino congrua; saltem quae ei non adversantur, contineat. Arg. l. 15. D. Condit. insit.
units.tr: Fit. c. erit. dist. 4. c. illas. dist. 15. Menoch. 2. Presumpt. 1. Tusc. litt. L. conclus. 252. n. 1; and Menoch. de Arbitr. 82. num. 17; Fontanell. de Pact. Anten. Clauf. 4. glos. 19. p. 2. n. 14; the doctors on c. sin. de Consuet.; Boër. decis. 132; Vivius decis. 66. n. 6.

units.la: Fit. c. erit. dist. 4. c. illas. dist. 1 5. Menoch. 2. Presumpt. 1. Tusc. litt. l. conclus. 252. n. 1. & Menoch. de Arbitr. 82. num. 17. Fontanell. de Pact. Anten. Clauf. 4. glos. 19. p. 2. n. 14. DD. ad c. sin. de Consuet. Boër. decis. 132. Vivius decis. 66. n. 6.
units.tr: Thus, if a custom is unjust, because it nourishes sin, it must be torn out as quickly as possible, lest it be drawn by the wicked into the force of a privilege or of law, as is the way. c. mala. distinct. 8.

units.la: Ut si iniqua, quia peccati nutritiva, citissime sit evellenda, ne in vim privilegii aut juris, uti moris est, ab impiis trahatur. c. mala. distinct. 8.
units.tr: For example, if an unjust custom, since it nourishes sin, must be most quickly uprooted, lest impious people draw it into the force of a privilege or of law, as is their habit. c. mala. distinct. 8.

units.la: 8. Si tamen de iniquitate consuetudinis inciderit dubium, & quidem in foro foli, ea res arbitrio judicis erit committenda. Scilicet, si videatur bonis moribus aut legibus civilibus adversari. vid. Meno.h. arbitr. judic. 2. caf. 82. Gail. 2. obf. 31. n. 13. Bacchov. ad Treutl. disp. 1. thes. 9. n. 9. litt. B.
units.tr: 8. If, however, doubt arises about the unfairness of a custom, and indeed in a court of law alone, the matter is to be left to the judge's discretion; namely, if the custom seems to be opposed to good morals or to civil laws. vid. Meno.h. arbitr. judic. 2. caf. 82. Gail. 2. obf. 31. n. 13. Bacchov. ad Treutl. disp. 1. thes. 9. n. 9. litt. B.

units.la: 9. Quod si quaeratur de consuetudine, num licita in conscientiâ, num juri naturæ ac divino repugnet, penes ecclesiasticas personas, congruenter sacræ Scripturæ regulis, vel legi morali, tanquam cujusdam casus conscientiæ erit decisio; ut quibus eloquia Dei sunt concredita, non judicibus terrenis; quorum mandata, aut jussa, ad naturalia & divina Præcepta sese non extendunt. Argum. l. 3. D. quæ sent. sine appell. rescind. vid. Gloss. in c. cum tanto. de Consuet. Benedict. de Capra in Tom. Comm. opin. v. consuet. p. 812.
units.tr: 9. If, however, the question is whether a custom is lawful in conscience, and whether it conflicts with natural or divine law, the decision on this matter, as a case of conscience, belongs to ecclesiastical persons, in agreement with the rules of Holy Scripture or the moral law. The oracles of God have been entrusted to them, not to earthly judges, whose commands or orders do not extend to natural and divine precepts. Argum. l. 3. D. quæ sent. sine appell. rescind. vid. Gloss. in c. cum tanto. de Consuet. Benedict. de Capra in Tom. Comm. opin. v. consuet. p. 812.

units.la: 10. 3. Requisitum consuetudinis erat, usus, seu mores utentium, quibus designatur requiri actus, ut introducatur consuetudo. Verum an unus actus sufficerit? Resp. Quod non: cum ne quidem actus a Principe gestus, introducat jus; multo minus a Privatis. init. instit. Codicil. Arg. l. 3. in sin. D. Offic. Prætor.
units.tr: 10. 3. The requisite of custom was usage, or the practice of those who use it, by which it is indicated that acts are required for a custom to be introduced. But is a single act sufficient? Answer: No. Not even an act performed by a Prince introduces law, much less one performed by private persons. init. instit. Codicil. Arg. l. 3. in sin. D. Offic. Prætor.

units.la: 11. An duo aut tres? Non equidem. Cum enim frequenter fieri dicatur, quod iterum atque sæpius, fit. Et illis vocibus plus quam secundus & tertius actus designetur. Etiam in consuetudine, plures quam duos aut tres desiderabimus. Quinimo licet adsit subditi cujusdam actus, & insuper actus Principis, penes quem summa potestas est, non tamen ex illis duobus actibus consuetudo formari poterit. init. instit. de Codicill. l. 1. Cod. quæ sit long. consuet. l. 3. Cod. de Ædif. Privat. l. 15. §. 22. D. injur.
units.tr: 11. Are two or three acts enough? Surely not. For when something is said to happen frequently, it is what happens again and again (sæpius). Those words designate more than a second and a third act. So even in custom we shall require more than two or three. Indeed, although there is an act of a subject and, in addition, an act of the Prince, in whom supreme power lies, a custom cannot be formed from those two acts. init. instit. de Codicill. l. 1. Cod. quæ sit long. consuet. l. 3. Cod. de Ædif. Privat. l. 15. §. 22. D. injur.

units.la: 12. Ut judicis arbitrio totum hoc negotium sit committendum. Arg. l. 1. D. de Jur. Deliberandi. Bartol. in l. 2. Cod. quæ sit long. consf. Duaren. ad tit. de legibus c. 11. Connan. 1. Comm. 10. n. 6. Mynsf. 6. obs. 41. num. 7. Bronchorst.
units.tr: 12. So the whole matter is to be committed to the judge's discretion. Arg. l. 1. D. de Jur. Deliberandi. Bartol. in l. 2. Cod. quæ sit long. consf. Duaren. ad tit. de legibus c. 11. Connan. 1. Comm. 10. n. 6. Mynsf. 6. obs. 41. num. 7. Bronchorst.

units.la: 1. Enant. 8. Bocerus class. 1. disp. 4. thes. 10. Speckhan. loc. antea citat. n. 28. Zoes. D. de leg. n. 6. & seqq. vid. Deßel. in notis ad Zoes. instit. de Jure Natural. Gent. & Civil. n. 27.
units.tr: 1. Enant. 8. Bocerus, class. 1, disp. 4, thes. 10. Speckhan, loc. cit. above, n. 28. Zoes, D. de leg., n. 6 and following. See Deßel, in the notes to Zoesius, Institutes, on natural, gentile and civil law, n. 27.

units.la: Nec obst. l. 12. D. de Testibus. Quod in probationibus judicialibus sufficiant duo testes, ubi frequentia, aut turba testium non requiritur. Uti nec obst. l. 3. Cod. Episc. Audient. Quia loquitur de assuefactione unius hominis, non totius universitatis. Neque c. abbas. de v. signif. Quia tantum loquitur narrative. Cujac. 20. obs. 1. Nisi quis ad objecta loca respondere malit cum Azon. in summ. Cod. quae sit long. conf. duos actus tum sufficere, cum populo aut Praesidi post duos actus placuit, sic judicandum esse in posterum. diss. ex parte Wurmser. nucleo juris controv. libr. 1. tit. 2. contr. 8. Et DD. admittunt actus duos, quando sunt notorii, & saepius non occurrunt aliter plures. Francisc. Vivius Comm. opin. libr. 2. opin. 75.
units.tr: Nor does l. 12. D. de Testibus stand in the way, which holds that two witnesses suffice in judicial proofs where a crowd or multitude of witnesses is not required. Nor does l. 3. Cod. Episc. Audient. stand in the way, because it speaks of the habituation of one man, not of a whole community. Nor does c. abbas, de v. signif., because it speaks only narratively. Cujacius, 20. obs. 1. Unless one prefers to answer the objected passages with Azo, in summ. Cod. quae sit long. conf., that two acts suffice when it has pleased the people or the President, after two acts, that it be so judged in future. diss. ex parte Wurmser. nucleo juris controv. libr. 1. tit. 2. contr. 8. And the doctors admit two acts when they are notorious and more do not otherwise often occur. Francisc. Vivius Comm. opin. libr. 2. opin. 75.

units.la: 13. Verum desiderabuntur ne plures actus judiciales, ut introducatur consuetudo? Neg.
units.tr: 13. But will more judicial acts be required in order for a custom to be introduced? No.

units.la: Nam quae solo consensu introducuntur, & quidem consensu tacito, praesentiam judicis non desiderant. Et quemadmodum lex introducitur, citra actum judiciarium, ita & consuetudo, quae legem imitatur. Ut si in lege de consensu constet per actum extra judicium, sic etiam de consensu in consuetudine constare possit. Ne dicam, quod in ll. ubi potissimum de consuetudine agitur, nulla fiat mentio judiciarii actus, & consuetudo a re judicata, separetur. Ut extra judicialibus abunde constituatur consuetudo. Modo ne sint difformes. l. 28. D. de Transf. Arg. l. si servus plurium. 50. §. sin. D. de leg. 1. l. 18. §. 1. 2. D. Instruct. vel instrum. legat. l. 32. l. 38. D. de legibus. Cujac. 10. obs. 1. Cevall. comm. contr. comm. q. 358. Baptista Villalob. in tom.
units.tr: For those things which are introduced by consent alone, and indeed by tacit consent, do not require the presence of a judge. Just as a law is introduced without a judicial act, so too custom, which imitates law. As consent in a law can be established by an act outside court, so consent in custom can also be established. Not to mention that in the laws where custom is chiefly treated, no mention is made of a judicial act, and custom is separated from a matter adjudged. So a custom is sufficiently established outside judicial proceedings, provided the acts are not inconsistent with one another. l. 28. D. de Transf. Arg. l. si servus plurium. 50. §. sin. D. de leg. 1. l. 18. §. 1. 2. D. Instruct. vel instrum. legat. l. 32. l. 38. D. de legibus. Cujac. 10. obs. 1. Cevall. comm. contr. comm. q. 358. Baptista Villalob. in tom.

units.la: E comm. opin. libr. 3. v. consuet. per Panormit. in c. sin. n. 16. de consuet. quem refert. Tiraq. de Primog. q. 91. in sin. Johan. Fichardus tom. comm. opin. libr. 3. v. consuet: Franc. Tursanus d. l. 3. v. consuetudo. ubi Cravett. consil. 55. n. 6. Burfat. 1. consil. 50. n. 27. Post eos. Mevius ad Lubec. quæst. Prælim. 7. n. 19. Mynsf. 6. observ. 41. in sin. Gail. 2. obs. 31. n. 8. in sin. Speckhan. centur. 1. q. 73. n. 29. Bronchorst. 1. Eniant. 10. Besold. oicon. jur. sit. 3. 4. libr. 1. Pand. n. 32. Bartol. in l. 2. Cod. quæ sit long Consuet. Mynsf 6. obs. 42. n. 3.
units.tr: From the Commentary on Opinions, book 3, under "consuetudo," by Panormitanus on c. sin., n. 16, de consuetudine, which Tiraquellus cites, De primogeniis, q. 91, at the end. Johannes Fichardus, Commentary on Opinions, tom. book 3, under "consuetudo." Franciscus Tursanus, on the same law, under "consuetudo," where Cravetta, Consilia 55, n. 6. Burfatus, Consilia 1, 50, n. 27. After them, Mevius on the Lübeck questions, Preliminary 7, n. 19. Myns. 6, Observations 41, at the end. Gail, 2, Observations 31, n. 8, at the end. Speckhan, Centuria 1, q. 73, n. 29. Bronchorst, 1 Enant. 10. Besold, Oeconomia juris, title 3, 4, book 1 of the Pandects, n. 32. Bartolus on l. 2 Cod. quae sit longa consuetudo. Myns. 6, Observations 42, n. 3.

units.la: 14. 4. Ad consuetudinem introducendam requisitum erat longus usus, mores diuturni, ut consuetudo sit inveterata. Neque enim subito enascitur, verum temporis aliquem requirit decursum. Hinc quæsitum, quod anni ad consuetudinem introducendam sint necessarii?
units.tr: 14. 4. For a custom to be introduced, a long usage was required, lasting customs, so that the custom is well established. For it does not arise suddenly, but requires some lapse of time. Hence the question arises how many years are necessary for introducing a custom.

units.la: 15. Sunt qui totidem annos requirunt, quot necessario requisiti ad præscriptionem, quam cum ipsa consuetudine confundunt. c. sin. de consuet. cum tamen manifestum sit, præscriptionem tantum jus acquirere præscribenti, consuetudinem omnibus in republica; eam esse juris strictissimi, hanc ad similia trahi & extendi; adversus eam minorem juvari, in quantum eâ non lædituer; adversus hanc eundem non juvari, adeoque per consuetudinem lædi posse. Negari tamen non poterit, quin quandoque præscriptione, vel tempore immemoriali, vetustate, introducatur consuetudo, adversus leges superioris. Cult. de consuet.
units.tr: 15. Some require as many years as are necessarily required for prescription, which they confuse with custom itself. Yet it is clear that prescription acquires a right only for the one prescribing, while custom binds everyone in the commonwealth; that custom is of the strictest law, and that it is extended and drawn to similar cases; that a minor is helped against it in so far as he is not harmed by it, but the same person is not helped against it, and so can be harmed by custom. Yet it cannot be denied that sometimes a custom is introduced against the laws of a superior by prescription, or by immemorial time, by antiquity. Cult. de consuet.

units.la: 16. Sunt qui requirunt decennium, quod illud tempus longum in jure appelletur Azo in summ. Cod. hic. Alexand. consil. 132. visa. vol. 1. Matth. Gribald. tom. Comm. opin. libr. 3. verb. Consuet. & Francisc. Vivius comm. opin. ibidem, & Baptist. Villalob. post gloss. in l. de quibus D. leg. & in l. 2. Cod. quae sit long. consuet. Benedict. de Capra tom. comm. opin. verb. consuetudo. p. 812. ibique varii. Donell. 1. comm. 10.
units.tr: 16. There are those who require ten years, because that period is called a "long time" in law. Azo, in the Summa on this title of the Code. Alexander, Consilia 132, seen in vol. 1. Matthaeus Gribaldus, tom. Commentary on Opinions, book 3, under "Consuetudo," and Franciscus Vivius, Commentary on Opinions, in the same place, and Baptista Villalobos, after the gloss on l. de quibus, D. de leg., and on l. 2 Cod. quae sit longa consuetudo. Benedictus de Capra, tom. Commentary on Opinions, under "consuetudo," p. 812, and the various writers there. Donellus, 1 Commentary 10.

units.la: 17. Sunt qui tempus immemoriale desiderant per l. 2. §. 1. D. Aquâ, & Aquâ Pluv. ibique DD.
units.tr: 17. Some require immemorial time. per l. 2. §. 1. D. Aquâ, & Aquâ Pluv. ibique DD.

units.la: 18. Sunt qui spatium centum annorum flagitant, quod hoc sit longissimum tempus vitæ humanæ. l. 56. D. Usufr. vid. Mynsf. 6. obs. 41. n. 9. 10. ibi Bartol. Bald. aliosque allegatos.
units.tr: 18. Some demand a space of a hundred years, since this is the longest span of human life. l. 56. D. Usufr. vid. Mynsf. 6. obs. 41. n. 9. 10. there Bartol. Bald. aliosque allegatos.

units.la: 19. Verum dicendum quantumcunque sufficere tempus, modo pluralis sit annorum numerus, cum actuum pluralitate & uniformitate conjunctus. Ut tamen hoc totum arbitrio judicis relictum malim. Arg. l. 1. D. jure deliber. Giurba ad Consuet. Messanensis in Proœm. p. 1. n. 14. post varios. Menoch. de Arbitr. cas. 83. n. 6. Coras. in l. 32. D. de legibus. Fachin. 7. cont. 67. Bronch. 1. Enant. 8. Bocerus, Class. 1. disp. 4. thes. 7. Specham. cent. 1. quæst. 73. n. 22. Befold. oicon. jur. ad tit. 3. 4. libr. 1. Pand. num. 13. Wurmser. Nucl. juris contr. libr. 1. tit. 2. controv. 8.
units.tr: 19. The truer view is that any length of time is sufficient, provided the number of years is plural and joined with a plurality and uniformity of acts. Yet I would prefer that this whole question be left to the judge's discretion. Arg. l. 1 D. de jure deliberandi. Giurba, on the Messina Customs, Proem. p. 1, n. 14, after various writers. Menochius, De arbitrariis casibus, 83, n. 6. Corasius, on l. 32 D. de legibus. Fachinus, Controversies 7, 67. Bronchorst, 1 Enant. 8. Bocerus, Class. 1, disp. 4, thes. 7. Speckhan, Cent. 1, quaest. 73, n. 22. Besold, Oeconomia juris, on title 3, 4, book 1 of the Pandects, n. 13. Wurmser, Nucleus juris controversi, book 1, title 2, controversy 8.

units.la: 20. Quid si dubitetur de consuetudine, num sit in usu, aut viridi observantia, uti loquuntur, quâ ratione, quove modo ea veniat probanda, multum disquiritur?
units.tr: 20. What if there is doubt whether a custom is in use, or in what they call "green observance"? By what reasoning or in what manner is it to be proved? This is much disputed.

units.la: Sunt qui statuunt, per testimonium viri excellentis consuetudinem probari posse; adeoque doctori eximio asserenti de consuetudine fidem esse adhibendam, secundum Decianum consil. 559. apud Matth. Gribald. in tom. comm. opin. libr. 3. verb. consuetudo. ubi plures.
units.tr: Some hold that a custom can be proved by the testimony of a distinguished man, and so the word of an eminent teacher asserting a custom is to be trusted, according to Decianus, consil. 559, cited in Matth. Gribald. in tom. comm. opin. libr. 3, verb. consuetudo, where there are many more.

units.la: Sunt qui dicto glossæ standum existumant, si de consuetudine testetur.
units.tr: Some think one should abide by the gloss, if it bears witness to the custom.

units.la: 21. Verum dicendum, & si negandum non sit multum tribui hic posse prætico eximio, in tantum, ut si quis ex peritioribus suo exemplo præcar, id agendo, quod consuetudini allegatæ, conforme est, sit præsumendum pro consuetudine; (exemplo Labeonis, qui cum fecisset codicillos, nulli dubium amplius erat, quin Codicilli optimo jure admitterentur. Init. Instit. de Codicill.)
units.tr: 21. But it must be said, and it cannot be denied, that a great deal of weight can be given here to an eminent practitioner, so far that if one of the more experienced, by his own example, acts in a way that conforms to the custom alleged, it is to be presumed in favour of the custom (by the example of Labeo, who, when he had made codicils, there was no longer any doubt that codicils were admitted by the best law). Init. Instit. de Codicill.

units.la: 22. Ut autem per testes consuetudo accurate probetur, quatuor à DD. requiruntur. Ut testes deponant de visu actus, cujus consuetudo allegatur. Quia plus est oculatus testis unus, quam auriti decem. Arg. §. fin. Instit. de Gradibus Cognat. Ut de frequentia actuum deponant; quod per dicta superius, plures actus de siderentur. Ut temporis poris diuturnitatem intervenisse deponant, quo consuetudo dicatur longa. Denique edoceant actus varios sic adhibitos fuisse, ut appareat, saltem consensum populi tacitum intervenisse; ne clam commissum consuetudinem operetur. Decian. Consil. 483. Matth. Gribald. in tom. comm. Opinion. libr. 3. verb. consuetudo. Emanuel Soares Thesaur. Recept. Sent. verb. consuetudo, ibique varii.
units.tr: 22. In order that a custom be accurately proved through witnesses, the doctors require four things. First, that the witnesses depose from sight of the act whose custom is alleged, because one eyewitness is worth more than ten who heard. Arg. §. fin. Instit. de Gradibus Cognat. Second, that they depose to the frequency of the acts, which the testimonies set out above, where several acts are described, make clear. Third, that they testify that a lengthy stretch of time has passed, by which the custom is called long. Finally, that they show the acts were performed in such a way that at least the tacit consent of the people appears to have intervened, so that something done in secret does not create a custom. Decian. Consil. 483. Matth. Gribald. in tom. comm. Opinion. libr. 3. verb. consuetudo. Emanuel Soares Thesaur. Recept. Sent. verb. consuetudo, and there various authors.

units.la: 23. Licet autem probetur sufficienter consuetudo, si de actubus extrajudicialibus satis constet; promptissime tamen per actus judiciales (non tamen si semel intra 10. vel 20. annos ita fuerit judicatum) eandem probari, statuendum erit. Quo refero l. 34. D. de legibus, l. 1. Cod. Qua sit long. Consuet. AZain summ. Cod. hic. signo *, in additamentis. & litt. a. in addit. Coras. ad l. 34. de legibus.
units.tr: 23. Although a custom is sufficiently proved if the extrajudicial acts are sufficiently established, it must nonetheless be laid down that it is proved most readily by judicial acts (though not if a judgment was given only once within 10 or 20 years). To this I refer l. 34. D. de legibus, l. 1. Cod. Qua sit long. Consuet. Azo, Summa Cod., here, under the sign *, in the additions, and letter a in the additions; Coras. ad l. 34. de legibus.

units.la: CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: 1. Consuetudo non minores habet vires, quam lex.
units.tr: 1. Custom has no less force than law.

units.la: 2 Interpretatur legem, contractum, testamentum, &c.
units.tr: 2. It interprets law, contract, testament, etc.

units.la: 3. Quandoque a lege superatur.
units.tr: 3. Sometimes it is overridden by law.

units.la: 4. Quandoque legem superat.
units.tr: 4. Sometimes it overrides law.

units.la: 2. In specie autem consuetudo legis verba ambigua interpretatur. l. 37. de legibus. c. cum dilectus. de Consuet. Et si non appareat, quid actum sit inter contrahentes, ad eam, tanquam rerum ac verborum dominam recurritur, l. Semper in stipulationibus. D. Reg. jur. Quam etiam in perscrutandâ testatoris voluntate, l. 50. §. 3. D. legi. 1. l. 18. §. 3. 3. in sin. D. Instruct. vel instrum. In exquirendâ rationum fide, l. 9. §. 2. in sin. D. Edend. In probandi modo, aliisque multis in casibus, sequimur l. 3. in sin. D. de Testibus, l. 6. D. de Evict. Johann. Bellonus in Tom. Comm. Opin. libr. 3. verb. consuet. p. 63. Pacius 1. Enant. 15. Mantic. de Tacit. & Ambig. libr. 3. tit. 9. Connan. 6. comm. 3. Claud. Cantiunc. Topic. legal. loc. cit.
units.tr: 2. In particular, custom interprets ambiguous words of law. l. 37. de legibus. c. cum dilectus. de Consuet. And if it does not appear what was agreed between the contracting parties, recourse is had to custom as the mistress of things and words. l. Semper in stipulationibus. D. Reg. jur. Custom is likewise used in searching out the will of a testator, l. 50. §. 3. D. legi. 1. l. 18. §. 3. 3. in sin. D. Instruct. vel instrum. in inquiring into the good faith of accounts, l. 9. §. 2. in sin. D. Edend. and in the mode of proof and many other cases. We follow it there, l. 3. in sin. D. de Testibus, l. 6. D. de Evict. Johann. Bellonus in Tom. Comm. Opin. libr. 3. verb. consuet. p. 63. Pacius 1. Enant. 15. Mantic. de Tacit. & Ambig. libr. 3. tit. 9. Connan. 6. comm. 3. Claud. Cantiunc. Topic. legal. loc. cit.

units.la: 3. Verum an consuetudo à lege superari poterit, tanquam à fortiori? Respondeo, si lex sit consuetudine posterior, eique directè adversetur, consuetudo superari poterit, adeoque per legem abrogari. Constitutiones quippe tempore posteriores potiores sunt hisce, quæ ipsas antecesserunt. l. sin. D. Princip. Constit. Vid. Hillig. ad Donell. 1. comm. 10. litt. i.
units.tr: 3. But can custom be overridden by law, as by something stronger? I answer: if the law is later than the custom and directly opposes it, the custom can be overridden and so abrogated by the law. Indeed, later constitutions take precedence over those which went before them. l. sin. D. Princip. Constit. Vid. Hillig. ad Donell. 1. comm. 10. litt. i.

units.la: Censent nihilominus DD. de jure canonum, legem generalem posteriorem non tollere specialem loci consuetudinem, cui adversatur. Quasi præsumendum sit legislatorem particulares ignorasse consuetudines, adeoque nec eas revocasse. c. 1. de constit. in 6. Bartol. ad l. 32. D. de legibus, lect. 2. n. 5. Covarr. 3. variar. Resol. cap. 13. n. 4. circa sin.
units.tr: Nevertheless the doctors of canon law hold that a later general law does not abolish a special custom of a place to which it is opposed, as if it were to be presumed that the legislator was ignorant of particular customs and therefore did not revoke them. c. 1. de constit. in 6. Bartol. ad l. 32. D. de legibus, lect. 2. n. 5. Covarr. 3. variar. Resol. cap. 13. n. 4. circa sin.

units.la: 4. An vice versâ unquam consuetudo vincet legem? Respondeo, si generalis sit consuetudo, & lege posterior, eam superabit: lex enim posterior abrogat priorem, si fit prioris correctoria. Consuetudinem autem cum lege parificari, antea fuit demonstratum. Ut consuetudo ejusdem cum lege sit efficaciæ. l. 3 2. l. 3 5. D. de legibus. l. sin. D. Princ. Constit. libr. 2. feudor. tit. 1. §. legum autem. Neque obst. l. 3. §. divus, D. Sepulchr. Violat. Quia non agit de consuetudine adversus legem introductâ, verum de statuto municipali, cui nulla vis est tributa superandæ Principis constitutioni. Non itidem obst, l. 2. Cod. Quæ sit longa Consuet. Quia d. Const. locum habet in statu Monarchico; in quo uti nulla est populi auctoritas, ita nulla vis consuetudinis, per tacitum populi consensum introducendæ. l. 3 2. in sin. D. de legibus. Cum solius sit Principis in regno leges ferre, easque interpretari. l. sin, Cod. de legibus. Tiraquell. de jure Primogenit q. 16. Cravett. consil. 969. n. 3. Bachov. ad Treutl. disp. 1. thes. 9. litt. D. Si tamen Princeps consuetudinem suâ confirmaverit auctoritate, eamque servari voluerit, tum demum ea vim legis in principatu est habitura, ut tamen ad jus scriptum seu sancitum referri debeat; quod simul & semel ab eo comprobatum, qui legis sanciendæ habet potestatem. Quo referri meo judicio non incongrue poterunt, Consuetudines jussu Ducis Albani collectæ, & in nonnullis Belgii Provinciis receptæ. Arg. Init. Instit. de Codicill. l. 1. Cod. Quæ sit long. consuet. l. 3. Cod. eod. vid. Baldum. in
units.tr: 4. Conversely, can custom ever prevail over law? I answer: if the custom is general and later than the law, it will overcome it, for a later law abrogates an earlier one if it is corrective of it. Now, it has been shown above that custom is to be equated with law, so that it has the same efficacy. l. 32. l. 35. D. de legibus. l. sin. D. Princ. Constit. libr. 2. feudor. tit. 1. §. legum autem. Nor does l. 3. §. divus, D. Sepulchr. Violat. stand in the way, because it does not treat of a custom introduced against law, but of a municipal statute, to which no force has been given to overcome a Prince's constitution. Nor does l. 2. Cod. Quæ sit longa Consuet. stand in the way, because that constitution has its place in a monarchical state. In such a state, as there is no authority of the people, so there is no force in custom introduced by the tacit consent of the people, since in a kingdom it belongs to the Prince alone to make laws and to interpret them. l. 32. in sin. D. de legibus. l. sin, Cod. de legibus. Tiraquell. de jure Primogenit. q. 16. Cravett. consil. 969. n. 3. Bachov. ad Treutl. disp. 1. thes. 9. litt. D. If, however, the Prince has confirmed a custom by his own authority and wished it to be observed, then at last it will have the force of law in the principality, yet it ought to be referred to written or sanctioned law, which has been approved once and for all by him who has the power of enacting law. To this class, in my judgment, the customs gathered by order of the Duke of Alba and received in some provinces of Belgium may not inappropriately be referred. Arg. Init. Instit. de Codicill. l. 1. Cod. Quæ sit long. consuet. l. 3. Cod. eod. vid. Baldum. in

units.la: Constant. ad sin. Lyclam. Membr. Eclog. 11. Cujac. 5. obs. 2. Donell. 1. comm. 10. Bronchorst. 1. Enant. 9. Befold. Oicon. jur. tit. 3. & 4. libr. 1. Pand. n. 29. 30. -- Vid. de Consuet. Ducis Albani. Radelant. decis cur. Ultraj. 3 1. Neostad. decis. Supremi Senat. 10.
units.tr: Constant. ad sin. Lyclam. Membr. Eclog. 11. Cujac. 5. obs. 2. Donell. 1. comm. 10. Bronchorst. 1. Enant. 9. Besold. Oicon. jur. tit. 3. & 4. libr. 1. Pand. n. 29. 30. -- Vid. de Consuet. Ducis Albani. Radelant. decis cur. Ultraj. 31. Neostad. decis. Supremi Senat. 10.

units.la: SECT. III. CAP. III.
units.tr: SECT. III. CAP. III.

units.la: 1. Quid sit stylus Curiæ?
units.tr: 1. What is the style of the Court?

units.la: 2. Qui probetur stylus Curis?
units.tr: 2. Which style is approved by the Court?

units.la: 3. Quandoque stylus Curiæ spectat litis decisoria.
units.tr: 3. The style of the Court sometimes concerns the deciding of suits.

units.la: 1. QUandoquidem consuetudinis species est stylus Curiæ, quam Imperator Justinianus formam & observantiam appellat, summis digitis, & quasi per indicem ipsam attingere mihi visum; quod aliqualis ejusdem cognitio, non contemnendum in foro præstet usum.
units.tr: 1. Since the style of the Court is a kind of custom, which the Emperor Justinian calls the form and observance, I thought I should touch on it lightly, as it were with the fingertips and by pointing. A certain knowledge of it is of no small use in the courts.

units.la: Estque stylus ille, nihil aliud, quam consuetudo, circa juris processum, seu modum procedendi in Curiâ servata. Ut non tam spectet momentum causæ, quam modum seu rationem instruendi litem. Sunt enim in jure duo consideranda, litis ordinatoria, & litis decisoria. Ad illa refertur stylus Curiæ, non ad hæc; quę ex legibus, & alio jure certo petenda. Vid. Zasium in l. 32. p. 76. n. 35. D. de legibus.
units.tr: That style is nothing other than custom concerning legal procedure, or the manner of proceeding observed in the Court. It concerns not so much the substance of the case as the manner or method of conducting the suit. For in law two things are to be considered: the ordering of the suit and the deciding of the suit. The style of the Court belongs to the former, not the latter, which are to be sought from the laws and other certain law. See Zasius on l. 32, p. 76, n. 35, D. de legibus.

units.la: 2. Quia vero Stylus ille Curiæ apertius in quotidiano judiciorum usu, in ipsis rerum documentis apparet, ideo hic maxime fidem merebuntur, Practici eximii qui in foro diu multumque versati sunt. Ut tamen ad eum probandum non unius licet præclari satis sufficiat auctoritas, verum plurium requiratur assertio, idque argumento eorum, quæ de probandâ consuetudine antea dicta fuerunt. §. fin. Instit. Satisfdat.
units.tr: 2. But because that style of the Court appears more plainly in the daily practice of the courts and in the very records of the cases, therefore the practitioners who have been long and much engaged in the courts deserve the greatest trust here. Yet to prove it, the authority of one outstanding man is not enough; the agreement of several is required, and this by the argument of what was said earlier about proving a custom. § fin. Inst. Satisdat.

units.la: Et quemadmodum istum procedendi modum ad unguem tenere, res est difficillima; ita habent Patroni causarum disertissimi, secundum Merulam, quod discant indices, ante forte non observatum. Vid. §. fin. Instit. de Satisdat. l. 2. Cod. Quemadm. testam. aperiant. l. 2. Cod. de bon. vacant. gloss. & DD. in c. Ecclesia sanctæ Mariæ. de Constit. apud Franciscum Vivium in Tom. comm. Opin. libr. 3. verb. consuet. Bald in l. 1. in fin. Cod. Quæ sit long. consuet. Gail. 1 obs. 65. n. 8. Petr. Paul. Parisius. in c. Illud autem. de Prescript. Tom. 4. Repet. jur. canon. n. 2. p. 256. ibique Fel. Abb. in c. ex litteris. de Constit. Treutl. part. 1. disp. 1. thes. 9. litt. a. Menoch. 2. Præsumpt. 8. n. 14. cum seqq. Everhard. in loc. à stylo curiæ. Merul. Prax. civil. libr. 1. c. 2. tit. 5. & DD. ad l. ult. in fin. Cod. de Injur. Goris adversf. 3. cap. 7. n. 5. Joseph. Ludov. decis. Lucens. 36.
units.tr: And just as it is very difficult to keep to that mode of proceeding exactly, so, according to Merula, the most eloquent advocates are in the habit of studying the indexes, which perhaps had not been noticed before. See §. fin. Inst. de Satisdatione; l. 2 Cod. Quemadmodum testamenta aperiantur; l. 2 Cod. de bonis vacantibus, gloss. and the Doctors on c. Ecclesia sanctae Mariae, de Constitutionibus; with Francis Vivius in the Commentary on Opinions, book 3, s.v. consuetudo; Bartolus on l. 1 in fin. Cod. Quae sit longa consuetudo; Gail, 1 obs. 65, n. 8; Peter Paul Parisius on c. Illud autem, de Praescriptionibus, Tom. 4 Repetitiones juris canonici, n. 2, p. 256, and there Felinus Abbas on c. ex litteris, de Constitutionibus; Treutler, part 1, disp. 1, thes. 9, lit. a; Menochius, 2 Praesumptiones, 8, n. 14 and following; Everhard, s.v. a stylo curiae; Merula, Praxis civilis, book 1, c. 2, tit. 5, and the Doctors on l. ult. in fin. Cod. de Injuriis; Goris, Adversaria 3, c. 7, n. 5; Joseph Ludovicus, Decisiones Lucenses 36.

units.la: 3. Dixi stylum Curiæ spectare litis ordinatoria, natoria, non decisoria. Nonnunquam tamen, quæ exceptio est à regulâ, ad litis decisoria stylus Curiæ referri poterit, in quantum respicit probandi modum & efficaciam; puta ut credatur tali instrumento, vel non credatur, ut libris mercatorum plena vel semiplena fides tribuatur; & in aliis similibus casubus. Argum. l. Quedam. §. Nummularios. D. Edendo, l. 3. in sin. D Testibus, post Bartolum in l. Ictus fustium. D. Qui notant infam. Baldum in l. 1. Cod. Quæ sit long. consuet. Franciscus Vivius in tom. comm. Opin. libr. 3. verb. consuetudo.
units.tr: 3. I have said that the style of the Court concerns the ordering of suits, not their decision. Sometimes, however, which is an exception to the rule, the style of the Court may be referred to the deciding of suits, insofar as it regards the mode and force of proof: for example, whether a particular document is to be believed or not believed, as when full or half proof is given to merchants' books; and in other similar cases. By argument from l. Quaedam, §. Nummularios, D. de edendo; l. 3 in fin. D. de testibus; after Bartolus on l. Ictus fustium, D. qui notantur infamia; Baldus on l. 1 Cod. Quae sit longa consuetudo; Francis Vivius in the Commentary on Opinions, book 3, s.v. consuetudo.

units.la: SECT. III. CAP. IV.
units.tr: SECT. III. CAP. IV.

units.la: 1. Æquitas commendatur.
units.tr: 1. Equity is commended.

units.la: 2. Distinguitur à dispensatione.
units.tr: 2. It is distinguished from dispensation.

units.la: 3. Est juris portio.
units.tr: 3. It is a part of law.

units.la: 4. Et quidem juris non scripti. 5. 6. Variæ proponuntur æquitatis acceptiones. (ostenditur. 7. Quî occasione æquitas sit introducta 8. Quid sit æquitas? 9. An juri communi contraria? 10. An ab omnibus judicibus adhibenda?
units.tr: 4. And indeed of unwritten law. 5. 6. Various meanings of equity are set out (as shown). 7. By what occasion equity was introduced. 8. What is equity? 9. Is it contrary to the common law? 10. Is it to be employed by all judges?

units.la: i. ALtera Species juris non scripti erat æquitas; quæ cum non adeo cuivis obvia, à paucis intellecta satis, à paucioribus exercita, tutius tamen est in eâ versari, etiam utilius, quam in variis juris subtilitatibus, Oldend. in formul. investig. Action. magisque; in explicatione statutorum ea locum obtinet, quam apices juris; de ipsâ, quantum ad explicationem ejus naturæ satis est, agendum erit.
units.tr: i. Another kind of unwritten law was equity. Since it is not so readily available to everyone, understood by few, and practised by still fewer, it is nevertheless safer and more useful to be conversant with it than with the various subtleties of the law. It holds a place in the explanation of statutes greater than the minutiae of the law. Oldendorp in Formulae investigationis actionum. Concerning equity itself, as far as is enough to explain its nature, something must now be said.

units.la: 2. Quæ licet aliqualem cum dispensatione convenientiam habeat, non tamen erit cum eâ confundenda. Dispensatio quippe Majestaticis annumeratur, soli Principi concessa. Interpretatio secundum æquitatem etiam judicibus tributa. Illa locum habet, etiam si manifestus sit legis sensus; adeoque & contra legem. Hæc vero legis sensum in mitiorem partem trahit, dum ejus contrarium non apparet. Ut si lex sit clara; licet iniquè scripta, eam judex contemnere nequeat, aut contra eandem judicare. l. 12. in Princ. D. qui & à quibus Manum. l. 1. Cod. de leg. l. nemo judex. Cod. Sent. & interloc. Fachin. 1. contr.
units.tr: 2. Although equity has some agreement with dispensation, it is not to be confused with it. Dispensation is counted among the rights of majesty and is granted to the Prince alone; interpretation according to equity is granted also to judges. The former applies even where the sense of the law is manifest, and so even against the law. The latter draws the sense of the law to the milder side, so long as the contrary does not appear. So, if a law is clear, though it is written unjustly, a judge cannot disregard it or give judgment against it. l. 12 in princ. D. qui et a quibus manumittuntur; l. 1 Cod. de legibus; l. nemo judex, Cod. de sententiis et interlocutionibus; Fachin. 1 contr.

units.la: 3. In antecessum vero inquirendum erit: Num æquitas sit aliqua juris portio? Respondendum, quod ita. Tum quia inter se se opponuntur; jus æquum & iniquum. Tum quia eam complectitur jurisprudentia, prositetur jurisconsultus, sibi in judicando propositam habet judex, eamque stricto[?] juri prælatam debet. l. 1. in init. & §. 1. D. de just. juft. & jure. l. 32. D. Rebus credit. l. 4. §. 1. D. de eo quod certo loc. dari oport. l. 91. §. 3. D. v. oblig. l. 8. Cod. de Judic. Bodin. juris univ. distrib. p. 14. Wurmf. Nucl. jur. contr. tit. 1. libr. 1. contr. 7. n. 17.
units.tr: 3. But first it must be inquired: is equity some part of law? It must be answered that it is. Both because the just law and the unjust are set against one another; and because jurisprudence embraces it, the jurist professes it, the judge has it before him in judging, and ought to set it above strict law. l. 1 in init. and §. 1 D. de justitia et jure; l. 32 D. de rebus creditis; l. 4 §. 1 D. de eo quod certo loco dari oportet; l. 91 §. 3 D. de verborum obligationibus; l. 8 Cod. de iudiciis; Bodin, de iuris universi distributione, p. 14; Wurmser, Nucleus iuris controversi, tit. 1, lib. 1, contr. 7, n. 17.

units.la: 4. Verum an portioni juris scripti, an non scripti, annumeranda? Retuli eam in mea distributione ad jus non scriptum. Dependet quippe æquitatis ratio, ex solâ animi deliberatione, secundum negotiorum circumstantias, infinitis modis variantes. Unde etiam in jure nostro tanquam invicem opposita considerantur æquitas & jus scriptum. Quod in tantum etiam verum est, ut si scribatur æquitas, nomen & naturam suam mutet. l. 12. §. 5. D. de Aquâ & Aquâ pluv. l. 7. in Princ. D. de Usur. l. 16. D. de Condit. & demonstr. Connan. 1. Comm. 11. Donell. 1. comm. 13. Duaren. 2. disp. Anniv. 18. Bronch. 1. Antin. 7. Petr. Faber in l. 90. D. Reg. jur. Gotefred. ad l. 8. Cod. judic. diss. Wurmser. Nucl. jur. contr. libr. 1. tit. 1. contr. 7. n. 65. & seqq. ibique plurimi. Jure nihilominus canonico æquitatem aliquam scriptam admittunt. vid. Duaren. d disp. Pezel. ad Melanton. in 8. de legibus Politic. p. mihi. 656.
units.tr: 4. But is equity to be counted as part of written law or of unwritten law? I have placed it, in my own division, under unwritten law. For the reasoning of equity depends solely on the deliberation of the mind, according to the circumstances of affairs, which vary in infinite ways. Hence in our law also equity and written law are considered as opposed to each other. This is true to such an extent that if equity is written down, it changes its name and its nature. l. 12 §. 5 D. de aqua et aquae pluviae arcendae; l. 7 in princ. D. de usuris; l. 16 D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus; Connanus, 1 Comm. 11; Donellus, 1 comm. 13; Duaren, 2 disp. Anniv. 18; Bronchorst, 1 Antinomies 7; Petrus Faber on l. 90 D. de regulis juris; Gothofredus on l. 8 Cod. de iudiciis, diss.; Wurmser, Nucleus iuris controversi, lib. 1, tit. 1, contr. 7, n. 65 and following; and there very many others. Nevertheless, by canon law they admit some written equity. See Duaren, d. disp.; Pezelius on Melanchthon, De legibus politicis, p. 656.

units.la: 5. Sed ut natura æquitatis magis innotescat, præmittendæ erunt duæ ejusdem acceptiones nostro instituto inservientes; relictis aliis, quas apud Althus. dicajol. libr. 1. c. 16 n. 16. n. 17. & 21. 22. reperire licebit. Certum enim aliquod jus semper esse æquum, idque sic appellari, quod ei conjuncta sit aliqua benignitas, id est ratio æqua, quæ tale jus suadeat. Nec tum distinguetur jus æquum, à jure naturali, gentium aut civili scripto. Quo etiam nomine exceptiones per æquitatem introductæ dicuntur etiam nonnullæ conditiones, licet sint juris civilis scripti, vel Prætorii. Init. Instit. de Exept. l. pen. in init. D. de Just. & jure. l. 14. l. 66. D. de Indeb. Cond.
units.tr: 5. But so that the nature of equity may become better known, two of its meanings serving my present purpose must be set out first; the others, which may be found in Althusius, Dicaeologica, book 1, c. 16, nn. 16, 17, and 21, 22, I leave aside. For there is always some law which is equitable, and it is called so because some kindness is joined to it, that is, a reasonable ground which recommends such a law. Nor is equitable law then distinguished from natural law, the law of nations, or written civil law. By this name also some conditions introduced through equity are called equitable, even though they belong to written civil law or to the praetorian law. Init. Inst. de exceptionibus; l. pen. in init. D. de justitia et jure; l. 14, l. 66 D. de indebito condictione.

units.la: 6. Aliter dein jus æquum dicitur, quod juri civili scripto, & quidem stricto, contradistinguitur, quod jus strictum Græcis ἀχεῖροδικαιον appellatur. Et habet locum, vel cum leges scriptæ, nimium severæ, & sine ullo moderamine positæ sunt, propter aliquam utilitatem publicam, quæ commodis anteponenda privatorum. l. 51. §. 2. v. quod si quis. D. Ad l. Aquil. l. 12. in init. D. Qui & quibus de caus. manum.
units.tr: 6. Equity is also taken in another sense, in which it is contrasted with written civil law, and strictly so. The Greeks call this strict law [ἀχεῖροδικαιον]. It applies when written laws are too severe and have been laid down without any moderation, for some public utility that is to be preferred to the advantages of private persons. l. 51. §. 2. v. quod si quis. D. Ad l. Aquil. l. 12. in init. D. Qui & quibus de caus. manum.

units.la: Vel cum leges per interpretationem sine ullo temperamento aut moderamine ad casus similes trahuntur, in quibus tamen ratione circumstantiarum est aliqua dissimilitudo; ut duriore interpretatione contra civium commodum trahantur ad severitatem. l. nulla, 25. D. de leg. l. 11. in init. D. de Pæn.
units.tr: Or it applies when laws are extended by interpretation, without any tempering or moderation, to similar cases in which, nevertheless, there is some dissimilarity because of the circumstances, so that by a harsher interpretation they are drawn to severity against the advantage of the citizens. l. nulla, 25. D. de leg. l. 11. in init. D. de Pæn.

units.la: Vel cum fraus fit legi, & salvis verbis legis, ejus sententia circumvenitur. Id quod à sophisophistis, & sycophantis fieri solet, qui nimis acutè leges intuentur. l. 19. 29. 30. D. de leg. l. 13. D. quod met causf. l. pen. D. Ad Exhibend. Auth. de litigiosis. §. omnes autem.
units.tr: Or it applies when a fraud is committed against the law, and while its words are kept, its sense is circumvented. This is what sophists and sycophants are accustomed to do, who look too sharply at the laws. l. 19. 29. 30. D. de leg. l. 13. D. quod met causf. l. pen. D. Ad Exhibend. Auth. de litigiosis. §. omnes autem.

units.la: 7. Duabus postremis juris rigidi acceptionibus consideratis, apparet satis, quâ ratione, quâve occasione jus æquum sit introductum; scil. suadente necessitate. Neque enim omnes casus, qui emergunt quotidie, legibus comprehendi poterunt. l. 10. l. 12. D. de legibus. Et natura indies novas formas edere deproperat. l. 2. §. 18. Cod. vet. jure Enucleand. Et quoniam leges generaliter latæ, casui singulari propter variationem circumstantiarum applicari forte nequeunt, interpretatione benigna tum statuendum erit, quod oportet. l. 11. D. de leg.
units.tr: 7. With the two last senses of rigid law considered, it is clear enough on what ground and for what occasion equity was introduced, namely, because necessity demanded it. For not all the cases that arise every day can be comprehended by laws. l. 10. l. 12. D. de legibus. And nature hastens to produce new forms each day. l. 2. §. 18. Cod. vet. jure Enucleand. And since laws laid down in general terms may by chance be unable to be applied to a singular case because of the variation of circumstances, then by a kindly interpretation what ought to be done must be determined. l. 11. D. de leg.

units.la: 8. Ut æquitas nihil aliud sit, quam juris universalis in certis casubus, in quibus illud vel contrarium est, vel deficit moderatrix; id ipsum propter circumstantias faciens quod ipse legislator, si adesset, facturus fuisset. Vel interpretatione quid statuendo certius; vel leges interpretando benignius; vel legis verbis neglectis, vim atque potestatem intuendo. l. pen. §. Prator etiam. D. Justit. & jure l. 2. §. 5. D. Aquâ & Aquâ pluv. l. 32. D Reb. credit. l. 18. D Ædil. Edict. l. 11. l. 17. l. 18. D. de legibus.
units.tr: 8. So equity is nothing other than the moderating of universal law in certain cases, in which that law is either contrary or deficient, doing on account of the circumstances the very thing the legislator himself would have done had he been present. This is done either by determining something more certainly through interpretation, or by interpreting laws more kindly, or, the words of the law being set aside, by looking to its force and power. l. pen. §. Prator etiam. D. Justit. & jure l. 2. §. 5. D. Aquâ & Aquâ pluv. l. 32. D Reb. credit. l. 18. D Ædil. Edict. l. 11. l. 17. l. 18. D. de legibus.

units.la: 9. Dixi, jus universale quandoque contrarium esse ejus quod per æquitatem deciditur.
