Non quidem in thesi; quod legi in thesi, & generaliter latæ non sit contrariandum, licet dura sit. l. 12. in init. D. qui & à quibus manum. verum in hypothesi, id est ratione circumstantiarum, quæ faciunt illius legis observationem in casu incidenti declinare, seu deficere. Ita verbi gratiâ, lex naturæ exigit, ut depositum repetenti restituatur. l. 1. D. depositi. Quid si itaque qui sanus, & compos mentis gladium depositerit, eumque furibundus repetat? Quid si criminis capitalis reus, quæ ante reatum fidei alicujus commendaverat, repetat? Quid si quæ spolia custodienda tradidit, sibi restitui velit? Nec illi gladius, nec isti bona, nec huic spolia sunt reddenda. l. 31. D. Depositi. vid. Alciat. 1. de verb. signif. n. 21.
units.tr: 9. I have said that universal law is sometimes contrary to what is decided through equity. Not indeed in thesi, for a law laid down in thesi and in general terms is not to be opposed, even if it is harsh. l. 12. in init. D. qui & à quibus manum. But it is so in hypothesi, that is, by reason of the circumstances which make the observance of that law decline or fail in an incident case. Thus, for example, the law of nature requires that a deposit be restored to the one who asks for it. l. 1. D. depositi. What if, then, someone who was sound and of sound mind deposited a sword, and a madman demands it back? What if a man accused of a capital crime demands back what he had entrusted to someone's faith before the charge? What if someone who handed over spoils to be kept wishes them to be restored to himself? Neither is the sword to be returned to the first, nor goods to the second, nor spoils to the third. l. 31. D. Depositi. vid. Alciat. 1. de verb. signif. n. 21.

units.la: Neque hic peccatur adversus legem, quia non adversus intentionem legislatoris, ut qui si adesset, vel tale quid eventurum prævidisset, facturus idem fuisset.
units.tr: Nor is a sin committed here against the law, because it is not against the intention of the legislator, who, if he were present, or had foreseen that such a thing would happen, would have done the same.

units.la: Quod dictum, si lex deficiat, aut declinet, æquitatis haberi rationem, id indistincte tamen admittendum non est, ne aliter leges inextricabili labyrintho implicentur.
units.tr: This being said, that if the law is deficient or declines, account is to be taken of equity, yet this is not to be admitted indiscriminately, lest the laws otherwise be entangled in an inextricable labyrinth.

units.la: Aut igitur lex deficit, quia generaliter lata, secundum DD. contrarie. Quando scilicet non tantum cessat ipsa legis ratio, sed & iniquè ageretur, si lex servaretur. Aut deficit lex, quia, universaliter lata est negative, in quantum incidit casus, in quo cessat legis ratio. Aut denique lex deficit, propter ambiguitatem, vel obscuritatem. Duobus prioribus casibus, æquitatis ratio juri strićto præferenda, atque à judice adhibenda. l. 8. Cod. de judic. l. 4. §. 1. D. de eo quod certo loc. l. 25. D. donat. l. 11. D. Servit. Præd. Ru- stic. l. 36. D. verb. oblig. l. in omnibus. 90. l. 143. D. Reg. jur.
units.tr: Either, then, the law is deficient because it was laid down in general terms, which according to the Doctors is the contrary case: namely, when not only the reason of the law has ceased, but it would also be unjust to act if the law were kept. Or the law is deficient because it is laid down universally in a negative way, insofar as a case falls in which the reason of the law ceases. Or finally the law is deficient on account of ambiguity or obscurity. In the two former cases, the reason of equity is to be preferred to strict law and applied by the judge. l. 8. Cod. de judic. l. 4. §. 1. D. de eo quod certo loc. l. 25. D. donat. l. 11. D. Servit. Præd. Rustic. l. 36. D. verb. oblig. l. in omnibus. 90. l. 143. D. Reg. jur.

units.la: Postremo casu, quo lex est dubia, aut obscura, non judicis partes, verum Magistratus supremi aut Principis interponendæ; cujus solius erit, inter æquitatem & jus rigidum interpretationem adhibere. l.
units.tr: In the last case, in which the law is doubtful or obscure, it is not the part of a judge but of the supreme magistrate or the Prince to intervene, and it alone belongs to him to apply interpretation between equity and the rigid law. l.

units.la: 10. Quoniam vero ex ante dictis paret à judice adhibitam fuisse æquitatem, & adhibendam ante omnia, ut suppleatur illud, in quo lex deficit; colligere licebit, eos hallucinari turpiter, qui nonnisi majores judices, & supremas curias, ex æquo & bono judicare posse, statuunt; immemores earum legum, quæ ab omnibus in judiciis æquitatem strićto juri præferendam suadent. d.l. 8. Cod. judic. l. 4. §. 1. D. quod certo loc. Nec obst. Auth. hodie. Cod. de judic. Eo quod, si recurratur ad authenticum, id est textum Græcum, unde illa ab Irnerio epitomatore de- sumsumpta, deprehendatur eam auth. socorditer translatam & compilatam esse: vid. Duaren. tit. de judic. c. de Var. Judic. Præcept. Conn. 1. Comm. 11.
units.tr: 10. Since, however, it is clear from what has been said above that equity was applied by the judge, and must be applied above all to supply what the law lacks, it may be concluded that those are shamefully mistaken who lay down that only the greater judges and the supreme courts can judge according to what is fair and good, forgetful of those laws which, in all courts, urge that equity be preferred to strict law. d.l. 8. Cod. judic. l. 4. §. 1. D. quod certo loc. Nec obst. Auth. hodie. Cod. de judic. For if one has recourse to the authentic text, that is, the Greek text from which that law was taken by Irnerius the epitomator, it will be found that the authentic text was carelessly translated and compiled. vid. Duaren. tit. de judic. c. de Var. Judic. Præcept. Conn. 1. Comm. 11.

units.la: SECTIO QUARTA.
units.tr: SECTION FOUR.

units.la: CAPUT PRIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER ONE.

units.la: 1. De voce statuti agitur.
units.tr: 1. The word statutum is discussed.

units.la: 2. Definitur statutum.
units.tr: 2. The statute is defined.

units.la: 3. Distinguitur à lege proprie dicta.
units.tr: 3. It is distinguished from law properly so called.

units.la: 4. Distinguitur à consuetudine.
units.tr: 4. It is distinguished from custom.

units.la: 5. Statutum & consuetudo pari passu ambulant.
units.tr: 5. Statute and custom walk side by side.

units.la: 6. Consuetudo nihilominus aliquo sensu potentior.
units.tr: 6. Custom is nevertheless in some sense the more powerful.

units.la: 7. Statutum est juris scripti portio.
units.tr: 7. A statute is a portion of written law.

units.la: 1. SEquitur jus particulare, seu non commune, quod uno vocabulo usitatissimo, Statutum, dicitur, quasi statum publicum tuens, secundum Andream ab Exea in c. canonum Statuta. de Constit. tom. 2. Repet. jur. can. p. 182. n. 46. Appellatur etiam jus municipale; ut hic tamen paulo latius sir acceptum. Forte apud Cæsarem in init. Belli Gallici, Instituti nomine designatum. Etiam in jure nostro dicta lex, seu lex municipii, quemadmodum in genere nere signat, jus communecietiam ipsum Principis rescriptum, quod statuti venit homine.l. 46. D. verb signif l. 3. §. Divus Hadrianus. D. Sepulcro violat. l. inter claras. Cod. summ. Trinit. l. unic. Cod. de Senator. l. 3. in init. Cod. de sent. ex pericul. Recitand. l. 10. Cod. de Murileg. libr. 11 Insuper, canones ecclesiae. c. canonum statuta. & ibi Andr. ab Exea loc. cit. n. 43. p. 182. &c. Statutum de Prebendis. in 6. De quo jure particulari DD. & interpretes agunt ex professo ad l. omnes populi. D. justitia & jure. Quasi in d. l. per jus proprium civitatis intelligatur jus statutarium. Verum sine fundamento, & adversus scopum & intentionem jurisconsulti, qui in d. l. jus partitur in commune & proprium: illad appellat jus naturale & gentium, quod omnibus hominibus est commune, hoc alicujus civitatis, quod appellat jus civile, quale erat Romanorum.
units.tr: 1. There follows the particular law, or non-common law, which is called by the very common single word Statutum, as if it were statum publicum tuens, "maintaining the public state," according to Andreas ab Exea on c. canonum Statuta, de Constit., tom. 2, Repet. jur. can., p. 182, n. 46. It is also called jus municipale; though here it is taken somewhat more broadly. Perhaps in Caesar at the beginning of the Gallic War it is designated by the name Instituti nomine designatum. Also in our law the terms lex, seu lex municipii, are used, just as statuti in general signifies common law, and even the Prince's rescript itself, which comes under the name of statute. l. 46. D. verb. signif.; l. 3. §. Divus Hadrianus, D. Sepulcro violat.; l. inter claras, Cod. summ. Trinit.; l. unic., Cod. de Senator.; l. 3. in init., Cod. de sent. ex periculo recitand.; l. 10. Cod. de Murileg. libr. 11. Besides, there are the canons of the Church: c. canonum statuta, and there Andreas ab Exea, loc. cit., n. 43, p. 182, etc.; Statutum de Prebendis, in 6. Concerning this particular law the doctors and commentators treat expressly on l. omnes populi, D. justitia et jure. It is as if in d. l. the "law of the particular city" were understood to be statutory law. But this is without foundation, and contrary to the aim and intention of the jurist, who in d. l. divides law into common and proper: the former he calls natural and of nations, which is common to all men; the latter belongs to some particular city, and he calls it civil law, such as was the law of the Romans.

units.la: 2. Verum ad statuti explicationem me conferam, quod hac finitione comprehendi poterit, est jus particulare, ab alio legislatore quam imperatore constitutum. Dico jus particulare, in quantum opponitur juri communi, non prout est gentium & naturale, sed prout est jus civile Romanorum, populo Romano commune, & omnibus qui illi populo parebant. Additur, ab alio legislatore, cum qui statuta condit, recte & suo modo legislator appellatur, uti ipsa statuta leges dicuntur municipiorum. Et quidem ab alio, quia regulariter statuta non condit imperator: excipe nisi municipibus jura det, statuta præscribat, secundum quæ ipsi sua regant municipia. Vid. clausul. Stat. Civitatis Ultrajectinæ. Denique adjicitur, quam imperatore, quod licet imperator solummodo dicatur legislator, id tamen non alio sensu obtineat, quam quod suis legibus non hunc aut illum populum, verum omnes constringat, quos suæ clementiæ regit imperium. l. 3. l. 6. D. decret. ab ordine faciend. l. 6. in Princ. D. quod cujusque univ. nomin. l. 25. D. Ad Munic. l. 9. D. Ad leg. Rhod. de jact. l. 1. in init. Cod. Summ. Trinit. §. 1. in sin. instit. Proœm. diss. Christin. Praelud. ad ll. Mechl. n. 3.
units.tr: 2. But I shall now turn to the explanation of the statute, which may be comprehended in this definition: it is a particular law, established by a legislator other than the emperor. I say particular law insofar as it is opposed to the common law, not as that is natural and of nations, but as it is the civil law of the Romans, common to the Roman people and to all who obeyed that people. It is added, by a legislator other than, since the one who enacts statutes is rightly and in his own way called a legislator, just as the statutes themselves are called laws of the municipalities. And indeed "other than", because as a rule the emperor does not enact statutes: except when he gives laws to the citizens and prescribes statutes by which they may govern their own municipalities. See the clauses of the Statutes of the City of Utrecht. Lastly, it is added, than the emperor, because although the emperor alone is called the legislator, this holds in no other sense than that by his laws he binds not this or that people but all whom the empire rules by his clemency. l. 3; l. 6. D. decret. ab ordine faciend.; l. 6 in princ. D. quod cujusque univ. nomin.; l. 25. D. ad municip.; l. 9. D. ad leg. Rhod. de jact.; l. 1. in init., Cod. Summ. Trinit.; §. 1 in fin., Instit. Proem.; diss. Christin.; Praelud. ad ll. Mechl., n. 3.

units.la: 3. Non tamen statutum sic definitum cum lege proprie dictâ confundetur, quod multiplex inter utrumque sit differentia. Lex enim generalis est, & omnes obligat, etiam ignorantes. Statutum, nec omnes, nec itidem ignorantes. Hinc censent DD. Simulac facta est statuti promulgatio, ejus præsumi scientiam, adeoque ad observantiam continuo municipes, obstringi, non tamen excluso modico tempore; perrationem quod facilis sit ejus scientia isto in loco, ita Menoch. 2. Arbitr. cas. 185. n. 5. & 6. Non autem simulac facta est legis promulgatio, ejus scientia præsumetur, ut duobus demum mensibus elapsis à publicatione, incipiat obligare. Novell. 66. §. 1. vid. tamen exc. apud Menoch. 2. arbitr. 185. Zoesius nihilominus ad exemplum legis post statuti promulgationem duorum mensium lapsum desiderat, ut obstringantur municipes. D. de constit. Princ. n. 37. vid l. 6. D. de Decret. ab ordin. faciend.
units.tr: 3. Yet a statute so defined is not to be confused with law properly so called, since there is a manifold difference between the two. For a general law binds all, even those who are ignorant of it; a statute binds neither all nor, likewise, the ignorant. Hence the doctors hold that as soon as a statute is promulgated, knowledge of it is presumed, and the citizens are at once bound to observe it, though not without a short interval of time, on the ground that its knowledge is easy in that place; so Menoch. 2. Arbitr. cas. 185. n. 5. & 6. But it is not that as soon as a law is promulgated its knowledge is presumed, so that it begins to bind only after two months have elapsed from publication. Novell. 66, §. 1; see however the exception in Menochius, 2 Arbitr. 185. Nevertheless Zoesius, following the example of the law, requires that after the promulgation of a statute an interval of two months should pass before the citizens are bound. D. de constit. Princ., n. 37; see l. 6. D. de Decret. ab ordin. faciend.

units.la: 4. Non itidem confundi oportet consuetudinem cum statuto, licet quandoque particularis sit loci consuetudo, costupme appellata. Statutum enim semper est non commune; consuetudo quandoque generalis, & generalissima. Statutum est jus sancitum, id est simul & semel latum; consuetudo jus non sancitum, id est sensim atque paulatim introductum, ut eam de necessitate antecedat actuum frequentia. Statutum obtinet etiam ubi imperium, & in imperio; consuetudo proprie in imperio non habet locum; id est non vincit legem anteriorem, nisi à Principe sit approbata; neque tum amplius erit consuetudo', sed jus aliquod sancitum. l. 3. & 9. Cod. de leg. §. 9. Instit. de jure nat. Gent. & civil. l. 32. D. de leg. l. 35. D. eod. Arg. §. pen. instit. Proem. l. 2. §. 10. Cod vet. jur. enucl. l. 2. Cod. quæ sit long. conf. Alex. consil. 108. vol. 3. in 2. column. & vol. 1. conf. 39. n. 13. Abbas in c. cum accessissent ult. not. de Constit. Connan. 1. comm. 10. n. 3. Cravett. de Antiq. tempor. part. 1 n. 42. Christin. loc. cit. n. 12. Dessel. in not. ad Zoes. instit. tit. de jure nat. gent. & civil. n. 37.
units.tr: 4. Nor likewise ought custom to be confused with statute, although a custom of a particular place, called costume, is sometimes particular. For a statute is always non-common; custom is sometimes general, and even most general. A statute is law enacted, that is, promulgated at once and in a single act; custom is law not enacted, that is, introduced gradually and little by little, so that it must of necessity be preceded by frequent acts. A statute holds also where there is an empire, and within an empire; custom properly has no place in an empire, that is, it does not overcome an earlier law unless it has been approved by the Prince; and then it will no longer be custom but some enacted law. l. 3. & 9. Cod. de leg.; §. 9. Instit. de jure nat. Gent. & civil.; l. 32. D. de leg.; l. 35. D. eod.; Arg. §. pen. Instit. Proem.; l. 2. §. 10. Cod. vet. jur. enucl.; l. 2. Cod. quae sit long. consuet.; Alex. consil. 108, vol. 3, in 2. column, and vol. 1, consil. 39, n. 13; Abbas on c. cum accessissent ult., not. de Constit.; Connan. 1. comm. 10. n. 3; Cravett. de Antiq. tempor. part. 1, n. 42; Christin., loc. cit., n. 12; Dessel. in not. ad Zoes. Instit. tit. de jure nat. gent. & civil., n. 37.

units.la: 5. Quia vero statutum dicitur à consuetudine differre tanquam expressum à tacito, ideo doctores statuunt à pari statutum cum eâ procedere. Argum. l. 32. in sin. D. de leg. post Decium consil. 694. n. 7. Decian. vol. 5. consil. 42. n. 24. Grammat. decis. 92. n. 4. Cravett. consil. 96. n. 6. Schraderus de feud. part. 10. sect. 8. n. 142. Tusc. litt. C. concl. 810. n. 1. litt. S. concl. 436. Giurba proæm. ad Senat. Messanien s. consuet part. 1. n. 22.
units.tr: 5. Since a statute is said to differ from custom as the expressed differs from the tacit, the jurists therefore hold that a statute is to be treated in the same way as custom, by parity of reasoning. Argument from the law 32, at the end, Digest, on laws; Post Decius, Consilium 694, no. 7; Decianus, vol. 5, Consilium 42, no. 24; Grammaticus, Decisio 92, no. 4; Cravetta, Consilium 96, no. 6; Schrader, On Feuds, part 10, section 8, no. 142; Tusc., Litt. C, Conclusio 810, no. 1; Litt. S, Conclusio 436; Giurba, Proemium to the Senate of Messina, on custom, part 1, no. 22.

units.la: 6. Inspecto nihilominus aliquo effectu, potentiorem volunt esse consuetudinem, quam est ipsa lex, vel statutum. Quia consuetudo suaviter & per se influit, per tacitum quasi omnium consensum, cum statutum quandoque invitis obtrudatur. Arg. l. 32. D. leg. c. 1. de feud. cognit. Bald. consil. 252. vol 2. Cravett. consil. 238. n. 7. Giurba loc. alleg. Menoch. de Arbitr. 71. n. 4.
units.tr: 6. Yet, looking at a certain effect, they hold that custom is more powerful than law itself or a statute. For custom flows in gently and of its own accord, through the tacit consent, as it were, of all, whereas a statute is sometimes forced upon the unwilling. Arg. l. 32. D. de leg.; c. 1. de feud. cognit.; Bald. consil. 252, vol. 2; Cravett. consil. 238, n. 7; Giurba, loc. alleg.; Menoch. de Arbitr. 71, n. 4.

units.la: 7. Quibus præmissis facile jam inteiri poterit, statutum esse portionem juris scripti, non quod scribi statutum sit necessum, verum quod simul & semel conditum sit & introductum. Ut tamen consultius sit statutum in scripturam redigi, etiam imprimi, quo facilius in civium notitiam pervenire queat. l. 2. §. 4. D. de orig. jur. confer. Treutl. vol. 3. disp. 1. thes. 5. litt. B. Christin. ad l. Mechlin in Prælud. n. 19.
units.tr: 7. With these premises it may now easily be understood that a statute is a portion of written law, not because it is necessary that the statute be written down, but because it has been enacted and introduced at once and in a single act. It is nevertheless more advisable that the statute be committed to writing and even printed, so that it may more easily come to the knowledge of the citizens. l. 2. §. 4. D. de orig. jur.; confer. Treutl. vol. 3, disp. 1, thes. 5, litt. B; Christin. ad l. Mechlin. in Praelud., n. 19.

units.la: SECT. IV. CAP. II.
units.tr: SECT. IV. CAP. II.

units.la: 1. Quot generum sint statuta ?
units.tr: 1. How many kinds of statutes are there?

units.la: 2. Refutantur hic doctores.
units.tr: 2. The doctors cited here are refuted.

units.la: 3. 4. Peculiaris auctoris sententia proponitur.
units.tr: 3. 4. The author's own opinion is set out.

units.la: 5. Species statutorum explicantur.
units.tr: 5. The kinds of statutes are explained.

units.la: 6. Traduntur regulæ in statutis persona-
units.tr: 6. The rules to be observed in personal statutes are laid down

units.la: libus observandæ.
units.tr: (see above).

units.la: 7. Nullum statutum sive reale, sive per-
units.tr: 7. No statute, whether real or personal, extends beyond its territory.

units.la: sonale, sese extendit extra territo-
units.tr: personal, extends itself beyond the

units.la: rium.
units.tr: territory.

units.la: 8. Mobilia comitantur personam, ubicun-
units.tr: 8. Movables accompany the person, wherever

units.la: que sita.
units.tr: they are situated.

units.la: 9. Statutum se extendit extra territori-
units.tr: 9. A statute extends itself beyond the territory

units.la: um, si utrinque subsit uni supremo
units.tr: if both sides are subject to one and the same

units.la: Principi.
units.tr: supreme Prince.

units.la: 10. Pœna subdito statuto imponi poterit
units.tr: 10. A penalty may be imposed on a subject by statute

units.la: propter gesta extra territorium.
units.tr: for deeds done beyond the territory.

units.la: 11. Etiam collectæ imponuntur subdito ra-
units.tr: 11. Even levies are imposed on a subject

units.la: tione bonorum extra territorium.
units.tr: by reason of goods beyond the territory.

units.la: 12. Statutum prohibens ne frumentum
units.tr: 12. A statute forbidding the export of grain

units.la: exportetur etiam obligat forensem.
units.tr: also binds a non-resident.

units.la: 13. Etiam statutum obligat forensem si
units.tr: 13. A statute also binds a non-resident if

units.la: consentiat.
units.tr: he consents.

units.la: 14. Si sit actus voluntarius jurisdictionis exercendis.
units.tr: 14. If it is a voluntary act for exercising jurisdiction.

units.la: 15. Si statuto contractus accesserit.
units.tr: 15. If a contract has been added to the statute.

units.la: 16. Bona statuto loci communia, etiam quæ alibi sita, ubi contrarium statutum expacto, communicanda.
units.tr: 16. Goods that are common under the statute of the place, even those situated elsewhere, are to be shared, where a contrary statute has not been agreed upon.

units.la: 17. Statutum loci extra territorium, ex comitate & æquitate sæpe servatum.
units.tr: 17. A statute of the place is often observed beyond its territory, out of courtesy and equity.

units.la: 1. PRæmissâ statuti finitione, tam nominali, quam reali, ad ejus me conferam divisiones varias, in quibus explicandis potissimum laborabo. Poterit alia desumpta esse à loco, quando statutum aliud provinciale, oppidanum, paganum, vicanum, quod provinciatim, oppidatim, pagatim, vicatim, condatur. Illud Lantrecht / istud Stadtrecht / hoc Dorfrecht / &c. appellatur. Lipsius, Monit. & exempl. c. 2. libr. 2. Alia ab accidenti, quod vel contra jus civile statutum sit introductum, vel præter, vel secundum jus civile. Alia ab adjuncto, quod aliud odiosum, aliud favorabile, aliud mixtum. Ab effectu, aliud pœnale, aliud non pœnale, aliud prohibitivum, aliud permissivum &c. Verum, quoniam hæ divisiones minoris sunt commatis, nec tantum habent usum in foro, adi ad aliam, quæ doctorum ingenia torsit, & torquet etiamnum, meum transferam laborem. Statuta vulgo dividuntur in realia, personalia, & mixta. Realia nonnulli ea appellant, in quibus à re orditur oratio, personalia, in quibus à persona. Exempli Gratiâ. Primogenitus succedat: erit personale. Bona decedentium venient ad primogenitum, erit reale secundum Bartol. in l. 1. Cod. Summ. trin. n. 42. Verum eam sententiam ex parte rejicit Salic. ad d. l. Cod. n. 13. 14. Arg. l. incola. D. Ad Municipal. quæ meritissime in totum rejicienda. Quod non verbis sed rebus leges sint impositæ; adeoque nec verba captanda. Cum scire leges non sit verba tenere, sed vim atque potestatem. Argum l. 17. 29. D. de legibus. l. 2. in sin. Cod. Comm. de Legat. vid. Gilken. ad l. 1. Cod. Summ. trinit. n. 68. 89. Christin. Prælud. ad Mechlin. n. 23. Burgund. 1. ad consuet. Flandr. Rodenb. tract. de jur. conjug. c. 1.
units.tr: 1. Having premised the definition of a statute, both nominal and real, I shall turn to its various divisions, and in explaining these I shall chiefly labour. A statute may be derived from the place, when it is made provincial, town, rural or village, that is, when it is enacted by province, town, country or village. The first is called Landrecht, the second Stadtrecht, this one Dorfrecht, and so on. Lipsius, Monit. & exempl. c. 2. libr. 2. Another division is from an accident: a statute may be introduced against the civil law, beyond it, or according to it. Another is from an adjunct: one statute is odious, another favourable, another mixed. From its effect: one is penal, another not penal, one prohibitive, another permissive, and so on. But since these divisions are of little compass and have little use in the courts, I shall turn to the other division, which has tormented and still torments the wits of scholars, and devote my labour to it. Statutes are commonly divided into real, personal and mixed. Some call real those in which the discourse begins from the thing, and personal those in which it begins from the person. For example: "The firstborn shall succeed" will be personal. "The goods of the deceased shall come to the firstborn" will be real, according to Bartol. in l. 1. Cod. Summ. trin. n. 42. But Salic. ad d. l. Cod. n. 13. 14. Arg. l. incola. D. Ad Municipal. partly rejects that opinion, and it deserves to be rejected altogether. For laws are imposed not by words but by things, and so words are not to be seized upon, since to know the laws is not to hold to the words but to their force and power. Argum. l. 17. 29. D. de legibus. l. 2. in fin. Cod. Comm. de Legat. See Gilken. ad l. 1. Cod. Summ. trinit. n. 68. 89. Christin. Prælud. ad Mechlin. n. 23. Burgund. 1. ad consuet. Flandr. Rodenb. tract. de jur. conjug. c. 1.

units.la: 2. Mixta vero statuta, licet admittant bene multi, non tamen ea satis accurate explicant, non equidem meo judicio legum studiosis aut mystis, aut pragmaticis satisfaciunt; an id ipse sim facturus, penes lectorem judicium esto. Mixta statuta appellat Argentræus, quæ de re & de persona fiunt, ut si dicatur: Minor ne alienet immobilia, quæ intra statuti territorium sunt. Burgundus paulo aliter, ea mixta appellat, quæ partim statuentis tuentis territorio continentur, partim extra territorium extenduntur. Qualia illi sunt: Ne conjux conjugi donet: ne minor annis 25. bona alienet. Ut illis mixta sint, quæ tam in rem quam in personam, qualia vix ulla reperiuntur. Effectum etenim & in statutis nos intueri oportet, eoque potissimum inspecto, mixtura consideranda, quæ etiam in multis obtinebit statutis. Verum in prænominatis, nullâ ratione effectus est mixtura,ut quæ non extra territorium statuentium sese extendunt; certum indicium, secundum illos doctores (de quo ego postmodum) illa tantum in rem esse, concepta, non in personam. Nec quicquam in contrarium movet illud Burgundi, quod statutum, ne minor 25. ann. bona alienet, sit personale,in quantum respicit mobilia, & ita sese extendit extra territorium; sit reale, in quantum respicit immobilia & sic intra territorium manet. 1. Quia & illa in territorio statuentis sita, à minore, ibidem domicilium habente, (qui casus est propositus) alienari non poterunt. Nec obstat, quod nec mobilia, quæ extra territorium reperiuntur, à minore in loco statuentis domicilium habente alienari nequeant. Id quippe non ideo locum habet, quod persona minoris afficiatur primario; neque enim magis afficitur persona per prohibitam mobilium alienationem, quam immobilium, quod utrobique ex æquo res afficiatur: verum
units.tr: 2. Mixed statutes, although many admit them, nevertheless do not explain them with sufficient accuracy; in my judgement they do not satisfy scholars of the law, whether theorists or practitioners. Whether I myself shall do so, let the reader judge. Argentraeus calls mixed those statutes which concern both thing and person, as when it is said: A minor shall not alienate immovables which lie within the territory of the statute. Burgundus, somewhat differently, calls mixed those which are partly contained within the territory of the enacting authority and partly extended beyond it. Such are: That a spouse shall not give to a spouse; that a minor under 25 years shall not alienate goods. So for them the mixed are those which affect both the thing and the person, and of these scarcely any are found. For we must look also at the effect in statutes, and with that chiefly in view the mixture is to be considered, which will also hold in many statutes. But in the aforementioned cases there is no mixture of effect for any reason, since they do not extend beyond the territory of the enacting authority. This is a sure sign, according to those doctors (of whom I shall speak later), that they are conceived as affecting the thing only, not the person. Nor does that argument of Burgundus move anything to the contrary, that the statute "that a minor under 25 years shall not alienate goods" is personal insofar as it regards movables, and so extends beyond the territory, and is real insofar as it regards immovables and so remains within the territory. First, because those immovables situated in the territory of the enacting authority cannot be alienated by a minor who has domicile there (which is the case proposed). Nor does it matter that movables found beyond the territory cannot be alienated by a minor who has domicile in the place of the enacting authority. This does not hold because the person of the minor is affected primarily; for the person is no more affected by the prohibited alienation of movables than of immovables, since in both cases the thing is equally affected. Rather,

units.la: 1. Quia & illa in territorio statuentis sitarum quod mobilia esse fingantur & intelligantur, intra statuentis territorium, ubi minor domicilium habet. Cumque secundum juris intellectum, res mobilis territorio incolatus contineatur, quoad illam etiam statutum erit reale, neque extra statuentis limites, aliquid operabitur. Verum instabit quispiam pro Burgundo & aliis: igitur effectu inspecto, adhuc poterit dici personale, quod sese extendat extra territorium. Resp. non sese extendit extra territorium, quod non extendatur ad bona, secundum juris intellectum alibi reperta. Qualia sunt immobilia; verum mobilia ibi censeatur esse, secundum juris intellectum, ubi is, cujus ea sunt, sedem atque larem suarum fortunarum collocavit. Instabit quis secundo, quod effectu inspecto, statutum de quo contentio, non differat à statuto personali. Verum respondeo, adhuc multum differet.:
units.tr: 1. Because those also, situated in the territory of the enacting authority, are feigned and understood to be movables within the territory of the enacting authority where the minor has domicile. And since, according to the understanding of the law, a movable thing is contained within the territory of one's residence, the statute will be real with respect to it too, and will have no operation beyond the limits of the enacting authority. But someone will press on behalf of Burgundus and others: therefore, with the effect considered, it can still be called personal, since it extends beyond the territory. I reply that it does not extend beyond the territory, since it does not extend to goods which, according to the understanding of the law, are found elsewhere. Such are immovables; but movables are deemed to be there, according to the understanding of the law, where he to whom they belong has established the seat and home of his fortunes. Someone will press a second point: that, with the effect considered, the statute in question does not differ from a personal statute. But I reply that it will still differ greatly.

units.la: Quod personale secundum illos ipsos, & plerosque Doctores, sese extendat extra territorium tam ratione bonorum immobilium, quam mobilium; hoc, de quo contentio, tantum secundum illos ad mobilia, non item ad immobilia extra territorium sita, extendatur. Ast uti dictum, ipsa mobilia, ibi esse intelliguntur, ubi quis domicilium fovet, nec sese ad immobilia alibi jacentia extendit statutum, & praeter illa, nulla alia reperiuntur bona; adeoque nec extra territorium vires res ullas exserere, statuendum erit; ut in terminis statuti realis, secundum communem sensum, consistere debeat. Argum. §. Quedam nationes. Instit. de Action. l. 1. D. sin. Regund. l. 29. in med. init. D. Comm. divid. Diss. Burg. ad cons. Flandr. tract. 1. n. 2. & n. 41. ibidemque Everhard. loc. leg. 79. Lambert. Goris Advers. part. 1. c. 6.
units.tr: For a personal statute, according to those same authors and most doctors, extends beyond the territory both by reason of immovable and of movable goods; this statute, which is in question, extends according to them only to movables, and not likewise to immovables situated beyond the territory. But as has been said, the movables themselves are understood to be where a person keeps his domicile, and the statute does not extend to immovables lying elsewhere; and beyond those there are no other goods to be found. Therefore it must be held that it does not exert any force beyond the territory, and so, in the terms of a real statute, according to common sense, it ought to stand. Argum. §. Quedam nationes. Instit. de Action. l. 1. D. sin. Regund. l. 29. in med. init. D. Comm. divid. Diss. Burg. ad cons. Flandr. tract. 1. n. 2. & n. 41. ibidemque Everhard. loc. leg. 79. Lambert. Goris Advers. part. 1. c. 6.

units.la: 3. Vt meum promam sensum, duplici respectu statuta considerabo, vel ratione objecti, quod afficiunt, vel ratione quorundam effectorum. Objecti; sic quædam erunt personalia, quædam realia; illa, quæ afficiunt personam, adeoque ei quasi inhærent; hæc quæ rem afficiunt: illa, quæ circa personam, potissimum quid disponunt, seu in ordine ad personam; hæc quæ circa rem, & potissimum, in ordine ad rem, aliquid statuunt. Et ita forte nulla dabuntur mixti generis statuta, quod vel magis rem quam personam, vel magis personam, quam rem afficiant; adeoque illi generi sint annumeranda, quod in iis prædominatur. Arg. §. 1. & 28. Instit. de Action. Quęque ibidem à Theoricis notantur, qui præter actiones in rem & in personam, alias nullas agnoverunt: idem quod secundum analogiam, quis non immerito statutis applicaverit.
units.tr: 3. That I may set forth my meaning, I shall consider statutes under a twofold respect: either by reason of the object they affect, or by reason of certain of their effects. As to the object: thus some will be personal and some real. Those which affect the person, and so as it were inhere in him, are personal; those which affect the thing are real. Those which lay down chiefly something concerning the person, or in relation to the person, are personal; those which decree something concerning the thing, and chiefly in relation to the thing, are real. And so perhaps there will be no mixed statutes that affect the thing more than the person, or the person more than the thing; so they are to be reckoned in that class which predominates in them. Arg. §. 1. & 28. Instit. de Action. And what the Theorists note there, who acknowledged no actions besides those in rem and in personam, someone may not unfairly apply to statutes by analogy.

units.la: Nisi quis eo aliquo modo referre voluerit, omnia illa statuta, quæ de solemnibus bis aut illis adhibendis disponunt; in quamquantum suo modo afficiunt omnes personas, in loco statuentis, aliquid agentes; & suo modo res, ubicunque locorum sitas. Licet, proprie loquendo, solemnitas adhibenda vel ex parte rei, vel personae, potius sit aliquod adjunctum, quam ut afficiat vel rem, vel personam.
units.tr: Unless someone chooses to relate all those statutes that lay down the solemnities to be used with persons or things in some way, insofar as they in their own fashion affect all persons, doing something in the place of the enacting authority, and in their own fashion affect things, wherever they are situated. Yet, properly speaking, a solemnity to be used, whether on the side of the thing or of the person, is rather an accessory than something that affects either the thing or the person.

units.la: 4. Quod si statuta ratione quorundam effectorum considerentur, sic meo sensu, alia erunt realia, alia personalia, alia mixta.
units.tr: 4. But if statutes are considered in terms of certain effects, then in my view some will be real, some personal, and some mixed.

units.la: Realia, quae non extra territorium statuentium vires suas exserunt. Sed tamen non subditos ligant, ratione bonorum immobilium, ibi sitorum. l. an in totum. D. Ædif. Priv. l. pupillo D. tutor. & Curat. dat. l. certa summa. Cod. jure fisci. l. rescripto. in sin. D. Muner. Honor. Mascard. conclus. 6. de interpret. Stat. n. 101. 102.
units.tr: Real statutes are those which do not exert their force beyond the territory of the enacting authority. Nevertheless, they bind not only subjects, but also with respect to immovable goods situated there. l. an in totum. D. Ædif. Priv. l. pupillo D. tutor. & Curat. dat. l. certa summa. Cod. jure fisci. l. rescripto. in sin. D. Muner. Honor. Mascard. conclus. 6. de interpret. Stat. n. 101. 102.

units.la: Personalia, quae etiam sese extendunt extra territorium, adeoque secundum DD. comitari dicuntur personam, ubique locorum, ut tamen respiciant subditos, non exteros, aut peregrinos, qui ab alieno territorio nullam qualitatem accipiunt:
units.tr: Personal statutes are those which also extend beyond the territory, and so, according to the doctors, are said to accompany the person everywhere, provided they regard subjects, not foreigners or strangers, who receive no quality from another territory:

units.la: Sicque mihi mixta dicentur, quae effectu aliquo inspecto, partim intra, partim extra territorium, vires exserunt. Intra, in quantum obstringunt omnes, sive incolas, sive forenses, ibi contendentes vel aliquid agentes; extra, in quantum sese extendunt ad omnia bona, ubicunque locorum jacentia.
units.tr: Thus those will be called mixed by me which, looking at some effect, exert their force partly within and partly outside the territory. Within, insofar as they bind all, whether residents or outsiders, contending or doing something there; outside, insofar as they extend to all goods, wherever situated.

units.la: Illud participando, de statutis realibus, hoc de personalibus.
units.tr: The former share in the nature of real statutes, the latter in that of personal ones.

units.la: 5. Verum ut magis innotescat statutorum ratio, principio illam divisionem ab objecto desumptam amplius elucidabo. Dicebantur illa realia, quæ rem afficiebant & quidem primo & principaliter, ut non statim si circa rem versentur, dicenda sint realia statuta, qualia sunt de solemnibus, in alienatione rei adhibendis; uti nec si rei aliqua in statutis fiat mentio, si modo principalis intentio statuentis non sit, de re aliquid disponere, aut ordinare, uti deinceps declarabitur.
units.tr: 5. But so that the reasoning behind statutes may become more evident, I shall further explain that division taken from the object. Those were called real which affected a thing, and that first and principally. Thus a statute is not at once to be called real merely because it concerns a thing, such as those about the solemnities to be used in alienating a thing; nor again if mention of a thing is made in statutes, provided the principal intention of the enacting authority is not to dispose or ordain anything about the thing, as will be declared afterwards.

units.la: Personalia statuta dicebantur, quae primario & per se afficiunt personam; ut non simulac verbum aliquod occurrit personae in statutis, aut fit personae mentio, judicandum sit, statutum esse personale. Quod autem persona dicitur affici, id ipsum varios continet modos.
units.tr: Personal statutes were those which affect the person primarily and of themselves. Thus, as soon as some word referring to a person occurs in statutes, or mention of a person is made, it must not be judged that the statute is personal. But that a person is said to be affected takes various forms.

units.la: Vel enim personae aliquid permittitur, ut filio-familias testari; qui de jure civili id non poterat. Vel tollit aliquod obstaculum, ut infamem restituere dignitati, spurium, bastardum legitimare. Vel habilitatem addit, ut Notario quo publicum faciat instrumentum. Vel inhabilitat aliquem ad actus varios eundem infamando; prodigum declarando, eidem interdicendo, arte, advocatiâ, negotiatione. Vel habilitat servatâ formâ, & inhabilitat, ea cessante. Utsi[?] minor aut mulier nequeat contrahere, sine consensu propinquorum. &c. Vel qualitatem aliquam imprimit puta, minori, ut habeatur pro majore, ignobili ut pro nobili agnoscatur; & in genere omnibus illis modis in personam statutum constituitur, quando tanquam de universali personae statu disponitur; sive ei aliquid addatur, sive detrahatur, sive permittatur, sive aliquod impedimentum auferatur, adeoque alius à priori statu inducitur vel alteratur prior, vid. Gabriel comm. opin. libr. 6. de Statu. concl. 8. Andreae ab Exea. in c. canonum. canonum Statuta. de Constit. tom. 2. Repet. jur. Canon. p. 189. n. 155.
units.tr: For either something is permitted to the person, as a son under power to make a will, which by civil law he could not do. Or an obstacle is removed, as when the infamous are restored to dignity, or a spurious child or bastard is legitimated. Or ability is added, as to a notary so that he may make a public instrument. Or someone is rendered incapable of various acts by branding him with infamy; by declaring him a spendthrift, by interdicting him, or by barring him from the arts, advocacy or trade. Or he is made capable when a form is observed, and incapable when it is absent: as a minor or a woman cannot contract without the consent of relatives, and so on. Or some quality is impressed, for instance on a minor, so that he is regarded as a major, or on a commoner, so that he is acknowledged as noble. And in general a statute is constituted on the person in all these ways when it is laid down as concerning the universal status of the person: whether something is added to him, or taken away, or permitted, or some impediment is removed, so that a status other than the prior one is introduced, or the prior one is altered. See Gabriel comm. opin. libr. 6. de Statu. concl. 8. Andreae ab Exea. in c. canonum. Statuta. de Constit. tom. 2. Repet. jur. Canon. p. 189. n. 155.

units.la: Non itaque si aliquâ ratione personâ assiciatur, id est prohibeatur aliquid facere, statim erit personale statutum: quale est; maritus, ne quid donet uxori: quia non universaliter de personae statu disponit, verum tantum in certo casu aliquid prohibet fieri, qui potissimum rem ipsam afficit.
units.tr: Thus if a person is affected in some way, that is, forbidden to do something, it will not at once be a personal statute. Such is: a husband may not give anything to his wife, because it does not dispose of the universal status of the person, but only forbids something to be done in a certain case, and principally affects the thing itself.

units.la: 6. Atque ita putem me clarum reddidisse quoad fieri poterit, quid in genere ad statutum personale referri debeat. Subjungam regulas aliquot generales, quae omni statuto personali applicari poterunt; dein in specie in varia inquiram statuta; denique tum jure civili, tum in plerisque ipsâ praxi, regulas à me traditas, confirmabo.
units.tr: 6. And so I think I have made clear, as far as possible, what in general is to be referred to a personal statute. I shall add some general rules which can be applied to every personal statute; then I shall inquire into various statutes in particular; and finally I shall confirm the rules I have laid down, both from civil law and, in most cases, from practice itself.

units.la: Prima regula est; statutum personale tantum afficit subditos territorii, ubi statutum conditum est, non autem forenses, licet ibidem aliquid agentes. Arg. l. 1. in sin. D. Tutor. & curator. dat. l. neque. Cod. qui dare tutores. Salicet. Cod. Summ. Trinit. l. 1. n. 10. Tom. comm. opinion. ex Consil. Marian. & Socini junior. verb. statutum:
units.tr: The first rule is: a personal statute affects only the subjects of the territory where the statute was enacted, and not foreigners, even though they act there. Arg. l. 1. in sin. D. Tutor. & curator. dat. l. neque. Cod. qui dare tutores. Salicet. Cod. Summ. Trinit. l. 1. n. 10. Tom. comm. opinion. ex Consil. Marian. & Socini junior. verb. statutum:

units.la: Secunda est; Statutum personale, non afficit personam extra territorium; sic ut pro tali non reputetur extra territorium, qualis erat intra. Arg. l. 1. 2. D. offic. Proconf. ubi qualitas addita Proconsuli, eum ibi tantum comitatur, ubi erit Proconsul, non alibi.
units.tr: The second is: a personal statute does not affect the person outside the territory, so that he is not regarded outside the territory as he was within it. Arg. l. 1. 2. D. offic. Proconf. where the quality added to the Proconsul accompanies him only where the Proconsul is, and not elsewhere.

units.la: bi. vid. Salic. Cod. ad l. 1. de Sum. Trinit. n. 11.
units.tr: There. See Salic. Cod. ad l. 1. de Sum. Trinit. n. 11.

units.la: Tertia est; Personalis qualitas non potest extra territorium addi personae non subjectae. Arg. l. sin. D. jurisd. Bartol. ad l. 1. Cod. summ. Trinit. n. 16. Gail. 2. obs. 124. n. 13. Zoes. D. qui testam. facere possunt. n. 51.
units.tr: The third is: a personal quality cannot be added outside the territory to a person not subject to it. Arg. l. sin. D. jurisd. Bartol. ad l. 1. Cod. summ. Trinit. n. 16. Gail. 2. obs. 124. n. 13. Zoes. D. qui testam. facere possunt. n. 51.

units.la: Quarta est; statutum personale ubique locorum personam comitatur, in ordine ad bona intra territorium statuentis sita, ubi persona affecta, domicilium habet. Vel etiam in ordine ad poenam à cive petendam, si poena civibus sit imposita. l. 2. 4. Cod. Commerc. & Mercat. Non tamen statutum personale; sese regulariter extendet ad bona immobilia, alibi sita. Dissentiunt ex parte DD. vid. Jacobum Marchisellum Sylv. quaest. Practic. 45. n. 1. 2. 3. Gabriel. comm. opin. libr. 6. de statutis concl. 8. n. 1. 7. 8. 9. & seqq. ibique varios.
units.tr: The fourth is: a personal statute accompanies the person everywhere, with respect to goods within the territory of the enacting authority where the affected person has his domicile; or also with respect to a penalty to be exacted from a citizen, if the penalty has been imposed on citizens. l. 2. 4. Cod. Commerc. & Mercat. Yet a personal statute as a rule does not extend to immovable goods situated elsewhere. The doctors disagree on this point. See Jacobus Marchisellus Sylv. quaest. Practic. 45. n. 1. 2. 3. Gabriel. comm. opin. libr. 6. de statutis concl. 8. n. 1. 7. 8. 9. & seqq. and the various authors cited there.

units.la: Sunt qui distinguunt, inter statutum favorabile & odiosum; quasi illud extendatur, non hoc. Mascard. de interpret. Statutor. concluf. 6. n. 120. 121. & seqq. ibique varii. Christin. ad Mechlin. in Praelud. n. 45.
units.tr: Some distinguish between a favourable and an odious statute, as if the former were extended and the latter not. Mascard. de interpret. Statutor. concluf. 6. n. 120. 121. & seqq. and the various authors cited there. Christin. ad Mechlin. in Praelud. n. 45.

units.la: 7. Verum quod indistincte procedat mea sententia, ex sequentibus patebit abunde. Quia nullum statutum, sive in rem, sive in personam, si de ratione juris civilis sermo instituatur, sese extendit ultra statuentis territorium. l. sin. D. de jurisdict. l. 27. in Princ.
units.tr: 7. But that the rule applies without distinction, in my opinion, will be abundantly clear from what follows. For no statute, whether concerning a thing or a person, if the matter is discussed according to the reason of civil law, extends beyond the territory of the enacting authority. l. sin. D. de jurisdict. l. 27. in Princ.

units.la: 8. Quin tamen ratione mobilium, ubicunque sitorum, domicilium seu personam domini sequamur, ut tamen spectentur loca, quo destinata, nullus iverit inficias; idque propter expressos textus juris civilis, quibus mobilia certo loco non alligantur, verum secundum juris intellectum personam comitatis eique adhaerere judicantur; id quod etiam mores ubique locorum sequuntur. l. 50. §. 1. D. judic. ubi Gothefred. in not. per ll. l. 19. §. rerum autem. D. hared. Institit. l. 41. §. legaverat. l. si fundus 44. D. leg. 3. l. 36. D. de Administr. tutel. Bald. in l. mercatores. Cod. Commerc. & Mercat. Alex. vol. 6. consil. 19. n. 9. & vol. 7. consil. 141. n. 20. Tiraquell. de Retract. §. 1. gloss. 7. n. 10. & seq. Gilken. ad init. tit. de Summ. Trinit. n. 85. Honded. consil. 31. n. 19. vol. 1. Gail. 2. obs. 124. n. 18. Chassan. ad Burgund. Rubric. 9. §. 16. verb. tant an meubles. n. 1. 2. Peck. testam. conjug. libr. 4. c. 35. n. 7. Peregrin de jure fisci. libr. 5. tit. 1. n. 14. Giurb. ad consuet. Messan. c. 1. gloss. 2. part. 1. n. 121. Zoes. D. qui testam. facere poss. n. 52.
units.tr: 8. Yet no one will deny that, by reason of movables wherever they are located, we follow the domicile or the person of the owner, provided that the places to which they are destined are also taken into account. This is so on account of the express texts of the civil law, by which movables are not bound to a fixed place, but are judged, according to the correct understanding of the law, to follow the person of the owner and to cling to him; and customs everywhere also follow this. Dig. 50.1.50 §1, with Gothofredus's note there; Dig. 1.19 §rerum autem; Institutes (the passage on legacies); Dig. 30.41 §legaverat; Dig. 31.44 l. si fundus; Dig. 26.36 on the administration of guardianship; Bald. on the law mercatores, Cod. de commerciis et mercatoribus; Alexander, vol. 6, consil. 19, n. 9, and vol. 7, consil. 141, n. 20; Tiraquellus, de retractu, §1, gloss 7, n. 10 f.; Gilkenius, at the start of the title de summa Trinitate, n. 85; Hondedei, consil. 31, n. 19, vol. 1; Gail, 2 obs. 124, n. 18; Chassanaeus on the Burgundian rubric 9, §16, verb. tant an meubles, n. 1, 2; Peckius, de testamentis conjugum, lib. 4, c. 35, n. 7; Peregrinus, de iure fisci, lib. 5, tit. 1, n. 14; Giurba on the custom of Messina, c. 1, gloss 2, part 1, n. 121; Zoesius, D. qui testamenta facere possunt, n. 52.

units.la: 9. Sic itidem statutum in rem & in personam, sese extra statuentis territorium extendet, in quantum a supremo Principe est confirmatum, qui utriusque territorii est dominus. Arg. l. 12. 13. 14. D. Testam. tutel. l. 7. 11. D. Custod & Exhibit. Reor. Nov. 134. c. 1. Campeg. de dote part. ult. q. 64. Tessaur. 2. quaest. forens. 5. n. 13.
units.tr: 9. Likewise a statute, whether in rem or in personam, extends beyond the territory of the enacting authority, insofar as it has been confirmed by the supreme Prince, who is lord of both territories. Arg. l. 12. 13. 14. D. Testam. tutel. l. 7. 11. D. Custod & Exhibit. Reor. Nov. 134. c. 1. Campeg. de dote part. ult. q. 64. Tessaur. 2. quaest. forens. 5. n. 13.

units.la: 10. Sic itidem potestas statuentium sese extendit extra territorium ad hunc effectum, ut pœna subdito imponatur, de gestis extra territorium, siquidem id expressum sit statuto, ut teneantur, si extra territorium deliquerint; non si simpliciter loquatur. l. relegatorum. §. intercedere. D. Interd. Relegat. l. 4. Cod. Comm. Mercator. ibique DD. Alciat. conf. 63. n. 3. 4. Chassan. ad Burgund. Rubric. 2. §. 1. n. 11. Cephall. consil. 309. n. 30. 35. Gabriel. comm. concl. tit. de statutis. Marc. Anton. Marscot. in c. ut animarum. de constit. tom. 5. Repet. jur. can. p. 111. n. 20. 22. 23. conclus. 8. n. 24. Mascard. d. libr. concl. 6. n. 115. & seqq. Jacob. Marchisell. Sylv. quaest. Pract. 45. n. 1. 2.
units.tr: 10. In the same way, the power of the enacting authority extends beyond its territory to this effect: a penalty may be imposed on a subject for acts done outside the territory, provided the statute expressly says so, so that they are bound if they have offended outside the territory. It does not apply if the statute speaks in general terms. l. relegatorum. §. intercedere. D. Interd. Relegat. l. 4. Cod. Comm. Mercator. And there the doctors: Alciat. conf. 63. n. 3, 4. Chassan. ad Burgund. Rubric. 2. §. 1. n. 11. Cephall. consil. 309. n. 30, 35. Gabriel. comm. concl. tit. de statutis. Marc. Anton. Marscot. in c. ut animarum. de constit. tom. 5. Repet. jur. can. p. 111. n. 20, 22, 23. conclus. 8. n. 24. Mascard. d. libr. concl. 6. n. 115, and following. Jacob. Marchisell. Sylv. quaest. Pract. 45. n. 1, 2.

units.la: 11. Sic etiam statutum afficit bona subditorum alibi sitorum, in quantum personae sibi subditae, ratione bonorum, in alieno territorio existentium, collectam imponit: quod tum demum obtinere vult Salicetus; si ibidem bonis collecta sit imposita. adl. 1, Cod. Summ. Trinit. n. 14. litt. a. in additam.
units.tr: 11. Likewise a statute affects the goods of subjects situated elsewhere, insofar as it imposes a levy on its subjects, on account of goods existing in foreign territory. Salicetus holds that this obtains only if the levy has been imposed on the goods there. adl. 1, Cod. Summ. Trinit. n. 14. litt. a. in additam.

units.la: 12. Non aliter, atque huic territorio subjacet forensis ratione bonorum, quae exportare nequit, contra statutum prohibens frumentum forte exportari, si modo in territorio aut ipse aut pars bonorum mobilium etiamnum reperiantur. Ad hunc effectum, ut de illicite gestis intra territorium, puniatur. Accedit, quod tale statutum non tam in personam, quam in rem latum esse videatur, ut forensem ratione rei ibidem sitae, constringat. Bartol. Koeland. à Valle, aliique apud Fabrum. Cod. de leg. def. 2. Vid. tamen diff. Tessaur. dec. ij. Pedemont. Senat. 152.
units.tr: 12. Not otherwise than as a foreigner is subject to this territory on account of goods which he cannot export, against a statute perhaps prohibiting grain from being exported, if either he himself or part of the movable goods are still found in the territory. This is so that he may be punished for what was done unlawfully within the territory. Add that such a statute seems to have been enacted not so much against the person as in rem, so as to bind a foreigner on account of a thing situated there. Bartol. Koeland. à Valle, aliique apud Fabrum. Cod. de leg. def. 2. Vid. tamen diff. Tessaur. dec. ij. Pedemont. Senat. 152.

units.la: 13. Insuper si non subditi, suâ sponte consentiant in judicem non suum, etiam tum statutum extra territorium ad non subditum vires exserit. Id quod obtinet in jurisdictione prorogatâ. l. 18. D. jurisd. l. 1. 2. D. judic.
units.tr: 13. Moreover, if non-subjects of their own accord consent to a judge who is not their own, then a statute extends its force even so to the non-subject. This holds in prorogated jurisdiction. l. 18. D. jurisd. l. 1. 2. D. judic.

units.la: 14. Amplius, si voluntariæ jurisdictionis actus exercendus, qui etiam extra territorium judicis exerceri poterat. l. 2. D. Ofsic. Proconf. nisi quis velit ea tantum obtinere, si quando plures judices uni Principi parent. Marcus Anton. Marscot in c. ut animarum. de Constit. in 5. tom. Repet. jur. can. n. 22. & seqq. p. 111. 112.
units.tr: 14. Further, if acts of voluntary jurisdiction are to be exercised, which could also be exercised outside the judge's territory. l. 2. D. Ofsic. Proconf. unless one wishes these to hold only if several judges obey one Prince. Marcus Anton. Marscot in c. ut animarum. de Constit. in 5. tom. Repet. jur. can. n. 22. & seqq. p. 111. 112.

units.la: 15. Ut etiam, si statuto in uno territorio, contractus accesserit, seu partium conventio, etiam si in rem sit conceptum, sese extendet ad bona, extra jurisdictionem statuentium sita; non ut afficiat immediate ipsa bona, quam ipsam personam, quoad illa; ad quæ contractus aut conventionis ratione jus est quæsitum. Arg. l. 13. in init. D. Comm. Prædior. Tessaur. 2. Forens. quæst. 5. n. 6. Giurb. ad Consuet. Senat. Messanensi. part. 1. c. 6. gloss. 8. n. 10; 11.
units.tr: 15. So also, if a contract or agreement of the parties has been made under a statute in one territory, even if it is conceived in rem, it extends to goods situated outside the jurisdiction of the enacting authorities. It does not affect the goods themselves immediately so much as the person in respect of them, with regard to those things to which a right has been acquired by reason of the contract or agreement. Arg. l. 13. in init. D. Comm. Prædior. Tessaur. 2. Forens. quæst. 5. n. 6. Giurb. ad Consuet. Senat. Messanensi. part. 1. c. 6. gloss. 8. n. 10; 11.

units.la: 16. Quâ ratione, si statuto hujus loci, inter conjuges bona sint communia, vel pactis antenuptialibus ita conventum sit, ut omnia, ubique locorum sita, communia forent; rent; etiam ad illa, quæ in Frisia jacent, ubi nonnisi quæsitorium est communio, dabitur actio ut communicentur. Argum. societatis universalis. l. 74. D. Pro socio. Argent. ad consf. Britton. artic. 218. n. 38. Christian Roodenburg de jure conjug. tit. 2. c. 5. n. 14. vid. sequentia. Malim tamen id indistincte obtinere, id est, etiam extra societatem universalem, & de moribus conjugalem; in quantum quis potest rebus extra territorium sitis, & ad se pertinentibus legem dicere, unde nascatur actio. l. 7. 12. D. Pact. dotal. l. 6. Cod. Pact. Conv. l. unic. Cod. Rei uxoriæ action. §. illo proculdubio. l. 1. Cod. Contrah. empt. l. sin. Cod. si quis alteri vel sibi.
units.tr: 16. For which reason, if by the statute of this place goods between spouses are common, or by antenuptial agreement it has been agreed that all goods, wherever situated, shall be common, then an action will be given that those goods lying in Friesland also be shared, where community extends only to acquired property. Argum. societatis universalis. l. 74. D. Pro socio. Argent. ad consf. Britton. artic. 218. n. 38. Christian Roodenburg de jure conjug. tit. 2. c. 5. n. 14. vid. sequentia. I would rather, however, that this hold without distinction, that is, also outside a universal partnership and by the customs of marriage, insofar as one may lay down law for things lying outside the territory and pertaining to oneself, from which an action arises. l. 7. 12. D. Pact. dotal. l. 6. Cod. Pact. Conv. l. unic. Cod. Rei uxoriæ action. §. illo proculdubio. l. 1. Cod. Contrah. empt. l. sin. Cod. si quis alteri vel sibi.

units.la: 17. Denique nonnunquam, dum populus vicinus vicini mores comiter vult observare, & ne multa bene gesta turbarentur, de moribus, statuta territorium statuentis, inspecto effectu, solent egredi. l. 7. §. sin. D. capt. & Postlim.
units.tr: 17. Finally, sometimes, while a neighbouring people courteously wishes to observe the customs of its neighbour, and so that many well-done acts are not disturbed, statutes concerning customs are accustomed, with regard to their effect, to go beyond the territory of the enacting authority. l. 7. §. sin. D. capt. & Postlim.

units.la: SECT. IV. CAP. III.
units.tr: SECT. IV. CAP. III.

units.la: 1. Veniæ impetratio ad testandum spectat solemnia.
units.tr: 1. Permission to make a will concerns the formalities.

units.la: 2. Statutum me conjux conjugi donet est reale.
units.tr: 2. The statute that a spouse may not give to the other spouse is real.

units.la: 3. Statutum ut minor sit major, est personale.
units.tr: 3. A statute that makes a minor a major is personal.

units.la: 4. Non sese tamen extendit extra territorium.
units.tr: 4. Yet it does not extend beyond the territory.

units.la: 5. Non etiam minor major effectus, ad omnem juris effectum censebitur esse major.
units.tr: 5. Nor is one made major by a statute, a minor, treated as major for every legal effect.

units.la: 6. Quando majori sic facto currat tempus restitutionis in integram?
units.tr: 6. When, for one thus made major, does the time for restitution in integrum begin to run?

units.la: 7. An qui major factus possit esse tutor?
units.tr: 7. Can one who has become major be a guardian?

units.la: 8. De moribus quorundam mater vidua, qua minorennis potest esse tutrix.
units.tr: 8. Under the customs of certain places, a widowed mother who is a minor can be a guardian (tutrix).

units.la: 9. Statutum de bonorum communione inter conjuges est reale.
units.tr: 9. The statute on community of goods between spouses is real.

units.la: 10. Statutum de successionibus ab intestato reale est.
units.tr: 10. The statute on intestate succession is real.

units.la: 11. Etiam de successionibus testamentariis.
units.tr: 11. The same holds for testamentary succession.

units.la: 12. Ut filius-familias faciat testamentum, est statutum reale.
units.tr: 12. That a son under paternal power may make a will is a real statute.

units.la: 13. An in uno loco inhabilis alibi, ubi jus civile obtinet, testari possit cum effectu?
units.tr: 13. Can one who is incapable in one place make a valid will elsewhere, where the civil law prevails?

units.la: 14. Forensis uti non poterit, alterius loci statuto.
units.tr: 14. A stranger (forensis) cannot use the statute of another place.

units.la: 15. Legitimatus in uno territorio non censetur esse legitimatus in alio, effectu inspecto.
units.tr: 15. One made legitimate in one territory is not deemed legitimate in another, looking to the effect.

units.la: 16. In uno loco nobilitatus, non ubique censetur talis.
units.tr: 16. One ennobled in one place is not deemed noble everywhere.

units.la: 17. Ancui in uno loco bonis interdictum, ad administrandum ubique censeatur inhabilis?
units.tr: 17. One who in one place is forbidden the use of goods: is he deemed incapable of administering them everywhere?

units.la: 18. An in uno loco notatus, alibi censeatur notatus?
units.tr: 18. One marked in one place: is he deemed marked elsewhere?

units.la: 19. An si alicui interdictum vel arte vel negotiatione, vel loco, id alibi locum habeat?
units.tr: 19. If someone is forbidden a trade or business, or a place, does that prohibition hold elsewhere?

units.la: 20. An Tabellio extra suum territorium recte conficiat instrumentum?
units.tr: 20. Does a notary (tabellio) validly draw up an instrument outside his own territory?

units.la: I. VErum ut magis de veritate hactenus explicatorum constet, superest ut in nonnulla inquiratur statuta; cujus illa sint generis, & ad quae, & quousque sese extendant?
units.tr: I. But so that the truth of what has been explained so far may be clearer, it remains to inquire into some statutes: what kinds they are, to what matters they extend, and how far.

units.la: Et quidem principio inquiram, Utrum statutum de veniae impetratione, ad testandum, quam octroy appellamus, quae in Provincia Ultrajectina, etiam quoad allodia, necessaria, statuto reali sit annumerandum? Respondeo, siquidem de personali & reali statuto foret quaestio, personali magis foret annumerandum, licet in ipsis licentiae litteris bonorum intra territorium jacentium fiat mentio; eo quod agat de licentia disponendi simpliciter seu testandi, quae est juris permissivi. missivi, in ordine personæ testantis. Malim tamen illam licentiam potius ad testandi formam, necessarium requisitum, seu solemnitatem referre. Sic enim de jure civili, veniæ illa impetratio per Principem concessa, surdo & muto, ad solemnia refertur, nunquam ad rem ipsam. Argum. tot. tituli, & §. item surdus. Instit. quibus non ost permiss. sacer. testam. & l. 7. D. qui testam. facere poss. Quo nomine miles, surdus & mutus, sine veniæ impetratione testari potest, quod ipsius testamentum sit privilegiatum, ipseque à juris solemnibus liberatus, §: 2. Instit. de Testam. militar. Accedit, quod Testamentum Hollandi in Hollandiâ factum, ubi tamen licentiâ opus non est, sese extendat etiam ad bonâ in provinciâ Trajectinâ jacentia: certum indicium, licentiam non rem afficere, sed partem facere solemnitatum. Ut non quæratur de quibus bonis testari liceat, sed quomodo? Id est, præhabitâ veniâ, adhibitâ licentiâ. Nutanter & vacillanter hâc in re, ut quid statuat, ipse dubitem. Ampliss. Rodenburch. tract. de jure conjug. c. 3. tit. 2. p. 113. & c. 4. n. 8. vid. tamen eundem p. 57. & seq. vid. & Zoes. D. qui testam. facere poss. n. 53. Sand. de feud. Gelriæ tit. 3. num. 74. pag. 149. 150.
units.tr: And first I shall inquire whether the statute on obtaining leave to make a will, which we call the octroy, required in the province of Utrecht even for allodial lands, is to be counted among real statutes. I answer: if the question concerned a personal or real statute, it would rather be counted among the personal, although the letters of licence themselves mention goods lying within the territory, because it concerns a licence to dispose or make a will simply, which belongs to the law of permission, in relation to the person of the testator. I would nonetheless rather refer that licence to the form of the will, as a necessary requirement or solemnity. For under the civil law the leave granted by the Prince to a deaf and dumb person is referred to the solemnities, never to the matter itself. Argument from the whole title, and from §. item surdus, Institutes, quibus non est permissum facere testamentum, and l. 7 D. qui testamenta facere possunt. On this account a soldier, deaf and dumb, can make a will without obtaining leave, because his will is privileged and he himself is freed from the formalities of law, §. 2 Institutes, de testamentis militaris. In addition, a will made in Holland by a Hollander, where no licence is needed, extends also to goods lying in the province of Utrecht: a sure sign that the licence affects not the thing but forms part of the solemnities. So the question is not as to which goods one may bequeath, but how: that is, with leave first obtained and licence applied. I hesitate in this matter and waver, so I am unsure what to decide. See the most distinguished Rodenburg, tract. de jure conjugum, c. 3, tit. 2, p. 113, and c. 4, n. 8; but see also the same, p. 57 and following; see also Zoesius, D. qui testamenta facere possunt, n. 53; Sande, de feudis Gelriae, tit. 3, n. 74, pp. 149–150.

units.la: 2. Ulterius utrum statutum: ne conjux conjugi donet, aut aliquid relinquat, quale est nostrum Trajectinum, sit in rem, an in personam conceptum ? Respondeo, licet forte de jure Romano tale statutum in personam possit esse. conceptum; quod ibidem alia ratio prohibitionis, atque apud nostrates, ibidem donatio valebat, ad instar mortis causa, adeoque morte confirmabatur, apud nostros, non item: nihilominus dicendum erit, hoc statutum de moribus esse mere reale. Inhibet quippe rerum alienationem & translationem, primario; versatur circa rem, tanquam objectum statuti principale; neque etiam extenditur, ad immobilia, extra statuentis territorium sita ubi contrarium obtinet statutum. Arg. l. ult. D. jurisd. l. 27. §.
units.tr: 2. Further: is the statute "that a spouse shall not give to a spouse, or leave anything to them," such as our Utrecht one, conceived as real or as personal? I answer: although perhaps under Roman law such a statute could be conceived as personal, because there the reason for the prohibition was different, and there a gift was valid like a gift in view of death, and was thereby confirmed by death, which was not so among our people; nevertheless it must be said that this statute on the customs is purely real. For it forbids, primarily, the alienation and transfer of things; it is concerned with the thing as the principal object of the statute; nor does it extend to immovables lying outside the territory of the enacting authority, where a contrary statute holds. Argument from l. ult. D. de jurisdictione, and l. 27 §. 1 D. de tutoribus et curatoribus dandis.

units.la: 1. D. Tutor & curat. dat. Hancque sententiam à multis observatam, usu approbatam, & magni senatus arrestis confirmatam, refert Peckius de Testam. conjug. libr. 4. c. 7. 10. 12. 28. 29. Gothefred. ad l. ult. D. de jurisd. verb. quid si municipum lege. dissentit ex parte Burgund. ad consf. Flandr. tract. 1. n. 41. qui statuit illud esse mixti generis. Dissentiunt alii in totum, qui id ipsum statuto personali annumerant. uti Bartolus in l. 32. D. de leg. in sin. Bald. in consil. 418, in Princ. libr. 4. Socin. lib. 4. consil. 131. n. 2, aliique apud Alderanum Mascardum, dubitantem, de interpret. statutor. concl. 4. n. 145. & concluf. 6. n. 15. vid. Christin. ad Mechlin, in prelud. n. 45. & tit. 17. artic. 2. n. 11. & artic. 3. n. 13. Rodenburg. tract. de jure conjugum tit. 2. cap. 5. n. 1. 2. Quae causa est, quod nuperâ ordinum nostrorū declaratione de an. 1659. Apr. 14. extra controversiam omnem hæc quæstio sit constituta, adeoq; statuto reali, hoc nostrum, annumeratum.
units.tr: 1 D. de tutoribus et curatoribus dandis. Peckius, de testamento conjugum, book 4, cc. 7, 10, 12, 28, 29, reports this view as observed by many, approved by use, and confirmed by decisions of the great senate; so too Gothofredus on l. ult. D. de jurisdictione, verb. quid si municipum lege. Partly dissenting is the Burgundian commentator on the consuetudo of Flanders, tract. 1, n. 41, who holds that it is of mixed kind. Others dissent altogether, classing it among personal statutes, as Bartolus on l. 32 D. de legatis, in fine; Baldus in consilium 418, in principio, book 4; Socinus, book 4, consilium 131, n. 2; and others cited by Alderanus Mascardus, who doubts, de interpretatione statutorum, concl. 4, n. 145, and concl. 6, n. 15. See Christinaeus on Mechlin, in prelude, n. 45, and tit. 17, art. 2, n. 11, and art. 3, n. 13; Rodenburg, tract. de jure conjugum, tit. 2, c. 5, nn. 1, 2. This is why, by the recent declaration of our lords the States of 14 April 1659, the question has been settled beyond all controversy, and this statute of ours has been counted among the real ones.

units.la: 3. Quale censebitur esse statutum, ut minor fiat major, 18. vel 20. ætatis anno, quale antehac nostrum Ultrajectinum, nuperâ itdem ordinum declaratione ann. 1659. April. 14. immutatum, an reale, an vero personale? Respondeo, & si qui per ætatem major est factus, eo ipso liberam rei suæ consequatur administrationem: quia tamen statuentium scopus est & intentio, personas de jure civili inhabiles, habilitare, easque primo & per se afficere aliquâ qualitate, personale statutum erit dicendum. vid Berlich. part. 1. decis. 6. n. 7. Rodenb. tract. de jure conjug. tit. 2. c. 1.
units.tr: 3. What is the character of the statute "that a minor shall become a major" at the age of 18 or 20 years, such as our former Utrecht statute, changed by the same declaration of the lords of 14 April 1659: is it real or personal? I answer: although one who has become major by age at once obtains free administration of his property, nevertheless, because the purpose and intention of the enacting authority is to make persons who are incapable under civil law capable, and to affect them first and directly with a certain quality, it must be called a personal statute. See Berlich, part 1, decis. 6, n. 7; Rodenburg, tract. de jure conjugum, tit. 2, c. 1.

units.la: 4. Verum, utrum eo ipso semet extendat extra statuentis territorium, idque ad omnem juris effectum, sic ut illa qualitas personam comitetur ubique locorum, id equidem, admodum dubium est. Et licet id permulti velint, illis tamen, invitâ jurisprudentiâ, non potero assentiri, per allegata superius. Quo etiam forte nomine Ordin. Ultrajectini suâ Constit. de ann. 1659. April. 14 art. 16. id reale appellant.
units.tr: 4. But whether, by that very fact, it extends beyond the territory of the enacting authority, and to every legal effect, so that the quality accompanies the person everywhere, is indeed very doubtful. And although very many wish it, I cannot assent to them, since jurisprudence is against it, for the reasons alleged above. For this reason, perhaps, the Ordinance of Utrecht, in its Constitution of 14 April 1659, art. 16, calls it real.

units.la: 5. Utrum itidem, qui ita statuto major est effectus, quoad omnem juris effectum pro majore habeatur, sic ut postquam 18. vel 20 ætatis annum implerit, perdat beneficium in integrum restitutionis ex edicto minoribus annis 25. competens, disquiri poterit? Meo judicio, in illis omnibus in quibus pro majore habetur, censendus est illud minoris ætatis beneficium amisisse. Ut tamen id extendi nolim rerum ad alienationē, maxime si illa etiamnum tali statuto sit restricta. Id quod antea statuto Ultrajectino obtinebat. Rubric. 28. artic. 6. Et videtur sententia hæc stabiliri Argum. l. 3, Cod. qui veniam ætat. Impetr. l. 5. in init. Cod. de Tempor. in integr. Restit. Montan. de Tutel. c. 33. n. 38. 619. Cuyck ad Cravettam consil. 722. Anton. Matth. disp. 5. de Curat. n. 22. ibique alii. DD. Zoes. D. de Minor. num. 20.
units.tr: 5. Likewise it may be asked whether one who has been made major by statute is held to be major for every legal effect, so that after he has completed the eighteenth or twentieth year of age he loses the benefit of restitution in integrum, which the edict grants to those under twenty-five years. In my judgment, he is to be regarded as having lost that benefit of minority in all those matters in which he is held to be major. Yet I would not have this extended to the alienation of things, especially if these are still restricted by such a statute, as under the former Utrecht statute. Rubric 28, art. 6. And this view seems to be confirmed by argument from l. 3 Cod. qui veniam aetatis impetrare possunt; l. 5 in init. Cod. de temporibus in integrum restitutionis; Montanus, de tutelis, c. 33, nn. 38, 619; Cuyck on Cravetta, consilium 722; Antonius Matthaeus, disp. 5, de curatoribus, n. 22, and the others there; Zoesius, D. de minoribus, n. 20.

units.la: 7. Idem quod dicendum, de statuto, quod
units.tr: 7. The same must be said of a statute which frees a minor from guardianship by marriage and holds him to be of full age.

units.la: quod minorem per nuptias tutelâ liberat, atque pro majori habet. Neque enim hoc iplum ad onera trahendum erit, quasi ante 25. ætatis annum tutelam sibi impositam subire debeat, aut etiam possit. Neque enim, nnâ posità juris civilis correctione, præsumenda erit altera, præsertim in materiâ odiosâ: cum sic interpretemur statuta, ut quam minimum à jure civili devient, nec in quorum favorem inducta, in eorum odium torquantur, per allegata quæstione superiori. Montan. de Tutel. c. 33. n. 619. Oddus de Restit. in integr. q. 23. n. 44. 47. & 50. Sand. libr. 2. tit. 7. def. 4. Mev. ad Lubec. 1. Rubr. 7. art. 6. n. 14. & seqq. aliique apud Anton. Matth. disput. 1. de Tutel. n. 7. 8.
units.tr: For it is not to be extended to the burdens, so that he would have to undertake, or even be able to undertake, a guardianship imposed on him before his twenty-fifth year. Nor, once the correction of civil law is granted, is another correction to be presumed, especially in an odious matter, since we must interpret statutes so that they depart from civil law as little as possible, and are not turned to the hurt of those for whose favour they were introduced, as the question above has shown. Montan. de Tutel. c. 33. n. 619. Oddus de Restit. in integr. q. 23. n. 44. 47. & 50. Sand. libr. 2. tit. 7. def. 4. Mev. ad Lubec. 1. Rubr. 7. art. 6. n. 14. & seqq. aliique apud Anton. Matth. disput. 1. de Tutel. n. 7. 8.

units.la: 8. Nec tamen, quod in transitu observandum, de moribus nonnullorum locorum excluditur mater vidua, & minor 25. annis à tutelâ suorum liberorum uti judicatum scribit Christin. 3. decis. 149. n. 7. Nec distinctionem inter minorennem & majorennem matrem admittendam esse, refert Faber in Cod. quando mulier. tutel. offic. etiam DD. apud Barbos. in collect. tit. eod. n. 7. Etiam cum aliquo temperamento in ditionibus nostri Belgii fœderati, Celsissimi Guilielmi Friderici Araufonienfium Principis pupilli, Regiæ Principiffe viduæ matri, tutela fuit concredita.
units.tr: 8. It should also be noted in passing that, by the custom of some places, a widowed mother who is under 25 is excluded from the guardianship of her own children; so Christin. writes that it has been decided, 3. decis. 149. n. 7. Christin. 3. decis. 149. n. 7. Faber, in his commentary on the Code, quando mulier tutelae officio, reports that no distinction is to be admitted between a mother who is a minor and one who is of full age, and the same is held by the doctors cited by Barbosa in his collection under the same title, n. 7. Faber in Cod. quando mulier. tutel. offic. etiam DD. apud Barbos. in collect. tit. eod. n. 7. Even in the provinces of our united Belgium, with some moderation, the guardianship of the pupil, the most illustrious William Frederick, Prince of Orange-Nassau, was entrusted to his mother, the widowed royal Princess.

units.la: 9. Verum quid statuendum de variarum
units.tr: 9. But what is to be decided concerning the custom, or rather the statute, of the various provinces in Belgium,

units.la: Provinciarum in Belgio consuetudine, vel potius statuto, quo inter conjuges, post celebratas nuptias, ut in Hollandia; post copulam, ut apud Ultrajectinos, bonorum inducitur communio, nisi pactis sit exclusa dotalibus, reali ne statuto adnumerabitur, an potius personali? Resp. Et si forte de jure civili tale statutum, ad exemplum societatis ad bona alibi jacentia se extenderet, in quâ societate, si ea sit omnium bonorum, etiam omnia continuo, per fictam aliquam traditionem, exceptis nominibus, communicabantur. l. 1. in sin. l. 2. l. 3. D. Pro socio.
units.tr: by which a community of goods between spouses is introduced after the marriage is celebrated (as in Holland) or after the union (as among the Utrechters), unless it has been excluded by dotal agreements: is it to be counted among real statutes, or rather among personal ones? Answer: even if such a law of civil right, following the pattern of a partnership, were to extend to goods lying elsewhere, in which partnership, if it embraces all goods, everything is at once communicated by some fictitious delivery, except debts. l. 1. in sin. l. 2. l. 3. D. Pro socio.

units.la: Etiam si pactum interveniat, ex eo nasceretur actio personalis, ad bonorum extra territorium jacentium, ubi contraria consuetudo locum habet communicationem, vel æstimationem &c. Arg. l. 7. 12. D. Pact. dotal. l. 6. Cod. de Pact. convent. Quia tamen illa communio statutaria potissimum rerum spectat alienationem, adeoque res ipsas assicit primario & principaliter, negari non poterit, quin reali statuto, hoc nostrum sit connumerandum; ut ad bona alibi sita, ubi contrarium obtinet statutum, reales essectus non exerat. per all. anterioribus positionibus: Argentr. artic. 218. ad conf. Britton. n. 38. Christin. vol. 2. Decis. 57. diss. Burgund. ad. Conf. Flandr. tract. 1. n. 15. vid. Amplis. Rodenburg. tract. de jure conjug. tit. 2. c. 1. Simonem van der Leeuwen Paratit. juris novis. libr. 4. artic. 1. cap. 15. 10. I.
units.tr: 10. Should the same be inferred about statutes which concern intestate succession? I answer that it should; for they affect the thing, not the person, so that they must be governed by the laws of the place where the goods are situated, or are understood to be. Immovables are governed by the statutes of the place where they lie, movables by the statutes of the place where the testator had his domicile. Tiraquell. de jure primogen. q. 46. Giurba ad Messan. c. 6. gloss. 8. part. 1. n. 3. vid. & Sand. libr. 4. decis. tit. 6. def. 7. Burgund. ad consuet. Flandr. tract. 1. n. 25. Christin. vol. 3. decis. 59. Christian. Rodenburg. h. tract. de jure conjug. cap. 2. tit. 2. n. 1. Omnino diss. Salicet, qui 5. argumentis in l. 1 Cod. de Summ. Trinit. n. 14. contendit, respici statutum originis, & domicilii defuncti. But this question, and the matter of the conflict of statutes, will offer a fuller occasion for discussion.

units.la: 10. Idem ne inferendum de statutis, quę spectant successiones ab intestato? Respondeo, quod ita; rem enim afficiunt, non personam, ut legibus loci, ubi bona sita sunt, vel esse intelliguntur, regi debeant. Immobilia statutis loci, ubi sita, mobilia loci statutis, ubi testator habuit domicilium. Tiraquell. de jure primogen. q. 46.
