Giurba ad Messan. c. 6. gloss. 8. part. 1. n. 3. vid. & Sand. libr. 4. decis. tit. 6. def. 7. Burgund. ad consuet. Flandr. tract. 1. n. 25. Christin. vol. 3. decis. 59. Christian. Rodenburg. h. tract. de jure conjug. cap. 2. tit. 2. n. 1. Omnino diss. Salicet, qui 5. argumentis in l. 1 Cod. de Summ. Trinit. n. 14. contendit, respici statutum originis, & domicilii defuncti. Verum de hoc quæsito, & in materia de concursu statutorum erit uberior occasio differendi.
units.tr: 11. The same must be inferred as regards testamentary succession. Suppose that making a will is permitted here, but not in Gelderland. If someone makes a will here, it will have no force with respect to the goods lying in Gelderland. Such a statute plainly concerns the goods themselves, and so will be real, not exerting its force beyond the territory of the lawgiver. Arg. l. sin. D. jurisd. Gotefred. ibid. Gabriel, Comm. opin. libr. 6. de statutis concl. 8. ubi varii. Zoes, D. qui testam. facere poss. n. 52. ibique alii.

units.la: 11. Idem quod inferendum, quoad successionem testamentariam; finge enim testamentum hic fieri permissum esse, in Geldria non ita? Hinc si quispiam hic fecerit testamentum, non capiet vires, ratione bonorum, in Gelria jacentium. Tale quippe statutum ipsectat ipsa bona, adeoque erit reale, non exserens vires ultra statuentis territorium. Arg. l. sin. D. jurisd. Gotefred. ibid. Gabriel, Comm. opin. libr. 6. de statutis concl. 8. ubi varii. Zoes, D. qui testam. facere poss. n. 52. ibique alii.
units.tr: 11. The same must be inferred as to testamentary succession. Suppose that making a will is permitted here but not in Gelderland. Then if anyone makes a will here, it will have no force with regard to goods lying in Gelderland. Such a statute indeed bears upon the goods themselves, and so it will be real, not exerting force beyond the territory of the one who enacts it. Arg. l. sin. D. jurisd. Gotefred. ibid. Gabriel, Comm. opin. libr. 6. de statutis concl. 8. ubi varii. Zoes, D. qui testam. facere poss. n. 52. ibique alii.

units.la: 12. Verum ut etiam exempla innotescant statutorum personalium, & eorundem effectuum, quo regulæ antea allegatæ, inductionibus demonstrentur; Inquiram utrum statutum; ut filius-familias possit facere testamentum, (quod personale esse judico, quia habilis ad testandum declaratur, qui erat de jure communi inhabilis, eique quid permittitur, de jure communi prohibitum): utrum, inquam, tale statutum, etiam locum habeat extra territorium, & dum alibi facit testamentum, & dum disponit in territorio, de bonis alibi sitis? Resp. quod ad primum quæsitum, non dubium, quin si alibi testetur, valeat dispositio illa, ratione bonorum intra territorium disponentis jacentium. Quod potestas aliquid disponendi circa suum civem, non præcise arctetur territorio. Arg. l. sin. D. de decret. ab ordin. faciend. l. 2. 4. Cod. Comm. & Mercat.
units.tr: 12. But so that examples of personal statutes, and of their effects, may also be known, and the rules alleged above be demonstrated by inductions, I shall inquire whether a statute that a son under paternal power may make a will (which I judge to be personal, because one who was by common law incapable of making a will is declared capable, and something is permitted which common law prohibited) also has effect outside the territory, both when he makes a will elsewhere and when he disposes, within the territory, of goods lying elsewhere. Answer to the first question: there is no doubt that if he makes the will elsewhere, that disposition is valid with regard to goods lying within the territory of the one disposing, since the power to dispose of something concerning one's own citizen is not strictly confined to the territory. Arg. l. sin. D. de decret. ab ordin. faciend. l. 2. 4. Cod. Comm. & Mercat.

units.la: Quod secundum speclat quæsitum, judicarem illam personæ habilitatem ad bona alibi sita sese non extendere, propter ll. & auctoritates superius allegatas. Adde Gail. 2. obs. 123. n. 13. & 124 Post Bartol. in l. 1. Cod. Summ. Trinit. n. 40. Bald. n. 80. Gilken. ibidem, n. 124. 91. Gomes. ad l. Tauri. 3. n 20. vid. tamen Rodenb. de jure conj. t. 1. c. 1. per totum. post Burgund. ibidem refutatum ex parte.
units.tr: As for the second question, I would judge that this capacity of the person does not extend to goods situated elsewhere, for the reasons of law and authority cited above. Add Gail, 2 obs. 123 n. 13 and 124; Post Bartol. on l. 1 Cod. Summ. Trinit. n. 40; Bald. n. 80; Gilken. ibid., n. 124, 91; Gomes ad l. Tauri 3 n. 20; but see Rodenb. de jure conj. t. 1 c. 1 throughout; after Burgund., refuted in part in the same place.

units.la: Atque hic videtur esse sensus constit. novæ ordin. Ultraj. de ann. 1659. April, 14. artic. 16.
units.tr: And this seems to be the sense of the new ordinance of Utrecht of 14 April 1659, article 16.

units.la: 16. Ubi statutum, de quo agendum subse‐ quenti quæstione, volunt esse reale: quod e‐quidem sic accipiendum existumarem, ut non sese extendat ad bona alibi sita de‐quibus forte testari poterit minor, licet nondum 16. aut 18. ætatis annum impleverit. Neque enim id esse reale hoc sensu probabile, quasi incola Hollandiæ aut loci alterius ratione bonorum hic jacentium testari non valeat, nisi sit 16. aut 18. annis major.
units.tr: 16. Where it wishes the statute, to be discussed in the following question, to be regarded as real. I would take this to mean that it does not extend to goods situated elsewhere, about which a minor who has not yet completed the sixteenth or eighteenth year of age may perhaps be able to make a will. For it is not probable that the statute is real in this sense, as if a resident of Holland, or of another place, could not make a will concerning goods lying here unless he were over sixteen or eighteen years of age.

units.la: 14. Quid si tamen forensis (qui qualis sit vid. apud Mascard. dict. tract. conclus. 6. n. 212. Barbof. ad l. 19. §. proinde D. judic.) uti velit loci alterius statuto, eo ne uti poterit, sic ut ei judex gratificari debeat? Non equidem; neque enim ibi quicquam introductum in gratiam forensis, aut exteri. Ut quemadmodum non potest nolle, ita nec possit velle, l. ejus est nolle. 3. D. de Reg. jur.
units.tr: 14. But what if a stranger (on who he is, see Mascard, loc. cit., concl. 6 n. 212; Barbof. ad l. 19 §. proinde D. judic.) wishes to use the statute of another place: can he use it, so that the judge ought to grant him this favour? Certainly not. For nothing has been introduced there for the sake of a stranger or an outsider. As he cannot be unwilling, so he cannot be willing, l. ejus est nolle 3 D. de Reg. jur.

units.la: Et quemadmodum forensis invitus non sentit incommodū ex statuto loci alterius, ita nec volens sentire poterit talis statuti commodum. Argum. à contrario sensu. Roeland. à Valle consil. 79. n. 35. libr. 3. Tiraq. de jure Primog. q. 44. n. 4. Marsil. singul. 519. incipit. Ille qui non sustinet. Alexand. 7. Consil. III.
units.tr: And just as a stranger, against his will, does not feel the disadvantage of another place's statute, so neither, though willing, can he feel its advantage. Argument from the contrary sense. Roeland. à Valle consil. 79 n. 35, libr. 3; Tiraq. de jure Primog. q. 44 n. 4; Marsil. singul. 519, beginning "Ille qui non sustinet"; Alexand. 7 Consil. III.

units.la: 15. Quid autem statuendum erit de legitimato in uno territorio, censebitur ne ratione bonorum alibi jacentium, ubi legitimatus non erat, statutum vires suas exserere; vel an illa qualitas seu habilitas, eum ubique locorum, comitabitur, quoad effectum consequendae dignitatis, vel succedendi ab intestato? Respondeo, etsi per legitimationem habilitetur persona, ut velint DD. qualitatem eam comitari ubique locorum: etiam ex comitate id servari possit: quia tamen potissimum illa legitimatio fit ad effectum vel honoris, vel hæreditatis consequendæ, in quam nihil juris habet is qui in suo territorio legitimavit; existumarem illam legitimationem ad honores subeundos & hæreditatem extra territorium capiendam non suffisufficere. Arg. l. ult. D. jurisd. l. communium, 9. Cod. Natur. liber. c. per venerabilem. qui filii sint legitimi. Bartol. in l. 1. Cod. Summ. Trinit. Gothefred. in comm. ad d. l. ult. Gabriel comm. opin. libr. 6. de Statut. conclus. 8. n. 18. Gilken. Cod. summ. Trinit. ad l. 1. n. 88. Mantic. de Conjectur. Ultim. volunt. libr. 11. tit. 10. n. 43. Cravett. consil. 119. Schepliz. ad Brandenb. Constit. folio 242. Perez. Cod. Natural. liber. n. 17. Besold. de jure Majestat. dissert. jurid. Politic.
units.tr: 15. What, then, must be decided about a man legitimated in one territory: is it judged that the statute exerts its force with respect to goods lying elsewhere, where he was not legitimated, or does that quality or capacity accompany him everywhere, as regards the effect of obtaining a dignity or succeeding on intestacy? I answer: although legitimation makes the person capable, as the doctors wish, so that the quality accompanies him everywhere, and although this may be observed out of courtesy, nevertheless, since that legitimation is made chiefly for the sake of obtaining honour or inheritance, over which he who legitimated in his own territory has no right outside it, I would judge that such legitimation is not sufficient for undertaking honours and taking an inheritance outside the territory. Argument from l. ult. D. de jurisdictione; l. communium, 9 Cod. de naturalibus liberis; c. per venerabilem, qui filii sint legitimi. Bartolus on l. 1 Cod. Summa Trinitas; Gothofredus in his commentary on the said l. ult.; Gabriel, Commentarii opinionum, lib. 6 de Statutis, concl. 8, n. 18; Gilkenius on Cod. Summa Trinitas, ad l. 1, n. 88; Mantica de conjecturis ultimarum voluntatum, lib. 11, tit. 10, n. 43; Craveta, consil. 119; Schepliz on the Brandenburg constitutions, fol. 242; Perezius, Cod. de naturalibus liberis, n. 17; Besold, de jure majestatis, dissertationes iuridico-politicae.

units.la: 16. Idem quod dicendum, de eo qui alibi extra territorium est nobilitatus. Etsi enim illa qualitas ei prosit, ibi locorum, ubi nobilitatur: non tamen proderit extra territorium nobilitantis. Sic enim alteri per alterum fieret praejudicium, & qui esset ad dignitates hic subeundas inhabilis, per forensem fieret habilis, etiam invito territorii domino. Ne dicam, quod quemadmodum lex non se extendit ultra territorium legislatoris; ita nec privilegium, aut beneficium in aliquem collatum; utpote quod nonnisi ab eo tribui solet, qui ferendae legis habet potestatem. Argum l. 1. D. de Constit. Princ. l. 1. §. 42. D. de Aqua quot. & aestiv. & per not. in seqq.
units.tr: 16. The same must be said of a person who has been ennobled elsewhere, outside the territory. For although that quality benefits him in the place where he was ennobled, it will not benefit him outside the territory of the one who ennobled him. For in that case one place would be prejudiced by another, and a person who was incapable of undertaking dignities here would become capable through a stranger, even against the will of the lord of the territory. Not to mention that, just as a law does not extend beyond the territory of its lawgiver, so neither does a privilege or benefit conferred on someone, since it is usually granted only by one who has the power of enacting law. Arg. l. 1 D. de Constit. Princ.; l. 1 §. 42 D. de Aqua quot. & aestiv., and the notes on what follows.

units.la: 17. Quid si in uno loco aliquis sit inhabilis ad administrandum declaratus, puta si ei prodige viventi, bonis sit interdictum: an ubique locorum, pro inhabili censetur, adeoque interdictum ad bona alibi sita extendetur? tendetur? Ita volunt DD. per l. is cui bonis. D. verb. oblig. l. 10. Curator. furiof. Gilken. in init. tit. Cod. de summ. Trinit. n. 59. Forte & ea sententia retinenda, non quod personae qualitas, eam ubique concitetur, etiam ratione bonorum alibi existentium; verum quod ubique locorum prodigo sit interdictum administratione; hic vero tantum agatur de modo probandi, aliquem esse prodigum, vel non esse: qui licet forte variet, pro locorum diversitate non tamen tollit effectum interdictionis; quod sufficiat circa probationes servari loci solemnia ubi fiunt. Arg. l. 3. in sin. D. de Testibus.
units.tr: 17. What if someone is declared incapable of administration in one place, for example if an interdict has been imposed on his goods because he lives as a spendthrift: is he regarded as incapable everywhere, so that the interdict is extended to goods situated elsewhere? The doctors hold so. Per l. is cui bonis D. verb. oblig.; l. 10 Curator. furios.; Gilken. in init. tit. Cod. de summ. Trinit. n. 59. Perhaps that opinion too should be kept, not because the quality of the person accompanies him everywhere, even as regards goods existing elsewhere, but because the interdict on administration applies everywhere; here the question concerns only the manner of proving whether someone is a spendthrift or not. This may vary with the diversity of places, yet it does not remove the effect of the interdict; for it suffices, as regards proofs, that the formalities of the place where they are made be observed. Arg. l. 3 in sin. D. de Testibus.

units.la: Malim tamen, id ita obtinere, non tam de jure, quam quidem de humanitate, dum populus vicini decreta populi comiter observat, ut multorum evitetur confusio.
units.tr: I would prefer, however, that this holds not so much by right as by courtesy, since the people of a neighbouring place observe the decrees of another people politely, so that much confusion may be avoided.

units.la: 18. Quid si quis in uno loco sit notatus infamiâ, an etiam in alio loco, non subdito priori, pro infami habebitur? Ita quidem velint DD. per l. 9. D. de Postul. l. 29. D. de Pœn. Bartol. Bald. apud Gilken. Cod. de summ. trinit. n. 120. 121. Contrarium potius colligo ex generali regulâ: quod judex nihil possit extra territorium, adeoque nec judicis sententia. l. sin. D. jurisd. l. 1. D. de officio Proconsul. l. 3. D. offic. Præsid. Quinimo uti poena tempore determinata, contra sententiae fidem non ulterius porrigitur, ita nec poena quae loco & territorio judicis sententiam proferentis est conclusa, l. 8. in sin. D. de Postul. Pariter enim passu ambulant tempus & locus, ut à tempore ad locum argumentum etiam procedat. l. 4. in medio. D. Condict. Tritic. Ne dicam argumentum ex d. l. 9. petitum commodè retorqueri posse. Ibi quippe prohibitus postulare in uno loco, adhuc in alio postulare non censetur esse prohibitus, eo quod sententia Præsidis, ejus provinciam quoad effectum non egrediatur.
units.tr: 18. What if someone is marked with infamy in one place: will he also be regarded as infamous in another place, not subject to the first? The doctors indeed hold so. Per l. 9 D. de Postul.; l. 29 D. de Pœn.; Bartol.; Bald., cited in Gilken. Cod. de summ. trinit. n. 120, 121. I rather infer the contrary from the general rule that a judge can do nothing outside his territory, and so neither can a judge's sentence. l. sin. D. jurisd.; l. 1 D. de officio Proconsul.; l. 3 D. offic. Præsid. Moreover, just as a penalty limited in time does not extend further against the terms of the sentence, so neither does a penalty confined to the place and territory of the judge pronouncing the sentence. l. 8 in sin. D. de Postul. For time and place go side by side, so that the argument may proceed from time to place as well. l. 4 in medio D. Condict. Tritic. Not to mention that the argument drawn from the said l. 9 can conveniently be turned back: for one who is forbidden to plead in one place is not regarded as forbidden to plead in another, since the sentence of the governor does not, as far as its effect goes, pass beyond his province.

units.la: 19. Quid si alicui interdictum arte, vel negotiatione, vel loco &c. an sententia servabitur extra territorium ejus, quicquam tulit aut pronunciavit? Respondeo, id quidem jure Romano obtinebat, in illo judice aut magistratum superiori, puta in Urbis præfecto, qui vice Principis regebat, ut si sententiam ferat, ea quandoque extra ejus territorium vires habeat, non tamen extra Principis territorium, qui illi id ipsum jure singulari concesserat. l. 1. §. 13. D. offic. Praef. Urbi.
units.tr: 19. What if someone has been forbidden a trade, a business, or a place, and the judge has given or pronounced a sentence: will that sentence be observed outside his territory? I answer that under Roman law this was so for that judge, or for a superior magistrate such as the Prefect of the City, who governed in the Prince's place. If such a judge pronounces a sentence, it may sometimes have force outside his territory, but not outside the Prince's territory, since the Prince had granted him this by a special law. l. 1. §. 13. D. offic. Praef. Urbi.

units.la: Verum tamen, ubi alter magistratus alteus non subest jurisdictioni, ibi equidem sententia pronunciantis limites egredi non potest. Atque in hunc sensum DD. statuunt; effectum Banni, extra territorium vires non habere. Arg. d. l. 1. D. off. Proconsf. l. 3. D. offic. Praef. l. 9. in sin. D. Postul. l. 7. §. 1. §. interdictum. §. seq. D. Interd. & Relegat. Bartol. in l. 1. Cod. summ. Trinit. n. 50.
units.tr: Yet where one magistrate is not subject to the jurisdiction of another, the sentence of the one who pronounces it cannot go beyond its limits. The doctors (DD.) lay down in this sense that the effect of a ban has no force outside the territory. Arg. d. l. 1. D. off. Proconsf. l. 3. D. offic. Praef. l. 9. in sin. D. Postul. l. 7. §. 1. §. interdictum. §. seq. D. Interd. & Relegat. Bartol. in l. 1. Cod. summ. Trinit. n. 50.

units.la: Gilken. ad d. tit. in init. n. 120. 121. Marcus Anton, Marscot. in c. ut animarum. de Constit. tom. 5. Repet. jur. can. p. 111. n. 20.
units.tr: Gilken. ad d. tit. in init. n. 120. 121. Marcus Anton, Marscot. in c. ut animarum. de Constit. tom. 5. Repet. jur. can. p. 111. n. 20.

units.la: Consuetudine tamen Germaniae, quoad relegationem, secus obtinere, sic ut & ultra Rhenum & Danubium, adeoque ultra locum, quam quo relegantis jurisdictio sese extendit, relegentur malefici, post Anton. Bernederum, Germaniae Practicum insignem, scribit Besold. in delib. jur. ex libr. 1. Pand. tit. de offic. Praef. Urbi. n. 45. Id quod etiam de moribus nostrarum Provinciarum, vel propter concordata, vel unionem quandoque obtinere, pro comperto est habitum.
units.tr: By the custom of Germany, however, relegation is handled otherwise, so that criminals are relegated even beyond the Rhine and the Danube, and so beyond the place to which the jurisdiction of the one relegating extends. Besold writes this, after Anton Bernederus, a notable German practitioner. Besold. in delib. jur. ex libr. 1. Pand. tit. de offic. Praef. Urbi. n. 45. It has been found, too, that this is also the practice in the customs of our own Provinces, sometimes by reason of concordats or union.

units.la: 20. Quid itaque de Tabellione seu notario, in uno loco habilitato ut instrumenta conscribat, dicendum: an extra locum, ubi erat habilitatus illud poterit? Non equidem. Absurdum quippe foret plus juris habere tabularium, quam is habet, qui eum constituit. Aut si tantundem juris haberet adeoque Tabularii habilitatio referretur ad actum jurisdictionis voluntariae, uti nonnulli censent: non tamen actus jurisdictionis illius voluntariae alicui inferiori concessus, extra territorium exerceri potuisset. Arg. l. 2. D. offic. Proconsf. Bartol. ad l. 1. Cod. Summ. Trinit. n. 34. Arg. l. sin. D. jurisd. Junct. l. nemo potest. 70 D. Reg. l. 4. §. 6. in med. D. Offic. Praef. Boer. decis. 242. n. 1. Gabriel. 1. comm. opin. tit. de fide instrum. conclus. 1. n. 5. Bartol.
units.tr: 20. What, then, should be said of a notary or tabellio, qualified in one place to draw up instruments: can he do so outside the place where he was qualified? Certainly not. It would be absurd for the notary to have more right than the one who appointed him. Or if he had the same right, and his qualification were referred to an act of voluntary jurisdiction, as some hold, still an act of that voluntary jurisdiction, granted to an inferior, could not have been exercised outside the territory. Arg. l. 2. D. offic. Proconsf. Bartol. ad l. 1. Cod. Summ. Trinit. n. 34. Arg. l. sin. D. jurisd. Junct. l. nemo potest. 70 D. Reg. l. 4. §. 6. in med. D. Offic. Praef. Boer. decis. 242. n. 1. Gabriel. 1. comm. opin. tit. de fide instrum. conclus. 1. n. 5. Bartol.

units.la: Bald. apud Gilken. ad init. tit. Cod. de summ. Trinit. n. 90. Coren Observat. Cur. Holland. 37, p. 294. 295. ibique Mascard. & alii.
units.tr: Baldus, cited in Gilken on the opening title of the Code, de summa Trinitate, n. 90; Coren, Observationes Curiae Hollandiae 37, pp. 294, 295, and there Mascardus and others.

units.la: SECTIO QUINTA
units.tr: SECTIO QUINTA

units.la: CAPUT PRIMUM.
units.tr: CAPUT PRIMUM.

units.la: 1. Utrum Princeps statuta condat super iis quae jure divino sunt introduc-ta?
units.tr: 1. Whether the Prince makes statutes validly concerning matters that have been introduced by divine law?

units.la: 2. Utrum recte statuta condat de negotiis mere ecclesiasticis?
units.tr: 2. Whether he makes statutes validly concerning purely ecclesiastical affairs?

units.la: 3. An statuto fiat licitum quod aliter in conscientia est illicitum?
units.tr: 3. Whether a statute can make lawful what is unlawful in conscience?

units.la: 4. An statuta recte condantur, circa ea quae spectant jus naturale, & gentium primaevum?
units.tr: 4. Whether statutes are validly made concerning those things that pertain to natural law and the primeval law of nations?

units.la: 5. An statutum valeat super negotiis, de quibus abunde jure civili cautum est?
units.tr: 5. Whether a statute is valid on matters on which the civil law has already provided fully?

units.la: 6. An statuta valeant, quae condita contra jus civile?
units.tr: 6. Whether statutes are valid which are made contrary to the civil law?

units.la: 1. POst explicatas difficultates quae naturam, id est definitionem, & divisiones statutorum, spectabant; ordo me deducit, ad obiecta statutorum; id est ut de rebus atque negotiis, licitis vel illicitis, super quibus statuta conduntur, meam proferam sententiam.
units.tr: 1. After the difficulties explained, which concerned the nature, that is the definition and divisions of statutes, the order of my treatment leads me to the objects of statutes. That is, I shall set out my opinion about the matters and affairs, lawful or unlawful, on which statutes are made.

units.la: Et quidem hic in vestibulo sese offert circa jus divinum, non una difficultas. Principio, num recte Princeps statuta condat super iis, quae jure divino sunt introducta? Ut ea confirmet magis & suae accommodet reipublicae, dubium nullum. Ut iis contraria statuta condat, non indistincte affirmandum, aut negandum erit.
units.tr: And indeed here, at the threshold, more than one difficulty presents itself concerning divine law. First, may the Prince validly make statutes on those things which have been introduced by divine law? That he may make statutes to confirm them more firmly and to adapt them to his commonwealth, there is no doubt. That he may make statutes contrary to them cannot be affirmed or denied without distinction.

units.la: Vel enim jus divinum, quod hic pro divino aliquo praecepto amplector, est mutabile & forte Judaicae reipublicae accommodatum, adeoque illi populo solummodo datum; & spectat negotia saecularia, aut versatur circa ecclesiastica, sed politice; & erit in Principis potestate, statutum condere illi praecepto contrarium.
units.tr: For either the divine law, which I here take to mean some divine precept, is changeable and perhaps adapted to the Jewish commonwealth, and so was given to that people only; and it concerns secular affairs, or it deals with ecclesiastical matters but in a political way. In that case it lies within the Prince's power to make a statute contrary to that precept.

units.la: Vel divinum praeceptum, est immutabile inter homines, universo generi humano latum, nituturque ratione naturali omnibus communi; nec erit in arbitrio Principis situm, statutum in contrarium condere. Neque enim juri naturali hominum immutabili, multo minus divino, Princeps adversari potest. Argum. §. 2. 1. Institut. jure natur. gent. civil. & §. 2. in sin. instit. de Usufr. verb. nec enim poterat. l. 15. D. de Condit. Institut. l.
units.tr: Or the divine precept is unchangeable among men, given to the whole human race, and rests on natural reason common to all. In that case it does not lie within the Prince's discretion to make a statute to the contrary. For the Prince cannot oppose the unchangeable law of nature among men, much less the divine law. Argument from §2, I. Institutes, On natural, civil and the law of nations; and from §2 at the end of the Institutes, On usufruct, the words "for he could not"; l. 15 D. De conditionibus institutionum; l.

units.la: 1. Cod. de Crimin. Sacril. l. 4. D. de Recept. Arbitr. Nov. 109. in init. Christian. ad Mechlin. chlin. in Prælud. num. 20. Collector. jur. consuet. Hungariæ & Transsylvaniæ. Prologi tit. 9.
units.tr: 1. Cod. De crimine sacrilegii; l. 4 D. De receptis arbitris; Nov. 109 at the beginning; Christian, on Mechlin, in Prælud. no. 20; Collector of the customary law of Hungary and Transylvania, Prologue, title 9.

units.la: 2 An igitur statuta condere poterit de negotiis mere ecclesiasticis, ut condendo statuta, conscientiæ casus quoad hominem internum decidat; aut articulos fidei determinet? Non equidem. 1. Quia ex præscripto imperatoris Justiniani sacerdotium ministrat rebus divinis, imperium nonnisi humanis. nov. 6. & in init. & nov. 42. vid. Grafwinck. de juris fundam. contra Jesuitam. p. 234. Ut utriusque distincte sint potestates, distincta officia, adeoque nec eorum confundendum exercitium. Confess. Belgica. artic. 30. 31. Ordin. Eccles. Synod. Dordrac. de ann. 1618. 1619. art. 28. Potestas quippe Sacerdotis Dei versatur circa negotia Dei, quæ talia; potestas Principis circa Principis negotia. Illa circa hominem internum, spiritualem; hæc circa externum, Politicum. Illa, à Christo ut Mediatore, hæc ut à Domino Deo, dependet. Illa, verbo, prece, predicatione obtestando, rogando, hortando, instruendo, dirigit hominem, ut incrementum capiat ratione vitæ spiritualis; hæc jubendo pro imperio, coercendo, cogendo, societati civili consulit. Illa, ut regnum gratiæ magis magisque capiat incrementum; hæc ut naturæ regno sua constet auctoritas. Illa quidem potestas est, & jurisdictio, suo modo, sed spiritualis, & quidem ministerialis ; hæc dominica, auctoritativa, seculcandidatis. Illa substitutum non habet, nec est in capite substituto; hæc substitutum admittit, ut vice regem, & poterit esse substituta.
units.tr: 2. Can the Prince, then, make statutes on purely ecclesiastical affairs, so that by making statutes he settles cases of conscience concerning the inner man, or determines the articles of faith? Certainly not. 1. Because by the prescription of the emperor Justinian, the priesthood ministers in divine things, the empire only in human things. Novels 6, at the beginning, and Novel 42; see Grafwinkel, On the foundations of law, against the Jesuit, p. 234. Thus the two powers are distinct, the offices distinct, and so their exercise must not be confused. Belgic Confession, articles 30 and 31; Ecclesiastical Ordinance of the Synod of Dort of 1618–1619, art. 28. For the power of the priest of God is concerned with the affairs of God, as such; the power of the Prince with the affairs of the Prince. The one is concerned with the inner, spiritual man; the other with the outer, political man. The one depends on Christ as Mediator, the other on the Lord God. The one, by word, prayer and preaching, by entreating, asking, exhorting and teaching, guides the man so that he may grow in the life of the spirit; the other, by commanding with authority, restraining and compelling, provides for civil society. The one aims that the kingdom of grace may grow more and more; the other that the kingdom of nature may keep its authority. The one is indeed a power and a jurisdiction, after its own manner, but spiritual, and indeed ministerial; the other is lordly and authoritative, secular. The one has no deputy and is not in a deputised head; the other admits a deputy, as a vice-king, and may have one.

units.la: 2. Quia statuta demum ecclesiastica seu canones ecclesiasticos, scil. ecclesiastice tantum illi condunt, qui negotia mere ecclesiastica tractant: quales personæ ecclesiasticæ, quæ votum habent in Synodis decisivum. Quales solum ecclesiasticæ personæ, non Princeps secularis, aut ejus commissarii. artic. 29. 30. 33. 47. 50. ordin. eccl. de ann. 1619.
units.tr: 2. Because ecclesiastical statutes, that is, canons, are made in the ecclesiastical manner only by those who deal with purely ecclesiastical matters: such persons as ecclesiastical persons who have a decisive vote in synods. Only ecclesiastical persons make them, not the secular Prince or his commissioners. Articles 29, 30, 33, 47 and 50 of the Ecclesiastical Ordinance of 1619.

units.la: 3. Quia non Princeps, verum sacerdos discernit inter purum & impurum, quid sanctum sit, quid prophanum, explicando. Ezechiel. c. 44. v. 23. Ut cui soli mysteriorum divinorum concredita est dispensatio. 1. Corinth. c. 4. v. 1. 2. ordin. Eccles. de ann. 1618. 1619. artic. 18.
units.tr: 3. Because it is not the Prince but the priest who, by explaining, discerns between the clean and the unclean, what is holy and what is profane. Ezekiel 44:23. As the dispensing of the divine mysteries has been entrusted to him alone. 1 Corinthians 4:1–2; Ecclesiastical Ordinance of 1618–1619, article 18.

units.la: 4. Quia sacerdos, Christi nomine, conscientiam hominis obligat cujus ministrum agit atque mandatarium; ut optime sensum sui domini scire præsumatur; adeoque non futurus secus hominum ductor, aut doctor, in via veritatis. Argum. l. 6. Cod. Sacrof. Eccles. 1. Corinth. c. 4. v. ult. 1. Corinth. c. 5. v. 20. Matth. c. 10. v. 5. & c. 18. v. 17. Luc. c. 10. v. 16. 1. Thessal. c. 5. v. 12. 13. Hebr. c. 13. v. 17.
units.tr: 4. Because the priest, in Christ's name, binds the conscience of the man whose minister and mandatary he acts; so he is presumed to know very well the mind of his Lord, and therefore will not be a leader or teacher of men on the way of truth in any other way. Argument from l. 6 Cod. De sacrosanctis ecclesiis; 1 Corinthians 4 last verse; 1 Corinthians 5:20; Matthew 10:5 and 18:17; Luke 10:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:12–13; Hebrews 13:17.

units.la: 5. Quia artifici credendum est in suâ arte & fidendum judicanti de negotio, cui præpositus. Ut hominis sit arrogantis, & extra terminos saltantis, qui tantum sibi de artificio in judicando auctoritatis assumpserit, quantum ipse artifex; quem in suâ arte peritum esse convenit, atque habere sensus exercitatos ad discretionem boni & mali. Argum l. 12. D. de stat. homin. l. 1. in med. init. D. de ventr. inspic. l. comparationes. l. plures. Cod. de fide Instrum. l. hac edictali. §. hic illud. Cod. de Secund. Nupt. Quinimo, non aliter atque si dubitetur, vulnus sit lethale, nec ne, ad medicorum recurritur judicium; si de finibus finium, ad mensorem itur; si de peritiâ studiosi, ad doctorem seu præceptorem. l. 4. Cod. sin. Regund. l. nemini. 14. Cod. Advoc. diverf. judic. Speculator tit. de Homicidio. verb. sed pone. Ita si de vitiis aut morbis vitæ spiritualis agatur, medicos animarum, atque vitæ spiritualis curatores in consilium adhibere oportebit, qui suo consilio decisivo, certum, declarabunt, congruenter verbo Dei, quod erat forte controversum. Et quod de Augustino Petrus Faber. 2. Semestr. ult. Optimus quidem ille Theologus, non æque bonus forsitan ipse jurisconsultus; id etiam sacerdos regeret jurisconsulto: Magnus quidem legislator Justinianus, magnus Constantinus, sed non magnus Ecclesiæ doctor. Alber. de Nupt. libr. 1. c. 10. in sin. vid. & Confess. Synod. Angliæ de ann. 1647. sub Rege Carolo, cap- 32. Id quod eleganter explicarunt imperatores Carol. & Ludovic. in Capitulari libr. 5. c. 63. Illud ad exemplum reducendum est, „quod in ecclesiastica historia Constantinus „imperator Episcopis ait: Deus constituit „vos sacerdotes & potestatem vobis dedit de „nobis quoque judicandi. Et ideo nos à „vobis recte judicamur. Et ex Prospero de „vita contempl. & actual. ipsis sacerdotibus „proprie animarum curandarum sollicitudo „est commissa, qui pondus populi sibi com„missi viriliter sustinentes, pro peccatis o„mnium, velut pro suis, infatigabiliter sup„plicant Deo: ac velut quidam Aaron, in„censum contriti cordis, & humiliati spiri„tus offerentes, quo placatur Deus, aver„tunt iram futuræ animadversionis à popu„lo. Qui per Dei gratiam fiunt divinæ vo„luntatis judices. & c. 170. honorem debi„tum episcopis absque ullâ simulatione aut „detrectatione impendant, eisque in omni„bus, ut patribus obediant: & quicquid pro „salute animarum monuerint, prout melius „potuerint ad implere satagant. Verum „subjungam exemplum nostri seculi, quo „magis constet, quid Principi quæsitum „circa sacra. Non illustre magis est, quam illud Jacobi, regis Angliæ in controversiis fidei satis versati qui ita scribit ad candidum lectorem ante Apol. pro juramento fidelit. „Chri„ Christiano cuique Regi, Principi ac „ Reipublicæ esse concessum, externam in „ rebus ecclesiasticis regiminis formam suis „ præscribere, quæ ad civilis administratio- „ nis quam proxime accedat, dummodo à „ Fidei veræque religionis fundamentis „ nec tantillum abscedat.
units.tr: 5. Because one must believe the craftsman in his own craft, and trust the one who judges a matter over which he is set. It belongs to an arrogant man, who leaps beyond his bounds, to assume for himself as much authority in judging of a craft as the craftsman himself has, who ought to be skilled in his own art and to have senses trained to discern good from evil. Argument from l. 12 D. De statu hominum; l. 1 in the middle and beginning D. De ventre inspiciendo; l. comparationes; l. plures Cod. De fide instrumentorum; l. hac edictali, §. hic illud Cod. De secundis nuptiis. Indeed, just as when it is doubted whether a wound is mortal or not, one has recourse to the judgment of doctors; if about the boundaries of fields, one goes to the surveyor; if about the skill of a student, to the teacher or tutor. l. 4 Cod. De sententiis et regundis; l. nemini 14 Cod. De advocatis diversorum iudiciorum; Speculator, title On homicide, the words "but suppose". So if the question concerns the faults or diseases of the spiritual life, it will be necessary to call in physicians of souls and curers of the spiritual life as counsel, who by their decisive judgement will declare, in agreement with the word of God, what was perhaps in dispute. And what Peter Faber says of Augustine, Second Semester, last part: that most excellent theologian was perhaps not equally good as a jurist; so a priest would rule a jurist in this matter. Justinian was a great lawgiver, and Constantine great, but not a great teacher of the Church. Alber. On marriage, book 1, ch. 10, at the end; see also the Confession of the Synod of England of 1647 under King Charles, ch. 32. This the emperors Charles and Louis have elegantly explained in the Capitulary, book 5, ch. 63. That must be brought back to this example: "that in ecclesiastical history the emperor Constantine said to the bishops: God has appointed you priests and has given you power, and so we too may rightly be judged by you. And from Prosper, On the contemplative and active life: the care of souls is entrusted properly to the priests themselves, who bravely bear the weight of the people committed to them and, for the sins of all as if for their own, unceasingly pray to God, and, like a certain Aaron, offering incense of a contrite heart and a humbled spirit, by which God is appeased, turn away the anger of future punishment from the people. These, by the grace of God, become judges of the divine will. And ch. 170: they should give the honour owed to bishops without any pretence or disparagement, and obey them in all things as fathers; and whatever they admonish for the salvation of souls, they should strive to carry out as well as they can." But I shall add an example from our own age, so that it may be clearer what is sought from a Prince concerning sacred things. Nothing is more illustrious than that of James, king of England, well versed in controversies of faith, who thus writes to the candid reader before the Apology on the oath of allegiance: "It is permitted to every Christian king, prince and commonwealth to prescribe for its subjects an external form of government in ecclesiastical matters, which comes as near as possible to civil administration, provided it does not depart even slightly from the foundations of the faith and the true religion."

units.la: 6. Quia causæ ecclesiasticæ, non sunt causæ Principis, adeoque nec ad seculare imperium, quale Principis est, referri debebunt. 2. Paralipom. c. 19. v. 11. Johann. c. 18. v. 36. 37. Ut quemadmodum indecens est personas ecclesiasticas sese negotiis secularibus immiscere: 2. Timoth. c. 2. v. 4. Marc. c. 10. v. 42. 43. Luc. c. 22. v. 25. 26. Ita etiam incongruum erit, Principem causis mere ecclesiasticis semet ingerere. Maxime cum uti dictum, jura Principis & Dei sint distincta: Argum. Matth. c. 22. v. 21. Quasi dicatur sano sensu divisum imperium cum Jove Cæsar habet. Unde qui iniquum esse censet, uti iniquum est, Aaronem in civilibus Mosi præfici, is etiam sciat æquum non esse, in negotio sacerdotali, Mosem Aaroni præficere. Utrobique enim par ratio est, & qui nec illud patitur, nec hoc affectet; argumento à naturâ oppositorum desumpto. Et quemadmodum nemo nostrum sacerdotem velit militem, ita nec militem cupiat sacerdotem. Non enim conveniunt, aut eâdem manu tractantur, cithera & gladius; arma spiritualia & temporalia. Quod si tamen quis existumet sic fieri debere, quia forte extra ordinem, peculiari quo instinctu & monitu, & jussu divino, Princeps ecclesiastica, & prophetica tractavit; id quod suadent exempla Davidis, Salomonis, aliorumque; is sciat & summum sacerdotem Jehojada, etiam extra ordinem, & jure tamen, negotia tractasse politica, quæque statutum regni spectarent, cum suis peregisse. Ut si posterius exemplum pro regulâ servari nolit, etam priora immerito ecclesiasticis personis obtruserit.
units.tr: 6. Because ecclesiastical causes are not the Prince's causes, they must not be referred to secular rule, which is the Prince's. 2 Chron. 19:11. John 18:36, 37. Just as it is unseemly for ecclesiastical persons to mix themselves in secular business (2 Tim. 2:4; Mark 10:42, 43; Luke 22:25, 26), so it will be incongruous for the Prince to thrust himself into purely ecclesiastical causes. Especially since, as has been said, the rights of the Prince and of God are distinct. Argument from Matt. 22:21. It is as if one were to say that Caesar holds a divided empire with Jove, in the sound sense. Hence whoever thinks it unjust (as it is unjust) that Aaron should be set over Moses in civil affairs, let him also know that it is not fair for Moses to be set over Aaron in priestly business. For the reasoning is the same on both sides: whoever does not allow the one should not aim at the other. This is an argument drawn from the nature of opposites. And just as none of us would want a priest to be a soldier, so let no one desire a soldier to be a priest. For the lyre and the sword do not agree, nor are they handled by the same hand: spiritual and temporal arms. But if anyone thinks it ought to be done so, because perhaps a prince handled ecclesiastical and prophetic matters outside the ordinary order, by some peculiar instinct, prompting and divine command, as the examples of David, Solomon and others suggest, let him know that the high priest Jehoiada too, even outside the ordinary order, yet rightfully, handled political affairs and carried out with his own people those matters which concerned the statutes of the kingdom. So if he will not have the later example kept as a rule, he is wrong to thrust the earlier ones upon ecclesiastical persons.

units.la: 3. An igitur Princeps statuto poterit facere licitum, quod aliter in conscientiâ est illicitum; & subditus parendo tali statuto, eo ipso, quod à Principe sit conditum, illæsam servabit conscientiam? Non equidem.
units.tr: 3. Can the Prince, then, by statute make lawful what is otherwise unlawful in conscience? And will a subject, by obeying such a statute, keep his conscience unharmed simply because it was established by the Prince? Certainly not.

units.la: Et quia subditus legi quidem civili, adeoque & statuto civitatis obsequium debet; sed tamen salvo jure superioris, puta Dei, cujus jussui ante omnia semet subjiciet: non aliter atque de jure feudali, qui fidelitatem jurat Seniori (nisi sit feudum ligium) semper excipit territorii dominum, aut imperatorem. Unde qui sequitur ductum statutorum humanorum, ita sequitur, si non devient à suo Principio, divinâ scilicet jussione. Nam quodcunque bene ordinatum est, oportet ut sit reducibile ad Principium, ex quo ducit originem. Et si ab illo dissentiat principio, errare potius, quam dirigere sit dicendum. c. sunt quidam. 25. q. 1. Fortun. Garcias. de ult. sin. juris civil. & canonic. p. 142. n. 201.
units.tr: For the subject owes obedience to civil law, and so to the statute of the state, but saving the right of the superior, namely God, to whose command he will submit himself before all else. It is just as in feudal law: one who swears fealty to his lord (unless it is a liege fief) always excepts the lord of the territory, or the emperor. Hence whoever follows the course of human statutes follows it only if he does not depart from its principle, namely divine command. For whatever is well ordained must be reducible to the principle from which it draws its origin, and if it dissents from that principle, it must be said to err rather than to direct. c. sunt quidam, 25 q. 1. Fortunatus Garcias, de ultimis sinibus juris civilis et canonici, p. 142, n. 201.

units.la: Et quia non potest Princeps ex injustitiâ facere justitiam, aut quod secundum legem Dei est inhonestum, honestare: nisi velit esse Papa in terris, eandemque sibi potestatem concessam, quam canonistæ Romano Pontifici, de cujus factis disputare, ad instar Sacrilegii foret, quod coeleste habeat arbitrium. gloss. inc. non nos beatam. dist. 40. Quem nemo potest reprehendere, licet suam & suorum fratrum salutem negligeret, & ad infernum secum traheret. c. si papa dist. 40. Et si dispensaret contra Apostolum, vetus testamentum Gloss. in 3. Decret. c. 4. de conc. ess. Prab. c. praepositi. Quin imo si aberraret, & mandaret vitia, vetaret virtutes, credendum esset vitia esse licita, virtutes esse illicitas. Bellarm. de Pontif. libr. 4. c. 5. contra. c. 5. de Testam. c. inter haec 33. q. 2. vid. Hottom. in Brut. fulmine. p. mihi. 13.
units.tr: And because the Prince cannot make justice out of injustice, or make honourable what is dishonourable according to the law of God, unless he wishes to be the Pope on earth, and to have the same power granted to him that the canonists grant to the Roman Pontiff. To dispute the Pontiff's acts would be like sacrilege, since he has a heavenly judgement. Gloss on inc. non nos, beatam, dist. 40. No one can rebuke him, even if he neglects his own salvation and that of his brothers and drags them with him to hell. c. si papa, dist. 40. And if he dispensed against the Apostle or the Old Testament, Gloss in 3 Decret., c. 4, de conc. ess. Prab.; c. praepositi. Indeed, even if he erred and commanded vices and forbade virtues, it would have to be believed that vices are lawful and virtues unlawful. Bellarmine, de Pontifice, lib. 4, c. 5; contra c. 5, de testamentis; c. inter haec, 33 q. 2. See Hotman, in Brutum fulmen, p. mihi 13.

units.la: Et quia non potest ullius Principis edictum, vel statutum quempiam eximere nexibus legis moralis; ut quae dispositioni terreni Principis non subest, cujus jussus à lege illa divina, etiam in omnibus causis atque casubus decidendis, habet dependentiam. Barbos. ad l. 4. Cod. de Summ. Trinit. Ut hic merito dicatur, jus divinum, pactis hominum immutari non posse; Arg. l. 38. D. de Pact. adeoque excedentem hac in parte suæ Potestatis limites, non exaudiri. l. ult. D. de jurisdict. l. 170. D. verb. signif. Exod. 1. v. 7.
units.tr: And because no edict or statute of any prince can exempt anyone from the bonds of the moral law, since it is not subject to the disposition of an earthly prince, and its command depends on that divine law in deciding all matters and cases. Hence it is rightly said here that divine law cannot be altered by the agreements of men, and so a prince who exceeds the limits of his power in this respect is not heard. Argument from l. 38 D. de pactis; l. ult. D. de jurisdictione; l. 170 D. de verborum significatione; Exod. 1:7.

units.la: 1. Samuel. 22. v. 17. Daniel. 3. v. 12. Actor. 4. v. 19. & 5. v. 29.

Unde etiam DD. statuunt, Principem de rebus fidei statutum non fecisse, licet id forte ita videatur, quod non sit præsumendum, statuentes id statuisse, super quibus & de quibus non habebant statuendi potestatem. Alex. vol. 5. consil 33. in sin. n. 16. Mascard. de statutor. interpret. conclus. 2. n. 261. & conclus. 1. n. 55. & seqq.
units.tr: Hence also the doctors (DD.) lay down that a prince has not made a statute concerning matters of faith, even if it may seem so, since it is not to be presumed that those who declare he has enacted it were enacting in matters over which, and concerning which, they had no power to enact. Alexander, vol. 5, consil. 33, in sin., n. 16. Mascardus, de statutorum interpretatione, concl. 2, n. 261, and concl. 1, n. 55 and following.

units.la: Et quia declarare aliquid esse licitum vel illicitum in conscientiâ, seu in foro Poli, nihil aliud est, quam dirigere actiones hominis intrinsecè, prout in ordine ad vitam spiritualem consideLantur. Verum id ipsum nulli seculari potestati concessum est, aut commissum ut cui primo & per se vitæ Politicæ salus & tranquillitas est curæ. Ut ad conscientiam tranquillandam, sola Dei vox audiri debeat, ab iis prolata, atque declarata, quibus Deus sua concredidit oracula. Matth. 15. v. 9. Rom. 13. 1. Corinth. 3. v. 5. & 4. v. 1. & 2. Corinth. c. 5. v. 20. 1. Petr. c. 2. v. 13. & c. 5. v. 2. 3. Actor. 15. à v. 6. Novel. 137. init. Daneus Ethic. Christian. libr. 2. c. 12. Amef. Medull. libr. 2. c. 17.
units.tr: And because to declare something lawful or unlawful in conscience, or in the forum of heaven, is nothing other than to direct human actions in themselves, insofar as they are considered in relation to spiritual life. But this itself has not been granted or committed to any secular power, since the safety and tranquillity of political life is its first and proper concern. So to calm the conscience, only the voice of God should be heard, uttered and declared by those to whom God has entrusted his oracles. Matt. 15:9. Rom. 13:1. 1 Cor. 3:5 and 4:1, 2. 2 Cor. 5:20. 1 Pet. 2:13 and 5:2, 3. Acts 15 from v. 6. Novel 137, init. Daneus, Ethica christiana, lib. 2, c. 12. Amesius, Medulla, lib. 2, c. 17.

units.la: Et quia Princeps in terris est Dei servus atque minister, qui sicuti quod agit, mandato peragit illius summi legislatoris; sic nec unquam fines mandati excedere debet, aut potest; multo minus quicquam agere contra legem sui domini, gloss. in Auth. ad hæc. Cod. de Usur.
units.tr: And because the Prince on earth is God's servant and minister, who, as what he does, he performs by the command of that supreme lawgiver, so he never ought or is able to exceed the limits of his command, much less to do anything against the law of his Lord. Gloss on Auth. ad haec, Cod. de usuris.

units.la: Quo nomine populus Israëliticus non secutus per omnia suum ducem Mosem, verum in quantum ea, quæ populo præscribebat, iis erant conformia quæ à Deo ipsi in mandatis erant data: textus expressius est, Numer c. 1. v. sin.
units.tr: For which reason the Israelite people did not follow their leader Moses in all things, but only insofar as the things he prescribed to the people conformed to what had been given to him by God in commands. The text is more explicit: Num. c. 1, v. sin.

units.la: Et denique, quia nihil magis in Principe fulget, quam recta & sincera fides. l. 4. Cod. summ. Trinit. Barbos. Cod. ibid. n. 5. Ut illius curæ incumbat, aliquid utile, & Deo placens & gratum peragere; quo divinum numen placari possit; quod in Deum spes, salus sit reipublicæ; & conformia juri divino statuta, mandatis divinis, conformes leges, tranquillitas sit eorum, qui à Domino Deo ejus curæ sunt concrediti. Sic loquuntur Christiani Principes, sic omnes agere oportet, & suam rempublicam administrare nec iram divinam in se, aliter agendo, provocent. l. 5. in Princ. Cod. Summ. Trinit. Nov. 8. in init. Novell. de lenonibus. 16. Nov. 135. in Princ. Nov. 109. Frederic, Imperator tit. de Pace tenend. in init. Nov. 77. in init. Nov. 85. in init. vid. Proæm. Carol. 7. Francor. ad Pragmat. Sanct. super. concil. Constant. & Basil. Facbin. 1 contr. 63. Quettam consil. 61. num. 5. 6. 5. 6. 7. 8. 9. 10. per Alex. Corneum, Abbas tem, Felin. in c. sin. de Præscript. Oldendorp. in Classe. in init. de juris ordinat. Rittersh. ad nov. parat. 2. c. 1. in init. Gothefred. ad nov. 105. c. 2. §. 4. litt. K. L. in comm. Amef. casuum conf. libr. 1. c. 2, n. 8. 9. & seq. & libr. 5. c. 41. n. 10. 11. 12. 13. 14. & seqq. Grot. de jure bell. & pac. libr. 2. c. 1. n. 14. Anton. Matth. tract. de judic. disp. 1. n. 32. Zoes. D. de Usucap. n. 55. 56. & seqq.
units.tr: And finally, because nothing shines more in a Prince than right and sincere faith, it is his care to do something useful, pleasing and acceptable to God, by which the divine majesty may be appeased, in which lies the hope in God and the safety of the commonwealth; and that statutes conformable to divine law and laws conformable to divine commands bring tranquillity to those whom the Lord God has entrusted to his care. Thus Christian princes speak, and thus all should act and administer their commonwealth, nor by acting otherwise provoke divine wrath upon themselves. l. 5 in princ. Cod. summa Trinitas; Nov. 8 in init.; Nov. de lenonibus 16; Nov. 135 in princ.; Nov. 109; Frederick, Emperor, tit. de pace tenenda in init.; Nov. 77 in init.; Nov. 85 in init.; see Proem. Carolus VII of France to the Pragmatic Sanction; super concilio Constantiensi et Basiliensi; Fachin, 1 contr. 63; Quettam, consil. 61, nn. 5, 6; 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, through Alexander Cornaeus, Abbas Panormitanus, Felinus in c. sin. de praescriptionibus; Oldendorp, in Classe, in init. de juris ordinatione; Rittershusius, ad nov. parat. 2, c. 1, in init.; Gothofredus, ad nov. 105, c. 2, §4, lit. K, L; in comm. Amesius, casuum conscientiae, lib. 1, c. 2, nn. 8, 9 and following, and lib. 5, c. 41, nn. 10–14 and following; Grotius, de jure belli et pacis, lib. 2, c. 1, n. 14; Anton. Matthaeus, tract. de judiciis, disp. 1, n. 32; Zoesius, D. de usucapione, nn. 55, 56 and following.

units.la: Hinc in hypothesi DD. statuunt; si statutum uni rem adimat sine causa, & alteri donet, non posse donatarium rem donatam in conscientia retinere. Petrus Anchoran. in c. canonum Statuta, de Constit. tom. 2. Repet. jur. canon. p. 105. n. 129. ubi plures.
units.tr: Hence, in this case the doctors lay down that if a statute takes a thing from one person without cause and gives it to another, the recipient cannot in conscience keep the thing given to him. Petrus Anchoran. in c. canonum Statuta, de Constit. tom. 2. Repet. jur. canon. p. 105. n. 129. ubi plures.

units.la: 4. Verum poterunt ne statuta condi circa ea, quæ spectant jus naturale aut gentium primævum? Respondeo, ut confirmient jus naturale, aut gentium in totum vel pro parte, dubitari non poterit. Quia & jus naturale & gentium, in civitatem recipitur, sicque comprobatione fit civile. Accedit, quod jus civile non in totum à jure naturali aut gentium recedat. Ne dicam, quod absurdum non sit, unam candemque rem diverso jure censeri; adeoque & juri naturæ, & gentium, & civili annumerari. §. 2. v. sic enim & jus. Institut. jure nat. gent. civil. l. 2. l. 3. l. 6. D. de justitiâ & jure. l. 45. D. Ad leg. Aquil.
units.tr: 4. But could statutes be made about those matters that belong to the natural law or the primary law of nations? I answer that there can be no doubt they may confirm the natural law or the law of nations, wholly or in part. For both the natural law and the law of nations are received into the commonwealth, and so by such approval they become civil law. Moreover, civil law does not depart from the natural law or the law of nations in every respect. I need not add that it is not absurd for one and the same thing to be judged under different laws, and so to be counted both under the law of nature, the law of nations and the civil law. §. 2. v. sic enim & jus. Institut. jure nat. gent. civil. l. 2. l. 3. l. 6. D. de justitiâ & jure. l. 45. D. Ad leg. Aquil.

units.la: Ut vero statuta tollant jus naturale, aut gentium primævum, & quidem in thesi, non videtur dicendum. Quia hoc ipsum ne quidem Princeps, aut Senatus Romanus per jus civile potuit; adeoque nec id statutis fieri poterit. §. 2. verf. ergo senatus. instit. de Usufr. §. sin. Instit. de legitim. agnat. Tutel. Quæ etiam ratio est, quod princeps jure naturæ & gentium teneatur; quod utrumque ipso principatu potentius sit; ut & omnibus illis, quæ ex utroque jure descendunt, quales sunt plerique contractus, obligetur. Bald. ad c. 1, §. sin. qui feud. dare posf. Castrens. ad l. digna vox Cod. de leg. Coraf. 2. Misc. 25. Tusc. conclus. 50. verb. Papa. Salmas. dissert. de fœnor. Trapezit. p. 401. Arthur. Duck. Anglus. in tract. de auctor. jur. civil. Roman. libr. 1. c. 3, n. 12.
units.tr: But that statutes may abolish the natural law or the primary law of nations, and that in principle, does not seem to be maintainable. For not even the Roman Prince or Senate could do this by civil law, and so it cannot be done by statutes either. §. 2. verf. ergo senatus. instit. de Usufr. §. sin. Instit. de legitim. agnat. Tutel. The reason is also that the prince is bound by the law of nature and the law of nations, both of which are more powerful than the principate itself; and he is bound to all those things that descend from either law, such as most contracts. Bald. ad c. 1, §. sin. qui feud. dare posf. Castrens. ad l. digna vox Cod. de leg. Coraf. 2. Misc. 25. Tusc. conclus. 50. verb. Papa. Salmas. dissert. de fœnor. Trapezit. p. 401. Arthur. Duck. Anglus. in tract. de auctor. jur. civil. Roman. libr. 1. c. 3, n. 12.

units.la: Quinimo uti judex non potest cum effectu sententiam ferre, aut quid jubere contra naturam l. 3. D. quæ sent. sine appell. rescind. Ita statuta non valent, nisi quæ juste & sancte sunt condita, adeoq; honestati naturali convenientia; prout ipsa demum lex valet, quæ jubet honesta & naturâ civilia, prohibetque contraria, quasi Dei munus & inventum. l.
units.tr: Indeed, just as a judge cannot effectually pass a sentence or order anything contrary to nature, so statutes are valid only if they have been justly and rightly made, and so agree with natural honesty; just as that law itself is valid which commands what is honourable and in accordance with nature, and forbids the contrary, being as it were a gift and invention of God. l.

units.la: Unde oportet ita statuta condita esse, ut à sapiente reprehendi nequeant, qualia sunt bonis moribus convenientia. Argam. l. 15. D. de Condit. institut. l. Salvius Aristo. D. de legat. Praestand. Hyp. Riminald. in c. quae in Ecclesiâ. de Constit. tom. 2. Repet. jur. canon. n. 5. p. 339. & in Rubr. de Constit. p. 83. 153. eod. tom. Menoch. de Praesumpt. libr. 2. praes. 1. n. 4. Roeland. à Valle libr. 3. consil. 72. n. 42. Alderan. Mascard. de statutor. interpret. conclus. 2. n. 256. 257. & seqq. & conclus. 6. n. 195. & concl. 7. n. 51. Canonista in c. quod clericis. de foro compet. Christin. ad Mevhl. in Praelud. n. 5. idem ad Epilog. n. 6.
units.tr: Hence statutes must be so framed that a wise person cannot find fault with them, as is the case with those that agree with good morals. See the argument from l. 15 D. de Condit. institut.; l. Salvius Aristo D. de legat. praestand.; Hyp. Riminald. in c. quae in Ecclesia de Constit. tom. 2 Repet. jur. canon. n. 5 p. 339, and in Rubr. de Constit. pp. 83, 153 of the same volume; Menoch. de Praesumpt. libr. 2 praes. 1 n. 4; Roeland. à Valle libr. 3 consil. 72 n. 42; Alderan. Mascard. de statutor. interpret. concl. 2 nn. 256, 257 and following, concl. 6 n. 195, and concl. 7 n. 51; the Canonist in c. quod clericis de foro compet.; Christin. ad Mevhl. in Praelud. n. 5, and the same author ad Epilog. n. 6.

units.la: 5. Quid si statutum aliquod conditum sit de casubus & negotiis, super quibus jure civili abunde est dispositum? Resp. Et si statutum primâ fronte videri possit inutile, in quantum praeter effectum per jus commune obtentum, nullum alium producit: quia tamen abundans cautela non nocet, & duo vincula magis ligant, quam unum; uti etiam provisio hominis, cum legis provisione concurrens, magis constringit; insuper tale statutum dici posset juris civilis probatorium, in quantum in civitatem receptum est; adeoque quod antea erat commune, jam factum est proprium, & aliquid operatur; in quantum inducit aliud remedium, praeter jus commune: tale statutum non prorsus inutile censeri, poterit. Hinc etiam in jure infrequens non est, ut una eademque res duabus legibus introducatur, aut confirmetur. Arg. §. 2. verb. nam furtivarum. Instit. de Usucap. & §. 5. verb. & lege antiquâ. Instit. de Exhared. liberor. §. 28. Instit. de legat. Baldus de Statutis. q. 3. & in l. 3. in sin. D. de leg. 1. August. Berous quest. 24. n. 3. Bursat. libr. 1. cons. 44. n. 37. Alexand. consil. 93. libr. 7. n. 8. Guid. Pape consil. 102. n. 1. Christin. ad Mechlin. in Epilog. n. 7. Bender. de Revis. conclus. 20. n. 98. diss. Hippol. tract. de fidejuss. n. 302. post. gloss. in Auth. de Exhibendis reis in §. quia vero. per rationes commentatoris in 8. ad 1. Reg. Cancell. Dictionarium Alberic. de Rofate in verb. Statutum in addit. ubi Bartol. in l. 1. Cod. de Thesaur. libr. 10. & in l. 3. §. si reg. D. leg. 3. l. 4, §. Prætor ait. D. damn. infect. Jafon in l. Properandum. §. sin autem. ubi etiam Bartol. & Alexand. Cod. judic.
units.tr: 5. What if a statute has been enacted about cases and transactions on which the civil law has already made ample provision? Answer: Even if a statute may at first sight seem useless, inasmuch as it produces no effect beyond that obtained by the common law, nevertheless, since excessive caution does no harm, and two bonds bind more tightly than one, just as a person's own provision, when it concurs with the provision of the law, binds more firmly; moreover, such a statute may be called a confirmation of the civil law, inasmuch as it has been received into the city; and so what was previously common has now become peculiar to it, and it has an effect, inasmuch as it introduces another remedy besides the common law. Such a statute may be judged not wholly useless. Hence it is not unusual in law for one and the same thing to be introduced or confirmed by two laws. See the argument from §. 2, verb. nam furtivarum, Inst. de Usucap.; and §. 5, verb. and by the ancient law, Inst. de Exhered. liberorum; §. 28, Inst. de Legatis; Baldus, de Statutis, q. 3, and on l. 3 in fine, D. de leg. 1; Augustinus Berous, quaest. 24, n. 3; Bursatus, lib. 1, cons. 44, n. 37; Alexander, cons. 93, lib. 7, n. 8; Guido Pape, cons. 102, n. 1; Christinaeus, ad Mechlin. in Epilog. n. 7; Bender, de Revis. concl. 20, n. 98, diss.; Hippolytus, tract. de fidejussoribus, n. 302; the gloss after Auth. de Exhibendis reis, in §. quia vero, by the reasons of the commentator in 8 ad 1 Reg. Cancell.; the Dictionarium of Alberic de Rosate, verb. Statutum, in the additions; where Bartolus on l. 1 Cod. de Thesaurís, lib. 10, and on l. 3 §. si reg. D. leg. 3; l. 4 §. Praetor ait, D. damn. infect.; Jason on l. Properandum §. sin autem, where also Bartolus and Alexander, Cod. judic.

units.la: 6. Quid si statuta sint condita adversus jus civile? Respondeo, Si statuta, aliquid introducant quod de jure civili non erat introductum; id est aliquem casum determinent, qui erat de jure civili vel omissus, vel non decisus; quo sensu etiam in jure aliquid dicitur esse juri contrarium in quantum non est ex illo jure: negari non poterit, quin illis, qui gaudent jure condendi statuta liceat aliquid disponere contra, id est præter jus civile. Quod si statuta disponant expresse contra jus civile, in quantum illi ex parte vel in totum derogant: talia non introducent munimunicipia, nisi hoc illis expresse sit concessum. Arg. §. 2. verb. quae sunt juri naturali contraria. Instit. de jur. natur. gent. civil. l. 3 2. D. de leg. l. 3. §. 5. D. de Sepulchr. violat. l. 4. D. de Decret. ab ordin. faciend. l. 3. in sin. Cod. de leg. Authent. navigia, Cod. de Furtis. l. 1, 2. Cod. de Decret. Decurion. libr. 10.
units.tr: 6. What if statutes are enacted against the civil law? I answer: if a statute introduces something that the civil law had not introduced, that is, determines some case which the civil law either left out or did not decide, then (in the sense in which something in law is also said to be contrary to law, insofar as it does not come from that law) it cannot be denied that those who enjoy the right of enacting statutes may lawfully provide something contrary to, that is, beyond, the civil law. But if statutes expressly provide against the civil law, so far as they derogate from it in part or in whole, such statutes will not be introduced by municipalities, unless this has been expressly granted to them. Cf. §. 2, verb. quae sunt juri naturali contraria, Inst. de jur. natur. gent. civil.; l. 32. D. de leg.; l. 3. §. 5. D. de Sepulchr. violat.; l. 4. D. de Decret. ab ordin. faciend.; l. 3. in fin. Cod. de leg.; Authent. navigia, Cod. de Furtis; l. 1, 2. Cod. de Decret. Decurion. lib. 10.

units.la: SECT. V. CAP. II.
units.tr: SECT. V. CHAP. II.

units.la: 1. Num valeat statutum, ne cum peregrino matrimonium contrahatur?
units.tr: 1. Is a statute valid that forbids marriage with a foreigner?

units.la: 2. Ne filiae nobilium civicae conditionis viris nubant?
units.tr: 2. That the daughters of nobles of civic rank may not marry men?

units.la: 3. Ne quis ducat alterius sectae foeminam?
units.tr: 3. That no one may marry a woman of another sect?

units.la: 4. Ut sponsalia pure contracta, mutuo consensu dissolvantur?
units.tr: 4. That sponsals purely contracted, which are called de praesenti, be dissolved by mutual consent?

units.la: 5. An ut matre nobili patre ignobili prognatus, sit nobilis?
units.tr: 5. That one born of a noble mother and an ignoble father is noble?

units.la: 6. An ut conjux ex maritii debito ante initum matrimonium contracto, etiam in solidum obligetur?
units.tr: 6. That a spouse is bound even for the whole of a husband's debt contracted before the marriage was entered into?

units.la: 7. An ut filius, licet non sit haeres patri, teneatur ad debiti paterni solutionem?
units.tr: 7. That a son, although he is not heir to his father, is bound to pay his father's debt?

units.la: 8. An ne civis originarius alio migret?
units.tr: 8. That a citizen by origin may not migrate elsewhere?

units.la: 9. An ut credatur libris mercatorum?
units.tr: 9. That credit is to be given to merchants' books?

units.la: 10. An ut appellandi facultas alicui sit adempta? 11. An
units.tr: 10. That the faculty of appeal be taken away from someone? 11. That

units.la: 11. An ut liberorum legitima diminuatur?
units.tr: 11. That the legitimate portion of children be diminished?

units.la: 12. An ut in totum tollatur?
units.tr: 12. That it be wholly abolished?

units.la: 13. An ne bona per laicos in personas ecclesiasticas transferantur?
units.tr: 13. That goods not be transferred by laymen into ecclesiastical persons?

units.la: 14. An ne Pontificius ordini alicui adscriptus, res immobiles extra familiam alienet?
units.tr: 14. That a Papist enrolled in some order may not alienate immovable property outside the family?

units.la: 15. An illicitum statutum, quo conventicula, pro secta cujusdam exercitio, vetantur?
units.tr: 15. Is an unlawful statute one by which conventicles are forbidden for the practice of someone's sect?

units.la: 16. An ut sectarii ab officiis vel honoribus arceantur?
units.tr: 16. That sectarians be debarred from offices or honours?

units.la: 17. An ut naufragorum bona fisco applicentur?
units.tr: 17. That the goods of shipwrecked persons be applied to the treasury?

units.la: 18. An ut in causa homicidii non nisi multa pecuniaria exigatur?
units.tr: 18. That in a case of homicide only a pecuniary fine be exacted?

units.la: 19. Quid judicandum de statuto, quod exigit, ut simplex furtum capite puniatur?
units.tr: 19. What is to be judged of a statute which requires that simple theft be punished by death?

units.la: 20. An statuto introduci possit, ut pater de delicto filii teneatur, usque ad legitimam?
units.tr: 20. Can it be introduced by statute that a father is liable for his son's delict, up to the legitimate portion?

units.la: 21. An ut fidejussor admittatur in causis criminalibus?
units.tr: 21. That a surety be admitted in criminal causes?

units.la: 22. Objectionibus respondetur.
units.tr: 22. Objections are answered.

units.la: 1. Dicta hactenus quantum ad generalia statutorum suffecerint objecta; in specie, & quidem secundum varias hypotheses in nonnulla statuta, quæ aliquam iniquitatem continere videbuntur inquirendum erit; quibus explicatis, cætera omnia ex rationis parilitate nullo negotio solvi poterunt.
units.tr: 1. The points said so far have been enough for the general matters concerning statutes. In particular, and according to various hypotheses, we must inquire into certain statutes which seem to contain some iniquity; once these have been explained, all the rest can be resolved without difficulty by parity of reason.

units.la: Et quidem primum inquirendum. An valeat statutum prohibitorium ne cum peregrino contrahatur matrimonium? Respondeo, valere. Neque enim illa lex iniqua videri poterit, quæ jubet ut inter cives tantum sit jus connubii. Ut idem operetur statutum circa qualitatem personæ, suæ jurisdictioni subditæ, quod Romana civitas, circa sibi subjectos. Quinimo si valeat hominis privati dispositio, ne Titia nubat Sejo, ne Sejus ex certo loco, ex certâ familiâ conjugem ducat, quid ni id ipsum expresso statuto caveri poterit. Argum. init. Instit. de Nupt. l. 6 ;. l. 64. D. de Condit. & Demonstr. l. adjicimus 7. §. 2. Cod. de Murilegul. lib. 11. Comment. marginalia in Sneidwin. Instit. de jur. natur. gent. & civil. num. 22. ibidemque Bald. in c. clerici. de judic. Alberic. de nupt. l. c. 18. p. 81. diff. videtur Petrus Wesemb. consil. 1. num. 39.
units.tr: And first we must inquire: is a prohibitive statute valid, forbidding marriage with a foreigner? I answer: it is valid. For that law cannot seem unjust which orders that the right of marriage belong only among citizens. The statute operates on the quality of a person subject to its jurisdiction just as the Roman state does with those subject to it. Indeed, if a private person's disposition is valid, that Titia not marry Seius, or that Seius take a wife from a certain place or family, why could the same not be secured by express statute? Argum. init. Instit. de Nupt. l. 6; l. 64. D. de Condit. & Demonstr.; l. adjicimus 7. §. 2. Cod. de Murilegul. lib. 11. Comment. marginalia in Sneidwin. Instit. de jur. natur. gent. & civil. num. 22. ibidemque Bald. in c. clerici. de judic.; Alberic. de nupt. l. c. 18. p. 81. diff.; videtur Petrus Wesemb. consil. 1. num. 39.

units.la: 2. An valebit statutum ne filiæ nobilium civicæ conditionis viris nubant, aut vice versâ? Respondeo, valebit. Cum enim præter nobilium liberos sint in civitate plures, & quidem dem honestæ conditionis puellæ quibus cum & prima & secunda dos confertur, non poterit hoc statutum videri iniquum, quasi libertati matrimonii ullum inferret præjudicium. d. l. 64, D. de Cond. & demonstr. l. 42. l. 44. l. 47. l. 49. D. de Ritu Nupt. l. 7. in init. Cod. de Murilegul. libr. 1. diss. Covarr. de Sponsal. part. 2. cap. 7. & Perez. in Praelect. ad tit. Cod. de Murileg. num. 23. per textum in cap. 29. de Sponsal. & Matrim. & l. 134. D. de verb. obligat. vid. tamen Alberic. de nupt. lib. 1. cap. 3. & Carpzov. jurisprud. Consistor. libr. 2. tit. 1. def. 9.
units.tr: 2. Will a statute be valid that the daughters of nobles may not marry men of civic rank, or vice versa? I answer: it will be valid. For since, besides the children of nobles, there are in the city many girls of honourable condition to whom both first and second dowries are given, this statute cannot seem unjust, as if it inflicted any prejudice on the freedom of marriage. d. l. 64, D. de Cond. & demonstr.; l. 42; l. 44; l. 47; l. 49. D. de Ritu Nupt.; l. 7. in init. Cod. de Murilegul. libr. 1. diss.; Covarr. de Sponsal. part. 2. cap. 7.; & Perez. in Praelect. ad tit. Cod. de Murileg. num. 23.; per textum in cap. 29. de Sponsal. & Matrim.; & l. 134. D. de verb. obligat. vid. tamen Alberic. de nupt. lib. 1. cap. 3.; & Carpzov. jurisprud. Consistor. libr. 2. tit. 1. def. 9.

units.la: 3, Anne quispiam ducat alterius sectæ fœminam? Respondeo, idem esse dicendum. Statutum enim tale quam maximè laudandum, quod amorem inter partes contrahentes vult sincerum, & concordantia cupit esse matrimonia. Præterquam quod tale statutum, intentionem contrahentium promoveat, quæ ut inter conjuges suadet omnium bonorum, atque corporis communicationem, ita etiam desiderat sacrorum omnino esse participationem. Ne jam addam, tale statutum, vel potius talem legem in populo Israelitico obtinuisse, ne cum alienigenis jungerentur. Quam etiam ex parte secutæ sunt leges civiles, quæ prohibent matrimonium Judæi cum Christianâ, & vice versâ. Ut tale statutum rationi & æquitati per omnia convenire, sit dicendum. Exod. 34. v, 16. Esr. cap. vap. 9. & 10. l. 1. D. de Rit. Nupt. l. 6. Cod. de Judæis. Gotefred. prolixe ad d. l. 6. ir bidemque varii allegati.
units.tr: 3. Whether anyone may marry a woman of another sect? I answer: the same must be said. For such a statute deserves the highest praise, since it wishes the love between the contracting parties to be sincere and desires marriages to be harmonious. Besides, such a statute promotes the intention of the contracting parties, who, as they urge between spouses the sharing of all goods and of the body, so also desire the full participation in sacred things. Not to add that such a statute, or rather such a law, held among the Israelite people, that they should not join themselves with foreigners. Civil laws too have followed this in part, which forbid marriage of a Jew with a Christian and vice versa. Hence it must be said that such a statute agrees in every way with reason and equity. Exod. 34. v. 16. Esr. cap. 9. & 10. l. 1. D. de Rit. Nupt. l. 6. Cod. de Judaeis. Gotefred. prolixe ad d. l. 6. ibidemque varii allegati.

units.la: 4. An ut sponsalia pure contracta, quæ appellant de præsenti, dissensu mutuo dissolvantur? Respondeo; & si unumquodque communiter eodem modo solvatur, quo ligatum est: quia tamen in casu pro propositio, vertitur commodum publicum, & eadem facilitate nuptiæ dissolverentur, quod secundum canones ratione vinculi sponsalia de Præsenti nuptiis æquiparentur: censerem tale statutum non admittendum esse; idque ex illo trito: Quod Deus conjunxit, homo ne separet. Arg. l. 31. D. de Reg. jur. Modestin. Pistor. consil. 42. num. 53. volum. 2. Mev. ad jus Lubecense lib. 1. tit. 4. num. 11. vid. Nobiliss. Schurmannum tractat. Weechschale des Heilichdoms.
units.tr: 4. Whether sponsals purely contracted, which they call de praesenti, are dissolved by mutual dissent? I answer: although each thing is commonly dissolved in the same way in which it was bound, yet because in this case the public advantage is at stake, and marriages would be dissolved with equal ease, and because according to the canons sponsals de praesenti are equated with marriages by reason of the bond, I would judge that such a statute is not to be admitted; and this from that trite saying: What God has joined together, let not man put asunder. Arg. l. 31. D. de Reg. jur.; Modestin.; Pistor. consil. 42. num. 53. volum. 2.; Mev. ad jus Lubecense lib. 1. tit. 4. num. 11.; vid. the most noble Schurmann's tractate The Balance of the Sanctuary.

units.la: 5. An ut matre nobili, patre vero ignobili prognatus nobilitatem consequatur? Respondeo; & si de jure civili justis nuptiis quæsiti, sequantur conditionem patris. Quia tamen juri gentium, aut naturæ non adversaretur, si matris conditionem sequerentur. Etiam de moribus quorundam locorum ita fit receptum, puta apud Tricassinos, Lovanienses, Campanos, aliosque ut filii melioris conditionis sequantur parentes. Nec in totum abhorreat jus civile, ut materna censeatur origo, idque ex privilegio: tale statutum nihil iniqui continere, judicarem. Argum. init. Instit. de Ingenuis. l. 1. §. 2. D. Ad Municipal. l. 22. l. 29. Cod. de Decurion. quam tamen legem abrogatam vult Cujuc. per nov. 38. l. 7. l. 12. Cod. de Muril. libr. 10. Tiraquell. Tract. de Nobilit. cap. 18. num. 23. Cravett. consil. 829. num. 2. Connan. 2. Comment. jur. civil. cap. 11. Gotefred. prolixe in comment. ad d. l. 1. §. 2. Cujac. ad libr. 4. feud. tit. 32. Deffel. in not. ad Zoef. Comm. instit. de ingen. Dissent. Bartol. in l. exempl. Cod. de Decurion. Quem sequitur Felinus citat. à Cravettâ. loc. all.
units.tr: 5. Whether one born of a noble mother but an ignoble father obtains nobility? I answer: if born of lawful marriage according to civil law, they follow the father's condition. Yet since it would not be contrary to the law of nations or of nature if they followed the mother's condition, and this has been received by custom in certain places, for instance among the Tricassini, the Lovanienses, the Campanians and others, so that children of the better condition follow their parents; and since civil law does not wholly abhor that maternal origin be counted, and that by privilege, I would judge that such a statute contains nothing unjust. Argum. init. Instit. de Ingenuis. l. 1. §. 2. D. Ad Municipal. l. 22. l. 29. Cod. de Decurion.; which law Cujac. wishes to be abrogated, per nov. 38.; l. 7. l. 12. Cod. de Muril. libr. 10.; Tiraquell. Tract. de Nobilit. cap. 18. num. 23.; Cravett. consil. 829. num. 2.; Connan. 2. Comment. jur. civil. cap. 11.; Gotefred. prolixe in comment. ad d. l. 1. §. 2.; Cujac. ad libr. 4. feud. tit. 32.; Deffel. in not. ad Zoef. Comm. instit. de ingen.; Dissent. Bartol. in l. exempl. Cod. de Decurion.; whom Felinus follows, cited by Cravetta, loc. all.

units.la: 7. An idem in simili dicendum de filio, ut æs alienum Patris solvere teneatur, etsi non probetur esse heres, aut semet ab hæreditate paterna abstinuerit vel eam repudiaverit? Ita videtur. d. l. fin. Cod. de Primipil. Petr. Anchor. deatur. Mynsing. 1. obs. 29. licet id ei durum viapud Gail. 1. observ. 36. num. 3. ibidemque Alexand. Bald. allegati.
units.tr: 7. Should the same be said in a similar case of a son, that he is bound to pay his father's debts even if he is not proved to be heir, or has abstained from the paternal inheritance or renounced it? It seems so. d. l. fin. Cod. de Primipil. Petr. Anchor. deatur. Mynsing. 1. obs. 29. Although this may seem harsh to him, Gail. 1. observ. 36. num. 3. and the passages cited there by Alexand. and Bald.

units.la: 8. An ne civis originarius alio migret, aut natale solum vertat? Respondeo, quamvis, non extante statuto, de jure, etiam generali consuetudine, libera cuique subdito facultas sit concessa, quo velit emigrandi, adeoque domicilium ad lubitum transferendi. Attamen si onus cæteris civibus impositum nimis grave foret diminuto civium numero, quod etiam damnosum est civitati; habita ratione publicæ utilitatis, non poterit videri tale statutum esse iniquum. Argum. §. ult. instit. de his qui sui vel alien. jur. l. 5. §. 3. D. de Captiv. & Postl. Reversi. l. 1. Cod. de Incol. l. ult. Cod. de Municip. & originar. Bartol. ad l. fin. D. de decret. ab ordine faciend. Gail. 2. Observ. 36. num. 10. Perez Prælect. in libr. 10. Cod. tit. de Munic. & originar. num. 17. & 18.
units.tr: 8. May a native citizen move elsewhere, or change his native soil? I answer: although, in the absence of a statute, by law and even by general custom, each subject is granted the free power to emigrate wherever he wishes, and so to transfer his domicile at pleasure, nevertheless, if the burden laid on the other citizens were too heavy because the number of citizens had been diminished, which is also harmful to the commonwealth, then, having regard to public utility, such a statute cannot be seen as unjust. Argum. §. ult. instit. de his qui sui vel alien. jur. l. 5. §. 3. D. de Captiv. & Postl. Reversi. l. 1. Cod. de Incol. l. ult. Cod. de Municip. & originar. Bartol. ad l. fin. D. de decret. ab ordine faciend. Gail. 2. Observ. 36. num. 10. Perez Prælect. in libr. 10. Cod. tit. de Munic. & originar. num. 17. & 18.

units.la: 9. An ut credatur libris rationum, seu registris uti loquuntur, mercatorum & artificum, licet probationibus testium non juventur? Respondeo, quamvis exemplo perniciosum esse videatur, quemque sibi privata testatione, sive adnotatione facere debitorem. Quia tamen hæc est mercatorum cura & opera, ut debiti & crediti rationes diligenter conficiant. Etiam in eorum foro & causis, ex æquo & bono est judicandum. Insuper non admisso aliquo litium accelerandarum remedio, commerciorum ordo & usus eveititur. Neque enim omnes præsenti pecunia merces sibi comparant. Neque cujusque rei venditioni testes adhiberi, qui pretia mercium noverint, aut expedit, aut congruum est. Non iniquum videbitur illud statutum, quo domesticis talibus instrumentis additur fides; modo aliquibus adminiculis juventur. Quod etiam ad Chartam partitam, fissos bacillos, & transversim crenis incisos, quos Kerfstocken appellamus, recte extenditur.
units.tr: 9. Should books of accounts, or registers as they are called, of merchants and craftsmen be believed, even though they are not supported by the testimony of witnesses? I answer: although it may seem a dangerous example that anyone should make himself a debtor by a private attestation or entry, nevertheless, since it is the care and business of merchants to draw up their debit and credit accounts diligently, and since in their own court and causes judgment is to be given according to equity and good conscience, and moreover, unless some remedy for speeding up lawsuits is admitted, the order and practice of commerce would be overthrown. For not everyone buys his goods with ready money, nor is it expedient or proper that witnesses who know the prices of goods be called to every sale of goods. That statute will not seem unjust by which faith is added to such domestic instruments, provided they are supported by some aids. This also rightly extends to the indented charter and to split sticks notched crosswise, which we call Kerfstocken.

units.la: Sic tamen hæc omnia procedent, ut judicis arbitrium maneat liberum, qui nonnunquam diversum decernere poterit, Si quid in contrarium circumstantiæ suadeant. Argum. l. 9. §. 2. l. 10, in init. & §. 1. D. de Eendend. l. 5. Cod. de Probat. Ordinat. Urb. Ultraj. super modo Procedendi de ann. 1623. art. 11. Zas. consil. 15. num. 53. volum. 1. Boër. decif.
