units.tr: Yet all these things will proceed in such a way that the judge's discretion remains free, since he may sometimes decide otherwise if the circumstances suggest the contrary. Argum. l. 9. §. 2. l. 10, in init. & §. 1. D. de Eendend. l. 5. Cod. de Probat. Ordinat. Urb. Ultraj. super modo Procedendi de ann. 1623. art. 11. Zas. consil. 15. num. 53. volum. 1. Boër. decif.

units.la: Argum. l. 9. §. 2. l. 10, in init. & §. 1. D. de Eendend. l. 5. Cod. de Probat. Ordinat. Urb. Ultraj. super modo Procedendi de ann. 1623. art. 11. Zas. consil. 15. num. 53. volum. 1. Boër. decif.
units.tr: Argument from D. 9.2 and D. 10 init. and D. 10.1 (de Eendend.); C. 5 (de Probat.); Ordinance of the city of Utrecht concerning the manner of proceeding, of 1623, art. 11; Zas. consil. 15 n. 53, vol. 1; Boër, decis.

units.la: eis. 105. Gail. 2. observ. 20. Francisc. Vivius in tom. Comm. opin. libr. 17. verb statutum. p. 334. ibique multa. Oldendorp. tractat. de Actionibus class. 1. act. 8. in sin. Gilken. in l. 5. Cod. de Probat. Cravett. de Antiq. tempor. part. 1. num. 27. & seq. p. mihi 32, 33. Hieron. Treutl. select. disput. volum. 2. disp. 4. thes. 2. conf. jurisc. Batav. part. 1. conf. 204. 313. diss. Hunn. ad Treutl. d l. p. 424. ibidemque alii.

Hunn. ad Treutler, d. l., p. 424, and the others cited there.

units.la: 10. An illicitum statutum, quo appellandi facultas alicui aufertur? Respondeo, quod non. Etsi enim statutum alicui auferre nequeat defensionem sui, cum id ipsum ne quidem possit Princeps, ut quae juris est naturae. Quia tamen non omnis defensionis modus, aut species est juris naturae; uti bellum. Etiam jus civile non in omni causa, nec ab omnibus admittit appellationem, ut aliquibus in casubus non sine ratione certum defensionis modum alicui deneget. Quin amplius, alicui concessum est appellationis remedio renunciare, tanquam beneficio sibi competenti. Nec minor est efficacia statuti in casu proposito, quam est privatae conventionis, si non major: quod secundum DD. statutum sit pacto potentius. Georg. natt. in c. quamvis. de Pact. in 6. Tom. 5. Repet. jur. canon. pag. 237. n. 39. Censerem licite appellandi licentiam statuto posse auferri. Neque hic distinguo inter causas civiles & criminales: cum etiam in criminalibus multarum civitatum moribus, jus appellandi sit sublatum. Argum. l. 1. § si quis. D. a quibus appell. non licet l. ult. §. ult. Cod. Tempor. Appell. l. 34. & seq. Cod. de Appell. tit. Cod. quorum appell. non recip. & tit. Cod. si de momentan. possess. l. fin. in fin. Cod. de fidejuss. Zoes. D. à quibus appell. non licet, num. 8. Hunn. ad Treutl. volum. Poster. disp. 33. quaest. 1. in fin. Christin. Prælud. ad ll. Mechl. num. 18. ibidemque varii. Volumen Consiliorum jurisc. German. part. 3. Consil. 22. num. 5. & consil. 15. disting. Bartol. in l. omnes populi. D. de justitiâ & jure num. 27. Matth. Wesembec. tom. 6. Consil. 328. num. 19. gloss. in Rubric. Cod. decret. Decurion. libr. 10. Mascard. conclus. 7. de interpret. Statutor. n. 41. Bort peculiari tractat. de appell. in caus. Crimin. Diss. units.tr: 10. Is a statute unlawful if it takes away from someone the power to appeal? I answer, no. For although a statute cannot take away from anyone the defence of his person, since not even the Prince can do that, as this belongs to natural law, yet not every mode or kind of defence belongs to natural law, as war does. Civil law too does not admit appeal in every case or from everyone, so that in some cases, and not without reason, it denies a certain mode of defence to someone. Moreover, a person may renounce the remedy of appeal, as a benefit that belongs to him. Nor is a statute in the case proposed less effective than a private agreement, if not more so, since according to the jurists a statute is more powerful than a pact. I would judge that the licence to appeal can be taken away by statute. Nor do I here distinguish between civil and criminal causes, since even in criminal matters, by the customs of many cities, the right of appeal has been abolished. See D. 1 (si quis), D. a quibus appellare non licet; C. last (Tempor. Appell.); C. 34 ff. (Appell.); C. (quorum appell. non recip.) and C. (si de momentan. possess.); C. (de fidejuss.); Zoesius, D. a quibus appellare non licet, n. 8; Hunnius, ad Treutler, vol. Poster., disp. 33, quaest. 1; Christinaeus, Prælud. ad ll. Mechl., n. 18, and the various authorities there; the Volumen Consiliorum juris German., part 3, consil. 22, n. 5, and consil. 15; Bartolus, on D. (omnes populi), n. 27; Wesembeck, tom. 6, consil. 328, n. 19; gloss on the rubric of C. (Decurion.), book 10; Mascardus, concl. 7, de interpret. statutorum, n. 41; Bort, in his separate treatise on appeal in criminal causes; Arumaeus, disc. public. 9, tom. 2, thes. 118; Mynsinger, 1 obs. 14; Ordinance of the Imperial Chamber, part 2, tit. 28; Jacobus Thomingius, consil. 24, throughout; Treutler, disput. 33, vol. 2, thes. 1, ad litt. a, and the various authorities cited there; and after him Antonius Matthaeus, tractatus de judiciis, disp. 12, nn. 20–21; on the side of Besold, delibatio juris, ad lib. 49, tit. 2, quaest. 3; Bender, tractatus de revisionibus, concl. 29, throughout.

units.la: Nullo tamen modo valere potest statutū, quo parte inaudita altera fertur sentetia commonatoria. Quia licet aliquis defensionis modus, alicui statuto possit auferri, qualis erat appellatio: non tamen illa defensio, quæ juris est naturalis; non tamen omnes defendendi modus, quem etiam suasit exemplum divinum. Genes. c. 3. v. 8. 9. 10. c. 1. de Cauf. Poss. & Propriet. Andr. ab Exea in c. canonum Statuta. de Constit. in 2. Tom. rep. jur. can. n. 246. & ibi Jason. Zas. Hyppol.
units.tr: Yet a statute by which a sentence of banishment is pronounced with the other party unheard can in no way be valid. For although some mode of defence may be taken away from someone by statute, such as appeal was, that defence which belongs to natural law cannot be taken away, nor can every mode of defending oneself, which even the divine example suggests. Genes. c. 3. v. 8. 9. 10. c. 1. de Cauf. Poss. & Propriet. Andr. ab Exea in c. canonum Statuta. de Constit. in 2. Tom. rep. jur. can. n. 246. & ibi Jason. Zas. Hyppol.

units.la: 11. An illicitum censeri poterit statutum quo liberorum legitima diminuitur? Respondeo, quod non. Neque enim legitima jure naturae praecise est determinata, ut augeri vel minui possit. Quin imo de jure civili fuit aucta, ut cum antea in omnibus liberis esset quarta, jam sit aut triens aut semis, pro numero liberorum. Cumque ejus quota subjaceat juris civilis dispositioni, negari non poterit, quin etiam juri statutario subesse possit. Argum. l. 8. D. de Reg. jur. Decius ad d. l. §. ult. Instit. de legit. Adgnat. tutel. l. 6. §. sin autem. Cod. de Secund. Nupt. Novell. 18. Mynsinger. cent. 5. observat. 43. Gail. 2. observ. 122. num. 11. Fachin. 4. controverf. 32. Zoes. D. de Inoffic. Querel. num. 109. vid. Hieron Treutler. consil. 41. num. 19. & num. 113. Volum. consil. jurisc. Germ. part. 3. consil. 65. num. 2. 3. Claud. Chifflet. de Portionibus. cap. 3. Gabriel. comm. Lopin. 6. de legitima, concluf. 1.
units.tr: 11. Can a statute that reduces the legitim of children be deemed unlawful? I answer, no. For the legitim is not precisely fixed by natural law, so that it cannot be increased or diminished. Indeed it was even increased by civil law: whereas formerly every child received a quarter, it is now a third or a half, according to the number of children. And since its amount is subject to the disposition of civil law, it cannot be denied that it may also be subject to statutory law. See D. 8 (de Reg. jur.); Decius on the last §. of Inst. de legit. agnat. tutel.; C. 6 §. sin autem (de secund. nupt.); Novell. 18; Mynsinger, cent. 5, observ. 43; Gail, 2 observ. 122, n. 11; Fachin, 4 controv. 32; Zoesius, D. de inofficioso querela, n. 109; see also Hieronymus Treutler, consil. 41, nn. 19 and 113; Volumen consiliorum juris German., part 3, consil. 65, nn. 2–3; Claudius Chifflet, de portionibus, cap. 3; Gabriel, comm. Lopin, 6 de legitima, concl. 1.

units.la: 12. An igitur in universum statuto tolli poterit? Id videtur dicendum. Cum enim legitima jure humano sit introducta, licet congruenter affectioni illi naturali, quam parens habet erga liberos. Et ab eo dependeat cjus obligatio, adeoque præstatio. Etiam ideoque dicatur ex legibus esse debita. Insuper miles, si militari jure testetur, liberis legitimam relinquere non tenetur; qui tamen in testamenti factione non nisi juris civilis solemnibus est solutus, ut jure naturæ debita videri non possit. Idem quod de matre illustri dicendum, in ordine ad spurium, modo habeat legitime natos. Jure itidem Mosaico non passim filiabus legitima paternæ hæreditatis concessa fuerit, quibus in totum extantibus masculis eadem adempta. Tale statutum nihil iniqui in se continere dicendum erit. Quod tamen sic accipi velim, ut non in omnibus casibus tale statutum valeat, verum quando urgens ratio, aut publica utilitas hoc suadet. Quo casu etiam quod jure naturæ seu secundum affectionem naturalem est debitum, qui sensus est l. 7. in sin. D. Si tabul. testam. null. extab. propter rationem fortionem poterit esse non debitum, ut in filio ingrato, qui etiam legitimâ, aliter sibi debitâ, justâ de causâ defraudatur. Inscript. l. 4. D. de Inoffic. Testam. l. 6. §. sin autem. Cod. de Secund. Nupt. l. 9. l. 24. Cod. de Inoffic. Testam. l. 5. Cod. Ad senat. Orfit.Numer. cap. 36. v. 6. 7. 8. 9. Alexander consil. 3. volum. 7. Beust. ad l. 1. D. de jurejur. p. 128. Fichard. in Tom. comm. opinion. libr. 17. verb. Statutum. p. 354. Bened. de Capra comm. opin. vero, legitima: Zoes. D. de Inoffic.
units.tr: 12. Can a statute therefore abolish legitim in general? That seems the right answer. For although legitim was introduced by human law, it accords with the natural affection a parent has for his children, and the parent's obligation, and hence his provision, depends on that affection. For this reason it is also said to be owed by law. Moreover, a soldier who makes his will under military law is not bound to leave legitim to his children, yet he is released from the formalities only of civil law, so it cannot seem to be owed by natural law. The same is to be said of an illustrious mother in relation to a bastard, provided she has legitimate children. Under Mosaic law too, daughters were not generally granted legitim from their father's inheritance, and it was taken away altogether when sons survived. Such a statute will be said to contain nothing unjust in itself. I would, however, have this understood to mean that such a statute does not hold in all cases, but only when a pressing reason or public utility suggests it. In that case, even what is owed by natural law or according to natural affection may, by reason of the cause, cease to be owed, as in the case of an ungrateful son, who is defrauded of his legitim, otherwise owed to him, for a just cause. Inscript. l. 4. D. de Inoffic. Testam. l. 6. §. sin autem. Cod. de Secund. Nupt. l. 9. l. 24. Cod. de Inoffic. Testam. l. 5. Cod. Ad senat. Orfit.Numer. cap. 36. v. 6. 7. 8. 9. Alexander consil. 3. volum. 7. Beust. ad l. 1. D. de jurejur. p. 128. Fichard. in Tom. comm. opinion. libr. 17. verb. Statutum. p. 354. Bened. de Capra comm. opin. vero, legitima: Zoes. D. de Inoffic.

units.la: 13. An illicitum statutum, (de quo controversia fuit, inter Pontificem, & Rempublicam Venetam) ne bona per laicos, uti loquuntur, transferantur in personas ecclesiasticas, sine licentia superioris? Respondeo, etsi libertati ecclesiae non facile debeat fieri praejudicium: si quae libertas jure debita est ecclesiae. Quia tamen bonum publicum tale fieri statutum nonnunquam exigit. Et civitates secundum illos, qui talia condunt statuta, subsidio carent collectarum, etiam subditorum numero: quod clerici secundum illos, etiam corum bona, sint exempta jurisdictioni magistratus Politici. Neque adversatur legibus personas ecclesiasticas, eorumque bona, suadente utilitate etiam collectis, aut tributis gravari. Existumarem tale statutum nihil illiciti continere. Argum. l. 1. D. Solut. Matrimon. l. 7. Cod. de SS. Eccles. Argum. c. si imperator. 96. distinct. c. pervenit de immun. Eccles. Argentr. ad consf. Brittan. art. 346. Goris tratt. 3. Adversf. cap. 8. Tholos. libr. 45. Synt: jur. cap. 2. n. 8. Arum. discurf. Academ. de jur. Publ. 9. num. 106. & sequent. part. 2. vid. Molin. ad consuet. Parisiens. §. 41. num. 90.91.92.93. 94 diff. apud Gail. 2. observ. 32. num. 3. Cevall. comm. contr. comm. q. 388. Anto. Matth. disp. ult. post succeff. n. 18. ibique DD.
units.tr: 13. Is an unlawful statute (about which there was a dispute between the Pontiff and the Venetian Republic) one forbidding that goods be transferred by laymen, as they say, to ecclesiastical persons without the permission of a superior? I answer: although the liberty of the Church ought not easily to be prejudiced, provided it is a liberty owed to the Church by law, nevertheless the public good sometimes requires such a statute to be made. According to those who enact such statutes, cities would otherwise lack the aid of levies, even from the number of their subjects, since the clergy, and their goods too, would be exempt from the jurisdiction of the political magistrate. Nor is it contrary to the laws that ecclesiastical persons and their goods should be burdened with levies or taxes, when public utility so suggests. I would judge that such a statute contains nothing unlawful. Argument from l. 1 D. Solut. Matrimon.; l. 7 Cod. de SS. Eccles.; argument from c. si imperator, 96 dist.; c. pervenit de immun. Eccles.; Argentré on the Consuetudines of Brittany, art. 346; Goris, tratt. 3, Adversf. ch. 8; Tholosanus, lib. 45, Synt. jur. ch. 2, no. 8; Arumaeus, Discurs. Academ. de jur. Publ. 9, nos. 106 ff., part 2; see Molinaeus on the Custom of Paris, §41, nos. 90–94, dispute cited in Gail, 2 observ. 32, no. 3; Cevallos, comm. contr. comm. q. 388; Antonius Matthaeus, disp. ult., post successiones, no. 18, and the jurists there.

units.la: 14. Anligitur illicitum censebitur in Belgio foederato statutum, quo prohibitum, ne Pontificius ordini alicui pseudo-ecclesiastico adscriptus, res immobiles extra familiam alienet? Resp. licet quisque sit arbiter & moderator rerum suarum, in tantum ut de iis disponendi liberam habeat facultatem. Neque cuiquam hominum, ne quidem per Principem facile jus sibi competens sit auferendum. Quia tamen respublica est suprema domina, & moderatrix. Etiam bonum publicum exigit ut tale condatur statutum. Insuper etiam familiarum conservatio id suadet. Dicendum erit ipsum nihil iniqui in se continere.
units.tr: 14. Will a statute be judged unlawful in the Dutch Netherlands which forbids a Papist, enrolled in some pseudo-ecclesiastical order, to alienate immovable property outside the family? I answer: although each person is the judge and manager of his own affairs, to the extent that he has the free power to dispose of them, and no one's right, not even a prince's, should easily be taken away, yet because the commonwealth is the supreme lord and governor, public good demands that such a statute be enacted. Moreover, the preservation of families also suggests it. It must be said that the statute itself contains nothing unjust.

units.tr: 15. AD

units.la: 15. An illicitum censebitur statutum, quo conventicula pro religionis, aut potius sectæ cujufdam exercitio privato vetantur? Respondeo, & fi conscientiæ libertas statutis tolli nec debeat, nec possit: ut quæ nulli mortalium, potentissimo licet, verum foli Deo subjecta est. Quia tamen conventus agere plus est, quam conscientiæ gaudere libertate. Etiam quam maxime interest reipublicæ tales conventus impediri: ut qui turbent reipublicæ tranquillitatem; inque seditiones facile erumpere queant. Non dubium quin tale statutum licite condatur. Argum. l. ita vulneratus. verb. multa autem. D. Ad l. Aquil. l. utilitas, Cod. de Primip. lib. 12. l. 2. in init. Cod. de Summ. Trinit. l. 3. 5. 6. Cod. de Haret. & Manich. l. 6. & 7. in sin. Cod. Pagan. Sacrific. Petrus Frederic. Mindan. de Proceff. Execut. libr. 1. cap. 30. Arum. difcurf. Academ.publ. 12. cap. 9. num. 20. part. 2.
units.tr: 15. Will a statute be judged unlawful which forbids private meetings for the exercise of a religion, or rather of some sect? I answer: although freedom of conscience neither should nor can be taken away by statute, since conscience is subject to no mortal, however powerful, but to God alone, yet because to hold a meeting is more than to enjoy liberty of conscience, it is also of the greatest concern to the commonwealth that such meetings be prevented, since they disturb the tranquillity of the commonwealth and can easily break out into sedition. There is no doubt that such a statute may lawfully be enacted. Argum. l. ita vulneratus. verb. multa autem. D. Ad l. Aquil. l. utilitas, Cod. de Primip. lib. 12. l. 2. in init. Cod. de Summ. Trinit. l. 3. 5. 6. Cod. de Haret. & Manich. l. 6. & 7. in sin. Cod. Pagan. Sacrific. Petrus Frederic. Mindan. de Proceff. Execut. libr. 1. cap. 30. Arum. difcurf. Academ.publ. 12. cap. 9. num. 20. part. 2.

units.la: 16. An illicitum judicandum statutum, aut contra jura civilia conditum, quo Hæretici & Sectarii ab officiis aut honoribus arcentur, vel etiam tabernas, aut officinas habere prohibentur? Respondeo, etsi eadem onera cum cæteris subire cogantur, ut etiam videantur ad honores aut officia exæquo esse admittendi. Quia tamen non eadem utrobique est ratio, quod hæresis sit odiosa, adco que indigna favore; sic ut in odium sectæ aut hæreseos onera cum cæteris subire cogantur. Etiam metus est dissensionis, & periculum perturbationis quietis reipublicæ. Cum ubi religionis dissensus, in diversa studia colliment dissentientes. Nec cuiquam subditorum fit injuria, præsertim si non admittatur, aliud dicendum si ejiciatur, ut cui liberum alio sese conferre. Dicendum, illud tanquam bono publico conveniens, non tantum licitum fore, tale statutum, sed etiam introducendum esse. l. Secundum naturam. D. de Regul. jur. ibidemque DD. Comment. Argum. l. unic. Cod. de infam. l. 12 Cod. de Decurion. l. 15. 19. & seq. Cod. Episcop. Audient. l. 8. Cod. de Defensor. civit. Argum. l. utilitas Cod. de Primipil. l. 1. & Authent. item Privilegium. l. 2. 4. in init. l. 7. l. 12. l. 18. 20. Cod. de Hæretic. & Manichæis l. ult. Cod. Judæis l. 9. Cod. de Diverf. offic. Nov. 37. in Princ. Martyr. classi. 2. loc. comm. c. 4. n 40. nec obst. l. 3. §. sin. D. l. 49. Cod. de decurion. Id enim per imperatores Christian. correctum. vid. Hunn. ad Treutl. de tutel. vid. Cujac. p. 800. nov. 45.
units.tr: 16. Is a statute to be judged unlawful, or enacted against the civil laws, by which heretics and sectaries are kept from offices or honours, or are even forbidden to keep shops or workshops? I answer: although they are compelled to bear the same burdens as others, so that they seem to be admitted to honours and offices on equal terms, yet the reason is not the same on both sides, since heresy is hateful and therefore unworthy of favour, so that they are compelled to bear burdens with others out of hatred of the sect or heresy. Also there is the fear of dissension, and the danger of disturbing the quiet of the commonwealth, since where there is a difference of religion, dissenters gather in different pursuits. Nor is any of the subjects wronged, especially if they are not expelled; it would be otherwise if they were expelled, since each is free to betake himself elsewhere. It must be said that such a statute would not only be lawful but should even be introduced, as agreeing with the public good. l. Secundum naturam. D. de Regul. jur. ibidemque DD. Comment. Argum. l. unic. Cod. de infam. l. 12 Cod. de Decurion. l. 15. 19. & seq. Cod. Episcop. Audient. l. 8. Cod. de Defensor. civit. Argum. l. utilitas Cod. de Primipil. l. 1. & Authent. item Privilegium. l. 2. 4. in init. l. 7. l. 12. l. 18. 20. Cod. de Hæretic. & Manichæis l. ult. Cod. Judæis l. 9. Cod. de Diverf. offic. Nov. 37. in Princ. Martyr. classi. 2. loc. comm. c. 4. n 40. nec obst. l. 3. §. sin. D. l. 49. Cod. de decurion. For this was corrected by the Christian emperors. vid. Hunn. ad Treutl. de tutel. vid. Cujac. p. 800. nov. 45.

units.la: 17. Verum an recte, statuto introducetur, ut naufragorum bona ad littus appulsa, fisco vindicentur? Respondeo, & si talem consuetudinem apud Anglos, Gallos, Hispanos, communem testentur; ut videatur idem statuto indici posse, quod consuetudine: Quia tamen hæc ipsa consuetudo impietatis & crudelitatis est plenissima, quod afflicto superaddat peraddat afflictionem, & alicui rem suam sine causâ, sine aliquo suo facto auferat. Nec fieri debeat statuto, quod non debet consuetudine. Dicendum erit, tale statutum omnino improbandum esse. l. id quod nostrum. 11. D. de Regul. jur. l. 8. D. Ad l. Rhod. de jactu. Authent. Navigia. Cod. de furt. Carol. 5. Constit. Crimin. art. 218. Et ita in Camerâ decisum esse refert Gail. 1. Observat. 18. per totum, ibidemque variii allegati. Arum. tom. 2, discurs. Academ. de jur. Publ. tom. 9. num. 115. & seq. part. 2. Zoes. D. Ad l. Rhod. de jact. num. 10. 11. 12. vid. & Bodin. 1. de Republ. cap. ult. Prolixe auctor Batavicæ Arcadiæ, ibique nostratium & aliorum mores allegati.
units.tr: 17. But is it right to introduce by statute that the goods of shipwrecked persons, cast up on the shore, shall be claimed for the treasury? I answer: even if they attest that such a custom is common among the English, French and Spanish, so that it may seem the same thing can be introduced by statute as by custom. Yet because this very custom is most full of impiety and cruelty, in that it adds affliction to the afflicted and takes a man's property from him without cause and without any act of his own, a thing ought not to be done by statute that ought not to be done by custom. It must be said that such a statute is wholly to be condemned. l. id quod nostrum. 11. D. de Regul. jur. l. 8. D. Ad l. Rhod. de jactu. Authent. Navigia. Cod. de furt. Carol. 5. Constit. Crimin. art. 218. And Gail reports that it was so decided in the Chamber, 1. Observat. 18, throughout, and various authorities are cited there. Arum. tom. 2, discurs. Academ. de jur. Publ. tom. 9. num. 115. & seq. part. 2. Zoes. D. Ad l. Rhod. de jact. num. 10. 11. 12. See also Bodin. 1. de Republ. cap. ult. The author of the Batavian Arcadia treats it at length, and there the customs of our countrymen and others are cited.

units.la: 18. An ut in causâ homicidii nonnisi multa quæ pecuniaria exigatur? Respondeo. Etsi quævis civitas sibi possit condere statuta, non tamen id poterit in omni casu. Præsertim in casu, quo statutum juri divino & gentium adversatur. Verum cum tale statutum, omni juri esset contrarium; insuper in perniciem tenderet humani generis; etiam ad delinquendum invitaret; sicque grande delictu, quasi impunitum foret: tale statutum in civitate condi non posse, dicendum erit. l. inter claras. & seq. Cod. de Summ. Trinit. l. jus agnationis. D. de Pactis, l. 2. Cod. de injus vocando. l. 51. D. Ad l. Aquil. l. 11. D. qua ut indign. Baldus de statutis. quaest. ult. num. 6.
units.tr: 18. Whether, as in a case of homicide, only a fine should be exacted? I answer: although any city may frame statutes for itself, it cannot do so in every case, especially where the statute is opposed to divine law and the law of nations. But since such a statute would be contrary to all law, would moreover tend to the ruin of the human race, and would also invite men to crime, so that a great crime would be as good as unpunished, it must be said that such a statute cannot be enacted in a city. l. inter claras. & seq. Cod. de Summ. Trinit. l. jus agnationis. D. de Pactis, l. 2. Cod. de injus vocando. l. 51. D. Ad l. Aquil. l. 11. D. qua ut indign. Baldus de statutis. quaest. ult. num. 6.

units.la: 19. Quid judicandum de statuto, quod exigit, ut simplex furtum capite puniatur? Respondeo, & si in causa servi de jure civili nonnunquam ad ultimum supplicium deveniatur: etiam Constitutio Frederici imperatoris idem fere decernat in libero homine: nec in totum ab ea recedat Carolina: & ei pro parte accedat statutum urbis Ultrajectinæ. l. pen. in init. D. de Condict. causa. dat. causa. non secut. libr. 2. tit. 27. §. 9. de Usibus feud. Statut. Ultraj. Rubric 39. Quia tamen jure divino secus obtinuit. Neque proportio est inter vitam & bona. Hominisque liberi corpus nullam recipit æstimationem. Malim in illam inclinare sententiam, quâ tale statutum improbatur: Nisi tamen propter consequentiam, & crescentibus delictis, pœna ultimi supplicii in fures decreta fuerit. Exod. 22. v. 1. & seq. Argum. l. 3. D. Si quadrup. pauper. fecisse. dicat, l. 13. D. Ad l. Aquil. l. ult. D. de deject. & essus. Petrus Martyr class. 2. cap. 11. num. 33. Danæus Ethic. Christian. ad 8. Præcept. Prolixe Anton. Matthæus tract. de Crimin. libr. 47. D. tit. 1. cap. 2. per totum. Et cap. 3. num. 10. — Argum. l. 1. D. de Abigeis. Vid. Artic. militar. cum Pappi comment.
units.tr: 19. What is to be judged of a statute that requires simple theft to be punished by death? I answer: although in the case of a slave, under civil law, the extreme penalty is sometimes reached, and although the constitution of the Emperor Frederick decrees nearly the same for a free man, and the Carolina does not wholly depart from this, and the statute of the city of Utrecht partly agrees with it, l. pen. in init. D. de Condict. causa. dat. causa. non secut. libr. 2. tit. 27. §. 9. de Usibus feud. Statut. Ultraj. Rubric 39. yet under divine law it has turned out otherwise. Nor is there any proportion between life and goods, and the body of a free man admits of no valuation. I would rather incline to that opinion by which such a statute is disapproved, unless perhaps, on account of its consequences and the growth of crime, the penalty of capital punishment has been decreed against thieves. Exod. 22. v. 1. & seq. Argum. l. 3. D. Si quadrup. pauper. fecisse. dicat, l. 13. D. Ad l. Aquil. l. ult. D. de deject. & effus. Petrus Martyr class. 2. cap. 11. num. 33. Danæus Ethic. Christian. ad 8. Præcept. Prolixe Anton. Matthæus tract. de Crimin. libr. 47. D. tit. 1. cap. 2. per totum. Et cap. 3. num. 10. — Argum. l. 1. D. de Abigeis. Vid. Artic. militar. cum Pappi comment.

units.la: 20. Verum an statuto induci poterit, ut pater legitimam post suam mortem filio debitam, bitam, vel pœnam pecuniariam ad legitimæ quantitatem teneatur persolvere, propter delictum à filio commissum? Respondeo, & si legitima filio non sit debita nisi post mortem patris. Nec delictum unius debeat alterum prægavare. Quia tamen delictum filii in potestate, quasi in delicto constituit patrem; urpote cui incumbebat filium bonis moribus induere. Etiam aliquis potest, de jure humano ob alterius crimen affici pœnâ quapiam pecuniariâ, si in legem latam consenserit. Et ubi tale statutum, etiam est consensus saltem tacitus, si non expressus, eorum, qui statuentibus subsunt; ut non habeant, quod conquærantur se propter delictum alterius puniri: dicentum erit, statuto recte id induci. Argum. §. final. Instit. de Obligat. quæ quas. ex delict. l. 5. §. 5. verb. ideo si filius familias. & §. 6. D. de obligat. & Action. vid. l. 58. D. de Reg. jur. ibidemque DD. l. 2. Cod. de libert. & ea r liber. Stat. ordin. Frisc. libr. 2. tit. 2. §. 28. Prolixè Covarr. variar. Resolut. lib. 2. cap. 8. num. 7. Treutl. vol. 1. disp. 13. thes. 17. & 24. thes. 14. vid. Peck. ad c. 86. de R. jur. in 6. Marsil. sing. 36. Vivium in tom. comm. opin. libr. 17. p. 349. verb. Statutum, cum variis limit. & dissentientibus ibid. Arg. c. 2. de Delictis Puerorum, ubi canonista. Cujac. ad l. unic. Cod. de Peric. eorum qui pro magistr. interv. libr. 11. Argentr. ad conf. Britt. grt. §26. n. 11. Anton. Maith. tract.
units.tr: 20. But can a statute be introduced whereby a father, on account of a crime committed by his son, is bound to pay a pecuniary penalty up to the amount of the legitim owed to the son after the father's death? I answer: yes, even if the legitim is not owed to the son except after the father's death, and even if the crime of one person ought not to burden another. Yet because the son's offence, being within the father's power, as it were places the father himself in fault, since it was his duty to train the son in good morals; and because a man can, by human law, be subjected to some pecuniary penalty on account of another's crime if he has consented to the law enacted; and because where such a statute is in force there is at least a tacit, if not an express, consent of those who are subject to the lawmakers, so that they have no ground for complaint that they are punished for another's crime, it must be said that such a statute is rightly introduced. Argum. §. final. Instit. de Obligat. quæ quas. ex delict. l. 5. §. 5. verb. ideo si filius familias. & §. 6. D. de obligat. & Action. see l. 58. D. de Reg. jur. and the Doctors there, l. 2. Cod. de libert. & ea r liber. Stat. ordin. Frisc. libr. 2. tit. 2. §. 28. Covarr. at length, variar. Resolut. lib. 2. cap. 8. num. 7. Treutl. vol. 1. disp. 13. thes. 17. & 24. thes. 14. See Peck. ad c. 86. de R. jur. in 6. Marsil. sing. 36. Vivius in tom. comm. opin. libr. 17. p. 349. verb. Statutum, with various limitations and dissenters there. Arg. c. 2. de Delictis Puerorum, where the canonist. Cujac. ad l. unic. Cod. de Peric. eorum qui pro magistr. interv. libr. 11. Argentr. ad conf. Britt. grt. §26. n. 11. Anton. Maith. tract.

units.la: 22. Verum, quid judicandum de statuto, quo admitteretur fidejussor in criminalibus causis, id est, ut sponsor sese submittat damno quocunque, per legem propter aliquod crimen infligendo? Sunt qui distinguunt inter fidejussorem de sistendo reo, & inter eum, qui ad pœnam irrogandam semet obligat. Sunt qui inter pœnam pecuniariam, & corporalem differentiam statuunt. Sunt denique qui inter jus Dei, & jus hominum discrimen faciunt. Quasi tribus prioribus modis procedat de jure fidejussio, non tribus posterioribus. Ego potius rejectis illis distinctionibus libere tuebor, hoc statutum, quo in criminalibus causis, etiā capitalibus, admittitur fidejussor, non omnino improbandum esse. Suadet hanc sententiam jus divinum, quo etiam in aliis facta & delecta aliorum puniri poterunt: crimina parentum in filiis; igitur & propter delicta parentum; auctoritate 2. Præcepti in Decalogo. Exod. 20. v. 5. non obstante loco Ezechiel. c. 18. v. 2. 3. 4. 5. Qui referendus ad Evangelicam promissionem, non ad legale præceptum; ad hoc quod Deus velit facere, non quid jure suo possit. Suadent divina exempla, quibus peccata prædecessorum posteris imputata fuerunt, adeoque alterius nomine, qui formaliter peccavit, licet posteri per imputationem, poenas sustulerint. Ita Sacrilegii nomine ab Achane commisso, Iosuæ c. 7. v. 20. non tantum ipse qui deliquerat, verum etiam utriusq. sexus liberi puniti fuerunt, v. 24.
units.tr: 22. But what is to be judged of a statute by which a surety is admitted in criminal cases, that is, by which a guarantor submits himself to whatever damage the law inflicts for some crime? Some distinguish between a surety for producing the accused and one who binds himself to the imposition of a penalty. Some make a difference between a pecuniary and a corporal penalty. Finally, some make a distinction between divine law and human law, as if suretyship proceeds lawfully in the first three ways but not in the latter three. I, however, setting those distinctions aside, shall freely maintain that this statute, by which a surety is admitted in criminal cases, even capital ones, is not wholly to be condemned. The divine law supports this view, since the deeds and choices of others may also be punished: the crimes of parents are visited on children, and therefore also on account of the parents' crimes, by the authority of the second precept of the Decalogue, Exod. 20. v. 5. This is not weakened by the passage in Ezekiel 18:2-5, which should be referred to the evangelical promise rather than to the legal precept, to what God wills to do rather than to what he may do by his right. Divine examples also persuade, in which the sins of forefathers were imputed to their posterity, so that, in the name of another who had formally sinned, the posterity, by imputation, bore the penalties. Thus, in the name of the sacrilege committed by Achan, Joshua 7:20, not only he who had sinned but also the children of both sexes were punished, v. 24.

units.la: Et quicquid commiserant primi nostri parentes, justo Dei judicio posteris imputatum fuisse, in iisque vindicatum, probat cap. 5. Ad Romanos. Ne jam exemplum proferam benedicti nostri Salvatoris, qui pro nobis apud Patrem, ut universi Rectorem, atque Moderatorem, pro nobis miseris peccatoribus, se statuit vadem, sponsorem, atque fidejussorem; eam poenam, quam nos laturi fuissemus, in se sponte & volens, non coactus, boni publici causa, & amoris erga nos suscipiendo.
units.tr: And that whatever our first parents committed was imputed to their posterity by the just judgment of God, and avenged upon them, is proved by Romans chapter 5. Not to mention the example of our blessed Saviour, who, before the Father as the universal Ruler and Governor, set himself up for us wretched sinners as bail, surety and guarantor, taking upon himself of his own accord and willingly, not under compulsion, for the public good and out of love toward us, the penalty which we would have had to bear.

units.la: Verum ut inclarescat magis hæc mea sententia, duas positiones formabo. Prima erit, quod fidejussor se possit obligare ad poenam capitis. Secunda, quod puniri possit capitis poenâ, idque alterius nomine.
units.tr: But so that my view may become clearer, I shall lay down two propositions. The first is that a surety can bind himself to the penalty of death. The second is that a person can be punished with death on another's behalf.

units.la: Prima positio vel hinc paret quod ut sese obligare possit ad poenam capitis aut ultimi supplicii, tantum desideretur ut faciat actum, qui possit mereri ultimum supplicium; idque vel ob delictum præsens, vel futurum. Sic de jure civili, qui aliquem capitalis criminis incusabat, in ipsum crimen inscribebat, ut si non probasset crimen, eam poenam esset subiturus, quam tulisset reus, si convictus sceleleris fuisset. l. sin. Cod. de Accus. Quinimo Commentariensis, custos rei criminalis, si eundem culpâ suâ dimisisset, etiam ultimo supplicio affici poterat. l. 12. D. de Custod. & Exhibit. Reor. l. 4. Cod eod. Et fidejussor, ni stiterit facinorosum; ultimi supplicii reum se facit; idque secundum sententiam Regiam. 1. Reg. c. 20. v. 38. & seqq. modo ita fuerit conventum. Quo etiam referri poterunt exempla. Genes. 42. v. 37. & 43. v. 9. Ios. 2. v. 12. & seqq. & 6. v. 22. 23. Id quod juri civili congruum, quo fidejussor, si aliquâ suâ culpâ vel dolo, reum non stiterit, quem sistere debebat, non tantum & pecuniariâ multâ venit condemnandus, sed & corporali poenæ quandoque subjiciendus. l. 4. D. Custod. & Exhib. reor. l. 13. Cod. fidejussor.
units.tr: The first proposition is shown as follows. To bind himself to capital punishment or the extreme penalty, a man need only perform an act that can deserve the extreme penalty, whether for a present or a future offence. Thus under the civil law, one who accused someone of a capital crime entered himself in the charge, so that if he failed to prove it, he would undergo the penalty the accused would have suffered had he been convicted. l. sin. Cod. de Accus. Indeed, if a commentariensis, the guard of a prisoner accused of a crime, had let him go through his own fault, he could even be punished with the extreme penalty. l. 12. D. de Custod. & Exhibit. Reor. l. 4. Cod. eod. And a surety who fails to produce a wicked man becomes liable to the extreme penalty himself, according to the sentence of the king, 1 Kings 20:38 and following, provided the arrangement was made in this way. Examples may also be cited here: Genesis 42:37 and 43:9; Joshua 2:12 and following, and 6:22, 23. This agrees with the civil law, under which a surety who, through any fault or fraud of his own, fails to produce the accused whom he was bound to produce, is to be condemned not only to a fine but sometimes also to bodily punishment. l. 4. D. Custod. & Exhib. Reor. l. 13. Cod. fidejussor.

units.la: Altera positio: scil. quod fidejussor poenâ capitis, propter alterius crimen, vel alterius nomine, possit affici. Tum jure civili, & canonico; tum rationibus; tum jure gentium, & exemplis; tum locorum statutis, confirmari poterit.
units.tr: The second proposition is that a surety may be punished with death on account of another's crime, or on another's behalf. This may be confirmed by the civil and canon law, by reasons, by the law of nations and by examples, and by the statutes of places.

units.la: Equidem jus civile, admittens primæ positionis veritatem, postremi positioni non adversatur. Si enim ex conventione quis semet potest ad capitis poenam obligare, quid ni etiam poterit semet eidem poenæ subjicere, quam reus principalis tulisset si modo tale quid fieri reipublicæ interfit. Neque enim illo casu magis est, membrorū suorum dominus, quam casu postremo. Et si propter aliquod suum factum, qui sistere promisit reum, sub capitis periculo, ultimum patitur supplicium. Quid ni propter hoc ipsum factum, hanc ipsam voluntatem, quod se in locum rei principalis substituat, eam perferret poenam, quam pertulisset criminis capitalis reus.
units.tr: Indeed, the civil law, while admitting the truth of the first proposition, does not oppose the second. For if by agreement a man can bind himself to the penalty of death, why should he not also be able to subject himself to the same penalty that the principal offender would have suffered, provided such a thing is in the interest of the commonwealth? For in that case he is no more the master of his own limbs than in the latter. And if, because of some act of his own, one who promised to produce the accused suffers the extreme penalty under threat of death, why should he not, on account of this very act and this very will, by which he puts himself in the place of the principal, undergo the penalty that the capital offender would have undergone?

units.la: Non equidem hic distinguit jus civile inter fidejussorem de judicio sisti, quasi ille tantum corporaliter possit puniri, & inter fidejussorem simpliciter datum, ad hoc ut subeat poenam, quam tulisset reus Principalis. Leges enim generaliter loquuntur, & totum hoc negotium pro personarum, & criminum qualitate, magistratus ejus, qui summum habet imperium, committunt arbitrio. Quod non fecissent, si in criminalibus capitis poenam concernentibus, nunquam admittendus esset fidejussor. tunc enim judicis arbitrium fuisset coarctatum.lex 1. D. Custod. & exhib. Reor. Et l. 3. D. eod. simpliciter fidejussorem admittit, exceptis causis gravissimis; non quod in iis non sit admittendus fidejussor, verum quod ille praeter poenam corporalem etiam meritus sit carceris squalorem. Haec est ratio jurisconsulti, non alia: qui si fidejussor in illa causa intervenire non potuisset, hanc rationem allegare debuisset, quod in causis poenam corporalem merentibus rentibus non sit admittendus fidejussor. Quin imo in illo crimine, quod exigit necessario custodiam, quale non semper est pecuniariuper. d. l. 3. & nov. 134 c. 9. si quispiam, vel quaepiam incusetur, fidejussorem dando simpliciter, liberabitur, gravissimo solummodo crimine excepto, proculdubio majestatis, quo casu custodiae mulicbri, aut claustris monasticis erit committenda. Nov. 134. c. 9.
units.tr: Indeed, the civil law does not here distinguish between a surety for appearance in court, as if only he could be punished bodily, and a surety given simply in order to undergo the penalty the principal offender would have suffered. For the laws speak in general terms, and they leave the whole matter to the discretion of the magistrate who holds supreme power, according to the character of the persons and the crimes. They would not have done so if, in criminal cases involving the death penalty, a surety could never be admitted; for then the judge's discretion would have been restricted. lex 1. D. Custod. & exhib. Reor. Et l. 3. D. eod. admits a surety simply, except in the most serious cases; not because a surety is not to be admitted in those cases, but because the accused, besides the bodily penalty, deserves the squalor of prison. This is the jurist's reason and no other: if a surety could not have intervened in that case, he ought to have given this reason, namely that a surety is not to be admitted in cases that deserve bodily punishment. Indeed, in that crime which necessarily requires custody, which is not always a matter of money, d. l. 3. & nov. 134 c. 9. if a man or woman is accused, he is freed by giving a surety simply, except for the most grievous crime, undoubtedly treason; in which case he is to be committed to a women's prison or a monastic cloister. Nov. 134 c. 9.

units.la: Nec dissentit jus canonum. in c. cum homo 23. q. 5. Ubi refert Augustinus, reum capitis suum decepisse fidejussorem, atque hunc pro isto, legitimo supplicio fuisse affectum. Non ex hypothesi, si forte alibi talis esset consuetudo, sed probando illam sententiam, quod judicem punientem fidejussorem, extra culpam constituat, qui judex, si jura nihil tale admitterent, extra culpam constitui nullo modo potuissel.
units.tr: Nor does the canon law disagree. in c. cum homo 23. q. 5. There Augustine reports that a man accused of a capital crime deceived his surety, and that this surety was put to a lawful death in his place. He does not say this as a hypothesis, as if such a custom existed somewhere, but in proving that opinion: that a judge who punishes the surety places himself outside the wrong. Had the laws admitted nothing of the kind, the judge could in no way have been placed outside the wrong.

units.la: Non item desunt rationes, quibus sententia mea confirmari potest. Si enim ex contractu, vel delicto, alicui potest imputari, idque sua voluntate, quod debebat alius quis, qui contraxit, vel deliquit, etiam ad hunc effectum, ut infamia afficiatur, quae ipsa morte major est. Quid ni etiam quod reus criminis debebat, alteri puta fidejussori imputari poterit, si velit in locum rei succedere; ejusque subire vices, idque publica consentiente auctoritate. Non aliter enim atque obligatio ex crimine est quid personale ita & ex delicto, vel contractu, quae officiis personae contrahentis inhaeret. Ut non magis haec ipsa alicui possit imputari eam in se suscipienti, atque illa. Aut si quis potest velle, hanc sibi imputari, etiam illam sibi imputari, quasi ipse crimen commisisset, velle poterit. Ita Apostolus Paulus sibi vult imputari delictum ab Onesimo servo commissum; quale etiam jure Romano, (erat enim fur & fugitivus,) poena corporis fuit punitum, ad l. 3. Cod. & Auth. seq. Cod. de serv. Fugitiv. Gothefr. in comm. Ut absurdum omnino non videatur, delictum unius, quod corporis meretur cruciatum, alterum in se recipere. Et si potest velle, alterius crimen sibi imputari alter; quid ni poterit alterius loco puniri. Tum quippe pro reo & nocente moraliter habetur; adeoque poena illa dignus; quam reus principalis subire debuisset. Exemplum iterum proferam in commentariensi, qui licet nihil dignum fecerit morte ut qui forte in culpa levi aut lata aut dolo, quae tamen singula mortem non merentur: attamen ultimo supplicio erit afficiendus. d. l. 4. Cod. de Cust. Reor. Non alia de causa, quam quod in se susceperit, sua conventione, sive expressa, sive tacita, dum in Commentariensem eligitur, custodiam rei, sub capitis periculo. Adeoque se paratum pati declaraverit ultimum supplicium, modo evaserit non fortuito, quem ad poenam perferendam exhibere atque sistere debuisset. Ut hic manifestum sit exemplum, quo quis propter alterum qui evasit non tamen propter suum factum, quod non merebatur capitis poenam, idque ex conventione vel quasi, (nam Aristoteles delicta contractus appellavit involuntarios) ultimo subjicitur supplicio. Quid quod ipsi milites custodes, eo ipso, de jure civili, periculo capitis sese subjiciant, si is cujus custodiam in se susceperant, lata eorum culpa, evaserit, & si illa culpa citra illam conventionem, expressam vel tacitam, seu citra officium, quod consensum requirit suscipientis, adeoque consensum in omnia negotia, quae comitanter officium, capitis poena vindicanda non esset. l. 12. l. 14. D Custod. & exhib. Reor. Arg. l. 7. D. de Tutei.
units.tr: Nor are there lacking reasons by which my opinion can be confirmed. For if, through a contract or a delict, something that another man, who contracted or offended, ought to bear can be imputed to someone, and that by his own will, even to this effect, that he be visited with infamy, which is greater than death itself, why should not the debt that the offender of a crime owed also be imputable to another, say a surety, if he is willing to take the place of the principal and stand in his stead, and this with the consent of public authority? For the obligation arising from a crime is personal, just as that arising from a delict or contract adheres to the person of the one contracting. So the one is no more imputable to a man who takes it upon himself than the other. Or if a man can will that another's offence be imputed to himself, he can equally will that it be imputed to himself as if he had committed the crime himself. So the Apostle Paul wills that the wrong committed by Onesimus the slave be imputed to himself; under Roman law such a slave, since he was a thief and a runaway, was punished with bodily pain. ad l. 3. Cod. & Auth. seq. Cod. de serv. Fugitiv. Gothefr. in comm. So it does not seem altogether absurd for one to take upon himself the wrong of another, which deserves bodily torture. And if one can will another's crime to be imputed to himself, why should he not be able to be punished in the other's place? For then he is morally regarded as the guilty and harmful party, and therefore worthy of that penalty which the principal offender ought to have undergone. I shall again cite an example from the commentariensis, who, although he has done nothing deserving death, as when through slight or gross fault or fraud, which singly do not merit death, he nonetheless is to be visited with the extreme penalty. d. l. 4. Cod. de Cust. Reor. This is for no other reason than that he has taken upon himself, by his agreement, whether express or tacit, when he is chosen as commentariensis, the custody of the accused under threat of capital punishment. And so he has declared himself ready to suffer the extreme penalty, provided that the man whom he was bound to produce and present for the penalty escaped not by chance. Thus the example is plain, by which a man, on account of another who escaped, though not on account of his own act, which did not deserve capital punishment, is nonetheless subjected to the extreme penalty by agreement, or as if by agreement (for Aristotle called such delicts involuntary contracts). What of the fact that soldiers who guard prisoners, by that very act, under the civil law, subject themselves to danger of death if the man whose custody they have undertaken escapes through their gross fault, and that fault is not without that agreement, express or tacit, or without the duty which requires the consent of the one undertaking it; and so, by consent to all the business that accompanies the duty, they would not be liable to capital punishment. l. 12. l. 14. D. Custod. & exhib. Reor. Arg. l. 7. D. de Tutel.

units.la: Accedit & altera ratio: Si quis semet potest pro incolumitate patriae devovere, sic permittente supremo magistratu, & suadente utilitate publica; quid ni etiam pro crimine capitalis reo, si in eo conservando, maxima patriae cernatur utilitas, ut praestet quasi unum perire, quam ut utilissimo reipublicae membro e medio sublato, universus populus periret. Arg. Johan. c. 18. v. 14. Nulla enim hic poterit dissimilis allegari ratio. Si enim dicatur, civi patriae vitam debere, respondebo, & amico nostro aliquo in casu, vitam debeti, ut illius vita, nostra debeat esse carior; id quod jure Romano in servis admissum, quorum vita domini vitâ erat postponenda. l. 1. §. 28. D. Silanian. Unde si talis sit amicus quem salvum esse, interfit reipublicæ, quid ni ejus loco extrema quis tulerit. Maxime si illi tantus debitor, quantus domino servus.
units.tr: There is also another reason. If a man can devote himself for the safety of his country, when the supreme magistrate permits it and public utility urges it, why should he not also do so for a man guilty of a capital crime, if in preserving that man the greatest advantage to the commonwealth is seen, so that it is better for one to perish, as it were, than for the whole people to perish when a most useful member of the commonwealth is removed from the midst? Arg. Johan. c. 18. v. 14. For no dissimilar reason can be alleged here. If it be said that a citizen owes his life to his country, I reply that in some case we also owe our life to a friend, so that his life should be dearer to us than our own; which the Roman law admitted in the case of slaves, whose lives were to be put before their masters' lives. l. 1. §. 28. D. Silanian. Hence, if such a friend is one whose safety is in the interest of the commonwealth, why should not someone undertake extreme measures in his place? Especially if he is as much in debt to him as a slave is to his master.

units.la: Quid quod gentium jura admiserint obsides, qui sub periculo capitis pro fide, atque promissis suorum concivium facti sunt sponsores. Ut etiam fidejussores in criminalibus sub poenâ mortis possint admitti. Neque argumentum hoc infrigitur, eo ipso, quod obsides dentur inviti, nec sint sponsores. Nihil quippe facit ad momentum causæ, quod inviti dentur. Quid si enim inter cives reperiantur, qui volentes vadimonium pro populo subire velint an ideo incipiet jus obsidum esse iniquum? Quin imo vel eo magis procedit nostrum argumentum, quod inviti subjiciantur poenæ, quam alius est meritus, multo magis volentes, modo publica auctoritas & utilitas hoc ipsum suadeat, ut propter delictum alterius, tali poenæ subjiciantur. Accedit, quod obsides fidem suam pro civibus interponant, & nihil aliud sint quam sponsores reipublicæ, uti fidejussor regulariter est privatorum sponsor. Ut in argumento ab obside desumpto, non sit ratio diversitatis in casu proposito. Ut enim obses consentit in poenam ex delicto suorum civium, si illi fidem fallant, & eo ipso habetur moraliter pro nocente : & ita sibi vult imputari, quod faciunt sui; ita & fidejussor, ad pœnam semet obligat, propter delictum alterius, quod ita accipi vult, quasi ipse hoc delictum commisisset, adeoque reatum in se transferri cupit interpretative.
units.tr: What of the fact that the laws of nations have admitted hostages, who, under penalty of death, became sureties for the good faith and promises of their fellow citizens? So too sureties may be admitted in criminal cases under penalty of death. Nor is this argument weakened by the fact that hostages are given unwillingly and are not sureties by choice. For it makes no difference to the point at issue that they are given unwillingly. What if there are citizens who, of their own will, wish to undertake bail for the people? Would the law of hostages then begin to be unjust? Indeed, our argument holds even more strongly here: that a man is subjected to a penalty against his will, which another has deserved, is all the more true when he is subjected to it willingly, provided that public authority and public advantage recommend that, on account of another's offence, he be subjected to such a penalty. Moreover, hostages pledge their faith on behalf of the citizens and are nothing other than sureties of the commonwealth, just as a surety is ordinarily the surety of private persons. So in the argument drawn from the hostage there is no reason for a difference in the case proposed. For just as a hostage consents to the penalty for the offence of his fellow citizens if they break faith, and by that very fact is held morally to be guilty, and so what his people do is imputed to him, so too a surety binds himself to a penalty on account of another's offence, which he wishes to be taken as though he had committed the offence himself, and so desires that the guilt be transferred to himself by interpretation.

units.la: Nec desunt exempla populorum, qui veluti tacito quopiam consensu, pro jure talia facta admiserunt. Celebrata sunt exempla Dæmonis & Eucriti, quorum ille pro Pythia, hic pro Euephemo, ad mortem damnatis, apud Dionysium, Siciliæ Tyrannum, mortis sponsores sese constituerunt.
units.tr: Nor are there lacking examples of peoples who, by a kind of tacit consent, have admitted such arrangements as lawful. The examples of Damon and Eucritus are well known: the one stood surety for Pythias, the other for Euephemus, when they had been condemned to death by Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, and became sureties of death.

units.la: Notissimum Appii Claudii Romani Consulis exemplum, qui obsides trecentos, ex gente Volscorum bellum redintegrantium, in forum adduxit, atque spectante Romano populo & approbante virgis cæsos, securi jussit percuti. Dionys. Halicarnass. libr. 6. Nec obscurum Eduardi, regis Angliæ factum, qui Scoti Guilielmi Setonii præfecti Bervici filium, obsidem sibi datum, in crucem egit, quod pater fidem datam non servasset. Buchan. Rerum Scotic. libr. 9.
units.tr: The example of Appius Claudius, Roman consul, is most notorious: he led into the forum three hundred hostages from the Volscian people, who had renewed the war, and, while the Roman people looked on and approved, had them beaten with rods and ordered them struck down with the axe. Dionys. Halicarnass. libr. 6. Nor is the deed of Edward, king of England, unknown, who, when the son of William Seton, governor of Berwick, had been given to him as a hostage, had him crucified because the father had not kept his promised faith. Buchan. Rerum Scotic. libr. 9.

units.la: Huc etiam referendi mores antiquorum, ubi vades in pœnam ultimi supplicii, & dati assumpti fuerunt. Teste Vallâ 6. Elegant. 32. vid. DD. apud Hering. de fidejuss. c. 3. n. 43. Gregor. Tholos. Synt. libr. 19. c. 13. n. 3. & libr. 24. c. 3. n. 12.
units.tr: To this should also be referred the custom of the ancients, where bail was given and taken on the penalty of capital punishment. On the testimony of Valla, 6 Elegant. 32; see the jurists cited by Hering, de fidejuss. c. 3. n. 43. Gregor. Tholos. Synt. libr. 19. c. 13. n. 3, and libr. 24. c. 3. n. 12.

units.la: Unde etiam statuto caveri posse, ut in caufis capitalibus admittantur fidejuffores, idque fub periculo capitis, eandem fcilicet poenam fubituri, quam reus meritus fuiffet, ftatuunt bene multi. apud Speckhan. loc. antea allegat. vid. & Minoch. 2. caf. 303. n. 15, 16. & Duen. 2. Regul. Fallent. juris Regula 323. circa finem. Grot. de Satisfactione Chrifti adrerfus Socinum. Acacium Enench. Baron. in uno cafu. tractat. de Priv. Parent. & liber. Privil. 3. c. 6.
units.tr: Hence many also hold that by statute it may be provided that sureties be admitted in capital causes, and that under penalty of death, that is, that they shall undergo the same punishment that the accused would have deserved. See Speckhan, loc. cited above; also Minoch. 2. cas. 303. n. 15, 16, and Duen. 2. Regul. Fallent. juris Regula 323, near the end; Grotius, de Satisfactione Christi adversus Socinum; Acacius Enench; Baron, in one case, tractat. de Priv. Parent. and liber. Privil. 3. c. 6.

units.la: Quinimo idipfum in regno Neapolitano obtinere, DD. allegati probant; hocque quondam Kennemerlandiae ftatuto obtinuiffe, refert Leeuwen Paratit. juris noviff. libr. 4. c. 2. part. 1. p. mihi prioris editionis 229, ubi ex archivis loca varia huc facientia allegat.
units.tr: Moreover, the jurists cited prove that the same obtains in the kingdom of Naples; and Leeuwen, Paratit. juris noviss. libr. 4. c. 2. part. 1, p. 229 of my earlier edition, reports that this was once the law in Kennemerland, where he cites from the archives various passages bearing on the point.

units.la: 22. Neque obftat l. 13. in init. D. Ad l. Aquilian. ubi dicitur, neminem effe dominum fuorum membrorum. Refpondeo enim 1. Nemo eft dominus fuorum membrorum, in quantum non poteft abfolute de fe ipfo difponere, nec in fe habet vitae aut necis poteftatem, nec eft in fuo ipfius dominio, aut proprietate, uti quidem olim erant mancipia, quorum membra, & omnia dominicae fuberant poteftati; & quidem in tantum, ut domini in eos vitae necifque haberent poteftatem, membris eorum, olim abuterentur ea, etiam in gratiam cujufdam, corporis cruciatibus fubjicere potuerint. Et si aliunde damnum ipsorum membris esset illatum, dominis in damnum inferentes daretur actio ex l. Aquilia, in quantum illa membra, illud corpus est æstimabile pretio, cum liberi hominis corpus non esset in commercio, adeoque nec re nummarià possit æstimari. l. 3. D. Si quadrupes pauper.
units.tr: 22. Nor does the rule in l. 13, at the beginning, D. Ad l. Aquilian., stand in the way, where it is said that no one is lord of his own limbs. For I reply, first: no one is lord of his own limbs insofar as he cannot dispose of himself absolutely, nor has power of life and death over himself, nor is he in his own dominion or property, as slaves once were, whose limbs and whole persons were subject to the power of their master. Indeed masters had such power of life and death over them that they could subject their limbs to torture, and abuse them even for someone's favour. And if damage were done to their limbs by someone else, an action under the lex Aquilia was granted to the masters against those causing the harm, insofar as those limbs and that body could be valued in money, since the body of a free man was not in commerce and so could not be estimated in money. l. 3. D. Si quadrupes pauper.

units.la: 2. Nemo sic est membrorum suorum dominus, ut non etiam respublica, aut summi rectores, sint domini supremi, quibus invitis uti de bonis non recte disponunt subditi, ita nec de suis membris. In quantum interest reipublicæ, ne quis suâ, & suis membris utatur male. Ut si interfit reipublicæ, aliquem in alterius delinquentis locum substitui, id etiam fieri possit. Arg. §. sin. instit. qui sui vel alien. jur. l. 1. D. qui sui vel alien. jur.
units.tr: Second: no one is so lord of his own limbs that the commonwealth, or the supreme rulers, are not also supreme lords, and subjects do not rightly dispose of their goods, or of their own limbs, against the will of those rulers. Insofar as it is in the interest of the commonwealth that no one misuse himself and his limbs, so if it is in the interest of the commonwealth that someone be substituted in place of another offender, this too may be done. Arg. §. sin. instit. qui sui vel alien. jur.; l. 1. D. qui sui vel alien. jur.

units.la: Non aliter atque repugnabat legibus, civem Romanum, patrem-familias, semet alterius potestati subjicere, adeoque semet adrogandum alteri dare, injussu populi Romani, cujus consensu, ut pro more adprobatione Principis adrogatio peragebatur, accedente consensu ipsius adrogandi. Ut ita designaretur, tum aliquem de se ipso, de suis membris, de suâ vita, alterius potestati subjicienda (nam jure antiquo pater in filiumfam. jus vitæ necisque habebit) posse disponere, cum accedit consensus Populi vel Principis. l. 2. in med. init & l. 21. ibique Gothefred. in not. D. de Adoption.
units.tr: It is no different from the fact that it was not contrary to the laws for a Roman citizen, a head of household, to subject himself to another's power, and so to give himself over to be adrogated by another without the command of the Roman people, whose consent was needed, and with the approval of the Prince, as the custom was for adrogation, together with the consent of the one adrogating. Thus it is shown that one may dispose of himself, of his own limbs and his own life, and subject himself to another's power (for under the ancient law a father will have the power of life and death over a son under his authority), when the consent of the People or of the Prince is added. l. 2. in med. init., and l. 21, with Gothofred's note, D. de Adoption.

units.la: 3. Non obstat regula proposita in d. l. Quia patitur exceptionem in casu extremæ necessitatis, in casu publicæ commoditatis, cui consulendum est, etiam cum damno privatorum. Quia & illo casu, aliquid fit licitum, quod aliter esset illicitum; & in thesi non admittendum, in hypothesi admittendum erit. Arg. l. 2. D. Iustit. & jur. junctâ l. 35. D. de Religios. & sumpt. funer.
units.tr: Third: the rule proposed in the said law does not stand in the way, because it admits an exception in the case of extreme necessity, and in the case of public advantage, which must be looked to even at the cost of private persons. For in that case also something is lawful which otherwise would be unlawful; what is not to be admitted in the thesis is to be admitted in the hypothesis. Arg. l. 2. D. Iustit. & jur., joined with l. 35. D. de Religios. & sumpt. funer.

units.la: 4. Nemo eo ipso, quod se sistat fidejussorem in causâ criminali, membrorum suorum vult offensionem, tanquam finem, verum tantum patitur, non invitus, membrorum offensionem, ut medium, ut conditionem antecedentem; non aliter atque qui periculo se subjicit mortis, pro patriæ incolumitate. Ut tantum pro fine sibi propositam habeat rem bonam, opus bonum, licitum, honestum, laudabile, salutem universitatis, propter quam periculum mortis, quæ per accidens advenit, intrepide vult subire.
units.tr: Fourth: no one, merely because he presents himself as surety in a criminal cause, wills injury to his limbs as an end; he only suffers, and not unwillingly, injury to his limbs as a means, as an antecedent condition. It is no different from one who exposes himself to the peril of death for the safety of his country. He has before him as his end only a good thing, a good, lawful, honourable, praiseworthy work, the safety of the community, for the sake of which he willingly undergoes the danger of death, which comes upon him by accident.

units.la: Non obst. 2. l. 20. l. 26. D. de Pænis l. sancimus. Cod. eod. Quod peccata suos teneant auctores. Adeoque non debeat absolvi nocens, & puniri innocens l. 5. D. de Pænis. Et quia qui se sistit fidejussorem, illo suo facto se reddidit nocentem: & moraliter obligationis auctor censetur, qui illam in se suscepit: & per interpretationem, & imputationem pro nocente habetur, qui in nocentis locum succedit, suâ voluntate, consentiente rectore supremo, & idsuadente publicâ, utilitate: non aliter atque id usu evenire observamus in obside à civitate dato, qui licet innocens, pro nocente tamen habetur, si respublica nocens declaretur. Quinimo uti actiones ex contractubus sunt personales & ossibus personae inhærentes, ceduntur, & ita cessione creditum transit in cessionarium, ac si ipse creditor esset, & debitum novatione factum transit in novantem, ejusdem voluntate; ita etiam delictum ab uno commissum boni publici gratiâ, volenti fidejussori imputatur. Neque dicendum inter obligationem ex contractu, ad poenam pecuniariam, & ex crimine ad poenam corporalem disparem esse rationem. Quod priori in casu detur repetitio, saltem possit dari, ejus quod datum est, non casu posteriori. Quia saepissime fidejussori in causis civilibus intercedent, nec datur nec dari potest regressus adversus reum principalem; quia id sibi, & suae facilitati imputare debebit, quod, cum sciret, se repetere non posse, quod vult expendere in gratiam rei, id tamen volens praestiterit. Exempla sunt in fidejussore, qui pro minore 25. annis, pro servo, pro furioso, pro impubere, proque omnibus illis, qui aliquâ personali exceptione tuti sunt, (quales, socii, maritus, cedens bonis suis, aliique l. 7. D. Except) intercessit.
units.tr: Nor do these stand in the way: 2. l. 20, l. 26, D. de Poenis; l. sancimus, Cod. eod., that sins bind their authors, and so the guilty ought not to be acquitted and the innocent punished, l. 5. D. de Poenis. For he who presents himself as surety has by that very act made himself guilty; and he who takes an obligation upon himself is regarded as its author in a moral sense; and by interpretation and imputation he is held to be guilty who, by his own will, with the supreme ruler consenting and public advantage urging, takes the place of the guilty. This is just as we observe happens in practice with a hostage given by a state, who, although innocent, is nevertheless held as guilty if the guilty commonwealth is declared so. Indeed, just as actions arising from contracts are personal and adhere to the person of the obligee, and so by cession the credit passes to the cessionary as if he were the creditor himself, and a debt made by novation passes to the one novating by the will of the same party, so too a crime committed by one is imputed to a volunteer surety for the sake of the public good. Nor is it to be said that between an obligation arising from contract to pay a fine and one arising from crime to bear bodily punishment there is an unequal reason, on the ground that in the former case repayment is given, or at least may be given, of what was paid, but not in the latter case. For very often sureties intercede in civil causes, and there is and can be no recourse against the principal debtor; the surety must impute this to himself and his own readiness, since, knowing he could not recover what he willingly paid out for the debtor's benefit, he nevertheless paid it. Examples are found in the surety who has interceded for a minor under twenty-five, for a slave, for a madman, for a minor below puberty, and for all those who are protected by some personal exception (such as partners, a husband, one ceding his goods, and others, l. 7. D. Except.).

units.la: Praeterquam, quod ad essentiam fidejussionis non spectet, repetitio ejus, quod pro reo principali est expensum. In eo quippe tantum consistit natura fidejussionis, ut quis solvere promittat, quod alius debet, salva manente principalis debitoris obligatione. Quæ tamen extincta censebitur, simulac, quod debebatur, fidejussor solverit. Etsi ejus recuperandi quod solvit, pro reo principali, non habeat mandati actionem. Id quod evenit, si pro nolente, & invito, semet ipsum interposuerit, adeoque forte amore rei fidejusserit. l. 40. l. 53. D. Mandati.
units.tr: Apart from the point that it does not pertain to the essence of suretyship, there is the matter of recovering what has been paid on behalf of the principal debtor. For the nature of suretyship consists solely in this: that someone promises to pay what another owes, while the principal debtor's obligation remains intact. Yet that obligation is regarded as extinguished as soon as the surety has paid what was owed. Even so, the surety does not have an action of mandate to recover what he paid on behalf of the principal debtor, if he put himself forward for a debtor who was unwilling and opposed, and so perhaps stood surety out of love for the matter. l. 40. l. 53. D. Mandati.

units.la: SECTIO SEXTA
units.tr: SECTIO SEXTA

units.la: CAPUT PRIMUM.
units.tr: CAPUT PRIMUM.

units.la: 1. Conficiendorum statutorum olim restrictior, quam moribus erat potestas.
units.tr: 1. The power of making statutes was formerly more restricted than it was under custom.

units.la: 2. Utrum condere statuta, sit jurisdictionis?
units.tr: 2. Is making statutes a matter of jurisdiction?

units.la: 3. Utrum Episcopus possit condere statuta?
units.tr: 3. Can a bishop make statutes?

units.la: 4. Utrum Rex, dux, marchio &c.?
units.tr: 4. Can a king, duke, margrave, etc.?

units.la: 5. Utrum Senatus in civitate liberâ?
units.tr: 5. Can the senate of a free city?

units.la: 6. Utrum municipia?
units.tr: 6. Can municipalities?

units.la: 7. Utrum Academia?
units.tr: 7. Can a university?

units.la: 8. Utrum familiæ singulares?
units.tr: 8. Can individual families?

units.la: 9. U9. Utrum Doctores & Professores?
units.tr: 9. Can teachers and professors?

units.la: 10. Utrum collegia licita?
units.tr: 10. Are lawful colleges able to?

units.la: 11. Objectionibus respondetur.
units.tr: 11. Objections are answered.

units.la: 12. An Synodi?
units.tr: 12. What of synods?

units.la: 13. An imperator possit canones condere?
units.tr: 13. Can an emperor make canons?

units.la: 14. Statuta dum conduntur à municipiis, omnes oportet esse vocatos, qui sunt de Municipio.
units.tr: 14. When statutes are made by municipalities, all who belong to the municipality must be called.

units.la: 15. Et valent, licet omnes non adfuerint.
units.tr: 15. And they are valid even though not all were present.

units.la: 16. Singulorum tamen requiritur consensus; Si tale quid exigat statutum.
units.tr: 16. Nevertheless the consent of each individual is required, if the statute so demands.

units.la: 17. In Senatum municipii, si jus condendi statuta collatum non opus erit civium presentiâ.
units.tr: 17. If the power of making statutes has been conferred on the senate of a municipality, the presence of the citizens will not be necessary.

units.la: 18. An requiratur Principis consensus, ut statuta valeant?
units.tr: 18. Is the consent of the prince required for statutes to be valid?

units.la: 19. An sufficiat antecedens, an & consequens requiratur?
units.tr: 19. Is the antecedent sufficient, or is the consequent also required?

units.la: 1. COnficiendorum statutorum potestas, olim erat restrictior, quod tantum praeter leges, non autem adversum leges ea condere fuerit permissum. l. 3. §. divus Hadrianus. D. Sepulcr. violat. l. 2. D. offic. Praef. Prætor.
units.tr: 1. The power of making statutes was formerly more restricted, in that it was permitted to make them only beyond the laws, not against the laws. l. 3. §. divus Hadrianus. D. Sepulcr. violat. l. 2. D. offic. Praef. Prætor.

units.la: Verum de moribus major condendorum statutorum licentia datur, ut quae juri civili decro derogant, quod nonnisi deficientibus statutis apud nos locum habet. Gail. 2.obs. 124.
units.tr: But by custom a wider licence to make statutes is granted, so that they may derogate from the civil law, which among us has effect only where the statutes are lacking. Gail. 2. obs. 124.

units.la: 2. Ego pecul. tract. de auctor. jur. civil. in Belg. fœder. Id quod etiam ex clausulis multorum statutorum plus quam manifestum est; in quibus statuitur deficientibus demum statutis in cæteris ad jus civile recurrendum esse. Quia vero potestas illa statutorum condendorum spectat causam efficientem, circa eam ad intellectum materiæ, varias examinabo difficultates.
units.tr: 2. I have treated this in a separate tract on the authority of civil law in the Belgian federation. This is more than plainly evident also from the clauses of many statutes, in which it is laid down that only when the statutes are lacking in other matters is recourse to the civil law to be had. But since that power of making statutes concerns the efficient cause, I shall examine its several difficulties with a view to understanding the matter.

units.la: 2. Et quidem in principio sese offert illa difficultas: Utrum statuta condere sit jurisdictionis, an simplicis tantum permissionis? Respondeo, cum passim in jure omnibus iis jus condendi statuta, sit tributum, quibus aliqualis competit jurisdictio. Negari non poterit, quin statuta condere sit jurisdictionis; id est, iis tantum concessum, qui gaudent aliquali jurisdictione. Non tamen id affirmandum erit ad exclusionem permissionis. In quantum nulli licitum, etiamsi habeat jurisdictionem, statuta condere, nisi cui hoc ipsum sit permissum. l. 1. D. de Damn. Infect. l. 32. in init. D. de leg. l. 26. D. Ad Municipal. Bartol. in l. omnes populi in 1. quest. Princ. num. 3. D. de Iustit. & Iur. & quos commemorat Iason in l. 2. Cod. quæ sit long. Consuet. Barbatia de Præstant. Cardinal. 8. 9. part. 1. n.
units.tr: 2. Indeed at the outset that difficulty presents itself: whether making statutes belongs to jurisdiction, or is merely a matter of permission. I answer: since the right to make statutes is everywhere in law granted to all those who possess some jurisdiction, it cannot be denied that making statutes belongs to jurisdiction; that is, it is granted only to those who enjoy some jurisdiction. Yet this is not to be affirmed to the exclusion of permission, since no one, even if he has jurisdiction, is allowed to make statutes unless this very thing has been permitted to him. l. 1. D. de Damn. Infect. l. 32. in init. D. de leg. l. 26. D. Ad Municipal. Bartol. in l. omnes populi in 1. quest. Princ. num. 3. D. de Iustit. & Iur. and those whom Jason cites in l. 2. Cod. quæ sit long. Consuet. Barbatia de Præstant. Cardinal. 8. 9. part. 1. n.

units.la: 3. Caeterum quis possit condere statuta, & quidem an Episcopus in sua Dioecesi seu Provincia ambigitur? Respondeo, affirmativa quidem illis placet, qui jurisdictionem aliam faciunt spiritualem, aliam secularem, seu ecclesiasticam vel civilem. Quales qui juris canonici auctoritatem sequuntur. Id quod admittunt, si quando consensus accedit capituli. Marc. Anton. Marescot. in c. ut animarum. de Constit. tom. 5. Repet. jur. can. n. 53. p. 116. Verum quia illam jurisdictionis distinctionem non agnoscimus; neque juris condendi potestas concessa est episcopis; ut qui nec forum, nec apparitionem, nec executionem habent; jure merito iisdem statuta condendi deneganda facultas l. 3. l. 8. Cod. de Episcop. Audient. & Cujac. in Parat. Cod. ibid. l. 25. in init. Cod. de Episc. & Cleric. nov. 123. cap. 21, & cap. 24. Quinimo in Nov. 123. c. 21. res executioni mandatur per judicem secularem. Et ipse Episcopus coram seculari ratione delicti communis conveniebatur. c. 24. d. nov. 123.
units.tr: 3. Further, it is disputed who may make statutes, and in particular whether a bishop may do so in his diocese or province. I answer: those who make jurisdiction twofold, one spiritual and the other secular, or ecclesiastical and civil, are inclined to the affirmative. Such are those who follow the authority of canon law, and they concede it if at any time the consent of the chapter is added. Marc. Anton. Marescot. in c. ut animarum. de Constit. tom. 5. Repet. jur. can. n. 53. p. 116. But since we do not acknowledge that distinction of jurisdiction, and since the power of making law has not been granted to bishops, who have neither a court, nor an official staff, nor execution, the faculty of making statutes is rightly denied to them. l. 3. l. 8. Cod. de Episcop. Audient. and Cujac. in Parat. Cod. ibid. l. 25. in init. Cod. de Episc. & Cleric. nov. 123. cap. 21, & cap. 24. Indeed in Nov. 123. c. 21. the carrying out of a matter is committed to a secular judge. And the bishop himself was sued before a secular court for a common crime. c. 24. d. nov. 123.

units.la: Nec obst. Nov. 79. Quia ut prior per subsequentes est explicanda.
units.tr: Nor does Nov. 79. stand in the way, since the earlier novel is to be explained by the later ones.

units.la: Non etiam obst. Nov. 8. c, 9. quia tantum in defectum judicum relatio fit ad Principem, qui coercebit delinquentes, non vero episcopus.
units.tr: Nor does Nov. 8. c. 9. stand in the way, because the reference to the Prince, who will punish offenders, is made only in default of judges, and not to the bishop.

units.la: Non obstat insuper, quod dicatur Episcopus habere forum l. 6. Cod. Episc. Aud. Ibi enim ad forum, non sequitur executio per eundem. Sic enim & Pedaneus forum habet in quantum quis coram pedaneo convenitur in loco judicii. Nec tamen Pedaneus habet executionem, aut jurisdictionem. Non denique obstat, quod episcopus coerceat delicta. Quia coercitio canonica, qualis est per excommunicationem, per censuram, nihil habet commune cum jurisdictione. Aliter & Patri, & Domino, & Praeceptori, competeret jurisdictio, quibus tamen jure tribuitur aliqua coercitio in suos, quae nihil aliud est, quam delictorium emendatio. tit. Cod. de Emend. Prop. & de Emend. Servor. Anton. Matth. Tract. de Judic. disp. 2. de Jurisd. num. 44. Diss. Jason in l. omnes populi. D. just. & jure. loc. ante cit. Octavian. Vestrius p. mihi 32. Bocer. Class. 1. disp. 3. num. 39.
units.tr: Nor does it stand in the way that a bishop is said to have a court. l. 6. Cod. Episc. Aud. For there the court is in view, but execution does not follow from it through the same person. Thus even a petty judge has a court, insofar as someone is sued before him in the place of judgment; yet a petty judge has neither execution nor jurisdiction. Finally, it does not stand in the way that a bishop restrains offences, because canonical restraint, such as by excommunication or by censure, has nothing in common with jurisdiction. Otherwise jurisdiction would belong also to a father, a master and a teacher, to whom by law some restraint over their own dependants is granted, which is nothing other than the correction of faults. tit. Cod. de Emend. Prop. & de Emend. Servor. Anton. Matth. Tract. de Judic. disp. 2. de Jurisd. num. 44. Diss. Jason in l. omnes populi. D. just. & jure. loc. ante cit. Octavian. Vestrius p. mihi 32. Bocer. Class. 1. disp. 3. num. 39.

units.la: 4. An id poterit Rex imperio subjectus in suo regno, Dux in ducatu, Marchio in marchionatu, Comes in comitatu, ut liber Baro in suo territorio? Respondeo, quod ita. Illi quippe immediate imperatori sunt subjecti, adeoque summi in sua ditione post imperatorem. Argum. l. 2. Cod. de Offic. Praef. Pretor. Orient. l. 16. Cod. de Judic. Ordin. Camera part. 1. tit. 57. de juram. judic. & Assess. sess. Bartol. in l. omnes populi num. 8. de Iust. & Iur. Cujac. 6. observ. 10. Jason. in d. l. omnes populi. §. 20. vid. Franc. Vivium in tom. Comm. opin. libr. 17. in verb. statutum. p. 342.
units.tr: 4. Could a king, subject to the empire in his own kingdom, a duke in his duchy, a margrave in his margraviate, a count in his county, or a free baron in his territory, do this? I answer that they could. For they are subject immediately to the emperor, and so are supreme in their own domains after the emperor. By argument from l. 2. Cod. de Offic. Praef. Pretor. Orient. l. 16. Cod. de Judic. Ordin. Camera part. 1. tit. 57. de juram. judic. & Assess. sess. Bartol. in l. omnes populi num. 8. de Iust. & Iur. Cujac. 6. observ. 10. Jason in d. l. omnes populi. §. 20. see Franc. Vivius in the Comm. opin. libr. 17. under statutum, p. 342.

units.la: 5. An id poterit Senatus in civitate imperiali liberâ, uti vocant, quæ nonnisi imperatorem recognoscit? Affirmativa placet. Tantundem enim is potest in suâ republicâ, quantum Imperator in Imperio. Accedit quod talis civitas introducere valeat consuetudinem, ut multo magis possit introducere statutum. l. 9. D. Ad leg. Rhod. de jact. l. 37. D. de Rebus Auctor. Iud. Poss. seu de Privil. cred. l. 3. §. 4. D. Quod vi aut clam. Bartol. in d. l. omnes populi. num. 2. Zas. ibidem num. 11. Gail. de Pac. Publica lib. 1. cap. 6. num. 10. & 11. ibidemque alii relati. Canonistæ, in c. quod clericis de Foro compet. Emanuel Soares Thesaur. Recept. Sent. in verb. statutum. ibique alii.
units.tr: 5. Could the senate of a free imperial city, as they call it, which acknowledges only the emperor, do this? The affirmative is accepted. For it can do as much in its own commonwealth as the emperor can in the empire. Moreover, such a city is able to introduce a custom, and so much more readily can it introduce a statute. l. 9. D. Ad leg. Rhod. de jact. l. 37. D. de Rebus Auctor. Iud. Poss. or de Privil. cred. l. 3. §. 4. D. Quod vi aut clam. Bartol. in d. l. omnes populi. num. 2. Zas. ibidem num. 11. Gail. de Pac.
