Publica lib. 1. cap. 6. num. 10. & 11. and the others cited there. The canonists, in c. quod clericis de Foro compet. Emanuel Soares Thesaur. Recept. Sent. under statutum, and the others cited there.

units.la: 6. An municipia? Idem dicendum. Sunt enim Magistratus in municipiis principes cæterorum. Ut quemadmodum appellatione conveniunt, ita & similiter re conveniant. Et quod lex in imperio, id erit in municipiis statutum seu decretum: quæ etiam ad exemplum, lex sæpissime appellatur. Ne dicam municipia ubique fere locorum jurisdictione munita esse, ut leges locales condere iis sit permissum. l. 15. §. 9. D. de Excus. Tutor. l. 6. in Princ. D. Quod Cujusque Univ. Nomin. l. 3.
units.tr: 6. Municipalities? The same must be said. For the magistrates in municipalities are princes of the rest. Just as they agree in name, so they likewise agree in fact. And what the law is in the empire, that in the municipalities is the statute or decree, which is also very often called a law by analogy. Not to mention that municipalities are almost everywhere fortified with local jurisdiction, so that it is permitted to them to make local laws. l. 15. §. 9. D. de Excus. Tutor. l. 6. in Princ. D. Quod Cujusque Univ. Nomin. l. 3.

units.la: 7. An Academia? Quod affirmandum, modo habeat aliqualem jurisdictionem. Pari enim passu ambulant, statuta condere, & aliqualem habere coercitionem. Scilicet, quæ sit jurisdictionis. Argum l. 6. D. Quod cujusque Universf. nom. l. 25. D. Ad Municip. juncti. l. 1. D. de damn. inf. l. 26. D. Ad munic. l. 17. §. 1. D. Qui & à Quibus Manum. Authent. Habitâ. verb. verum tamen. Cod. Ne filius pro patre. Besold. dissert. jurid. Polit. de jurisd. Academ. cap. 6.
units.tr: 7. Whether an academy (Academia) does? It should be affirmed, provided it has some jurisdiction. For they walk on equal footing: to enact statutes and to have some kind of coercive power. Namely, what sort of jurisdiction it is. Arg. l. 6. D. Quod cujusque Universf. nom. l. 25. D. Ad Municip., read together with l. 1. D. de damn. inf. l. 26. D. Ad munic. l. 17. §. 1. D. Qui & à Quibus Manum. Authent. Habitâ, verb. verum tamen. Cod. Ne filius pro patre. Besold, dissert. jurid. Polit. de jurisd. Academ. cap. 6.

units.la: 8. An familiæ singulares? Resp. Non defuerunt qui illud asserrerent. Inter quos allegati apud Jason. in l. omnes populi. D. just. & jure. n. 42. Verum cum familiæ nec jurisdictionem, adeoque nec coercitionem habeant, de quâ, in l. ult. D. de offic. ejus cui Mand. est jurisd. Dicendum videtur, etsi certa pacta sint familiarum, iis tamen vim statutorum non inesse. Ast si accesserit supremi consensus & auctoritas, negandum non erit quin illis pactis juri publico possit derogari. l. 38. D. de Pact. l. 20. in init. D. de Relig. & sumt. fun. l. 55. D. de legat. 1. l. 15. §. 1. D. Ad leg. Falcid. Zas. consf. 1. volum. 2. Gail. 2. observ. 127. Schrader. de Feud. part. 7. cap. 4. 4. num. 54. Rosenthal. de feud. c. 7. axiom. 57. vid. Taraquell. de jure primog. q. 16. n. 17. Vult. de feud. libr. 1. cap. 7. n. 48. Heigius quaest. 23. num. 40. & seq.
units.tr: 8. Are individual families (familiae singulares) able to make statutes? The answer: there were not wanting those who asserted it. Among them are those cited at Jason on l. omnes populi, D. de iustitia et iure, n. 42. But since families have neither jurisdiction nor, therefore, coercive power (on which see l. ult. D. de officio eius cui mandata est iurisdictio), it seems right to say that, although families may have certain agreements, those agreements do not have the force of statutes. But if the consent and authority of the supreme power be added, it cannot be denied that those agreements may be derogated from by public law. l. 38. D. de pactis. l. 20. in init. D. de religioso et sumptibus funerum. l. 55. D. de legatis 1. l. 15. §. 1. D. ad legem Falcidiam. Zas. consil. 1. vol. 2. Gail. 2. observ. 127. Schrader. de Feud. part. 7. cap. 4. 4. num. 54. Rosenthal. de feud. c. 7. axiom. 57. vid. Taraquell. de jure primog. q. 16. n. 17. Vult. de feud. libr. 1. cap. 7. n. 48. Heigius quaest. 23. num. 40. & seq.

units.la: 9. An Doctores & Professores, idque in gratiam suorum discipulorum? Non videtur. Neque enim privati jus statuta condendi habent, ut qui omni carent jurisdictione, Sic ut illi, in quorum gratiam ea condunt, ad obedientiam cogi non possint. Ex officio tamen, id est honestatis ratione si quas regulas studiorum gratia, suis praescribant discipulis, illi semet talibus subjicient; non aliter atque parentibus obsequia praestant liberi. Argum. l. liberto. & ibi gloss. D. de obseq. Parent. Praest. l. 4. Cod. locat. in simili Boër. decis. 155. num. 29. Angelus & Alexander in l. si non speciali. 9. & l. ult. Cod. de Testam apud Schneidewin. numer. 19. ad §. jus autem civile. Instit. de jur. nat. cent. civil.
units.tr: 9. Whether teachers and professors, and that for the sake of their students? It does not seem so. For private persons do not have the right to enact statutes, since they lack all jurisdiction; so those in whose favour such rules are made cannot be compelled to obedience. Nevertheless, out of duty, that is, for reasons of decency, if they prescribe certain rules of study for their students, the students will submit themselves to them, just as children render obedience to their parents. Arg. l. liberto. & ibi gloss. D. de obseq. Parent. Praest. l. 4. Cod. locat. in simili Boër. decis. 155. num. 29. Angelus & Alexander in l. si non speciali. 9. & l. ult. Cod. de Testam apud Schneidewin. numer. 19. ad §. jus autem civile. Instit. de jur. nat. cent. civil.

units.la: 10. An collegia licita, qualia sunt corpora Pistorum, Naviculariorum &c.? Resp. Etsi talia collegia sibi aliquem ordinem praescribant, decreta condant, & secundum ea qui sunt in collegiis, invicem sint obstricti. Censerem tamen illa decreta statutorum vim non obtinere. Neque enim talia collegia publica sunt, nec singuli in collegiis, publicis funguntur muneribus. Quicquid sit, id certum est, non eandem esse rationem collegiorum, quae est municipiorum. Ut dicendum sit collegiorum jura potius pactorum seu conventionum, quam statutorum nomen mereri. l. ult. D. de Colleg. & Corpor. l. ult. Cod. de juri-sd. Diss. Sneidwin. ad §. jus autem civile. num. 15. Instit. de jur. nat. gent. & civil. Bocer. Classs. 1. disp. 3. de form. & mod. const. jur. num. 40. & varii citati apud Berlich. decis. 150.
units.tr: 10. Whether licensed guilds (collegia licita), such as the corporations of bakers, shipmen and so on? The answer: although such colleges prescribe some order for themselves, enact decrees, and those within the colleges are bound to one another according to them, I would judge that those decrees do not have the force of statutes. For such colleges are not public, nor do their individual members discharge public offices. Whatever the case, it is certain that the reason for colleges is not the same as that for municipalities. So it must be said that the rights of colleges deserve the name of pacts or agreements rather than of statutes. l. ult. D. de Colleg. & Corpor. l. ult. Cod. de juri-sd. Diss. Sneidwin. ad §. jus autem civile. num. 15. Instit. de jur. nat. gent. & civil. Bocer. Classs. 1. disp. 3. de form. & mod. const. jur. num. 40. & varii citati apud Berlich. decis. 150.

units.la: 11. Nec obstat quod Collegium alicujus negotiationis judices dare possit, adeoque jurisdictionem habere videatur. l. 3. in sin. D. jurisdict. l. ult. Cod. de jurisd. omn. judic. Neque enim d. l. ult. asserit à negotiatoribus vel opificibus judices dari posse; sunt enim illi omnes privati. l. 3. Cod. eod. Verum municipia, rempublicam, judices dare posse, negotiatores, opifices, qui de talibus negotiis judicent, id vero innuit. Idque non sine ratione, quod illi artifices optime de rebus spectantibus ipsorum opificium & negotiationem possint judicare: siquidem artifici credendum in arte suâ. Arg. l. 1. in init. D. de Pœnit. inspiciend.
units.tr: 11. Nor does it stand in the way that a guild of some trade can appoint judges, and so seem to have jurisdiction. For the last-cited law does not assert that judges can be appointed by merchants or craftsmen; for these are all private persons. But that municipalities and the commonwealth can appoint judges, and merchants and craftsmen to judge such matters, that the law does indeed hint at. And not without reason, since those craftsmen can best judge matters concerning their own craft and trade; for one should trust a craftsman in his own art. Arg. l. 1. in init. D. de Pœnit. inspiciend.

units.la: 12. Verum, an non collegia vel potius ecclesiasticæ congregationes, qualia Concilia aut Synodi, statuta condere poterunt ecclesiastica? Respondeo, ut proprie loquendo sint statuta, quibus etiam quis in foro sol-li ligetur, & coërceatur, si eadem violaverit, non videtur affirmandum. Ut tamen in conciliis ecclesiasticos canones, seu regulas, condant, spectantes fidei normam & mores & disciplinam ecclesiæ, quibus obstringantur ecclesiæ membra, quoad hominem internum ; idque spirituali aliquá jurisdictione, suo modo ; (quæ tamen non est species jurisdictionis illius, quæ externum hominem coërcet) etiam, si approbatæ ab Imperatoribus, quoad externum hominem, modo verbo Dei congruè atq; convenientes sint constitutæ ; de omni jure indubitatum est. l. 7. §. 4. Cod. Summ. Trinit. l. 8. §. 3. Cod. Eod. Nov. 42. in sin. Nov. 83. c. 1. Nov. 131. c. 1. Actor. cap. 15. Inscriptio Ordin. Eccles. Synod. Dordrac. de ann. 1618. 1619. & artic. sin. dict. ordin.
units.tr: 12. But are colleges, or rather ecclesiastical assemblies such as councils or synods, able to enact ecclesiastical statutes? I answer: that properly speaking they are statutes, by which someone is bound and coerced in the courts if he violates them, is not to be affirmed. Yet that in councils they enact ecclesiastical canons or rules concerning the norm of faith, morals and the discipline of the Church, by which the members of the Church are bound as regards the inner man, and that with some spiritual jurisdiction in its own way (which, however, is not a species of that jurisdiction which coerces the outer man), and also that, if approved by the emperors as regards the outer man, they are constituted fittingly and agreeably with the Word of God, is beyond all doubt by any law. l. 7. §. 4. Cod. Summ. Trinit. l. 8. §. 3. Cod. Eod. Nov. 42. in sin. Nov. 83. c. 1. Nov. 131. c. 1. Actor. cap. 15. Inscriptio Ordin. Eccles. Synod. Dordrac. de ann. 1618. 1619. & artic. sin. dict. ordin.

units.la: 13, An idem de imperatore statuendum? Ut condat ea, quæ externum hominem spectant, adeoque extrinsecè circa ecclesiæ negotia ordo servetur, pacique publicæ istâc ratione consulatur, in quantum ex illo Constantini, est Episcopus extra, nemo protestantium ambigit. Ut vero canones ecclesiasticos, formaliter sic dictos constituat, fidei doctrinam, & ecclesiæ regimen intrinsecum spectantes, nemo dixerit, nisi qui imperatorem in rei veritate, formaliter, & eminenter velit Papam, aut ecclesiæ Patrem spiritualem. Ratio est, quia in conciliis ubi canones & regulæ ecclesiasticæ conduntur, solummodo Christus est univoce ecclesiæ Princeps, in re spirituali; supremus autem præses atque judex Deus per Scripturam; quandoque externi ordinis, præses imperator; & ecclesiasticæ personæ ibidem congregatæ donis & vocatione instructæ, quales Apostoli, Presbyteri, ecclesiæ doctores, sub Christo judicio ministeriali judices, ut quibus solis Christus domus suæ spiritualis administrationem demandavit. Ut præter personas enumeratas aliæ non desiderentur, quæ regulas ad substantiam rei ecclesiasticæ spectantes, constituant.
units.tr: 13. Is the same to be said of the emperor? That he may enact those things which concern the outer man, so that order is kept externally in ecclesiastical affairs and public peace is provided for in this way, insofar as he is, from the saying of Constantine, "bishop outside", no Protestant doubts. But that he should formally establish so-called ecclesiastical canons, concerning the doctrine of faith and the inner government of the Church, no one would say except one who wishes the emperor, in truth, formally and eminently, to be the Pope or spiritual Father of the Church. The reason is that in councils, where ecclesiastical canons and rules are enacted, Christ alone is, univocally, Prince of the Church in spiritual matters; the supreme president and judge is God through Scripture; the president of external order is sometimes the emperor; and the ecclesiastical persons gathered there, furnished with gifts and calling, such as Apostles, Elders and teachers of the Church, are judges under Christ in a ministerial judgment, since to them alone Christ entrusted the administration of his spiritual house. So, beyond the persons enumerated, no others are required to establish rules pertaining to the substance of ecclesiastical matters.

units.la: 2. Quia uti distincta sunt collegia, nec invicem subordinata adeoque toto genere diversa, respublica & ecclesia, ita & diversæ ipsorum regulæ, diversa jurisdictio; illa secularis, hæc spiritualis, illa dominica mixtum vel merum imperium habens conjunctum; hæc ministerialis, sine ullâ externâ coërcitione: ut alterum in alterius jura involare nequeat. Artic. 30 Confess. Belgicæ. artic. 71. ordin. Eccles. de ann. 1618. 1619. Et quemadmodum sacerdotium non fert imperio leges, nec quidem in iis negotiis, ad quæ oportet utriusque concurrere administrationem, aliâ tamen atqne alia ratione: ita nec imperium sacerdotio præscribit canones ecclesiasticos, quos à solo Christo, & ministris seu mandatariis Christi, sufficienti mandato instructis, accipit.
units.tr: 2. Because just as colleges are distinct and not subordinate to one another, and so wholly different in kind, so too the commonwealth and the Church, and their rules and jurisdictions are different: the one secular, the other spiritual; the one holding lordly power, mixed or pure, the other ministerial, without any external coercion; so that the one cannot encroach upon the rights of the other. Artic. 30 Confess. Belgicæ. artic. 71. ordin. Eccles. de ann. 1618. 1619. And just as the ministry does not impose laws on the magistrate, not even in those matters in which the administration of both must concur, yet in different ways, so neither does the magistrate prescribe ecclesiastical canons to the ministry, which it receives from Christ alone, and from the ministers or mandatories of Christ, furnished with sufficient commission.

units.la: 3. Quia si imperator regulas ecclesiasticas conderet, sequeretur, eas non amplius esse regulas ecclesiasticas, verum leges: cum quicquid imperatori placet, legis habeat vigorem. l. 1, De Princip. Constit. Verum eas ipsas leges non esse, quod legibus imperatoriis, & ab imperatore latis contradistinguantur, patescit ex Nov. 131. c. 1. Ubi sancivit imperator Justinianus, ut canones vicem legum obtinerent; scilicet qui antea solum ab ecclesiasticis erant conditi, eosdem postmodum sicut leges vult observari imperator. Cum tamen quae decreta ab imperatore condita, non ut leges observanda, sed quia revera ab initio leges erant. Ut canones vicem legum habere dicantur, postquam ab imperatoribus sunt probati, non ante, quod tantum ab iis conditi, qui legum serendarum potestatem non habebant, quales erant in officiis ecclesiasticis constitutae personae. 4 Quia & ipsi imperatores Christiani exserte statuunt in Conciliis, in Synodis, à Sanctis Patribus, Episcopis, Presbyteris, ecclesiae doctoribus non à se, factas esse regulas. l. 3. §. 3. l. 7. §. 4. Cod. de Summ. Trinit. Eaque synodorum non sua appellant dogmata. Nov. 131. c. 1, à conciliis expositas aut firmata, quae ipsi ibidem sequuntur, non faciunt.
units.tr: 3. For if the emperor were to lay down ecclesiastical rules, it would follow that they were no longer ecclesiastical rules but laws, since whatever pleases the emperor has the force of law. l. 1, De Princip. Constit. That these very things are not laws is clear from the fact that they are distinguished from imperial laws and from laws enacted by the emperor, as shown by Nov. 131. c. 1. There the emperor Justinian ordained that the canons should take the place of laws; that is, the emperor wills that those canons which had previously been drawn up only by churchmen should afterwards be observed as laws. Yet decrees enacted by the emperor are not observed as laws because they were, in truth, laws from the beginning. The canons are said to take the place of laws only after they have been approved by the emperors, and not before, because they were drawn up by men who did not have the power of making laws, such as persons appointed to ecclesiastical offices. 4. Likewise the Christian emperors themselves expressly state that the rules were made in councils and synods by the holy Fathers, bishops, presbyters and teachers of the Church, and not by themselves. l. 3. §. 3. l. 7. §. 4. Cod. de Summ. Trinit. And they call them the doctrines of the synods, not their own. Nov. 131. c. 1, set forth or confirmed by councils, which they themselves follow there, and do not make.

units.la: Cui consona ordin. Eccles. de ann. 1618, 1619. Quae id juris ecclesiasticis collegiis tribuit. art. 49. 50. Eoque etiam nomine iisdem, ampliatio, diminutio, alteratio, distorum canonum ecclesiasticorum concedi-turtur. artic. sin. d. ordin. 5. Quia imperator, vel summus magistratus dum ordinis ratione conciliis præest, ne qua causa detur confusionis, aut tumultus, neve ad rixas & contentiones transeant ecclesiastic (alio in conciliis Præside collegii ecclesiastici constituto in quantum ibidem de negotiis agitur ecclesiasticis, quibus non præsidet imperator nov. 6. in init.) tantum suffragio quo gaudet deliberativo, non vero decisivo. artic. 54. 41. 50. ordinat. Eccles. de ann. 1618, 1619. quod illis tantum competit, qui debitis pietatis & doctrinæ donis, legitimâ vocatione instructi, ecclesiasticis causis atque quæstionibus decidendis dati sunt. Ut iniquum sit virum Principem illis semet immiscere. Actor. 15. l. 4. verb. vam injuriam facit. Cod. de Summ. Trinit. Daneus ad 2. Quæst. sibi Propos. de auct. Magistrat. in Synod. & Class.
units.tr: The Church Order of 1618 and 1619 agrees with this, and it grants this right of decision to ecclesiastical assemblies. art. 49. 50. And for this same reason the power to extend, diminish or alter the said ecclesiastical canons is granted to them. artic. sin. d. ordin. 5. For the emperor, or the supreme magistrate, when he presides over councils by virtue of his office, lest any occasion of confusion or tumult arise, or lest the churchmen pass into quarrels and contentions (a president of the ecclesiastical college being appointed in the councils, insofar as ecclesiastical matters, over which the emperor does not preside, are being treated there, nov. 6. in init.), has only a deliberative vote, and not a decisive one. artic. 54. 41. 50. ordinat. Eccles. de ann. 1618, 1619. A decisive vote belongs only to those who have been appointed, equipped with the due gifts of piety and learning and with lawful calling, to decide ecclesiastical causes and questions. So it is wrong for a prince, a man, to thrust himself into these matters. Actor. 15. l. 4. verb. vam injuriam facit. Cod. de Summ. Trinit. Daneus ad 2. Quæst. sibi Propos. de auct. Magistrat. in Synod. & Class.

units.la: Negari tamen non poterit, quin imperator, vel supremus in suo territorio, canonibus ecclesiasticis auctoritatem suam accommodet, quo publice serventur, quo singula ecclesiæ membra obligent; & si quæ eos negligant, coërceantur, pœnâ in eorum violatores statutâ, artic. 4. Constit. Urbium quarundam in Holland. circa jus Magistr. in Ecclesiastic.
units.tr: Yet it cannot be denied that the emperor, or the supreme authority in his own territory, may lend his authority to ecclesiastical canons, so that they are publicly observed and bind each member of the Church; and if any neglect them, they may be restrained by a penalty laid down against their violators. artic. 4. Constit. Urbium quarundam in Holland. circa jus Magistr. in Ecclesiastic.

units.la: Ut quemadmodum contemptus canonum per ecclesiasticos censurâ vindicatur ecclesiastica: sic etiam eorum transgressores, postquam canones sunt confirmati, civili aliqua poena multarentur. Quo etiam nomine imperator Justinianus canones tanquam leges servari voluit, eas sua sanctione probavit, confirmavit, etiam contemtores eorum gravi poena coercendos statuit. l. 7. §. 4. Cod. l. 8. §§. 3. Cod. Summ. Trinit. Nov. 42. in sin. Nov. 83. c. 1. nov. 115. c. 3. §. 14. nov. 131 c. 1. Danaeus. Resp. ad tertiam quaest. de potest. Magistr. circa canones eccles. constit. Francisc. Junius de jur. Magistr. in Eccles.
units.tr: Just as the contempt of canons is punished by ecclesiastical censure, so too their transgressors, once the canons have been confirmed, may be fined with some civil penalty. For this reason also the emperor Justinian wished the canons to be observed as laws; by his sanction he approved and confirmed them, and he also decreed that their contemners be restrained by a heavy penalty. l. 7. §. 4. Cod. l. 8. §§. 3. Cod. Summ. Trinit. Nov. 42. in sin. Nov. 83. c. 1. nov. 115. c. 3. §. 14. nov. 131 c. 1. Danaeus. Resp. ad tertiam quaest. de potest. Magistr. circa canones eccles. constit. Francisc. Junius de jur. Magistr. in Eccles.

units.la: Neque tamen per hanc ipsam imperatoriam confirmationem regulae ecclesiasticae, in quantum tales, incipiunt esse Imperatoriae: non magis atque tutor à Patre testamento datus imperfecto, sed confirmatus à Praetore, desinit esse testamentarius: Arg. l. 3. D. conf. tutor. Neque obstabit, quod quis ea sua faciat, quibus suam accomodat auctoritatem. Argum. §. pen. instit. proem. ut videantur esse canones imperatoriae, seu Politicae, in quantum ab imperatore, vel à politica potestate sunt comprobatae. Quia nec imperator, nec politica ulla potestas, unquam facit illos canones esse regulas ecclesiasticas; utpote, quae tales erant, simulac ab ecclesiasticis essent conditae. Verum hoc efficit tantum, ut qui canones antea nonnisi regulae ecclesiasticae membris ecclesiae suadendae, omni vi coactiva, omni externa coercitione, destitutae, ut quae penes ecclesiasticos nulla, jam adinstar legum obligent ecclesiae membra, in quae, si ea neglexerint, etiam Politice, erit animadvertendum.
units.tr: Nor, however, do ecclesiastical rules, as such, begin to be imperial through this very imperial confirmation, any more than a tutor given by a father in an unfinished will, but confirmed by the praetor, ceases to be a testamentary tutor. Arg. l. 3. D. conf. tutor. Nor does it stand in the way that someone makes their own those things to which he lends his authority, so that the canons may seem to be imperial, or political, insofar as they have been approved by the emperor or by the political power. Argum. §. pen. instit. proem. For neither the emperor nor any political power ever makes those canons ecclesiastical rules, since they were such as soon as they were drawn up by churchmen. Rather, this only brings about that canons which before were nothing more than rules to be urged upon the members of the Church, lacking all coercive force and all external compulsion, and which, since there was no power of enforcement in the hands of churchmen, now bind the members of the Church in the manner of laws. If they neglect them, the civil authority too will have to take action against them.

units.la: Atque haec ipsa, quam jam explicui communis est reformatorum sententia, Belgii foederati praxis; à qua qui deviat Theologus inBelgio, jure merito heterodoxias manifestæ, contra subscriptionem à se factam, est insimulandus. Ut hic reprehendendus veniat D. Samuel Maresius, qui decreta Magistratus Politici inter canones recipit p. 3. in sin. Allocut. ad Lectorem in vindic. Responsi de Canonicis Ultrajectt. Idem, quod satis innuit, p. 42. Epistol. de Reconcil. inter se & Celeberrimum Voetium; quæ ut mendaciorum est plena, ita etiam continet, lubricas & periculosas locutiones. Et licet eadem Epistola scribat, sibi nihil mecum esse negotii, Theologo cum Jurisconsulto; non tamen ægre laturus est, si cum hic docere voluerim, & commonstrare, quam non deviet ab orthodoxia, ibique tanquam viator vectorem monere.
units.tr: This very view which I have now explained is the common opinion of the Reformed, and the practice of the United Netherlands; a theologian in the Netherlands who departs from it is rightly to be charged with manifest heterodoxy, contrary to the subscription he has made. Here the one who must be rebuked is D. Samuel Maresius, who admits decrees of the political magistrate among the canons. p. 3. in sin. Allocut. ad Lectorem in vindic. Responsi de Canonicis Ultrajectt. He hints at the same thing, as is quite clear, at p. 42 of his letter on reconciliation between himself and the most celebrated Voetius; a letter which is as full of lies as it is of slippery and dangerous expressions. And although the same letter writes that he has no business with me, a theologian with a jurisconsult, he will not be displeased if I undertake to teach him here, and to show how far he departs from orthodoxy, admonishing the passenger as a fellow traveller would.

units.la: Neque enim existumare debebit, me adeo rudem esse in negotiis Theologicis, ut non ejus errores varios, multasque heterodoxias possem, si vellem, detegere; quas etiam penes me ex ipsius scriptis excerptas asservo. Ne hic videar minus honorifice de ejus sentire erudițione, id sciat & si sic illi visum, experimentum à me capiat, me illos etiam in Hebraicis, atque Rabbinicis progressus fecisse, ut licet velit esse ille Senior in theologia doctor, facili negotio ejus ignorantiam detegerem; quę tanta est, ut ne quidem recte scribat voces Hebraicas, in ejusdem Systemate latinis litteris occurrentes.
units.tr: For he should not think that I am so inexperienced in theological matters that I could not, if I wished, uncover his various errors and many heterodoxies, which I also keep in my possession, excerpted from his own writings. Lest I seem to speak less honourably of his learning here, let him know this as well, and let him, if it so pleases him, take this as a test: I have made such progress in Hebrew and rabbinic studies that, though he wishes to be that senior doctor of theology, I would with little effort expose his ignorance, which is so great that he cannot even write correctly the Hebrew words that occur in Latin letters in his own System.

units.la: Quod quam turpe sit Theologiæ Professori, ut ipsos sacræ scripturæ fontes, adire & consulere nequeat, nemo est qui ignorat.
units.tr: No one is unaware how shameful it is for a professor of theology not to be able to approach and consult the very sources of Holy Scripture.

units.la: Præterquam quod D. Maresius, pro mendacissimo & hac in parte sit habendus, ut qui & directe, & per consequentiam, me multis calumniis & contumeliis gravet. Quid enim hoc est, si non putidum mendacium, quod meorum librorum, qui plerique inscio Reverendo meo Parente à me editi, saltem ab eo nunquam visi, antequam essent editi, Parentem facit autorem, & cooperatorem? Quinimo contra veritatem, quod meum factum concernit, narrat formulam à se oblatam Synodicam fuisse.
units.tr: Besides, D. Maresius must be held to be a most lying man, also in this matter, since he burdens me, both directly and by inference, with many calumnies and insults. For what is this, if not a foul lie, that makes my Reverend Father the author and co-worker of my books, which I published for the most part without my Reverend Father's knowledge, and which at least he had never seen before they were published? Indeed, contrary to the truth, as regards my own act, he says that the formula was offered by himself to the synod.

units.la: Ipse enim meis oculis vidi formulæ 'contentum & summam D. Marefii manu descriptam, ejusque stylo & phrasibus consignatam fuisse, sicque quoad potiorem partem in belgicum per Deputatos translatam. Etiam grande mendacium est, reconciliationis formulam à Rev. Parente oblatā, minus gratam suisse DD. Deputatis Groninganis; cum Viri illi Reverendi, in consistorio nostro Ultrajectino, præsentibus nostris DD. Deputatis, conceptis verbis mihi gratias egerint maximas, „quod pacis & concordiæ studio, hunc labo,, rem sumpsissem, & formulam talem concepissem, (nam Parens id mihi negotii commiserat, quod aliis esset occupatus) quæ Parenti exhibita placeret, quæque finiendis litibus inserviret; quamque gratam & acceptam fore D. Maresio, nulli dubitabant, ut quam primum eandem per Maresium subsignatam essent remissuri. Provoco hic ad scientiam & conscientiam utrinque DD. Deputatorum, & coram Deo testor, rem ita sese habere, prout eam enarravi.
units.tr: For I myself saw with my own eyes that the contents and the summary of the formula were written out in the hand of D. Maresius, and drawn up in his style and phrasing, and so were, for the most part, translated into Dutch by the deputies. It is also a great lie that the formula of reconciliation offered by my Reverend Father was less welcome to the Groningen deputies. For those Reverend men, in our consistory at Utrecht, with our deputies present, thanked me most warmly in these words: "because I had taken on this labour out of zeal for peace and concord, and had drawn up such a formula (for my Father had entrusted this business to me, since he was occupied with other matters), which might be pleasing when presented to my Father, and which would serve to end the disputes; and they did not doubt that it would be most welcome and acceptable to D. Maresius, so that they would send it back as soon as possible, countersigned by Maresius." I here appeal to the knowledge and conscience of the deputies on both sides, and I call God to witness that the matter stands just as I have related it.

units.la: Verum quod præterire non possum, quia per consequentiam me tangit, ut Maresius inter calumniatores primum locum reperiret, eadem epistola, etiam dum pacem offert, suo pravo more, exemplo Judæ proditoris, & Joabi dolosi Rever. Parentem, præter jus & fas, mille contumeliis una phrasi onerat, asserendo p. 4. se hactenus in Parentem nihil non legitimè & jure scripsisse. Scilicet in principio caudati scorpii lingua lambunt, interim dum arcuata cauda venenum immittunt. Quin imo non erubuit, quod probitatem & pietatem omnem hac in parte exuerit, calumniatorum ille Senior, (præter alias diabolicas fabulas & calumnias, in Reverendum meum Parentem, ejusque Patrem honestissimum, cujus manes quiescere debuissent, emissas, & repetitas, licet antea à me refutatas) Epistolæ suæ inserere (id enim apprime ad conciliationem facicfaciebat,) quod Reverendus mihi Parens, eo tempore, quo turbabatur ecclesiæ Status Ultrajecti, videretur periclitari de famâ & fortunâ; [quodque à supremis suis dominis Stigmate fuerit notatus. O diabolicam calumniam? O sceleratam linguam, & pennam, in fidelem Christi servum, instinctu carnis, & dæmonis armatam? Venia mihi detur, quod hic mitius loqui nequeam. Si enim Maresio vitium Rev. meum Parentem, qui in illum ron scripserat hoc insignire epitheto, quod sit calumniatorum & Sycophantiarum archidiabolus suæ ling.abortiv. p.16. Quis equidem Mortalium, nisi invidus, & malevolus, pietatis hostis acerrimus, innocentiæ oppressor, & scelerum Maresianorum propugnator iniquus, id cuiquam vitio verterit, quod duro nodo durum adhibeat cuneum. Si enim homines male feriati maledicere fas esse judicant, saltem id tacite probant, nefas equidem non erit remaledicere. Et si diabolica spargere mendacia, scelera innocentibus impingere, (eo scil. abiere seculi mores) pro ludo & joco habetur; quid culpandum in illo, qui dum defensionis jure atque viribus nititur, opera mendacii diabolica appellat, adeoque operarium & inventorem talium diabolum.
units.tr: But I cannot pass over what touches me by implication: Maresius has taken first place among the slanderers. In the same letter, even while offering peace, he follows his usual perverse custom, like the traitor Judas and the crafty Joab, and loads our Reverend Father with a thousand insults in a single phrase, asserting on p. 4 that until now he has written against the Father nothing that was not lawful and by right. Of course, scorpions lick at the start while the curved tail injects the poison. Indeed, that elder of the slanderers did not blush to strip himself of all probity and piety in this matter. Besides other diabolical fables and calumnies put out and repeated against my Reverend Father and his most honourable father, whose ashes ought to have been left in peace, though I had refuted them earlier, he inserted into his letter (since this was especially conducive to reconciliation) the claim that my Reverend Father, at the time when the church of Utrecht was in turmoil, "seemed to be in danger of his reputation and fortune, and had been branded by his supreme lords." O diabolical calumny! O wicked tongue and pen, armed by the flesh and the devil against a faithful servant of Christ! Let me be pardoned for not being able to speak more mildly here. For if Maresius brands with this epithet my Reverend Father, who had written against him, calling him "the archdevil of slanderers and sycophants, abortive of his own tongue, p. 16," who among mortals, unless he were envious and malicious, a bitter enemy of piety, an oppressor of innocence and an unjust champion of Maresian crimes, would hold it against anyone that he applies a hard wedge to a hard knot? For if men judge it lawful to curse when they are roughly handled, they at least tacitly approve, so it will surely not be unlawful to curse back. And if spreading diabolical lies and fastening crimes on the innocent (to such a pass have the morals of this age come) is treated as sport and jest, what is to be blamed in him who, relying on the right and the strength of defence, calls such works of lying diabolical, and so calls the devil their worker and inventor?

units.la: An igitur censet ille Satanas(ut ad rem redeam) incusator fratrum, libertatis ecclesiæ proditor, homo mundanus, praxeos pietatis ofsor,famam Viro honestissimo,idque ad lubi-tum tum virorum inimicorum adimi? Aut Christo & Apostolorum existimationi quicquam fuisse derogatum, quod illis populi primores minarentur, classicum ad hoc canentibus Pharisæis? An jura ignorat, quæ statuunt, famam nonnisi per judicis sententiam, per leges, aut certum genus pœnæ adimi? An ignorat mores totius fere Belgii, quibus ne quidem, discedere jussi, minimâ infamiæ macula, afficiuntur? Nisi & apostoli è Synagoga ejecti, nisi Salvator per Gadarenos exire jussus, perpetua infamiæ maculâ laborarit. Verum quid de stigmate hic narrat sycophanta? Venerandum illum Senem, & quidem innocentissimum, si causæ spectes justitiam, inaudit um, & indefensum stigmate notare, idlequidem esset summæ impietatis & iniquitatis: quod adscribere velle (id enim non egerat defensor ecclesiæ Trajectinæ) Provinciarum & urbium rectoribus, esset non tantum grande dedecus, sed & iniquitas maxima. Quod si unquam tale quid evenisset, non defuisset innoxiis justa defensio, non tantum adversus Maresium malarum causarum Tertullum, sed etiam adversus omnes, qui in bonos & fideles Dei servos sine modo, sine causâ grassantur. Majori ego jure de ipso Maresio dixero, quod de fama & fortunis, & vita (si jure cum ipso fuisset actum) ipsius actum fuisset; non propter quæsitas incusandi occasiones, quæsitos prætextus, verum propter crimen infamans, publicum, & capitale, cum Principis Leodiensis decretum publice affixum, falsificasset; sicque de novo imprimi curaslet, per typothetem ibidem. Qui miser homo, illo auctore & instigatore, propter incæptum facinus & consummatum punitus est, licet mitius. Ille autem maculæ exemptus propter honorem ordinis & ministerii; licet duplici pœna dignus. Et quia sceleris fuit auctor, & quia aliis laudator pessimi extitit propositi. Hæc vera sunt, neque à me probanda, cum ipse se ipsum ubique prodat, nec facinus unquam fuerit inficiatus, verum libellum (la Chandelle mise fuble boisseau.) potissimum in sui purgationem emiserit; ubi utramque facit paginam, illa defensio palliativa, qua facinus mitigare studet.
units.tr: Does that Satan, then (to return to the matter), the accuser of the brethren, the traitor to the liberty of the church, the worldly man, the enemy of the practice of piety, think that he may strip a most honourable man of his reputation, and that at the whim of hostile men? Or was anything taken from the standing of Christ and the apostles because the chief men of the people threatened them, the Pharisees sounding the trumpet for this? Does he not know the laws, which establish that reputation can be taken away only by a judge's sentence, by law, or by a certain kind of penalty? Does he not know the customs of almost all Belgium, by which even those ordered to leave are not stained with the least blot of infamy? Otherwise the apostles, cast out of the synagogue, and the Saviour, ordered out by the Gadarenes, would have laboured under a perpetual stain of infamy. But what does this sycophant say here about branding? To brand that venerable old man, and indeed a most innocent one, unheard and undefended, would be, if you look at the justice of the case, the height of impiety and injustice. To wish to ascribe this (for the defender of the church of Utrecht had not done it) to the rulers of provinces and cities would be not only great disgrace but the greatest injustice. If anything of the kind had ever happened, the innocent would not have lacked just defence, not only against Maresius, the Tertullus of bad causes, but also against all who rage without measure or cause against the good and faithful servants of God. I could say with greater right of Maresius himself that his reputation, fortune and life would have been dealt with, had the case been brought against him in law. This is not on account of sought occasions for accusing or sought pretexts, but on account of his infamous, public and capital crime: he forged the decree of the Prince of Liège, publicly posted, and had it reprinted there through a printer. That wretched man, at whose instigation and urging the thing was done, was punished for the crime undertaken and completed, though more mildly. But he himself was freed from the stain because of the honour of his order and ministry, though he deserved a double penalty, both because he was the author of the crime and because he praised its most wicked purpose. These things are true and need no proof from me, since he betrays himself everywhere. He never denied the deed, but published a little book, la Chandelle mise sous le boisseau, chiefly for his own purgation, in which both pages make that palliating defence by which he tries to soften the deed.

units.la: Ut nullæ hic aliæ judicis superessent partes, nisi in condemnando. Quia igitur ipse nocentissimus est, & lacera illius famæ carina, (sic alibi de Parente loquitur) id conatur, ut in consortium trahat venerandum meum [Parentem, nullius delicti, multo minus infamantis sibi conscium. Imitatus in eo fures & raptores, qui dum comites periculi quærunt, in levamen pœnæ, etiam non rogati, socios quandoq; per mendacium nominant, qui extra noxam constituti. Verum nolim ipsum aliis onerare, ne videat occasionem quæsisse & non in eam incidisse illum redarguendi. guendi. Dabitur quondam otium illius mores, & doctrinam exagitandi, licet sub potentiorum quorundam clypeo lateat, dum gnatonem & parasitum agit, atque ad instar Zedekiæ apud Achabos Michæ malum & invidiam conciliat,
units.tr: So no other part of the judge would remain except to condemn. Since he himself is most guilty, and a shattered hulk of reputation (as he says elsewhere of the Father), he tries to draw my venerable Father into partnership, though the Father is conscious of no offence, much less of any infamy. In this he imitates thieves and robbers who, seeking companions in their danger and hoping to lighten their punishment, sometimes name by lie, even unasked, those who stand outside the guilt. But I would not wish to burden him with others, lest he see that I had sought an occasion to refute him and had not fallen into one. There will someday be leisure to expose his morals and teaching, although he hides under the shield of certain more powerful men while he plays the flatterer and the parasite, and, like Zedekiah among the Ahabs, wins for himself the evil and the ill will that belonged to Micaiah.

units.la: 14. Cæterum quo casu civitates aut universitates jus condendi statuta consequuntur, non ea legitime condunt, nisi convocatis omnibus municipibus, seu civibus universitatis; iisque omnibus consentientibus, aut saltem parte majori. Et si quidem agatur de re majoris momenti, duabus tertiis præsentibus. Omnium enim censetur voluntas moralis, quæ est plerorumque in universitate. Cum ea lege in unum convenerint, ut quod pars potior statuerit, id, quasi omnium nomine statutum, robur sit habiturum. Arg. init. instit. de Attil. Tutor. & §. 1. verb. quod si non fuerit. Instit. de Satisd. Tutor. vel Curat. l. 106. §. 1. D. de Reg. jur. l. de unoquoque D. de Re Judic. l. 7. §. sin. & l. 8. D. de Pact. l. 32. D. de leg. l. 3. & 4. D. quod cujusque univ. nomin. l. 19. Ad Munic. l. 2, & 3. D. de Decret. ab Ordin. Faciend. l. 2. Cod. de Decur. Neque obstat l. 8. D. de Pact. l. 19. Cod. de Decur. Ubi & minor suffragantium pars vincit majorem. Si enim a minori creditorum, vel civium numero aliquid adversus majorem partem opponatur, & quidem secundum æquitatem & rationem, tum ut creditorum, sic minor & sanior pars civium prævalebit majori, si modo ostendatur majorem partem non bona ratione motam fuisse. Atque hic est sensus. ll. objectarum. Argum. l. 1. §. sed neque. Cod. de vet. Jur. Enucl. vid. Perez. de Decret. Decur. super immun. n. 4.
units.tr: 14. Moreover, in whatever case cities or corporations acquire the right to enact statutes, they do not enact them lawfully unless all the citizens or members of the corporation have been convoked, and all consent, or at least the greater part. And if the matter is of greater moment, two-thirds must be present. For the moral will of all is regarded as that of the majority in a corporation, since they have come together under the agreement that what the stronger part decides shall have force as if decided in the name of all. Arg. init. instit. de Attil. Tutor. & §. 1. verb. quod si non fuerit. Instit. de Satisd. Tutor. vel Curat. l. 106. §. 1. D. de Reg. jur. l. de unoquoque D. de Re Judic. l. 7. §. sin. & l. 8. D. de Pact. l. 32. D. de leg. l. 3. & 4. D. quod cujusque univ. nomin. l. 19. Ad Munic. l. 2, & 3. D. de Decret. ab Ordin. Faciend. l. 2. Cod. de Decur. Nor is there an obstacle in l. 8. D. de Pact. l. 19. Cod. de Decur., where the smaller part of those voting prevails over the greater. For if something is opposed by a smaller number of creditors or citizens against the greater part, and indeed according to equity and reason, then, as with creditors, so the smaller and sounder part of the citizens will prevail over the greater, provided it is shown that the greater part was not moved by good reason. And this is the sense. ll. objectarum. Argum. l. 1. §. sed neque. Cod. de vet. Jur. Enucl. vid. Perez. de Decret. Decur. super immun. n. 4.

units.la: 15. Quid si omnes quidem fuerint citati, non tamen omnes adfuerint, imo ne quidem duæ partes decurionum aut civium in re leviori fuerint præsentes: An quod ab illis statutum, ratum erit, quasi omnium nomine gestum esset? Id dicendum videtur. Inspicitur enim, regulariter, quod à majori parte eorum qui præsentes fuerunt, actum est. Ut cæteri, qui venire recusant, pro contumacibus, adeoque pro ficte consentientibus sint habendi. l. 160. §. 1. D. de Reg. jur. l. penult. & l. ult. Cod. de legat. Argum. l. 11. §. 4. D. de Interrogat. in jur. fac. Clarus. §. sin. quæst. 32. Hieron. Cagnol. & Faber in Comment. ad d. l. 160.
units.tr: 15. What if all indeed were summoned, but not all were present, and not even two-thirds of the decurions or citizens were present in a matter of lesser importance? Is what has been decided by them to be ratified, as if done in the name of all? That seems to be the right view. For, as a rule, what was done by the greater part of those who were present is what is looked at, so that the others who refuse to come are to be held as contumacious, and so as feigning consent. l. 160. §. 1. D. de Reg. jur. l. penult. & l. ult. Cod. de legat. Argum. l. 11. §. 4. D. de Interrogat. in jur. fac. Clarus. §. sin. quæst. 32. Hieron. Cagnol. & Faber in Comment. ad d. l. 160.

units.la: 16. Si tamen lex vel statutum caveat, omnium & singulorum consensum adhibendum esse, requiritur ut ab omnibus, saltem ab iis qui præsentes sunt consensus adhibeatur. Nec poterunt pluralitate suffragiorum prævalere, ex vi talis statuti. Idem quod dicendum, si interfit singulorum, qui sunt de municipio. Cum quod omnes tangit, ab omnibus debeat approbari. l. 5. D. de de-cret.
units.tr: 16. If, however, a law or statute provides that the consent of all and each must be obtained, it is required that consent be obtained from all, or at least from those who are present. Nor can they prevail by a majority of votes by virtue of such a statute. The same must be said if the matter concerns each individual who belongs to the municipality. What touches all must be approved by all. l. 5. D. de de-cret.

units.la: cret. ab ordin. faciend. c. quod omnes. de Reg. jur. in 6. l. 11. D. de Servit. Prædior. Rusticor. l. 28. D. Commun. Dividund. Gotefred. ad l. 19. D. Ad Municipal. Perez. Cod. de Decurion. n. 26.
units.tr: Decretals, "On the ordering of things to be done by the ordinary," ch. Quod omnes; "On rules of law," in the Sixth Book; Digest 11, "On rural servitudes"; Digest 28, "On the division of common property"; Gothofredus on Digest 19, "On the municipal law"; Perez on Code, "On decurions," n. 26.

units.la: 17. Quod si cives jus statuta condendi, vel in Consules civitatis contulerint, sive tacitè, patiendo id fieri, sive expressè, id declarando: neque singulorum amplius citatione, neque ullorum opus erit præsentia, ad valorem statutorum. Quod enim quis per alium facit, in quem tanquam Procuratorem, aut actorem consenserit, id per se facere videtur. Ut hoc casu nihil interfit, an ipsi cives statuta condant, an illi, quibus id negotii commiserunt. §. Senatusconsultum. Instit. de jur. natur. gent. & civil. l. 2, §. deinde quia difficile. D. de Origin. jur. l. 6. §. 1. D. quod cujusque Universf. nomin. l. 18. D. Mandat. c. qui per alium de Reg. jur. in 6. l. 180. D. eod. l. 56. l. 64. D. de Solut.
units.tr: 17. But if the citizens have conferred the power of enacting statutes upon the consuls of the city, either tacitly, by allowing it to be done, or expressly, by declaring it, then neither the summoning of each individual nor the presence of any one of them is needed for the validity of the statutes. For what someone does through another, to whom he has consented as his procurator or agent, he seems to do himself. So in this case it makes no difference whether the citizens themselves enact the statutes or those to whom they have entrusted the business. §. Senatusconsultum. Instit. de jur. natur. gent. & civil. l. 2, §. deinde quia difficile. D. de Origin. jur. l. 6. §. 1. D. quod cujusque Universf. nomin. l. 18. D. Mandat. c. qui per alium de Reg. jur. in 6. l. 180. D. eod. l. 56. l. 64. D. de Solut.

units.la: 18. Cæterum, an qui jus habent condendi statuta, absque superioris consensu id possint, satis est controversum? Distinctione rem expediendam esse censeo. Aut enim qui statuta condunt, sunt liberi Principes, & domini; liberæque civitates, quæ regalia habent; & condere sibi quascumque leges proprio jure possunt. Aut sunt civitates municipales & subditæ alicui populo, nec habent jus statuta condendi sine consensu supremi, vel generali, vel speciali. Idque tam procedit, si ea statuta juri communi conveniant, quam si eidem adversentur. Illo casu ea condunt, ex generali legis concessione. Hoc casu, nonnisi speciali consensu accedente: l. omnes populi. D. de just. & jur. Quae Lex tantum loquitur de populo libero. Ut hic omnes fere DD. errent, qui aliter sentiunt. l. 9. D. Ad l. Rhod. l. Antiochensium. D. de Privil. credit. l. 4. D. de decret. ab ordin. faciend. l. 3. §. 5. D. de Sepulchr. viol. Authent. Navigia. Cod. de Eurt. Baro ad l. 3. D. quod cujusq. universit. nomin. Zasius ad l. de quib. num. 15. & 16. D. de leg. Jacobus Thoming. tom. 1. Consil. 24. quaest. 5 vid. & Collectorem consuet. Hungar. & Transylv. part. 3. tit. 2.
units.tr: 18. Moreover, is it quite disputed whether those who have the power of enacting statutes may do so without the consent of a superior? I think the matter should be settled by a distinction. For either those who enact the statutes are free princes and lords, and free cities which hold regalia, and they can by their own right make whatever laws they like for themselves. Or they are municipal cities subject to some people, and they have no power of enacting statutes without the consent of a superior, either general or special. This holds whether the statutes agree with the common law or oppose it. In the former case they enact them by the general grant of the law; in the latter case only when special consent is added. l. omnes populi. D. de just. & jur. Quae Lex tantum loquitur de populo libero. Hence almost all the jurists who think otherwise are wrong. l. 9. D. Ad l. Rhod. l. Antiochensium. D. de Privil. credit. l. 4. D. de decret. ab ordin. faciend. l. 3. §. 5. D. de Sepulchr. viol. Authent. Navigia. Cod. de Eurt. Baro ad l. 3. D. quod cujusq. universit. nomin. Zasius ad l. de quib. num. 15. & 16. D. de leg. Jacobus Thoming. tom. 1. Consil. 24. quaest. 5 see also Collectorem consuet. Hungar. & Transylv. part. 3. tit. 2.

units.la: Nec obstat, quod statutis nonnullis aliquid contra jus civile, dicatur inductum: ubi tamen nulla mentio specialis concessionis. Id enim intelligendum est, vel in quantum salvâ suâ lege municipes in ditionem populi Romani pervenerunt, vel in quantum ea statuta civitatum Princeps approbavit. l. 3. §. plane. D. quod vi aut clam. l. lucius. in sin. D. Ad Munic. l. semper. §. legem. D. de jur. immun d. l. 9.
units.tr: Nor is it an obstacle that some statutes are said to introduce something contrary to the civil law, where there is no special mention of a concession. For that must be understood either insofar as the municipes came under the rule of the Roman people with their own law preserved, or insofar as the Prince approved those statutes of the cities. l. 3. §. plane. D. quod vi aut clam. l. lucius. in sin. D. Ad Munic. l. semper. §. legem. D. de jur. immun d. l. 9.

units.la: 19. Verum amplius inquiritur, an sufficiat consensus antecedens, an praeter illum ad statutorum vim & robur opus sit consensu subsequenti, id est superioris confirmatione? Respondeo, eo ipso, quo generalis consensus sus antecessit, in iis, quæ juri publico non adversantur, nulla opus est confirmatione. Quæ enim semel placuerunt, amplius, nisi gravi de causâ, displicere non possunt. Arg. l. 2. ff. de constit. Princ. De moribus tamen adhiberi solere adeoq; prudenter desiderari, statutorum confirmationem & approbationem, docent Pragmatici. Bocer. Class. 1. disp. 3. num. 41. de form. & modo constit. jur. ibidemque Fason. Coler. Coras. cituti. Merula Prax. Civil. lib. 1. tit. 4. cap. 5. num. 1. 2. Petrus Heigius quæst. 23. Christin. Prælud. ad Consuet. Mechl. num. 5. & in Epilogo ad dd. ll. num. 11. vide tamen hic Mevium destinguentem ad jus Lubecense. Prælim. quæst. 2. num. 55. & seq.
units.tr: 19. But it is further asked whether prior consent suffices, or whether, besides that, subsequent consent, that is, confirmation by the superior, is needed for the force and validity of statutes. I answer: by the very fact that general consent came first, in those matters which do not oppose public law, no confirmation is needed. For what has once pleased cannot further displease, unless for a serious reason. l. 2. ff. de constit. Princ. The Pragmatici teach that by custom the confirmation and approval of statutes is usually sought, and so prudently desired. Bocer. Class. 1. disp. 3. num. 41. de form. & modo constit. jur. and there Fason. Coler. Coras. cituti. Merula Prax. Civil. lib. 1. tit. 4. cap. 5. num. 1. 2. Petrus Heigius quæst. 23. Christin. Prælud. ad Consuet. Mechl. num. 5. & in Epilogo ad dd. ll. num. 11. but see here Mevium distinguishing for the law of Lübeck. Prælim. quæst. 2. num. 55. & seq.

units.la: SECTIO SEPTIMA.
units.tr: SECTION SEVEN.

units.la: CAPUT PRIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER ONE.

units.la: 1. Necessaria est statutorum interpreta-tio.
units.tr: 1. The interpretation of statutes is necessary.

units.la: 2. Quotuplex sit interpretandi ratio?
units.tr: 2. How many kinds of interpretation are there?

units.la: 3. Utrum etiam Municipiis interpretari liceat statuta?
units.tr: 3. May municipalities also interpret their statutes?

units.la: 4. Quotuplex sit interpretationis modus?
units.tr: 4. How many modes of interpretation are there?

units.la: 5. Quæ sit restrictiva statuti interpreta-tio? 6. Quæ extensiva?
units.tr: 5. What is restrictive interpretation of a statute? 6. What is extensive interpretation?

units.la: 7. Quæ sit statuti actiua interpretatio?
units.tr: 7. What is active interpretation of a statute?

units.la: 8. Quæ passiva?
units.tr: 8. What is passive interpretation?

units.la: 9. Quæ declarativa, seu significativa?
units.tr: 9. What is declarative, or explanatory, interpretation?

units.la: 10. Quæ correctiva seu emendativa?
units.tr: 10. What is corrective, or amendatory, interpretation?

units.la: 11. An si statuentes dictènt litteraliter accipiendum esse statutum, etiamnum admittat interpretationem?
units.tr: 11. If the framers direct that the statute be taken literally, does it still admit of interpretation?

units.la: QUandoquidem pari passu ambulant, statutorum constitutio, & eorundem interpretetatio; nec minor est auctoritas interpretantis, quam statuentis: ea propter postquam de efficiente causa statutorum actum est, de eorundem agendum erit interpretatione. Arg. l. ult. Cod. de legibus.
units.tr: Since the making of statutes and their interpretation go hand in hand, and the authority of the interpreter is no less than that of the framer, therefore, after treating of the efficient cause of statutes, I shall now treat of their interpretation. Arg. l. ult. Cod. de legibus.

units.la: Eam ubique adhibendam esse, tum dictat necessitas, tum sapientum suadet auctoritas. l. 2. §. his legibus. D. Origin. jur. Quo nomine duo evitanda extrema. Et illa Franciscì opinio, qui animum agens, fratribus monachis interdixisse fertur, ne quis in traditis à se regulis aut quæreret aut reciperet aliam interpretationem c. exiit. §. caeterum. de verbor. signif. in 6. Alberic. de Rosat. ad l. quamvis D. in jus vocand. n. 6.
units.tr: That interpretation must be applied everywhere is required both by necessity and recommended by the authority of the wise. l. 2. §. his legibus. D. Origin. jur. On this head two extremes must be avoided: first, the opinion of Francis, who, as he is said to have done in his own mind, forbade the brothers and monks to seek or accept any other interpretation of the rules laid down by him. c. exiit. §. caeterum. de verbor. signif. in 6. Alberic. de Rosat. ad l. quamvis D. in jus vocand. n. 6.

units.la: Et illa quorundam captiosa & inepta interpretatio, quæ præter sophisticam, & Sycophanticam redolet nihil. Quæque non tam juris est interpretatio, quam ejusdem correctio, censura, eversio. Quam hodierno tempore nonnulli Aristarchi male morati, qui juri explicando dati sunt, nimium licentiose adhibere solent; & loco utilium scriptorum, praeter cerebrinos mores, & in utopia Mori, vel in idea Platonis, admissos, proferunt nihil. Parum memores prohibuisse imperatorem ne quispiam in leges a se editas sic scribat, aut evulget commentarios. l. 1. §. nostra autem Cod. de vet. jure Enucl.
units.tr: Second, that captious and silly interpretation of certain people, which smells of nothing but sophistry and sycophancy, and which is not so much an interpretation of law as its correction, censure, and overthrow. Some ill-mannered Aristarchuses, appointed to explain the law, are accustomed in our own day to use this far too licentiously; and instead of useful writings they produce nothing but brainsick fancies, admitted in the Utopia of More or the Idea of Plato. They forget too much that the emperor forbade anyone to write or publish commentaries on the laws he had enacted. l. 1. §. nostra autem Cod. de vet. jure Enucl.

units.la: Ut itaque in statutorum interpretatione ordine progrediar, & evitem quod in aliis improbandum, atque perstringendum censui, in quasdam inquiram difficultates. 1. Cui incumbat statutorum vera interpretatio? 2. Quomodo interpretatio adhibenda?
units.tr: So that I may proceed in order in the interpretation of statutes, and avoid what I have judged deserving of rebuke and censure in others, I shall inquire into certain difficulties: 1. To whom does the true interpretation of statutes belong? 2. How is interpretation to be applied?

units.la: 2. Quod primum spectat quaesitum, idque ratione personarum, quibus id juris est concessum; ibi multiplex interpretandi ratio consideranda. Vel enim est interpretandi ratio decisoria, vel scholastica, vel forensis. Illa est, quando auctor statuti illud interpretatur, sic ut ejus interpretatio tam sit obligatoria, atque ipsum statutum, adeoque sit juris decisoria. Qualis etiam interpretatio consuetudini tributa, ut quae certissima & optima legum interpres. l. si de interpretatione 37. D. de legibus.
units.tr: 2. As to the first question, which concerns the persons to whom this right has been granted, several kinds of interpretation must be considered. Interpretation is either decisive, scholastic, or forensic. The first is when the author of a statute interprets it himself, so that his interpretation is as binding as the statute itself and so has the force of law. Such interpretation is attributed to custom, as being the most certain and best interpreter of laws. l. si de interpretatione 37. D. de legibus.

units.la: 3. Ubi quaesitum, utrum Populi aut Principis, solius sit interpretari statuta, utrum id etiam concessum ip sis Municipiis? Respondeo, licet solius sit populi, aut Principis, prout variat reipublicæ forma, leges interpretari, quia tamen statuta non sunt leges; & Municipiis privilegium statuta condendi est concessum, quod de necessitate comitari oportet jus interpretandi. Arg. l.
units.tr: 3. Where it is asked whether the interpretation of statutes belongs solely to the people or the prince, or whether this right is also granted to the municipalities themselves: I answer that, although the power to interpret laws belongs solely to the people or the prince, according as the form of the commonwealth varies, yet, since statutes are not laws, and the privilege of enacting statutes has been granted to the municipalities, the right of interpretation must of necessity accompany it. Arg. l.

units.la: 2. D. jurisd. l. 2. §. his legibus. D. orig. jur. l. ult. Cod. leg. Etiam id ipsum Municipiis esse concessum, arg. dictarum legum, negari non potest. disp. Canones secundum Panormit. in cap. ex parte. de verbor. signif. Bartol. in l. omnes Populi. D. de jurisd. & jure. Paul. Winmeck. Theolog. jurisconf. part. 2. c. 5. vid. Merul. Prax. civil. libr. tit. 4. cap. 1 art. 15. Vinn. quaestion. Select. libr. 1. cap. 2.
units.tr: 2. D. jurisd. l. 2. §. his legibus. D. orig. jur. l. ult. Cod. leg. That this very power has also been granted to municipalities cannot be denied, by the argument of the laws just cited. Disp. Canons, according to Panormitanus in cap. ex parte, de verbor. signif.; Bartolus in l. omnes populi, D. de jurisd. & jure; Paul Winmeck, Theolog. jurisconf. part 2, c. 5; see Merula, Prax. civil. lib. 1, tit. 4, cap. 1, art. 15; Vinnius, Quaestion. select. lib. 1, cap. 2.

units.la: Interpretatio Scholastica est, quando juris anrecessor in academiâ verba & sensum statutorum, ex legum collatione explicat, subjectis forte ejusdem statuti rationibus. Qualis ipsi imperatoriâ concessa auctoritate. tot tit. Cod. de Profess. Qui in Urbe Constantin. libr. 10. Forensis interpretatio duplex est, vel quando jurisconsultus, tanquam vir bonus & æquus, cui de jure respondendi à Principe facultas est concessa, æquum ab iniquo secernit, justum ab injusto separat; atque ita suo modo statutum casui sibi oblato applicat, Arg. l. 1. §. 1. D. justit. & jure. l. 2. §. 5. D. origin. jur. Vel quando judex, si de statuto dubitetur, illud ex officio ad casus sus similes extendit. l. 10, l. 12. l. 13. D. de legibus. Nulla tamen harum interpretationum futura decifpria, id est, nulla earundem erit virium cum ipso statuto, quid interpretandi licentia jurisconsultis, aut judicibus tribuenda, quæ olim. Befold. in oicon. jur. ad l. 7. 8. tit. 1. libr. 1. Dig. n. 9. in sin. post Bufium 1. Subtil. 3.
units.tr: Scholastic interpretation is when the professor of law in the university explains the words and sense of statutes by comparing the laws, perhaps with the reasons of the same statute set out. Such was the interpretation granted to the professors by the emperor's own authority. tot tit. Cod. de Profess. who in the city of Constantinople, libr. 10. Forensic interpretation is of two kinds: either when a jurisconsult, as a good and fair man to whom the prince has granted the right of giving legal opinions, separates the fair from the unfair and the just from the unjust, and so applies the statute in his own way to a case put before him, Arg. l. 1. §. 1. D. justit. & jure. l. 2. §. 5. D. origin. jur. or when a judge, if a statute is doubtful, extends it by his office to cases like it. l. 10, l. 12, l. 13. D. de legibus. None of these interpretations, however, will be decisive, that is, none will have force equal to the statute itself, since the licence to interpret is to be granted to jurisconsults or judges in the same way as formerly. Befold. in oicon. jur. ad l. 7. 8. tit. 1. libr. 1. Dig. n. 9. in sin. post Bufium 1. Subtil. 3.

units.la: 4. Verum ad interpretandi modum memet conferam, ubi de tribus agendum. 1. De variis interpretationum modis. 2. De iis, quæ in ipsa interpretatione observanda, & ad quæ attendendum, ut intellectus statuti appareat. 3. De interpretatione quorundam statutorum in specie.
units.tr: 4. I now turn to the mode of interpretation, where three things must be treated: 1. the various modes of interpretation; 2. the things to be observed in the interpretation itself and to which attention must be paid, so that the sense of the statute may appear; 3. the interpretation of certain statutes in particular.

units.la: 1. Interpretationis modus in genere duplex, vel naturalis vel civilis. Ille est, quando vel ratio superior, vincit inferiorem; ut si boni publici causâ aliquid statuatur, contra privatorum commodum, statuto comprehensum. Vel quando regulam juris naturæ in thesi consideratam moderamur secundum hypothesin; ut si dicatur, non occides, & in hypothesi, occides tamen, modo aliter periculum nequeas evadere. Modus interpretandi civilis est, quando statutum aut legem incertam, ex probabilibus circumstantiis, declaramus. vid. Althus. dicajol. libr. 1. c. 16. 17. Atque talis interpretandi modus, vel potius talis ex modo interpretatio potissimum, vel Restrictiva, vel Extensiva. vid. Albe.
units.tr: 1. The mode of interpretation in general is twofold, either natural or civil. The natural mode is when a higher reason overcomes a lower one, as when something is enacted for the sake of the public good, against the advantage of private persons, and this is included in the statute. Or when we qualify a rule of natural law, considered in the abstract, according to a hypothesis: for instance, if it is said, thou shalt not kill, and in the hypothetical case, yet kill, provided that you cannot otherwise escape danger. The civil mode of interpretation is when we declare a statute or an uncertain law from probable circumstances. See Althus. dicajol. libr. 1. c. 16. 17. And this mode of interpretation, or rather the interpretation arising from this mode, is chiefly either restrictive or extensive. See Albe.

units.la: Albericum de Rosate. ad l. qui duos. n. 3. D. leg. 3. sol. 70. D. inforciati. Hillig. ad Donell.
units.tr: Albericus de Rosate, ad l. qui duos. n. 3. D. leg. 3. sol. 70. D. inforciati. Hillig. ad Donell.

units.la: 1. Comm. 13. 14. ibique alii.
units.tr: 1. Comm. 13. 14. and the others there.

units.la: 5. Illa, quando generalis statuti oratio & sententia, ad certas tantum species sub eadem oratione generali contentas reducitur.
units.tr: 5. Restrictive interpretation is when the general wording and meaning of a statute is reduced to certain species only, contained under that same general wording.

units.la: Quod accidit, cum ratio statuti, & mens statuentis in quibusdam cessat casubus, qui tamen sub genereli oratione comprehendebantur. Tumque necessum est dictum limitari secundum ejusdem rationem, quod oratione potentior sit mens dicentis. Arg. l. 50. §. 1. D. leg. 1. l. 24. D. de Rebus dubiis. l. 6. §. 2. D. jur. Patronat. Claud. Cantiuncul. loc. legal. à sent. contrascriptum.
units.tr: This happens when the reason of the statute and the intention of the framer cease in certain cases which were nevertheless included under the general wording. Then the saying must necessarily be limited according to the same reason, because the intention of the speaker is more powerful than the wording. Arg. l. 50. §. 1. D. leg. 1. l. 24. D. de Rebus dubiis. l. 6. §. 2. D. jur. Patronat. Claud. Cantiuncul. loc. legal. à sent. contrascriptum.

units.la: Poterit autem illa ratio ad quam attenditur vel esse expressa in ipso statuto; vel in alio statuto tradita; vel per interpretem ex rerum conditione collecta; vel anceps & dubia.
units.tr: The reason to which we attend may be either expressed in the statute itself, or set out in another statute, or gathered by the interpreter from the condition of things, or uncertain and doubtful.

units.la: Si primum: tum ubicunque locum habebit ratio, etiam locus erit statuto. Argum. l. 12. in init. & §. 1. D. qui & à quibus manum. Ut deficiente ratione in aliquo casu, etiam deficiat statutum, à quo impune judex recedet. Arg. l. non dubium. Cod. de legibus & ibi gloss. in verb. amplexus. Dynus circa Reg. sin. de Reg. jur. in 6.
units.tr: If the first: then wherever the reason applies, the statute will also apply. Argum. l. 12. in init. & §. 1. D. qui & à quibus manum. So that if the reason fails in some case, the statute too fails, and the judge may depart from it without penalty. Arg. l. non dubium. Cod. de legibus and the gloss there on the word amplexus. Dynus on Reg. sin. de Reg. jur. in 6.

units.la: Si secundum; idem, quod in casu primo, statuendum erit. Arg. l. 26. l. 27. l. 28. D. de legibus.
units.tr: If the second: the same must be decided as in the first case. Arg. l. 26, l. 27, l. 28. D. de legibus.

units.la: Si tertium; nec diversum quid à casu primo mo & secundo statuendum, modo adeo certa sit interpretatio, ut certior reddi nequeat. Arg. l. 11. l. 12, l. 13. D. de legibus. & Arg. l. milites. 9. D. de Re Milit. l. nominatim. D. lib. & Posthum. hared. instit.
units.tr: If the third: nothing different from the first and second case is to be decided, provided the interpretation is so certain that it cannot be made more certain. Arg. l. 11, l. 12, l. 13. D. de legibus. and Arg. l. milites. 9. D. de Re Milit. l. nominatim. D. lib. & Posthum. hared. instit.

units.la: Si quartum; in dubio statuti verba non erunt aliquâ restringenda interpretatione. Quia verba generalia, generaliter sunt accipienda. Et ubi statutum non distinguit, aut restringit, nostrum non est distinguere aut restringere. Bald. in l. non dubium. Cod. de leg. & alii apud Alderan. Mascard de Statutor. interpret. conclus. 5. n. 1. 2. cum variis limitationibus. Lagus Method. jur. p. 1 c. 9. per totum. vid. Sanson, ad Turon. tit. 1. § 5. gloss. 4. p. 9, 10. 11. 12.
units.tr: If in the fourth case, in doubt the words of a statute are not to be restricted by any narrowing interpretation, for general words are to be taken generally. And where the statute does not distinguish or restrict, it is not for us to distinguish or restrict. Bald. in l. non dubium. Cod. de leg. & alii apud Alderan. Mascard de Statutor. interpret. conclus. 5. n. 1. 2. cum variis limitationibus. Lagus Method. jur. p. 1 c. 9. per totum. vid. Sanson, ad Turon. tit. 1. § 5. gloss. 4. p. 9, 10. 11. 12.

units.la: 6. Interpretatio statuti extensiva est, quando quidem verba statuti sunt specialia, sic ut iis non omnia comprehendantur, quæ comprehendi potuissent, verum tamen subjecta ratio est generalis, ut ad alios casus, ad alias personas verbis non comprehensas, extendi non incommode possit. Neque enim tam verba, quam sensum, quam rationem nos intueri oportet. Argum. tit. instit. de legit. Patron. tutel. § 1. in sin. instit. qui sui vel alien. jur. l. 17. l. 29. l. 30. D. de legibus. Ut enim lege omnes casus exprimi non posse certum est, ut ideo ex ratione legis, ad similia progredi liceat; ita etiam in statuto, si ratio sit manifesta, extensionem ad similia admittemus. Arg. l. 10. 11. 12. 13. 27. D. de legibus.
units.tr: 6. An extensive interpretation of a statute occurs when the words of the statute are specific, so that not everything that could have been included is comprehended by them, but the underlying reason is general, so that it can fairly be extended to other cases and other persons not covered by the words. For we ought to regard not so much the words as the sense and the reason. Argum. tit. instit. de legit. Patron. tutel. § 1. in sin. instit. qui sui vel alien. jur. l. 17. l. 29. l. 30. D. de legibus. For just as it is certain that not every case can be expressed in a law, so that it is permissible to proceed from the reason of the law to similar cases, so too in a statute, if the reason is manifest, we shall admit extension to similar cases. Arg. l. 10. 11. 12. 13. 27. D. de legibus.

units.la: Quâ etiam ratione ab uno correlativorum ad aliud facienda est extensio. Arg. l. sin. D. Accept. l. sin. Cod. de Cupress. ex luco Daphnensi. & l. sin. Cod. in dist. induit. Gabriel. comm. opin. libr. 6. de leg. & Constit. concl. 3. cum limit. & etiam tit. de Statutis. Anton. de Rosellis de successt. ab intestato. n. 156. sol. 244. vol. 8. tractat. Stephanus Coste tract. de ludo. §. 2. n. 17. vol. 1. tract.
units.tr: By this same reasoning, an extension must be made from one of two correlatives to the other. Argument from l. sin. D. Accept., l. sin. Cod. de Cupress. ex luco Daphnensi, and l. sin. Cod. in dist. induit.; Gabriel, comm. opin. libr. 6, de leg., and Constit. concl. 3, with the limitation. And also tit. de Statutis. Anton. de Rosellis, de successt. ab intestato, n. 156, sol. 244, vol. 8, tractat.; Stephanus Coste, tract. de ludo, §. 2, n. 17, vol. 1, tract.

units.la: 7. Ut tamen non indistincte id admittat. Bartol. in l. omnes populi. D. de justiti & jure. q. ult. Secundum quem alia est statuti extensio activa, alia passiva, quam etiam distinctionem post alios admittit. Alderanus Mascard. de Gener. Statut. interpret. concl. 2. n. 256. Illam appellat, per quam statutum per commodam similitudinis accomodationem ad casus in ipso non expresse comprehensos transfertur. Id quod tum verum, cum illi casus non sunt jure communi, aut aliis statutis decisi. per l. alleg. Gloss. ad l. non possunt D. de leg. Cum si ita decisi forent, non alia quaerenda foret casuum decisio, quae dispositioni juris communis relinquenda. Arg. l. 21. D. de Testam. Militar. In qua lege de Privilegiis militum agitur, quibus concessum ut testamenta ipsorum, militiae facta valerent etiam post missionem, idque intra annum. Id quod ad eos non erat extendendum, qui acceptis successoribus militare desierant, quod is casus esset decisus. l. 20. in init. D. eodem eodem vid. & l. 64. §. 9. D. Solut. Matri-monn.
units.tr: 7. Yet this is not to be admitted indiscriminately. Bartol. in l. omnes populi. D. de justiti & jure. q. ult. According to him, one extension of a statute is active and another passive, a distinction which he also admits following others. Alderanus Mascard. de Gener. Statut. interpret. concl. 2. n. 256. The former he calls that by which a statute is carried over, by a fitting accommodation of likeness, to cases not expressly comprehended in it. This is true when those cases are not decided by common law or by other statutes. per l. alleg. Gloss. ad l. non possunt D. de leg. For if they had been so decided, the decision of such cases would not be sought elsewhere, since it is to be left to the disposition of common law. Arg. l. 21. D. de Testam. Militar. In that law the privileges of soldiers are discussed, to whom it was granted that their wills made during military service should remain valid even after discharge, and that within a year. This was not to be extended to those who, after accepting successors, had ceased to serve, because that case had been decided. l. 20. in init. D. eodem eodem vid. & l. 64. §. 9. D. Solut. Matri-monn.

units.la: Maxime autem extensio statuti in casu propositio locum habet cum quod statuto inductum, effectum commode sortiri nequit, si non ad ea quoque quæ in illo non sunt expresse posita, extendatur. Id quod etiam in iis de jure obtinent, quæ aliter strictam admittunt interpretationem. Argum. l. 32. §. 15. D. de Recept. qui arbitr. l. 22. in init. D. Usu & habit. l. si stipulatum. 11 1. D. verb. obligat.
units.tr: Most especially does the extension of a statute to a case proposed take place when what was introduced by the statute cannot conveniently obtain its effect unless it is extended also to those things which are not expressly set down in it. This also holds in those matters of law which otherwise admit a strict interpretation. Argum. l. 32. §. 15. D. de Recept. qui arbitr. l. 22. in init. D. Usu & habit. l. si stipulatum. 11 1. D. verb. obligat.

units.la: Sunt tamen qui eam appellant activam interpretationem, quando statutum in aliud statutum influit, & illud explicat, & informat. Petr. Anchor. in c. canonum Statuta, de Constit. Tom. 2. Repet. jur. canon. p. 124. n. 264. & p. 132. n. 340. & seqq.
units.tr: There are, however, those who call this the active interpretation, when a statute flows into another statute and explains and shapes it. Petr. Anchor. in c. canonum Statuta, de Constit. Tom. 2. Repet. jur. canon. p. 124. n. 264. & p. 132. n. 340. & seqq.

units.la: 8. Passivam statuti extensionem tum admittit Bartol. cum unum statutum ad aliud, quod de eodem agit negotio, trahitur; adeoque ab illo moderamen aliquod, & interpretationem nanciscitur. Finge, statutum licentiam tribuere conjugibus invicem gratificandi, idque illimitate, non expressa certa quantitate; quod tamen non accipiendum illimitate, quasi etiam ille gratificandi modus, in detrimentum legitimæ filiorum, possit admitti: cum statutum de legitima liberis relinquenda, huc trahendum; secundum quod illud primum explicandum. Sic
units.tr: 8. Bartolus admits passive extension when one statute is drawn to another which deals with the same matter, and so receives from it some moderation and interpretation. Suppose a statute grants spouses licence to make gifts to one another, and does so without limit, no certain amount being stated. This is not, however, to be taken as without limit, as if that mode of giving could also be admitted to the detriment of the children's legitim, since the statute on the legitim to be left to children is to be drawn in here, and according to it the first statute must be explained. Thus

units.la: Paulus JC. jubet extendi leges testamentarias ad testamentum, citra observationes juris communis conditum, ex alia lege, puta Cornelia, firmum, ut tamen illud juxta easdem leges moderetur. l. 1. §. lex Falcidia. D. Ad l. Falcid. Et JC. Hermogenianus, mores atque leges civitatum de muneribus intelligi vult ex illis, quae per ipsum de muneribus alibi erant relata. l. 1. §, 2. in sin. D. de Muner. & Honoribus. Lagus Method, jur. part. 1. cap. 10. Licet meo judicio haec statuti interpretatio potius restrictiva quam extensiva sit dicenda, dum unum statutum illimitate positum, per aliud restringitur, & coarctatur.
units.tr: Paulus the jurist orders the testamentary laws to be extended to a will made without the observances of common law, which is valid by another law, say the Cornelian, yet so that it is moderated according to those same laws. l. 1. §. lex Falcidia. D. Ad l. Falcid. And the jurist Hermogenianus wills that the customs and laws of cities concerning offices be understood in the light of those things about offices which he had related elsewhere. l. 1. §, 2. in sin. D. de Muner. & Honoribus. Lagus Method, jur. part. 1. cap. 10. Although in my judgment this interpretation of a statute should rather be called restrictive than extensive, since one statute, put without limit, is restricted and confined by another.

units.la: 9. Praeter jam enumeratos interpretationis modos, quibus statutum, vel ampliatur, vel arctatur, doctores addidere alios duos modos scilicet unum declarativum, seu significativum, quem Grammaticalem appellant, alterum correctivum, seu emendativum statuti. Jason in l. omnes populi. §. 2. D. just. & jure. n. 60. Varii apud Alderan. Mascard. de interpret. statutor. concl. 2. num. 78. 79. Petrus Anchoran. in c. canonum statuta. de Constit. Tom. 2. Repet. jur. can. p. 124. n. 264. p. 132. n. 340. & seqq. Illum appellant, quando verba, dictiones, & phrases statuti explicantur, grammatice, litteraliter, historice, ut veritas sermonis statuto comprehensi innotescat.
units.tr: 9. Beyond the modes of interpreting already enumerated, by which a statute is either enlarged or narrowed, the doctors have added two other modes: one declarative or significative, which they call grammatical, and another corrective or emendatory of the statute. Jason in l. omnes populi. §. 2. D. just. & jure. n. 60. Varii apud Alderan. Mascard. de interpret. statutor. concl. 2. num. 78. 79. Petrus Anchoran. in c. canonum statuta. de Constit. Tom. 2. Repet. jur. can. p. 124. n. 264. p. 132. n. 340. & seqq. They call the former when the words, expressions and phrases of a statute are explained grammatically, literally and historically, so that the truth of the language comprehended in the statute may become known.

units.la: 10. Hunc appellant, quando statutum aliquam manifestam in se continens iniquitatem, vel manifestum casum excludens, sic explicatur, ut illa auferatur, hic casus includatur &c. Verum studio in generali à me proposita divisione illos omisi modos. Et quia qui litteraliter statutum explicat, & declarat, circa sensum statuti nihil agit, ut ea proprie non sit interpretatio. Quo etiam nomine à DD. talis admissa verbalis interpretatio, licet omnis ab ipso statuente & quidem expressis verbis interpretatio sit exclusa. Er quia statutum emendare aut corrigere, non tam est interpretari quam id ipsum abrogare, vel ei obrogare, vel derogare. Quod juris equidem nonnisi statuti conditori reservatum est. Non negandum tamen, quin de jure civili quandoque Prætori, qui quodammodo viva vox erat juris civilis & ejus interpres l. 8. D. de just. & jure. talis emendatio & correctio juri civilis fuerit concessa: l. 7. §. 1. D. just & jure. Non tamen primario sed per consequentiam, non propalam, verum indirecte, & per obliquum, ne juris civilis majestatem laedere, aut quicquam adversum illud statuere deprehenderetur, tantum ejusdem custos & moderator.
