units.tr: 10. They call the latter when a statute containing some manifest iniquity, or excluding a manifest case, is explained so that the iniquity is removed and the case is included, and so on. But in the general division I proposed I have omitted these modes, for the sake of study. And because one who explains and declares a statute literally does nothing to its sense, such an explanation is not properly an interpretation. By this name too the doctors admit such a verbal interpretation, although every interpretation by the framer himself, and indeed in express words, is excluded. And because to amend or correct a statute is not so much to interpret it as to abrogate it, or to repeal or derogate from it, a power which indeed is reserved solely to the author of the statute. Yet it must not be denied that under civil law such an amendment and correction was sometimes granted to the Praetor, who was in a way the living voice of civil law and its interpreter. l. 8. D. de just. & jure. l. 7. §. 1. D. just & jure. Yet not primarily but by consequence, not openly but indirectly and obliquely, lest he be found to injure the majesty of civil law or to decide anything against it, he was only its guardian and moderator.

units.la: init. instit. de bonor. Possess.
units.tr: init. instit. de bonor. Possess.

units.la: 11. Occasione distinctionis modorum interpretandi statutum, inquirunt interpretes, num si statuentes dicent, litteraliter intelligendum esse statutum, omnis interpretandi ratio exclusa censeri debeat? Resp. Quia in statuentium est potestate, taliter condere statutum, qualiter ipsi volunt, sibique omnem omnino reservare interpretationem. Et qui concedunt jus interpretandi, etiam illud denegare valent; dicendum videtur omnem omnino exclusam esse rationem interpretandi. Arg. l. 1. l. ult. Cod. de leg. & l. 3. ibique DD. D. de Regul. jur. Non tamen meo judicio censebitur exclusa declarativa interpretatio, ut quae est litteralis, seu verborum significativa Bartol. in l. omnes populi. D. de just. & jur. n. 65. Felyn. in Prooem. decret. n. 22. Alex. consil. 50. vol. ult. num.
units.tr: 11. On the occasion of the distinction between modes of interpreting a statute, the interpreters inquire whether, if the framers should say that the statute is to be understood literally, every mode of interpretation ought to be deemed excluded. Answer: since it lies in the power of those who make a statute to frame it as they wish, and to reserve to themselves all interpretation whatever, and since those who grant the right of interpreting can also deny it, it seems right to say that every mode of interpretation is wholly excluded. Arg. l. 1. l. ult. Cod. de leg. & l. 3. ibique DD. D. de Regul. jur. In my judgment, however, declarative interpretation will not be deemed excluded, since it is literal, that is, it signifies the words. Bartol. in l. omnes populi. D. de just. & jur. n. 65. Felyn. in Prooem. decret. n. 22. Alex. consil. 50. vol. ult. num.

units.la: 12. Aliique apud Mascard. de interpret. statut. concl. 2. n. 80. & concl. 4. n. 107. Uti nec extensiva vel restrictiva censebitur exclusa, casu quo neutra admissa, iniquitas & injustitia ex statuto oriretur. Eam enim voluisse statuentes aut affectasse, credibile non est. Arg. l. 15. D. Condit. instit. l. 19. D. de leg. Menoch. 1. conf. 11. Bald. de statut. n. 13. Nec unquam censebitur esse exclusa interpretatio, si ex collatione alterius statuti, à quo prius declaretur, aut suppleatur, ea commode haberi possit. post Baldum Mascard. concl. alleg. num. 81. 82.
units.tr: 12. And others in Mascardus, On the Interpretation of Statutes, concl. 2, n. 80, and concl. 4, n. 107. Nor will an extensive or restrictive interpretation be deemed excluded in a case where, if neither is admitted, injustice and iniquity would arise from the statute. For it is not credible that the framers intended or aimed at such a result. Arg. l. 15 D. Condit. instit.; l. 19 D. de leg.; Menoch. 1 conf. 11; Bald. de statut. n. 13. Nor will an interpretation ever be deemed excluded if it can conveniently be had by comparison with another statute, by which the matter is declared or supplied. Following Baldus, Mascardus, concl. alleg. nn. 81, 82.

units.la: SECT. VII. CAP. II.
units.tr: SECT. VII. CHAP. II.

units.la: 1. Quænam spectanda, si de vero sensu statuti difficultas?
units.tr: 1. What is to be considered if there is difficulty about the true sense of a statute?

units.la: 2. Si sensus statuti investigari nequeat, ad statuti conditorem erit recurrendum.
units.tr: 2. If the sense of a statute cannot be discovered, recourse must be had to the author of the statute.

units.la: 3. An si statutum sit juris communis derogatorium, extensivam admittat interpretationem?
units.tr: 3. If a statute derogates from the common law, does it admit an extensive interpretation?

units.la: 4. Si sensus dubius talis adhibenda interpretatio, quæ juri communi minus adversetur.
units.tr: 4. If the sense is doubtful, such an interpretation is to be adopted as is less opposed to the common law.

units.la: 5. Et statutum, quod simpliciter loquitur, intelligendum est secundum jus commune.
units.tr: 5. A statute which speaks simply is to be understood according to the common law.

units.la: 6. Statutum, quo victus victoriin expensas tenetur, sic accipiendum, si non habuerit justam litigandi causam.
units.tr: 6. A statute by which the losing party is bound to pay the expenses of the victor is to be taken to apply if he had no just cause for litigating.

units.la: 7. Statutum continens verba taxativa, quandoque extensivam admittit interpretationem.
units.tr: 7. A statute containing restrictive words sometimes admits an extensive interpretation.

units.la: 8. Si statutum dictet in casubus non expressis ad jus commune recurrendum esse ; per jus commune solet intelligi Romanum.
units.tr: 8. If a statute directs that in cases not expressed recourse must be had to the common law, the common law is usually understood to mean the Roman law.

units.la: 9. Si quis in instrumento juris auxiliorenunciaverit, non censetur juri statu-tario renunciasse.
units.tr: 9. If someone has renounced the aid of the law in a legal instrument, he is not deemed to have renounced the statutory law.

units.la: 10. 11. Si de moribus in statuto juris fiat mentio, an jus intelligi debeat provinciale?
units.tr: 10, 11. If mention of customs is made in a statute, ought the law to be understood as provincial?

units.la: 12. 13. Jus statutarium super adveniens juri communi, quandoque hoc tollit, quandoque non.
units.tr: 12, 13. A statutory law supervening on the common law sometimes abolishes it, sometimes not.

units.la: 14. Statutum de moribus desiderans Tabellionem cum duobus testibus, ad testamenti factionem, non excludit solemnia juris civilis.
units.tr: 14. A statute on customs requiring a notary and two witnesses for the making of a will does not exclude the solemnities of the civil law.

units.la: 15. Succurritur objectionibus.
units.tr: 15. Objections are answered.

units.la: 16. Num extendatur statutum de casu vero ad casum fictum?
units.tr: 16. Is a statute concerning a real case extended to a fictitious case?

units.la: 17. Affirmativa sententia explicatur.
units.tr: 17. The affirmative opinion is explained.

units.la: 18. Statutum, quod extantibus masculis excludantur foemina, non admittit masculos adoptivos.
units.tr: 18. A statute providing that females are excluded while males survive does not admit adoptive males.

units.la: 19. 20. 21. 22. 23. Statuta si invicem contraria, qui conciliando, vel explicanda sint?
units.tr: 19, 20, 21, 22, 23. If statutes are mutually contrary, how are they to be reconciled or explained?

units.la: 24. An in statutis tempus compositionis,
units.tr: 24. Whether in statutes the time of composition

units.la: 25. Rejiciuntur varia dd. limitationes circa statuti posteriora, correctoria priorum. 26. Si statutum expressam sui derogatio- nem exigat, posteriori statuto de- bebit esse inserta clausula prioris revocatoria.
units.tr: 25. Various limitations by the doctors concerning later statutes that correct earlier ones are rejected. 26. If a statute requires an express repeal of itself, a clause revoking the earlier statute must be inserted in the later one.

units.la: 1. ALterum quod circa interpretandi modum observandum, spectabat ea, quæ in genere circa statuti interpretationem observanda, quo sensus & intellectus genuinus, innotescat. Et quidem spectanda sunt in statuto, de cujus sensu laboramus, antecedentia, & consequentia; examinanda Rubrica; præfatio, quæ ut plurimum causam finalem continet, ut mens statuentis innotescat; accipienda verba in sensu ordinario, & proprio, à quo non est recedendum, licet statutum videatur odiosum, aut à jure communi exorbitare; nisi tamen manifestum sit, id voluisse statuentem, quod improprius exprimit sermo; vel nisi proprio servato sermone, vel impossibilitatem, vel iniquitatem, vel absonum sensum contineret statutum: quod nunquam admittendum. Spectandus is sensus statuti, qui rei gerendæ accommodatior; qui benignior; qui vitio caret. Spectanda consuetudo, quæ retro in civitate obtinuit; tenenda
units.tr: 1. Next, concerning the manner of interpretation, there are the general rules to be observed in interpreting a statute, so that its genuine sense and meaning may become known. In the statute whose sense we are examining, one must consider what goes before and what follows; the rubric must be examined; the preface, which for the most part states the final cause, must be read so that the mind of the lawgiver may become known; words must be taken in their ordinary and proper sense, from which one must not depart, even if the statute seems harsh or departs from the common law. Unless, however, it is clear that the lawgiver meant what his wording expresses improperly, or unless, keeping the proper sense of the words, the statute would contain an impossibility, an iniquity, or an absurd meaning, which must never be admitted. That sense of the statute is to be preferred which is better suited to the conduct of affairs, which is more benign, and which is free from fault. The custom which has prevailed in the state in former times is to be considered; the practice, as they say, or observance is to be maintained; another statute of the same place is to be looked at; the common law is to be considered; the law of the royal city, that is, the statute of the metropolis or ruling city, is to be considered; and finally the custom of neighbouring cities or peoples.

units.la: 2. Quod si omnibus conditionibus & requisitis expensis, atque examinaris, adhuc dubius & incertus remaneat statuti, de quo agitur, sensus, ad auctorem & conditorem statuti recurrendum erit, qui sua interpretatione, quod certius est, statuet. Argum. l. 11. D. de legibus. l. 1. 9. 10. 11. 12. Cod. eod. l. 2. §. 18. Cod. de veter. Jur. Enucleando.
units.tr: 2. But if, after all the conditions and requisites have been weighed and examined, the sense of the statute in question still remains doubtful and uncertain, recourse must be had to the author and maker of the statute, who will settle it by his own interpretation, which is most certain. Argument from law 11 de legibus; laws 1, 9, 10, 11, 12 Cod. eodem; law 2 § 18 Cod. de veteri iure enucleando.

units.la: 3. Verum quoniam circa statuti explicationem in genere consideratam, superfunt etiamnum aliquod difficultates, eas ne quid intactum maneat, in sequentibus explicabo. Quid si statutum sit juris communis derogatorium; an sicut aliud statutum, extensivam admittet interpretationem? Respondeo, id quidem communiter negant, quasi hic de casu expresso ad non expressum non fiat transitus. Alii distinguunt, inter statutum favorabile & odiosum. Quasi illud, non hoc admittat extensionem. Sic Anton. de Roselli de successs. ab intestato. sol. 246. n. 215. vol. 8. tract. Et allegati apud Aideran. Mascard. de interpret. statut. conclus. 4. 5. per tot. & n. 86. 141. 4. concl. ubi explicatur, quid sit favorabile, quid odiosum? Alii distinguunt inter statutum quod adjuvat jus gentium, vel potius coarctat. Quasi illud, non hoc sit extendendum, Anton. de Canario. de insinuation. q. 20. num. 27. sol. 163. vol. 1. tract. Verum, quandoquidem statutum nonnunquam a jure communi deviat, quod id ipsum forte non satis accommodatum nostrae reipublicae formae; quodque jus commune rationi & aequitati minus congruum; etiam statutum de moribus nostris quasi jus commune, in loco, ubi conditum, non obstante jure communi, ad similia trahi & referri poterit. Tritum enim illud Doctorum: argumentum ab identitate rationis, in statutis esse admittendum. Argum. tit. instit. de legitim. Patron. tutel. l. 13. D. de leg. l. 6. §. 1. D. verb. Signif. l. ut gradatim, §. et si lege. D. Muner. & Honor. l. 1. §. mutuum. D. Ad Senat. Macedon. Bald. tract. de statut. n. 1. 2. Bartol. ad l. omnes populi. n. 53. & seq. units.tr: 3. But since, concerning the explanation of statutes considered in general, some difficulties still remain, I shall explain them in what follows, so that nothing is left untouched. What if a statute derogates from the common law: will it, like any other statute, admit an extensive interpretation? I answer that most writers deny this, as if there were no transition here from an expressly stated case to one not expressed. Others distinguish between a favourable and an odious statute, holding that the former admits extension but not the latter. So Antonius de Rosellis, de successionibus ab intestato, sol. 246, n. 215, vol. 8 tract. [and those cited by Alderanus and Mascardus, de interpretatione statutorum, concl. 4, 5 throughout, and nn. 86, 141; concl. 4, where it is explained what is favourable and what odious]. Others distinguish between a statute that supports the law of nations and one that restricts it, holding that the former, not the latter, is to be extended: Antonius de Canario, de insinuationibus, q. 20, n. 27, sol. 163, vol. 1 tract. But since a statute sometimes departs from the common law, perhaps because that law is not sufficiently suited to the form of our commonwealth, and since the common law is less in accord with reason and equity, a statute concerning our customs may, like the common law in the place where it was enacted, be drawn and referred to similar cases, notwithstanding the common law. For the well-worn saying of the doctors is that argument from identity of reason must be admitted in statutes. [Cited in support: Inst. de legitima tutela; D. 1.3 law 13; D. 50.16 law 6 §1; law ut gradatim; D. 50.5 law 1 §mutuum; Baldus, tract. de statutis, nn. 1, 2; Bartolus on law Omnes populi, nn. 53 ff.; Cravetta, de antiquitate temporum, part 4; Matthaeus Wesembeck, vol. 5 consil. 220, n. 14; Treutler, consil. 89, n. 3; Goris, adversus tract. 4; Christinaeus on the custom of Mechlin; Merenda; Sande, de feudis, Gelria; Groenewegen; Chassanaeus on the custom of Burgundy; Molinaeus on Paris; Argentré on Brittany.]

units.la: 4. Id tamen secundum plerosque doctores erit statuendum, ut si statuti sensus sit obscurus vel dubius, talem admittat interpretationem, quæ juri communi recepto, non sit contraria. Legum quippe correctio, ut odiosa, non facile inducenda, ne quidem per ipsas leges. Nisi tamen illa correctio, vel expressis verbis probetur, vel ipso facto, id est urgentibus conjecturis, potissimum à causa finali statuti, desumptis. Quo etiam nomine argumentum à contrario sensu nonnunquam in statutis erit admittendum; quia & in pactis dotalibus, licet ipsa sint stricti juris. Maxime, si verba, unde sumi debet argumentum, sunt proposita causative, & contrarium argumentum non est contra jus commune. Argum. l. 32. in sin. Cod. de Appellat. l. quamvis. Cod. de Testam.
