units.tr: 4. Nevertheless, according to most doctors, the rule is this: if the sense of a statute is obscure or doubtful, it should be given an interpretation that is not contrary to the common law received in practice. For the correction of laws, being odious, is not to be lightly introduced, not even by the laws themselves. Such a correction must, however, be proved either in express words or by the fact itself, that is, by pressing conjectures drawn chiefly from the final cause of the statute. On this ground an argument from the contrary sense will sometimes have to be admitted in statutes too, since it is also admitted in dotal pacts, although these are of strict law. This holds especially if the words from which the argument must be drawn are put causally, and the contrary argument is not against the common law. Argument from l. 32 in fin. Cod. de Appellationibus; l. quamvis, Cod. de Testamentis; Laurus de Palatiis, on the Statute of Italy, that males being extant females do not succeed, part 2, Principium, n. 7, p. 7, p. 49, vol. 1, tractatus; Petrus Antibolus, de Muneribus, §. 4, n. 10, vol. 10, tract., p. 30; Gail, 2 obs. 138, n. 7; Quetta, Consil. 27; Cravetta, de Antiquis temporibus, part 4, §. absolutus, n. 42; Menochius, de Recuperanda Possessione, remedium 9, n. 387 et seq.; Treutler, consil. 19, n. 104, and consil. 41, n. 49; Andreas Kolb, Exercitationes legales 2, n. 35; Berlich, part 2, decis. 203, and the various authors there; Jacob Thomming, consil. part 1, conf. 1, n. 60, and conf. 34, n. 35; Matthias Wesembeck, part 6, conf. 296; Christinaeus, Prolixe, vol. 1, decis. 113, n. 20 et seqq., and vol. 2, decis. 54, at the end; the same author on Mechlin, in Epilogo, n. 8; Mevius, Praelim., quaest. 9, n. 33 et seq., on the law of Lübeck; Antonius Matthaeus, tract. de Auctionibus, lib. 1, c. 21, n. 33; l. 26 §. 2 D. de Pactis Dotalibus, and there, after Baldus, Gothofredus at length; Mascardus, de interpretatione statutorum, concl. 4, n. 69 et seqq.

units.la: -5. Hinc itidem consequitur, statutum quod simpliciter loquitur, intelligi, restringi, & modificari debere secundum jus commune; ad quod ante omnia recurrere soliti statuentes. Nisi ut in antecedentibus dictum, sit juris communis derogatorium. Tunc enim in illo individuo, in quo disponit, contra jus civile, per illud & secundum illud non explicabitur. Vel nisi jus commune servatum in dicto statuto manifestam contineret iniquitatem.
units.tr: 5. From this it likewise follows that a statute which speaks simply is to be understood, restricted and modified according to the common law, to which the lawmakers were accustomed to have recourse before all else. Unless, as said above, it is derogatory to the common law. For then, in that particular case in which it disposes contrary to the civil law, it will not be explained through that law or according to it. Or unless the common law retained in the said statute would contain manifest injustice.

units.la: Vel nisi evidens sit statuentes a jure communi muni recedere voluisse. Matthesilanus de success. ab intestato. 3. Artic. Principal. num. 5. vol. 3. tract. Et Chassan. ad Burg. Rubric. 2. §. 1. n. 12. Panormit. in c. in nostris. de injur. & alii in Dictionario Albericide Rosate verb. statutum dubium. in Addit. post Bursatum consil. 12. vol. 1. n. 53. Mascardus de interpret. statut. general. concl. 2. n. 20. 226. 244.
units.tr: Or unless it is evident that the framers of the statute wished to depart from the common law. Matthaeus Wesembeck... Matthesilanus, de successionibus ab intestato, 3 Articulus Principalis, num. 5, vol. 3, tractatus; and Chassanaeus on Burgundy, Rubric 2, §. 1, n. 12; Panormitanus on c. in nostris, de iniuriis; and others in the Dictionary of Albericus de Rosate, under "statutum dubium," in the Additions after Bursatus, consil. 12, vol. 1, n. 53; Mascardus, de interpretatione statutorum generalium, concl. 2, n. 20, 226, 244.

units.la: 6. Quâ etiam ratione statutum, quod disponit simpliciter, ut victus victori in expensas sit condemnandus, hunc sensum admittit, si non habuerit justam litigandi causam; hic quippe sensus juri communi est conformis, & rationi conveniens. §. 1. instit. de Pæn. temer. litig. l. 13. l. 15. Cod. de Judic. l. 73. §. 2. D. de leg. 2. Bald. in l. terminato. Cod. de fructibus & lit. Expens. Alciat. in praxi juris utriusque tit. de expensis. p. 275. & seqq. Lanfranc. ab Ariadno de Expens. fol. 221. vol. 9. tract. Mascard. d. libr. concl. 2. n. 41. & concl. 12. n. 1. 2. 3. 4. Pacius. disp. 24. ad Instit. n. 15. Gudel. de jure novis. libr. 4. c. 13 ibique Covarr. Pract. quest. 27. Christin. vol. 2. decis. 54. n. ult. idem prolixe tit. 1. art. 29. ad l. Mechlin.
units.tr: 6. For the same reason, a statute which simply provides that the loser is to be condemned to pay the winner's costs admits this sense, namely, if the loser had no just cause for litigating; for this sense is in accordance with the common law and agrees with reason. §. 1 Inst. de Poena temere litigantium; l. 13, l. 15 Cod. de Iudiciis; l. 73 §. 2 D. de legatis 2; Baldus on l. terminato, Cod. de fructibus et litis expensis; Alciatus, in Praxi iuris utriusque, tit. de expensis, p. 275 et seqq.; Lanfrancus ab Ariadno, de Expensis, fol. 221, vol. 9, tract.; Mascardus, op. cit., concl. 2, n. 41, and concl. 12, n. 1, 2, 3, 4; Pacius, disp. 24 ad Institutiones, n. 15; Gudelinus, de iure novissimo, lib. 4, c. 13, and there Covarruvias, Practicarum quaestionum 27; Christinaeus, vol. 2, decis. 54, n. last; the same author at length, tit. 1, art. 29, on the law of Mechlin.

units.la: 7. Quid si statutum contineat verba taxativa, an unquam extensivam admittet interpretationem; adeoque de casu expresso ad non expressum, verum tamen similem, transferetur? Respondeo, licet verba taxativa sint aliorum casuum exclusiva, si respiciamus casus disparatos; non tamen erunt casuum similium exclusiva. Per vulgatum illud DD. & Philosophorum; exclusiva quidem excludit genere diversa, non tamen concomitantia. Id quod obtinet quam maxime, si non admissa extensione & ampliatione statuti, idque ad II. similitudinem, absurdus admitteretur sensus, adeoque vitio statutum non careret. Ut si non rationis statuti sit dissimilitudo, quia par aut major ratio, similis etiam casus ad statutum sit referendus.
units.tr: 7. What if a statute contains restrictive words; will it ever admit an extensive interpretation, and so be transferred from an expressed case to a case not expressed but nevertheless similar? I answer: although restrictive words exclude other cases when we look at dissimilar cases, they will not exclude similar cases. By the common saying of the doctors and philosophers: exclusives exclude things of a different kind, but not those that accompany them. This holds above all if, without admitting an extension and enlargement of the statute, and by reason of similarity, an absurd sense would be admitted, and the statute would not be free from fault. Thus, if there is no difference in the reason of the statute, because the reason is equal or greater, a similar case is also to be referred to the statute.

units.la: Id quod alii tantum in favorabilibus, alii etiam in odiosis causis admittunt. Arg. §. porro. verb. sed quia. libr. 2. feudor. tit. 24. l. 12. l. 19. D. de legibus, l. oö as. 12. Cod. de Præd. Minor. & ibi Gothefr. in comm. l. 1. Cod. de bonor. Possess. contr. Tabul. & ibi gloss. & DD. Alexander, Jason, Bald. Castrens. apud Gomes. variat. Resol. tom. 1. c. 11. n. 12. & 13. Alderan. Mascard, de interpret. statutor. conclus. 4. n. 158. 159. -- DD. ad §. 28. instit. de Action. & Novell. 115. c. 3. in sin. init. diff. Zoes. in simili, D. de liber. & Posthum. hared. instit. n. 13. 14.
units.tr: Some admit this only in favourable causes, others also in odious causes. Compare §. porro, verb. sed quia, lib. 2 Feudorum tit. 24; l. 12, l. 19 D. de legibus; l. 1 Cod. de praediis minorum; and the Cod. 12, Cod. de praediis minorum; and there Gothofredus in commentary on l. 1 Cod. de bonorum possessione contra tabulas, and there the gloss and the doctors; Alexander, Jason, Baldus, Castrensis, in Gomesius, Variae resolutiones, tom. 1, c. 11, n. 12 and 13; Alderanus; Mascardus, de interpretatione statutorum, concl. 4, n. 158, 159. — The doctors on §. 28 Inst. de actionibus; Novell. 115, c. 3 at the end and beginning; Diffinitio Zoesius, in simili, D. de liberis et postumis heredibus; Institutiones, n. 13, 14.

units.la: 8. Quid si statutum dicet, in casibus non expressis ad jus commune vel civile recurrendum esse; id ne de jure alio statutario communiori puta Provinciali, de Principum constitutionibus in illa itidem civitate receptis erit intelligendum, an potius de jure civili Romanorum? Respondeo, quoniam in Provinciis vinciis Belgii fœderati, regulariter deficientibus locorum statutis, jus Romanum, ut in plerisque partibus æquissimum, est receptum: & passim statutorum conditores statutis hanc clausulam subjiciunt, ut in casubus non expressis ad jus commune scriptum, sit recurrendum : quod ibidem jus Cæsareum, jus Justinianæum appellatur : nec præter illud reperitur aliud quippiam commune, apud nos receptum, quod juris communis nomen meretur : affirmandum erit intrepide, per jus commune, civile Romanorum seu Justinianæum, seu Cæsareum intelligendum esse.
units.tr: 8. What if a statute says that in cases not expressed recourse must be had to the common or civil law: is this to be understood of other statutory law that is more general, for example the provincial law, or the constitutions of the princes received in that same city, or rather of the civil law of the Romans? I answer: since in the Provinces of the United Netherlands, where local statutes are generally lacking, the Roman law is received, as being most equitable in many respects; and since the framers of statutes everywhere append to their statutes this clause, that in cases not expressed recourse must be had to the written common law, which there is called the Imperial law, the Justinianic law; and since no other common law is found among us besides that, which deserves the name of common law: it must be affirmed boldly that by the common law is to be understood the civil law of the Romans, whether Justinianic or Caesarean.

units.la: Argum. §. sed quoties, instit. de jure natur. gent. & civil. Auth. Præsides. Cod. Episc. Audient. in med. l. rem non novam, in sin. init. Cod. judic. Jason in l. omnes populi. D. just. & jur. n. 20. 21. 22. Sanson. ad Turonensf. §. 14. gloss. 1. p. 24. Ordin. Curiæ Ultraj. Provinc. in sin. Constit. ordin. Provinc. Ultraj. super matrimon. de ann. 1584. Octobr. 6. art. 24. 29. Ordinat. Urbis Ultraj. in sin. Christin. ad II. Mechlin. in Pralud. n. 38. ibidemque varii, idem in Epilogo. n. 20. & seq. Zoes. D. de Pæn. n. 13. idem. D. de Testam. milit. in sin. Auctor Batavicæ Arcadiæ p. mihi. 598. in medio. vid. & Menoch. 2. Præsumpt. 6. num. 11. 12. ego in meo tract. de auctorit. juris civilis & canonici in Belgio fœderat.
units.tr: Argument from §. sed quoties, Inst. de iure naturali, gentium et civili; Authentica Praesides, Cod. Episcopis et clericis; l. rem non novam in medio et fine, Cod. de iudiciis; Jason on l. omnes populi, D. de iustitia et iure, n. 20, 21, 22; Sanson on the Turonensis, §. 14, gloss 1, p. 24; Ordinance of the Court of Utrecht, Provincial, at the end; Constitution of the Province of Utrecht concerning marriage, of 1584, October 6, art. 24, 29; Ordinance of the City of Utrecht at the end; Christinaeus on the Mechlin laws, in Praeludio, n. 38, and the various authors there, the same in Epilogo, n. 20 et seq.; Zoesius, D. de poenis, n. 13; the same, D. de testamento militis, at the end; the author of the Batavian Arcadia, p. 598 in the middle; see also Menochius, 2 Praesumptiones 6, n. 11, 12; I in my treatise de auctoritate iuris civilis et canonici in Belgio foederato.

units.la: 9. Unde secundum Baldum, si quispiam in instrumento omnis juris auxilio renunciaverit, non censebitur statuti beneficio renunciasse. in l. sed & si quis. § quæsitum D. si quis cautionibus:vid. tamen prolixe. Andreä de ExeaTom. 2. Repet. jur. canonic. p. 132. n. 48. & seqq. Gothefr. ad l. 1. §. 1. D. Quæ in Testamento delent.
units.tr: 9. Hence, according to Baldus, if someone in an instrument has renounced all the aid of law, he is not deemed to have renounced the benefit of a statute. In l. sed & si quis. § quaesitum D. si quis cautionibus: but see at length Andreas de Exea, Tom. 2 Repet. jur. canonic. p. 132 n. 48 and following; Gothofredus on l. 1 §. 1 D. Quae in Testamento delent.

units.la: Neque officiunt huic sententiæ quæ occurrunt apud Corenium, obs. 30. cur. Holl. ob. 234. n. 68. Neque enim ibi agitur de statuti sensu, sed de partium conventione; in quâ forte, si casus aliquis sit omissus, pro omisso habebitur; ex jure communi patrio, id est vel provinciali, vel consuetudinario generali decidendus.
units.tr: Nor do the passages in Corenius, obs. 30, cur. Holl. ob. 234 n. 68, stand in the way of this opinion. For there the question is not about the meaning of a statute but about the agreement of the parties. If some case has perhaps been omitted from that agreement, it will be regarded as omitted and must be decided by the common law of the fatherland, that is, either the provincial law or the general customary law.

units.la: Idque rationi juris congruum est; cum illa partium conventio supra se habeat jus patrium provinciale, vel consuetudinarium generale, ad quod, probabile est, partes respexisse, & cui probabiliter se confirmare voluerunt. Verum statuta, quæ partim urbana, partim provincialia, supra se aliud jus commune præter Cæsareum, seu civile Romanorum, non agnoverunt, ut ad illud collimare in defectum juris proprii videantur. Et licet jus Provinciale dici possit, quasi commune nobis, uti loc. alleg. scribit Coren, non tamen est commune, sic absolute dictum, quale est Romanorum. Nisi tamen addatur, aut occurrat hæc phrasis, jus regionis commune, aut jus commune patriæ, <bl>gemeyn</bl> <bl>lants recht</bl>. Tum quippe probabile statuentes jus provinciale statutarium respexisse.
units.tr: This accords with the reason of law, since that agreement of the parties stands above the provincial native law or the general customary law. It is probable that the parties had regard to that law and wished to be confirmed by it. But statutes which are partly urban and partly provincial recognised no other common law above them besides the Caesarean law, that is, the civil law of the Romans, so that they seem to aim at that law when their own law is lacking. And although provincial law may be called "common" as it were to us, as Corenius writes in the place cited, it is not common in the absolute sense, as Roman law is. Unless, however, it is added, or this phrase occurs: common law of the region, or common law of the fatherland, gemeyn lants recht (common law of the land). Then it is probable that those who enacted the statute had regard to the provincial statutory law.

units.la: 10. Si tamen de moribus in statuto mention fiat juris simpliciter, sine ullo additamento, tum probabile etiam jus aliud statutarium provinciale, vel generale consuetudinarium intelligi: quia & hoc ipsum juris venit appellatione: l. ult. D. de Decret. ab ordin. faciend. l. 3. §. 5. D. Sepulchr. violat. Jason in loc. alleg. n. 23. 24. Maxime cum de moribus statuentes dum intendunt jus civile, id non sine additamento, civilis, Cæsarei, communis scripti, Justinianei, imperialis, secularis, exprimant.
units.tr: 10. If, however, a statute mentions law in general, simply "law" without any addition, then it is probable that some other provincial statutory law or general customary law is meant, because this too comes under the name of law: l. ult. D. de Decret. ab ordin. faciend. l. 3. §. 5. D. Sepulchr. violat. Jason in loc. alleg. n. 23. 24. This is especially so since those who enact statutes, when they intend civil law, do not express it without some addition: civil, Caesarean, of the common written law, Justinian's, imperial, secular.

units.la: 11. Quin tamen quandoque facta mentione juris communis, ad provinciale, vel generale consuetudinarium sit recurrendum, negari non poterit. 1. Si, absurdus sensus statuti oriretur, recurrendo ad jus commune. Aut praeter casum statuto expressum, jus civile injustitiam foveret. Arg. l. 19. D. de legibus. 2. Si per generalem consuetudinem juri civili in caeteris casibus statuto non expressis esset derogatum. 3. Si fraute tali statuto, nihilominus in illa regione, vel civitate, soliti sint recurrere ad jus Provinciale. Quia servanda est consuetudo, & quod diu retro in civitate obtinuit, pro lege habetur. l. 23. l. 35. l. 37. D. de legibus. post Decian. Jason, aliosque Masc. conclus. 2. num. 92. & seqq.
units.tr: 11. Yet it cannot be denied that when mention is made of common law, one must sometimes have recourse to provincial or general customary law. (1) If an absurd sense of the statute would arise by recourse to the common law, or if civil law, outside the case expressed in the statute, would foster injustice. Arg. l. 19. D. de legibus. (2) If civil law has been derogated by general custom in other cases not expressed in the statute. (3) If, despite such a statute, the people of that region or city are accustomed to have recourse to provincial law. For custom must be observed, and what has long prevailed in a city is held as law. l. 23. l. 35. l. 37. D. de legibus; after Decianus, Jason, and others; Mascard. conclus. 2. num. 92. and following.

units.la: 12. Quid si jus statutarium superadveniat juri communi, an per illud jus commune sublatum censebitur, an potius aliquid ei superadditum vel adjectum esse dicetur? Respondeo. Aut jus statutarium idem dicit, quod jus commune, nec alterum per alterum videbitur esse sublatum: quod quemadmodum lex legi, pactum legi adjicitur, etiam de superfluo, licet unum per aliud non abrogetur, sed stabiliatur magis; ita etiam statutum juri civili de superfluo superadditum, confirmet illud magis, ex eoque confirmetur, in quantum eadem tum restrictiones tum limitationes admittet, quas admisit jus civile. Sic ut tamen appellandum sit statutum, non jus commune, in quantum fortius vinculum ei, quod jure communi cautum est, adjicitur. Arg. §. 2. instit. de Usucapion. l. 19. in init. D. de Usufruct. Barbatia. de Præstant. Cardinal. quæst. 1. part. 1. n. 13. p. 41. vol. 6. Tractat. ibique Bartol. Baldus. aliique.
units.tr: 12. What if statutory law supervenes upon common law: is it deemed to have been abrogated by that common law, or should it rather be said that something has been added or appended to it? I answer: either the statutory law says the same thing as the common law, and neither will be seen to have been abolished by the other. Just as law is added to law, and pact to law, even concerning what is superfluous, yet one is not abrogated by the other but rather is strengthened, so also a statute added to civil law concerning what is superfluous confirms that law more, and is confirmed by it, insofar as it admits the same restrictions and limitations that civil law admitted. Yet it must be called a statute, not common law, insofar as a stronger bond is added to what is provided by common law. Arg. §. 2. Instit. de Usucapion. l. 19. in init. D. de Usufruct. Barbatia de Praestant. Cardinal. quaest. 1. part. 1. n. 13. p. 41. vol. 6. Tractat., and there Bartolus, Baldus, and others.

units.la: 13. Aut jus statutarium aliquid adjicit juri communi, quod ut plurimum est exististumandum, per Marsil. singul. 121. inc. habens justam causam. & sing. 207. init. victus. Tumque aut versamur in favorabilibus causis, aut in casibus odiosis.
units.tr: 13. Or the statutory law adds something to common law; this is for the most part to be assumed, see Marsil. singul. 121. inc. habens justam causam, and singul. 207. init. victus. Then we are dealing either with favourable causes or with odious cases.

units.la: Si illud, non censebitur per statutarium, jus commune anterius, esse sublatum. Quod in suo vigore manebit, ut jure communi quis uti valeat, & eo recurrere, neglecto statuto, ejus loci, in quo domicilium habet.
units.tr: If the former, the earlier common law is not deemed to have been abolished by the statute. It will remain in force, so that one may be able to use the common law and have recourse to it, disregarding the statute of the place where one has domicile.

units.la: Quia cum cuivis liceat favori introducto pro se renunciare, etiam illi licebit negligere tale statutum, quod solummodo ejus respicit favorem. Arg. l. 41. D. oblig. & Action. l. 91. D. de Reg. jur. l. pen. Cod. de Pact.
units.tr: Because, since anyone may renounce for himself a favour introduced in his favour, so it will also be permitted to him to disregard such a statute as regards only his own favour. Arg. l. 41. D. oblig. & Action. l. 91. D. de Reg. jur. l. pen. Cod. de Pact.

units.la: Si hoc, censebitur jus statutarium tollere jus civile commune. Odiosa quippe, qualia poenalia, sunt restringenda. Et quae poenae arbitrio judicis essent irrogandae, frustra statuto civitatis determinatum modum accepissent. Arg. l. 13. l. 42. D. de Pæn. l. 155. §. sin. D. de Reg. jur. l. final. Cod. de Modo Multar.
units.tr: If the latter, the statutory law will be deemed to remove the common civil law. For odious matters, such as penal ones, are to be restricted. And penalties which were to be imposed at the judge's discretion would have received a fixed mode in vain from the statute of the city. Arg. l. 13. l. 42. D. de Pæn. l. 155. §. sin. D. de Reg. jur. l. final. Cod. de Modo Multar.

units.la: 14. Hinc etiam vice versa, in causa favorabili statutum, de moribus ad testamenti conficiendi solemnitatem desiderans Tabellionem, & duos testes, non excludit testamenti faciendi rationem secundum solemnia juris civilis: ut etiam alicui liceat coram septem testibus condere testamentum, etsi Tabellio non fuerit adhibitus; modo tamen in hâc nostrâ Provinciâ, prius litteras licentiæ, seu veniæ impetraverit, id quod in omni testamenti factione coram Notario, & testibus, etiam est necessarium.
units.tr: 14. Hence also, conversely, in a favourable cause a statute which, as to custom, requires a notary and two witnesses for the solemnity of making a will does not exclude the making of a will according to the solemnities of civil law. So it is also permitted to someone to make a will before seven witnesses, even though no notary has been called in, provided only that in this our Province he first obtains letters of licence or permission, which is also necessary in every making of a will before a notary and witnesses.

units.la: 15. Nec obstat quod ait Montan. cap. 33. de Tutel. num. 38. 39, 40. Solemnitatem ultra jus commune requiri cumulative, adeòque statutum à jure communi suppleri. Id enim tum demum verum est, cum per statutum alicui magis prospectum voluere statuentes. Id quod accidit, si forte plures solemnitates requirat statutum ad alienationem bonorum minoris, quam lex desiderat. Finge enim statutum velle, ne qui major hic quondam erat masculus, decimo octavo ætatis anno, sua immobilia alienet, citra consensum propinquorum. Statut. Ultraject. Rubric. 28. n. 6. Quo casu non videtur alia exclusa solemnitas, de jure communi ad alienationem immobilium minorum requisita. Et ita dicendum, solemnitatem juris statutarii superaddendam solemnitati civili. Quasi inducta ad unum finem, non debeant operari ejus contrarium. Arg. l. cum tale. §. 8. D. Condit. Demonstrat. Cassrenf. strens. consil. 278. aliter. 271. col. 1. 2. Decius consil. 110. n. 1. apud Masc. concl. 2. n. 58. 59.
units.tr: 15. Nor does what Montanus says, cap. 33. de Tutel. num. 38. 39. 40., stand in the way: that a solemnity beyond common law is required cumulatively, and so the statute supplements the common law. For this is true only when the enacting authorities have wished to provide more for someone by the statute. This happens if, for example, the statute requires more solemnities for the alienation of a minor's property than the law demands. Imagine a statute wishing that a male who was formerly a minor, in his eighteenth year of age, should not alienate his immovables without the consent of relatives. Statut. Ultraject. Rubric. 28. n. 6. In this case no other solemnity, which common law requires for the alienation of minors' immovables, seems to be excluded. And so it must be said that the solemnity of statutory law is to be added on top of the civil solemnity, since what is introduced for one end ought not to work the contrary. Arg. l. cum tale. §. 8. D. Condit. Demonstrat. Cassaneus, strens. consil. 278, aliter 271, col. 1. 2. Decius consil. 110. n. 1. apud Mascard. concl. 2. n. 58. 59.

units.la: 16. Sed anxie circa extensivam interpretationem statuti DD. inquirunt, num de casu vero procedat unquam ampliatio ad casum non verum, id est, ad casum fictum. Resp. Sunt bene multi, qui censent statutum, quod loquitur de casu vero, non extendi ad casum fictū, quod statutum stricti juris sit, adcoque strictam admittat interpretationem. Id quod etiam admittendum videtur, si statutum requirat casum verum, non fictum. Vel in casu fiḉto adhibito, absurdus statuti census oriretur. Vel statutum esset admodum odiosum, adeoque nec extendendum; vel contra jus commune sit introductum. Arg. l. 3. §. hac verba. D. Neg. Gest. l. pen. D. de Pæn. l. 14. D. de legibus. Alexand. cons. viso statuto. 189. vol. 7. Bartol. ad d. l. 3. Vivius in tom. comm. opin. libr. 17. verb. statutum, p. 343. Quo forte referri poterunt varii apud Christinæum ad Mechlin: in Prælud. n. 37. allegati. vid. Hyppol. in c. atsi clerici. de Judic. n. 82. Tom. 3. Repet. jur. canon. & volum. consil. jurisc. German. parte 3. consil. 15. Hartm. Pistor. libr. 1. q. 25. n. 20. Berlich. 2. Practic. concl. 18. n. 28. ibique varii.
units.tr: 16. But people anxiously inquire among the doctors about the extensive interpretation of a statute: whether an extension ever applies from a true case to a case that is not true, that is, to a fictitious case. Answer: there are quite many who hold that a statute which speaks of a true case is not extended to a fictitious case, because a statute is of strict law and so admits only strict interpretation. This also seems to be admitted if the statute requires a true and not a fictitious case. Or, if a fictitious case were admitted, an absurd result would follow from the statute. Or the statute would be very odious and so should not be extended, or it would be introduced against the common law. Argument from l. 3, §. hac verba, D. Neg. Gest.; l. pen. D. de Pæn.; l. 14, D. de legibus; Alexander, consilium viso statuto, 189, vol. 7; Bartolus on the said l. 3; Vivius in the Tomus communium opinionum, book 17, under statutum, p. 343. To this may perhaps be referred the various authorities cited by Christinaeus on Mechlin, in Prælud. n. 37. See Hippolytus on c. atsi clerici, de Judic., n. 82; Tom. 3 of the Repetitions on the canon law; the volume of German legal consilia, part 3, consilium 15; Hartmann Pistorius, book 1, q. 25, n. 20; Berlich, 2 Practicae, concl. 18, n. 28, and the various authors there.

units.la: Sunt alii, qui existumant statutum in casu vero etiam referri ad casum fictum quando idem disponit, quod jus commune, vel loquitur in juris materiâ, in quâ casus verus & fictus æquiparantur. vid Bald. Panormitan. Jasonem, apud Alberic. de Rosate in Diction. verb. statutum. in addit. Et post Romanùm consil. 105. n. 2. Felyn. in c. insinuavi. n. 2. & alios. Alder. Mascard. de statut. interpret. n. 72. & n. 211. 212. & seqq. cum limit. & concluf. 10. n. 1. 2. & seqq. Costal. adl. 3. 5. D. Neg. Gestis. Gomes. adl. 70. Tar. n. 17. Christin. in Prel. ad Mechlin. n. 37.
units.tr: Others think that a statute which speaks of a true case is also referred to a fictitious case when it lays down what the common law lays down, or when it speaks in a matter of law in which a true and a fictitious case are treated as equal. See Baldus, Panormitanus, Jason, cited by Alberic de Rosate in the Dictionarium under statutum, in the additions. And afterwards Romanus, consilium 105, n. 2; Felinus on c. insinuavi, n. 2, and others; Alderisius; Mascardus, de statutorum interpretatione, n. 72 and nn. 211, 212 and following, with limitations; and conclusion 10, nn. 1, 2 and following; Costalius on l. 3, D. Neg. Gestis; Gomesius on l. 70; Tiraquellus, n. 17; Christinaeus in Prelud. ad Mechlin., n. 37.

units.la: 17. Sic tamen malim sentire; quia statutum regulariter interpretationem recipit ex jure communi, quod etiam admittit extensionem de casu vero, ad fictum. Et fictiones suadente æquitate sunt introductæ, quæ maxime in statuto dominantur. Et statutum nobis est veluti lex quæpiam civilis. Etiâ statutum de casu vero ad fictum referri poterit; si modo neq; ex verbis, neque ex mente, aut intentione statuentis, neque ex ratione ipsius statuti, neque ex naturâ rei, quia est odiosa, sit exclusa fictio. Arg. l. 11. §. 7. D. interrog. in jur. faciend. l. 15. D. de Rebus cred. l. Gallus. §. & quid si in sin. D. liber. & Posster. hared. instit. Arg. §. namque si. 4. & seq. instit. Action. §. ult. instit. Quibus non est permiss. facere testam. Jason in l. omnes populi. D. just. & jur. n. pen. & ult. Cataldinus de Boncompagnis de Syndicatu. n. 76. post Baldum in l. Gallus. 29. §. quid si is. D. liber. & Posthum. Hared. Costal. ad l. 3. D. Neg. Gestis. Everhard.
units.tr: 17. Yet I would rather hold this view: since a statute ordinarily admits interpretation by the common law, which also admits extension from a true case to a fictitious one. Fictions, introduced at the prompting of equity, are especially prevalent in statutes, and a statute is for us like some civil law. Even a statute speaking of a true case may be referred to a fictitious one, provided that the fiction is not excluded by the words, nor by the mind or intention of the one who enacted it, nor by the reason of the statute itself, nor by the nature of the matter, because it is odious. Argument from l. 11, §. 7, D. interrog. in jur. faciend.; l. 15, D. de Rebus cred.; l. Gallus, §. & quid si, in fin., D. liber.; and Posthumus, hered. instit.; argument from §. namque si, 4 and following, Instit.; Action, §. ult., Instit.; to whom it is not permitted to make a will; Jason on l. omnes populi, D. just. & jur., n. pen. and ult.; Cataldinus de Boncompagnis, de Syndicatu, n. 76, after Baldus on l. Gallus 29, §. quid si is, D. liber. & Posthum. hered.; Costalius on l. 3, D. Neg. Gestis; Everhard.

units.la: Everhard. Consil. 78. paulo post init. & loco à vi fictionis. p. mihi. 379. lin. 20. Molin. ad Consuet. Parisi. tit. 1. §. 11. num. 29. p. 245. & §. 36. num. 10. p. 509. Zoes. D. Solut. Matrim. num. 4. vid. & Anton. Matth. disp. 3. de quasi Usufr. n. 18. ubi aliæ allegationes.
units.tr: Everhard, Consilium 78, a little after the beginning, and in the place from the force of the fiction, p. mihi 379, line 20; Molinaeus on the Consuetudo Parisiensis, tit. 1, §. 11, num. 29, p. 245, and §. 36, num. 10, p. 509; Zoesius, D. Solut. Matrim., num. 4. See also Antonius Matthaeus, disp. 3, de quasi Usufructu, n. 18, where there are other allegations.

units.la: 18: Unde si statutum dictet extantibus masculis excludi fœminas, tale statutum non extantibus legitimis & naturalibus simul, non extendetur, ad filios, qui tales juris fictione, quales sunt legitimi tantum, seu adoptivi. Hæc quippe causa est odiosa, & præjudicium grande allatura liberis justo quæsitis matrimonio. Quinimo ea ipsa extensio statuti, æquitati naturali adversatur, & illi parentum affectui, quo liberis ex se quæsitis, sua relicta cupiunt. Nec minus liberorum justis nuptiis quæsitorum, circa successionem spem deminuit, quam quisque obsequio parat sibi; adeoque & everit debitam obedientiam], omni succedendi via resecatâ. l. 15. D. de inoffic. Testam. l. 7. in sin. D. Si Tabul. Testam. null. extab. Unde liber. l. 17. §. 3. D. de Adopt. vid. ad similia. Treutl. vol. 2. disp. 16. thes. 3. in notis. Et ex professo, de hoc statuto, ejusque interpretatione. Laurus de Palatiis per totum, prim. vol. tractat.
units.tr: 18. Hence, if a statute provides that, where males exist, females are excluded, such a statute is not extended, when legitimate and natural children are not present together, to those children who exist only by a legal fiction, such as adopted or legitimated children alone. For this case is odious and would bring great prejudice to children lawfully born of marriage. Indeed that very extension of the statute is contrary to natural equity and to that affection of parents by which they wish their property to be left to children begotten by themselves. Nor does it less diminish the hope of succession that lawful children born in marriage have from the obedience that each one renders to himself, so that the due obedience is also overturned, all way of succeeding being cut off. L. 15, D. de inoffic. testam.; l. 7 in fin., D. Si tabul. testam. null. extab.; hence liberi, l. 17, §. 3, D. de Adopt.; see on similar matters Treutler, vol. 2, disp. 16, thes. 3, in the notes. And expressly, concerning this statute and its interpretation: Laurus de Palatiis throughout, first volume, tractatus.

units.la: 19. Quid si reperiatur in statutis oppositio vel saltem aliqua contrarietas appareat; id est, in iisdem reperiatur vel antiromia, vel enantiophania? Respondeo, vel unum tantum statutum est, in quo aliqua continetur contrarietas, sic ut verba priora posterioribus adversentur. Tumque nihil in illo statuto valere contendunt, sic ut nihil servari velint, quod contraria continens scriptura perplexe comparetur. Arg. l. hac verba. D. verb. signif. l. 16. D. Condit. instit. l. ubi repugnantia. D. Regul. juris. Quam tamen legem postremam, alii scripturae vel instrumento applicatam velint, ubi falsitatis est suspicio, non statuto, quod ab universitate conditum. l. qui falso vel varie. 16. D. de Testibus. Sic ut ultimum statuti capitulum, anterius corrigere velint, per l. 24. D. de legibus. cui potius adjiciam l. 15. in sin. D. de Praescript. vid. Alberic. de Rosate ad l. etsi. Cod. Testam. Tutel. n. 4.
units.tr: 19. What if there is found in the statutes some opposition, or at least some contrariety appears; that is, if in the same statutes there is found either antinomy or enantiophany? I answer: either there is only one statute in which some contrariety is contained, so that the earlier words oppose the later. Then some contend that nothing in that statute is valid, so that they wish nothing to be kept which a writing containing contrary provisions makes confused. Argument from l. hac verba, D. verb. signif.; l. 16, D. Condit. instit.; l. ubi repugnantia, D. Regul. juris. Yet some wish this last rule to be applied to a writing or instrument where there is suspicion of falsity, not to a statute enacted by a corporate body. l. qui falso vel varie, 16, D. de Testibus. So they wish the last chapter of a statute to correct the earlier one, by l. 24, D. de legibus; to which I would rather add l. 15 in fin., D. de Praescript. See Alberic de Rosate on l. etsi, Cod. Testam. Tutel., n. 4.

units.la: 20. Vel plura sunt statuta; & videndum num ad concordiam aliquo modo reduci possint. Quod praesumendum ut plurimum, unum statutum alterius esse declaratorium, uti una pars statuti ab alia declaratur. Nec facile praesumenda correctio, nisi expresse constet, statuentes per posterius statutum prius corrigere voluisse. Adeoque omnia tendanda esse prius, dispiciendumque, num vel aliqua limitatione, vel distinctione inter se conciliari possint; etiam ipsas particulas taxativas negligendo, vel disjunctivas in copulativas, & vice versa resolvendo. Argum. §. 15. de confirmat. D. Ad Senat. & Popul. & §. 15. Const. ad Magnum Senat. l. 26. 28. D. de leg. Ubi Bartol. & Bald. l. si servus plurium. §. sin. D. leg. 1. l. 32. in sin. Cod. Appel l sancimus. Cod. de Testam. l. sepe D. verb signif. Alex. 4. consil. 4. n. 7. Franciscus Vivius in tom. comm. opin. libr. 17. p. 133. ibique Bartol. in l. 1. §. partis. D. quod vi aut clam. Alex. vol. 5. conf. 107. n. 6. Alberic, de Rosate in l. scripturæ. Cod. fide instrum. num. 4. vid. Everhard. in loc. legali: à naturâ dictionis taxativa.
units.tr: 20. Or there are several statutes, and it must be considered whether they can in some way be reduced to agreement. This should ordinarily be presumed: that one statute is declaratory of another, just as one part of a statute is declared by another. Nor is correction easily presumed, unless it clearly appears that those who enacted it wished to correct the earlier by a later statute. Accordingly, every effort must be made first, and it must be examined whether they can be reconciled with one another by some limitation or distinction, even by disregarding the restrictive particles, or by resolving disjunctives into copulatives and vice versa. Argument from §. 15, de confirmat., D. Ad Senat. et Popul., and §. 15, Const. ad Magnum Senatum; l. 26, 28, D. de leg. Where Bartolus and Baldus; l. si servus plurium, §. sin., D. leg. 1; l. 32 in fin., Cod. Appel.; l. sancimus, Cod. de Testam.; l. sepe, D. verb. signif.; Alexander, 4 consilium, n. 7; Franciscus Vivius in the Tomus communium opinionum, book 17, p. 133, and there Bartolus on l. 1, §. partis, D. quod vi aut clam; Alexander, vol. 5, consilium 107, n. 6; Alberic de Rosate on l. scripturae, Cod. fide instrum., n. 4. See Everhard in loco legali: from the nature of a restrictive expression.

units.la: 21. Quod si plura sint statuta, quæ invicem contraria: vel non erunt æque valida, ut in uno forte desint requisita debita; nec tum maximopere erit laborandum, quod unū propter defectum requisitorum, nullius sit efficaciæ. Id quod etiam obtinere volunt, si unum sit publicatum, alterum non æque. Ut illud tantum liget, non hoc. Per DD. in l. omnes populi. D. just. & jure. nov. 66.
units.tr: 21. But if there are several statutes which are contrary to one another, either they will not all be equally valid, as when one perhaps lacks the required formalities, and then one need not labour greatly over the fact that, because of the lack of requisites, one of them has no force. The doctors also wish this to hold if one has been promulgated and the other has not been equally promulgated, so that only the former binds and not the latter; see the doctors on l. omnes populi, D. just. et jure; Novella 66.

units.la: 22. Vel illa plura statuta non erunt æque generalia; tumque posterius speciale non derogabit priori, quod generi per speciem non derogetur: ut hic stricte loquendo, non sit contrarietas, nisi statutum posterius, priori non derogaret, quod esset inutiliter & frustra conditum. c. generi. de Reg. juris in 6. l. in toto jure 80. D. Reg. jur. l. 41. D. de Pœnis. Alex. 6. consil. 58: 89. Mascard. de interpret. statut. concl. 8 per totum.
units.tr: 22. Or those several statutes may not be equally general. In that case the later special statute does not derogate from the earlier one, since a general law is not derogated from by a special one. Strictly speaking, therefore, there is no contrariety unless the later statute would derogate from the earlier one, which would otherwise be enacted uselessly and in vain. c. generi. de Reg. juris in 6. l. in toto jure 80. D. Reg. jur. l. 41. D. de Pœnis. Alex. 6. consil. 58: 89. Mascard. de interpret. statut. concl. 8 per totum.

units.la: 23. Aut statuta quae invicem contraria, aeque sunt generalia, aeque firma, ut nihil in solemnibus, in requisitis desit; tumque si posterius priori ex parte adversetur, etiam ex parte tollit; si in totum, etiam in totum destruit prius, l. ult. D. de Princ. Constit. l. pacta novissima. Cod. de Pact. l. 28. D. de leg. l. 27. in med. Cod. de Testam. l. Sancimus. verb. reliquum vero. Cod. Donat. Clem. dudum. §. nos enim de Sepultur. vid. Christin. ad Mechlin. in Prael. n. 34. 51. Honded. conf. 196. n. 4. Surd. conf. 568. n. 9. Menoch. conf. 196. n. 4. apud Marium. Giurbam obs. 45. n. 17.
units.tr: 23. Or the contrary statutes are equally general and equally firm, and nothing is lacking in the solemnities or the requisites. In that case, if the later statute opposes the earlier one in part, it also repeals it in part; if it opposes it wholly, it also destroys it wholly. l. ult. D. de Princ. Constit. l. pacta novissima. Cod. de Pact. l. 28. D. de leg. l. 27. in med. Cod. de Testam. l. Sancimus. verb. reliquum vero. Cod. Donat. Clem. dudum. §. nos enim de Sepultur. vid. Christin. ad Mechlin. in Prael. n. 34. 51. Honded. conf. 196. n. 4. Surd. conf. 568. n. 9. Menoch. conf. 196. n. 4. apud Marium. Giurbam obs. 45. n. 17.

units.la: 24. Id quod procedere volunt interpretes, etiamsi illa duo statuta eodem tempore confirmata; quod tempus compositionis statuti, non confirmationis velint attendi Arg. l. confirmantur. §. si miles. D. Codic. Bartol. in l. omnes populi. D. just. & jure. n. 35. Verum e contrario dicendum, potius confirmationis, quam compositionis tempus esse spectandum, ut id posterius sit statutum, quod quidem forte primo compositum, postremo tamen fuit confirmatum. Ea quippe demum nostra facimus, quibus nostram impartimur auctoritatem, ut ante confirmationem nihil nostrum censeri debeat, §. pen. Instit. Proem. ibique DD.
units.tr: 24. The interpreters want this to hold even where the two statutes were confirmed at the same time, and they want the time of the drafting of the statute, not of its confirmation, to be considered. Arg. l. confirmantur. §. si miles. D. Codic. Bartol. in l. omnes populi. D. just. & jure. n. 35. On the contrary, it must be said that the time of confirmation, rather than the time of drafting, is to be regarded, so that the statute is the later one which, though perhaps first drafted, was confirmed last. For we make our own those things to which we impart our authority, so that nothing is to be counted as ours before its confirmation. §. pen. Instit. Proem. ibique DD.

units.la: 25. Ut hic etiam rejiciendae veniant omnes illae Doctorum limitationes, qui sine ullo juris aut legum fundamento asserunt,
units.tr: 25. Here too should be rejected all those limitations of the teachers, who assert, without any foundation in law or statute, that:

units.la: 1. Si prius statutum æquias, per posterius, sed durius, non corrigi. Lex quippe servanda, licet dura, & ita etiam statutum. Arg. l. 51. in sin. D. Aquil. l. 12. §. 1. in sin. D. Qui & à quibus manumiss. 2. Si unum statutum prius compilatum, licet postremum in librum redactum, censeri tamen esse prius. Quod equidem non verum, si tempus confirmationis, cum tempore redigendi in librum conjungantur, per dicta anterius. 3. Si prius favorabile, posterius odiosum. 4. Si unum prohibitivum, mandans alterum. Quia er⁣bescimus sine lege loqui. nov. 18. c. 5. in init. dist. varii apud Musc. libr. alleg. concl. 8. n. n. 42. 43 & 4. 5. & seqq. per totum.
units.tr: 1. If an earlier statute is made equitable by a later one but in a harsher way, it is not corrected. For a law must be observed even if it is harsh, and so too a statute. Arg. l. 51. in sin. D. Aquil. l. 12. §. 1. in sin. D. Qui & à quibus manumiss. 2. If one statute was compiled earlier, it is still to be counted as the earlier one even though it was later put into the book. This is certainly not true if the time of confirmation is joined with the time of putting it into the book, according to the cited passages. 3. If the earlier statute is favourable and the later one odious. 4. If one statute is prohibitive and the other mandatory, because we are ashamed to speak without law. nov. 18. c. 5. in init. dist. varii apud Musc. libr. alleg. concl. 8. n. n. 42. 43 & 4. 5. & seqq. per totum.

units.la: 26. Si tamen statutum prius conditum & confirmatum expressam sui velit derogationem, adeoque sit posterioris derogatorium, tunc equidem per posterius non censebitur correctum aut revocatum, nisi posteriori inserta sit expressa derogationis clausula; idque de moribus procederet ad exemplum testamentorum. Arg. l. 22. D de leg. 3. & l. si mihi & tibi. §. in legatis. D. leg. 1. Bartol. in l. omnes populi. D. just. & jur. n. 3. Anton. Burges Repet. Jur. Canon. Tom. 2. in c. cum omnes, de Constit. p. 295. n. 330. & seqq. vid. Guidon. Papa de Compulsorial. litteris. quaest. 1. num. 4. vol. 9. tractat.
units.tr: 26. If, however, an earlier statute, both drafted and confirmed, expressly wishes to be derogated from, and so is derogatory to a later one, then indeed it will not be considered corrected or revoked by the later one, unless an express clause of derogation is inserted in the later one. This would hold according to custom, by analogy with wills. Arg. l. 22. D de leg. 3. & l. si mihi & tibi. §. in legatis. D. leg. 1. Bartol. in l. omnes populi. D. just. & jur. n. 3. Anton. Burges Repet. Jur. Canon. Tom. 2. in c. cum omnes, de Constit. p. 295. n. 330. & seqq. vid. Guidon. Papa de Compulsorial. litteris. quaest. 1. num. 4. vol. 9. tractat.

units.la: SECT. VII. CAP. III.
units.tr: SECTION VII. CHAPTER III.

units.la: 1. Qualem statutum admittat interpretationem, quod vel alterutrum oculum eruendum esse, vel alterutrum manum amputandam, statuit?
units.tr: 1. What interpretation does a statute admit that orders either one of a man's eyes to be put out or one of his hands to be cut off?

units.la: 2. Quale membrum sit amputandam, si simpliciter de membri amputatione statutum loquatur?
units.tr: 2. If a statute speaks simply of cutting off a limb, which limb is to be cut off?

units.la: 3. Si manum amputandam statutum dicet, qualis amputanda veniat?
units.tr: 3. If a statute says a hand is to be cut off, which hand is to be taken?

units.la: 4. Si pœnam imponat percutienti, an sese extendat ad impellentem, ut quis percutiatur?
units.tr: 4. If a statute imposes a penalty on one who strikes another, does it extend also to one who urges someone else to strike?

units.la: 5. Si vetet exportari frumentum &c. an referatur ad illud, quod quis proprii usus gratia exportavit?
units.tr: 5. If a statute forbids the export of flax, oil, grain, etc., does it refer to what someone has exported for his own use?

units.la: 6. Statutum prohibens rem suam vendere, non extenditur ad casum, quo quis eam rem vendidit, ad quam personalem habebat actionem.
units.tr: 6. A statute forbidding a man to sell his own property does not extend to the case in which someone sells a thing against which he had a personal action.

units.la: 7. An si rei per statutum legari prohibita, debeatur æstimatio?
units.tr: 7. If the bequest of a thing is prohibited by statute, is its value owed?

units.la: 8. Statutum exigens probationes per scripturam, ptuVam, num excludat alias species probationum?
units.tr: 8. Does a statute requiring proof by writing exclude other kinds of proof?

units.la: 9. Statutum quod in numero plurali loquitur, etiam ad numerum singularem extendendum.
units.tr: 9. A statute speaking in the plural number is also to be extended to the singular number.

units.la: 10. An quod statutum de filiis loquitur, etiam comprehendat nepotes?
units.tr: 10. Does a statute that speaks of sons also include grandsons?

units.la: 11. Unde statutum jubens, ut in solidum succedant filii, nepotes excludit.
units.tr: 11. Hence a statute ordering that sons succeed in full excludes grandsons.

units.la: 12. Si tamen deficiant filii, admitti poterunt nepotes.
units.tr: 12. If, however, the sons fail, grandsons may be admitted.

units.la: 13. Non tamen ordinarie filiorum appellatione filiae continebuntur.
units.tr: 13. Yet daughters are not ordinarily included under the name of sons.

units.la: 14. An si statutum vocet agnatum ad hæreditatem, excludatur frater uterinus, reliquique cognati?
units.tr: 14. If a statute calls an agnate to the inheritance, is a uterine brother excluded, along with the other kinsmen?

units.la: 15. Statutum de lucro dotis, qualiter explicandum?
units.tr: 15. How is a statute concerning the gain from a dowry to be explained?

units.la: 16. An statutum quod Advocatos quoad actiones personales Curiae Provinciali subjicit, etiam quoad crimina eo dem subjiciat eidem foro?
units.tr: 16. Does a statute that subjects advocates to the provincial court in personal actions also subject them to the same court in criminal charges?

units.la: 1. SUbsequitur membrum tertium, quod in statutorum interpretatione considerandum erat. Scilicet quorundam statutorum sensus erat eruendus, adeoque exempla empla nonnulla in hypothesi proponenda, ex quibus constaret, quid in aliis similibus explicandis obtinere debeat. Et quidem ex innumeris quæstionibus, quæ ad certum ordinem, ad classes certas redigi non commodé poterunt, illustriores, & usum non contemnendum in foro habituras, subjiciam. Quarum prima hæc est.
units.tr: 1. There follows the third point to be considered in the interpretation of statutes. Namely, the sense of certain statutes had to be drawn out, and so some examples are to be put forward in a hypothetical case, from which it may be made clear what ought to hold in explaining other similar statutes. Indeed, out of the countless questions which cannot conveniently be reduced to a fixed order or to certain classes, I shall set out the more notable ones, which will have a use not to be despised in the courts. The first of these is this.

units.la: 1. Si statutum disponat alicui alterutrum oculum eruendum esse, aut manum alterutram amputandam, qualem admittat interpretationem, casu quo, is qui delinquit, altero oculo, vel altera manu caret? Respondeo, licet pœnæ communiter interpretatione molliori temperandæ sint, adeoque in mitiorem partem accipiendæ, quia ut plurimum odiosæ; & in casu proposito, rei durior sit causa in ordine pœnæ statutariæ, quam alterius cujusdam, qui membris orbatus non est, aut mutilus. Quia tamen pœna quæ à statuto imposita, non est eâ gravior, quæ ratione commissi criminis est debita: licet forte accidat, id quod hic non attenditur, eam esse huic facinoroso duriorem. Et reipublicæ quam maxime interest delicta non manere impunita: quæ res est favorabilis. Hac vero occasione accideret, sceleratos ordinarias pœnas evitaturos esse; adeoque spe impunitatis, amplius peccaturos. Dicendum videtur, secundum juris rigorem, alterum oculum eruendum esse, vel alteram manum amputandam. Argum. § 9. Institut. Ad leg. Aquil. l. 23. §. 3. l. 51. §. 2. D. eod. & ita tenuit Bald. in Authent. Sed novo jure. Cod. de furt. & Serv. fugit. & tractat. de statutis, quæst. 5. Etiam hanc sententiam judicando tenuisse consilium Neapolitanum scribit Grammat. decis. 94. Clarus §. Sent. §. final. quæst. 60. num. 5. licet ipse per Principem pœnam temperandam censeat, ideoque in partem mitiorem inclinare videatur. vid. Paulum Grillandum de Relaxat. Carcerator. libr. 5. q. 4. in 4. vol. tract.
units.tr: 1. If a statute provides that one of a man's eyes or one of his hands is to be taken, what interpretation is admitted in the case where the offender lacks one eye or one hand? I answer: although penalties are commonly to be tempered by a milder interpretation, and so are to be taken in the milder sense, because they are for the most part odious; and in the case proposed the defendant's position is harder under the statutory penalty than that of another man who has not lost a limb or been maimed. Yet because the penalty imposed by the statute is not heavier than the one due by reason of the crime committed, even if it happens (which is not considered here) that it is harsher for this wrongdoer. And it is above all in the interest of the commonwealth that crimes do not remain unpunished; this is a favourable matter. Moreover, on this occasion it would come about that criminals would avoid the ordinary penalties, and so, hoping for impunity, would sin further. It seems to be said that, according to the strictness of the law, one eye is to be put out or one hand cut off. Argument from § 9, Institutes, On the Lex Aquilia; l. 23 § 3; l. 51 § 2, D. eod. And so Bartolus held in the Authentica "Sed novo jure," Cod. de furt. et Serv. fugit. and in his treatise de statutis, question 5. Grammaticus, decision 94, writes that the Neapolitan council also held this opinion in judging. Clarus, § Sententia, final question 60, number 5, although he himself thinks the penalty is to be tempered by the Prince, and so seems to incline toward the milder part. See Paulus Grillandus, de Relaxatione Carceratorum, book 5, question 4, in volume 4 of the tracts.

units.la: 2. Quid si statutum absolute loquatur de membri amputatione, vel mutilatione, non expresso membro; quod nam veniat amputandum, disquiritur? Respondeo, quia statutum in dubio talem admittit interpretationem, qualis juri communi maxime est conformis; quo jure non facile, ad membri amputationem proceditur, aut si procedatur, ad ejus membri amputationem, quod quam minimum usum corporis laedit, aut impedit ejusdem officia: dicendum videtur, cum qui deliquit, abscissione potius manus, quam alterius membri puniendum esse. Nisi tamen ipsa criminis qualitas, aliud membrum amputandum esse suaderet. Uti lingua in blasphemo, in perjuro digiti primores. Arg. l. 42. D. de Pœn. Auth. sed novo jure. Cod. De Serv. fugitiv. Novell. 134. c. ult. Gothefred. ibid. & ad l. 3. Cod. eod. Paulus Grillandus de de Relaxat. Carcerat. loc. cit. Gregor. Tholof. Synt. jur. libr. 31. c. 16. n. 6.
units.tr: 2. What if the statute speaks absolutely of cutting off or maiming a limb, without naming the limb; the question is which limb is to be cut off? I answer: because in doubt a statute admits that interpretation which is most in conformity with the common law; and under that law one does not readily proceed to amputation of a limb, or if one does proceed, to the amputation of that limb which harms the use of the body least or impedes its functions least. It seems to be said that the one who has offended is to be punished by the cutting off of the hand rather than of another limb. Unless, however, the very nature of the crime should suggest that another limb is to be cut off: as the tongue for blasphemy, the first fingers for perjury. Argument from l. 42, D. de Poenis; Authentica "Sed novo jure," Cod. de Serv. fugitiv.; Novella 134, last chapter; Godefroy on the same and on l. 3, Cod. eod.; Paulus Grillandus, de Relaxatione Carceratorum, loc. cit.; Gregorius Tholosanus, Syntagma juris, book 31, chapter 16, number 6.

units.la: 3. Quid si statutum dicet alicui facinoroso manum esse amputandam, an dextram, an vero sinistram amputabimus? Respondeo, quia in odiosis, favorabilem communiter sententiam amplectimur, manum sinistram amputandam esse, suadebit interpretatio benigna. Nisi tamen delicti qualitas aliam admitteret interpretationem. Puta, si forte notarius falsi crimen commisisset, & ex forma statuti exigeretur manus amputatio. Tum enim dextram, in quâ peccavit amputandam esse, juris rationi foret congruum. Unde etiam dicendum, in casu quo statutum iuferret manum alicujus esse mutilandam, qui in militiâ turpiter gladium abjecisset, eum pollice truncandum esse ut fiat poltronus, quasi pollice truncus, militiâ indignus, quod eâ parte videatur deliquisse; adeoque æquum esse, ut in eâ parte luat, quâ peccavit. l. interpretatione. D. de Pæn. l. in ambiguis. D. de leg. l. semper in dubiis. l. ea quæ. §. in re dubiâ D. de Reg. jur. Argum. l. & in his D. de Condit. & Demonstr. l. fugitivis. Cod. de serv. sugit. Auth. omnes peregrini. in sin. Cod. Commun. de succeff. c. imperialem. §. Scriba. de prohibit. feud. alienat. libr. 2. feud. Paulus Grilland. de Relaxat. Carcerator. loc. antea alleg. Perez. Cod. de falsf. n. 19. Gothefred. in not. ad nov. 134. c. ult. Gabriel. Naud. de Re Militar.
units.tr: 3. What if the statute says that a hand is to be cut off from some criminal: shall we cut off the right hand or the left? I answer: since in odious matters we commonly embrace the more favourable opinion, a benign interpretation will suggest that the left hand is to be cut off. Unless, however, the nature of the offence admits another interpretation. For instance, if a notary had committed the crime of forgery, and the form of the statute required amputation of the hand, then it would accord with the reason of law that the right hand, in which he sinned, be cut off. Hence it must also be said that, where a statute ordered that the hand of a man who had shamefully thrown away his sword in military service be maimed, he is to be cut off at the thumb so that he becomes a poltronus, as if "thumb-truncated" and unworthy of soldiering, because he seems to have sinned in that part; and so it is fair that he pay in that part with which he sinned. l. interpretatione, D. de Poenis; l. in ambiguis, D. de legibus; l. semper in dubiis; l. ea quae, § in re dubia, D. de Regulis juris; argument from l. et in his, D. de Conditionibus et Demonstrationibus; l. fugitivis, Cod. de Serv. fugit.; Authentica "omnes peregrini," in fine, Cod. Commun. de successionibus; c. imperialem, § Scriba, de prohibita feudi alienatione, book 2 of the Feuds. Paulus Grillandus, de Relaxatione Carceratorum, loc. antea alleg.; Perez, Cod. de falsis, number 19; Godefroy, note on Novella 134, last chapter; Gabriel Naudé, de re militari.

units.la: 4. Quid si statutum poenam imponat percutienti, aut vulneranti, an se se extendet ad eum, qui aliquem stimulando, incitando, causam dedit, ut alius percutiatur & vulneretur. Respondeo, etsi qui occasionem, & causam mali praebet, nonnunquam eadem poenâ dignus judicetur, qua qui malum commisit. Quia tamen id ipsum tum demum secundum jus civile admittitur, cum lex expresse de eo qui causam mali praebuit, loquitur; quod obtinet in l. Cornelia de Sicariis. Et statutum non majorem admittit interpretationem, quam ipsa lex. Etiam distincta sunt, quid fieri vere, & per consequentiam seu interpretative. Neque de casu posteriori statutum loquitur. Stimulatorem talem ordinariâ statuti poenâ non teneri, probabilius videbitur. l. qui occidit. §. pen. l. ult. D. Ad l. Cornel. de Sicar. l. ult. D. de vi bonor. Raptor. l. 1. §. rejicitur. D. de vi & de vi armata. Baldus tract. de Statutis. Quaest. 1. num. 12. & seq. & in simili casu. quaest. 11.
units.tr: 4. What if a statute imposes a penalty on one who strikes or wounds, does it extend also to one who, by goading or inciting someone, gave the occasion for another to be struck and wounded? I answer: although one who offers the occasion and cause of evil is sometimes judged worthy of the same penalty as the one who committed the evil, yet because this is admitted by the civil law only when the law speaks expressly of one who gave the cause of the evil, which holds in the lex Cornelia de sicariis, and because a statute admits no wider interpretation than the law itself; also because it is one thing to do a thing truly and another to do it by consequence or by interpretation, and the statute does not speak of the latter case. It seems more probable that the one who urges on such a man is not bound by the ordinary penalty of the statute. l. qui occidit, § pen.; l. ult., D. ad l. Corneliam de sicariis; l. ult., D. de vi bonorum raptorum; l. 1 § rejicitur, D. de vi et de vi armata. Baldus, tract. de Statutis, question 1, numbers 12 and following, and in a similar case, question 11.

units.la: 5. Quid si statutum sub poena pecuniariâ vetet exportari linum, oleum, frumentum, an etiam extendetur ad ea, quae quispiam vel proprii usus gratia, vel gratiâ familiae exportavit? Respondeo, quia per allegata superius, statutum accipit interpretationem ex jure civili, & quidem talem, quae rationi & aequitati, sit consentanea. Improbum autem censeri posset, nemini licere ad usum proprium um necessaria secum ferre, exĩstumarem cum in poenam statuto comprehensam non incidere, qui gratia sui quid extulit, aut exportavit. l. 4. §. 1. D. de Publican. l. 5. Cod. de vectigal. & Commiss. per Bartol. Alexandr, Jason Natt. allegatos à Christineo ad ll. Mechl. in Prælud. num. 22.
units.tr: 5. What if a statute, under a pecuniary penalty, forbids the export of flax, oil, or grain, does it extend also to those things which someone has exported for his own use or for the use of his family? I answer: because, by what has been said above, the statute takes its interpretation from the civil law, and indeed such an interpretation as accords with reason and equity. It could, however, be judged unreasonable that no one may carry with him the things necessary for his own use; I would judge that one who has taken or exported something for his own needs does not fall into the penalty comprehended in the statute. l. 4 § 1, D. de publicanis; l. 5, Cod. de vectigalibus et commissis; as cited by Bartolus, Alexander, and Jason, Natta, and by Christinaeus on the Mechlin laws, in the Prelude, number 22.

units.la: 6. Quid si statutum sub certa poena prohiberet aliquem rem suam divendere extraneo, aut peregrino, an sese extenderet ad eum, qui rem vendidit, ad quam personalem habebat actionem id est, qui ipsam actionem vendidit? Respondeo, Etsi quandoque aequiparentur res, & actio ad rem, per regulam juris, quod qui habet actionem, ipsam rem habere videatur. Quia tamen ea regula non tam procedit secundum veritatem, quam secundum juris interpretationem. Et impropria est illa locutio, notam impropriietatis, videtur, conjunctam habens. Statuti autem verba proprie sunt accipienda, si non verborum proprietas absurdum contineat sensum. Etiam interpretatio adhibenda secundum veritatem; quâ inspecta, minus est actionem, quam ipsam rem habere. Dicendum erit, statuti poena eum non teneri, qui ad rem actionem vendidit extraneo. l. 15. D. de Reg. jur. l. 204. D. eod. Bartol. Alexander, & alii ad l. 29. §. videndum. D. de liber. & Posthum. hæred. instit. Hieronym. Cagnol. comment. D. ad Reg. jur. 18, num. 16.
units.tr: 6. What if a statute, under a fixed penalty, forbade anyone to sell his property to a foreigner or non-citizen? Would it extend to the person who sold the thing for which he had a personal action, that is, who sold the action itself? I answer: although things and actions are sometimes treated as equivalent, by the rule of law that one who has an action is regarded as having the thing itself. Yet that rule holds not so much according to truth as according to legal interpretation, and the expression "is regarded as" carries the mark of impropriety. Statutory words are to be taken in their proper sense, unless that proper sense yields an absurd meaning. Interpretation must also be made according to truth, and when truth is considered, having an action is less than having the thing itself. It must therefore be said that the statute's penalty does not bind one who sold an action for a thing to a foreigner. l. 15. D. de Reg. jur. l. 204. D. eod. Bartol. Alexander, & alii ad l. 29. §. videndum. D. de liber. & Posthum. hæred. instit. Hieronym. Cagnol. comment. D. ad Reg. jur. 18, num. 16.

units.la: & 9. Petrus Faber. Comment. ad d. l. 15.
units.tr: And 9. Peter Faber, Commentary on the said law 15.

units.la: 7. Quid si statutum rem aliquam legari vetet, puta, rem immobilem ecclesiæ super addita clausula irritante; an saltem ejus rei legatæ debebitur æstimatio? Respondeo, Etsi communiter ita interpretemur ultimas voluntates, ut potius valeant, quam ut pereant: saltem aliquem sortiantur effectum. Etiam rei alienæ legatæ nonnunquam ab hærede præstanda sit æstimatio. Insuper pro legatario plerumque sit præsumendum, quem honorare voluit testator. Et maximus in plerisque sit favor piæ causæ. Tamen quia propter clausulam irritantem tale legatum est ipso jure nullum; & ita quod fieret in fraudem talis statuti. Dicendum erit, ejus legati ne quidem deberi æstimationem.
units.tr: 7. What if a statute forbade the bequest of some thing, for instance an immovable to the Church, with an added irritating clause? Would at least the estimated value of the bequeathed thing be owed? I answer: although we commonly interpret last wills so that they stand rather than fail, so that at least they have some effect; and the value of another's property bequeathed is sometimes to be paid by the heir. Moreover, in favour of the legatee it is generally to be presumed whom the testator wished to honour, and there is very great favour for a pious cause. Yet because by reason of the irritating clause such a legacy is void by law itself, and because what was done would be done in fraud of such a statute, it must be said that not even the estimated value of that legacy is owed.

Sand. decis. 4. lib. 4. tit. 4. ibidemque varii allegati. disp. Wamesius consil. 409. num. 3. & consil. 416. num. 11. De Testamentis. vid. Menoch. de Præsumpt. libr. 4. præsumpt. 20. n. 5, 6. Mantic. de Conjectur. Ultim. volunt. libr. 9. c. 9. n. 9. Renatum Choppinum de Moribus Parisi. 1. tit. 1. n. 8. & de Sacra Politiâ libr. 3. tit. 1.

units.la: 8. Qui si statutum exigat probationes per scripturam seu instrumenta: (quale est statutum Trajectense, & Vianense in causâ locationis & conductionis) an talem admittet interpretationem, ut excludat cæteras omnes probationum species, quales sunt, per binarium testium numerum, per certa indicia; vel etiam probationem factam interpositione juris jurandi voluntarii, secundum sensum Græcorum intellecti? Respondeo, quamvis etiam instrumentorum nomine veniant testes; qui in exequendis litibus, eandem vim obtinent, quam instrumenta. Ut absurdum videatur plus fidei mereri pellem animalis mortui, quam hominis vivi. Quia tamen statuta commemorata loquuntur prohibitive seu negative, id est, ne alia species probationis sit admittenda, quam quæ est per instrumentum locationis; exclusi videbuntur duo testes, etiam conjecturæ & præsumptiones. Quia tamen potissimum ratio & mens statuentium est inspicienda, quæ non alia, nisi ut forte calumniis iretur obviam, & celerius res possit expediri. Probationum itidem materia quantum potest fieri est amplianda, non coangustanda. Nosque insuper oportet statutum sic interpretari, ne absurdū sensum contineat, & ut in casu non expresso, juri civili se accommodet. Insuper nemini est, denegatum, saltem non est denegandum, ut adversarium in propria causa judicem eligat. Nec ad probationis speciem jusjurandum voluntarium refertur: cum ne quidem sit probationis legitimæ spe-cies.
units.tr: 8. But if a statute requires proof by writing or instruments (such as the Utrecht and Viana statutes in a case of letting and hiring), would it admit such an interpretation as to exclude all other kinds of proof, such as by two witnesses or by certain indications, or even proof made by the interposition of a voluntary oath, understood in the sense of the Greeks? I answer: although witnesses also come under the name of instruments, and in carrying out lawsuits they have the same force as instruments, so that it would seem absurd for the hide of a dead animal to deserve more credit than a living man. Yet because the statutes mentioned speak prohibitively or negatively, that is, that no other kind of proof is to be admitted than that by the instrument of lease, two witnesses seem excluded, and conjectures and presumptions too. But the reason and intention of the lawmakers must chiefly be examined, which was none other than that calumnies might perhaps be met and the matter settled more quickly. The matter of proofs, likewise, is to be enlarged as far as possible, not narrowed. We must also interpret the statute so that it does not contain an absurd sense, and so that in a case not expressed it accords with civil law. Moreover, no one is denied, or at least must not be denied, the choice of a judge for his adversary in his own cause. Nor is a voluntary oath referred to a species of proof, since it is not even a species of lawful proof.

units.la: 9. Quid si statutum loquatur in numero plurali,
units.tr: 9. What if the statute speaks in the plural number?

units.la: plurali, an etiam interpretatione extendendum erit ad numerum singularem? Respondeo, aut præcise statutum exigit numerum pluralem, ut si testes ad actus celebrationem adhiberi velit; & dubium non est, quin ad minimum duo adhiberi debeant. Aut statutum ita loquitur in numero plurali, ut eadem ratio, quæ statuto inest, numero singulari applicari possit; tumque ad numerum singularem extendetur. Ita si multam ei imponat, qui verba contumeliosa alicui dixerit; sufficerit hic vel unum verbum contumeliæ gratia illatum. Injuria enim eo ipso illata censebitur, cui statutum obviam ire voluit. Idque propterea quod impunitum aliter esset maleficium: ac facile statuti verba in alterius detrimentum eluderentur, quod fieri non oportuit. Argum. l. ubi numerus. D. de testib. §. 3. in sin. instit. de Testam. Ordin. l. 1. §. 1. D. de Negot. Gest. l. 2. §. quod ait. D. de vi bonor. Raptor. l. 3. in init. D. de Abigeis. Arg. l. 50. in sin. D. Ad leg. Aquil. l. non tantum. D. De legib. Bald. de Statut. Quæst. 9, ibidemque alii allegati.
units.tr: Must it also be extended by interpretation to the singular number? I answer: either the statute expressly requires the plural, as when it wishes witnesses to be present at the performance of an act, and there is no doubt that at least two must be present; or the statute speaks in the plural in such a way that the same reason which underlies it can be applied to the singular, and then it will be extended to the singular. Thus if it imposes a fine on one who has spoken insulting words to another, a single insulting word uttered to injure him will suffice. For the injury will be deemed to have been inflicted by that very act which the statute wished to prevent. This is because otherwise the wrong would go unpunished, and the words of the statute could easily be evaded to another's detriment, which ought not to happen. Argum. l. ubi numerus. D. de testib. §. 3. in sin. instit. de Testam. Ordin. l. 1. §. 1. D. de Negot. Gest. l. 2. §. quod ait. D. de vi bonor. Raptor. l. 3. in init. D. de Abigeis. Arg. l. 50. in sin. D. Ad leg. Aquil. l. non tantum. D. De legib. Bald. de Statut. Quæst. 9, ibidemque alii allegati.

units.la: 10 Quid si statutum filiorum faciat mentionem, an etiam eorum appellatione veniant nepotes? Respondeo; & si negandum non sit, aliquando in jure filiorum appellatione nepotes comprehendi. Quia tamen ubique non est par ratio filiorum & nepotum, quod illi sint gradu proximiores, hi remotiores. Et à proprietate verborum ad improprietatem, in præjudicium filiorum non est recurrendum. Nisi aliud suadeat mens statuentis, vel præsumptio & justâ interpretatio; appellatione filiorum excludendos esse nepotes existumarem. §. sin. Instit. de Testam. Tutel. l. 6. D. de Testam. Tutel. l. 220. §. 1. D. de verb. signif. l. 59. D. de Ritu. Nupt. l. 41. §. 5. D. de leg. 3. l. 201. D. de verb. Signif. l. 6. Cod ad Sen. Macedon. l. 34. Cod. de inoff. Testam. Prolixe Gabriel comm. opin. libr. 6. de verb. signif. conclus. 1. cum limit. & sublim.
units.tr: 10. What if the statute makes mention of sons: are grandsons also included under the name of sons? I answer: if it cannot be denied that sometimes in law grandsons are comprehended under the name of sons, yet the position of sons and grandsons is not everywhere the same, since the former are nearer in degree and the latter more remote. And one must not pass from the proper meaning of words to an improper one to the prejudice of sons. Unless the intention of the one enacting the statute, or a presumption and just interpretation, suggests otherwise, I would judge that grandsons are excluded by the name of sons. §. sin. Instit. de Testam. Tutel. l. 6. D. de Testam. Tutel. l. 220. §. 1. D. de verb. signif. l. 59. D. de Ritu. Nupt. l. 41. §. 5. D. de leg. 3. l. 201. D. de verb. Signif. l. 6. Cod ad Sen. Macedon. l. 34. Cod. de inoff. Testam. Prolixe Gabriel comm. opin. libr. 6. de verb. signif. conclus. 1. cum limit. & sublim.

units.la: 11. Unde quæsitum: an si statutum disponat, ne pater valeat efficere, quin filii sui in totum succedant, nepotes jure merito cum filiis admittere possit, aut hæreditatem universam relinquendo nepotibus, statuto satisfacere? Respondeo, quoniam Statutum principaliter, in gratiam filiorum est conditum. Etiam sufficienter verificari potest in filiis, licet interpretatione non extendatur, ad nepotes. Et quod in cujusdam favorem est introductum, in eorum torqueri nequit præjudicium. Multo minus adversus intentionem statuentis impropriam & latissimam admittere significationem. Præsertim cum tale statutum sese conformet juris communis dispositioni, per quod ad successionem vocantur soli filii: dicendum parentem nepotibus gratificando, statuto non satisfecisse. Argum. l. 201. D. de verb. Signif. l. 12. D. liber, & Posthum. hared. Nov. 118. c. 1. Gotefred. in comm. ad l. 6. D. de Testament. Tutel. & ad l. 84. D. de verb. Signif. Menoch. 4. præsumpt. 94. n. 15. Cravetta, in simili. consil. 588. Tessaurus libr. Singul. Quæst. Forensi. 91. per totum.
units.tr: 11. Hence the question arises: if a statute provides that a father may not act so that his sons do not succeed entirely, may he rightly admit grandsons along with the sons, or may he satisfy the statute by leaving the whole inheritance to the grandsons? I answer: since the statute was enacted principally for the sake of sons, it can be sufficiently fulfilled in sons, even though it is not extended by interpretation to grandsons. What was introduced for the favour of certain persons cannot be turned to their prejudice. Much less may one admit against the intention of the one enacting it an improper and very broad meaning. Especially since such a statute conforms itself to the provision of common law, by which only sons are called to the succession; so it must be said that a parent who gratifies grandsons has not satisfied the statute. Argum. l. 201. D. de verb. Signif. l. 12. D. liber, & Posthum. hared. Nov. 118. c. 1. Gotefred. in comm. ad l. 6. D. de Testament. Tutel. & ad l. 84. D. de verb. Signif. Menoch. 4. præsumpt. 94. n. 15. Cravetta, in simili. consil. 588. Tessaurus libr. Singul. Quæst. Forensi. 91. per totum.

units.la: 12. Quid si itaque statutum disponat, ut mater filiis sua bona relinquat, an non saltem ipsis deficientibus, relinquenda erunt nepotibus? Respondeo, licet verba statuti strictam admittant interpretationem, dum agitur de præjudicio filiorum; dumque exorbitat à jure communi rationabili. Quia tamen, si versamur in favorabilioribus, appellatione filiorum nonnunquam continentur nepotes. Dicendum erit, iis non existentibus, hosce admittendos esse. l. 84. D. de Verbor. Signif. l. 7. Cod. de Secund. Nupt. l.
units.tr: 12. What if, then, a statute provides that a mother shall leave her goods to her sons: must they not, at least when the sons are lacking, be left to the grandsons? I answer: although the words of the statute admit a strict interpretation while the matter concerns the prejudice of sons, and while it departs from reasonable common law, yet if we are dealing with more favourable matters, grandsons are sometimes included under the name of sons. It must be said that, when sons do not exist, grandsons are to be admitted. l. 84. D. de Verbor. Signif. l. 7. Cod. de Secund. Nupt. l.

units.la: 13. Verum, an etiam si statutum filiorum faciat mentionem, eorum appellatione fœminæ continebuntur? Respondeo, etsi communiter in jure sub verbo masculino etiam comprehendatur fœmininum. Quia tamen permulta locorum statutis,masculis sunt concessa, quæ fœminis, quarum conditio in multis juris articulis est deterior, sunt denegata. Ex mente statuentium ubi de jure prælationis agitur, fœminas exclusas esse, vero similius est. Ita statutum feudum deferens filiis, censetur exclusisse filias. Et statutum Trajectense aliquid tribuens filio natu majori jure præcipui, non continebit filiam natu majorem. Cum enim non indefinitè, sed specificè statutum loquatur, exclusa etiam filia censebitur. l. 1. l. 172. D. de verbor. signific. l. 9. D. de Stat. Homin. l. 116. D. de verbor. Signif. l. 122. D. eod. Gotefred. in comment. ad l. 1. D. de verb. signif. lit. m. Nizol. Allegat. 19. num. 76. 77. vid. tamen Baldum de statut. Quæst. 10. Gabriel. commun. Opinion. libr. 6. conclus. 7. num. 4. Cujac. accurate in sin. libr. 2. tit. 11. feud. Molin. ad consuet. Parisf. tit. 1. §. 12. num. 1. p. 247. vid. Anton. Merend. libr. 10. c. 8. 9. contr. jur. tom. 2,
units.tr: 13. But is it also the case that, if a statute mentions sons, daughters are included under the name "sons"? I answer: although in law the masculine term commonly includes the feminine as well, nevertheless, since in very many places statutes have granted things to males that have been denied to females, whose position is worse in many articles of the law, it is more likely that, according to the intention of the lawmakers where the right of precedence is concerned, females are excluded. Thus a statute granting a fief to sons is held to exclude daughters. And a Utrecht statute that grants something to the eldest son by right of preciput will not include the eldest daughter. For since the statute speaks not indefinitely but specifically, the daughter will also be deemed excluded. L. 1, l. 172, D. de verb. signific.; l. 9, D. de Stat. Homin.; l. 116, D. de verb. Signif.; l. 122, D. eod.; Gothofredus, commentary on l. 1, D. de verb. signif., lit. m; Nizolius, Allegat. 19, num. 76, 77. But see Baldus, de statut., Quaest. 10; Gabriel, Commun. Opinion., lib. 6, concl. 7, num. 4; Cujacius, accurately at the end of lib. 2, tit. 11 of the feuds; Molinaeus on the Custom of Paris, tit. 1, §. 12, num. 1, p. 247. See also Antonius Merenda, lib. 10, c. 8, 9, Contr. jur., tom. 2.

units.la: 14. Quid si statutum agnatum vocet ad hæreditatem, excludetur ne frater uterinus, reliquique cognati? Respondeo; etsi de jure civili differentia sit sublata inter agnatos & cognatos, effectu aliquo inspecto; sic ut ex æquo ad intestati bona admittantur, si modo in eodem sint gradu. Etiam fratres uterini in tantum habeant jura agnationis, ut ulterioris gradus agnatis præferantur; licet cum fratribus utroque parente junctis, non admittantur. Si tamen statutum expresse vocet agnatum; & statuti verba sensu propio sint accipienda: nec agnatorum nomine veniant cognati. Dicendum erit existentibus agnatis, licet gradu remotioribus, uterinos fratres caeterosque cognatos exclusos esse. l. 15. §.
units.tr: 14. What if a statute calls the agnate to the inheritance: is the uterine brother excluded, and the other cognates as well? I answer: although in civil law the difference between agnates and cognates has been abolished, as far as the effect goes, so that they are admitted equally to the goods of one who dies intestate, provided they are in the same degree; and uterine brothers even have rights of agnation to such an extent that they are preferred to agnates of a more remote degree, although they are not admitted together with brothers joined to the deceased by both parents. If, however, the statute expressly calls the agnate, and the words of the statute are to be taken in their proper sense, then cognates do not come under the name of agnates. It must be said that, where agnates exist, even though more remote in degree, uterine brothers and the other cognates are excluded. L. 15. §.

units.la: 15. Quid si statutum de lucro dotis vel ex parte mariti, vel ex parte uxoris, disponat, id quod de moribus in multis obtinet territoriis; qualis admittenda sit interpretatio, disquiritur anxie? Respondeo, quia in illo statuto explicando alii ex professo laborarunt, omnesque casus explicarunt prolixe, nolim hic, quod nostris jam moribus, frequentatur nimium, plagiarium, aut collectorem agere; atque adeo bonos auctores, qui consulendi, lectoris avidi manibus excutere, in gratiam quorundam ignavorum, qui soliti non res ipsas, sed numerum dd. ponderare. vid. Bald. in l. 1. Cod. de Condit. ob causs. Johann Campegium de dote. part. 5. q. 8. 9. 10. 11. Et an habeat locum in bonis feudalibus?
