Cacialupi. tract. de feud. cognit. artic. 5 n. 11. vol. 2. tract. p. 119. & p. 121, n. 24, videatur tur. etiam Boer.ad Bituricens.tit. 8.§.4.Roland. à Valle.de lu:ro dot. Gilken.ad l.1.Cod.Summ. Trinit. Francisc. Vivius. in vol. comm. opin. libr. 17.verb.statutum.p, 339. Quetta conf. 63.n. 5.
units.tr: 15. What if a statute on the gain from a dowry disposes of it, either on the husband's side or on the wife's, as is the custom in many territories? What interpretation is to be admitted is a question much anxiously debated. I answer: since others have expressly worked on the explanation of that statute and have explained all its cases at length, I would not wish here to play the plagiarist or compiler, which is practised all too often in our present age, nor to snatch good authors, who are to be consulted, from the hands of an eager reader, for the sake of certain lazy men who are accustomed to weigh not the matters themselves but the number of doctors. See Bald. on l. 1, Cod. de Condit. ob causam; Johannes Campegius, de dote, part. 5, q. 8, 9, 10, 11. And whether it has a place in feudal goods: Cacialupus, tract. de feud. cognit., artic. 5, n. 11, vol. 2; tract. p. 119, and p. 121, n. 24; see also Boerius on Bituricensis, tit. 8, §. 4; Rolandus a Valle, de lucro dotis; Gilkenius on l. 1, Cod. Summ. Trinit.; Franciscus Vivius, in vol. Comm. Opin., lib. 17, verb. statutum, p. 339; Quetta, conf. 63, n. 5.

units.la: 16. Concludam materiam de interpretatione statutorum insigni & inter practicos agitata quæstione; An si statutum disponat (quale est Curiæ Ultraj. Rubr. de Advoc. n. 13.) Advocatum in actione, vel in omni actione personali, conveniri non debere, coram judice inferiori, eundem eximat judicis inferioris jurisdictioni, id est urbis Ultrajectinæ, quoad crimina? Respondeo, Ut si negari non poterit, quin statutum admittat declarationem & interpretationem, nonnunquam etiam prorogationem seu extensionem de uno casu in alium, per superius allegatos textus & doctores. Etiam actionis nomine quandoque veniat accusatio. l. qui accusant. juncta gloss. Cod. Edend. Rubr. Cod. quando civil. actio crimin. præjudicet. Censeri tamen (salvo meliore judicio) Advocatum in criminalibus coram judicibus inferioribus conveniri posse, imo debere.
units.tr: 16. I will conclude the discussion of interpreting statutes with a notable question much debated among the practitioners. If a statute (such as that of the Court of Utrecht, Rubric. on Advocates, n. 13) provides that an advocate ought not to be sued in an action, or in every personal action, before a lower judge, does it exempt him from the jurisdiction of the lower judge, that is, of the city of Utrecht, as regards crimes? I answer: it cannot be denied that a statute admits declaration and interpretation, and sometimes also prorogation or extension from one case to another, by the texts and doctors cited above. Also, under the name of action, accusation is sometimes included: l. qui accusant, with the gloss, Cod. Edend.; Rubr. Cod. quando civil. actio crimin. praejudicet. Nevertheless, it is my view (saving a better judgment) that an advocate may be sued in criminal matters before inferior judges, and indeed must be.

units.la: 1. Quia statutum non est interpretatione extendendum de casu in casum toto genere diversum, multo minus contrarium, per superius allegata. Verum certum est, causas civiles valde diversas esse à causis criminalibus. Unde etiam aliæ dilationes in civilibus, aliæ in criminalibus admittuntur. Aliaque etiam est causa delinquendi, alia contrahendi. Ut diversorum diversa esse debeat ratio. l. 1. in sin. & l sin. D. de fer. l. 2. 3. Cod. Ut intra cert. temp. crimi. causf. l. 13. Cod. de jud. Bald. quaest. 1. de Statut. num. 10. & quaest. 4. num. 1. & 2.
units.tr: 1. Because a statute is not to be extended by interpretation from one case to another wholly different in kind, much less to a contrary one, as the authorities above show. It is certain that civil causes are very different from criminal causes. Hence other delays are admitted in civil matters and others in criminal ones. The cause of committing a crime is also different from the cause of contracting, so the reasoning must differ for things that differ. l. 1 in sin. & l. sin. D. de fer. l. 2, 3 Cod. Ut intra cert. temp. crimi. causf. l. 13 Cod. de jud. Bald. quaest. 1. de Statut. num. 10 & quaest. 4 num. 1 & 2.

units.la: 2. Quia statuti verba proprie sunt accipienda, non abusive, nisi urgens ratio contrarium suaderet per allegata superioribus dispp. Verum certum est, in jure negotiorum nomine non venire delicta aut crimina publica, aut actionis verbo accusationem, nisi dura admodum catachresi, quam statutis applicare velle, ubi commodus ejus sensus haberi potest, absurdum est. Rubric. & tot. tit. Instit. de Action. Eadem Rubrica D. Rubric. D. & Cod. & Decretal. de Accusat. §. 1. & 15. Instit. de Action. l. 25. l. 37. D. eod. l. 178. §. 1.
units.tr: 2. Because the words of a statute are to be taken properly, not abusively, unless a pressing reason suggests otherwise, as the authorities cited above show. It is certain that in law the word "business" (negotia) does not cover public offences or crimes, nor does the word "action" cover accusation, except by a very harsh catachresis. It is absurd to want to apply such a catachresis to statutes where a more convenient sense is available. Rubric. & tot. tit. Instit. de Action. Eadem Rubrica D. Rubric. D. & Cod. & Decretal. de Accusat. §. 1. & 15. Instit. de Action. l. 25. l. 37. D. eod. l. 178. §. 1.

units.la: 2. Verb. signif. Rubr. Cod Ut nemo invitus agere vel accusare cogatur. Jason. ad Inst. Inst. de Action. Sneidwin. Instit. eod. ad § actio. n. num. 1. Bacchov. Vinn. aliique eod. loc.
units.tr: 2. Verb. signif. Rubr. Cod. Ut nemo invitus agere vel accusare cogatur. Jason on the Institutes, Institutes, De actionibus; Sneidwin, on the Institutes of the same title, on the words "actio", number 1; Bacchov, Vinnius and others in the same place.

units.la: Quinimo quando statutum utitur verbis legalibus, intelligendum est secundum naturam istorum terminorum. Nisi ex indiciis aut circumstantiis aliud quid colligi possit. Ut ita mens statuentium fiat clara. Bald consil. 212. in sin. lib. 5. cit. à Jacob Schulz. observ. forens. 31. num. 4.
units.tr: Moreover, when a statute uses legal terms, it is to be understood according to the nature of those terms, unless something else can be gathered from indications or circumstances, so that the intention of the enactors becomes clear. Bald consil. 212 in sin. lib. 5. cit. à Jacob Schulz. observ. forens. 31. num. 4.

units.la: 3. Id quod procedit, si quando ne quidem in una parte statuti sub actionibus crimina comprehenduntur. Ut hinc sumatur indicium, quid velint statuentes per actiones intelligere. Cumque in libro statutorum unum ab alio accipiat interpretationem, per allegata superioribus thesibus, etiam id hic obtinere, congruum erit. vid. Cur. Provinc. Ultraj. Rubric. 3. artic. 24. & Rubric. de Advoc. art. 13. junct. Rubric. Statuti Ultraj. civitat. Rubric. 21.
units.tr: 3. This holds good where crimes are not included under actions in any part of the statute. From this an indication may be drawn of what the enactors mean by actions. And since in a body of statutes one takes its interpretation from another, as shown in the theses above, it will be fitting for this to hold here too. Vid. Cur. Provinc. Ultraj. Rubric. 3. artic. 24. & Rubric. de Advoc. art. 13. junct. Rubric. Statuti Ultraj. civitat. Rubric. 21.

units.la: 4. Accedit, quod unum statutum ab alio, etiam non eodem libro contentum recipiat interpretationem. Et quidem ita, ut debeant illa justa interpretatione & distinctione inter sese conciliari. Neque enim credendum est statuentes in uno aut altero statuto sibi fuisse contrarios, aut sese correxisse, nisi illa correctio expresse probetur. Jason. in l. triticum. 94. num. 6. D. de verb. obligat. - Cravett. Consil. 307. num 3. -- Alexand. in l. 1. in Princ. num. 4. D. Oper. Nov. Nunciat. Memoch. lib. 6. Praef. 38. num. 2. vid. & anteriora.
units.tr: 4. Add that one statute receives interpretation from another, even one contained in a different book. And indeed they must be reconciled with one another by a just interpretation and distinction. For it is not to be believed that the enactors contradicted themselves in one statute or another, or corrected themselves, unless that correction is expressly proved. Jason in l. triticum. 94. num. 6. D. de verb. obligat. - Cravett. Consil. 307. num 3. -- Alexand. in l. 1. in Princ. num. 4. D. Oper. Nov. Nunciat. Memoch. lib. 6. Praef. 38. num. 2. vid. & anteriora.

units.la: 5. Quod in tantum etiam procedit, ut licet forte statuti verba (de jure civili accepta) talem sensum admitterent, qualem pars adversa illi tribuit, (contra quam obtinet in casu propositio) non tamen ille sensus procedere deberet, propter aliud statutum, ab eodem auctore conditum, ex quo deberet declarari.
units.tr: 5. This holds to such an extent that, even if the words of a statute (taken in the sense of civil law) would admit the meaning which the opposing party gives them, against which the proposition in this case holds, that meaning ought nonetheless not to prevail, on account of another statute enacted by the same author, by which it ought to be declared.

units.la: Bald. Consil. 408. num. 9. v. & in hanc. vol.
units.tr: Bald. Consil. 408. num. 9. v. & in hanc. vol.

units.la: 1. Castrens. Consil. 468. num. 9. volum. 1. & consil. 94. num. 2. eod. vol. Berlich. decis. 115. num. 11. Nam si statutum suppleri debeat à jure communi, multo magis ab alio statuto ejusdem conditoris: quale jam allegatum d. Rubric. 21. Ordinarie quippe præsumendum statuentem velle potius conservare, statuta; quæ à se profecta, quam jus commune. Arg. l. Si hominem. D. Mund. l. forma. Cod. off. Præf. Prætor. Anchor. consil. 93. in v. non obstat. Romän. consil. 399. apud Montan. de Tutel. c. 33. n. 40.
units.tr: 1. Castrens. Consil. 468. num. 9. volum. 1. & consil. 94. num. 2. eod. vol. Berlich. decis. 115. num. 11. For if a statute must be supplemented by the common law, much more must it be supplemented by another statute of the same enactor, such as the Rubric. 21 already cited. For it is ordinarily to be presumed that the enactor wishes rather to preserve the statutes that proceeded from himself than the common law. Arg. l. Si hominem. D. Mund. l. forma. Cod. off. Præf. Prætor. Anchor. consil. 93. in v. non obstat. Romän. consil. 399. apud Montan. de Tutel. c. 33. n. 40.

units.la: 6. Quicquid sit negari non poterit, quin ita sint interpretanda statuta, ne quid inde proveniat absurdi, iniqui, aut ea condita censeantur in alterius præjudicium. Quod adeo verum est, ut hac de causa etiam à propria significatione recedere liceat. Maxime cum etiam ipsa principalia rescripta sic interpretari soleamus, quæ aliter latissime dicuntur accipienda. Unde si tale statutum Curiæ Provinc. Ultraj. ita interpretaremur, ut sub actionibus continerentur crimina, tenderet interpretatio prejudicii jurisdictionis urbi quondam concessæ in criminalibus, eo ipso, quod advocati per illud Provincialis Curiæ statutum eximerentur. l. nec audiendus. D. de oper. lib. l. nam absurdum. D. de bon. libert. Argum. l. pen. D. de Constit. Princ. l. 2. §. 10. & 16. D. Ne quid in loc. Publ. Bartol. aliique liique citati apud Andr. Kolh. declar. const. March. post pact. dot. & succ. conjug. quest. 7. num 14. & seq. Quinimo si ratione delictorum, jurisdictio praesertim criminalis concessa fuisset Curiae Provincialis Senatoribus, in Advocatos, non utique hoc ita frigide propositum fuisset dicta ordinatione, nulla meri imperii facta mentione. Quod cum specialem legem desideret, nec contineatur generali & indefinita oratione, eo etiam trahi non debuit. Arg. l. 2. D. off. ejus cui mand. jurisd. l. 6. D. Pignor. & hypoth. l. ult. D. Supell. leg. Molin. ad Consf. Paris. §. 1. Gloss. 5. num. 48.
units.tr: 6. Whatever be the case, it cannot be denied that statutes must be interpreted in such a way that nothing absurd or unjust follows from them, and that they are not thought to have been enacted to the prejudice of another. This is so true that, for this reason, it is permissible even to depart from their proper meaning, since we are accustomed to interpret even principal rescripts of the prince in this way, although otherwise they would be understood in the widest sense. Hence, if we were to interpret the statute of the Provincial Court of Utrecht so that crimes were contained under the actions, the interpretation would tend to the prejudice of the jurisdiction once granted to the city in criminal matters, for the very reason that advocates were exempted by that statute of the Provincial Court. See the law "nec audiendus," D. de operis libertorum; the law "nam absurdum," D. de bonis libertorum; the argument from the law "pen.," D. de constitutionibus principum; the law 2, §§ 10 and 16, D. ne quid in loco publico; Bartolus and others cited by Andreas Kolh, declaration on the Constitution of March after the pact of dowry and succession of spouses, question 7, numbers 14 and following. Moreover, if jurisdiction, especially criminal jurisdiction by reason of offences, had been granted to the senators of the Provincial Court over advocates, that ordinance would certainly not have been so coldly framed without any mention of mere imperium. Since this would require a special law, and is not contained in a general and indefinite expression, it ought not to be drawn into that sense either. See the argument from the law 2, D. officium ejus cui mandata est jurisdictio; the law 6, D. de pignoribus et hypothecis; the last law, D. de supellectile legata; Molinaeus on the Consuetudines of Paris, §1, Gloss 5, number 48.

units.la: SECTIO OCTAVA.
units.tr: SECTION EIGHT.

units.la: CAPUT PRIMUM.
units.tr: CHAPTER ONE.

units.la: 1. Quae statutorum requisita, ut ullarum sint virium?
units.tr: 1. What requirements must statutes meet in order to have any force?

units.la: 2. Utrum statuta statim obligent atque sunt publicata?
units.tr: 2. Do statutes bind at once, as soon as they are published?

units.la: 3. Utrum statuta referenda sint ad sutura tantum negotia; an etiam ad praeterita? cum variis limitt. & Sublimit.
units.tr: 3. Are statutes to be referred only to future transactions, or also to past ones? With various limitations and sub-limitations.

units.la: 4. An quod esi contra statuta gestum, sit ipso jure nullum?
units.tr: 4. Is that which is done contrary to a statute null by the very force of law?

units.la: SECT. VIII. CAP. I.
units.tr: SECT. VIII. CAP. I.

units.la: 1. POstquam de conditoribus statutorum eorumque variis interpretandi modis actum est, quæ equidem materia est optima, & subtilis, Sainson. ad Turon. tit 1. §. 5. p. 9. suadet bona methodus, ut post causas, essectus varii inde resultantes primum in genere; dein in specie explicentur. Nullorum tamen ulla erit vis aut efficacia, nisi tria adsint requisita. Quorum unum si desit, viribus statuta destituentur. Primum est, ut condantur rite, & juste ab iis qui condendi habent auctoritatem. Secundum, ut condita promulgentur. Tertium, ut promulgata, recipiantur. DD. apud Muscard. de Statutor. interpret. conclus. 8. seqq.
units.tr: 1. Now that we have discussed the founders of statutes and the various ways of interpreting them, which is indeed a most excellent and subtle subject (Sainson on Tours, tit. 1, §5, p. 9), sound method suggests that, after the causes, the various effects resulting from them be explained first in general and then in particular. Yet statutes will have no force or efficacy unless three requisites are present. If any one of these is lacking, the statutes are deprived of their force. The first is that they be enacted duly and justly by those who have authority to enact them. The second is that what has been enacted be promulgated. The third is that what has been promulgated be received. (The doctors, cited in Muscardus, De interpretatione statutorum, concl. 8 et seq.)

units.la: 2. Secundi requisiti consideratione, occurrit illa difficultas, utrum statuta obligent simulac lata sunt, & publicata? Respondeo, quandoquidem statuta non obligant, antequam fuerint intellecta, adeoque innotuerint, id quod statim fieri non potest l. 9. Cod. de leg non etiam videbuntur statuta simulac promulgata sunt ad obedientiam sui municipes obligare. Nec tamen quemadmodum in legum promulgatione, duorum mensium spatium erit exspectandum. Novell. 66. verum tempus modicum, quo commode in notitiam incolarum perveniant. Arg. l. 2. §. 4 D. origin. jur. Idque propterea, ne probabilis ignorantia possit allegari: quæ transgressores excusaret. DD. l. 8. 9. D. & Cod. jur. & facti. ignor.
units.tr: 2. In regard to the second requisite, the difficulty arises whether statutes bind as soon as they have been enacted and published. I answer: since statutes do not bind before they have been understood, and so have become known, which cannot happen immediately (l. 9 Cod. de legibus), they are not to be regarded as binding the obedience of their subjects the moment they are promulgated. Nor, however, must an interval of two months be awaited, as in the promulgation of laws (Novell. 66); rather a short time is to be allowed in which they can conveniently come to the knowledge of the inhabitants (cf. l. 2 §4 D. de origine juris). This is so that a plausible ignorance may not be pleaded, which would excuse transgressors (the doctors, l. 8, 9 D. and Cod. de juris et facti ignorantia).

units.la: Et maxime in recens incolâ facto præsumitur, ignorantia, nisi aliquam jam moram fecerit, in illo municipio. Ut tamen hic nihil certi circa tempus sit determinandum, verum quicquid in dubium trahitur, judicis prudentis relinquendum veniat arbitrio.vid. Gail.2.obs.48. Menoch. 2.Præsumpt. 3.n. 8. & prolixe Mascardum de interpret. Statutor. conclus. 6. n. 144. & seqq. quem hic transcriptum nolui.
units.tr: And especially in the case of a newly arrived inhabitant, ignorance is presumed, unless he has already spent some time in that municipality. Yet nothing certain is to be fixed here regarding the time; whatever is brought into doubt must be left to the discretion of a prudent judge. See Gail, 2 obs. 48; Menochius, 2 Praesumpt. 3, n. 8; and, at length, Muscardus, De interpretatione statutorum, concl. 6, n. 144 et seq., whom I have chosen not to transcribe here.

units.la: 3. Subsequitur altera nec minor, sed intricatior longe, difficultas, quæ etiam in materia legum occurrit: num quæ statuta lata sunt & promulgata, etiam ad præterita, referri debeant negotia? Respondeo, si statuta simpliciter loquantur, ad exemplum legum, nonnisi ad futura negotia referri debebunt. l. leges. Cod de leg. l. antep. & pen. Cod. de Sacrof. Eccles. DD. in Auth. de Nupt. in Princ. §. duo igitur. c. sin. de Constit. Clement. 2. in sin. de judic.
units.tr: 3. There follows another difficulty, no less but far more intricate, which also arises in the matter of laws: do statutes that have been enacted and promulgated apply to past transactions? I answer: if statutes speak simply, after the manner of laws, they ought to be referred only to future transactions (l. leges Cod. de legibus; l. antepenult. and penult. Cod. de sacrosanctis ecclesiis; the doctors on Auth. de nuptiis in princ., §duo igitur; c. sin. de constitutionibus; Clem. 2, in fin. de judiciis).

units.la: Nec tamen ad omnia futura; saltem non ad ea quibus homines ad delinquendum invitarentur. Finge, statuta remittere male facta, de præterito, veniam dare delictis, non equidem illa trahenda ad futura. Arg. l. 27. §. 3. in sin. & §. 4. D. de Pact. l. cum lex. D. de leg. ibi Bartol. & Bald. Salicet. in l. 2. Cod gener. Abolit.
units.tr: Nor, however, do they apply to all future matters; at least not to those by which men would be invited to commit offences. Suppose statutes remit wrongs done in the past and pardon past crimes; these certainly are not to be extended to the future (cf. l. 27 §3 in fin. and §4 D. de pactis; l. cum lex D. de legibus, where Bartolus and Baldus; Salicetus on l. 2 Cod. de generali abolitione).

units.la: Quod dictum statuta nonnisi ad præterita referri id varias admittit exceptiones, quas omnes, saltem plerasque recensebo.
units.tr: That statutes are referred only to past matters admits various exceptions, all of which, or at least most of them, I shall list.

units.la: 1 Excipe, nisi nominatim ad praeterita referantur. d. l. leges. Quod tamen non intelligendum de praeteritis diu & antiquis negotiis, aut quorum memoria non amplius extat; quod hinc occasio litium & confusionis omnium rerum, atque jurium oriretur. l. minime. l. sed & ea quae longa. D. leg. Nisi tamen & in iis id ipsum suaderet evidens necessitas, vel publica utilitas. Arg. l. 2. D. de Princ. Constit.
units.tr: 1. Let it be excepted: unless they are expressly referred to past matters (said l. leges). This, however, is not to be understood of past affairs that are long ago and ancient, or whose memory no longer survives, since occasion for lawsuits and confusion of all things and rights would thence arise (l. minime; l. sed et ea quae longa D. de legibus). Nevertheless, even in these cases the same is to be done if clear necessity or public utility should so advise (cf. l. 2 D. de principum constitutionibus).

units.la: Quod etiam non intelligendum esse censent doctores, in praeteritis, duris, rigidis, & odiosis; de quibus tamen addubitarem. vid. Bartol. in l. omnes populi. D. just. & jur. n. 51. quaest. 5. in Princ. Masc. libr. all. concl. sin. n. 59. 61. 62.
units.tr: This too the doctors think is not to be understood of past matters that are harsh, rigid and odious; yet I would doubt this. See Bartolus on l. omnes populi D. de justitia et jure n. 51, quaest. 5 in princ.; Muscardus, lib. all. concl. fin., nn. 59, 61, 62.

units.la: Quod etiam non intelligendum de praeteritis pendentibus, quod res non sit integra; nisi & expresse pendentia sint excepta. Masc. concluf. 13.
units.tr: This also is not to be understood of past matters that are pending, since the affair is not yet whole, unless pending matters are also expressly excepted (Muscardus, concl. 13).

units.la: Multo minus de praeteritis jam decisis, aut brevi terminandis: puta si fuerit renunciatum allegationibus utrimque, si conclusum sit in causa. Abbas & DD. in c. sin. de Constit n. 9. Nisi tamen expresse statuta ad decisa referantur d. l. 7. Cod. leg. Ut tamen decisis, non laedatur jus tertio jam quaesitum. Aut si laedatur, id fiat publica suadente utilitate, per notata a me in tit. de Princ. Constit. circ. sin.
units.tr: Much less of past matters already decided, or soon to be concluded: for instance, if the pleadings have been closed on both sides, and the cause has been concluded (the abbot and the doctors on c. sin. de constitutionibus n. 9). Unless, however, statutes are expressly referred to matters already decided (d. l. 7 Cod. de legibus). Yet, once matters are decided, the right already acquired by a third party is not to be injured; or if it is injured, that happens because public utility urges it, as I have noted in my title de principum constitutionibus, near the end.

units.la: Quid si, casu quo ad pendentia negotia referendum sit statutum, quod in priori instantiâ decisum est, pendeat coram judice appellationis: an etiam ad illam causam referri debebit, quasi adhuc pendentem? Resp. Quod non. Judex quippe appellationis judicans de sententiæ iniquitate, sese referre debebit ad illa jura, quæ tempore prioris instantiæ obtinebant, ut sententia à judice inferiori lata, iniquitatis arguatur. Neque enim si tempore prioris sententiæ, eam tulisset judex, aliter eam ferre potuisset, nisi juri ltum obtinenti congruenter. Ut nihil aliud facere debeat in secundâ instantiâ, quam quod judex primæ instantiæ fecit, & facere debuit, quo sententia legibus esset conformis. Appellatio enim nihil aliud est, quam ab iniquitate sententiæ provocatio. l. 1. in init. D. Appell. Auth. ut cum de appell. cognosc. in init. seu nov. 115. Bartol. in l. omnes populi. D. just. & jur. n. 40. ibique post Gloss. Alexand. consil. 96. libr. 2, n. 3. Masc. ult. concl. n. 31. 32.
units.tr: What if, in a case where a statute must be referred to pending business, a matter which was decided in the first instance is pending before the judge of appeal: must the statute also be referred to that case, as though it were still pending? Answer: no. For the judge of appeal, judging whether the sentence is unjust, must refer himself to those laws which held in force at the time of the first instance, so that the sentence delivered by the inferior judge may be shown to be unjust. For if the judge had pronounced the sentence at the time of the first instance, he could not have pronounced it otherwise than in accordance with the law then in force. Thus in the second instance he ought to do nothing other than what the judge of the first instance did and ought to have done, so that the sentence might conform to the laws. For appeal is nothing other than a challenge to the injustice of a sentence (l. 1 in init. D. de appellationibus; Auth. ut cum de appellationibus cognoscitur in init., or Nov. 115; Bartolus on l. omnes populi n. 40 and there after the Gloss; Alexander, consil. 96, lib. 2, n. 3; Muscardus, ult. concl. nn. 31, 32).

units.la: 2, Excipe, nisi statuta posteriora sint prioris alicujus statuti declaratoria: utpote quæ ex sui natura respiciunt lata, adeoque præterita. Arg. l. hæres palam D. Testam. Auth. de ea quæ raptor. seu nov. 150. in sin. Auth. de filiis ante detul. instrum. nat. §.
units.tr: 2. Let it be excepted: unless the later statutes are declaratory of some earlier statute; for by their nature they look back to what was enacted and so to past matters (arg. l. haeres palam D. de testamentis; Auth. de ea quae raptor, or Nov. 150 in fin.; Auth. de filiis ante detulit instrumenta nat. §.

units.la: 1. Canonistæ inc. sin de Constit. Felinus, aliique ibid. Bartol. in l. non dubium. Cod. de leg. Jason in d. l. n. 10. Masc. ult. conclus. n. 41.
units.tr: 1. The canonists on c. sin. de constitutionibus; Felinus and others there; Bartolus on l. non dubium Cod. de legibus; Jason on that law n. 10; Muscardus, ult. concl. n. 41.

units.la: Idem quod de confirmatoriis statutis est affirmandum, l. bene à Zenone. Cod. Quadrien. Præscript c. 1. de Transslat. Prælat, Bartol in l. omnes populi. D just. & jur. n. 46:
units.tr: The same must be affirmed of confirmatory statutes (l. bene a Zenone Cod. quadriennii praescriptione; c. 1 de translatione praelatorum; Bartolus on l. omnes populi D. de justitia et jure n. 46).

units.la: Non idem tamen dicendum, ratione pœ-ne adjectæ ; ut quæ ad præterita referri non debebit. Quid enim peccavit antiquitas, quę præsentis legis ignara, pristinam secuta est obseruantiam. l. jubemus. 29. in sin. Cod. de Testam. Arg. l. 9. Cod. de leg. Zoes, D. de leg. n. 43. 44.
units.tr: Yet the same is not to be said with regard to the penalty attached; for it ought not to be referred to past matters. For what did antiquity sin, which, ignorant of the present law, followed the earlier custom? (l. jubemus 29 in fin. Cod. de testamentis; arg. l. 9 Cod. de legibus; Zoesius D. de legibus n. 43, 44.)

units.la: 3. Excipe, nisi annullarent actum ex causa de præterito, factum scil. contra dispositionem prius existentem, & ipsum actum annullantem. l. pen. Cod. Incestuos. Nupt. Auth. de Alien. & Emphyt. §. si vero aliquid. c. 5. de Usur. c. peccat. de Regul. juri in 6. Bartol. l. d. omnes populi. n. 44.
units.tr: 3. Let it be excepted: unless they annul an act on account of a past matter, namely an act done contrary to a prior disposition that exists, and annul the act itself (l. penult. Cod. de incestis nuptiis; Auth. de alienatione et emphyteusi, §si vero aliquid; c. 5 de usuris; c. peccat. de regulis juris in 6; Bartolus, l. omnes populi n. 44).

units.la: 4. Excipe, nisi statuta posteriora respicerent judicii ordinatoria, quæ etiam quoad illa ordinatoria locum habent in omnibus litibus futuris, licet de præteritis & pendentibus sint negotiis. Arg. l. unic. de Errore calculi. Bartol. in d. l. omnes populi. n. 44. Mascard. de interpret. Statut. concl. ult. n. 49. 50.
units.tr: 4. Let it be excepted: unless later statutes concern rules of judicial procedure, which hold also as to those rules in all future lawsuits, even though they concern past and pending matters (arg. l. unic. de errore calculi; Bartolus on d. l. omnes populi n. 44; Muscardus, de interpretatione statutorum, concl. ult. nn. 49, 50).

units.la: 5. Excipe, nisi statuta de præterito, complementum accipiant de futuro, ut tamen ante gestum in duriori & asperiori statu non constituatur, nec gerendum cum gesto omnino sit connexum; tum quippe de gerendo, tanquam de gesto judicabitur. Bartol. in d l. n. 47. Bald. ibid. n. 52. Laurus de Palatiis super Statuto Italiæ: Quod Extant. Masculis fœminæ non succedant. 2. part. Princip. n. 12. Masc. d conclus. n. 52. &seqq.
units.tr: 5. Make an exception, unless the statutes concerning the past receive their completion in regard to the future; yet a thing is not to be established in a harsher and more rigorous condition before it has been done, nor is the thing to be done wholly connected with the thing done; for then what is to be done will be judged as if it had been done. Bartolus on the said law, n. 47. Baldus, ibid. n. 52. Laurus de Palatiis on the statute of Italy, "Quod extant. Masculis foemina non succedant," part 2, Princip. n. 12. Masc. on the said conclusion, n. 52 et seqq.

units.la: 6. Excipe, nisi statuta introducerent aut tollerent aliquam exceptionem, in ordine ad negotia: tum enim ratione negotiorum de præterito etiam illa exceptio locum habebit. Scilicet, ut tempus exceptionis incipiat currere, à tempore conditorum statutorum. Nisi tamen aliud quidpiam expresse statuto foret cautum. Argum. l. pen. Cod. Usur. l. testium, Cod. de Testibus. l. fiscus. D. de Jure fisc. Abb. Felin in c. sin. de Constit. Masc. d. conclus. sin. n. 55.
units.tr: 6. Make an exception, unless the statutes introduce or remove some exception in relation to affairs; for then, in respect of affairs concerning the past, that exception will also apply. Namely, so that the time of the exception begins to run from the time of the enacted statutes, unless something else has been expressly provided in the statute. By argument from l. pen. Cod. Usur., l. testium, Cod. de Testibus, l. fiscus, D. de Jure fisc., Abb. Felin. on c. sin. de Constit., Masc. on the said conclusion, sin. n. 55.

units.la: Hinc patescit ratio artic. 21. in med. nuperæ constit. ordin. Ultraj. de ann. 1659. april. 14. Quo introducta exceptio biennii vel 6. mensium, quibusdam contractibus, etiam ante initis, objiciendum; quæ exceptio in ordine ad ante gesta, à die editæ constitutionis currere incipiet. vid. de tali exceptione. Pichard. accurate ad tit. instit. de litterar. obligat. n. 16. 17. Et de æquitate vel iniquitate talis statuti. Francisc. Cosc. in c. Cognosc. de Constit. Tom. 2. Repet. jur. Canon. n. 23. p. 295. Petrum de Ubald. in c. si diligenti de Præscript. Tom. 4 Repet. Juris Canon. n. 68. p. 320.
units.tr: Hence is made clear the reason of art. 21, in the middle of the recent ordinance of Utrecht of 14 April 1659, by which an exception of two years or six months was introduced to be objected against certain contracts, even those entered into earlier; this exception, in relation to acts done before, will begin to run from the day the constitution was issued. See on such an exception Pichardus, accurately on the title of the Institutes concerning literal obligations, n. 16, 17; and on the equity or iniquity of such a statute Francisc. Cosc. on c. Cognosc. de Constit., Tom. 2 Repet. jur. Canon. n. 23, p. 295; Petrus de Ubaldis on c. si diligenti de Praescript., Tom. 4 Repet. Juris Canon. n. 68, p. 320.

units.la: 7. Excipe, nisi essent introducta favore cujusdam liberationis; maxime si non ad delinquendum invitarent. Ut si dictarent: quicunque pacem ab offenso habuerit, liberetur. Quicunque bannitus fuerit, liberetur, si solverit decem. Gloss. in l. cum secundi. D. Injust. Testam.
units.tr: 7. Make an exception, unless they were introduced in favour of some release, especially if they did not invite to wrongdoing. As, if they should lay down: whoever has obtained peace from the offended party shall be released; whoever has been banished shall be released if he pays ten. Gloss on l. cum secundi, D. Injust. Testam.

units.la: 8. Excipe, nisi aliter absurdus intellectus inde resultaret, si non ad praeterita referretur. Marcus Anton. Marscot. post Jasonem & alios. in c. ut animarum. de constit. Tom. 5. Repet. jur. can. p. 116 n. 62.
units.tr: 8. Make an exception, unless an otherwise absurd sense would result from it, if it were not referred to the past. Marcus Anton. Marscot., after Jason and others, on c. ut animarum, de constit., Tom. 5 Repet. jur. can. p. 116, n. 62.

units.la: 4. Tertia generalis difficultas est, an simulac statuta lata sunt, & promulgata, etiam in notitiam civium venerunt, sic ut nulla probabilis ignorantia possit allegari, quicquid adversus statuta factum est, vel gestum, sit ipso jure nullum?
units.tr: 4. The third general difficulty is whether, as soon as statutes have been enacted and promulgated, and have come to the notice of the citizens, so that no probable ignorance can be pleaded, whatever has been done or transacted against the statutes is null by the very law itself?

units.la: Respondeo, uti leges sunt duum generum, ita & statuta. Vel enim erunt minus quam perfecta, vel perfecta. Illa, quae quidem aliquid fieri vetant, non tamen si quid factum sit, illud quod factum est, rescindunt, verum poenam delinquenti imponunt. Et dubium nullum, quin indistincte, hoc casu quod contra statuta factum, non sit ipso jure nullum. Ulpian. in Fragment. tit. 1. de leg. l. sanctio legum. D. de Poen. Quinimo quaedam sunt prohibita inchoati, quae tamen non prohibita, postquam inchoata, confirmari, ut, postquam facta sunt, teneant. Quae etiam, licet contra statuta facta, non sunt ipso jure nulla. l. unic. Cod. de Contract. judic. l. & si contra, Cod. de Nupt. Arg. l. 1. §. biduum. D. quando Appell. Azo in summ. Cod. de leg. n. 7.
units.tr: I reply: just as there are two kinds of laws, so there are of statutes. For they will be either less than perfect or perfect. Those which indeed forbid something to be done, but do not, if something has been done, annul what was done, rather impose a penalty on the offender. And there is no doubt that, in this case, what has been done contrary to the statutes is not null by the very law itself, without distinction. Ulpian, in Fragments, tit. 1, de leg.; l. sanctio legum, D. de Poen. Indeed, some things are forbidden as inchoate, which, not being forbidden once begun, are confirmed so that they hold once done. These too, although done contrary to statutes, are not null by the law itself. l. unic. Cod. de Contract. judic.; l. & si contra, Cod. de Nupt.; Arg. l. 1 §. biduum, D. quando Appell.; Azo in summ. Cod. de leg. n. 7.

units.la: Quod si statuta sint perfecta, sic jam loquar ad imitationem Ulpiani, illa iterum non unius erunt ordinis, aut generis.
units.tr: But if the statutes are perfect, then, to imitate Ulpian, I shall speak thus: those again will not be of one order or kind.

units.la: Vel enim continent alicujus favorem, vel publici boni causa sunt introducta. Illo casu, quae contra statuta gesta, non sunt ipso jure nulla, si modo partis aut partium adsit consensus, eorumq; quorum interest, quisque juri pro se introducto poterunt renunciare, l. pen. Cod. de Pact. Hoc casu, aut permittunt, consulunt; aut prohibent, praecipiunt, mandant. Si permittant, proprie nihil fit contra statuta: quia quae permittuntur, non subjacent juris necessitati, uti nec illa, quae per modum consilii suadentur, licet & haec postrema quandoque partium favore sint introducta. Arg. §. sin. instit. verb. obligat. Quae vero prohibent aliquid fieri, aut fieri mandant. Vel quod contra factum est, rescindi volunt, adeoque non erit etiam, quod contra factum est, ipso jure nullum, rescindetur tamen. Arg. l. 1. D. quod Met. causa gest. Nov. 115. §. 3. in sin.
units.tr: For they either contain the favour of someone, or are introduced for the sake of the public good. In the former case, things done contrary to the statutes are not null by the law itself, provided there is the consent of the party or parties, and those whose interest it is may renounce the law introduced in their own favour. l. pen. Cod. de Pact. In this case the statutes either permit or advise, or else forbid, command or order. If they permit, strictly speaking nothing is done contrary to the statutes, because what is permitted is not subject to the necessity of the law, nor are those things which are urged by way of counsel; although these latter also are sometimes introduced for the sake of the parties. Arg. §. sin. instit. verb. obligat. But those which forbid something to be done, or order it to be done: either they wish what was done contrary to them to be rescinded, and so what was done contrary is not null by the law itself, yet it will be rescinded. Arg. l. 1 D. quod Met. causa gest.; Nov. 115 §. 3 in sin.

units.la: Vel nihil statutis illis est adjectum; vel adjecta est clausula irritans, & annullans id quod gestum est. Utroque casu, quod contra gestum est, ipso jure non valet, & pro nullo habetur. l. non dubium. Cod. de leg. ibique DD. c. quae contra jus. de Reg. jur. in 6.
units.tr: Or nothing has been added to those statutes; or an irritant clause has been added, annulling what was done. In either case, what was done contrary is not valid by the law itself, and is held as null. l. non dubium, Cod. de leg., and there the Doctors; c. quae contra jus, de Reg. jur. in 6.

units.la: Id quod procedit, si in conditionali statuto conditio non servetur, modo talis sit conditio, quae formam internam det statuto, adeoque necessaria sit, ut vel ex verbis, vel intentione statuentis, inesse aut adesse debeat. Barbos. in axiom. jur. verb. forma. Baldus in Auth. matri. Cod. quando. mul. off. tutel. Tiraquell. de Retract. § 1. gloss. 21. n. 13. Bartol. in l. 1. n. 9. D. Condit. & Demonstr.
units.tr: This holds good if, in a conditional statute, the condition is not observed, provided that the condition is of such a kind as to give the statute its internal form, and so is necessary, such that it ought to be present or to be inherent, either from the words or from the intention of the one who enacts it. Barbosa, on the axiom of law, verb. forma; Baldus, on Auth. matri, Cod. quando mul. off. tutel.; Tiraquellus, de Retract. §1 gloss 21 n. 13; Bartolus, on l. 1 n. 9, D. Condit. & Demonstr.

units.la: Idem quod ut plurimum servatur, si statuta contineant ablativos absolutos, quę saepissime inferunt aliquam necessitatem. l. evictis agris. D. de Evict. l. testatore. D. Condit. & demonstr. vid. Boer. ad Bituricens. tit. 8. §. 1. p. 109. Chassan. ad Burgund. Rubric. 7. §. 5. in textum. Ne peut faire. n. 1. 2. Mascard. conclus. 9. n. 2. 3. 4. & seqq. n. 19. & seqq. Zoes. D. de legibus, n. 47. 48. 49. 50. Sanden. 2. def. 6. tit. 1. Vinnius Select. quaest. 1.
units.tr: The same holds, as a rule, if statutes contain ablative absolutes, which very often imply some necessity. l. evictis agris, D. de Evict.; l. testatore, D. Condit. & demonstr.; see Boer on Bituricens. tit. 8 §1 p. 109; Chassan. on Burgund. Rubric. 7 §5 in textum, Ne peut faire, n. 1, 2; Mascard. conclus. 9 n. 2, 3, 4 et seqq., n. 19 et seqq.; Zoes. D. de legibus, n. 47, 48, 49, 50; Sanden. 2 def. 6 tit. 1; Vinnius Select. quaest. 1.

units.la: SECT. VIII. CAP. II.
units.tr: SECT. VIII. CAP. II.

units.la: 1. Utrum statuta laicorum, uti loquuntur personas ligent ecclesiasticas?
units.tr: 1. Whether the statutes of laymen, as they speak of persons, bind ecclesiastical persons?

units.la: 2. Utrum cives Academici, territorii statutis ligentur?
units.tr: 2. Whether academic citizens are bound by the statutes of the territory?

units.la: 3. Utrum ratione suorum bonorum immobilium?
units.tr: 3. Whether they are so bound by reason of their immovable goods?

units.la: 4. Quid de Principe statuendum, & ejus familitio? 5. Quid de Nobilibus?
units.tr: 4. What is to be decided concerning the Prince and his household? 5. What about the nobles?

units.la: 6. Quid de subditis extra territorium quid committentibus?
units.tr: 6. What about subjects who commit something outside the territory?

units.la: 7. Quis effectus statuti, ne cives invicem extra territorium conveniant?
units.tr: 7. What is the effect of a statute that forbids citizens to meet one another outside the territory?

units.la: 8. Quid si animal extra territorium portaverit civis, quo ibidem parareet, an nihilominus, id persolvere tenea-tur, pro nato animali, ad quod in territorio, si pareret, erat obligatus?
units.tr: 8. If a citizen carries an animal outside the territory and it gives birth there, is he nonetheless bound to pay for the newborn animal, to which he would have been obligated had it been born within the territory?

units.la: 9. An statutum liget subditos, ne extra territorium frequentent cauponas &c.?
units.tr: 9. Does a statute bind subjects not to frequent taverns outside the territory, and so on?

units.la: 1. PRæmissis generalibus statutorum effectubus, in specie quorundam effectus examinandi, idque in ordine personarum, quæ statutis ligari, vel non ligari dicuntur. Ubi occurrit, illa inter canonistas, & legum doctores agitata quæstio: Num statuta laiorum uti loquuntur, personas ligent ecclesiasticas? Respondeo, cum Ecclesia sit in republica, etiam ecclesiastici ut reipublicæ membra considerari debeant, quidni ut pars civitatis Politico magistratui, adeoque eorum statutis erunt subjecti. Id tamen negari non poterit, quin posteriores Imperatores plus nimium indulserint Episcopis, id impense procurantibus, ne per omnia secularium culariūm legibus essent alligati. tot. tit. Cod. Episc. Audient. Clapmar. de Arcan. Reipublic. lib. 3. cap. 5. Mev. Prælim. quæstion. 3. adjus Lubecense. num. 3. & seqq. diff. Christianeus cum multis aliis allegatis ad l. Mechlin. in Prælud' num. 41. ubi etiam pro parte affirmativa varios enumerat.
units.tr: 1. Having set out the general effects of statutes, we must now examine the effects of certain statutes in particular, taking them by the order of the persons who are said to be bound or not bound by statutes. Here arises the question much debated among the canonists and the doctors of law: whether the statutes of laymen, as they speak, bind ecclesiastical persons? I answer: since the Church is within the commonwealth, ecclesiastics too must be regarded as members of the commonwealth, and why should they not, as part of the state, be subject to the political magistrate and therefore to its statutes? Yet it cannot be denied that the later emperors indulged the bishops far too much, and zealously sought that they should not be bound in every respect by the laws of secular men. See the whole title of the Code, De episcopali audientia; Clapmar, De arcanis rerum publicarum, book 3, chapter 5; Mevius, Praelectiones, question 3, on the Lübeck law, number 3 and following; the disputation of Christinaeus, with many others cited on the Lex Mechlin, Praeludia, number 41, where he also lists various authors on the affirmative side.

units.la: 2. Num Academici cives ejus loci seu territorii statutis, teneantur, ubi domicilium fovent ? Respondeo, si Præfectorum imperio & jurisdictioni subsint, quorum in loco habitant, dubium nullum est, quin & eorum statutis sese accommodare debeant, quia subjectiigratione quippe subditorum statuta tenent, eosque constringunt. Quod si tam in civilibus quam criminalibus causis exempti reperiantur, id quod ratione privilegiorum illis concessorum in multis obtinet Academiis: etiam non obstringentur illorum locorum statutis quæ in locis obtinent Academiæ. Certum enim est statuta deficere & cessare ratione non subditorum. Cum quos non continet jurisdictio, eos non constringat constitutio. Et licet sint intra limites territorii, quod Academia pro Domicilio agnovit, non tamen sunt de illo territorio, ratione jurisdictionis; ut nec quoad statuta, ibidem condita, quod ea non receperint. Uti igitur, nec forum ibidem sortiuntur, nec judicem, ita nec legibus loci tenebuntur. Arg. l. sin. D. de jurisdict. Authentic. Habita Ibidemque D.
units.tr: 2. Are academic citizens bound by the statutes of the place or territory where they keep their domicile? I answer: if they are subject to the authority and jurisdiction of the magistrates in whose place they live, there is no doubt that they too must conform to those magistrates' statutes, since statutes hold and bind subjects by reason of subjection. But if they are found to be exempt both in civil and in criminal causes, as is the case in many universities by reason of the privileges granted to them, then they will not be bound by the statutes of the places in which the university is situated. For it is certain that statutes fail and cease to apply to those who are not subjects; a constitution does not bind those whom jurisdiction does not embrace. And although they are within the limits of the territory which the university has acknowledged as its domicile, they are not of that territory by reason of jurisdiction, and so not as regards the statutes enacted there, since they have not received them. Therefore, just as they acquire neither the forum nor the judge there, so they are not bound by the laws of the place. Compare the law Sin, De jurisdictione; Authentic Habita; and the authorities on the Code, Ne filius pro patre; Besold, Politica, tractate on the jurisdiction of universities; Mevius, on the Lübeck law, question Praelim. 3, numbers 1 and 24, and the others cited there.

units.la: DD. Cod. Ne filius pro patre. Besold. in Polit. tract. de Jurisd. Academ. Mev. ad jus Lubecense, quaest. Prælim. 3. num. 1. & num. 24. ibidemque alii allegati.
units.tr: The Doctors; Cod. Ne filius pro patre. Besold, in Politicus tractatus de jurisdictione Academiarum. Mevius, ad jus Lubecense, quaest. praelim. 3, n. 1 and n. 24, and the others cited there.

units.la: 3. Verum, an non Academici cives,(qui subditi non sunt, ut dictum, si personas intueamur, etiam res mobiles, quæ conditionem personarum comitantur,) subesse cogentur statutis, idque ratione bonorum immobilium, in loco domicilii Academiæ sitorum? Respondeo, cum civium Academicorum privilegia tantum sint personalia: quod ibidē immobilia non præsumantur possidere, cum pleriq; sint exteri; in quorum potissimū gratiam illa privilegia sunt concessa. Neque ullo privilegio constet immobilia territorii, juri civitatis esse exempta. Dicendum est, eos immobilium ratione statutis loci domicilii subjectos esse. Arg. l. ult. D. de jurisd. Authet. Habita Cod. Ne filius pro patre. Ex parte Pingiz-erus quaest. Saxonic. 29. num. 40. & seq. Eam tamen sententiam usu multorum locorum abrogatam esse, scribit Mev. in quaest. Prelim. 3. num. 30. Ad jus Lubec, vid. Richterum ad d. Auth.
units.tr: 3. But are academic citizens, who (as has been said, if we look to their persons) are not subjects, also compelled to submit to the statutes by reason of immovable goods situated in the place of the university's domicile? I answer: since the privileges of academic citizens are merely personal, it is not presumed that they possess immovable goods there, since most of them are foreigners, for whose sake in particular those privileges were granted. Nor does any privilege establish that immovable property within the territory is exempt from the law of the state. It must be said that, by reason of immovable goods, they are subject to the statutes of the place of their domicile. Compare the Ne filius pro patre, the Authentic Habita, and the last law De jurisdictione; Pinggerus, Saxon questions, 29, numbers 40 and following. Yet Mevius writes, in his Praelectiones question 3, number 30, that this opinion has been abrogated by the custom of many places; on the Lübeck law, see Richter on the said Authentic.

units.la: 4. Quid de Principe dicendum, anne cum statutis locorum subjectum judicabimus? Resp. Quia cessante jurisdictione, etiam cessat statutum. Nec quispiam inferiorum Principem legibus, adeoque nec suæ jurisdictioni subjecit. Nec superior inferioris mandato ligatur. Etiam in generali sermone communiter non censetur esse comprehensa persona loquentis. Sequetur Principem statutis obligatum non esse, licet in civitate contraheret, aut domicilium foveret. Idem quod ministris, & universo Principis famulitio DD. applicatum volunt. Nisi tamen vel sponte se subjecerit Princeps, vel statuta quid contineant juri divino & naturali conforme, id est, honestatem naturalem. l. 18. D. de Minor. l. 4. D. de Recept. Arbitr. l. 19. Cod. de Testamen. §. sin. Instit. quibus mod. Testam. infirm. l. 14. D. de jurisd. l. 4. Cod. de leg. - Argum. l. 2. Cod. de Offic. Magistr. milit. l. 1. in sin. Cod. Si quacunque præd. potestat. in v. cum suam, suorumque domin. inquisitio. Cod. de Solut. l. 4. Cod. de leg. Andr. de Exea in Repet. jur. canon. tom. 2. in c. canonum Statuta, de Constit. p. 189. n. 248. Petr. Heigius part. 2. quæst. 25. per totum. Menoch. libr. 2. Præsumpt.
units.tr: 4. What must be said of the Prince: shall we judge him subject to the statutes of the places? I answer: because when jurisdiction ceases, the statute also ceases. Nor does any inferior subject the Prince to his laws, and so not to his jurisdiction. Nor is a superior bound by the command of an inferior. Even in general speech the person speaking is not commonly understood to be included. It follows that the Prince is not bound by the statutes, even if he contracts in the city or keeps a domicile there. The doctors hold the same for his ministers and the whole household of the Prince. Unless, however, the Prince submits himself of his own accord, or the statutes contain something not in accordance with divine and natural law, that is, with natural honesty. Compare Minor, D. 18; De receptis arbitris, D. 4; Code De testamentis, 19; Institutes, Quibus modis testamenta infirmantur, final section; De jurisdictione, D. 14; De legibus, Code 4; the argument from Code De officio magistri militum, 2; Code Si quacunque praedicta potestate, 1, at the end, on the words "cum suam suorumque dominorum inquisitio"; Code De solutionibus; De legibus, Code 4; Andreas de Exea in Repetitio on the canon law, vol. 2, on the chapter Canonum statuta, De constitutionibus, p. 189, n. 248; Petrus Heigius, part 2, question 25, throughout; Menochius, book 2, Praesumptiones.

units.la: 5. Imbert. instit. Forens. libr. 1. cap. 1. in comment. Peck. de jur. sistend. cap. 22. num. 23 & seq. Christin. ad Mechlin. in Epilog. num. 25. Zoes. D. de Princip. Constit. num. 38.
units.tr: 5. Imbert. instit. Forens. libr. 1. cap. 1. in comment. Peck. de jur. sistend. cap. 22. num. 23 & seq. Christin. ad Mechlin. in Epilog. num. 25. Zoes. D. de Princip. Constit. num. 38.

units.la: 5. An igitur & nobiles statutis suæ civitatis, tenebuntur? Resp. Si incolæ sint civitatis ipso incolatu, nisi exemptionem jure certo docere possint, non tantum ratione bonorum, verum etiam ratione personarum, ejus loci, ubi habent domicilium, & jurisdictionem, & statuta agnoscere tenentur. Quod in tantum verum est, ut nullis civitatis oneribus sint exempti; etiam propter munera sibi impositâ, quæ subire detrectant, pœnâ quâ pecuniariâ constringantur: l. 3. §. 1. l. 16. D. de Muner. & Honor. l 10. D. de Vacat. & Excuf. Muner. l. 9. Cod. de Excuf. Muner. l. 3. Cod. de quibus muner. nulli lic. l. 1: Cod. de Decret. Decur. super Immun. Novell. 15. cap. 1. & 6. in fin. Merul. lib. 4. Prax. civil. distr. 2. tit. 1. cap. 5. Baptist. Cæsar. Consil. Illustr. 70. part. 2. Christin. decif. 102. volum. 1. Mev. quæst. Pralim. 4. ad jus Lubec.
units.tr: 5. Are the nobles, then, also bound by the statutes of their own city? I answer: if they are residents of the city by residence itself, they are bound to acknowledge the statutes, and the jurisdiction, of the place where they have their domicile, not only by reason of their goods but also by reason of their persons, unless they can show an exemption by certain law. This holds so far that they are not exempt from any burdens of the city; even on account of offices imposed on them, which they refuse to undertake, they may be compelled by a penalty, whether pecuniary or otherwise. Law 3, §1; law 16, De muneribus et honoribus; law 10, De vacatione et excusatione munerum; Code law 9, De excusationibus munerum; Code law 3, De quibus muneribus nullus licet; Code law 1, De decretis decurionum; on the immunities, Novel 15, chapters 1 and 6 at the end; Merula, book 4, Praxis civilis, distinction 2, title 1, chapter 5; Baptista Caesar, Consilia, 70, part 2; Christinaeus, decision 102, vol. 1; Mevius, question Praelim. 4, on the Lübeck law.

units.la: 6. Verum an unquam statuta, verbi gratia prohibitoria, aut præcipientia subditos obstringent, aliquid extra territorium committentes? Respondeo, quemadmodum lex omnes Imperio subjectos ligat, ubicunque locorum versentur, & ideo etiam ab iis, qui forte in peregrinatione hærent observari debet: ita etiam statutum nonnunquam obligat subditos extra territorium, præsertim si id exprimatur, ne quid sub pœnâ, extra territorium committant. Argum. Init. v. Nam cum decederet in Africa, & v. propter magnas. Institut. de Codicill. l. 13. D. qui testam. facere possl. l. fin. D. de decret. ab Ordin. faciend. l. 2. l. Mercatorem 4. Cod d. Commerc. & Mercator. Alexander. Consil. 41. libr. 6, Baldus. de Angel. in Prato super primo libr. Cod. ad l. 3. de legibus. Peck. de jur. sistendi cap. 8. Christin. [illegible, ~10 letters] Schlin. tit. 12. artic. 9. num. 7. vid. [illegible, ~10 letters] Gabriel, comm. opinion. libr. 6. con-clus. clus. 8. ibidemque varias limitationes. vid. mea antecedentia.
units.tr: 6. But do statutes, for example prohibitory or commanding ones, ever bind subjects who do something outside the territory? I answer: just as the law binds all subject to the empire, wherever they are, and so must be observed even by those who happen to be abroad, so too a statute sometimes binds subjects outside the territory, especially if it is expressly stated that they shall commit nothing outside the territory under penalty. Compare the argument from Init. and Cum decederet in Africa, and propter magnas, Institutes De codicillis; D. 13, Qui testamenta facere possunt; the last law De decretis ab ordine faciendis; Code 2 and Mercatorem 4, De commerciis et mercatoribus; Alexander, Consilia 41, book 6; Baldus de Angelis, in Pratum on the first book of the Code, on law 3, De legibus; Peckius, De jure sistendi, chapter 8; Christinaeus [illegible]; Schlinck, title 12, article 9, number 7; see [illegible]; Gabriel, Commune opinionum, book 6, conclusion 8, and the various limitations there; see my preceding remarks.

units.la: 7. Unde quæsitum, an si statutum disponat, ne concives invicem judicio conveniant extra territorium; quale est concessum Brabantinis, læto introitu, Philipp. II. Hisp. Regis, quale etiam apud Hollandos, aliosque obtinet; aliquid operetur extra territorium statuentis? Resp. Si spectemus concives invicem extra Provinciam sistentes; eo usque efsectum sortietur hoc statutum ut concives in loco statuentis mandato poenali impetrato invicem ad hoc cogant, ut refusis expensis, liti extra territorium inchoatæ renuncient. Id quod etiam obtinet secundum aureamn bullam Caroli IV., verb. cum per duos Romanos Imperat., ubi quia omnes uni subsunt Imperatori, actus in contrarium declaratur nullus. Quod si spectemus judices exteros, statutum nihil operabitur quoad illos, quia illi extra territorium statuentis, adeoque insuper habito tali statuto, adhuc arrestum personæ, admittent. Ut id ipsum de re arrestanda, multo magis sit dicendum; nisi obstent concordata. Et quia extra territorium jus dicenti, impune non paretur. Et quia actio realis in loco rei sitæ intentari potest. Et quia tale statutum, quod meo judicio admodum anomalum, non facile ad correctionem juris civilis est extendendum, si in ordine ad cives statuentis adhuc aliquid operetur. l. ult. D., de de jurisd. l. ult. Cod. Ubi in rem act. l. 38. D. de jud. Tiraq. de jure Primog. q. 48. n. 7. Zanger. de Except. part. 2. cap. 1. num. 259. n. 283. 284. Aurea bull. Carol. V. de ann. 1530. Latus introitus Philipp. II. Hisp. Reg. artic. 24. & 32. Vivien. in comm. ad let. introit. prolog. -- vid. Jason. Consil. 201. num. 16. vol. 2. 4. Panorm. in cap. ex pacto 31. de verb. signif. num. 2, 3. Matth. Wesemb. consi. 201. per totum. Nicol. Everhard. consi. 45. n. 4. Sententia in Hollandia lata de ann. 1549. Mart. 13. Grot. Antiq. Batav. cap. 5. p. mihi 36. 37. Berlich. decis. aurear. part. 2. dec. 245. Mevius ad jus Lubec. lib. 5. tit. 3. 4. art. 4. n. 8. Itaque in Vianensi Camera intelleximus. ann. 1660. dec. 19.
units.tr: 7. Hence the question arises whether, if a statute provides that fellow citizens may not sue one another outside the territory (as was granted to the Brabanters at the Joyous Entry of Philip II, King of Spain, and as also holds among the Hollanders and others), it has any effect outside the territory of the enacting authority. Answer: If we consider fellow citizens appearing before one another outside the province, the statute will have effect to this extent: the citizens, by a penal mandate obtained in the place of the enacting authority, compel one another to this, so that, with expenses refunded, they renounce a suit begun outside the territory. This also holds according to the Golden Bull of Charles IV, in the words cum per duos Romanos Imperat., where, since all are subject to one Emperor, an act to the contrary is declared null. But if we consider foreign judges, the statute will have no effect as regards them, because they, outside the territory of the enacting authority, and so disregarding such a statute, will still admit the arrest of a person. The same must be said, even more so, of arresting property, unless concordats stand in the way. And because one who pronounces law outside his territory is not obeyed with impunity. And because a real action may be brought in the place where the thing is situated. And because such a statute, which in my judgment is quite anomalous, is not easily to be extended so as to correct the civil law, if it still has some effect with regard to the citizens of the enacting authority. l. ult. D., de de jurisd.; l. ult. Cod. Ubi in rem act.; l. 38. D. de jud.; Tiraq. de jure Primog. q. 48. n. 7.; Zanger. de Except. part. 2. cap. 1. num. 259, 283, 284; Golden Bull of Charles V, of the year 1530; Joyous Entry of Philip II, King of Spain, articles 24 and 32; Vivien, in the commentary on the Joyous Entry, prologue; see Jason, Consil. 201. num. 16. vol. 2; Panormitanus in cap. ex pacto 31. de verb. signif. num. 2, 3; Matth. Wesemb. consil. 201, throughout; Nicol. Everhard, consil. 45. n. 4; sentence pronounced in Holland in the year 1549, March 13; Grot. Antiq. Batav. cap. 5, my page 36, 37; Berlich, decis. aurear. part. 2, dec. 245; Mevius on the law of Lübeck, lib. 5, tit. 3, art. 4, n. 8. Accordingly we have so understood it in the Vianen Chamber, in the year 1660, decision 19.

units.la: 8. Hinc si statutum dicet, quae communis est opinio, ut proprietarius pro quolibet animali, in territorio nato, aliquid persolvere debeat, obligabitur ad solutionem summae impositae, licet animal praegnans extra territorium portaverit, ut ibi pareret. Commissum quippe in fraudem statuti extra territorium, ligat subditum, ad poenam in territorio subeundam. l. 2. Cod. de Eunuch. Bartol. in l. satis. n. 13. Cod. de Agricol. & censit. allegat. a Baldax. de Angel. Neapol. in Prato super 1. libr. Cod. ad l. 3. Cod, de legibus. Gabriel. comm. opin. libr. 6. conclus. 8.
units.tr: 8. Hence, if a statute says, as is the common opinion, that the owner must pay something for each animal in the territory where it was born, he will be bound to pay the sum imposed, even if he carried a pregnant animal outside the territory so that it might give birth there. For an act committed outside the territory in fraud of a statute binds the subject to the penalty to be undergone in the territory. l. 2. Cod. de Eunuch.; Bartol. in l. satis, n. 13, Cod. de Agricol. et censit.; allegations of Baldus, de Angelis of Naples, in Prato on the first book of the Code, on law 3, Cod. de legibus; Gabriel, comm. opin. lib. 6, conclus. 8.

units.la: 9. Quae etiam ratio est, quod statutum valeat, & omnino subditos constringat, eti-amam extra territorium, quo iisdem interdicitur, ne vel molendinis extra jurisdictionem civitatis positis, utantur, vel cauponas extra territorium exercitas, ubi cervisia vili venditur, frequentent. Est enim statutum, quasi personale, saltem poenale, quod ligat subditos territorium exeuntes, ratione poenae eidem appositae. Arg. l. 2. Cod. de Eunuch. l. 2. 4. Cod. Comm. Mercat. Alex. vol. 2. consil. 211. in sin. Praef. Everhard. consil. 45. vid. & à me alleg. superius in cap. de Stat. divis. Diss. ex parte Hartman. Pistor. observat. 200. post alios ibidem allegatos.
units.tr: 9. This is also the reason why a statute is valid and binds subjects altogether, even outside the territory, where they are forbidden to use mills situated outside the jurisdiction of the city, or to frequent taverns outside the territory where beer is sold cheaply. For the statute is quasi-personal, or at least penal, and binds subjects who leave the territory, by reason of the penalty attached to it. Arg. l. 2. Cod. de Eunuch.; l. 2. 4. Cod. Comm. Mercat.; Alex. vol. 2. consil. 211, in sin.; Praef. Everhard. consil. 45; see also what I have cited above in the chapter on the division of statutes; Diss. ex parte Hartman.; Pistor. observat. 200, after the others cited there.

units.la: SECTIO NONA. CAPUT PRIMUM.
units.tr: Section Nine. Chapter One.

units.la: 1. Quis ordo servandus in effectubus statutorum comparatis?
units.tr: 1. What order is to be observed in the effects of comparable statutes?

units.la: 2. Si contentio de re, aut in rem actione, aut de actione personali, sed in rem scriptâ, quale spectandum statutum?
units.tr: 2. If the dispute concerns a thing, whether by an action in rem or by a personal action that is written in rem, which statute is to be regarded?

units.la: 3. Quale in successione ab intestato?
units.tr: 3. Which statute applies in succession on intestacy?

units.la: 4. Quale in successione testamentariâ?
units.tr: 4. Which applies in testamentary succession?

units.la: 5. Quale si bona sint feudalia?
units.tr: 5. Which applies if the goods are feudal?

units.la: 6. Feuda per omnia patrimonialibus non comparantur. 7. Quale, si de missione in possessionem feudi?
units.tr: 6. Fiefs are not to be compared with patrimonial goods in every respect. 7. Which applies in the case of missio in possessionem of a fief?

units.la: 8. Quale, si de bonis mobilibus, controversia?
units.tr: 8. Which applies if the controversy concerns movable goods?

units.la: 9. Quid statuendum, casu quo duobus in locis quis habet domicilium?
units.tr: 9. What is to be decided where someone has a domicile in two places?

units.la: 10. Casus deciditur, quo jure Aesdonico & Scabinico, in mobilia succeditur, ratione statuti loci, ubi quis moritur.
units.tr: 10. The case is decided in which, under Aesdonic and Scabinic law, succession to movables follows the statute of the place where the person dies.

units.la: 11. Quale statutum spectandum, si de nominibus & actionibus contentio?
units.tr: 11. Which statute is to be regarded if the dispute concerns debts and actions?

units.la: 12. Traditur casus exceptus.
units.tr: 12. An excepted case is laid down.

units.la: 13. Quale spectandum statutum, si de annuis reditibus contentio?
units.tr: 13. Which statute is to be regarded if the dispute concerns annual rents?

units.la: 14. Quenam mobilium aut immobilium veniant nomine?
units.tr: 14. What things are included under the name of movables or immovables?

units.la: 1. HActenus explicui,& quidem facili negotio statutorum effectus absolutos; sunt etiam difficultates evolvendae, circa effectus statutorum comparatos; dum variorum locorum statuta dissonantia, circa unam eandemque rem, vel personam, vel negotia, concurrunt; quae longe prioribus sunt explicatione difficiliores. Quoad tamen fieri poterit, plerasque ex quibus de caeteris facile judicandum, in ordinem redigam, sicque me praestitisse, quod ante me forte non alius, judicabit ille, qui extra partes constitutus mea legerit, & perlegerit accurate. In quibus ne quid intactum manet, hanc servabo methodum: ut agam. 1. De negotiis realibus. 2. De Solemnibus, negotiorum. 3. De personalibus statutis. 4. De causis judicialibus. 5. De delictis, eorumque poenis.
units.tr: 1. Hitherto I have explained, and indeed with little difficulty, the absolute effects of statutes. There are also difficulties to be worked out concerning the comparative effects of statutes, where the conflicting statutes of various places apply to one and the same thing, person or transaction. These are far harder to explain than the earlier ones. Nevertheless, as far as I can, I shall reduce most of them to order, from which the rest may easily be judged; and he who reads my work from outside the parties, and reads it through carefully, will judge whether I have accomplished what perhaps no one before me has. So that nothing remains untouched, I shall keep this method: I shall treat (1) of real transactions; (2) of the solemnities of transactions; (3) of personal statutes; (4) of judicial causes; (5) of delicts and their penalties.

units.la: 3. Quid si circa successionem ab intestato, statutorum sit difformitas? Spectabitur loci statutum, ubi immobilia sita, non ubi testator moritur. Unde primogenitus in Anglia, tantum patri succedit, ratione bonorum rum Anglicanorum. Ratione bonorum in Belgio jacentium, pari jure cum fratribus concurret, nec gaudebit jure præcipui, nisi in specie id illi deferat statutum, mobilium quorundam ratione. Arg. ll. allegatarum. Covarr. de Sponsal. part. 2. c. 7. n. 8. Gabriel. comm. opin. libr. 6. de Statut. conclus. 9. ibique varii. Gilken. ad init. Tit. Cod. de Summ. Trinit. n. 78. & seqq. & n. 83. 84. Barbos. ad l. hæres absens. §. proinde. in articul. de foro ratione rei sitæ, per totum. D. de Judic. vid. de illo Angliæ statuto, ejusque explicatione distinguentem, sed perperam, Bertachin. tractat. de Episcop. 2. part. libr. 4. q. 18. n. 50. vol. 5. tractat. Martinum Laudensem. de Primogen. q. 28. vol. 6. tractat. Prolixe Johann. le Cirier de Primogen. libr. 2. q. 6. 7. 8. sol. 175. vol. 8. tractat. Grav. 2. conclus. 123. Matth. Stephani de jurisd. 33. n. 54. Bacchov. ad Treutl. 1. disp. thes. ult. litt. e. Muscard. d. concl. 6. n. 203. & seqq. Ubi casum excipit, quo statuto expresse cautum est, ne forensis ita ut municeps succederet, n. 207. diss. Schultet. 1. quaest. pract. 24. n. 5. & seqq. qui domicilii locum vult spectari, per l. 50. D. Pet. hæred. Neque obst. l. 28. Cod. Episc. Cleris. Quia omnes suberant uni imperatori; nec dicam quod etiam favor piæ causæ quid operetur.
units.tr: 3. What if there is a difference between the statutes concerning succession on intestacy? The statute of the place where the immovable property lies is to be considered, not the place where the testator dies. Hence in England the eldest son succeeds only to his father, by reason of English goods. By reason of goods lying in Belgium, he concurs with his brothers on equal terms and does not enjoy the right of primogeniture, unless the statute grants it to him specifically, by reason of certain movables. Cf. the laws cited above. Covarr. de Sponsal. part. 2. c. 7. n. 8. Gabriel. comm. opin. libr. 6. de Statut. conclus. 9. and the various authors there. Gilken. ad init. Tit. Cod. de Summ. Trinit. n. 78. ff. and n. 83. 84. Barbos. ad l. hæres absens. §. proinde. in the article on jurisdiction by reason of the thing situated, throughout. D. de Judic. See on that English statute, and its explanation, those who distinguish it, but wrongly: Bertachin. tractat. de Episcop. 2. part. libr. 4. q. 18. n. 50. vol. 5. tractat. Martinus Laudensis, de Primogen. q. 28. vol. 6. tractat. Johann. le Cirier, at length, de Primogen. libr. 2. q. 6. 7. 8. sol. 175. vol. 8. tractat. Grav. 2. conclus. 123. Matth. Stephani de jurisd. 33. n. 54. Bacchov. ad Treutl. 1. disp. thes. ult. litt. e. Muscard. d. concl. 6. n. 203. ff. Where he excepts the case in which a statute expressly provides that an outsider shall not succeed as a citizen does, n. 207 of the dissertation. Schultet. 1. quaest. pract. 24. n. 5. ff., who wants the place of domicile to be considered, by the law 50 D. Pet. hæred. Nor does law 28 Cod. Episc. Cleris. stand in the way. Because all were subject to one emperor; nor should I say what even the favour of a pious cause may achieve.

units.la: 4. Quid si testamento bona immobilia relicta, diversis subjaceant statutis? Idem dicendum; nihil enim interest, testatus quis an intestatus decedat, ut locus sit regulæ: extra territorium jus dicenti, impune non paretur. l. ult. D. jurisd.
units.tr: 4. What if immovables left by will are subject to different statutes? The same answer must be given. For it makes no difference whether someone dies testate or intestate, so the rule holds: one who declares law outside his territory is not obeyed with impunity. l. ult. D. jurisd.

units.la: 6. Non tamen probo quorundam rationem, qui ideo censent & feudum statuto loci ubi situm est, regi, quod de moribus patrimonialibus annumeretur. Quia licet nonnulli feudum velint ad instar patrimonii, ut Burgund. ad Flandr. tract. 3. n. 18. 19. Neost. feud. Holl. c. 1. in fin. Zoes. D. Contr. Empt. n. 17. Id tamen non per omnia procedit, ut particula fere, adjici debuerit, secundum Sand. de feud. Gelr. tract. 1. cap. 1. n. 3. & tract. 2. tit. 1. c. 1. n. 14. p. 271. Goris. Adv. 3. c. 7. n. 7.
units.tr: 6. I do not, however, approve the reasoning of some writers who think that a fief is governed by the statute of the place where it lies, because it is counted among patrimonial customs. Although some wish a fief to be treated like a patrimony, as Burgundus on Flanders, tract. 3, nn. 18, 19; Neostadius, Feud. Holl. c. 1, at the end; Zoesius, D. Contr. Empt., n. 17, this does not hold in every respect. The particle "almost" ought therefore to have been added, according to Sandérus, De feud. Gelr., tract. 1, c. 1, n. 3, and tract. 2, tit. 1, c. 1, n. 14, p. 271; Goris, Adv. 3, c. 7, n. 7.

units.la: 7. Si tamen de missione in possessionem bonorum feudalium controversia; an statuta domus mortuariae, an rei sitae spectanda, disquiritur? Resp. Reformatores Zutphaniensēs respexerunt locum domicilii, Transisulani, locum rei sitæ, ut in quæstione propositâ, mores varient. vid. Sand. ad consf. feud. Gelr. tract. 3. c. 1. §. 4. n. 21.
units.tr: 7. But if the question is whether the statutes of the place of death or of the place where the thing lies are to be considered in the matter of putting someone into possession of feudal goods? Answer: the Reformers of Zutphen looked to the place of domicile, the Transisulani to the place where the thing lies, as in the question proposed; customs vary. See Sandérus on the Gelderland feudal consultation, tract. 3, c. 1, §. 4, n. 21.

units.la: 8. Verum an quod de bonis immobilibus dictum, idem de mobilibus statuendum erit? Resp. Quod non. Quia illorum bonorum nomine nemo censetur semet loci legibus subjecisse. Ut quæ certum locum non habent, quia facile de loco in locum transferuntur, adeoque secundum loci statuta regulantur, ubi domicilium habuit defunctus. Nisi tamen perpetui usus gratiâ ex destinatione patris familias in uno loco manere debeant; quo casu immobilibus comparabuntur. Vel nisi arresto inclusa, de moribus, ibi censeantur esse, ubi detinentur, non tamen in ratione succedendi. Vel nisi secundum jus antiquum Hollandicum bona mobilia dirigantur ad successionem statuti loci illius, ubi quispiam supremum diem clausit; licet forte ibi transiverit tantum, aut ad animi relaxationem semet eo contulerit. l. ex facto. 35. verb. 3. 4. D. Hered. instit. l. 32. D. de Pignor. & Hypothec. l. 89. D. de leg. 3. l. 19. §. 2. D. de Judic. l. 1. & 2. Cod. de Rer. & verbor. signific. Tiraquell. de jure primog. q. 47. 48. 49. Gail. 2. obs. 124. n. 18. Burgund. ad consf. Flandr. tract. 1. n. 36. & tract. 2. 32. Sand. libr. 4. tit. 8. def. 7. Petrus Wesemb. consil. 1. n. 65.
units.tr: 8. But should what has been said of immovable goods be held to apply equally to movables? Answer: no. For no one is regarded as having submitted himself to the laws of a place by reason of such goods. Things which have no fixed location, because they are easily carried from place to place, are therefore governed by the statutes of the place where the deceased had his domicile. Unless, however, by the settled purpose of the head of the household they must remain in one place for a lasting use, in which case they will be compared to immovables; or unless, being held under arrest, they are considered, as to their customs, to belong to the place where they are detained, though not in respect of succession; or unless, according to the old Holland law, movable goods are directed to the succession of the statute of that place where a person breathed his last, although perhaps he had only passed through it or had gone there for relaxation of mind. L. ex facto 35, verb. 3, 4, D. Hered. instit.; l. 32, D. de Pignor. et Hypoth.; l. 89, D. de leg. 3; l. 19, §. 2, D. de Judic.; l. 1 and 2, Cod. de Rer. et verbor. signif.; Tiraquellus, De jure primog., q. 47, 48, 49; Gail, 2 obs. 124, n. 18; Burgundus on the Flanders consultation, tract. 1, n. 36, and tract. 2, n. 32; Sandérus, lib. 4, tit. 8, def. 7; Petrus Wesembecius, consil. 1, n. 65.

units.la: 9. Occasione praecedentis difficultatis, duae subjungendae quaestiones. Primo, quid statuendum foret, casu quo quispiam duobus in locis haberet domicilium? Respondeo, etsi de jure Romano in concursu loci originis, & domicilii, potior esset ratio originis, quam quidem domicilii; ut illic potissimum quis esse intelligeretur, saltem reputaretur. l. cum satis. in Princ. Cod. de Agric. censi. Boer. decis. 13. n. 49. Barbof. ad l. 19. §. proinde artic. de foro ration. origin. n. 36. ibique plures. Qui d. l. 19. sin. §. n. 61. & seqq. distinguit, Quia tamen de moribus locus originis non consideratur & amissus censetur. si quispiam per annum & diem alibi se contulerit, animo domicilium figendi, nec in loco originis foverit domicilium. Dicendum videtur, si duobus in locis habuerit domicilium, alterum alteri non praevaliturum. Atque adeo secundum dum statuta cujusque loci, mobilia ubi sita ex destinatione patris-familias dirigenda esse. Uno tamen casu excepto secundum naturam juris Aesdonici, quo ad successionem loci dirigantur mobilia, ubi quis obiit, non ubi domicilium habebat defunctus. l. 17. §. 3. D. Ad Munic. Choppin. ad Mores Parisiens. libr. 1. tit. 1. num. 11. Burgund. ad consuet. Flandr. tract. 2. num. 1. 2. Gail. 2. observ. 36. Mev. ad jus Lubec. libr. 3. tit. 1. art. 10. & 11. & post illos. Ad Grot. introd. jurispr. Holland. libr. 2. part. 26. Groenw. in not. Christ. Rodenb. cap. 2. tit. 2. alleg. tract. Vid. tamen de foro ratione originis, quod moribus vix obtinet. Barbos. d. l. 19. art. de foro origin.
units.tr: 9. Arising from the preceding difficulty, two further questions should be added. First, what is to be decided if someone has a domicile in two places? I answer: although under Roman law, in a conflict between the place of origin and the place of domicile, the reason of origin prevailed over that of domicile, so that a person was understood, or at least regarded, as belonging chiefly to the place of origin (l. cum satis, in princ., Cod. de Agric. et censit.; Boerius, decis. 13, n. 49; Barbosa on l. 19, §. proinde, art. de foro ration. origin., n. 36, and the many authors there cited), who in d. l. 19, at the end, §. n. 61 et seqq., distinguishes this: because by custom the place of origin is not considered and is held to be lost if someone has moved elsewhere for a year and a day with the intention of fixing his domicile, and has not kept his domicile in the place of origin. It seems right to say that if someone has had a domicile in two places, neither will prevail over the other; and so the movables located in each place are to be directed, by the settled purpose of the head of the household, under the statutes of each place. There is, however, one case excepted: under the nature of the Aesdonic law, movables are directed to succession by the place where a person died, not by the place where the deceased had his domicile (l. 17, §. 3, D. Ad Munic.; Choppinus on the Paris customs, lib. 1, tit. 1, n. 11; Burgundus on the Flanders customs, tract. 2, nn. 1, 2; Gail, 2 observ. 36; Mevius on the Lübeck law, lib. 3, tit. 1, arts. 10 and 11, and those after them; Grotius, Introd. jurispr. Holland., lib. 2, part 26; Groenewegen in notes; Christianus Rodenburg, cap. 2, tit. 2, alleg. tract.; see also). Yet concerning the forum, the rule of origin, which hardly prevails by custom, is seen in Barbosa, d. l. 19, art. de foro origin.

units.la: 10. Unde secundo quaesitum in hypothesi; num si Roterodami habitans impubes, ubi pater filio non succedit secundum jus Scabinicum, sese Leidam conferat, ubi pater secundum jus Aesdonicum filio succederet, ibique in fata concedat, jus Leidense, num vero Roterodamense sit spectandum? Respondeo, licet communiter spectetur statutum loci, ubi bona immobilia sita sunt, quoad successiones tam ab intestato, quam ex testamento, uti idipsum fuit probatum per ll. & DD. allegatos disquisitione superiori. Et locus statuti, quoad bona mobilia, ubi defunctus habuit domicilium. Quia tamen secundum jura Aesdonica & Scabinica id speciale est, ut quoad bona mobilia spectetur loci statutum, ubi quis defungitur: ideo non secundum jus Roterodamense, sed potius Leidense, pater ratione mobilium filio succedet. Nisi tamen, casus notandus est, pupillus vel sine tutorum consensu, seu camerae pupillaris, sese Leidam contulerit; & id ipsum videatur in fraudem statuti factum. Quo casu statutum Roterodamense suas vires obtinere deberet. Consultat. jurisconf Batav. part. I. consil. 152. per ibidem allegatos. Bartol. Panormit. Boër. Mascard. vid. casum similem in causa testati apud Peckium de Testam. Conjug. lib. 4. cap. 29. num. 2. Groenweg. in notis ad Grot. introd. jur. Holl. libr. 2 part. 26. in sin. vid. & in simili Christ. Rodenburch d. tract. cap. 1. num. 5. & cap. 2. part. ult. tit. 2. Simon van der Leeuwen Paratit. jur. novissi. lib. 3. part. 3. cap. 4. num. 3.
units.tr: 10. Hence a second question arises on the following case: if a minor residing at Rotterdam, where by the Scabinic law a father does not succeed his son, moves to Leiden, where by the Aesdonic law the father would succeed the son, and dies there, is the law of Leiden or that of Rotterdam to be considered? I answer: although, as the jurists and doctors cited in the preceding inquiry have proved, the statute of the place where the immovable goods lie is generally considered for successions, both on intestacy and by will; and for movable goods the statute of the place where the deceased had his domicile. Yet since under the Aesdonic and Scabinic laws it is a special rule that movables are governed by the statute of the place where a person dies, the father will succeed his son in respect of movables not under the law of Rotterdam but rather under that of Leiden.
