units.tr: tollend. Argument from l. 44, D. Religiosis, by analogy. Socinus, Bartolus, Baldus, Alexander, Covarruvias, Practical questions, q. 36, nn. 1, 2; Tiraquellus on l. si unquam, Cod. de revocandis donationibus, n. 192; Gail, 2 obs. 130; and countless others in Salgado de Somoza, Labyrinthus creditorum concurrentium, part 1, c. 4, nn. 15–18 and following, and the same c. 4, §§2, 3; Rodenburg, de jure conjugum, tit. 2, c. 5, n. 15, p. 92.

units.la: Si tamen judices alterius loci etiam de causa cognoverint, nullo remedio cogentur, modo omnes æque supremi nec superiorem recognoscant. Nisi per litteras requisitoriales, quas appellant litteras mutui compassus requisiti, ex æquo & bono abstineant, vel secundum morem atque stylum id observare soleant, vel quod comiter habeant vicinarum civitatum sententias. Id quod nostrarum Provinciarum moribus sic observari notum est. vid. Samosa. d. tract. p. 1. c. 5.
units.tr: If, however, judges of another place have also taken cognizance of the cause, they cannot be compelled by any remedy, provided that all are equally supreme and acknowledge no superior; unless, by letters requisitorial, which they call letters of requested mutual courtesy, they refrain out of equity and good conscience, or are accustomed to observe this according to custom and practice, or courteously respect the judgments of neighbouring cities. That this is observed in this way under the customs of our Provinces is well known: see Somoza, the said tract, part 1, c. 5.

units.la: 5. Finge tamen creditorem habere pignus aut hypothecam, quae in loco domicilii creditoris sita est, an in judicio concursus creditorum, una cum suâ hypothecâ sequi tenebitur cæteros creditores, an vero ratione suae hypothecae, in loco sui domicilii, agere poterit, adeoque sibi consulere? Respondeo, si judicium inter creditores sit universale, & hypothecarius creditor actione intentet personalem, eam intentabit coram judice debitoris. Si judicium particulare, nec per eum concursus sit formatus, alibi per ante dicta, intentare poterit actionem. Quod si in rem actione hypothecam persequatur, licet judicium sit universale, exististumarem illum, coram judice sui domicilii, ubi hypotheca, jacet, experiri posse. Cum juris sit indubitati in rem actionem in loco rei sitae posse intentari. Accedit, quod nemo creditori hypothecario praejudicare valeat, cui in bonis immobilibus jus quaesitum, servatur illaesum; & onus rei impositum sequatur locum rei sitae. Neque possit creditoris conditio ea propter reddi deterior, quod debitor factus sit non solvendo. Ut aeque secundum legem sui territorii, hypothecam excutere valeat, coram judice suo, atque si debitor adhuc esset solvendo.
units.tr: 5. Suppose, however, that a creditor has a pledge or mortgage situated in the place of the creditor's domicile: in a concursus judgment, is he bound to follow the other creditors together with his own mortgage, or can he rather act on account of his mortgage in the place of his own domicile, and so provide for himself? I answer: if the judgment among creditors is universal, and the mortgage creditor brings a personal action, he will bring it before the debtor's judge. If the judgment is particular, and no concourse has been formed through it, he may bring the action elsewhere, by what was said above. But if he pursues the mortgage by a real action, although the judgment is universal, I would think he can sue before the judge of his own domicile, where the mortgage lies, since it is an indubitable rule of law that a real action can be brought in the place where the thing lies. Add that no one can prejudice a mortgage creditor, whose right acquired in immovable goods is preserved unharmed, and the burden imposed on a thing follows the place where the thing lies. Nor can the creditor's position be made worse for this reason, that the debtor has become insolvent, so that he may equally, under the law of his own territory, enforce the mortgage before his own judge, just as if the debtor were still solvent.

units.la: 1. D. de judic. Gotefred. ibid. Salgado de Somosa part. 2. c. 12. num. 35. vid. & eundem part. 1. c. 12. Barbos. ad l. 19. n. 44. 45. & seqq.
units.tr: 1. D. de judic. Gotefred. ibid. Salgado de Somosa part. 2. c. 12. num. 35. see also the same author part. 1. c. 12. Barbos. ad l. 19. n. 44. 45. & following.

units.la: seqq. D. de judic. vid. Mev. ad Lubec. libr. 3. tit. 1. §. 10. n. 59. 60. Anton. Matth. de Auctionibus libr. 1. c. 11. n. 80. in sin. & disput. de judic. 4 n. 13. 14. 15. & seq. Rodenb. p. mihi. 92.
units.tr: seqq. D. de judic. See Mevius on the Lübeck law, book 3, title 1, §10, nn. 59, 60. Anton Matthaeus, on Auctions, book 1, ch. 11, n. 80 at the end, and on judgments, disputation 4, nn. 13, 14, 15 et seq. Rodenburg, p. 92.

units.la: Neque obstat, quod propter causæ continentiam ad eundem judicem sit eundum, quo multa evitentur incommoda. Arg. l. 5. Cod. Arbitr. tutel. l. 2. D. de quibus rebus ad eund. judic. eat. l. 10. Cod. de judic. Quia & fortior obstat regula, quod alteri per alterum non inferatur iniqua conditio. Nec mutatio forte domicilii à debitore facta, præjudicium adferre debeat creditori ratione juris in rem quæsiti. Nec dissentit Mev. loc. alleg. n. 59. 60, ut qui respicit bonorum massam in ordine ad creditores chirographarios, qui tantum in personam habent actiones.
units.tr: Nor does it stand in the way that, for the sake of the connection of the case, one must go before the same judge, by which many inconveniences are avoided. Arg. l. 5. Cod. Arbitr. tutel. l. 2. D. de quibus rebus ad eund. judic. eat. l. 10. Cod. de judic. For a stronger rule opposes it: that one party's unfair position is not to be imposed on another by the other. Nor should a change of domicile made by the debtor cause prejudice to the creditor by reason of a right acquired in rem. Nor does Mev. dissent in the passage cited, n. 59, 60, since he looks to the mass of goods with regard to chirographary creditors, who have only personal actions.

units.la: 7. Et quidem si de feriis pro statutorum diversitate, variantibus, contentio, spectandus locus judicii. Ut si forte quis vocatus sit e loco ubi stylus obtinet Julianus, adeoque dies feriatus est, ad locum ubi Gregorianus obtiobtinet, adeoque dies forte non est feriatus, venire debeat. Præter allegatos, Abbas in c. sin. col. sin. de feriis. Mascard. de stat. interpret. conclus. 7. n. 52. Duaren. tit. Cod. de Testibus c. 2. Sand. 1. decis. def. 5. tit. 12.
units.tr: 7. And indeed, if there is dispute about holidays, which vary according to the diversity of statutes, the place of the court is to be regarded. For example, if someone is summoned from a place where the Julian style prevails, and so the day is a holiday, to a place where the Gregorian style prevails, and so the day perhaps is not a holiday, he ought to come. Besides the authors cited: Abbas in c. sin. col. sin. de feriis. Mascard. de stat. interpret. conclus. 7. n. 52. Duaren. tit. Cod. de Testibus c. 2. Sand. 1. decis. def. 5. tit. 12.

units.la: Censet nihilominus Besoldus incivile esse, citare partem illo tempore, quo circa conscientiæ negotia est occupata, sic ut in contumaciam procedi non debeat, si emanserit. in delibat. jur. ad 2. libr. Pand. tit. 12. n 10. in sin.
units.tr: Besold nevertheless holds it uncivil to summon a party at the time when he is occupied with matters of conscience, so that one ought not to proceed to default if he has failed to appear. in delibat. jur. ad 2. libr. Pand. tit. 12. n 10. in sin.

units.la: 8. Si de cautionibus; tales exigendæ, & interponendæ, quales postulat, stylus curiæ, ubi litigatur. § pen. & ult. instit. de Satisdat. DD. allegati.
units.tr: 8. If concerning securities: such securities are to be demanded and given as the practice of the court where the suit is brought requires. § pen. & ult. instit. de Satisdat. DD. allegati.

units.la: 9. Si de probationibus, & quidem testibus; sic eas adhibebit, sic examinabit hosce, prout exigit forum judicis, ubi producuntur. l. 3. in sin. D. de Testibus.
units.tr: 9. If concerning proofs, and indeed witnesses: thus one will admit them and thus examine them, as the forum of the judge where they are produced requires. l. 3. in sin. D. de Testibus.

units.la: 10. Si de instrumentis; sic exhibenda, sic edenda, ut fert loci statutum, ubi exhibentur, vel eduntur. l. 2. Cod. Testam. Quemad. Aperiant.
units.tr: 10. If concerning documents: they are to be exhibited and produced in the manner that the statute of the place where they are exhibited or produced requires. l. 2. Cod. Testam. Quemad. Aperiant.

units.la: 11. Quid si tamen in uno loco factum sit instrumentum coram notario, qui ibidem est habilis, an extendetur vis illius instrumenti, ad alium locum, ubi censetur inhabilis, sic ut publicum ibidem nequeat facere instrumentum?
units.tr: But what if an instrument was made in one place before a notary who is competent there? Does the force of that instrument extend to another place, where he is deemed incompetent, so that he cannot make a public instrument there?

units.la: Sunt qui id adfirmant, Ut Jason. in l. 1. Cod. summ. Trinit. n. 23. post Johann. Andr. in addit. Specul. tit. de instrum. edit. Bald. in l. si non speciali, inz. Col. Cod. de Testam. Quasi loci consuetudo, dans robur scripturæ, etiam obtineat extra territorium.
units.tr: Some affirm that it does, as Jason on l. 1. Cod. summ. Trinit. n. 23, after Johann. Andr. in the addition to the Speculum, title de instrum., edition of Bald. on l. si non speciali, inz. Col. Cod. de Testam. as if the custom of the place, which gives force to a writing, also held good outside the territory.

units.la: Sunt qui id ideo adfirmant, quod non tam de habilitate & inhabilitate notarii laboremus, quam de solemnibus. Quod si verum foret, res extra dubitationis aleam esset collocata. l. 2. Cod. quemadm. Testam. Aperiunt. post. Bartol. Bald. Jasonem. Gilken. ad tit. Cod. Summ. Trinit. 90.
units.tr: Some affirm this for the reason that we are concerned not so much with the competence or incompetence of the notary as with the formalities. If that were true, the matter would be placed beyond the risk of doubt. l. 2. Cod. quemadm. Testam. Aperiunt. after Bartol., Bald., Jason. Gilken. on the title Cod. Summ. Trinit. 90.

units.la: Verum ut quod res est dicam, existumem hic agi, non tam de solemnibus, quam probandi efficaciâ; quæ licet in uno loco sufficiens, non tamen ubique locorum, quod judex unius territorii nequeat vires tribuere instrumento, ut alibi quid operetur. Arg. l. ult. D. jurisdict. dixi ad tit. de divis. Statutor.
units.tr: But to tell the truth as it stands, I think the question here concerns not so much the formalities as the efficacy of the proof. Though this is sufficient in one place, it is not so everywhere, since a judge of one territory cannot give force to an instrument so that it operates elsewhere. Arg. l. ult. D. jurisdict. I have said on the title de divis. Statutor.

units.la: Hinc etiam mandatum ad lites, coram notario & testibus hic sufficienter factum, non tamen erit validum in Gelriæ partibus, ubi notarii non admittuntur, ut coram lege loci, hic confectum esse oporteat, quo in Geldriâ sortiatur effectum.
units.tr: Hence also a mandate for lawsuits, made here sufficiently before a notary and witnesses, will not be valid in the parts of Guelders, where notaries are not admitted. So, to take effect in Guelders, it must have been drawn up here in accordance with the law of the place.

units.la: Quemadmodum enim personam non subditam, non potest quis alibi inhabilitare; ita nec personam subditam potest alibi facere habilem. Bald. in l. 1. Cod Summ. Trinit. Johannes le Cerier. de Primogen. q. 24. n. 5. vol. 8. tractat.
units.tr: For just as one cannot render a person not subject to one's jurisdiction incompetent elsewhere, so too one cannot make a subject person competent elsewhere. Bald. in l. 1. Cod Summ. Trinit. Johannes le Cerier. de Primogen. q. 24. n. 5. vol. 8. tractat.

units.la: 12. Si de sententiæ pronunciatione, sic itidem pronunciabit judex, prout exigit sui territorii consuetudo. Loquor de ordine, puta, ta, an stans an sedens, an aperto capite, an ipse per se, an per alium recitet sententiam: Argum. dd. ll. & DD.
units.tr: 12. If the sentence is pronounced, the judge will likewise pronounce it as the custom of his territory requires. I speak of the order: for instance, whether he speaks standing or sitting, with head bared or covered, and whether he himself or another reads out the sentence. Argument from the cited laws and the Doctors.

units.la: 13. Quod si de causæ meritis agatur, quæ spectant ipsam decisionem negotii principalis, adhibendæ distinctiones antea propositæ. Ut si in rem agatur, spectetur loci consuetudo, ubi res sita. Si in personam ex contractu, locus contractus, vel ratione initii, vel implementi. Si de iis, quæ culpâ vel morâ rei accidunt, locus statuti, ubi mora vel culpa contracta, &c. per ll. & DD. allegatos. Johan. Bertachin. de Episcop. libr. 4. part. 2. q. 18. n. 45. Barbof. ad l. 65. D. judic. n. 112. 113.
units.tr: 13. But if the matter concerns the merits of the case, which bear on the decision of the principal business, the distinctions proposed earlier must be applied. Thus, if the action is in rem, the custom of the place where the thing is situated is observed. If it is in personam arising from a contract, the place of the contract, whether by reason of its beginning or its fulfilment. If it concerns things that happen through the fault or delay of the party, the place of the statute where the delay or fault was incurred, etc., as the laws and Doctors cited there. Johann Bertachin, On Bishops, book 4, part 2, q. 18, n. 45. Barbosa on law 65, D. de judiciis, nn. 112, 113.

units.la: 14. Si de executione ratione solemnium servandum statutum loci judicii, in quo fit executio; si de causæ meritis jure Romano, id quod sententiâ juri congruenter, & secundum ante datas distinctiones præseiptum, servandum est, licet, ubi fit executio, aliud quid servaretur. l. 15. §. sententiam. D. Re judic. l. argentarium. 45. in sin. D. judic. l. properandum. §. sin. Cod. judic. vid. Bartol. in l.
units.tr: 14. If the matter is one of execution, the statute of the place of judgment, where the execution takes place, must be observed with regard to the solemnities. If it concerns the merits of the case under Roman law, what is prescribed by law, in agreement with the sentence and according to the distinctions given above, must be observed, even though something else would be observed where the execution takes place. Law 15, §. sententiam, D. de re judicata; law argentarium, 45, at the end, D. de judiciis; law properandum, §. sin., Cod. de judiciis; see Bartolus on law 1, Cod. de summa Trinitate, n. 30; Baldus on the law missi opinatores, Cod. de exactionibus tributorum, book 10; Masc., the tractate, conclusion 7, nn. 78, 79, 80.

units.la: 1. Cod. Summ. Trinit. n. 30. Baldum in l. missi opinatores. Cod. de Exact. Tribut. libr. 10. Masc d. tract. concl. 7. n. 78. 79. 80. Ratio est, quia omnes judices de jure Romano uni suberant imperatori. Ut de moribus nostris dicendum sit ex humanitate per requisitoria lia judices alterius territorii sententiam alibi latam executioni mandare solere, ut tamen ad hoc non sint obstricti. Unde etiam Geldri per requisitoria desiderati sententiam in nostro territorio latam, exequi detrectabunt. vid. Barbof. ad l. 19. §. 1, D. judic. n. 93. & seqq. & ad l. 65. D. eod. n. 113. 114. & seqq.
units.tr: The reason is that all judges under Roman law were subject to one emperor. So, as regards our customs, it must be said that out of courtesy, through letters requisitorial, judges of one territory are accustomed to have a sentence passed elsewhere carried into execution, yet they are not bound to do so. Hence also the judges of Gelderland, when asked by letters requisitorial to execute a sentence passed in our territory, will refuse. See Barbosa on law 19, §. 1, D. de judiciis, nn. 93 ff., and on law 65, D. eod., nn. 113, 114 ff.

units.la: Multo minus de moribus judex sententiam alterius territorii exequetur, si lata sit contra sui territorii statutum, ratione rerum in suo territorio sitarum. Idque obtinet in vindicationibus, successionibus ab intestato, successionibus ex testamento; etiam in contractubus, in quibus, eorum ratione, quae causae spectant decisionem, ex antedictis, non servabitur statutum loci judicii, verum loci contractus.
units.tr: Much less, by custom, will a judge execute a sentence of another territory if it was passed against the statute of his own territory, by reason of things situated in his territory. This holds in vindications, in intestate successions, and in testamentary successions; and even in contracts, in which, by reason of the matters that bear on the decision, as said above, the statute of the place of judgment will not be observed but that of the place of the contract.

units.la: 15. Si super appellatione contentio, dubium nullum, quin ratione solemnium spectetur forma servari solita, in curia suprema, ad quam appellatum est, per allegatos textus & DD. Quod si circa causae momentum, ejusque decisionem incidat controversia, spectabitur statutum judicis a quo, non qui appellatur. Per textum & ibi notata in Auth. Ut cum de appell. Nov. 11 §. in init. Addit ad Bartol. ibique alii in l. 1. Cod. summ. Trinit. num. 13. vid. & a me antea notata.
units.tr: 15. If the dispute concerns an appeal, there is no doubt that the form customary by reason of the solemnities is observed in the supreme court to which the appeal is made, according to the cited texts and Doctors. But if the controversy arises over the substance of the case and its decision, the statute of the judge from whom the appeal is made will be observed, not that of the court appealed to. By the text and the notes there, in the Authentic "Ut cum de appellationibus," Novel 11, §. in init. Addition to Bartolus and others there, on law 1, Cod. de summa Trinitate, n. 13; see also what I noted earlier.

units.la: 16. Verum quid statuendum erit de citatione, quae vel ante vel post litem contestatam locum habet, etiam post sententiam, an ea fieri debebit jussu & auctoritate judicis, ubi litigatur, an ubi domicilium habet reus, si forte alibi, ubi reperiebatur, & contraxerat, sit conventus, vel ubi bona habet sita? Resp. Sunt qui distinguunt inter judices, qui uni supremo parent, quasi, illi etiam extra domicilium citare valeant. Sunt qui absolute negant judicem extra suum territorium citare posse, quid ibi cesset authoritas: ut mittere debeat litteras deprecatorias ad judicem in cujus territorio quis est citandus, ut debitorem citari faciat. Quae postrema sententia verissima, & communis Canonistarum, & usu fori recepta. Arg. l. sin. D. jurisd. l. 3. D. offic. Praesid. Felin. c. sin col. 1. de foro compet. Covarr. pract. quaest. 10. n. 7. Clarus. prax. Crimin. §. sin. q. 31. n. 19. Rebuff. 2. tom. ad l. Gall. tit. de litter. Requisf. gloss. 3. n. 11. Barbos ad l. 19. §. 1. n. 84. Ut tamen prior, quae Bartoli in l. 1. D. Req. reis, procedat, si id judici inferiori permittat Princeps supremus territorii utriusque. Panorm. in c. sin. de for. compet. n. 41.
units.tr: 16. But what is to be determined about citation, which takes place either before or after litis contestatio, and even after sentence: must it be made by the order and authority of the judge where the suit is brought, or where the defendant has his domicile, or, if he was perhaps sued elsewhere where he was found and had contracted, or where his goods are situated? Answer: some distinguish between judges who obey one supreme authority, since these may cite even outside their domicile. Others absolutely deny that a judge can cite outside his own territory, since his authority ceases there; so he ought to send letters deprecatory to the judge in whose territory the person is to be cited, so that the judge there has the debtor cited. This latter opinion is most true, is the common view of the Canonists, and is received in the practice of the courts. Argument from law sin., D. de jurisdictione; law 3, D. de officio praesidis; Felinus on chapter sin., col. 1, de foro competenti; Covarrubias, practical questions, 10, n. 7; Clarus, practice in criminal matters, §. sin., q. 31, n. 19; Rebuffus, 2nd tome, on the French law, title de litteris requisitoriis, gloss 3, n. 11; Barbosa on law 19, §. 1, n. 84. Yet the former opinion, which is Bartolus's view on law 1, D. de requisitoriis reis, holds good if the supreme prince of both territories permits this to the inferior judge. Panormitanus on chapter sin., de foro competenti, n. 41.

units.la: SECTIO UNDECIMA
units.tr: SECTIO UNDECIMA

units.la: CAPUT PRIMUM.
units.tr: CAPUT PRIMUM.

units.la: I. An qui crimen commisit extra locum domicilii, secundum locum delicti, ubi ubi deprehenditur, sit puniendus?
units.tr: I. Whether one who has committed a crime outside his domicile is to be punished according to the place of the offence, wherever he is caught?

units.la: 2. Quid si tamen delictum non sit commune?
units.tr: 2. What if, however, the offence is not common?

units.la: 3. An qui mandat delictum, puniendus secundum locum mandati, an impleti delicti?
units.tr: 3. Is one who orders an offence to be punished according to the place of the order, or the place where the offence is carried out?

units.la: 4. An qui extra territorium delinquit, reversus ad locum domicilii, poena domicilii sit puniendus?
units.tr: 4. Is one who offends outside his territory, and then returns to his place of domicile, to be punished with the penalty of his domicile?

units.la: 5. Quid si forensis alibi deliquerit, & alibi deprehendatur, qua poena afficiendus?
units.tr: 5. What if a stranger offends elsewhere and is caught elsewhere: with what penalty is he to be visited?

units.la: 6. Remissiones de jure civili erant necessitatis, moribus sunt humanitatis.
units.tr: 6. Remissions under the civil law were a matter of necessity; under custom they are a matter of humanity.

units.la: 7. An delinquens ratione bonorum alibi sitorum conveniri possit?
units.tr: 7. Can an offender be sued on account of goods situated elsewhere?

units.la: 8. Quid si in suo territorio sagittam emiserit, in alio per eam occiderit?
units.tr: 8. What if he shoots an arrow in his own territory and kills someone with it in another?

units.la: 2. Quod si tamen delictum non sit commune, vel si commune, poena statuti non sit delicti proportionata, saltem quae non ordinarie infligi solet, adeoq; contineat in loco statuti quidpiam speciale, non tenebitur reus, ordinaria poena, l. 1. §. 1. D. Effract.
units.tr: 2. But if the offence is not common, or, if it is common, the penalty of the statute is not proportionate to the offence, or at least is one not ordinarily inflicted, and the statute in its place contains something special, the offender will not be bound to the ordinary penalty. l. 1. §. 1. D. Effract.

units.la: Nisi tamen aliquo tempore in loco delicti fuerit commoratus, ut cogitam habere potuerit illius statuti poenam. Arg. l. 2. Cod. Ubi de Crimin. l. 1. Cod. ubi Senator, l. 9. 10. D. Extraord. Crimin. Argum. l. 4. §. sin. D. de Re Milit. l. 14. §. tyroni. eod. Mev. ad Lubec. quaest. 4. prælim. n. 11. alii apud Gilken. d. l. 1. Cod. summ. Trinit. n. 96.
units.tr: Unless, however, he had at some time stayed in the place of the offence, so that he could have been aware of the penalty of that statute. Arg. l. 2. Cod. Ubi de Crimin. l. 1. Cod. ubi Senator, l. 9. 10. D. Extraord. Crimin. Argum. l. 4. §. sin. D. de Re Milit. l. 14. §. tyroni. eod. Mev. ad Lubec. quaest. 4. prælim. n. 11. others cited in Gilken. d. l. 1. Cod. summ. Trinit. n. 96.

units.la: Vel etiam vero similiter cogitare potuisset & debuisset, talem statuto poenam delicto impositam esse. Ut hoc casu ignorantia veniam non meretur. Arg. l. interdum. §. licet. §. divi. D. Publican. - l. sin. D. de decret. ab ordine faciend. gloss. ibid.
units.tr: Or even if he could and ought to have thought in a similar way, that such a penalty had been attached to the offence by the statute. In this case ignorance does not deserve pardon. Arg. l. interdum. §. licet. §. divi. D. Publican. - l. sin. D. de decret. ab ordine faciend. gloss. ibid.

units.la: 4. Quid si qui extra territorium deliquit, ad locum domicilii revertatur, ibique prehensus, coram sui domicilii judice sistatur, an puniendus erit secundum sui domicilii statutum, an secundum loci statutum, ubi deliquit? Resp. licet nonnulli censeant eum in loco domicilii, secundum ejusdem statutum puniri non oportere, quod ibidem non deliquerit, de quo casu Bartol. Bald. & ex professo Salicet. in l. 1. Cod. de Summ. Trinit. n. 8. & prolixe Barbos. ad l. 19. §. proinde, in artic. de foro delict. n. 53. ibique plures. D. judic. Id quod forte obtineret, si delictum non esset commune, sed illius civitatis proprium in quâ deliquit, casu quo locus esset arbitrariæ poenæ. Arg. l. 1. §. expilatores. 1. D. Effract. Aut certus tantum judex à Supremo Principe sit constitutus, qui de tali delicto solus judicet, non alius. l. 8. Cod. de Diverf. offic. libr. 12.
units.tr: 4. What if one who has offended outside his territory returns to his place of domicile, and there, being caught, is brought before the judge of his domicile: is he to be punished according to the statute of his domicile, or according to the statute of the place where he offended? I answer: although some think that he ought not to be punished in his place of domicile under its statute, because he did not offend there, Bartolus, Baldus, and especially Salicetus on l. 1. Cod. de Summ. Trinit. n. 8, and at length Barbosa on l. 19. §. proinde, in the article on the forum of the offence, n. 53, and the several authorities there cited, have treated of this case. This would perhaps hold if the offence were not common but peculiar to the city in which it was committed, in a case where the place has an arbitrary penalty. Arg. l. 1. §. expilatores. 1. D. Effract. Or if only a certain judge has been appointed by the supreme Prince to judge such an offence alone, and no other. l. 8. Cod. de Diverf. offic. libr. 12.

units.la: Aut si inter civitates quæ invicem non parent, aut uni Principi supremo non subsunt concordata sint concepta, de puniendis invicem subditis pari pœna, ex delicto pari. Arg. l. non dubito. in sin. D. Captiv. & Postlim. licet in d. l. forte adhuc aliqua subjectio.
units.tr: Or if, between cities which do not obey one another, or which are not subject to one supreme Prince, agreements have been made concerning the punishment of each other's subjects with an equal penalty for an equal offence. Arg. l. non dubito. in sin. D. Captiv. & Postlim. although in the said law there is perhaps some further subjection.

units.la: Quia tamen reus criminis se videtur retulisse ad statutum sui domicilii quod optime noverat, & ad quod reverti decreverat, adeoque pœnam statuto decretam respexisse, ut ei semet subjicere voluerit: etiam pœnâ domicilii, eundem afficiendum existumarem. Arg. l. 1. Cod. Ubi de Crimin. l. 65. D. judic. Maxime, quod aliter delicta manerent impunita, & civis delinquere volens, extra territorium se conferret, ibique adversarium provocando, statutum sui loci eluderet. Contra l. 51. D. Ad l. Aquil. diff. Matth. Gribald. in tom. comm. opin. libr. 17. verb. statutum. p. 331. ex parte Mascard. d. tract. conclus. 6. n. 60. & seqq.
units.tr: Yet, since the offender seems to have referred himself to the statute of his domicile, which he knew very well and to which he had resolved to return, and so to have had regard to the penalty decreed by that statute, as a sign that he wished to subject himself to it, I would judge that he should be punished also with the penalty of his domicile. Arg. l. 1. Cod. Ubi de Crimin. l. 65. D. judic. Especially since otherwise offences would remain unpunished, and a citizen wishing to offend would betake himself outside the territory and, by provoking his adversary there, would evade the statute of his own place. Contra l. 51. D. Ad l. Aquil. diff. Matth. Gribald. in tom. comm. opin. libr. 17. verb. statutum. p. 331. partly from Mascard. d. tract. conclus. 6. n. 60. & seqq.

units.la: 5. Quid si forensis alibi deliquerit, an punietur secundum pœnam sui domicilii, an delicti commissi, an statuti, ubi deprehenditur? Respondeo, sunt qui censent, illum puniri non posse alibi, quam ubi deliquit: ut si alibi deliquerit, sit dimittendus, Salicet. ad l. 1. Cod. Summ. Trinit. n. 8. Matth. Gribald. loc. cit. Barbof. ad l. hæres absens. tit. alleg. D. judic. per totum. p. 470. & seqq. Neque id aliter admittunt, quam si statuto alicujus loci cautum fuerit, ut qui delictum alibi commisit, & hoc territorium ingreditur, eâdem poenâ sit puniendus. Bald. in d. l. 1. Cod. n. 97. post eum Salicet. apud Masc. d. concl. 6. n. 72. Licet non tam propter commissum delictum puniatur, quam propter illud ipsum factum, quod territorium ingrediatur, sicque de novo judicem offendat. Dicendum nihilominus videtur, cum ubique locorum, ubi fuerit deprehensus, puniri posse. Et quia non tantum omnium interest, maleficia non relinqui inulta, quam singulorum, propter cognationem illam naturalem, quam natura inter homines constituit, ut hominem homini insidiari, ubique nefas sit judicatum; adeoque ab homine beneficio affici, interfit hominis. l. 51. D. Adl. Aquil. l. 3. D. de Just. & jur. l. 7. in sin. D. Servis Export. Accedit, quod conveniat magistratubus, suum locum flagitiosis hominibus purgare. Ast flagitiosi sunt & illi, qui alibi deliquerunt; ut & alibi sint puniendi. l. 13. D. offic. Præsid.
units.tr: 5. What if a stranger (forensis) commits an offence elsewhere? Will he be punished according to the penalty of his domicile, of the place where the crime was committed, or of the statute of the place where he is caught? I answer: some hold that he cannot be punished anywhere but where he offended, so that if he offended elsewhere he must be let go, Salicet. ad l. 1. Cod. Summ. Trinit. n. 8. Matth. Gribald. loc. cit. Barbof. ad l. hæres absens. tit. alleg. D. judic. per totum. p. 470. & seqq. Nor do they admit this otherwise than where a statute of some place has provided that whoever has committed an offence elsewhere, and enters this territory, is to be punished with the same penalty. Bald. in d. l. 1. Cod. n. 97. after him Salicet. apud Masc. d. concl. 6. n. 72. Although he is punished not so much on account of the offence committed as on account of that very act of entering the territory, and so offends the judge afresh. Nevertheless it seems to me that the rule should be stated thus: he can be punished wherever he is caught. For it concerns not only all but each individual that wrongdoings should not go unpunished, on account of that natural kinship which nature has established among men, so that it has been judged wrong everywhere for one man to lie in wait for another, and so it concerns a man that a man should be harmed by a man. l. 51. D. Ad l. Aquil. l. 3. D. de Just. & jur. l. 7. in sin. D. Servis Export. In addition, it befits magistrates to rid their place of wicked men. But those also are wicked who have offended elsewhere, so they too are to be punished where they are caught. l. 13. D. offic. Præsid.

units.la: Et quidem eundem poenâ loci statuti ubi deprehenditur, puniri posse, judicarem. Tum quia poena etiâ est ad exemplū est infligenda, ut si puniatur alibi, ea poena, quę ibidē obtinet, videatur esse puniedus, quod aliter subditi ibi locorum non deterrerentur, nec metus ad omnes pervenirent. Arg. l. 29. §. sin. D. de Pœn.
units.tr: And indeed I would judge that the same person may be punished with the penalty of the place of the statute where he is caught. First, because a penalty is also to be inflicted as an example: if he is punished elsewhere, the penalty that obtains there would seem to be the one to be inflicted, since otherwise the subjects of that place would not be deterred, and the fear would not reach everyone. Arg. l. 29. §. sin. D. de Pœn.

units.la: Tum quia magistratus punientis non est inquirere unde sint flagitiosi, ut non habita ratione domicilii, aut loci delicti, eos punire valeat, secundum delicti qualitatem, adeoque secundum qualitatem illi delicto in suo territorio per pœnam impositam. l. 2. Cod. Ubi de crim. l. 1. Cod. Ubi Senator. l. 3. D. offic. Præf. Argum. l. 12. in sin. D. de Testibus. nov. 8. c. 12, Auth. Quà in Provinc. Cod. Ubi de Crimin. exceptô casu juris canonici in c. placuit. 6. q. 3.
units.tr: Second, because it is not the business of a punishing magistrate to inquire where wrongdoers come from, so that he could punish them, disregarding domicile or the place of the crime, according to the nature of the offence, and so according to the penalty imposed for that offence in his own territory. l. 2. Cod. Ubi de crim. l. 1. Cod. Ubi Senator. l. 3. D. offic. Præf. Argum. l. 12. in sin. D. de Testibus. nov. 8. c. 12, Auth. Quà in Provinc. Cod. Ubi de Crimin. excepting the case of canon law in c. placuit. 6. q. 3.

units.la: Si tamen alibi delictum non tantam merentur pœnam, quam ubi deprehensus est reus, vel ibi pœna non satis sit illi delicto proportionata, quia dura nimium & aspera, judicis arbitrio relinquendum id esse censerem, quâ pœnâ facinorosum punire velit. Arg. l. 1. § 1. D. Effract. Uti forte etiam vel ex comitate, vel concordatorum ratione pœnam domicilii rei criminalis infligere poterit. Arg. l. 7. in sin. D. Capt. & Postl. Rev. vid. Bald. in l. Mercatores. Cod. Commerc. & Mercat. & in l. 2. Cod. Eunuch. & in l. si quis in hoc genus. Cod. Episc. Cleric. Alberic. de Rosate 2. part. D. nov. sol. 239. Johan. Bertachin. de Episcop. 2. part. libr. 4. q. 18. n. 51.
units.tr: If, however, the offence committed elsewhere does not deserve as great a penalty as the place where the accused is seized, or if the penalty there is not sufficiently proportionate to that offence, because it is too harsh and severe, I would think it should be left to the judge's discretion with what penalty he wishes to punish the criminal. Arg. l. 1. § 1. D. Effract. Perhaps also, out of courtesy or by reason of agreements, he may inflict the penalty of the domicile of the accused criminal. Arg. l. 7. in sin. D. Capt. & Postl. Rev. vid. Bald. in l. Mercatores. Cod. Commerc. & Mercat. & in l. 2. Cod. Eunuch. & in l. si quis in hoc genus. Cod. Episc. Cleric. Alberic. de Rosate 2. part. D. nov. sol. 239. Johan. Bertachin. de Episcop. 2. part. libr. 4. q. 18. n. 51.

units.la: 6. Jure tamen civili notandum, remissionibus locum fuisse de necessitate, ut reus ad locum, ubi deliquit, sic petente judice, fucerit fuerit mittendus, quod omnes judices uni subessent imperatori. Et omnes provinciae Romanae unitae essent accessorie, non principaliter. Nov. 60. 6. 1. nov. 134. c. 5. Auth. quâ in Provinc. & l. 1. Cod. Ubi de Crimin. l. 1. Cod. Ad l. Jul. Repet. l. 28. §. sin. D. de Pœn. vid. Gothefr. ad d. l. 1. Cod. & ad l. 7. D. de Custod. & Exhib. reorum. Clarum §. sin. q. 38. n. 19. Grammat. decis. 26. Thoming. decis. 5. n. 9. Gomes. 3. Resol. 1. n. 8. Donell. 17. comm. 16.
units.tr: 6. Yet it must be noted that by the civil law remissions were of necessity had, so that the accused, if the judge asked, was to be sent back to the place where he offended, since all judges were subject to one emperor, and all the Roman provinces were united as accessories, not as principals. Nov. 60. 6. 1. nov. 134. c. 5. Auth. quâ in Provinc. & l. 1. Cod. Ubi de Crimin. l. 1. Cod. Ad l. Jul. Repet. l. 28. §. sin. D. de Pœn. vid. Gothefr. ad d. l. 1. Cod. & ad l. 7. D. de Custod. & Exhib. reorum. Clarum §. sin. q. 38. n. 19. Grammat. decis. 26. Thoming. decis. 5. n. 9. Gomes. 3. Resol. 1. n. 8. Donell. 17. comm. 16.

units.la: 7. Verum an unquam, qui delictum commisit, ratione bonorum, alibi sitorum conveniri poterit, sic ut ibidem secundum statutum bonorum veniat puniendus, licet non ibidem reperiatur? Non equidem. Quamvis enim quis sortiatur forum, ubi subditus non est, aut non reperitur, idque ratione rei immobilis, ubicunque ea sita sit, tit. Cod. Ubi in rem Actio. Nullibi tamen legitur aliquem sortiri forum ratione delicti, nisi vel ubi domicilium habet, vel ubi deliquit, vel alibi, si modo alibi deprehendatur. Arg. l. libertas. §. sola. D. Ad Munic. l. rescripto. §. sin. D. Muner. & Honor. Alexand. Consil. 138. col. 3. libr. 1. Cravett. consil. 27. Alder. Masc. tract. all conclus. 6. n. 46. 62.
units.tr: 7. But can anyone who has committed an offence ever be sued on account of goods situated elsewhere, so that he is to be punished there according to the statute on goods, even though he is not found there? Certainly not. For although someone may have a forum where he is not a subject, or where he is not found, and that on account of immovable property, wherever it is situated, tit. Cod. Ubi in rem Actio. yet nowhere do we read that anyone acquires a forum on account of an offence, except where he has his domicile, or where he offended, or elsewhere, if he is indeed caught elsewhere. Arg. l. libertas. §. sola. D. Ad Munic. l. rescripto. §. sin. D. Muner. & Honor. Alexand. Consil. 138. col. 3. libr. 1. Cravett. consil. 27. Alder. Masc. tract. all conclus. 6. n. 46. 62.

units.la: Id quod tum maxime locum habet, cum statuti pœnâ, intra suam dioecesin, aut alibi fuit punitus. Durum quippe foret, unius delicti nomine, quem duplici pœnâ pupiri: Marcus Anton. Marscot. in c. ut animarum. de Confis. Stit. 5. tom. Repet. jur. canonic. p. 116. n. 50.
units.tr: This holds especially when someone has already been punished by the penalty of the statute within his own diocese, or elsewhere. For it would be harsh to punish a man twice on account of one offence. Marcus Anton. Marscot. in c. ut animarum. de Confis. Stit. 5. tom. Repet. jur. canonic. p. 116. n. 50.

units.la: 8. Quid si quispiam è suo territorio sagittam emiserit, vel sclopum exoneraverit, sic ut aliquem in alieno territorio consistentë, vel vulneraverit, vel occiderit? An spectandū erit statutum, ratione pœnæ infligendæ, ejus loci, ubi constitit, qui deliquit, an potius ejus loci, ubi quis est vulneratus, vel occisus? Respondeo, statutum loci, in quo deprehenditur esse respiciendū, ut locus debeat esse præventioni. Ibi, quia affectus & animus fuit occidendi, qui pœnam meretur. Hic, quia delictum est consummatum. Arg l. 1. l. 8. D. Ad l. Cornel. de Sicar. tit. Cod. Ubi de Crimin. Abbas in c. licet. n. 25. de foro compet. vid. Clarum q. 38. verb. item pone, quod aliquis. Sunt tamen qui respiciunt locum patientis, per l. eum qui. §. pen. D. Injur. Mascard. tract. alleg. conclus. 7. n. 25.
units.tr: 8. What if someone shoots an arrow from his own territory, or discharges a gun, so that he wounds or kills a person standing in another territory? Is the statute to be regarded, for the penalty to be inflicted, of the place where the one who committed the offence stood, or rather of the place where the person was wounded or killed? I answer that the statute of the place where he is caught is to be regarded, so that that place should have priority. There, because the intention and purpose of killing is what deserves punishment; here, because the offence has been completed. Arg l. 1. l. 8. D. Ad l. Cornel. de Sicar. tit. Cod. Ubi de Crimin. Abbas in c. licet. n. 25. de foro compet. vid. Clarum q. 38. verb. item pone that someone... Yet there are those who look to the place of the one who suffered the harm, per l. eum qui. §. pen. D. Injur. Mascard. tract. alleg. conclus. 7. n. 25.

units.la: SECT. XI. CAP. II.
units.tr: SECTION XI, CHAPTER II.

units.la: 1. Quale tempus spectandum, an delicti, an sententiæ, dum agitur de pœnâ infligendâ?
units.tr: 1. What time is to be considered, that of the delict or that of the sentence, when a penalty is to be inflicted?

units.la: 2. Cujus loci statutum de jure Romano spectandum circa bonorum confiscationem?
units.tr: 2. Which place's statute is to be considered under Roman law concerning confiscation of goods?

units.la: 3. Cujus loci statutum de moribus, quoad immobilia? 4. Cujus loci statutum, quoad mobilia?
units.tr: 3. Which place's statute concerning customs is to be considered, as regards immovables? 4. Which place's statute, as regards movables?

units.la: 5. An quisque fiscus teneatur sui territorii creditoribus?
units.tr: 5. Whether each fisc is bound to the creditors of its own territory?

units.la: I. UT in delictis ratione diversitatis locorum, diversæ etiam pœnæ infligendæ veniunt, prout jam examinatum est, & ostensum; ita etiam temporum ratione pœnæ quandoque variabunt, unius ejusdemque delicti contemplatione. Quid si igitur, alia pœna delicto imposita tempore delicti, alia tempore condemnationis; quænam erit facinoroso infligenda? Respondeo, ea, quæ obtinebat ex vi statuti, tempore delicti. Tum quippe obligatio ad illam pœnam erat nata, non aliter atque actio, simulac contractus est celebratus, licet in diem dilata solutio. Accedit, quod statutum tempore latæ sententiæ conditum, referretur ad præterita, si pœna delicto præterito, ex statuto de futuro, esset irroganda; id quod esse contra naturam statuti simpliciter loquentis, antea fuit deductum, per l. 9. Cod. de leg. l. 1. D. de Pæn. Videtur tamen obstare l. pen. D. si ex Noxal. causa agatur. Quæ secundum DD. respicit pœnam tempore latæ sententiæ debitam.
units.tr: I. Just as in delicts different penalties come to be imposed by reason of the diversity of places, as has already been examined and shown, so also by reason of time the penalties sometimes vary, with regard to one and the same delict. What then if one penalty was imposed for the delict at the time of the delict, and another at the time of condemnation? Which penalty is to be inflicted on the wrongdoer? I answer: the one that held by force of the statute at the time of the delict. For at that time the obligation to that penalty had arisen, just as an action arises as soon as a contract has been made, even though payment is deferred to a later day. Moreover, a statute enacted at the time of the sentence would refer to past events, if a penalty for a past delict were to be inflicted under a statute speaking of the future; and this has already been shown to be contrary to the nature of a statute speaking simply, from l. 9 Cod. de leg. l. 1 D. de Pæn. Yet l. pen. D. si ex Noxal. causa agatur seems to stand in the way. According to the jurists, this passage concerns the penalty owed at the time of the sentence.

units.la: Aut pœna delicto est propria & proportionata, atque adeo pœna ordinaria; & inspicitur statutum temporis delicti. l. si quis decurio. D. de Falsi.
units.tr: Either the penalty is proper and proportionate to the delict, and so is an ordinary penalty; and then the statute of the time of the delict is looked to. l. si quis decurio. D. de Falsi.

units.la: Aut quædam est adjectio vel diminutio pœnæ,ex aliquâ novâ qualitate personæ accedenti, vel ex aliâ aliquâ causâ ; & inspicitur statutum tempore sententiæ conditum. per d.l.pen. D. si ex noxal. cauf. Id quod ad servum delinquentem, postmodum liberum factum , & per rationem ad ignobilem, postmodum nobilitatum recte retuleris.
units.tr: Or there is some addition or diminution of the penalty, arising from some new quality of the person or from some other cause; and then the statute enacted at the time of the sentence is looked to. This is in accordance with d.l.pen. D. si ex noxal. cauf. which you may rightly apply to a slave who offended and was afterwards made free, and by analogy to a commoner who was afterwards ennobled.

units.la: Quasi propter novam aliquam qualitatem mitius, quam antea puniendus esse videatur. d. l. 11. D. Sepulcr. violat. l. 1. §. 3. D. Ambigeis. l. 1. in sin. D. Furibus balnear.
units.tr: As when, because of some new quality, he seems to be punishable more mildly than before. d. l. 11. D. Sepulcr. violat. l. 1. §. 3. D. Ambigeis. l. 1. in fin. D. Furibus balnear.

units.la: Hinc etiam merito Theorici statuunt in d. l. pen. non agi, de pœnâ mutata, sed personæ conditione. Pacius Antin. cent. 1. q. 74. & Nicol. de Passeribus, qui variorum reprehendit solutiones.
units.tr: Hence the Theorists also rightly hold, in d. l. pen., that the matter concerns not a changed penalty but a change in the condition of the person. Pacius, Antin. cent. 1. q. 74. and Nicolaus de Passeribus, who criticised the solutions of various writers.

units.la: Id tamen secundum Bartolum certa veritate niti statuit, quod statutum temporis delicti sit spectandum. d. l. 1. D. Pœn. Nicol. de Passer. in suo conciliatore n. 20. n. 31. p. mihi 27. Per rationem, quod si pœna sit certa, reus simulac deliquit, ad illam sit adstrictus; si incerta, demum ad illam quam judex tempore sententiæ determinaverit. l. sin. Cod. Contr. Empt. vid. Bald. in l. 1. D. de Pœn. Castrensf. & Alexand. ad d. l. pen. si ex noxal. Mascard. conclus. 4. n. 62. diss. ex parte Clarus. §. sin. q. 85. n. 4. Everh, consil. 451 n. 11. Zoes. D. de Pœn. n. 38.
units.tr: Yet according to Bartolus this is settled on a certain truth: that the statute of the time of the delict is to be looked to. d. l. 1. D. Pœn. Nicolaus de Passeribus in his Conciliator n. 20, n. 31, p. mihi 27. The reason is that if the penalty is fixed, the offender is bound to it as soon as he offends; if it is uncertain, he is bound only to that which the judge determines at the time of the sentence. l. sin. Cod. Contr. Empt. See Baldus on l. 1. D. de Pœn.; Castrensis and Alexander on d. l. pen. si ex noxal.; Mascardus, conclus. 4. n. 62. diss. ex parte; Clarus, §. sin. q. 85. n. 4.; Everhard, consil. 451. n. 11.; Zoesius, D. de Pœn. n. 38.

units.la: 2. Claudat agmen circa delicta, controversia de bonorum confiscatione. Finge, quempiam in uno loco fuisse majestatis condemnatum, ejusque bona fisco addicta; an quæ habet omnia, fisco loci, ubi condemnatus est, applicabuntur, an vero quæ bona extra territorium sita, fisco alieni dicasterii applicabuntur? Respondeo, de jure Romano, proposita quæstio nullam in se difficultatem continebat, quod omnes Provinciæ, uni subessent imperatori, adeoque omnia commissa uni fisco applicabantur. l. 1. & seq. D. bon. Damn. l. 5. in Princ. Cod. l. Jul. Majest. Nov. 134. cap. 13. circa sin. l. si quando. Cod. de bon. vacant. libr. 10. vid. Chassan. ad Burgund. Rubric. 2. §. 1. & seqq.
units.tr: 2. The question of confiscation of goods closes the discussion of delicts. Suppose someone was condemned for treason in one place and his goods were adjudged to the fisc: will all the goods he has be applied to the fisc of the place where he was condemned, or will the goods lying outside that territory be applied to the fisc of another jurisdiction? I answer: under Roman law the question as put contained no difficulty in itself, since all the provinces were subject to one emperor, and so all forfeited property was applied to one fisc. l. 1. & seq. D. bon. Damn. l. 5. in Princ. Cod. l. Jul. Majest. Nov. 134. cap. 13. circa fin. l. si quando. Cod. de bon. vacant. libr. 10. See Chassanaeus on Burgundy, Rubric. 2. §. 1. & seqq.

units.la: 3. De moribus tamen distinguendum foret, inter immobilia & mobilia bona. Illa quia judici loci subjacent, etiam fisco cujusque territorii applicabuntur; adeoque totidem erunt confiscationes, quod sunt distinctæ, nec invicem subjectæ ditiones. Etsi enim qui deliquit, ejus loci pœnis, ubi delictum commissum, se subjecisse censeatur; non tamen id extendendum videtur ad immobilia alibi jacentia, utpote in quæ nunquam judex qui condemnat imperium habuit, nec delinquens ea territorio cui subjacent exemit, aut eximere potuit. Nam si alibi sita immobilia pœnali statuto afficerentur, illud statutum tanquam reale extra statuentis territorium extendetur: quod absurdum dum esse ex anterioribus abunde patet. Arg. tit. Cod. ubi in rem actio. l. ult. D. de jurisd. l. 30. §. 1. D. de Excus. Tutor. l. 9. in init. Cod. de Pagan. l. 8. §. universi. Cod. Hæret. l. 20. Cod. de Episc. & Cleric. Cravett. consil. 128. n. 10. Boerius ad Bituric. tit. 2. §. 10. Natta in c. quamvis. col. 61. verf. 6. Gothefred. ad d. l. 30. Zoes. D. Ad l. Jul. Majest. n. 18. Anton. Matth. tract. de Auctionib. libr. 2. cap. 4. n. 31. & de Criminibus. libr. 2. tit. 20. cap. 4. n. 17. 18. 19. & de Judiciis disp. ult. n. 119. per Clarum, Imbertum &c. Gilken. prolixe ad l. 1. Cod. Summ. Trinit. n. 120. 121. 122. 123. & seqq. ibique varii.
units.tr: 3. But concerning customs one must distinguish between immovable and movable goods. The former, because they are subject to the judge of the place, will be applied to the fisc of each territory; and so there will be as many confiscations as there are distinct jurisdictions, not subject to one another. For although one who commits a delict is held to have submitted himself to the penalties of the place where the delict was committed, this does not seem to extend to immovables lying elsewhere: the judge who condemns never had authority over them, and the offender could not, and did not, withdraw them from the territory to which they are subject. For if immovables situated elsewhere were subjected to a penal statute, that statute would be extended as a real statute beyond the territory of the one who enacted it, and that this is absurd is abundantly clear from what has gone before. Arg. tit. Cod. ubi in rem actio. l. ult. D. de jurisd. l. 30. §. 1. D. de Excus. Tutor. l. 9. in init. Cod. de Pagan. l. 8. §. universi. Cod. Hæret. l. 20. Cod. de Episc. & Cleric. Cravetta, consil. 128. n. 10.; Boerius on Bituric. tit. 2. §. 10.; Natta on c. quamvis, col. 61, verf. 6.; Godefroy on d. l. 30.; Zoesius, D. Ad l. Jul. Majest. n. 18.; Antonius Matthaeus, tract. de Auctionib. libr. 2. cap. 4. n. 31. and de Criminibus, libr. 2. tit. 20. cap. 4. n. 17, 18, 19, and de Judiciis disp. ult. n. 119., per Clarus, Imbertus etc.; Gilkens, prolixly on l. 1. Cod. Summ. Trinit. n. 120, 121, 122, 123, & seqq., and the various writers there.

units.la: 4. Quod si de mobilibus alibi positis contentio, non idem videtur. Mobilia quippe judici domicilii, vel condemnanti cedere debebunt, quod sequantur personam, & ibidem esse fingantur, ubi quisque sedem suarum fortunarum collocavit. Arg. l. in lege 203. D. de verb. signif. l. 7. D. de incol. l. ex facto. 25 §. rerum. D. Hared. infit. l. 186. D. de leg. 3. Arg. l. 50. §. 1. verb. cum non loci. D. de judic. Bald. in l. Mercatores. Cod. de Comm. & Mercat. Costal. in l. 8. D. Ex quibus caus. major. Burgund. ad Consuet. Flandr. tract. 2. n. 25.
units.tr: 4. But if the dispute concerns movables situated elsewhere, the position does not seem to be the same. Movables must indeed yield to the judge of the domicile, or to the judge who pronounced the condemnation, because they follow the person and are deemed to be where each has fixed the seat of his property. Arg. l. in lege 203, D. de verb. signif.; l. 7, D. de incol.; l. ex facto 25 §. rerum, D. Hered. instit.; l. 186, D. de reg. iur.; Arg. l. 50 §. 1, verb. cum non loci, D. de judic.; Bald. in l. Mercatores, Cod. de Comm. et Mercat.; Costal. in l. 8, D. Ex quibus caus. maior.; Burgund. ad Consuet. Flandr., tract. 2, n. 25.

units.la: Huc referam casum quo quis condemnatus in uno loco, beneficio privatur quod alibi obtinet, ut tamen per alium judicem executio privationis illius beneficii fiat. c. Postulasti. Stulasti de foro Compet. Arg. c. sin. eod. Barbof. ad l. 19. §. 1. n. 6. D. de judic. vid. mea superius allegata.
units.tr: To this I refer the case in which someone condemned in one place is deprived of a benefit he holds elsewhere, yet the execution of that deprivation is carried out by another judge. c. Postulasti. Stulasti de foro Compet. Arg. c. sin. eod. Barbosa on l. 19. §. 1. n. 6. D. de judic.; see my own works cited above.

units.la: Dissentiunt hic alii, qui censent judicem bona quaevis sive mobilia sive immobilia, in suo reperta territorio retinere posse. Id quod facile concesssero, si de absoluta loquamur potestate, quam quisque in suo potest exercere; ut non teneatur, nisi ex aequitate, mobilia cedere judici distincti territorii. Clarus §. sin. q. 78. n. 27. Peregrin. de jure fisc. libr. 5. c. 1. post Bursat. consil. 43. n. 13. & alios ibid. vid. Tiraqueli. de jure Primogen. q. 48. 49. Id saltem sic obtinere de moribus locorum nonnullorum in Gallia post Baldum in l. ex facto. D. Hared. instit. Alexandr. vol. 1, conf. 31. Chassan. ad. § 16. tit. de Manumortua. n. 32. Consuet. Burgund. scribit. Choppin. de Mor. Paris. 1. tit. 1. n. 4.
units.tr: Others dissent here, holding that a judge may retain any goods, whether movable or immovable, found within his territory. I would readily concede this if we speak of the absolute power which each may exercise in his own territory, so that he is not bound, except by equity, to hand over movables to a judge of a distinct territory. Clarus, §. sin. q. 78. n. 27.; Peregrinus, de jure fisc. libr. 5. c. 1., following Bursatus, consil. 43. n. 13., and others there; see Tiraqueau, de jure Primogen. q. 48, 49. That this at least is the rule under the customs of some places in France, following Baldus on l. ex facto. D. Hared. instit., is written by Alexander, vol. 1, conf. 31.; Chassanaeus on § 16, tit. de Manumortua, n. 32.; the Consuetudines of Burgundy and Choppin, de Mor. Paris. 1. tit. 1. n. 4.

units.la: Quod si tamen bonorum publicatio non sit facta de jure communi, verum de jure speciali; scil. ut civitatis statuto in hoc aut illo casu praeter jus commune, bona delinquentis sint fisco loci applicanda; forte non erit sententia confiscationis ad bona extra territorium applicanda: nisi & ubi sunt bona sita etiam jure speciali ad publicationem & confiscationem auctoritate domini illius territorii procedatur. Franciscus Lucanus de fisco & ejus Privileg. 2. part. de Publicat. bo-nor. n. 4. p. 112, volum. 1. tract, Giiken. ad init. tit. Cod. Summ. Trinit. n. 131. 132, 133. ibique varii.
units.tr: If, however, confiscation of goods has not been made under the common law but under a special law, namely where a city statute, in this or that case and in addition to the common law, directs that the goods of an offender are to be applied to the fisc of the place, then perhaps the sentence of confiscation will not extend to goods outside the territory. The exception is where, for goods situated there, seizure and confiscation are also carried out under a special law, by the authority of the lord of that territory. Franciscus Lucanus de fisco & ejus Privileg. 2. part. de Publicat. bonor. n. 4. p. 112, volum. 1. tract, Giiken. ad init. tit. Cod. Summ. Trinit. n. 131. 132, 133. ibique varii.

units.la: 5. Verum an casu quo bona confiscata in diversis territoriis sita, duobus aut pluribus fiscis applicantur, quisque fiscum tenebitur tantum ex suis confiscatis, sui territorii creditoribus, qui fisco poenam persequenti sunt potiores, an omnibus creditoribus indistincte; id est non tantum suis, sed & forensibus? Resp. Fiscus, etiam alieni territorii, omnibus etiam alterius territorii creditoribus, condemnati debitoris, obligatur; eo quod inter fiscos facta divisio bonorum contemplatione, creditoribus nequeat praejudicare. per l. 50. §. 1. D. de judic. l. si pro rata. D. de Religios. l. si vir uxori. D. Ad leg. Falcid. Alex. consil. 32. n. 16. libr. 1. Tiraquell. de jure Primogen. q. 35. n. 31. Peregrin. de jure fisc. libr. 5. tit. 1. n. 144. Salgado de Somosa labyr. concurs. creditor. part. 2. c. 12. n. 34, 35. diff. Clarus Pract. crim. q. 78. verb. sed quaero. Bald. Angel. in l. ex facto. D. Haered. institut, vid. Choppinum de Moribus Paris. 2. tit. 5. n. 24.
units.tr: 5. But whether, in the case where confiscated goods lying in different territories are applied to two or more fisci, each fiscus shall be bound only to pay its own creditors of its own territory out of its own confiscated goods (creditors who are preferred to the fiscus pursuing the penalty), or to all creditors without distinction, that is, not only its own but also those from elsewhere? Answer: a fiscus, even of another territory, is bound to all creditors of the condemned debtor, including those of the other territory, since a division of the goods made between the fisci cannot prejudice the creditors. See l. 50 §1 D. de judiciis; l. si pro rata D. de religiosis; l. si vir uxori D. ad legem Falcidiam; Alexander, consil. 32 n. 16 lib. 1; Tiraquellus, de jure primogeniorum q. 35 n. 31; Peregrinus, de jure fisci lib. 5 tit. 1 n. 144; Salgado de Somoza, labyrinthus creditorum concursus part. 2 c. 12 n. 34, 35; Clarus, practica criminalis q. 78 verb. sed quaero; Baldus and Angelus on l. ex facto D. de haeredibus instituendis; see Choppinus, de moribus Parisiensibus lib. 2 tit. 5 n. 24.

units.la: Quandoque tamen cessabit hoc jus creditorum, sic ut nequeant ad universum patrimonium defuncti recurrere, verum ad certam bonorum portionem, loco & qualitate à caeteris distinctam. Id quod ex privilegio in bonis militis obtinere colligitur ex l. 17. §. Julianus. D. Testam. Milit. l. 26. §. si miles. miles. D. Familiæ Erciscę. Quod privilegium cum exceptionem inducat à regulâ, certum erit regulam in aliis casibus non exceptis non vitiari.
units.tr: Sometimes, however, this right of creditors will cease, so that they cannot have recourse to the whole estate of the deceased, but only to a certain portion of the goods, distinguished from the rest by place and kind. That this holds for the privilege in a soldier's goods is gathered from l. 17. §. Julianus. D. Testam. Milit. l. 26. §. si miles. miles. D. Familiae Erciscundae. Since this privilege introduces an exception to the rule, it will be certain that the rule is not impaired in other cases that are not excepted.

units.la: SECTIO XII. Caput Primum.
units.tr: SECTION XII. Chapter One.

units.la: 1. Jura non facile immutanda.
units.tr: 1. Laws are not to be changed easily.

units.la: 2. Cujus sit statuta tollere?
units.tr: 2. Whose right is it to repeal statutes?

units.la: 3. An decurionum?
units.tr: 3. Is it the right of the decurions?

units.la: 4. An Principis?
units.tr: 4. Is it the right of the Prince?

units.la: 5. An si statuta sint jurata?
units.tr: 5. What if the statutes have been sworn to?

units.la: 6. An statuta extendantur ultra vitam statuentium?
units.tr: 6. Do statutes extend beyond the lifetime of those who enacted them?

units.la: 7. An sic unquam condantur, ut nunquam tollantur?
units.tr: 7. Can statutes ever be enacted so that they are never repealed?

units.la: 1. ETsi non facile ea sint immutanda, quæ diu placuerunt, & nonnisi propter evidentem aliquam reipublicæ utilitatem. l. 2. D. de Princip. Constit. Nec jurium aut statutorum in dubio præsumenda correctio, utpote quæ odiosa. Arg. l. 32. in sin. Cod. de Appellat. Andreas ab Exea in c. canonum statuta, de Constit. Repet. jur. canon. tom. 2. p. 190. n. 173. Merul. prax. civil. libr. 1. tit. 4. c. 1. art. 25. Montan. de Tutel. cap. 4. n. 50. Rittershuf. ad Nov. in Proœm. c. 3.
units.tr: 1. Although those things which have pleased for a long time should not easily be changed, and only for some clear advantage to the commonwealth: Digest, de Principum Constitutionibus, law 2. Nor is a correction of laws or statutes to be presumed in doubt, since it is odious: cf. Code, de Appellationibus, law 32, at the end. Andreas ab Exea, on c. canonum statuta, de Constitutionibus, Repetitio of the canon law, vol. 2, p. 190, n. 173. Merula, Practice of Civil Law, book 1, title 4, ch. 1, art. 25. Montanus, de Tutela, ch. 4, n. 50. Rittershusius, on the Novels, Preface, ch. 3.

units.la: Quia tamen nihil constans est & stabile, nihil perfectum in rerum natura, quæ vel indies novas deproperat ed re formas, vel quod antea confusum, declarare, quod imperfectum perficere, quod antiquatum forte renovare. nov. 7. in init. §. 13. 18. Cod. de vet. jur. Enucl. Ideo non sic unquam leges vel statuta ferri poterunt, ut non quondam mutationi, vel emendationi, subjaceant. Quā etiam ratione postquam de statutorum constitutione, naturā, & effectubus dictum est, non poterunt omitti, quæ eorundem vel obrogationem, vel derogationem, vel abrogationem spectarent,
units.tr: nov. 7. in init. §. 13. 18. Cod. de vet. jur. Enucl. But since nothing in the nature of things is constant and stable, and nothing is perfect, which either daily hastens to new forms or needs to declare what was confused, to complete what was imperfect, or perhaps to renew what has grown obsolete, laws or statutes can never be enacted in such a way that they are not at some time subject to change or amendment. For this reason, after we have spoken of the enactment, nature, and effects of statutes, we cannot omit those matters which concern their modification, derogation, or abrogation.

units.la: 2 Ubi primitus in genere inquiritur, cujus sit statuta tollere vel abrogare? Respondeo, ejus est statuta tollere, cujus est constituere: quod nihil tam naturale sit, quam unumquodque eodem modo solvi, quo ligatum est. Ut etiam eadem in revocando solemnitas requiratur, quæ in condendo. §. 1. instit. quibus mod. tollitur oblig. l. nihil tam naturale. D. Regul. juris. l. 3. D. eodem. l. ult. Cod. de legibus. DD. ad d. l. nihil.
units.tr: 2. Here we first inquire in general whose right it is to repeal or abrogate statutes. I answer: it belongs to the one whose right it is to enact them, since nothing is so natural as that each thing be dissolved in the same way in which it was bound. Likewise the same solemnity is required in revoking as in enacting. §. 1. instit. quibus mod. tollitur oblig. l. nihil tam naturale. D. Regul. juris. l. 3. D. eodem. l. ult. Cod. de legibus. DD. ad d. l. nihil.

units.la: Unde qui condere statuta nequit si non accedat Principis supremi confirmatio, eadem sine ejusdem authoritate tollere non potest. Natta. consil. 534. n. 32. vol. 3. Mascard. de Statut. interpret. conclus. 8, n. 39, ubi plures.
units.tr: Natta. consil. 534. n. 32. vol. 3. Mascard. de Statut. interpret. conclus. 8, n. 39, ubi plures. Hence one who cannot enact statutes, unless the confirmation of the supreme Prince is added, cannot repeal the same without the authority of that Prince.

units.la: Nisi tamen, uti statuunt DD. statuentes ad jus commune velint recurrere, aut ad statutum antiquum ; quasi tunc non opus esset supremi Principis in abrogando auctoritate. Abbas, Felinus. in c. cum accessissent. de Constit. Johan. Crot. in c. conquestus. de Usur. n. 12. tom. 4. Repet. jur. canon. p. 756. Mascard. d. tract. concl. 8. n. 93. Quod tamen non potest non displicere, propter regulam generalem antea traditam, à quâ quisquis deviaverit, is mihi exceptionem aut limitationem, aliqua lege, aut legis argumento probaverit.
units.tr: Abbas, Felinus. in c. cum accessissent. de Constit. Johan. Crot. in c. conquestus. de Usur. n. 12. tom. 4. Repet. jur. canon. p. 756. Mascard. d. tract. concl. 8. n. 93. Unless, however, as the jurists state, those who enacted the statutes wish to have recourse to the common law, or to the earlier statute; in such a case there would seemingly be no need of the authority of the supreme Prince in repealing them. Yet this cannot but displease me, on account of the general rule laid down above, from which whoever departs must prove to me an exception or limitation, by some law or by an inference from law.

units.la: 3. An igitur per Decuriones, aut civitatis consilium, quod statuta condidit, eadem immutari, vel tolli poterunt? Respondeo, (casu quo supremi Principis confirmatio fuit necessaria) vel sunt condita statuta per decuriones in favorem civitatis ; in quantum hoc illis Princeps permisit; & revocari poterunt; siquidem cuivis licitum est favori pro se introducto, adeoque privilegio sibi per Principem tributo, renunciare. Vel statuta simpliciter introducta sunt in bonum communitatis, nec tantum Principe talia permittente, verum etiam eadem expresse comprobante. Neque à statuentibus tolli poterunt, nisi etiam Principis accedat auctoritas. Per regulam antea traditam, quod unumquodque eadem solemnitate tollatur, quâ constitutum est. d. l. nihil tam naturale. D. de Regul. jur. §. 1. & ult. Instit. quibus mod. testam. infirm. l. 1. §. 6. Cod. de veter. jur. Enucl. Paulo tamen aliter aliter hæc explicat Baldus de Statut. q. 26. num. 3. Bartol. in l. omnes populi. D. just. & jur. n. 33. vid. Anton. Burges. in c. cum accessisset. de Constit. 2. Tom. Repet. jur. can. p. 391. n. 72. Hieron. Pantsman. quæst. jur. contr. libr. 2. q. 17. n. 60. Zoes. D. de Princ. Constit. n. 35. Perez. Cod. de officio juridic. Alexandr. num. sin.
units.tr: 3. Can statutes enacted by the decurions, or by the council of the city, then be changed or repealed by the same? I answer: (in the case where the confirmation of the supreme Prince was necessary) either the statutes were enacted by the decurions for the benefit of the city, so far as the Prince allowed this to them, and they may be revoked, since anyone may renounce a favour introduced on his own behalf, and so a privilege granted to him by the Prince. Or the statutes were introduced simply for the good of the community, and not merely with the Prince permitting such things but also expressly approving them. These cannot be repealed by those who enacted them unless the authority of the Prince also be added, by the rule laid down above, that each thing is removed by the same solemnity by which it was established. d. l. nihil tam naturale. D. de Regul. jur. §. 1. & ult. Instit. quibus mod. testam. infirm. l. 1. §. 6. Cod. de veter. jur. Enucl. Baldus, however, explains these matters otherwise, de Statutis, q. 26, n. 3. Bartolus, on law Omnes populi, D. de justitia et jure, n. 33. See also Antonius Burgensis, on c. cum accessisset, de Constitutionibus, 2nd vol. of the Repetitio of the canon law, p. 391, n. 72. Hieronymus Pantsmann, Quaestiones juris controversi, book 2, q. 17, n. 60. Zoesius, D. de Principum Constitutionibus, n. 35. Perez, Cod. de officio juridici. Alexander, n. at end.

units.la: 4. An itaque Princeps, qui statuta confirmat, eadem tollere poterit? Respondeo, quia talia statuta non sunt statuta, nisi Principis consensus expressus vel tacitus accedat. l. 3. Cod. Silent. libr. 12. Etiam ejus est tollere, cujus erat constituere. Dicendum erit, Principem de plenitudine potestatis talia statuta posse abrogare. Modo se hoc velle expresserit; quod id in specie sit exprimendum, Principem ea velle abrogare. Ejus quippe est nolle, cujus erat velle. l. 3. D. de Regul. juris. ibique DD. l. 35. l. 153. D. eod. vid. Merul. Praxi Civil. libr. 1. tit. 4. c. 2. n. 4. Christin. vol. 2. decis. 53. n. 6. Qui tamen nonnihil à se ipso dissidere videtur in Prælud. ad Mechlin. n. 8. & in Epilog. n. 24.
units.tr: 4. Can the Prince, then, who confirms statutes, repeal the same? I answer: since such statutes are not statutes unless the consent of the Prince, expressed or tacit, is added: l. 3. Cod. Silent. libr. 12. It belongs to the one whose right it was to enact, to repeal. It must be said that the Prince, by the fullness of his power, can abrogate such statutes, provided that he has expressed that he wishes this; and that in the particular case it must be stated that the Prince wishes to abrogate them. For it is the part of one who was able to will, to be able to refuse. l. 3. D. de Regul. juris. ibique DD. l. 35. l. 153. D. eod. vid. Merul. Praxi Civil. libr. 1. tit. 4. c. 2. n. 4. Christin. vol. 2. decis. 53. n. 6. Yet he seems somewhat to disagree with himself in Prælud. ad Mechlin. n. 8. & in Epilog. n. 24.

units.la: 5. Quid si statuta sint jurata, an nihilominus eadem tollere poterit supremus Princeps? Quid ni, cum eadem sit ratio statutorum juratorum, quam non juratorum: quod jusjurandum sequatur naturam actus cui apponitur. Id quod etiam in collegiis admittunt, si statutis collegialiter contraveniant, qui cacondiderunt.l, ult. Cod. de non numer. Pecun. Afflict. decis. 361. n. 9. Panormit. in c. dilecto. Col. sin. verò. sed adverte. de Præb. Andr. ab Exea, in c. canonum statuta. de Constit. in Tom. 2. Repet. jur. can. n. 161. p. 189. Cravett. consil. 238. n. 11 Baldus vol. 4. consil. 430. Giurb. ad Messanien. Senat. consuet. Proœm. part. 1. n. 27.
units.tr: 5. What if the statutes have been sworn to: could the supreme Prince nevertheless repeal them? Why not, since the reason for sworn statutes is the same as for unsworn ones, because an oath follows the nature of the act to which it is attached. This is also admitted in the case of colleges, if those who enacted the statutes act contrary to them collectively. l. ult. Cod. de non numerata pecunia. Afflictis, decis. 361. n. 9. Panormitanus, on c. dilecto. Col. sin. verò. sed adverte. de Praebendis. Andreas ab Exea, on c. canonum statuta. de Constitutionibus, in vol. 2 of the Repetitio of the canon law, n. 161, p. 189. Cravetta, consil. 238. n. 11. Baldus, vol. 4, consil. 430. Giurba, on the Messina Senate customs, Preface, part 1, n. 27.

units.la: 6. Verum an quæ statuta justo Decurionum numero condita, & à Principe confirmata, ultra statuentium vitam extenduntur, an potius iis defunctis, obligandi vires amittunt? Respondeo, licet Prætorum edicta olim fuerint annalia, nec ultra extendebantur, quod nonnisi annuum eorum esset imperium. §. 1. instit. de Perpet. & tempor. Action.
units.tr: 6. But do statutes that were enacted by a lawful number of decurions and confirmed by the Prince extend beyond the lifetime of those who enacted them, or rather, once those men are dead, do they lose their binding force? I answer: although the edicts of the praetors were once annual, and were not extended beyond that, because their power lasted only a year: §. 1. instit. de Perpet. & tempor. Action.

units.la: Quia tamen ista ratio Triboniani forte minus accurata. Quod sæpe ultra tempus jurisdictionis potestas majorum magistratuum extendatur, effectu inspecto. Etiam Prætores antiqui, edicta condiderunt, actiones introduxerunt, quæ in perpetuum obtinerent. Nec semper finito officio, ea exspirant quæ gesta sunt officii nomine. Etiam ipsa decurionum universitas non interit, licet in illa capita singula extinguantur; quod jus nihilominus universitatis continuatâ serie maneat, & in uno decurione conservetur. Dicendum erit statuentium morte statuta suas vires non amisisse. d, §. 1, instit. Perpet. Tempor. action. l. moris. 9. D. de Pœn. l. 1. D. de Postul. l. 49. §. 1. l. 76. D. judic. Arg. l.
units.tr: But since this reasoning of Tribonian is perhaps less accurate: the power of the greater magistrates often extends beyond the period of their jurisdiction, looking to the effect. The ancient praetors also enacted edicts and introduced actions which were to hold in perpetuity; nor do those things that were done in the name of the office always lapse when the office ends. Even the body of the decurions does not perish, although individual members in it die; and the right of the body remains through a continuous succession and is preserved in any one decurion. It must be said that statutes do not lose their force by the death of those who enacted them. d. §. 1, instit. Perpet. Tempor. action. l. moris. 9. D. de Poenis. l. 1. D. de Postulando. l. 49. §. 1. l. 76. D. judic. Arg. l.

units.la: 2. Rep. jur. can. p. 102. n. 107. vid. Christin. ad Mechlin. in Epilog. n 13. & distinguentem. Arumæum discurs. Academic. de jure Public. 9. vol. 2. thes. 102.
units.tr: 2. Rep. jur. can. p. 102. n. 107. vid. Christin. ad Mechlin. in Epilog. n 13. & distinguentem. Arumaeum discurs. Academic. de jure Public. 9. vol. 2. thes. 102.

units.la: 8. Quid si tamen statuta transiverint in contractum? Certum est, ea ne quidem à Principe posse revocari.
units.tr: 8. What if, however, statutes have passed into a contract? It is certain that they cannot be revoked even by the Prince.

units.la: Idem quod statuendum, si introducta sint statuta, vel civitatibus permissa, per modum privilegii. Nisi tamen contrarium publica suadeat necessitas,quæ legem non fert, & ex illicito,aliquid faciat licitum. Mascard. post alios. conclus. 8. n. §2. & seqq. vid. mea superius in cap. de Privileg.
units.tr: The same must be held if statutes have been introduced, or granted to cities, by way of a privilege. Unless, however, public necessity, which does not bear a law, suggests otherwise, and makes lawful something that was unlawful. Mascard. post alios. conclus. 8. n. §2. & seqq. vid. mea superius in cap. de Privileg.

units.la: SECT. XII. CAP. II.
units.tr: SECT. XII. CHAP. II.

units.la: 1. Non præsumenda est mutatio statutorum, sed probanda?
units.tr: 1. Is a change of statutes to be presumed, or must it be proved?

units.la: 2. Quid si statuta quidem condita, verum usu non recepta?
units.tr: 2. What if statutes have indeed been enacted but never received in use?

units.la: 3. An id obtineat, si decennium interlabatur?
units.tr: 3. Does this hold if a decade has elapsed?

units.la: 4. Abolentur statuta desuetudine, vel usu contrario.
units.tr: 4. Statutes are abolished by disuse or by contrary usage.

units.la: 5. Quod nam tempus ad desuetudinem requiratur?
units.tr: 5. What length of time is required for disuse?

units.la: 6. An ad contrarium usum introducendum sufficiat unus actus?
units.tr: 6. Is one act sufficient to introduce a contrary usage?

units.la: 7. An statuta tollantur partium renuntiatione?
units.tr: 7. Are statutes repealed by the renunciation of the parties?

units.la: 8. An si civitas armis sit subacta?
units.tr: 8. What if the city has been subdued by arms?

units.la: 9. An revocatis statutis, reformationes censeantur revocata? 10. An
units.tr: 9. When statutes are revoked, are reforms considered revoked? 10. Whether

units.la: 10. An revocatis statutis censeantur an- te gesta revocata? 11. An allegans statuta abolita incidat in crimen falsi?
units.tr: 10. When statutes are revoked, are acts done before them considered revoked? 11. Does one who pleads abolished statutes incur the crime of forgery?

units.la: 1. ETsi nonnunquam statuta possint ad lubitum statuentium revocari, quae juris erat quaestio, non tamen praesumendum erit, eadem esse revocata, nisi id ipsum per probationes manifeste constet. Tum quia odiosa est mutatio, adeoque non praesumenda. Tum quia statuta sunt legum instar, quae semper durare praesumuntur. Arg. l. 2. D. de Princ. Constit. l. 32. in sin. Cod. Appellat. l. Ariani. in sin. Cod. de Haret. c. erit autem lex. dist. 4. Menoch. 2. Praesumpt. 2. in sin. & 2. Praesumpt. 16. n. 15. Bartol. in l. certa forma. n. 11. Cod. jure fisci. libr. 10. Masc. de statut. interpret. conclus. 11. n. 35.
units.tr: 1. Although statutes can sometimes be revoked at the pleasure of those who enacted them, it is not to be presumed that they have been revoked, unless this is clearly shown by proofs. This is because a change is odious and therefore not to be presumed. It is also because statutes stand in the place of laws, which are always presumed to endure. Arg. l. 2. D. de Princ. Constit. l. 32. in sin. Cod. Appellat. l. Ariani. in sin. Cod. de Haret. c. erit autem lex. dist. 4. Menoch. 2. Praesumpt. 2. in sin. & 2. Praesumpt. 16. n. 15. Bartol. in l. certa forma. n. 11. Cod. jure fisci. libr. 10. Masc. de statut. interpret. conclus. 11. n. 35.

units.la: 2. Quid si statuta quidem condita, verum usu non recepta vel observata? An egent ulla abrogatione, an potius pro nullis habenda? Posterius affirm. Quia pro talibus habentur, ac si facta non essent, adeoque non alleganda. Maxime si casus exstiterit, ut municipes iis uti potuerint. Deest quippe requisitum ad statuta necessarium quam maxime; scilicet ut sint recepta. Arg. l. 1. §. 9. in sin. Cod. Cad. Toll. per DD. antea allegatos. Adde Alex. vol. 1. consil. 6. n. 2. Felin. ad c. 1, de Treug. & Pace. Mascard. libr. all. concl. 8. n. 28. & seqq. Mev. 4. Prælim. 9. n. 65. 75.
units.tr: 2. What if statutes have indeed been enacted, but not received or observed in use? Do they need any abrogation, or are they rather to be held as void? The latter is affirmed. Because they are held as if they had never been made, and so they are not to be pleaded. This is especially so if there has been a case in which the citizens could have used them. For the requirement necessary for statutes is wholly lacking, namely that they be received. Arg. l. 1. §. 9. in sin. Cod. Cad. Toll. per DD. antea allegatos. Adde Alex. vol. 1. consil. 6. n. 2. Felin. ad c. 1, de Treug. & Pace. Mascard. libr. all. concl. 8. n. 28. & seqq. Mev. 4. Prælim. 9. n. 65. 75.

units.la: 3 Id quod obtinere volunt DD. Si lapsus intersit decennii à die conditi cujusdam statuti. Argum. l. 2. de Nundin. ibique DD. Menoch. 1. consil. 75. n. 9. Purpur. consil. 449. DD. in c. sin. de Consuet. in 6. Masc. d. tract. conclus. 6. n. 77. 78. 79. & seqq. & conclus. 11. n. 5. 6.
units.tr: 3. The doctors wish this to hold if a decade has elapsed from the day a certain statute was made. Argum. l. 2. de Nundin. ibique DD. Menoch. 1. consil. 75. n. 9. Purpur. consil. 449. DD. in c. sin. de Consuet. in 6. Masc. d. tract. conclus. 6. n. 77. 78. 79. & seqq. & conclus. 11. n. 5. 6.

units.la: 5. Ut tamen ad desuetudinem desiderent lapsum decennii, per l. 2. D. de Nundin. Alexand. consil. 132. visa facti narratione. libr. 1. Cephal. consil. 155. n. 17. aliique apud Mascard. d. concl. 6. n. 83.
units.tr: 5. But so that they may require the lapse of a decade for desuetude, see l. 2. D. de Nundin.; Alexand. consil. 132, having considered the narrative of the facts; Cephal. libr. 1, consil. 155, n. 17; and others cited in Mascard. d. concl. 6, n. 83.

units.la: Desiderarem tamen potius vetustatem, seu tempus immemoriale; quod pro lege est. l. 2. in init. D. de aquâ & aquâ pluv. arcend. vel secundum mores plerorumque spatium tertiae partis centum annorum ; quo omni juri præ- scribi solet.
units.tr: I would rather require antiquity, or immemorial time, which has the force of law. l. 2. in init. D. de aquâ & aquâ pluv. arcend. Or, according to the custom of most places, a space of a third part of a hundred years, by which every right is wont to be barred.

units.la: 6. An igitur per contrarium usum statuta censebuntur abrogata, modo unus actus universitatis sit in contrarium ? Id videtur dicendum : quia non aliter atque statuta legum instar, ab universitate simul & semel introducuntur ; ita etiam simul & semel ab eâ tolluntur. Arg. l. nihil tam naturale. D. de Reg. jur. Id quod tum maxime verum,cum actus in contrarium ab universitate est adhibitus scienter, & quidē citra vim aut metum, aut citra protestationem juris sui conservandi gratia adhibitam. Argum. l. 6. §. ult. D. Adquir. vel omitt. Hæredit. ibique Gothefred. in not. Abbas in c. pro illorum. in ult. not. de Præbend. aliique apud Mascard. d. tract. concluf. 11, num. sin. vid. Gail. 2. obs. 31. Mynsing. 6. obs. 41. Grev. 2. Pract. conclus. 31.
units.tr: 6. Are statutes, then, to be considered abrogated by a contrary usage, provided that a single act of the community is contrary to them? It seems that this should be said: because, just as statutes, standing in the place of laws, are introduced by the community together and at once, so too they are removed by it together and at once. Arg. l. nihil tam naturale. D. de Reg. jur. This holds especially true when the contrary act has been performed by the community knowingly, and indeed without force or fear, or without a protest made to preserve its right. Argum. l. 6. §. ult. D. Adquir. vel omitt. Hæredit. ibique Gothefred. in not. Abbas in c. pro illorum. in ult. not. de Præbend. aliique apud Mascard. d. tract. concluf. 11, num. sin. vid. Gail. 2. obs. 31. Mynsing. 6. obs. 41. Grev. 2. Pract. conclus. 31.

units.la: 7. Verum an non statuta tolli poterunt renunciatione partium, quæ statuti commodis utuntur ?
