Respondeo, si quando statutis aliquid est introductum, quod spectat commodum & utilitatem partium contrahentium, illis non uti poterunt: si modo non promiserint se contenta statutorum esse servatuüras. Anton. Burges. Tom. 2. Repet. jur. can. in c. sicut Romana. de Rescript. p. 424. n. 148. Quod si de jure tertii, vel jure publico disponant statuta, non recte eadem omittunt, vel disponendo vel contrahendo, qui negotium aliquod gerunt. Ut tamen neutro casu statuta tolli dicantur: quod ejus tantum sit tollere, cujus est constituere. l. pen. Cod. de Pact. l. 38. l. 46. D. eodem. l. 55. D. de leg. 1. -- Arg. l. nihil tam naturale. l. 23. D. de leg. l. ult. Cod. eod. Marant. part. 4. distinct. judic. 12. n. 26. Gail. 1. obs. 40. & obs. 39. Merul. Prax. civil. libr. 4. distinct. 2. tit. 1. c. 13. n. 3. Hering. de fidejuss. c. 17. n. 56. Honded. vol. 1. consil. 28, n. 34. Mev. ad Lubec. q. 7. prael. n. 16. & q. 9. n. 75. 76. & seqq.
units.tr: 7. But can statutes not be repealed by the renunciation of the parties who enjoy the benefits of the statute? I answer: if something has been introduced by statutes which concerns the advantage and benefit of contracting parties, they may decline to use it, provided they have not promised that they will observe the terms of the statutes. Anton. Burges. Tom. 2. Repet. jur. can. in c. sicut Romana. de Rescript. p. 424. n. 148. But if the statutes dispose of the right of a third party, or of public right, those who transact some business do not validly omit them, whether in disposing or in contracting. Yet in neither case are the statutes said to be repealed, because it belongs only to one who can establish to repeal. l. pen. Cod. de Pact. l. 38. l. 46. D. eodem. l. 55. D. de leg. 1. -- Arg. l. nihil tam naturale. l. 23. D. de leg. l. ult. Cod. eod. Marant. part. 4. distinct. judic. 12. n. 26. Gail. 1. obs. 40. & obs. 39. Merul. Prax. civil. libr. 4. distinct. 2. tit. 1. c. 13. n. 3. Hering. de fidejuss. c. 17. n. 56. Honded. vol. 1. consil. 28, n. 34. Mev. ad Lubec. q. 7. prael. n. 16. & q. 9. n. 75. 76. & seqq.

units.la: 8. Quid si municipium vel civitas, quæ statuta condidit, armis fuerit devicta, an eo ipso sua statuta vel privilegia censebitur amisisse? Resp.
units.tr: 8. What if a municipality or city that has enacted statutes is conquered by arms: is it then deemed to have lost its statutes or privileges by that very fact? Answer:

units.la: Aut se subjecit civitas ex conventione, salvis suis juribus & privilegiis, tumque statuta servat illibata, ut propriis legibus regatur. Standum quippe est pactis, quæ etiam hostibus illibata servanda; in l. 5. Cod. de Pact. Hottom, illustr. quæst. 7. Grot. de jure Bell. libr. 3. c. 19. Zoes. D. pact. n. 55.
units.tr: Either the city has submitted by agreement, with its rights and privileges preserved, and then it keeps its statutes unimpaired so that it may be governed by its own laws. For agreements must be kept, and these are to be observed unimpaired even toward enemies; see l. 5 Cod. de Pactis; Hottoman, Illustrium quaestionum 7; Grotius, De iure belli libr. 3 c. 19; Zoesius, D. de pactis n. 55.

units.la: Aut non expressa ulla conditione hostibus semet subjecit; & nisi Princeps patiatur civitatem uti suis legibus & statutis, ea sublata censebuntur; adeoque ipsa jus sequetur victoris. Arg. l. 9. D. Ad l. Rhodiam de jactu. ibique DD. Grot. de jure belli & Pacis, libr. 3. cap. 8. & 15. ibique plures.
units.tr: Or the city has submitted to its enemies without any condition being expressed; and unless the prince allows the city to use its own laws and statutes, those are considered abolished, and the city itself follows the right of the victor. Cf. l. 9 D. Ad legem Rhodiam de iactu, and the doctors there; Grotius, De iure belli et pacis libr. 3 cap. 8 and 15, and several others there.

units.la: 9. Verum an revocatis statutis, uno ex præprædictis modo, etiam reformationes circa statuta factæ, revocatæ censebuntur? Respondeo, quod ita. Sublato quippe principali, tollitur accessorium, adeoque omnia corruunt concomitantia. l. cum principalis. D. de Reg. jur. ibique Decius & DD. §. fidejussores. instit. fidejuss. Pichard. ad §. si quis. alium. instit. Inst. stipulat. n. 32. Regul. accessorium. q. 2. de Reg. jur. in 6. Barbos. Princ. & axiom. juris in verb. accessorium. Addit. ad Abbatem in c. 1. de Constit. Princ. & alii apud Mascard. d. tract. conclus. 11. n. 36. vid. Ludovic. Gomes. in c. Statutum. de Rescript. libr. 6. n. 95. tom. 5. Repet. jur. canonic. p. 180. & p. 312. n. 11.
units.tr: 9. But if the statutes are revoked in one of the aforesaid ways, are the reforms made to the statutes also deemed revoked? I answer that they are. For when the principal is removed, the accessory is removed too, and so everything that accompanies it falls. See l. cum principalis D. de regulis iuris and Decius there, and the doctors; §. fidejussores Inst. de fidejussoribus; Pichardus on §. si quis alium Inst. de stipulationibus n. 32; Regula "accessorium" q. 2 de regulis iuris in 6; Barbosa, Principia et axiomata iuris, under "accessorium"; the Addition to Abbas on c. 1 de constitutionibus, Principe; and others cited by Mascardus in his tract, conclusion 11 n. 36; see Ludovicus Gomesius on c. Statutum de rescriptis libr. 6 n. 95; Repetitio iuris canonici tom. 5 p. 180 and p. 312 n. 11.

units.la: 10, An igitur statutorum revocatio, retrotrahetur, id est ad ante gesta, referetur? Resp. Uti leges regulariter futuris dant formam negotiis, sic etiam statuta. l. 7. Cod. de leg. nov. 73. §. obtineto. nov. 75. nov. 115. in init.
units.tr: 10. Does the revocation of statutes then take effect retrospectively, that is, does it refer back to past acts? Answer: just as laws ordinarily give form to future transactions, so do statutes. See l. 7 Cod. de legibus; Novel. 73 §. obtineto; Novel. 75; Novel. 115 in init.

units.la: Nisi tamen statutorum revocatio per expressa verba referatur ad præterita negotia, sicuti ad pendentia trahi poterunt, eodem modo. d.l. 7. l. 18. in sin. Cod. Sacrof. Eccles. l. ult. in sin. Cod. eod. nov. 113. §. ad hæc & illud. nov. 99. c. 1. §. 2. nov. 115. c. 1. Cujac. ad nov. 66.
units.tr: Unless, however, the revocation of statutes by express words refers to past transactions, in which case it may reach pending matters in the same way. See the said l. 7; l. 18 in fin. Cod. Sacrosanctae Ecclesiae; l. ult. in fin. Cod. eod.; Novel. 113 §. ad haec et illud; Novel. 99 c. 1 §. 2; Novel. 115 c. 1; Cujacius on Novel. 66.

units.la: Unde probabile Constit. Ordinum Trajectin. de ann. 1659. April. 14. quâ artic. 13 (contra quam antea obtinebat) mares & fœminæ demum post 25. ætatis annum censentur majores, non trahi ad ante gesta negotia, per illos, qui statuto civitatis, 18. vel 20. ætatis anno, censebantur majores, vid. Bald. in l. jus civile. n. 3. D. justit. & jure. Stephanum. de Coste de Affinit. n. 17. sol. 23. vol. 1. tract. Mascard. conclus. 8. n. 103. & conclus. 11. de statut. interpret.
units.tr: Hence it is probable that the Constitution of the Orders of Utrecht of 14 April 1659, by which article 13 (contrary to what held before) provides that men and women are deemed adults only after the twenty-fifth year of age, does not reach back to past transactions, so as to affect those who, under a city statute, were deemed adults in their eighteenth or twentieth year. See Baldus on l. ius civile n. 3 D. de iustitia et iure; Stephanus de Costa, De affinitate n. 17; Sol. 23 vol. 1; Mascardus' tract, conclusion 8 n. 103 and conclusion 11 de statutorum interpretatione.

units.la: 11. An denique casu quo statuta sunt abolita seu antiquata, qui eadem in judiciis allegat, dissimulatis statutis corrigentibus, incidet in crimen falsi? Respondeo, cum legibus & abrogatis constitutionibus uti non liceat, citra crimen falsi; & statutorum eadem sit vis in municipiis, quæ est legum vel constitutionum, in imperio. Dicendum videtur allegantem statuta, quæ posterioribus sunt abrogata, falsi criminis teneri. l. sin. D. de Falsi. l. 1. Cod. de Justin. Codic. confirm. vid. Novell. 115. in init. & cap. 1. Bartol. in l. omnes populi. in sin. D. de justit. & jure, idem in d. l. sin. Hippol. Riminald. in c. canonum statuta, de Constit. n. 121. tom. 2. Repert. jur. canon. p. 238. Oldendorp. in init. Classif. Actionum. Præfat. de Ordin. juris. n. 9. in sin. Christin. ad Mechlin. in Epilog. n. 17. & seq.
units.tr: 11. Finally, in the case where statutes have been abolished or obsolete, will one who cites them in judgment, while concealing the corrective statutes, incur the crime of forgery? I answer: since it is not permitted to use laws and abrogated constitutions without the crime of forgery, and since statutes in municipalities have the same force as laws or constitutions in the empire, it seems right to say that one who cites statutes which were later abrogated is liable for the crime of forgery. See l. sin. D. de falsis; l. 1 Cod. de iustiniano codice confirmando; see Novel. 115 in init. and cap. 1; Bartolus on l. omnes populi in fin. D. de iustitia et iure, and the same on the said l. sin.; Hippolytus Riminaldus on c. canonum statuta de constitutionibus n. 121, tom. 2 Repertorium iuris canonici p. 238; Oldendorp in init. Classificationum actionum, Praefatio de ordine iuris n. 9 in fin.; Christinaeus on Mechlin, Epilogue n. 17 et seq.

units.la: Nisi tamen pro parte tantum correcta dicantur. Vel non principaliter allegarentur, ad causæ decisionem, sed tantum in argumentii trahantur; si non & hoc expresse prohibitum. Vel tantum ad illustrationem & declarationē de novo conditorum allegentur. Vel dubitetur, an sint correcta, vel abrogata. Vel ea imperator allegaverit, qui vetera allegando, videtur nova facere. Argum. d. l. 1. Cod. & §. 5. instit. Proœm. init. instit. de Testam. §. 5. instit. Exhered. liberor. l. ult. Cod. leg. l. 32. in sin. Cod. Appell. Hippol. Riminald. in c. canonum Statuta. de Constit. tom. 2. Repet. jur. canon. p. 238. n. 122. & seqq.
units.tr: Unless, however, they are said to be corrected only in part; or they are not cited principally for the decision of the case, but are merely brought in as an argument; provided this is not also expressly forbidden; or they are cited only for the illustration and explanation of newly enacted statutes; or it is doubtful whether they have been corrected or abrogated; or the emperor himself has cited them, since by citing old laws he seems to make new ones. See by argument the said l. 1 Cod.; §. 5 Inst. Proemium in init.; Inst. de testamentis §. 5; Inst. de exheredatione liberorum; l. ult. Cod. de legibus; l. 32 in fin. Cod. de appellationibus; Hippolytus Riminaldus on c. canonum statuta de constitutionibus, tom. 2 Repetitio iuris canonici p. 238 n. 122 et seq.

units.la: Atque ita favente Deo Opt. Max. per quem sum, hoc quod sum, tractatum meum de statutis ad finem perduxi. In quo conscribendo non aliena scrinia compilavi, aut ab aliis probe dicta, mea feci, suppressis auctorum nominibus; verum candide, quod aliorum erat, illis reliqui. Id autem affectavi quam maxime, ne prolixis verborum ambagibus aut floscVulis quibusdam oratoriis in hac materia practica, nullum usum praebentibus, studiosum juris detinerem. Paucis equidem multa complectivolui, non multis pauca. Imitatus in hoc scribendi genere Stoicos antiquos, qui non tam verbis quam rebus, atque sententiarum pondere superare contendebant. Tu lector judiciose, hisce meis utere vel tantum ad indicium; & cogita me tibi ad interiora praxeos aditum pandisse, quae tute per tuam industriam ipse magis excolas & exornes.
units.tr: And so, with the favour of God, Best and Greatest, through whom I am what I am, I have brought my treatise on statutes to its end. In writing it I have not plundered other men's chests, nor made my own what others had said well, with the authors' names suppressed; rather I have candidly left to each what was theirs. I have especially aimed to ensure that I did not detain the student of law with long-winded verbal circumlocutions or with certain rhetorical flourishes, which offer no use in this practical matter. I have wished to embrace much in few words, not few things in many. In this manner of writing I have imitated the ancient Stoics, who strove to excel not so much in words as in things and the weight of their opinions. You, judicious reader, use these my pages only as an index; and consider that I have opened to you the way into the inner parts of practice, which you yourself, by your own diligence, may cultivate and adorn further.
